pronunciation.approximation: 'FEN-reer' — a short e as in 'fen', both r's trilled, and the final nominative -r sounded as a light syllabic trill, as in Icelandic.
pronunciation.note: Fenrir is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The name itself is a transparent compound of fen, 'marsh, moor', with the agentive suffix -ir: 'fen-dweller, the one of the fen' (Cleasby–Vigfusson, Zoëga, Simek, Orchard). The wolf's fame is cosmic; his orthography is humble.

domains.title: Wolf, Destruction, Binding
domains.subtitle: The Wolf Who Cannot Be Held
domains.lead: Fenrir is the monstrous wolf of Norse myth — the son of Loki and the giantess Angrboða, reared in the gods' own stronghold because no one dared do otherwise. When the prophecies said he would be Óðinn's death, the Æsir bound him: two fetters of iron broke like string, and the third — Gleipnir, the ribbon made of six things that do not exist — held, at the price of Týr's right hand. Gagged with a sword and chained to a stone beneath the earth, he lies on the isle of Lyngvi until Ragnarök, when he breaks free, swallows the Father of the Slain, and is torn jaw from jaw by Víðarr, the silent avenger.

cards.name: Gleipnir
cards.desc: Smooth and soft as a silken ribbon, made of six impossibles — the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, a mountain's roots, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, a bird's spittle. Iron failed twice; impossibility held.

cards.name: The Pledge of the Hand
cards.desc: Týr alone laid his right hand in the wolf's jaws as surety that the fetter was no trap. When Gleipnir held, the wolf bit it off — the gods laughed, says Snorri, all but Týr.

cards.name: The Gagging Sword
cards.desc: Wedged in the raging jaws, hilt against the lower gum, point against the upper — and from the foam that runs from his mouth flows the river Ván, Expectation, until the world's end.

cards.name: The Torn Jaws
cards.desc: At Ragnarök the wolf swallows Óðinn; Víðarr sets his foot on the lower jaw, seizes the upper, and tears the beast apart — the son avenging the father, as the poems always said he would.

symbols.name: Gleipnir
symbols.meaning: The fetter of six things that do not exist — proof that what binds the unbindable is not strength but impossibility

symbols.name: Týr's hand
symbols.meaning: The pledge that made the trap honest — justice's price paid in the god of justice's own flesh

symbols.name: The gagging sword
symbols.meaning: The wolf silenced but never tamed: the gods could stop his bite, not his doom

symbols.name: The river Ván
symbols.meaning: 'Expectation' — the stream of the bound wolf's slaver, flowing from Lyngvi until Ragnarök

symbols.name: Gjǫll and Þviti
symbols.meaning: The slab and the boulder driven deep into the earth — the world itself recruited as an anchor for the chain

mythology.lead: Fenrir's mythology is a single arc told in two registers: Snorri's prose gives the binding in full narrative, while the poems — older, allusive, apocalyptic — carry the prophecy and the end. Together they make the most complete monster-story the North preserves: birth, fostering, fetters, pledge, gag, and the waiting that ends at Ragnarök.

myths.title: The Brood of Angrboða
myths.text:
Hyndluljóð says it in a line: Loki begot the wolf with Angrboða — the giantess 'herald of sorrow' who dwells in Járnviðr, the Ironwood. Snorri names all three children of that union: the wolf Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr the world-serpent, and Hel, who is half the colour of the living and half of the dead. Because all were of giant stock and Loki's, and because the gods had heard prophecies that great harm would come of them, Óðinn had the children fetched.

He cast the serpent into the deep sea that lies around all lands, where it grew until it girdled the world; Hel he threw down into Niflheimr and gave her power over nine worlds. But the wolf the Æsir brought home with them and reared in their own stronghold — and only Týr had the courage to go to him and give him food.

myths.title: Lœðingr and Drómi
myths.text:
The wolf grew at a pace the gods could watch, and the prophecies grew plainer: he was fated to harm them. So the Æsir made a strong fetter called Lœðingr and brought it to the wolf, challenging him to test his strength against it. The wolf judged himself equal to it, let them bind him, braced himself, kicked — and the fetter sprang apart; he was loose from Lœðingr.

The gods made a second fetter, half again as strong, called Drómi, and told the wolf he would win great fame if he broke it — such a fetter, they said, would not hold even a beast of his power. The wolf reasoned that fame was worth the risk, let them bind him, dashed himself against the ground, kicked — and Drómi flew in pieces far away. It is from this, Snorri says, that the saying comes: to break loose from Lœðingr or to dash out of Drómi, when things are pushed to the utmost.

lore.culturalLegacy: Fenrir is the North's most famous monster, and his afterlife runs on two tracks. The scholarly track never stopped: the binding of the wolf was a set-piece of the Victorian Norse revival — the Kearys' Heroes of Asgard (1857) made the fetters and the pledge of Týr's hand a children's classic — and every handbook since has treated Gleipnir's six impossibles as the Edda's signature riddle-image. The popular track is enormous: Marvel's comics gave Thor a recurring Fenris Wolf; J. K. Rowling named her most savage werewolf Fenrir Greyback; the wolf fights through Final Fantasy (where Fenrir is a summoned beast), Smite, and Assassin's Creed Valhalla, and God of War: Ragnarök (2022) built part of its end-of-days on him. The idiom of the bound monster who must not be killed for fear of worse has become a standing political and moral metaphor — the fettered danger whose release is the prophecy. In modern Heathenry Fenrir is no object of cult but the corpus's fixed figure of doom: the destruction the gods themselves are keeping, chained, until the chain is the last thing left.
lore.archaeology: Fenrir is an entirely textual monster: no cult site, votive deposit, or runic inscription invokes him, and wolves in the Scandinavian material record are read as Fenrir only by interpretation, never by name. Two famous carvings are the standing candidates. The Gosforth Cross in Cumbria (c. 900–950) carries a panel of a figure rending the jaws of a great beast — a spear in hand, one foot on the lower jaw — within what is widely read as a Ragnarök programme, and the identification with Víðarr and the wolf, argued by Bailey and most subsequent scholars, remains the standard reading, though it is an interpretation, not an inscription. Thorwald's Cross at Kirk Andreas on the Isle of Man (Manx Cross 128, tenth century) shows a figure with a bird on his shoulder and his foot in a wolf's mouth, commonly read as Óðinn devoured at Ragnarök, with his raven still upon him; the Ledberg stone (Ög 181, Sweden) has likewise been given a Ragnarök reading, more controversially. On the textual side, Vǫluspá, Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál, and Lokasenna survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), Hyndluljóð in the Flateyjarbók, and Snorri's account of the binding in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister codices of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.
lore.syncretism: Fenrir's closest relative inside his own corpus is the hound Garmr, who breaks his chain before Gnipahellir at Ragnarök and fights Týr to mutual death: Vǫluspá's refrain 'now Garmr howls loud' announces the end, and scholars from Lindow onward have debated whether Garmr is a doublet of the bound wolf or a second beast of the same kennel. The chase-wolves of the sky — Skǫll, who pursues the sun, and Hati Hróðvitnisson, who will take the moon — belong to the same apocalyptic pack, and Vafþrúðnismál gives Fenrir himself the sun-swallowing role, a distribution of doom the sources never fully harmonize. Wider comparisons are made and immediately qualified: Cerberus is the obvious Mediterranean analogue for a chained hell-hound, and the Ironwood's brood of wolves in Vǫluspá has been set beside every Indo-European wolf-pack of the world's end — but Fenrir's story is structurally unique: a monster the gods themselves foster, bind by trickery, and preserve for the apocalypse, because killing him is the one thing their own holiness forbids. His kin in the lexicon are his family: [[loki|Loki]], [[angrboda|Angrboða]], [[jormungandr|Jǫrmungandr]], and [[hel|Hel]] — and [[tyr|Týr]], whose hand is the fetter's true price.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Fenrir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚠᛁᚾᚱᛁᛦ (f-i-n-r-i-R: the ᛁ rune covers both e and i, and ᛦ writes the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: fenrir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

variants.note: Modern stress form: the acute marks the stressed vowel in the conventional vocalization "Ra". The Egyptological spelling records only the consonants rꜥ.

etymology.derivation: From Egyptian rꜥ "sun, day". The solar creator god.

steps: The name is written rꜥ (𓂋𓂝) with the sun-disk (𓇳) as a determinative/rebus for 'sun'.
The consonantal skeleton r-ꜥ is vocalised as Ra in Egyptological convention; the original vocalisation is unknown.
Coptic ⲣⲏ provides a late phonetic reflex.
From the New Kingdom onward Ra is frequently combined with Amun as Amun-Ra.

provenanceSources.title: Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian

pronunciation.approximation: 'rah-ʿA' — a rolled or tapped 'r', then a deep throaty 'ah' like the Arabic ع.
pronunciation.note: Rꜥ is a Tier-1 restoration. Egyptologists vocalise the name as Ra or Rꜥa, but the hieroglyphs record only rꜥ. The ayin (ꜥ) is the defining non-English sound — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses; the acute variant Rá is a modern stress marker, not an ancient vowel sign.

domains.title: Sun, Creation, Kingship
domains.subtitle: The domain of Rꜥ
domains.lead: Rꜥ is the sun as sovereignty: creator of the ordered world each dawn, father of the king who rules in his name, and nightly conqueror of the serpent of chaos. Egyptian theology unfolded him in three acts — Khepri the scarab at dawn, Rꜥ reigning at noon, Atum the aged creator at dusk — one god in three phases.

cards.name: Solar Barque
cards.desc: Ra sails the Mandjet by day and the Mesektet through the underworld, defeating Apophis each night (Book of the Dead, spell 15).

cards.name: Khepri, Ra, Atum
cards.desc: He is the scarab at dawn, the reigning sun at noon, and the weary creator at evening — one solar life in three bodies.

cards.name: Eye of Ra
cards.desc: His eye, embodied as Sekhmet or Hathor, punishes rebellion and returns as the protective uraeus on his brow (Book of the Heavenly Cow).

cards.name: Kingship
cards.desc: The pharaoh rules as Ra's son — the royal titulary names him heir of Ra — and every obelisk is a frozen ray of the sun-god's first light.

symbols.name: Solar barque (Mandjet)
symbols.meaning: The morning boat in which Ra crosses the sky from east to west

symbols.name: Scarab beetle (khepri)
symbols.meaning: The self-begetting form of the sun at dawn, pushing the disk like dung

symbols.name: Falcon head with sun-disk
symbols.meaning: Ra as sky-falcon, the dominant icon of the solar god

symbols.name: Bennu heron
symbols.meaning: The soul of Ra and the prototype of the phoenix, rising from the Persea tree

symbols.name: Eye of Ra (wedjat)
symbols.meaning: The aggressive solar eye that destroys enemies and restores cosmic order

mythology.lead: Rꜥ's theology is Egypt's most complete vision of order (maat): the sun's daily circuit is a voyage, a kingship and a war. Each dawn the god is born in the east; each night he dies and must be defended; every royal tomb and solar temple re-stages that victory on earth.

myths.title: The Barque of Millions of Years
myths.text: The central image of Rꜥ theology is the barque called Mandjet, 'Boat of Millions of Years', in which the god sails the sky by day, and the Mesektet, in which he crosses the underworld by night. The underworld books — the Amduat and the Book of Gates — map the twelve hours of darkness: at each gate Rꜥ must pass guardians, recite their names, and survive the waiting ambush of Apopis, the serpent of chaos who rises from the primordial waters to swallow the sun. Other gods row; the souls of the justified dead join his crew; and at the twelfth hour the scarab Khepri rolls the renewed sun up from the eastern horizon (Book of the Dead, spell 15; Book of Gates). The theology makes every sunrise a contested event: light is not a fact but a nightly victory, re-won while humanity sleeps.

myths.title: The Distant Goddess and the First Men
myths.text: In the myth called 'The Destruction of Mankind', preserved in royal tombs of the Nineteenth–Twentieth Dynasties and on the gilded shrine of Tutankhamun (the 'Book of the Heavenly Cow'), humankind plots rebellion against Rꜥ — who, he says, has grown old, 'his bones silver, his flesh gold, his hair true lapis'. He sends his Eye against them as a raging lioness, the goddess Sekhmet, who slaughters until the gods fear nothing human will survive. Rꜥ halts her by stratagem: seven thousand jars of beer are dyed red with ochre and flooded across the field; Sekhmet drinks, believing it blood, and wakes gentle as Hathor — the returning Eye that becomes the uraeus coiled on the king's brow. The myth is a theology of measured wrath: the same solar power that nearly annihilates the world is tricked into mercy and worn thereafter as protection. Divine anger, Egyptian theology insists, must be outwitted into becoming grace.

lore.culturalLegacy: Rꜥ never ceased shining on the world's capitals. Rome took his obelisks — Augustus set one up in the Circus Maximus, and its red-granite siblings from Luxor now stand in London and on the Place de la Concorde, re-erected as trophies of Egyptomania rather than of the sun. The pyramid silhouette and the solar disk became the universal shorthand for Egypt itself, deployed from Masonic iconography to Hollywood; modern Egyptology restored his theology from texts and tombs, while new religious movements claimed him as ancestor of solar monotheism and films cast 'Ra' as everything from starship tyrant to enlightened lawgiver. The common thread is appropriation: every age has repolished the sun's name for its own mirror.
lore.archaeology: Solar cult is visible in the pyramid complexes of the Old Kingdom, the solar temple of Nyuserre at Abu Ghurab, and the great temples of Heliopolis, Karnak and Abu Simbel — whose facade colossi face the sun's rays at the equinoxes. The colossal obelisks of Heliopolis and Luxor, single shafts of Aswan granite, stood before the sun's temples; pairs from Luxor now stand in London and Paris. The Amarna boundary stelae and the Great Hymn to the Aten preserve Akhenaten's solar theology, and tomb paintings from the Valley of the Kings show Ra in his day- and night-barks, surrounded by protective deities.
lore.syncretism: Rꜥ absorbed and was absorbed. At Heliopolis he fused with Atum, 'the All', and with the scarab Khepri; in the New Kingdom the Theban god Amun merged with him into Amun-Rꜥ, 'king of the gods', the composite patron of empire whose priests would one day rival the crown. The compound Ra-Horakhty — 'Rꜥ, Horus of the Horizon' — folded the royal sky-falcon into the sun. Greeks and Romans read him through Helios: Herodotus already treats the phoenix's visit to Heliopolis as a solar event, and Plutarch retells Rꜥ's wanderings as Greek myth in Egyptian dress. The most radical reform was also solar: Akhenaten's Aten cult of the fourteenth century BCE — one disk, no image — was a revolution carried out entirely in Rꜥ's theological vocabulary, and the swiftness of its erasure shows how tightly solar doctrine bound the state. Through it all the name held: five thousand years of theology circle the same two consonants, r and ꜥ.

God of the underworld and resurrection

entries.meaning: Egyptian god of embalming and the necropolis; the name's etymology is uncertain (his epithet tpy-ḏw=f means He who is upon his mountain)

Full phonetic spelling can include 𓇋𓈖𓊪𓅱
God of mummification and guide of the dead

provenanceSources.title: Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian

pronunciation.approximation: The name is a consonant skeleton: ꜣ-n-p-w; the Greeks vocalized it as Anubis.
pronunciation.note: Egyptian ꜣnpw is conventionally vocalized "Anupu" or "Anup"; the Greek rendering Anoubis gives English "Anubis." The initial ꜣ (aleph, Gardiner G1) is a glottal consonant Egyptology once ignored and now transcribes — the restoration ꜣnpw keeps the ancient consonantal skeleton exactly as the hieroglyphs write it.

domains.title: The Jackal of the Necropolis
domains.subtitle: Embalming, the Scales, and the Guiding of Souls
domains.lead: ꜣnpw is the oldest funeral god of Egypt: lord of the necropolis before Osiris ever ruled it, master of embalming, and the steady hand at the scales where every human heart is weighed against a feather. His black jackal watches from the edge of the desert where the dead were always buried.

cards.name: The Jackal
cards.desc: The desert canid seen at the graves' edge — feared for what it digs, honoured as the grave's defender.

cards.name: The Weighing
cards.desc: He steadies the scales in the Hall of Two Truths: heart against Maat's feather, exact to the grain.

cards.name: The Embalmer
cards.desc: He wrapped Osiris himself — the first mummy — and every priestly embalmer wore his mask.

cards.name: The Psychopomp
cards.desc: "Foremost of the Westerners" — guide of souls through the night roads of the dead.

symbols.name: The black jackal
symbols.meaning: Black as the fertile Nile silt and the embalmed flesh — the colour of rebirth, not evil

symbols.name: The flail
symbols.meaning: His authority over the necropolis as its shepherd

symbols.name: The scales
symbols.meaning: Judgment made precise — his unwavering hand at the beam

symbols.name: The imiut fetish
symbols.meaning: The headless skin on a pole — the embalmer's ancient emblem, older than his myths

symbols.name: The embalmer's mask
symbols.meaning: The jackal-headed mask of the chief embalming priest — the rite performed by visibly divine hands

symbols.name: The Western mountain
symbols.meaning: The necropolis ridge his title tpy-ḏw=f claims — the desert edge where the dead were always buried, and where he keeps watch

mythology.lead: In the earliest religion ꜣnpw simply is the god of the dead; when the Osiris cycle rose, he was written into it — as embalmer, son, and guide — without ever losing his seniority at the grave.

myths.title: The First Embalming
myths.text: Isis had gathered all the pieces of Osiris' body that Set had scattered — save one, swallowed by a fish of the Nile — when ꜣnpw came to perform the rite no god had yet done. He washed the god's flesh, anointed it with oils, wrapped it in fine linen and breathed the first funerary formula over it: the first mummy, and the template of every burial Egypt would ever perform (Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride 13–14; the older Pyramid Texts already call ꜣnpw 'he who is upon his mountain', watcher of the god's booth). In temple ritual the connection stayed literal for three thousand years: the chief embalmer, the 'overseer of the mysteries', wore the jackal mask, so that the hands wrapping the dead were visibly Anubis' own. The myth makes the funerary craft a divine inheritance: mummification is not technique applied to religion but religion continued by technique.

myths.title: The Feather of Maat
myths.text: Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead — whose vignettes multiply from the Eighteenth Dynasty onward — fixes his most famous office. In the Hall of the Two Truths the deceased recites the Negative Confession, forty-two denials of sin before forty-two judges; then ꜣnpw, he who counts the hearts, leads the dead to the scales and steadies the beam while the heart is weighed against the single feather of Maat. Thoth records the verdict; a heart heavy with lies tips the pan, and Ammit the Devourer — crocodile's head, lion's foreparts, hippopotamus' hindquarters — waits beside the scales to eat it, annihilating the sinner's afterlife. A true-of-voice heart passes on to Horus and Osiris. That the terrible reading of the scales belongs to the jackal-god is the theology in one image: the watcher at the desert's edge, feared in life as a digger among bodies, is in death the incorruptible accountant of souls.

lore.culturalLegacy: He is, for most of the world, the face of ancient Egypt: Tutankhamun's recumbent jackal shrine — black wood, gilded ears, guarding the royal canopic chest — is among the most reproduced objects on earth, and the mummy-genre of cinema, from Karloff's Imhotep to modern franchises, works entirely in his territory. The modern image of justice borrowed his instrument: every balanced beam in courthouse iconography unconsciously quotes his scales. Egyptology has spent two centuries correcting the horror-movie caricature — feared on screen as a monster, he was antiquity's most trusted guardian, the gentle final attendant of every Egyptian who could afford the rite. His jackal still patrols the edge of the desert at Saqqara, exactly where the watchers always stood.
lore.archaeology: Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) yielded the Anubis shrine: a life-size black wooden jackal, gilded ears and collar, guarding the canopic equipment — now in Cairo. The Anubeion at Saqqara, excavated over decades, preserves catacombs of mummified dogs and jackals offered to him — estimates run to millions of animals across Egypt's canine catacombs. Vignettes of spell 125, with his hand on the scales, survive in hundreds of Books of the Dead, from the papyrus of Ani in the British Museum to the papyrus of Hunefer.
lore.syncretism: The Greeks, finding a jackal-headed guide of souls, fused him at once with Hermês: Hermanubis — kerykeion in one paw, jackal head on his shoulders — received cult at Alexandria and in Rome, an identification so natural that Coptic speakers simply called the god-form Anoup. In the Isiac mysteries he served as mystagogue: Apuleius, initiated at Cenchreae, describes the grand procession in which Anubis, herald and messenger 'between the gods above and the gods below', walked before the goddess in gold and black (Metamorphoses 11.11). Early Coptic Christianity quietly absorbed his office into the archangel Michael — weigher and guide of souls — so that a jackal-god of the third millennium BCE ended, unbroken, as an angel with scales. Egyptomania later restored him to European consciousness through Belzoni's exhibitions and the decipherment of the hieroglyphs.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written ꜣ-n-p-w with the recumbent jackal (Gardiner E16) as determinative, over the hotep offering sign in the fuller orthographies. The Greeks heard it as Anoubis; Coptic preserved it as Anoup. The jackal is not decorative: it is the god himself, present in his own spelling.

etymology.derivation: From Egyptian ḥr, written with the falcon sign and interpreted as 'the distant/high one' or 'falcon'; the original vowels are not recorded in hieroglyphs.

steps: The Egyptian name is written 𓅃 in hieroglyphs.
Hieroglyphs combine logograms, phonograms, and determinatives; the exact function of each sign depends on context.
Egyptian writing does not record vowels; the vocalised form is a modern convention reconstructed from Coptic and Greek evidence.
The Unicode restoration Ḥr uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com.

provenanceSources.title: Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAH-roo' — the first syllable is throaty and drawn out, the second light and ascending, like a falcon rising.
pronunciation.note: Horus is Tier 1 because the Egyptian Ḥr preserves the underdotted ḥ — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The name is onomatopoeically apt: the throaty ḥ and the final u suggest a cry from far above. The Greek borrowing Hōros adds an omega, but the original Egyptian root is simply ḥr.

domains.title: The Distant One
domains.subtitle: Sky · Kingship · Falcon
domains.lead: Ḥr is the falcon of the sky, whose eyes are the sun and the moon, whose wings outspread are the heavens, and whose incarnation on earth is the living pharaoh. He is not one god but a constellation of related gods — Horus the Elder, the primordial sky; Horus the Younger, son of Osiris and Isis; and Re-Horakhty, the solar synthesis. Through all his forms he stands for one thing: legitimate authority defending cosmic order against chaos.

cards.name: The Sky
cards.desc: Horus soars across the heavens; his right eye is the sun, his left the moon, and his body the luminous air.

cards.name: Divine Kingship
cards.desc: Every pharaoh is the 'Living Horus'; the Horus-name is the first and oldest of the five royal names.

cards.name: The Falcon
cards.desc: The lanner or peregrine falcon — swift, far-seeing, and deadly — is Horus's living embodiment.

cards.name: The Wedjat Eye
cards.desc: The restored eye of Horus is Egypt's supreme symbol of protection, wholeness, and royal health.

symbols.name: Falcon
symbols.meaning: The sky itself and the king's predatory vigilance

symbols.name: Double crown (pschent)
symbols.meaning: The unity of Upper and Lower Egypt under Horus's rule

symbols.name: Wedjat eye
symbols.meaning: Healing, restoration, and protection; the eye wounded by Set and made whole by Thoth

symbols.name: Serekh
symbols.meaning: The palace-façade frame that encloses the king's Horus-name

symbols.name: Sun disk with wings
symbols.meaning: Re-Horakhty, Horus fused with the sun-god Re

mythology.lead: Horus's mythology is the political theology of Egypt made personal. It tells how the rightful heir, born from a murdered father and a resourceful mother, defeats the usurper and restores the throne. The story was never merely entertainment; it was the charter of kingship, replayed in temples for three thousand years.

myths.title: Elder and Younger
myths.text: Two falcons answer to the name Ḥr, and the Egyptians rarely troubled to separate them. Horus the Elder (Ḥr-wr) is the primordial sky of the Pyramid Texts, brother of Osiris and Set, whose eyes are the sun and the moon — when he weeps, the Nile rises. Horus the Younger (Ḥr-pꜣ-ꜥd, 'Horus the child') is the son of Osiris and Isis, avenger of his father. By the New Kingdom the two had merged into a single royal figure: the Horus of Edfu is at once the ancient sky and the young heir. The fusion was not confusion but policy — the king's god had to be older than creation yet younger than his own succession. The myth means that legitimacy in Egypt drew on two wells, antiquity and inheritance, and Horus drew from both.

myths.title: Eighty Years Against Set
myths.text: When Set murders Osiris and seizes the throne, the infant Horus is hidden in the Delta marshes of Chemmis, guarded by Isis and the scorpion Serqet. Grown to manhood, he claims his inheritance, and the dispute goes before the Ennead. The New Kingdom satire The Contendings of Horus and Set (Papyrus Chester Beatty I) turns the cosmic lawsuit into eighty years of grotesque trials: the hippopotamus duel in the river's depths, the shameful episode of the lettuce, Isis disguised as a maiden tricking Set into judging against himself, and the tribunal's own judges oscillating 'like lunatics.' Set tears out Horus's eyes; at last the verdict favours legitimacy over force, and the gods divide the inheritance — Horus the black land, Set the desert. Plutarch retells the whole contest in Greek (De Iside 19–20), already calling it ancient. The myth is Egypt's constitution in narrative form: the crown follows the bloodline of Osiris, and chaos must settle for the frontier.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Eye of Horus is arguably the most widely recognised symbol of ancient Egypt. It appears on jewellery, tattoos, amulets, and corporate logos across the globe, usually as a generic sign of protection. In popular culture, Horus features in films, comics, and games as a falcon-headed warrior or sky-god. For modern Kemetics and Egyptian pagans, Horus remains a living deity of kingship, justice, and rightful authority. The name has also entered astronomy: the asteroid 1924 Horus reminds us that the distant one still watches from above.
lore.archaeology: The falcon-god Horus is attested from the earliest dynastic period: the Narmer Palette shows a falcon protecting the king, and the serekh with Horus-name became the oldest royal titulary. The temple of Horus at Edfu, built during the Ptolemaic period, preserves the longest surviving ancient Egyptian temple inscription, including the myth of Horus defeating Set. Falcon mummies and votive falcon coffins have been found at Saqqara, Abydos, and Hierakonpolis — the latter city being Horus's ancient cult center.
lore.syncretism: Horus absorbed and was absorbed by many gods. As Re-Horakhty he united the falcon with the solar disk; as Harpocrates he became the finger-to-lips divine child of Greco-Roman Egypt; as Sokar and Montu he shared falcon imagery with other deities of death and war. Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride transmitted the Osiris-Horus myth to the Greek and Roman world, where it influenced conceptions of divine sonship and resurrection. Some later interpreters, from early Christians to modern comparative mythologists, have drawn parallels between Horus and other divine-child figures, though many of these claims are exaggerated or unsupported by Egyptian evidence.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name ḥr is written with the falcon-on-perch hieroglyph (Gardiner G5), often used as a logogram for the god himself. The initial ḥ is a voiceless pharyngeal fricative; the final r is an alveolar liquid. Because Egyptian does not write vowels, the pronunciation has to be reconstructed from Coptic forms such as ϩⲱⲣ and from Greek Ὧρος. The meaning 'distant one' or 'one on high' is well attested.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-set' — begin with a slight catch in the throat (the alef), then 'set' with a crisp or silent final t. The variant 'EE-set' is also widely defended.
pronunciation.note: This entry is the Egyptian goddess ꜣst (Aset/Iset), not the later Greek name Isis. Hieroglyphs record only ꜣ-s-t; the vowel evolution is reconstructed as Rūsat > Rūsaʾ > ʾŪsaʾ > ʾĒsə, whence Coptic ⲎⲤⲈ and Greek Ἶσις. The ꜣ is a glottal stop, and the final -t is a feminine marker often silent in speech. PUNICODEX uses the registrable alef ꜣ (U+A723) to signal the historic consonant; this is a Tier 1 restoration, the alef being a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. Sources: Allen, Middle Egyptian (2014); Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. ꜣst; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache I, s.v. ꜣst; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), on the representation of Egyptian alef in Semitic transcriptions.

domains.title: The Throne Made Flesh
domains.subtitle: Magic, Motherhood, and Kingship
domains.lead:
Ꜣst is the throne that walks. Her very name is written with the hieroglyph of a seat (O29), and the king sits on her lap as on the throne of Egypt itself. She is the sister-wife of Osiris, the mother of Horus, and the most formidable magician in the Egyptian cosmos — a goddess who knows the secret names of things and is not afraid to use them.

Where other gods rule by force or decree, Ꜣst rules by devotion, cunning, and love. She reassembles the murdered Osiris, hides her infant son from Set, and outwits the sun-god Re himself to extract his hidden name. Her story is the Egyptian closest approach to a gospel: a god who dies, a mother who saves, a child who inherits.

cards.name: The Throne
cards.desc: Her name and form are bound to the royal seat; every pharaoh is enthroned on Isis.

cards.name: Words of Power
cards.desc: She commands heka, the force that animates ritual speech, and knows names that even Re keeps secret.

cards.name: Mother of Horus
cards.desc: She conceives Horus after Osiris's death and nurses him in the papyrus thickets of Chemmis.

cards.name: The Protectress
cards.desc: With outspread wings she shelters the living, the dead, and especially children and kings.

symbols.name: Throne hieroglyph
symbols.meaning: Her name and body; the seat on which the king is established

symbols.name: Outspread wings
symbols.meaning: Protection of the living and the dead; the winged goddess sheltering Osiris or the king

symbols.name: Ankh
symbols.meaning: The life she grants to Horus, the king, and the justified dead

symbols.name: Sistrum
symbols.meaning: Musical power used to frighten enemies and celebrate the goddess

symbols.name: Tyet knot
symbols.meaning: The 'blood of Isis,' a protective amulet associated with her menstrual and life-giving power

mythology.lead: Isis's mythology is the central drama of the Osirian cycle: love, murder, fragmentation, and restoration. It is also a handbook of magical power, because Isis does not accept loss as final — she out-searches the dismembered, out-waits the sun, and out-heals the poisoned, and does it all as a mother whose throne is the seat of kings.

myths.title: The Lament and the Search
myths.text: When Set murdered Osiris, dismembered the body, and scattered the pieces across the nomes, Isis did what no other power in the cosmos would do: she went looking. The Pyramid Texts (Utterances 364 and 593) already picture her and Nephthys keening beside the bier at Busiris, and the Late Period ritual Lamentations of Isis and Nephthys (Berlin Papyrus 3008) expands the mourning into antiphonal liturgy. Plutarch (On Isis and Osiris 13–19) gives the fullest narrative: piece by piece, nome by nome, Isis recovered her husband — all but one member, lost to the Nile fish, which is why, his priests said, the river's flood itself is fertile. She reknit the body, anointed it, and by her magic conceived Horus upon it. The tradition's sources differ in detail — the number and locations of the pieces, the role of Anubis — but the core is constant across three thousand years. The myth means that Isis makes wholeness out of what was torn apart, and that the act of gathering, not any weapon, is the deepest magic in Egypt.

myths.title: Chemmis
myths.text: Pregnant and hunted by Set's agents, Isis fled to the marshes of Chemmis in the Delta, where she gave birth to Horus in secret (Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris 19; the tradition is far older, staged across the Horus-stelae of the first millennium BCE). She hid the child in the papyrus thickets, nursed him, and fought off scorpions, snakes, and sickness; the great Metternich Stela tells of her all-night vigil, reciting spells over the stricken child until the sun itself stood still in sympathy. From this refuge came the image that conquered the ancient world: Isis lactans, the goddess seated on her throne suckling the divine child — an icon so potent that early Christian artists borrowed its posture for Mary and the Christ child without changing a line. The myth means that Egypt's salvation begins not in battle but in a mother's successful secrecy: the throne hides its heir until he is strong enough to claim it.

lore.culturalLegacy: Isis gave the ancient Mediterranean one of its first truly international mystery religions. Her temples offered initiation, personal salvation, and a goddess who heard individual prayers. After Egypt became Christian, her images were redeployed for the Virgin and Child. In modern times the name 'Isis' has been borrowed by terrorist groups, a sad irony that has nothing to do with the goddess. Contemporary Pagans, Kemetics, and feminist theologians reclaim her as a goddess of magic, motherhood, and political resistance. Her throne hieroglyph still sits at the center of every royal image in which a king is 'established' on the goddess herself.
lore.archaeology: The temple of Isis at Philae, relocated to Agilkia by UNESCO, preserves the last known hieroglyphic inscription (394 CE). Earlier shrines flourished at Abydos, Behbeit el-Hagar, and Giza. The Great Hymn to Osiris on the Stela of Amenmose (Louvre C 286, Eighteenth Dynasty) and the Metternich Stela celebrate her magical protection of Horus. Bronze statuettes of Isis lactans, faience amulets, and temple reliefs from the Delta to Nubia attest her popularity across three millennia.
lore.syncretism: Ꜣst absorbed or was identified with many goddesses: Hathor in her solar-mother aspect, Mut as consort of Amun, and Serqet in protective magic. Greeks identified her with Demeter, both searching goddesses of grain and mourning, and with Aphrodite in her erotic power. Roman Egypt made Isis a universal saviour whose cult spread across the Mediterranean, reaching Pompeii, London, and the Danube. Early Christianity drew on her iconography for the Virgin Mary: the nursing mother, the queen of heaven, the star-crowned woman of Revelation. The Copts rendered her name as ⲎⲤⲈ, a sound that still haunts the modern name 'Isis.'
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written with the throne hieroglyph (O29), functioning as a phonogram ꜣ, followed by s and t: ꜣ-s-t. The throne sign is also the name's semantic core: Isis is the throne. The initial ꜣ is an Egyptological alef, a glottal stop represented in PuniCodex by U+A723. Coptic writes the name ⲎⲤⲈ (Ēse), while Greek Ἶσις gave rise to the modern 'Isis.' Because hieroglyphs omit vowels, the precise pronunciation of the pharaonic form is reconstructed; the registrable Ꜣst preserves the consonantal skeleton and the throne icon embedded in the goddess's identity.

pronunciation.note: Ḏḥwtj is Tier-1: the underdotted ḏ and ḥ are distinctive letters the ASCII form loses. Egyptian writing records only the consonants ḏ-ḥ-w-tj; the vowels are reconstructed from Coptic and Greek sources. The initial palatal ḏ and the pharyngeal ḥ are both non-English sounds preserved in the Unicode form.

domains.title: Lord of the Sacred Word
domains.subtitle: Writing, Wisdom, Moon, and Judgment
domains.lead: Ḏḥwtj is the ibis-headed scribe of the gods, the measurer of time, the reckoner of accounts, and the moon whose light lets humans see at night. He invented writing, preserved the laws of Maat, and stands beside Osiris in the Hall of Judgment to record the verdict of the heart. Where Ptḥ creates by speaking, Thoth creates by writing: he is the god who makes knowledge durable.

cards.name: Moon and Measurement
cards.desc: Thoth is the moon that measures months, festivals, and the night hours of the Duat.

cards.name: Scribe of Maat
cards.desc: He records the weighing of the heart and knows the spells that protect the justified dead.

cards.name: Mediator and Healer
cards.desc: He intervenes in disputes among gods, restores the Eye of Horus, and masters medicine and magic.

cards.name: Hermopolis
cards.desc: His city Khemenu, 'Eight-Town,' was a center of learning and the cult of the Ogdoad.

symbols.name: Ibis
symbols.meaning: The bird whose curved beak and measured step made it emblematic of writing and calculation

symbols.name: Baboon
symbols.meaning: Thoth's other sacred animal, associated with the dawn and the rising moon

symbols.name: Scribal palette and reed pens
symbols.meaning: The tools of the divine scribe who records all deeds and spells

symbols.name: Crescent moon and disk
symbols.meaning: The lunar phases by which Thoth measures time and renews the cosmic order

symbols.name: Eye of Horus (wedjat)
symbols.meaning: Restored by Thoth after the conflict of Horus and Seth, symbolizing wholeness regained

mythology.lead: Thoth moves through Egyptian myth as the indispensable companion: he is present at creation, mediates divine quarrels, heals the wounded eye, and judges the dead. His stories are less about his own ambition than about the power of knowledge, writing, and measured speech to resolve conflict and preserve order.

myths.title: The Word That Organized Creation
myths.text: Egyptian creation had many authors — Atum of Heliopolis, Ptḥ of Memphis, the eight of Hermopolis — and Ḏḥwtj is the one indispensable technician in all of them. The Shabaka Stone's Memphite Theology makes him effectively the tongue of Ptḥ: the creator conceives in his heart, and it is Thoth's word that carries the conception into speech, 'which created all that exists.' Elsewhere he is credited with inventing hieroglyphs, numbers, and the calendar — the tools by which humans keep Maat on earth — and the Hermopolitan cosmogony makes his own city, Khemenu, the mound that first rose from the flood. Creation, in this theology, is not only a making but a record: nothing made is secure until it is written. The myth means speech without a scribe is unfinished creation — the word that is not written down has not yet fully happened.

myths.title: The Mediator of the Gods
myths.text: In the New Kingdom narrative The Contendings of Horus and Set (Papyrus Chester Beatty I), Ḏḥwtj is the divine institution that keeps the brawl from becoming apocalypse: he is scribe to the Ennead's tribunal, messenger between the courts above and below, and healer of both combatants — restoring Horus's torn eye and Set's injured testicles with the same professional calm. When the gods deadlock for years, it is Thoth who carries the correspondence with Osiris in the Duat, and Thoth who records the final verdict that seats Horus on the throne. His prestige is the point: the text is a comedy in which kings, warriors, and even the sun's council behave like litigants, and only the scribe behaves like a god. The myth defines a specific kind of sacredness: not the hand that throws the spear but the hand that writes the verdict — the power that ends wars by making decisions legible.

lore.culturalLegacy: Thoth lives on as the patron of writers, scholars, librarians, and occultists. The figure of Hermes Trismegistus shaped Western esotericism for nearly two millennia, and the word 'hermetic' still signals sealed, secret knowledge. In popular culture, Thoth appears as a wise moon-god, a keeper of arcane books, and a judge of souls. For Egyptologists, he embodies the Egyptian conviction that writing is a form of magic: the right words, properly recorded, can preserve a person beyond death.
lore.archaeology: Thoth's principal cult center was Khemenu (Hermopolis Magna) in Middle Egypt, where remains of his temple and the nearby ibis and baboon cemeteries have been excavated. Thousands of mummified ibises and baboons were deposited as votive offerings at Saqqara, Tuna el-Gebel, and other sites. Temple reliefs from the New Kingdom onward show Thoth as scribe, healer, and lunar measurer. The Graeco-Roman Hermetic texts and Coptic references preserve his later reputation as Hermes Trismegistus.
lore.syncretism: Thoth's most enduring syncretism is with the Greek Hermes, producing Hermes Trismegistus, 'Thrice-Great Hermes,' the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus. This Graeco-Egyptian figure became a cornerstone of late antique mysticism, alchemy, and astrology, and was reclaimed by Renaissance humanists such as Ficino and Pico della Mirandola. In Coptic Egypt, Thoth's month name (Thōout) survived in the Christian calendar. His ibis and baboon forms influenced medieval bestiaries and early modern emblem books.

pronunciation.approximation: ah-MOON — begin with a soft glottal catch, then a long 'moon' without the final glide.
pronunciation.note: Ꜣmun is Tier-1: the initial Egyptological alef (Ꜣ) is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The alef marks the consonant that Coptic and Greek sources vocalize as 'A'. Egyptian hieroglyphs record only j-m-n; the vowels are reconstructed from later witnesses.

domains.title: The Hidden One
domains.subtitle: Wind, Kingship, and the Invisible Power
domains.lead: Ꜣmun begins as a local Theban wind god and ends as the king of the Egyptian pantheon, fused with Ra as Amun-Ra. His very name means 'Hidden One': he is the power that cannot be seen, the breath behind the storm, the unseen source of royal and cosmic authority. Where solar gods blaze in the sky, Amun moves in the air, the temple shadows, and the oracle's whisper.

cards.name: Lord of the Breath
cards.desc: Amun's wind aspect links him to invisible force, royal fortune, and the breath that animates the cosmos.

cards.name: Karnak and Thebes
cards.desc: The great temple complex at Karnak was his principal seat; each pharaoh added to its forest of pylons and obelisks.

cards.name: Amun-Ra
cards.desc: Fused with the sun god, Amun becomes the hidden power within the visible disk, worshipped across Egypt.

cards.name: The Oracle of Siwa
cards.desc: His desert oracle at Siwa was consulted by Greek colonists and famously by Alexander the Great.

symbols.name: Two tall plumes
symbols.meaning: Amun's distinctive crown, combining the white crown of Upper Egypt with twin ostrich feathers

symbols.name: Ram with curved horns
symbols.meaning: His sacred animal, especially at Thebes and Nubia, symbolizing fertility and kingship

symbols.name: Goose
symbols.meaning: The 'great cackler' associated with Amun as a creator god who laid the cosmic egg

symbols.name: Solar barque
symbols.meaning: Amun-Ra as the hidden power steering the sun through the hours of night

mythology.lead: Amun's rise from provincial wind god to universal king is one of the great success stories of Egyptian religion. By the Middle Kingdom he is national; by the New Kingdom he is Amun-Ra, hidden lord of the cosmos; by the Late Period his oracles and priesthoods rival pharaonic power. His myths revolve around concealment, revelation, and the transmission of authority.

myths.title: The Hidden God Who Becomes King
myths.text: Amun's beginnings are almost comically modest. His first attestations are Old Kingdom: in the Pyramid Texts he stands quietly beside his consort Amaunet among the eight 'Elder Gods' — the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, frog- and snake-headed powers of the primordial waters. He is a god of air and invisibility, one of eight, local to Thebes, a provincial town. Then history intervened. When the Theban dynasty of Mentuhotep II reunified Egypt (c. 2055 BCE), Amun rode the rise; when the New Kingdom pharaohs of the Eighteenth Dynasty built an empire, his theologians proclaimed him 'King of the Gods', his hiddenness the mark of a supreme being too vast to be fully known. The myth of Amun is thus a success story about invisibility: the god you cannot see became the god you cannot avoid, and the ancient world learned that the unseen is often the most powerful thing in the room.

myths.title: Amun and the Returning Eye
myths.text: The Theban temples inscribed their own version of Egypt's most beloved story, the 'Distant Goddess' cycle (preserved in first-millennium temple inscriptions of the Eye of Ra, e.g. at Edfu). The sun-god's eye — his daughter, the fierce lioness — grows angry and flees south toward Nubia, and Egypt withers without her: crops fail, the Nile slackens, the gods' laughter stops. A messenger goes to bring her back; in the Theban reading the returning eye is identified with Mut, and she is appeased and united to the waiting god — Amun of Karnak — so that rage becomes alliance and the land blooms again. The myth was not merely read: it was staged, in the great processions when Amun's bark sailed from Karnak to Luxor at the Opet festival, the god visiting his consort Mut across the river. The royal theology fused the wandering eye with the king's own vital force: the empire's order was the marriage of returning rage to the patient hidden god.

lore.culturalLegacy: The name Amun echoes in the Hebrew Amen, the Coptic liturgy, and the Greek Ammon. Karnak remains one of the largest religious complexes ever built, a stone testament to his prestige. In modern spirituality, Amun is invoked as a god of hidden knowledge, occult power, and the unseen forces that shape events. Egyptologists study his priesthood as an early example of a religious institution that accumulated wealth and political influence comparable to a state within a state.
lore.archaeology: Amun's principal sanctuary was Karnak in Thebes, a vast complex of temples, pylons, obelisks, and sacred lakes developed over more than a millennium. The temple of Luxor, the Khonsu temple, and the Mut precinct formed the southern counterpart. His oracular temple at Siwa in the Libyan desert attracted Greek and later Roman visitors. Ram statues line the processional way at Karnak, and temple inscriptions record Amun's oracular responses and royal legitimation. In Nubia, temples at Jebel Barkal and Meroë continued his cult into the first millennium CE.
lore.syncretism: Amun's greatest syncretism is Amun-Ra, the fusion of Theban invisibility with Heliopolitan solar power. He was also paired with Mut and Khonsu as the Theban triad, and with Min as Amun-Min, an ithyphallic fertility god. Greeks identified him with Zeus under the name Zeus Ammon, and his oracle at Siwa drew visitors from across the Mediterranean. In Nubia and Kush, Amun remained a royal god long after Egypt's pharaonic decline, and the kings of Meroë claimed his patronage.

Egyptian writing does not record vowels; the vocalised form is a modern convention reconstructed from Coptic and Greek evidence.
The Unicode restoration Ptḥ uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com.

provenanceSources.title: Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian

pronunciation.approximation: puh-TAHKH — the final consonant is a dry, breathy 'kh' made in the back of the throat, not the soft 'h' of English.
pronunciation.note: Ptḥ is Tier-1: the pharyngeal ḥ preserved in the Unicode form is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The vowels are supplied by convention from Coptic and Greek transcriptions; Egyptian writing records only p-t-ḥ.

domains.title: Lord of the White Wall
domains.subtitle: Craft, Creation, and the Speaking Heart
domains.lead: Ptḥ is the creator god of Memphis, the ancient capital whose white walls enclosed Egypt's foremost workshop of stone and bronze. Unlike solar creators who speak light into being, Ptḥ creates through the heart's intention and the tongue's command: every god, every city, every craft is first thought, then pronounced, then made. He is therefore the patron of sculptors, metalworkers, carpenters, and architects — the one who shapes the raw stuff of the world into enduring form.

cards.name: The Speaking Creator
cards.desc: Ptḥ fashions the gods and their kas through heart and tongue; the Memphite Theology calls him the source of every creative word.

cards.name: Patron of Craftsmen
cards.desc: Sculptors, goldsmiths, carpenters, and shipwrights claimed Ptḥ as their divine foreman; his priests guarded the secrets of the craft.

cards.name: Memphis and the White Wall
cards.desc: His temple at Hut-ka-Ptḥ, 'the mansion of the ka of Ptḥ,' gave Egypt its Greek name Aígyptos.

cards.name: Ptḥ-Sokar-Osiris
cards.desc: In mortuary cult he merges with Sokar and Osiris, guardian of mummification and the nocturnal regeneration of the dead.

symbols.name: Djed pillar
symbols.meaning: Stability and the backbone of Osiris; Ptḥ is often shown grasping it as a maker of lasting order

symbols.name: Was scepter
symbols.meaning: Dominion and the power to command matter into form

symbols.name: Artists' tools
symbols.meaning: The chisel, level, and square of the sculptor and architect

symbols.name: Bull (Apis)
symbols.meaning: The living Apis bull was worshipped as Ptḥ's earthly herald at Memphis

symbols.name: Scarab and mummiform shape
symbols.meaning: Ptḥ-Sokar-Osiris as the nocturnal regenerator of the dead

mythology.lead: Ptḥ's mythology is less a cycle of adventures than a theology of making. His great text, the Memphite Theology, claims that Ptḥ's heart conceived and his tongue pronounced the gods, cities, and sacred rites of Egypt. Creation here is not a battle with chaos but an act of authoritative speech: what Ptḥ names, exists.

myths.title: The Heart and Tongue That Made the Gods
myths.text: The Shabaka Stone, now in the British Museum, is a granite slab on which a Twenty-Fifth-Dynasty king had 'this writing' copied, he says, 'because it was found worm-eaten' — and posterity received the Memphite Theology, a text far older than its copyist. In it, Ptḥ of Memphis stands above Atum: the older creator made the gods 'through that which came forth from his mouth' — semen, spittle, breath — but Ptḥ creates by intention and utterance. 'There came into being as the heart, there came into being as the tongue,' the text says: the heart conceives the thought, the tongue speaks it, and what is spoken is instantly real — every god, every nome, every offering ritual, 'down to the carving of the eye-pupil.' The claim is not poetic decoration but a philosophy of language seven centuries older than Plato's Cratylus: speech is the technology of reality, and Memphis its inventor.

myths.title: Ptḥ and the Birth of Royalty
myths.text: In royal ideology the king is the bodily son of Rē, but Memphis supplied the king's ka — and Ptḥ is its smith. Temple reliefs from Karnak to Luxor show the god leading the king by the hand, inscribing his titulary on the leaves of the ished tree so that the name cannot rot, and fashioning the royal statue into which the royal essence can descend. The coronation liturgy makes Ptḥ 'he who establishes the King of Upper and Lower Egypt upon the throne of Horus forever'; the craftsmen's stelae make him foreman of every workshop that shaped a royal monument. The theology is quietly radical: dynasty is blood, but kingship is craft — and what is crafted can be made well or badly, which is why Egypt wanted its kings supervised by a god of quality control.

lore.culturalLegacy: The very name Aígyptos derives from Ptḥ's temple, Hut-ka-Ptḥ. His city, Memphis, remained a religious capital for millennia, and his craftsmen shaped the temples and tombs that still define Pharaonic visual culture. In modern Egyptology, Ptḥ stands as the theologian-creator, the god who thinks and speaks the world into order. Contemporary artists, architects, and makers continue to find in him a patron of the patient transformation of raw material into meaning.
lore.archaeology: Ptḥ's primary cult center was the temple complex at Hut-ka-Ptḥ in Memphis, where remains of a vast enclosure, colossal statues of Ramses II, and the Serapeum where Apis bulls were buried have been excavated. The Shabaka Stone, now in the British Museum, preserves the Memphite Theology. Statues, stelae, and offering tables from workshops across Egypt invoke Ptḥ as patron of craftsmen, while composite Ptḥ-Sokar-Osiris figures are common in funerary assemblages from the Late and Ptolemaic periods.
lore.syncretism: Ptḥ absorbed and was absorbed by neighboring gods. With Sokar and Osiris he formed the mortuary triad Ptḥ-Sokar-Osiris. With the Apis bull he produced Osiris-Apis, the Hellenistic Sarapis worshipped across the Mediterranean. Greeks identified him with Hephaestus because both were divine craftsmen, and Roman Egypt exported the syncretic Sarapis as far as Britain and the Rhine. Ptḥ's creative theology also influenced later Platonic and Judeo-Christian ideas of the demiurge and the Logos, though the connections are debated.

pronunciation.approximation: 'sakh-MAHT' — 'sakh' as in 'Bach' with an s, then 'maht' with a long 'ah' and a crisp or silent final t.
pronunciation.note: The name is the feminine form of the root sḫm, 'to be powerful'. Hieroglyphs record S-ḫ-m-t; the vowels are reconstructed from Coptic Ⲥⲁⲭⲙⲓ and from Egyptian feminine-participle patterns. The ḫ is a voiceless velar fricative, not English 'k'. In PUNICODEX the Sḫmt spelling preserves the historic ḫ (U+1E2B) as a Tier 1 restoration — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses; the ASCII fallback is 'sekhm(t)'. Sources: Allen, Middle Egyptian (2014); Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. sḫm; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache IV, s.v. sḫm; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), on Egyptian ḫ in Semitic orthography.

domains.title: The Lioness Who Heals
domains.subtitle: War, Vengeance, and the Physician's Hand
domains.lead: Sḫmt is the solar eye when it has had enough. A lioness-headed goddess crowned with the sun disk and uraeus, she is the most terrifying expression of divine force in Egypt: plague-bringer, battlefield devourer — and, paradoxically, one of the most skilled healers in the pantheon. Her name means 'the powerful one', and power is rarely gentle.

cards.name: The Eye of Ra
cards.desc: She is the sun-god's burning gaze, sent to punish rebellion and to protect cosmic order.

cards.name: Destroyer of Mankind
cards.desc: The Destruction of Mankind myth tells how Re unleashed her and almost lost control.

cards.name: Lady of Life
cards.desc: Her priests practiced medicine; spells invoke Sekhmet to turn away disease and poison.

cards.name: Fire and Fever
cards.desc: Heat, fever, and the parching wind of the desert are hers; so is their relief.

symbols.name: Lioness
symbols.meaning: Her primary form and the animal embodiment of solar ferocity

symbols.name: Sun disk and uraeus
symbols.meaning: Her identity as the eye of Re, the burning emanation of the sun

symbols.name: Ankh
symbols.meaning: The life she can grant after she has taken it

symbols.name: Red beer
symbols.meaning: The pacifying drink that turned her rage into festival

symbols.name: Arrow
symbols.meaning: The plague and punishment she sends as Re's messenger

mythology.lead: Sekhmet's mythology is dominated by one stupendous story and its aftermath: the day the sun-god sent her to punish humanity, and the trick that turned genocide into festival. Around that core the tradition built a practical theology — the statue garrisons of Thebes, the daily appeasement rites, the physicians' prayers — because a goddess of plague cannot be merely told about; she must be managed, fed, and ritually kept calm.

myths.title: The Day the Eye Did Not Stop
myths.text: In the Book of the Heavenly Cow — inscribed in the tombs of Seti I (KV17) and Ramesses VI (KV9) and on the gilded shrines of Tutankhamun (KV62) — the aging Re learns that humanity plots against him and sends his Eye, the lioness, against the rebels. Her fury is absolute, and the text's numbers are a theology of excess: seven thousand jars of salvation-brew are ordered against the slaughter. When even the gods grow afraid that mankind will be extinguished, Re relents and deploys Egypt's oldest technology: fermentation. The fields are flooded with beer dyed red with ochre until the land stands red as blood. The lioness, sworn to drink only blood, drinks, wakes drunk, wakes pacified; Re greets the returning eye by a new and gentler name — Hathor — while Sekhmet remains the name of her wrath. The festival of drunkenness at Thebes kept the transformation liturgically alive. The myth's mercy is a technology: brewed, dyed, and poured — violence inebriated into harmlessness and commemorated, thereafter, with a hangover.

myths.title: One Statue for Every Day and Night
myths.text: At Karnak, in the precinct of Mut, stands Egypt's most startling devotional infrastructure: hundreds of black granite statues of Sekhmet, seated and standing, crowned with the sun disk, so many that one tradition holds a statue was dedicated for each day and night of the year, so that her protective gaze would never sleep. Most were commissioned by Amenhotep III, whose long reign also endured plague — the Amarna letters speak of pestilence in Egypt — and scholars have connected the vast program to the king's prayers for deliverance and to his sed-festivals, in which Sekhmet embodied royal power renewed. The statues were not decoration but stationed force: a distributed garrison of the goddess, each figure a sentry to be approached, addressed, and offered to daily. When Egyptologists count them by the hundred — in the British Museum, the Louvre, and the Luxor cache — they are counting the material form of a theology of vigilance: protection is not an event but a roster, and dangerous power is honored by being permanently employed.

lore.culturalLegacy: Sekhmet strides through modern culture as the archetype of righteous rage: lioness-warrior in games and fantasy novels, patroness of a fury that protects rather than wounds, invoked in wellness and feminist spirituality as the power women are still told to suppress. Scholars of ancient medicine study her priesthood as an early case of temple healing and of ritual epidemic management — her distributed garrison of statues reads today like an ancient public-health program. Artists return to her granite faces in museum storerooms and find the most human expression in Egyptian art: not serene like the gods, but barely restrained. In a culture still negotiating whether female anger is pathology or immunity, Sekhmet offers the older answer — it is the immune system of the cosmos: dangerous, necessary, and owed daily offerings.
lore.archaeology: The most striking material witnesses are the hundreds of granite statues of Sekhmet from the Mut precinct at Karnak, many now in museums worldwide, including the British Museum and the Louvre, with further examples from the Luxor cache. Bronze amulets, votive ears, and healing stelae come from Saqqara, Memphis, and Deir el-Medina. The Book of the Heavenly Cow survives on the walls of the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62), Seti I (KV17), and Ramesses VI (KV9), preserving the Destruction of Mankind narrative in royal burial contexts. Amenhotep III's statue program is documented by its own inscriptions and by the Amenhotep III colossi at the temple's entrance.
lore.syncretism: Sekhmet and Hathor are two sides of the same solar eye: the destroyer and the lover, the lioness and the cow. In Thebes she fuses with Mut; in Memphis with Bastet and Wadjet as protective forces. The Greeks sometimes compared her to Athena for her martial aspect, but the comparison is inexact: Athena is strategist, Sekhmet is conflagration. Later magical texts from Roman Egypt invoke her under Greek names and with syncretic attributes, blending her lion-roar with the names of Jewish and Greek angels. In modern goddess spirituality she has become the archetype of the angry, healing feminine.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written s-ḫ-m-t, with the seated-lioness determinative (E6). The root sḫm means 'to be powerful'; the final -t marks the feminine form. The ḫ is a voiceless velar fricative, rendered in PuniCodex by h-breve (U+1E2B). Coptic preserves a late form Ⲥⲁⲭⲙⲓ (Sakhmi). Because the name is also the word for power, the registrable Sḫmt is at once a proper noun and a theological statement: this goddess is might.

entries.meaning: She of the ointment jar (Egyptian bꜣstt)

steps: The Egyptian name is written 𓎯𓏏𓏏𓁐 in hieroglyphs.
Hieroglyphs combine logograms, phonograms, and determinatives; the exact function of each sign depends on context.
Egyptian writing does not record vowels; the vocalised form is a modern convention reconstructed from Coptic and Greek evidence.
The Unicode restoration Bꜣstt uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com.

provenanceSources.title: Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian

pronunciation.approximation: 'boo-ISS-tee' — say 'boo', then a tiny catch before 'iss', ending with 'tee' (the final t is often silent).
pronunciation.note: Allen (The Ancient Egyptian Language: A Historical Study, 2013, p. 74) reconstructs the earliest form as buʔístit or buʔístiat; by the first millennium the name had become *Ubaste and then Coptic ⲟⲩⲃⲁⲥⲧⲉ (Oubaste) /ʔuˈβastə/. The meaning of the name remains uncertain; the lexicon glosses it 'She of the ointment jar'. The final -t is a feminine marker often silent in speech, and the ꜣ represents a glottal stop. PUNICODEX uses the registrable alef ꜣ (U+A723); the double -tt- is orthographic. This is a Tier 1 restoration — the alef is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. Sources: Allen 2013, p. 74; Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. bꜣstt; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache III, s.v. bꜣstt; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), for the phonological background of Egyptian alef and feminine -t.

domains.title: Goddess of the Hearth and the Claw
domains.subtitle: Cats, Childbirth, and Domestic Sanctity
domains.lead: Bꜣstt begins as a lioness and ends as a cat. In the Old Kingdom she is a fierce daughter of Re, one of the raging eyes of the sun; by the Late Period she has become the benevolent lady of the home, her round face and upright ears copied by millions of household cats. The transformation is not a decline but an expansion: she learns to keep watch at the cradle as well as at the battlefield — and to receive her pilgrims with music and wine.

cards.name: The Cat
cards.desc: Bastet's later animal form; the cat protects the home from vermin and evil, and embodies solar warmth.

cards.name: The Lioness
cards.desc: Her older, fiercer aspect as a daughter of Re who fights the chaos serpent Apep.

cards.name: Music and Ecstasy
cards.desc: Her festivals featured sistrums, drums, and dancing; she is a goddess of controlled revelry.

cards.name: Guardian of the Home
cards.desc: Amulets of Bastet protected women in childbirth and children against malign forces.

symbols.name: Cat
symbols.meaning: Her later, domestic form; guardian of the home and hearth

symbols.name: Lioness
symbols.meaning: Her older solar-warrior aspect as an eye of Re

symbols.name: Sistrum
symbols.meaning: Music, trance, and the rattling sound that drives away evil

symbols.name: Ointment jar
symbols.meaning: Perfume, cosmetics, and the guarded substances of feminine space

symbols.name: Ankh
symbols.meaning: The life and fertility she grants to households

mythology.lead: Bastet's myths are fewer and more fragmented than those of Isis or Horus — Egypt never wrote her a great cycle — but what survives is vivid: the wandering solar eye that must be talked home, the red beer that ends a massacre, and the festival that Herodotus judged the merriest in Egypt.

myths.title: The Lioness Talked Home
myths.text: In the theology of the solar eye, the goddess who is Re's own eye grows angry and abandons Egypt for the Nubian desert, taking leonine form; the sun dims and the land withers behind her. The gods send the eloquent Thoth — disguised, in the Late Ptolemaic Papyrus Jumilhac, as a baboon — to coax her back with a flood of words and stories. When the eye returns she comes home in gentler form: the cat, Bastet, the pacified one, and the homecoming itself becomes festival. The same pattern, without her name, underlies the Book of the Heavenly Cow, where the eye must be retrieved before creation itself can be repaired. The Jumilhac account is late — a mythological manual of the Ptolemaic age — but the grammar it preserves is old: wrath departs south, eloquence retrieves it, and the returning goddess is gentler than the one who left. The myth reads Bastet's two bodies, lioness and cat, as a single biography — ferocity that has been talked home, and asked to stay.

myths.title: Red Beer on the Field of Slaughter
myths.text: When humanity plots against the aging Re, the sun-god sends his eye against them, and the eye — a lioness whom later tradition variously names Sekhmet or Bastet — falls upon mankind in a slaughter so complete that even the gods grow afraid the earth will be emptied. In the version painted on the royal tomb walls of the Book of the Heavenly Cow — Seti I (KV17), Ramesses VI (KV9), and the gilded shrines of Tutankhamun (KV62) — Re halts the carnage with a stratagem: the gods brew seven thousand jars of beer, dye them red with ochre, and flood the fields until the land lies red as blood. The eye, sworn to drink only blood, drinks, wakes drunk, wakes changed — and the text itself renames her Hathor, the rejoicing one, while her wrath keeps the name Sekhmet. The festival of drunkenness at Thebes kept this transformation liturgically alive. The myth's theology is precise and unnerving: divine violence is never defeated, only inebriated into harmlessness — and then commemorated, every year, with a hangover.

lore.culturalLegacy: Bastet is the ancestor of every famous cat. Her image underlies the seated feline statuette, the 'cat lady' archetype, and the double reputation of cats as guardians and familiars; medieval Europe, forgetting her temples, made the cat ambiguous — demonic in one legend, protective in the next — precisely the double nature Bastet had refined two thousand years earlier. Modern Kemetic and Neopagan practice invokes her for home protection, fertility, and pleasure; her name brands cat sanctuaries, museum exhibitions, and a small industry of bronze reproductions. The excavations at Tell Basta continue to yield her votive cats and jewelry, studied as evidence of the ancient animal-cult economy and of some of history's earliest pet-keeping. Bastet endures because her theology never needed rescuing from metaphor: the divine can sit on a windowsill, purring, and still be a daughter of the sun.
lore.archaeology: The temple of Bastet at Tell Basta (Per-Bastet/Boubastis) has yielded statues, jewelry, and one of the largest animal cemeteries in Egypt: hundreds of thousands of mummified cats deposited as votives from the Late Period into Roman times. Bronze cat statuettes, often inlaid with gold earrings, are common in museum collections; examples come from Saqqara, Thebes, and Tanis. Reliefs in the Valley of the Kings show Bastet as a daughter of Re in the solar barque, and the temple foundations Herodotus praised (Histories 2.137–138) have been partially excavated at the modern tell.
lore.syncretism: Bastet overlaps with Sekhmet as the pacified form of the solar eye; one text's destroyer is another's house-cat. She was also identified with Hathor in her musical and erotic aspects, and with Isis as protector of the child Horus. Greeks equated her with Artemis, another virgin huntress with a fierce streak, and sometimes with Aphrodite because of her festivals' sexual license. In Roman Egypt her cult spread alongside that of Isis, and her cat iconography influenced medieval European images of the cat as both demonic and protective. The Coptic name Oubaste preserves her sound long after her temples closed.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written b-ꜣ-s-t-t, often with an ointment-jar determinative (V30) that gives rise to the gloss 'she of the ointment jar.' Allen reconstructs an early pronunciation close to buʔístit, with a glottal stop represented by the alef ꜣ (U+A723). The doubled t is orthographic; the final consonant is a feminine marker often silent in speech. Coptic writes ⲟⲩⲃⲁⲥⲧⲉ (Oubaste). The meaning of the root remains uncertain, and PuniCodex preserves the historic spelling Bꜣstt as a Tier 1 restoration that signals the alef — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses — and the feminine ending.

The Unicode restoration Mꜣꜥt uses Egyptological alef/ayin and other registrable characters; the hieroglyphic form is not registrable in .com.

provenanceSources.title: Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian

pronunciation.approximation: 'mah-ʿAHT' — a soft 'm', a deep throaty 'ah' in the middle, and a crisp final 't'.
pronunciation.note: Mꜣꜥt is a Tier-1 restoration of a consonantal Egyptian word. The Egyptological alef (ꜣ) and ayin (ꜥ) are both preserved, marking two different throat sounds that English lacks — distinctive letters the ASCII form loses. The final -t is the feminine abstract ending; the word literally means 'straightness' or 'rightness'.

domains.title: Truth, Justice, Order
domains.subtitle: The domain of Mꜣꜥt
domains.lead: Mꜣꜥt is the Egyptian cosmos made moral: truth, straightness, the even plumb line, the feather against which the heart is weighed. Not a law code but a state of being — the king upholds her, the priest recites her, the scribe writes her, and the justified dead speak her name before the gods. To live in Maat is to move in harmony with the structure of reality itself.

cards.name: Feather of Truth
cards.desc: The heart of the deceased is weighed against Maat's feather; only the light heart passes the tribunal.

cards.name: Cosmic Order
cards.desc: Re 'lives on Maat' each morning; without her, the sun would not rise and chaos would rush back in.

cards.name: Straightness
cards.desc: Maat is the plumb line, the even measure, the straight path that kings, priests, and scribes must keep.

cards.name: Kingly Offering
cards.desc: Pharaohs presented small figures of Maat to the gods, ritually restoring order to its divine source.

symbols.name: Ostrich feather
symbols.meaning: The feather of truth weighed against the heart in the judgement hall

symbols.name: Set-scales
symbols.meaning: The balance on which the heart is tested before Osiris

symbols.name: Kneeling goddess with feather
symbols.meaning: Maat as the personification of cosmic order, often shown kneeling or winged

symbols.name: Primeval mound (benben)
symbols.meaning: The first land rising from chaos, ordered by the presence of Maat

symbols.name: Pharaoh offering Maat
symbols.meaning: The ritual gesture by which the king upholds truth and renews the cosmos

mythology.lead: Maat has no cycle of adventures — she is Egypt's most abstract major power, a principle wearing a woman's face. Her 'myths' are therefore texts: the creation theology that makes order prior to the world, the judgement scene that made her feather the most famous image of Egyptian religion, and the wisdom literature that turned her into the common man's cause.

myths.title: Order Before the World
myths.text: Egyptian creation theology insists that order precedes the world rather than following it. On the Shabaka Stone — the Late Period copy of the Memphite Theology — Ptah conceives creation 'through the heart' (thought) and 'through the tongue' (the commanding word), and the text closes its account with the consequence in the vocabulary of Maat: justice is done for the one who does what is loved, and punishment for the one who does what is hated. Sun hymns make the dependence still more intimate. The great hymn of Book of the Dead spell 15B addresses the sun as one who lives upon Maat, and temple tradition calls Maat the daughter of Re — the very air the sun-god breathes, set at his nose. Without her the sun would not rise and the chaos before creation would rush back: Maat is not a rule the cosmos obeys but the medium it breathes. The theology turns morality into physics — and physics, remarkably, into something worth keeping.

myths.title: The Weighing of the Heart
myths.text: The most famous scene in Egyptian religion survives on the Papyrus of Ani (BM EA 10470, c. 1250 BCE) at the head of Book of the Dead spell 125. The scribe Ani's heart — his conscience made organ — is set in the pan of a balance against a single ostrich feather, Maat herself, the minimum possible weight of a life. Anubis crouches at the scales, adjusting the plumb line; Thoth, ibis-headed, waits with palette to record the verdict; behind the god crouches Ammit the Devourer, crocodile-headed, lion-fronted, hippopotamus-backed, for the hearts that fail. Before the tribunal's assessors the deceased recites the Negative Confession — 'I have not committed evil against men... I have not diminished the offerings in the temples... I have not made anyone weep' — forty-two denials for the forty-two judges. A heart exactly level with Maat is declared 'true of voice' and crosses to the Field of Reeds. The scene's genius is its unit of measurement: a feather. Ethics is weighed not in laws broken but in lightness — the only guilt is heaviness.

lore.culturalLegacy: Maat's feather is among the most recognized images on earth — the badge of Egyptian judgement, stamped on museum merchandise and book covers, invoked wherever an emblem of conscience is needed. Her name powers a modern ethical revival: Afrocentric and Kemetic movements place Maat at the center of a living moral philosophy, sometimes with an 'ideals of Maat' list derived from the Negative Confession; courts, schools, and community organizations invoke her as the ancient warrant that justice is older than any state. Egyptologists — Assmann's classic study above all — treat her as the key to everything Egyptian: art that renders 'the right way', architecture aligned to cosmic axes, a state whose ideology was a promise of order. And because her name means simply 'right, straight, true', she survives in every language's plea that things be set right. Few abstract nouns have ever carried so much divinity.
lore.archaeology: The material record of Maat is a record of repetition — which is her point. The weighing scene survives in dozens of New Kingdom Book of the Dead papyri, most famously the Papyrus of Ani (BM EA 10470) and of Hunefer (EA 9901,3); temple walls from Karnak to Abydos carry the offering-of-Maat scene from Seti I through Ramesses II; and small votive figures of the kneeling goddess — a woman with a single feather — were dedicated in the thousands, from the gold and lapis amulets of Tutankhamun's treasures to the humble faience examples of Deir el-Medina. The Hall of the Two Maats in the Osireion at Abydos names the standard twice, as if for emphasis. Even scribal palettes and builders' plumb bobs invoke her. An abstract goddess leaves abstract archaeology: not a temple she can call her own, but a civilization aligned, wall by wall, to her axis.
lore.syncretism: Maat resisted translation. The Greeks, who happily equated Amun with Zeus and Hathor with Aphrodite, had no goddess of cosmic correctness to offer, and later writers reach instead for abstractions — Dikē, Justice, or the Stoic notion of a rational order governing gods and men alike; Plutarch's treatise on Isis discusses Maat-like concepts under Greek ethical categories rather than any divine name. Inside Egypt the syncretisms ran the other way: late theology fused Maat with Isis as 'the great god's mother, lady of Maat', and paired her constantly with Thoth — the divine couple of the two intellectual virtues, cosmic order and divine utterance, scholarship married to its standard. In Coptic, Maat survives not as a goddess but as the ordinary word for truth, ⲙⲉ. A deity can be absorbed into the language and disappear from the pantheon in the same gesture — that is Maat's fate, and fittingly, her triumph.
