Akkadian variant reflecting late pronunciation

etymology.derivation: Standard Assyriology transliterates the god as Enlil (𒀭𒂗𒇸). The Sumerian signs EN.LIL mean 'lord wind/air,' and the Akkadian rendering is Ellil. The length of the second vowel is reconstructed from comparative and orthographic evidence, not explicitly encoded in the cuneiform; the macron on Enlīl is a pedagogical mark that makes that open question visible, not a claim of canonical spelling.

steps: The name is written as the Sumerogram EN.LÍL (𒂗𒆤), literally 'lord of the wind/air'.
The divine determinative 𒀭 (dingir) marks the name as a deity; it is silent in pronunciation.
In Akkadian scholarly tradition the long vowel is marked with a macron: Enlīl.
Enlīl was the chief god of the Sumerian pantheon, dwelling in the Ekur temple at Nippur.

pronunciation.approximation: 'en-LEEL' — the second syllable is drawn out, like a sustained breath across the plain.
pronunciation.note: Enlīl is Tier 1: the macron on the second i is a diacritic the ASCII form loses. It is a pedagogical mark: a visible question that invites discussion about how the name was pronounced in Sumerian and Akkadian. Standard Assyriology writes Enlil; the Unicode form Enlīl belongs to PuniCodex's phonological reconstruction hub.

domains.title: ENLĪL — The Phonological Reconstruction Hub
domains.subtitle: Wind, Storm, Kingship
domains.lead:
The name is written 𒂗𒇸. Standard Assyriology transliterates it as Enlil. But in the phonological grammar of Sumerian and Akkadian, the length of the second vowel remains an open question — and it is here, in the space between the written sign and the spoken sound, that this temple operates. This node of PuniCodex is dedicated to the phonological reconstruction and didactic grammar of the ancient Near East. We mark vowel length not because it is certain, but because it is discussable. The macron is a question mark made visible.

Enlīl is nevertheless the king of the Sumerian gods, the invisible sovereign whose breath is the wind and whose word is fate. He rules from the Ekur, the 'Mountain House' at Nippur, the cosmic axis where heaven and earth meet. Storms are his messengers; kingship is his gift.

cards.name: The Wind
cards.desc: The air that animates the world and carries the voice of command across the Mesopotamian plain; his seven winds sweep the disobedient flat.

cards.name: The Ekur
cards.desc: The 'Mountain House' at Nippur, the temple whose foundations root in the netherworld and whose peak touches heaven — the axis of the cosmos.

cards.name: Kingship
cards.desc: The grantor of the me of kingship; no Sumerian city could rule without Enlīl's mandate, pronounced at Nippur and recorded in the King List.

cards.name: Storm and Decree
cards.desc: The thunderous voice that pronounces destinies and sends the destructive storm when order is violated; his word admitted no appeal.

symbols.name: Horned crown
symbols.meaning: The multi-horned tiara (agû) of divine rank — the number of horn-pairs marks a god's station, and Enlīl's is the supreme pair of all.

symbols.name: Storm winds
symbols.meaning: The seven winds (im-hul) released at his word — the hurricane that flattens rebels and the breeze that carries every royal proclamation.

symbols.name: Mountain
symbols.meaning: The Ekur at Nippur — his 'Mountain House,' rooted in the netherworld and peaked in heaven, the physical tether of cosmic order.

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: The wild bull whose bellow is thunder: the procreative, irresistible strength of the king of the gods.

symbols.name: Scepter and crook
symbols.meaning: The shepherd's crook and scepter of legitimate rule — the insignia handed to kings at Nippur and returned when a dynasty fell.

mythology.lead: Enlīl's myths are myths of sovereignty and consequence. He gives kingship, but he also sends the flood; he decrees fate, but he must answer to the assembly of the gods. His power is supreme within the Sumerian cosmos, yet it is not arbitrary — it is bound to the custody of order.

myths.title: Enlīl and Ninlil
myths.text: In the Sumerian poem Enlīl and Ninlil (ETCSL 1.2.1), the young god sees the goddess Ninlil bathing in the pure canal of Nippur and desires her. He woos her, she conceives, and the assembly of the gods, scandalized, banishes the lord of the air from his own city. What follows is the strangest courtship in Sumerian literature: in the Underworld Enlīl meets Ninlil in the guise of the gatekeeper, then of the river-man of the netherworld's river, then of the ferryman of the dead — and each time she recognizes him and welcomes him. From these unions are born the three great gods of the world below: Nergal the warlike plague-god, Ninazu the serpent-god, and Enbilulu, lord of the river and canals. The poem closes with Ninlil's proud declaration that her husband's exile has now filled the netherworld with deities of his own line. The myth explains how the lord of heaven came to plant his seed in the Great Below: sovereignty is only complete when it fathers its own counterpart in darkness.

myths.title: Enlīl Sends the Deluge
myths.text: In the Akkadian epic Atrahasis (tablets I–III, Old Babylonian copies from Nippur and later recensions), humankind, created to relieve the gods of toil, multiplies until 'the land bellowed like a bull' and the noise keeps Enlīl from sleeping. Three times he persuades the divine assembly to reduce the population — first plague, then drought, then at last the flood, the weapon released 'like a raging storm' against the cities. Each time Enki quietly undermines the plan from below; only the flood drowns all but Atrahasīs, whom Enki warns through the reed wall of his house. When Enlīl discovers the survivors, his fury gives way to negotiation: humanity will live, but under permanent controls — disease, stillbirth, and the socially infertile classes enumerated in the epic's grim final tablet. The myth is Mesopotamia's great theodicy: mortality is not cruelty but crowd control, and the god who cannot sleep becomes the god who defines the human condition.

lore.culturalLegacy: Enlīl's legacy is the idea of legitimate kingship as a sacred mandate. The doctrine that the ruler derives authority from the chief god of the pantheon influenced Israelite, Persian, and later Christian theories of monarchy. The Ekur at Nippur remained a symbolic center long after political power shifted to Babylon and Assyria. In modern fantasy, Enlīl often appears as the storm-king, the patriarchal sky-father whose breath is the wind. PuniCodex keeps the macron not as a settled fact but as an invitation: every visitor is invited into the philological conversation. The name still means: the authority that fills the air.
lore.archaeology: The Ekur sanctuary at Nippur — excavated by the University of Pennsylvania (1889–1900) and later Iraqi teams — remains the central archaeological witness to Enlīl's cult. Its mud-brick ziggurat, temple platform, and surrounding tablet houses yielded thousands of Sumerian hymns, royal inscriptions, and school texts invoking Enlīl as king of the gods; the Pennsylvania expedition shipped some thirty thousand tablets from the scribal quarter alone. Votive statuettes and foundation figurines from the site name him as grantor of kingship to Ur-Nammu, Shulgi, and later rulers, while Old Babylonian copies of Enlīl and Ninlil and the Anzu epic found at Nippur fix his mythology in datable manuscripts.
lore.syncretism: The Unicode form Enlīl is a reconstruction node: standard Assyriology writes Enlil, while the macron makes visible the open question of vowel length. The Akkadians called him Ellil and continued to venerate him as king of the gods well into the first millennium BCE. The Assyrians identified their national god Aššur with Enlīl, so that the king of Assyria ruled by Enlīl-Aššur's mandate. In Hittite and Hurrian sources, Enlīl's functions were distributed among Taru, Kumarbi, and Teššub. Later Greek and Roman writers had no direct equivalent: Zeus/Jupiter overlaps in sovereignty, but Enlīl's specific association with wind, air, and the mountain temple has no precise Mediterranean counterpart.

entries.meaning: Reconstruction node for the Akkadian deity Ea (Sumerian Enki): the macron marks a discussable vowel length, not a canonical spelling.

variants.note: Standard Assyriological transliteration

etymology.derivation: Standard Assyriology transliterates the god as Ea (𒀭𒂍𒀀). The Sumerian counterpart is Enki (EN.KI), 'lord of the earth.' The length of the first vowel in Akkadian Ea is an open phonological question; the macron on Ēa is a pedagogical mark that makes that question visible, not a claim of canonical spelling.

steps: The name is written 𒀭𒂍𒀀 in cuneiform.
Sumerian logograms may be read with Akkadian values; the divine determinative 𒀭 marks theonyms.
Macrons in the Unicode restoration mark long vowels inferred from Akkadian and Sumerian convention.
The Unicode restoration Ēa is registrable in .com; the cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

provenanceSources.title: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia
Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (ETCSL)

pronunciation.approximation: 'EH-ah' — two level syllables, with the first vowel held slightly longer to signal the open question of length.
pronunciation.note: Ēa is Tier 1: the macron is a diacritic the ASCII form loses. It is a pedagogical mark: a visible question that invites discussion about how the name was pronounced in Akkadian. The standard Assyriological spelling is Ea; the Unicode form Ēa belongs to PuniCodex's phonological reconstruction hub.

domains.title: ĒA — The Phonological Reconstruction Hub
domains.subtitle: Abzu, Crafts, Incantations
domains.lead: The name is written 𒀭𒂍𒀀. Standard Assyriology transliterates it as Ea. But in the phonological grammar of Akkadian, the first vowel's length remains an open question — and it is here, in the space between the written sign and the spoken sound, that this temple operates. This node of PuniCodex is dedicated to the phonological reconstruction and didactic grammar of the ancient Near East. We mark vowel length not because it is certain, but because it is discussable. The macron is a question mark made visible.

cards.name: The Abzu
cards.desc: The subterranean freshwater ocean; Enki's temple at Eridu, the E-abzu, was built over it.

cards.name: Wisdom and Counsel
cards.desc: The god who knows the secret plans of the universe and whispers them to the righteous king.

cards.name: The Craftsman
cards.desc: Patron of exorcists, potters, smiths, and scribes; the divine engineer who devises solutions.

cards.name: Magic and Incantation
cards.desc: The ashipu-priest invokes Enki to undo sickness, demons, and the curses of fate.

symbols.name: Goat-fish (suhurmašu)
symbols.meaning: The hybrid sea-goat, Capricorn's ancestor, linking the Abzu with the stars

symbols.name: Flowing water
symbols.meaning: Streams issuing from his shoulders or a vase — life-giving freshwater

symbols.name: Tortoise
symbols.meaning: A creature of the marshy border between water and land, sacred to Enki

symbols.name: Eridu
symbols.meaning: His primordial city, the first city in Sumerian king lists and cosmology

symbols.name: Caduceus-like staff
symbols.meaning: The rod of magic and authority, sometimes twined with serpents

mythology.lead: The myths of Ea / Enki are stories of intelligent intervention — and they are also data. Every text that names him, from the Sumerian Enki and the World Order to the Babylonian Enuma Elish, is evidence for how the name was read, pronounced, and transmitted. This temple treats those texts as a phonological corpus: each occurrence is a clue to the vowels, stress, and syllable weight that cuneiform signs leave underspecified.

myths.title: Enki and Ninhursag
myths.text: In the Sumerian myth Enki and Ninhursag (ETCSL 1.1.1), the land of Dilmun is a paradise without sickness or death but also without water. Enki impregnates Ninhursag, and a line of daughters follows — Ninsar, Ninkurra, and finally the young goddess Uttu — until eight plants sprout from Enki's own seed set in the marsh. When Enki eats the plants, Ninhursag curses him with eight ailments, one for each afflicted part of his body, and withdraws; only later, persuaded to return, does she seat him by her vulva and bear from his wounded limbs eight healing goddesses, among them Ninti, 'the lady of the rib'. The Sumerian pun is famous: ti means both 'rib' and 'life', the oldest known wordplay on the human condition. Eight diseases, eight remedies, one body of the god — sickness and cure issued from the same source, and the myth reads like a medical text in reverse: the pharmacopoeia is the god's own anatomy, and the healer is the one he wronged.

myths.title: Enki Warns the Flood's Survivor
myths.text: In the Atrahasis epic and the Sumerian Eridu Genesis, the gods, worn out by the noise of humankind, decree a flood to destroy their creation, and Enki is bound by the assembly's oath of silence. He breaks it anyway — not face to face, but through the reed wall of the pious king's house, so that technically the warning goes to a wall (Atrahasis, Tablet I; Eridu Genesis, where the deity speaks to Ziusudra in a dream). The king builds his boat, rides out the deluge, and offers sacrifice when the waters fall; and here the gods learn the counter-lesson — without humans there is no one to feed them (Atrahasis III). This is the earliest known flood narrative in world literature, centuries before Noah, and its theology is startling: the god who saves mankind is the one who cheated, and heaven's survival, not just man's, is the argument for mercy. Loyalty, in Enki's ethics, outranks protocol.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ea survives most visibly as a method: the deity who knows secrets and uses them to save rather than destroy. The flood story, transmitted through Atrahasis and the Epic of Gilgamesh, entered the biblical Noah narrative. The goat-fish became the constellation Capricorn. In modern scholarship, Ea has become a test case for how cuneiform signs map onto spoken sound. The macron on Ēa is our contribution to that conversation — a way of marking uncertainty honestly while keeping the question in view. The name still means: the intelligence that moves in deep water.
lore.archaeology: The E-abzu temple of Enki at Eridu, excavated by Iraqi and British teams across the twentieth century, lies at the edge of the ancient marshland. Its sequence of shrines, bitumen-lined platforms, and fish-offering deposits marks one of Mesopotamia's longest continuous cults. Babylonian cylinder seals depict Enki/Ea with water streams or in the goat-fish (suhurmašu) form; temple libraries at Nineveh and Babylon preserve the Adapa myth and incantations invoking his wisdom.
lore.syncretism: Ea is the Akkadian pronunciation and reinterpretation of the Sumerian Enki. The shift from EN.KI to E-a is not only theological; it is phonological — a new language pronouncing an old name with new vowels. Greek writers later identified him with Poseidôn because of his aquatic domain, though Ea's freshwater wisdom is quite unlike Poseidon's saltwater tempests. In Hellenistic and Gnostic currents, Ea/Enki was linked with Oannes, the fish-tailed culture-bringer described by Berossus. His iconography — water flowing from the shoulders — influenced later depictions of river gods. Each syncretism is a data point in the long history of how the name was heard.

etymology.derivation: Man (from Proto-Polynesian *tane)

pronunciation.approximation: 'TAH-neh' — hold the first vowel long, keep the t soft and unaspirated, and pronounce the final e as a clear 'eh.'
pronunciation.note: Tāne is one of the simplest and oldest theonyms in the corpus: a Proto-Polynesian common noun for 'man' or 'male' elevated to divine status. The macron on ā marks the long vowel that distinguishes the name in Māori. Tier 1: the single long vowel is the distinctive prosodic feature preserved in the Unicode restoration.

domains.title: Forests, Birds, First Man
domains.subtitle: Creator, Separator, and Ancestor
domains.lead: Tāne is the forest made conscious, the bird made ancestor, and the man made god. In Māori cosmology he is the child who separated earth and sky, the father of humankind who shaped the first woman from clay, and the lord of every tree and winged thing. He stands at the axis of nature and culture, the one who makes space for life by pushing upward.

cards.name: Separator of Earth and Sky
cards.desc: He pushed Ranginui upward with his legs, creating the space in which the world exists.

cards.name: Lord of Forests and Birds
cards.desc: Tāne-mahuta rules the trees and all creatures that live among them, especially birds.

cards.name: Creator of Humankind
cards.desc: He formed the first woman, Hineahuone, from red clay at Kurawaka and breathed life into her nostrils.

cards.name: Seeker of Knowledge
cards.desc: He climbed through the layered heavens to obtain the three baskets of knowledge for humankind.

symbols.name: Kauri tree
symbols.meaning: The great forest tree most closely identified with Tāne-mahuta, the lord of the forest

symbols.name: Birds and feathers
symbols.meaning: Creatures of the forest canopy and markers of sacred prestige, especially the huia and kiwi

symbols.name: Red clay
symbols.meaning: The substance from which Tāne shaped the first woman, Hineahuone

symbols.name: The three baskets of knowledge
symbols.meaning: The repositories of ritual, memory, and cosmic understanding brought down from the heavens

symbols.name: Tōtara and rātā, the forest's spine
symbols.meaning: The great canopy trees whose trunks stand between earth and sky like his legs still holding them apart

mythology.lead: Tāne's myths are central to Māori cosmogony. He is the active principle of separation, the ancestor of humankind, and the culture hero who brings knowledge from the sky. The narratives are preserved in nineteenth-century written versions of oral tradition.

myths.title: The One Who Pushed the Sky
myths.text: Tāne was born in the darkness between Ranginui and Papatūānuku, and it was he who ended it. His brother Tūmatauenga urged killing their parents; Rongo, Tangaroa, and Haumia-tiketike tried and failed to force them apart. Then Tāne lay on his back between the two great bodies and pressed upward with his legs — and Ranginui rose into the sky, and the space between became the world, and light came in. The recitations linger on the aftermath: Rangi's tears falling as rain, Papa's mist rising to meet him, and the new order's first casualty — the broken embrace. Tāwhirimātea, refusing the separation, made war from the sky; it was Tāne who had to live with what his success cost. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1.) The myth's insight is that creation is violent even when no one is killed: to make room is to amputate an embrace.

myths.title: The Making of Hineahuone
myths.text: Tāne sought a companion and found none among the gods, so he made one from the earth. At Kurawaka — the place where Papatūānuku's female essence was understood to be concentrated — he took the red ochre clay and shaped it into the form of a woman: Hineahuone, 'Earth-formed woman.' Then he pressed his nose to hers in the hongi and breathed his own breath into her nostrils, and she woke, and the first couple stood together in the new world. Their daughter was Hinetītama, the dawn-maiden, and from her the whole human line descends. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology; Best, Māori Religion and Mythology.) The myth makes humanity a collaboration of body and breath — clay from the mother, spirit from the father — and locates the first birth at the earth's most emphatically female place.

lore.culturalLegacy: Tāne is one of the most widely known Māori deities, especially through the famous kauri tree named Tāne Mahuta in Waipoua Forest, a major spiritual site visited by thousands each year. His image appears in carving, painting, dance, and environmental advocacy throughout Aotearoa. The story of the separation of Rangi and Papa is taught in schools as a founding narrative, and Tāne's quest for knowledge informs contemporary discussions of Māori education and intellectual tradition — the whare-wānanga, the Māori university colleges, bear the name of the very schools whose lore his myth charters. He has become an emblem of the living forest in an age of deforestation and climate change: to defend the ngahere, the forest, is to defend his body.
lore.archaeology: As with Papatūānuku, Tāne's primary preservation is oral and environmental rather than monumental — no temple was built to him, because the forest was the temple. The Waipoua kauri forest in Northland contains the tree named Tāne Mahuta, one of the largest and oldest living kauri, a natural shrine; the rātā and tōtara forests of the islands were managed as his body under customary regimes that fused religion and conservation. Māori wharenui, waka taua (war canoes), and carving invoke him through tree and bird imagery — the house itself is his standing form, ridge-beam as spine, posts as limbs. The nineteenth-century records of Grey, Best, White, and Smith remain the principal textual witnesses, taken down while the whare-wānanga schools still taught the full cycle.
lore.syncretism: Tāne's name is one of the oldest in the corpus: Proto-Polynesian *tane, the common word for 'man,' raised to divinity. Eastward it becomes the Hawaiian Kāne, the great creator god of the island pantheon, and the Tahitian Ta'ane, patron of beauty and craftsmanship. The western islands divided the forest-and-craft domains differently — Tonga and Samoa know Tangaloa there, a name the Māori keep separately as Tangaroa, lord of the sea — so in Aotearoa Tāne absorbed portfolios that other Polynesian cultures assigned elsewhere. Contemporary Māori spirituality, environmentalism, and the arts invoke Tāne-mahuta as the living forest and the ancestor of indigenous ecological knowledge; the Māori Marsden tradition reads his separation of the parents as the primordial act by which structure, and therefore meaning, entered the cosmos.

etymology.derivation: Stand, erect (from Proto-Polynesian *tuu)
Trickster hero (from Proto-Polynesian *maaui)
Peace, news (from Proto-Polynesian *longo)

pronunciation.approximation: 'RAW-ngaw' — tap the r lightly, keep both o's short and pure, and sound the ng as in 'singer'. Stress falls on the first syllable.
pronunciation.note: Rongo is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Māori spelling carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter that plain ASCII loses — the capital marks a proper name, not a sound. What the restoration keeps is the god's own Polynesian name, unrespelled and unanglicized.

domains.title: Rongo
domains.subtitle: Agriculture
domains.lead: Rongo is the Māori god of cultivated foods and of peace — the kūmara in the ground, the stored harvest, the quiet field. One of the sons of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, he is the brother who hid from the storm inside the Earth and became, in the people's telling, the very food dug from her bosom. Across Polynesia his name resounds as Hawaiian Lono and Tahitian Ro'o: the god of what is planted.

cards.name: The Kūmara
cards.desc: The sweet potato is his body in Māori telling; the first-fruits rites invoke Rongomatāne before a single tuber is lifted.

cards.name: Peace
cards.desc: His name from Proto-Polynesian *longo, 'news, hearing' — the settled season when tidings travel instead of war-parties.

cards.name: The Hidden Brother
cards.desc: Rongo and Haumia thrust themselves into the Earth to escape Tāwhirimātea's storm; the digging-stick and the karakia bring them back as food.

cards.name: The Polynesian Circuit
cards.desc: One god under many names: Rongo in Aotearoa, Lono in Hawai'i, Ro'o in Tahiti — the oldest shared deity of the Pacific.

symbols.name: Kūmara
symbols.meaning: The sweet potato, staple crop of the Māori; Rongo is the kūmara's guardian, and the garden's tapu is his.

symbols.name: The digging-stick (kō)
symbols.meaning: The tool that finds the hidden god; planting with the kō is a ritual approach to Rongo, not mere labour.

symbols.name: The storage pit (rua kūmara)
symbols.meaning: The earth-store where the harvest sleeps safe through winter — the tangible shape of the peace Rongo guards.

symbols.name: The Makahiki images
symbols.meaning: Hawaiian Lono's woven standards, carried around the islands in the season when war is suspended and games begin.

mythology.lead: Rongo stands at the junction of garden and peace. His cycle — born in darkness between Sky and Earth, hidden from the storm, dug up as food — makes cultivation itself a rescue of hidden gods, and the planted field a treaty renewed every spring.

myths.title: A Son Between Sky and Earth
myths.text: In the Māori creation told by Wiremu Maihi Te Rangikāheke and printed by George Grey, the Sky Father Ranginui and the Earth Mother Papatūānuku lay locked in an embrace, and their children — among them Rongo, Tāne, Tangaroa, Haumia-tiketike, Tāwhirimātea, and Tūmatauenga — lived crushed in darkness between them. Rongo's fiercest brother Tū urged the final solution: kill the parents and have done. The others recoiled at the thought of slaying their own father and mother, and the gentler plan of Tāne prevailed — the parents would be forced apart, not slain. Rongo stood with Tāne's party. Tāne braced his head against the earth and his feet against the sky and thrust, and light came pouring in where darkness had been (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, the legend of the children of Rangi and Papa). In this telling the gods of food are born of suffocation: Rongo's whole mythology begins in a space too tight to live in, and every field he blesses is a little of that darkness opened to the sun.

myths.title: Hidden in the Bosom of the Earth
myths.text: Tāwhirimātea, god of winds, had opposed the separation of his parents, and when it was done he took war to his brothers. Tangaroa fled to the sea; Tāne withdrew into the forests; but Rongo and Haumia-tiketike thrust themselves into the open bosom of their mother the Earth, and there they hid (Grey, Polynesian Mythology). When the storm at last spent itself, it was Tūmatauenga, the one brother who had stood his ground, who turned on the hidden gods: he dug with a sharp stake into the earth and dragged them out — Rongo's kūmara and Haumia's aruhe, the fern-root — and so those foods were given to humankind. The myth is exact about its meaning: agriculture is not a theft from nature but a rescue of hidden gods. The digging-stick wounds the mother gently, and what it brings up is a brother.

lore.culturalLegacy: Rongo's legacy is a foodway. The kūmara — a tropical plant coaxed to fruit in temperate Aotearoa — remains the emblem of Māori horticulture, and the storage pits that held it still pock the volcanic fields around Tāmaki Makaurau. In Hawai'i the Makahiki has been publicly revived since the 1970s, with canoes and schoolchildren carrying Lono's images round the coast as of old. Rongo endures as a given name across Polynesia, and the scholarship built on Grey, Tregear, and Beckwith keeps his cycle — separation, storm, hiding, harvest — the standard account of how the Pacific's peoples explain their bread. Few gods live so quietly and so persistently: in the ground, in the storehouse, in the season of peace.
lore.archaeology: Rongo leaves no temples — Polynesian religion built few — but his archive is underfoot. Thousands of rua kūmara (storage pits), dug into the volcanic soils of the Auckland region and preserved by the geochemistry that protected the crop, survive from the fourteenth century onward and mark the god's territory field by field. In Hawai'i the heiau platforms dedicated to Lono survive along the Kona coast, among them Hikiau Heiau above Kealakekua Bay, beside which Cook's party recorded the Makahiki rites in 1779; its stone terraces still overlook the water. The digging-stick itself, the kō, survives in museum collections — a plain agricultural tool whose every use was once prayer.
lore.syncretism: Rongo is one half of the oldest Polynesian pairing: the agriculture-god beside the sea-god Tangaroa. From Aotearoa to Hawai'i his name barely changes — Māori Rongo, Hawaiian Lono, Tahitian Ro'o, Cook Islands Rongo — a stability that marks him as a first-generation deity carried in the great voyaging canoes (Tregear; Beckwith; Henry, Ancient Tahiti). In Mangaia, strikingly, Rongo is the paramount god of war as well as of the cultivated field — the inversion shows the two faces of the planted life, which must be defended as well as tended. The Hawaiians pressed him furthest: Lono's Makahiki circuit made him a visiting king whose arrival ends warfare, and the eighteenth-century encounter with Cook turned the old theology into world history. Christian missionaries suppressed the cult, but the name survived in whakataukī, in the school calendars of the Hawaiian Renaissance, and in the revived Makahiki itself.

etymology.derivation: God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)

pronunciation.approximation: 'tah-ngah-ROH-ah' — say ng as in 'singer,' tap the r, and let the last two vowels glide together.
pronunciation.note: Tangaroa is the Māori continuation of Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa — the same name the Tahitians lengthen into Ta'aroa the creator and the Tongans keep as Tangaloa. No vowel length distinguishes the Māori form, so the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII spelling loses: Tier 2, a display fact only. The ng is not two letters but one sound, the velar nasal English lacks.

domains.title: Tangaroa
domains.subtitle: Ocean
domains.lead: Tangaroa is the sea given will: lord of ocean, fish, and all that swims, son of the Sky Father and Earth Mother, and the brother who fled to the deep when his parents were torn apart. Every fish is his child, every canoe his guest, and every storm over the water is family business.

cards.name: Lord of Ocean
cards.desc: He took the sea for his domain when his parents were separated, vowing in the recitations never to return to the land.

cards.name: Father of Fishes
cards.desc: With Hine-moana, the ocean woman, he is ancestor of every finned and swimming creature the nets take.

cards.name: The Exiled Brother
cards.desc: Tāwhirimātea's war drove him from the coast; his grandchildren scattered to sea and shore, splitting into fish and lizard.

cards.name: One Name, Many Islands
cards.desc: Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Tangaloa in Tonga and Samoa, Kanaloa in Hawai'i — one ocean god under four island names.

symbols.name: The fish-hook (matau)
symbols.meaning: The carved hook with which his descendants take his children from the sea — every catch a petition, every offering a repayment.

symbols.name: The whale and the shark
symbols.meaning: His largest and most feared children; the whale (tohorā) and the shark (mangō) carry his mana in bulk.

symbols.name: The canoe (waka)
symbols.meaning: The vessel that crosses his domain; canoes were tapu and addressed as kin, because the sea is a relative who must be asked.

symbols.name: The tide
symbols.meaning: Tangaroa-whakamau-tai, 'Tangaroa who fixes the tides' — one of his names, and the rhythm by which fishermen read him.

symbols.name: The lizard (ngarara)
symbols.meaning: His grandchildren who hid ashore: the lizards, fish that chose the land — kin, yet forever on the wrong side of the beach.

mythology.lead: Tangaroa's stories are the Māori ocean chapter of the great separation cycle — and then the cycle widens: the same name, in other dialects, becomes the supreme creator of the whole Polynesian triangle. The Māori knew what the comparison would later prove.

myths.title: Born Between the Embrace
myths.text: Tangaroa was born into the darkness that lay between Ranginui, the Sky, and Papatūānuku, the Earth, whose embrace left no room and no light for their children. With his brothers Tāne, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo, and Haumia-tiketike he grew to manhood in that cramped twilight, and with them he debated how to escape: Tūmatauenga counseled killing the parents outright, Tāne proposed forcing them apart. When Tāne at last pushed Ranginui into the sky and light flooded the world, Tangaroa looked at the dry land his brother had won and chose the other half of creation: he went down into the ocean, and took it for his own. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1; Smith, The Lore of the Whare-wānanga.) The myth reads the coastline as a family wound: the sea is not the land's opposite but its brother, still angry.

myths.title: The Children Who Split in Two
myths.text: Not all the brothers accepted the separation. Tāwhirimātea, the wind, remained with his father in the sky and made war on the others, and Tangaroa's domain was his first battlefield: the sea boiled under the storm. In the rout, Tangaroa's grandchildren — the children of his son Punga — split forever. Ikatere, father of the fish, fled into the deep and cried 'swim, my children'; Tū-te-wehiwehi, father of the reptiles, scrambled ashore into Tāne's forests and cried 'hide, my children.' Hence the hostility the myth sees everywhere along the tideline: fish devour the lizards cast into the sea, and the sea never forgives the land. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1.) What looks like natural enmity is re-read as a family separated under fire — every fish a refugee, every lizard a deserter's child.

lore.culturalLegacy: Tangaroa remains the most-seen of the Māori gods — in every coastal marae's imagery, in the school-taught separation cycle, and in the everyday word moana for the sea. Fishermen still speak of him half-jokingly and not entirely jokingly; the Māori fisheries claim and its settlement wrote his descendants' relationship with the sea into law. In Hawai'i, where his form is Kanaloa, the modern voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sails by the same star-compass the old navigators read — the sea-god's ancient craft, relaunched. Across the Pacific the name survives in hundreds of personal names, in ships, in the naming of research vessels, and in the quiet conviction of island peoples that the ocean is not empty water but occupied country.
lore.archaeology: No temple of Tangaroa survives, and Māori religion built none — but his archaeology is the archaeology of the sea. Coastal middens record the fisheries his priests regulated; the bone and shell of his children, stacked in heaps over centuries, are the oldest testimony to the relationship. Fish-hooks (matau) of bone, stone, and shell, many of superb workmanship, turn up wherever Māori camped on a coast; the great shank-hooks for snapper are functional sculpture. Rock shelters in the South Island preserve fish imagery read as ancestral. The canoe itself — the waka of the great voyages, surviving in fragments, adzes, and drilled hull-plugs — is his true monument: a technology of family visits.
lore.syncretism: Tangaroa's syncretic career runs in two directions. Westward, in Tonga and Samoa, his name — Tangaloa — remained the supreme creator's, and Samoan Christians long prayed to a God they still sometimes called Tangaloa, a continuity the missionaries alternately welcomed and fought. Eastward, the Māori had already demoted him: from creator of the cosmos to lord of one domain, a brother among brothers, because the separation cycle re-hierarchized the gods around the family drama. In modern Aotearoa the name rides the cultural renaissance: Tangaroa appears in carving, kapa haka, and marine policy as the person of the moana, the sea that feeds and must be fed. The Treaty of Waitangi fisheries settlements of the 1980s and 90s, and the doctrine of kaitiakitanga over the marine estate, gave him a legal afterlife: his name is now cited wherever the sea is spoken of as an ancestor rather than a commodity.

entries.meaning: One who shapes the sacred land (Hawaiian)

pronunciation.approximation: 'PEH-leh' — two light syllables, each vowel pure, stress on the first; no glide, no diphthong.
pronunciation.note: Hawaiian Pele carries no ʻokina or kahakō, and the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses: Tier 2, a display fact only. The tradition's fuller style is Pelehonuamea, 'Pele of the sacred land'; 'Pele' alone is how the chants and the volcano address her.

domains.title: Pele
domains.subtitle: Volcanoes
domains.lead: Pele is the volcano as a person: goddess of fire, lava, and lightning, patron of the hula through her sister Hi'iaka, and the most feared and loved deity of Hawai'i. She sailed from Kahiki in search of a home, dug her crater with a digging stick, and still receives offerings at Kīlauea today.

cards.name: The Digger of Craters
cards.desc: With her digging stick Pā'oa she sank pits across the islands, seeking a fire-pit no water could kill; at Kīlauea she found it.

cards.name: Mistress of Kīlauea
cards.desc: Halema'uma'u, the crater-within-the-crater, is her house; its lava lake is her body and her mood.

cards.name: The Wrathful Sister
cards.desc: Her feud with Nāmakaokaha'i filled the sea with steam; her jealousy burned Lohi'au and turned her sister's friend Hopoe to stone.

cards.name: Patron of the Hula
cards.desc: Through her youngest sister Hi'iaka she claims the dance: the pahu drum and the ʻōlapa chant are her family's voice.

symbols.name: The digging stick Pā'oa
symbols.meaning: The sacred staff with which she sank her fire-pits island by island; her house Halema'uma'u, 'house of the ʻāma'u fern,' stands where it last struck.

symbols.name: The ʻōhiʻa lehua blossom
symbols.meaning: The red flower of the volcano forest — in the famous legend born from Lehua, the lover Pele turned into a tree; to pick it carelessly is to call her rain.

symbols.name: Halema'uma'u crater
symbols.meaning: Her house within Kīlauea; the rising and falling of its lava lake is read as her presence arriving or withdrawing.

symbols.name: Lava (Pelehonuamea)
symbols.meaning: Her full name means 'Pele of the sacred land': the flow that destroys is the same substance that builds new earth.

symbols.name: The pahu hula drum
symbols.meaning: The temple drum of the hula, claimed for her family through Hi'iaka — dance and volcano as sisters in rhythm.

mythology.lead: Pele's mythology is a migration epic, a love tragedy, and a fire-against-water duel at once — preserved in the great nineteenth-century tale-cycles of Hawai'i and still performed in chant and hula today.

myths.title: The Canoe from Kahiki
myths.text: Pele came to Hawai'i from Kahiki — the ancestral homeland the Hawaiians left in the deep past — voyaging in a canoe with her brothers and sisters. Behind her she left a feud: her sister Nāmakaokaha'i, a sea goddess, held Pele to account for a seduction in the old country, and the ocean pursued the canoe across the archipelago. At island after island Nāmaka caught up, and Pele's fires were quenched in steam; in the long versions the sea caught her at last and tore her apart, and only her bones, gathered by her brothers, were carried on to be made alive again. (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes.) The migration myth makes the goddess an exile: Hawai'i is not where Pele was born but where she finally outran the sea.

myths.title: The Digging Stick Pā'oa
myths.text: From island to island Pele dug with her sacred digging stick Pā'oa, sinking deep pits in search of a fire-pit the sea's creatures could not kill. Kaua'i, O'ahu, the channels of Maui — at each, the water found her out and drove her on, the steam of her drowning fires rising as the islands' mists. At last, on the great island of Hawai'i, she sank her pit into the flank of Kīlauea, and the sea could not reach it. There she built her house, Halema'uma'u — 'house of the ʻāma'u fern' — and there she has lived ever since, adding land to the island at every eruption. (Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology.) The myth reads the archipelago's volcanology as a house-hunt: every crater on the chain is a rejected rental, and Hawai'i the only one whose landlord is deeper than the ocean.

lore.culturalLegacy: Pele is the most visible Hawaiian deity in the modern world: her name brands everything from hot sauces to football teams, while the real goddess receives offerings at her crater in every season. The Merrie Monarch hula festival and a hundred hālau keep her family in the dance; the published epics of Hi'iaka keep the migration cycle in print. During the 2018 Kīlauea eruption, which destroyed some seven hundred homes, residents framed the event in her terms: the land is hers, and the land taking itself back is not disaster but the goddess working. The ʻōhi'a forests she burns and blesses are defended against an alien wilt fungus partly because they are her forests. No figure in Polynesia so fully owns her element, and none has so successfully refused to become folklore.
lore.archaeology: Pele's archaeology is volcanic and ongoing. The Kīlauea caldera preserves shrine features and offering deposits on its rims; the 1790 ash layers — footprints hardened in the fallout of an eruption that caught a war party of Keōua on the caldera floor — are among the most haunting archaeological traces in Polynesia (Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park). Museum collections hold her family's images: the Bishop Museum and the British Museum keep carved wooden ki'i of Pele, Hi'iaka, and the pig-god Kamapua'a collected in the nineteenth century. Mauna Loa's 1881 flow, which stopped short of Hilo after public offerings were made to her, is the goddess's most famous 'documented' intervention. The lava itself is the archive: every flow is dated, and the chants date with it.
lore.syncretism: Protestant missions spent a century casting Pele as a demon, and nineteenth-century law punished her worship; yet she survived better than almost any Polynesian deity, because her cult needed no temple — only the crater. In the twentieth century she re-emerged as the central figure of the Hawaiian renaissance: the battles over geothermal drilling inside Kīlauea in the 1970s and 80s were fought explicitly in her name, with kūpuna chanting at the wellheads. Modern folklore — much of it twentieth-century in origin, popularized by rangers and hoteliers rather than recorded from traditional sources — warns that removing her lava rock brings misfortune, a 'curse' that has nonetheless genuinely reduced souvenir-taking. Hula hālau open major performances with chants to her family; and where Hawaiians once propitiated her, many now simply keep her company, leaving flowers, gin, and food at the rim of Halema'uma'u — a living cult older than any church in the islands.

etymology.derivation: From Japanese 大阪 "large hill"; ancient commercial capital.

Each kanji carries both a semantic meaning and Sino-Japanese (on'yomi) and native Japanese (kun'yomi) readings.
Hepburn romanisation with macron marks long vowels, which the ASCII form loses.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OH-sah-kah' — the first vowel is long; the following syllables are short and level in pitch.
pronunciation.note: Ōsaka is Tier 1 because the Hepburn restoration preserves the long initial vowel ō. As with other Japanese entries, the macron records length rather than pitch accent, which is not registrable at the DNS root.

domains.title: The Nation's Kitchen
domains.subtitle: Merchant Capital · Port of Naniwa · Castle Town
domains.lead: Ōsaka began as the ancient port of Naniwa, briefly an imperial capital, and grew into the merchant city par excellence of early modern Japan. Where Kyōto was aristocratic and Edo samurai, Ōsaka was the place where money, rice, and popular culture flowed together.

cards.name: Ōsaka Castle
cards.desc: Hideyoshi's fortress rose on the ruins of the Ishiyama Hongan-ji and became the symbol of Toyotomi ambition.

cards.name: Port of Naniwa
cards.desc: The ancient harbour received envoys, Buddhism, and trade from Korea and China before the city was called Ōsaka.

cards.name: Bunraku and Kabuki
cards.desc: Merchant patronage made Ōsaka a cradle of popular theatre, especially the puppet art of bunraku.

cards.name: Merchant Culture
cards.desc: The Dōjima rice exchange and canal-side warehouses turned Ōsaka into Japan's financial and distribution hub.

symbols.name: Castle tower
symbols.meaning: The reconstructed donjon of Ōsaka Castle, icon of the city's warrior and merchant history

symbols.name: Bunraku puppet
symbols.meaning: The articulated puppet of the National Bunraku Theatre, symbol of Ōsaka's popular arts

symbols.name: Merchant's scale
symbols.meaning: The balance of the Dōjima rice exchange, where futures trading first took shape in Japan

symbols.name: Glico running man
symbols.meaning: The neon athlete glowing above Dōtonbori since 1935 — Ōsaka's most photographed sign and emblem of its merchant showmanship

symbols.name: Kuidaore Taro
symbols.meaning: The clown drummer of Dōtonbori in his striped costume, mascot of the eat-yourself-bankrupt creed

mythology.lead: Ōsaka began as the ancient port of Naniwa, gateway to the Asian continent and briefly an imperial capital. It later became the merchant city par excellence — the 'kitchen of the nation' — and the fortress from which Toyotomi Hideyoshi sought to rule a unified Japan. Its 'myths' are historical episodes, told here with the same reverence as legend.

myths.title: Naniwa, the First Imperial Port
myths.text: Long before it was called Ōsaka, the delta at the mouth of the Yodo River was Naniwa — 難波, 'the rapids'. The Man'yōshū ('Collection of Ten Thousand Leaves', c. 759) preserves the city's oldest surviving poem: 'At Naniwa's ford these flowers bloomed, winter-bound, and now, with spring come, they bloom' (Man'yōshū 1.52), a courtly welcome staged at the port where envoys from Korea and China stepped ashore. South of the port the earth itself keeps royal memory: the Daisenryō Kofun of the Mozu cluster, traditionally attributed to Emperor Nintoku (r. early fifth century), is the largest tomb on earth, a keyhole-shaped island of forest nearly five hundred metres long. In 645 Emperor Kōtoku made Naniwa Nagara Toyosaki his capital — Japan's first planned imperial city — and Empress Saimei rebuilt the Naniwa palace in the 650s (Nihon Shoki). Ōsaka thus begins not as a town but as a doorway: everything continental — writing, Buddhism, metallurgy, ceramics — passed this threshold before it became Japanese.

myths.title: Shitennō-ji and Prince Shōtoku
myths.text: In 593, tradition says, Prince Shōtoku founded Shitennō-ji, 'Temple of the Four Heavenly Kings', on Naniwa's ground, making Ōsaka one of the first places in Japan where Buddhism put down institutional roots. The temple was a political theology built in wood: the Four Kings were guardians of the state, and their temple announced that the new faith would defend the realm — a diplomatic as much as a devotional statement, aimed at the continental powers whose models Japan was adopting. Tradition credits Shōtoku's foundation with works of mercy alongside worship — relief for the poor, care for the sick, a pharmacy — so that the temple doubled as Japan's first public infrastructure. Shitennō-ji's five-storey pagoda still rises over the ward that bears its name. The episode fixes a pattern the city never lost: in Ōsaka, religion arrives as logistics — imported, organised, and immediately put to work at the waterfront.

lore.culturalLegacy:
Ōsaka is the city that taught Japan to laugh, eat, and trade.

Its merchant culture produced bunraku, manzai comedy, and the regional cuisine celebrated in takoyaki, okonomiyaki, and kushi-katsu. The Dōjima rice exchange pioneered futures markets, and the city's canals and warehouses shaped the physical landscape of Kansai. Today Ōsaka is a global business hub, the gateway to the Kansai region, and a rival to Tōkyō in sports, food, and popular culture. It represents the Japan of merchants and migrants as much as the Japan of emperors and samurai.
lore.archaeology: Naniwa Palace Ruins Park preserves the Daigokuden audience hall, warehouse complexes, and wharf remains of Emperor Kōtoku's capital. The Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group, including the Daisenryō Kofun attributed to Emperor Nintoku, dominates the southern plain. Excavated Toyotomi stone walls, granite ramparts, and the reconstructed donjon of Ōsaka Castle document the city's transformation from port to mortuary landscape to fortress.
lore.syncretism:
Ōsaka's identity was forged by mixing sacred and commercial cultures.

Prince Shōtoku's Shitennō-ji made it one of Japan's earliest Buddhist centres, while the port received continental technologies, Chinese learning, and Korean crafts. In the Edo period the city became a meeting ground for samurai, merchants, and entertainers; its comedy, food, and theatre borrowed from Kyōto, Edo, and the immigrant communities of Nankinmachi. Modern Ōsaka remains Japan's most openly mercantile major city, proud of its dialect, its food, and its history of making deals across boundaries.

etymology.derivation: From Japanese 京都 "capital city"; the imperial capital for over 1,000 years.

steps: The name is written with the kanji 京都.
Each kanji carries both a semantic meaning and Sino-Japanese (on'yomi) and native Japanese (kun'yomi) readings.
Hepburn romanisation with macron marks long vowels, which the ASCII form loses.
The Unicode restoration Kyōto is used for DNS because the kanji form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KYOH-toh' — the first syllable is long and lightly pitched; the second is short and unstressed.
pronunciation.note: Kyōto is Tier 1 because the Hepburn restoration preserves the long vowel ō. Japanese pitch falls on the first mora, but the registrable form marks length rather than pitch, following the project's convention for Japanese entries.

domains.title: The Thousand-Year Capital
domains.subtitle: Imperial Centre · Buddhist-Shinto Synthesis · Aristocratic Culture
domains.lead: Kyōto was Japan's imperial capital from 794 to 1868, a city laid out on a Chinese grid and guarded by shrines at its four directions. It became the stage on which emperors, aristocrats, monks, and shoguns performed the art of traditional Japan.

cards.name: Heian Grid
cards.desc: Kammu's capital was modelled on Tang Chang'an, with north-south avenues defining a geomantically ordered city.

cards.name: Temple and Shrine
cards.desc: Kiyomizu-dera, Kinkaku-ji, Shimogamo, and Kamigamo anchor more than a millennium of Buddhist and Shinto culture.

cards.name: Tea and Court Culture
cards.desc: The Way of Tea, Noh theatre, and ikebana were refined here after political power moved to the samurai east.

cards.name: City of Craft
cards.desc: Nishijin textiles, Kiyomizu pottery, and yuzen dyeing turned Kyōto into a living museum of Japanese artisanship.

symbols.name: Torii
symbols.meaning: The red gate of Fushimi Inari and the Kamo shrines, marking the city's sacred boundaries

symbols.name: Five-story pagoda
symbols.meaning: The Buddhist tower visible above the city, a reminder of Kyōto's monastic wealth and patronage

symbols.name: Chrysanthemum
symbols.meaning: The imperial crest, linking the city to the Japanese throne even after the court moved to Tōkyō

symbols.name: The Kamo River
symbols.meaning: The eastern water-boundary of the geomantic plan, where the Kamo shrines' purification rites still mark the city's northern edge each May

mythology.lead: Kyōto was Japan's imperial capital for more than a thousand years, a city planned according to Chinese geomancy, guarded by shrines at its four directions, and later celebrated as the soul of traditional Japan. Its history is not merely administrative; it is a story of deliberate cosmic placement, aristocratic culture, and survival through war and modernization.

myths.title: Heian-kyō, the Capital of Peace
myths.text: In 794 CE Emperor Kammu moved the court from Nagaoka-kyō to a new site modelled on the Tang-dynasty capital Chang'an, as the Shoku Nihongi (797) records. He named it Heian-kyō, 'Capital of Peace and Tranquillity' — the city we now call Kyōto. The location was chosen with feng-shui geomancy in mind: mountains to the north, east, and west, the Kamo River to the east, and a grid of avenues designed to mirror cosmic order. The great central boulevard aligned the palace with the city's southern gate, so that the emperor sat at the axis of heaven and earth. The founding act was cosmological before it was administrative: the capital was laid out so that the realm would possess a fixed, centered point around which the seasons of rule could turn. That Chinese-inspired grid remains the skeleton of the modern city, a plan older than any building on it.

myths.title: Guardians of the Four Directions
myths.text: Kammu enlisted two local clans, the Hata and the Kamo, and established protective shrines at key geomantic points to shield the new capital from malign influences. Matsunoo Taisha and Fushimi Inari guarded the west and south-east, while the Kamo shrines — Shimogamo and Kamigamo — stood to the north; the tenth-century Engishiki lists them among the highest ranks of the realm's shrines. These sanctuaries still anchor Kyōto's sacred geography and are among the seventeen UNESCO World Heritage sites that define the city's historic landscape. The choice set the pattern for a thousand years: the capital's safety was negotiated with the local gods as partners and protectors, not conquered subjects, and the Hata and Kamo lineages who kept the shrines kept a share of the city's soul — and its politics — for centuries.

lore.culturalLegacy:
Kyōto is the city modern Japan uses to remember itself.

With seventeen UNESCO World Heritage sites, thousands of temples and shrines, and living traditions such as geiko districts, tea ceremony, and Noh, Kyōto is the material archive of pre-modern Japanese civilization. It survived the Ōnin War, the Meiji Restoration, and the Second World War to become the cultural capital of the nation. For visitors and Japanese alike, Kyōto represents the aesthetic and spiritual values that industrial modernity threatened but did not erase.
lore.archaeology: The Heian-kyō grid survives in Karasuma Street postholes and palace foundations excavated by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute. The Daigokuden audience hall of the former imperial palace has been reconstructed on its archaeological footprint, while Kiyomizu-dera's wooden stage, Kinkaku-ji's golden pavilion, and the Kamo shrines' Tadasu no Mori forest anchor more than a millennium of imperial, Buddhist, and Shinto material culture.
lore.syncretism:
Kyōto is a palimpsest of Chinese, Buddhist, Shinto, and aristocratic layers.

The city's grid and geomancy came from Tang China; its shrines were staffed by local clans who wove kami worship into an imperial frame. Buddhism arrived from Korea and China, and by the Heian period esoteric schools such as Tendai and Shingon shaped both court ritual and mountain practice. The later fusion of Zen, tea, and warrior taste produced a culture that exported itself back to China and on to the West. Modern Kyōto markets this synthesis as 'traditional Japan', even as the city remains a centre of research, sake brewing, and manga production.

domains.title: Port of the God-Door
domains.subtitle: Shrine Estate · Maritime Threshold · Global Crossroads
domains.lead: Kōbe stands where the Rokkō mountains meet the Inland Sea, a city whose name remembers the families who served the Ikuta Shrine and whose history has turned on thresholds: between shrine estate and port, between seclusion and openness, between destruction and recovery.

cards.name: Ikuta Shrine
cards.desc: The ancient Shinto shrine whose kanbe families lent their title to the city; its forest is Kōbe's mythic origin point.

cards.name: Maritime Gateway
cards.desc: Owada-no-tomari and the medieval port made Kōbe the arrival point for continental envoys, Buddhism, and trade.

cards.name: Foreign Settlement
cards.desc: The 1868 opening of the port brought Western merchants to Kitano-ijinkan-gai, creating Japan's most cosmopolitan hillside.

cards.name: Resilience
cards.desc: The 1995 Great Hanshin Earthquake levelled districts and broke the port, yet Kōbe rebuilt as a model of urban recovery.

symbols.name: Torii
symbols.meaning: The sacred gate of Ikuta Shrine, marking the threshold from the everyday world to the divine

symbols.name: Ship
symbols.meaning: The vessel that turned a small shrine bay into a gateway for continental culture and modern global trade

symbols.name: Western-style house
symbols.meaning: The ijinkan mansions of Kitano, concrete reminders of the port's opening to the world in 1868

symbols.name: The Rokkō wall
symbols.meaning: The steep mountain range sheltering the harbour — protection and, as an active fault scarp, the source of the city's deepest trauma

symbols.name: The anchor
symbols.meaning: The working port — from Owada anchorage to one of the world's great container harbours, the weight that holds a threshold city in place

mythology.lead: Kōbe has no myth in the divine sense — its lore is the documentary record of a port that became a threshold: a shrine estate whose serving families gave the city its name, a medieval harbour where a warlord briefly planted a capital, and a modern port-city rebuilt from earthquake ruins.

myths.title: The Shrine at the God-Door
myths.text: The foundation tradition recorded in the Nihon Shoki makes Empress Jingū the foundress of Ikuta Shrine in AD 201, on her return from the Korean campaign; the shrine enshrines Wakahirume, the heavenly weaving maiden. Its sacred grove, Ikuta-no-mori, stood at the only flat ground between the Rokkō mountains and the sea, and for sailors crossing the Inland Sea it was the landmark of shelter. The families hereditarily charged with the shrine's upkeep bore the title kanbe — written 神戸, 'god' plus 'door' or 'household' — and it was their title, not a ruler's, a battle, or a river, that became the city's name. The mythless fact is the striking one: a city named for its caretakers, a threshold that took the name of the people who kept it. Even now the shrine's spring rice-planting festival replays that founding, the caretakers' service renewed as civic ceremony.

myths.title: Owada Anchorage and the Capital That Failed
myths.text: By the Heian period the harbour below Ikuta appears in court records as Owada-no-tomari, the anchorage where ships bound between the capital and western Japan rode out the weather; it grew rich on Inland Sea tolls and, under the Taira, on trade with Song China. In 1180 Taira no Kiyomori — now the realm's chief minister — moved the imperial capital itself to his own estate at Fukuhara, in modern Kōbe, hoping to hold court and commerce in one hand (Heike monogatari; Azuma Kagami). The courtiers loathed the damp exile, the experiment collapsed within months, and the court returned to Kyōto amid the opening campaigns of the Genpei War. Yet Fukuhara's failure was diagnostic: everyone who tried to rule or trade there learned what Kōbe's bay offered — deep shelter one day's sail from the capital.

lore.culturalLegacy:
Kōbe is the city Japan built to face outward.

It was one of the first ports to reopen to the world in the modern era, and it remains a symbol of cosmopolitan openness and disaster resilience. The Great Hanshin Earthquake recovery became a global textbook for urban reconstruction. Kōbe beef, Arima Onsen, and the Kitano ijinkan attract visitors, while the port keeps the city economically tied to East Asia. In Japanese popular memory, Kōbe represents both the rewards and the risks of living on a fault line, literal and historical.
lore.archaeology: Ikuta Shrine's cultic deposits anchor the city's 'god-door' toponym, while Sakuragaoka's Yayoi bronze bells and the Goshikizuka kofun attest early elite authority around the harbour. Medieval Kyōgashima anchorages and the Kitano foreign-settlement excavations trace Kōbe's evolution from shrine estate to maritime threshold. The 1995 earthquake recovery layers document modern urban reconstruction directly above earlier port installations.
lore.syncretism:
Kōbe has always been a place where worlds overlap.

Shinto and Buddhism shared the city's sacred landscape for centuries, with Ikuta Shrine and nearby Buddhist temples serving overlapping communities. After 1868, Western Christianity, Islam, Judaism, and Freemasonry established visible presences alongside native traditions. The result is a layered city: a Shinto shrine stands a short walk from a mosque, a synagogue, and a former foreign consulate. Kōbe's culinary fame — Kōbe beef, sake from Nada, Chinese food in Nankinmachi — is itself a product of this long encounter.

steps: 日光 is a Sino-Japanese compound: 日 'sun' + 光 'light', hence 'sunlight'.
The standard Hepburn romanisation is Nikkō, with a macron over the final o marking a long vowel.
The geminate consonant -kk- reflects the sequential voicing assimilation of 日 (nichi) + 光 (kō) → Nikkō.
The place name Nikkō is famous for the Tōshō-gū shrine, dedicated to Tokugawa Ieyasu.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NEE-koh' — the first syllable is quick with a soft 'ny' color; hold the final 'koh' long, as if pronouncing two k's in a row.
pronunciation.note: Nikkō is Tier 1 because the final ō is long. In Japanese, the double k (kk) is a geminate consonant that creates a brief pause before the long vowel. The name refers both to the town in Tochigi Prefecture and to the sacred mountain complex that made it famous.

domains.title: Sacred Sunlight
domains.subtitle: Mountain Shrine, Tokugawa Memorial, and Living Heritage
domains.lead:
Nikkō is the town, the mountain, and the luminous name that binds them. In Japanese, the word means simply 'sunlight,' but by the 17th century it had become synonymous with one of Japan's most spectacular religious sites: the Tōshōgū shrine complex, where Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, was enshrined as the deified Tōshō Daigongen, 'Great Illuminating Deity of the East.'

Nikkō is where nature and politics meet in gold. Cedar avenues, waterfalls, and mountain mists frame shrines and mausoleums built with the wealth and craftsmanship of a newly unified Japan. It is a place of sunlight filtered through forest, of ancestral power made beautiful, and of Shinto-Buddhist synthesis at its most ornate.

cards.name: Tōshōgū
cards.desc: The lavish shrine-tomb of Tokugawa Ieyasu, a UNESCO World Heritage site and masterpiece of early Edo art.

cards.name: Three Wise Monkeys
cards.desc: The famous 'see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil' carving on the sacred stable.

cards.name: Cedar Avenue
cards.desc: Thousands of giant cryptomeria trees line the approach, turning the path itself into a sacred corridor.

cards.name: Sacred Bridge
cards.desc: The Shinkyō, a vermillion lacquered bridge over the Daiya River, marks the boundary between worlds.

symbols.name: Shinkyō (Sacred Bridge)
symbols.meaning: The vermillion bridge that marks the entrance to the sacred precinct and the crossing from mundane to holy space

symbols.name: Three wise monkeys (sanzaru)
symbols.meaning: The carved monkeys embodying the proverb 'see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil'

symbols.name: Sleeping cat (nemuri-neko)
symbols.meaning: The famous carved cat attributed to Hidari Jingorō, guarding Ieyasu's mausoleum

symbols.name: Yōmeimon Gate
symbols.meaning: The 'Gate of Sunlight' (yōmei, 陽明), lavishly carved and gilded, symbolizing the wealth of the shogunate and the light of the east that names the shrine.

symbols.name: Cedar trees (sugi)
symbols.meaning: The ancient avenue of cryptomeria linking the town to the shrines, a living sacred architecture

mythology.lead: Nikkō's mythology is both ancient and recent. The mountain had long been a site of Buddhist-Shinto practice, but its modern identity was forged by the apotheosis of Tokugawa Ieyasu and the extraordinary building campaign that followed his death.

myths.title: Shōdō Shōnin and the Sacred Bridge
myths.text: According to tradition, the Buddhist monk Shōdō Shōnin founded the first temple at Nikkō in the 8th century. When he could not cross the turbulent Daiya River, the mountain deity appeared in a dream and offered two serpents to form a bridge. The Shinkyō, the vermillion lacquered bridge at the entrance to the shrine complex, commemorates this divine assistance and marks the boundary between the secular world and the sacred mountain.

myths.title: The Deification of Tokugawa Ieyasu
myths.text: After his death in 1616, Tokugawa Ieyasu was enshrined at Nikkō as Tōshō Daigongen, a manifestation of the Buddhist divinity Yakushi Nyorai and the Shinto sun goddess Amaterasu. His grandson Iemitsu rebuilt the complex between 1634 and 1636 with staggering opulence, employing thousands of craftsmen. The result was both a mausoleum and a political statement: the shogun's power now rested in a sacred mountain bathed in sunlight.

lore.culturalLegacy: Nikkō is one of Japan's most visited sacred sites and a UNESCO World Heritage property. Its autumn maples, snow-covered gates, and the famous proverb Nikkō wo mizu shite kekkō to iu nakare (日光を見ずして結構と言うなかれ — 'don't say «splendid» until you've seen Nikkō') continue to shape Japanese aesthetics. The Three Wise Monkeys have become a global visual proverb, and images of the Shinkyō and Yōmeimon appear in travel literature, photography, and advertising worldwide. For Japanese nationalism, Nikkō is a symbol of the Tokugawa peace and imperial continuity; for contemporary visitors, it is a place where nature, art, and history converge. The Unicode restoration Nikkō preserves the long vowel and geminate consonant that distinguish the place name from ordinary nikkō ('sunlight').
lore.archaeology: The Tōshōgū complex as it exists today is primarily an Edo-period creation (1634–1636), though it rests on older religious layers. The main hall, Yōmeimon gate, five-storied pagoda, and Okumiya inner shrine are outstanding examples of early Edo architecture and polychrome decoration. The Shinkyō bridge, rebuilt in 1904, preserves the form of the original sacred crossing. Archaeological and architectural study of the site has documented the materials, craftsmen, and techniques employed in Iemitsu's rebuilding, while the surrounding cedar avenue (planted in the 17th century) remains one of Japan's most impressive designed landscapes.
lore.syncretism: Nikkō is a textbook case of shinbutsu shūgō, the medieval Japanese synthesis of Shinto and Buddhism. Tōshō Daigongen was simultaneously a Shinto kami and a Buddhist avatar; the shrine's architecture borrows from both traditions. This synthesis was forcibly dismantled in the Meiji period but survives in the layered art and ritual of the site. Nikkō also sits within a broader East Asian culture of mountain sacredness, where peaks serve as boundaries between worlds and repositories of ancestral power. The cedar avenues and vermillion bridges echo Chinese and Korean models, while the specific cult of Ieyasu is uniquely Japanese.

pronunciation.approximation: hok-KAI-doh, with the long final ō.
pronunciation.note: Hokkaidō 北海道 — "North Sea Road" — carries a long final ō, the doubled vowel the macron preserves. The name dates only from 1869, when the explorer Matsuura Takeshirō proposed it for the island the Ainu long called Ainu Mosir, "the quiet land of humans." The long ō of dō is a doubled vowel in kana (どう); the macron is the romanization of that extra beat.

domains.title: The North Sea Road
domains.subtitle: Ainu Mosir, the Frontier, and the Snow Country
domains.lead: Hokkaidō is Japan's youngest name on its oldest ground: an island inhabited for twenty thousand years, homeland of the Ainu, mapped into the Japanese state only in 1869 — a frontier whose ancient name, Ainu Mosir, still names the deeper country beneath the modern one.

cards.name: The Snow Country
cards.desc: Drift ice, powder snow, and the Sapporo Snow Festival — the island's signature climate.

cards.name: Ainu Mosir
cards.desc: "The quiet land of humans" — the Ainu name for the island, older than any map of Japan.

cards.name: The Kaitakushi
cards.desc: The Colonization Commission of 1869: the frontier office that made Ezochi into Hokkaidō.

cards.name: Shiretoko
cards.desc: The peninsula UNESCO calls one of the world's richest temperate ecosystems — Ainu for "the end of the land."

symbols.name: The bear
symbols.meaning: Kim-un-kamuy, the mountain god of the Ainu — honoured in the iomante ceremony

symbols.name: The drift ice
symbols.meaning: The winter sea that feeds the whole food chain of the north

symbols.name: The lavender field
symbols.meaning: Furano's summer signature — the cultivated frontier in bloom

mythology.lead: Hokkaidō's mythology is Ainu: a kamuy-cosmos where every animal, fire, and tool has a spirit-owner, and where the human world is maintained by right exchange with the unseen.

myths.title: Ainu Mosir and Kamuy Mosir
myths.text: Ainu oral tradition divides existence between Ainu Mosir, the land of humans, and Kamuy Mosir, the land of the spirits — and teaches that kamuy visit the human world wearing animal bodies as gifts. The bear is the mountain god's greatest visitation; the fire goddess, Ape-huci-kamuy, keeps every hearth and carries every prayer to the spirit world. The island itself is a borderland between the two realms.

myths.title: Iomante
myths.text: The iomante — "sending off" — returns the visiting bear-spirit to Kamuy Mosir with songs, prayers, and gifts, so that the god will tell the other kamuy of human courtesy and come again in generous flesh. Long misread by outsiders as cruelty, it is among the most studied hunting ceremonies on earth: a theology of gratitude in which killing and honouring are the same act.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hokkaidō supplies a third of Japan's food from a tenth of its land; Sapporo beer, the Snow Festival's ice palaces, and the lavender of Furano are national brands. The 2020 opening of Upopoy, the National Ainu Museum and Park at Shiraoi, gave the island's first people their first national institution. In the history of colonialism, the Kaitakushi is studied worldwide as Japan's own frontier — the laboratory where it practiced the modernization it later exported.
lore.archaeology: Hokkaidō holds some of the world's oldest pottery: Jōmon-period cord-marked vessels from sites like Taishō date beyond 14,000 years, among the earliest ceramic traditions on earth. The Shiretoko peninsula is a UNESCO World Heritage site for its marine-terrestrial food web; the Oshoro stone circles and the Ofuna shell middens mark the island's deep ritual past. Hakodate's Goryōkaku — the star fort of the last Tokugawa loyalists (1869) — is where the old Japan made its final stand on the new island.
lore.syncretism: Ainu religion absorbed and resisted Japanese and Russian pressure in equal measure: Orthodox missions among the Kuril Ainu, Buddhist temples on the coasts, and the yukar epics — sung in an isolate language with no close relatives — keeping the older world intact in verse. The twentieth century added a third strand: the Ainu cultural revival, led by figures like the poet and legislator Kayano Shigeru, made the island's first culture a national conversation.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 北海道: north, sea, road — the three kanji of the Meiji-era name. The older indigenous toponymy is Ainu: Ainu Mosir ("land of the humans"), and the island's pre-modern Japanese name Ezochi ("land of the Ezo") survives in the history books the new name replaced.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SHEE-koh-koo' — three crisp syllables.
pronunciation.note: Shikoku is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. Its significance is geographic and pilgrimage-based.

domains.title: Island of the Eighty-Eight Temples
domains.subtitle: Pilgrimage, Rural Japan, and the Cult of Kūkai
domains.lead: Shikoku is Japan's smallest main island, a place of mountains, coast, and rural quiet. For more than a thousand years it has been walked by pilgrims on the henro, the 88-temple circuit associated with Kūkai, the founder of Shingon Buddhism. Shikoku means 'four provinces,' and its identity is inseparable from the spiritual geography of the pilgrimage.

cards.name: Shikoku Henro
cards.desc: The 88-temple pilgrimage circuit honoring Kūkai; in Shingon numerology the 88 stands for the bonnō, the delusions each temple is walked to release.

cards.name: Kūkai's Island
cards.desc: The birthplace and spiritual home of the Shingon founder, born at Zentsū-ji in Sanuki in 774.

cards.name: Mountain Asceticism
cards.desc: Ishizuchi-san and ridges like Yokomine-ji (temple 60) preserve the Shugendō layer beneath the Buddhist circuit.

cards.name: Four Provinces
cards.desc: Awa, Tosa, Iyo, and Sanuki — the ancient kuni that gave the island its name and that the pilgrimage stitches into one body.

symbols.name: Pilgrim's staff and sedge hat
symbols.meaning: The kongō-zue staff rings for the dead who walk with the henro, and the sugegasa shades the white-robed pilgrim.

symbols.name: Osettai
symbols.meaning: The free food, lodging, and small gifts islanders offer walkers — the gift economy that sustains the circuit.

symbols.name: Eighty-eight temples
symbols.meaning: The sacred circuit that defines Shikoku's spiritual geography, one temple for each of the bonnō.

symbols.name: Naruto whirlpools
symbols.meaning: The famous tidal whirlpools at the island's eastern edge, where the Seto Inland Sea meets the Pacific.

symbols.name: The white robe (byakue)
symbols.meaning: The pilgrim's garment, worn as a funeral shroud for the self — the walker dies to ordinary life at temple one.

mythology.lead: Shikoku's mythology is the mythology of Kūkai and the Buddhist pilgrimage that bears his memory — documented history, medieval hagiography, and mountain legend fused into a single sacred geography that thousands of pilgrims in white still walk each year, temple by temple, around the island.

myths.title: Kūkai: The Boy of Zentsū-ji
myths.text: Kūkai (774–835), later venerated as Kōbō Daishi, was born in the village of Byōbugaura in Sanuki province — present-day Zentsū-ji city, where temple 75 still marks the family home. The medieval biographies wrap his life in marvel: as a youth he was sent by a despairing kinsman into the mountain wilderness, and there, tradition says, the esoteric teachings came to him in visionary form. The documentary core is solid: in 804 he sailed to Tang China, studied Sanskrit and esoteric Buddhism at the Qinglong monastery in Chang'an under the Indian master Huiguo, returned in 806 laden with scriptures and ritual implements, founded the Shingon school, and in 816 received imperial leave to open a mountain monastery on Kōya-san. His own early writings — the Sango Shiiki of 797 and the Shōrai Mokuroku of 806 — are among the founding documents of Japanese Buddhist literature. When he died on Kōya-san in 835, tradition refused the word: the master had entered eternal samādhi in the Okunoin and would sit there until the coming of the future Buddha. The hagiography makes the point the pilgrims still act on: on Shikoku, Kūkai never left.

myths.title: The Eighty-Eight Temples and the Companion Beside You
myths.text: The Shikoku Henro links 88 temples in a circuit of some 1,200 kilometres, and the number is itself theology: in Shingon numerology there are eighty-eight bonnō, the delusions that bind the heart, and each temple is understood to release one. The circuit as pilgrims walk it took shape in the Edo period, when temple associations, printed guidebooks such as the Shikoku Reijōki, and the island-wide institution of osettai — free food and lodging offered to walkers — made the henro a mass practice. Pilgrims wear the white byakue and sugegasa hat and carry a kongō-zue staff whose metal rings announce the dead traveling with them, and they address the Daishi not as a memory but as a companion: the walk's first principle is dōgyō ninin, 'two traveling together' — yourself and Kūkai. Walking tales insist the Daishi appears along the road as a child, a beggar, or a stranger who vanishes around the bend. The circuit turns a whole island into one ritual body: to walk Shikoku is to walk through Kūkai's biography, one delusion at a time.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Shikoku Henro remains one of Japan's most important pilgrimages, walked by tens of thousands each year — on foot, by bus, in section over a lifetime — and studied worldwide as a model of living religious practice (Statler, Japanese Pilgrimage, 1983; Reader & Tanabe, Practically Religious, 1998). The island's rural culture, its udon, its vine bridges and thatched Iya villages are celebrated as the 'hidden Japan' of slow travel. Kūkai's bequest runs beyond religion: tradition credits him with perfecting the kana syllabaries and founding Japan's first school open to commoners, and the Daishi's name opens esoteric rites across the country. Shikoku has become the national emblem of a counter-rhythm — the island where the answer to speed is not nostalgia but a walking staff.
lore.archaeology: The material record of the island's sacred culture is continuous and visible. Zentsū-ji (temple 75) preserves the Kūkai birth precinct, the Miedō hall with the birth room still shown to pilgrims, and Tairyū-ji (temple 21) on its eastern ridge guards the vajra said to have flown there when the young Kūkai prayed for a sign. Henro temples from Ryōzen-ji (temple 1, early 9th c.) onward preserve Daishi halls where food is offered daily to Kūkai as one still present — because he is believed to be. On Ishizuchi-san, the summit shrine and the chained final ascent mark the Shugendō layer of the cult. Across the water, the Okunoin of Kōya-san — Kūkai's mausoleum, part of the UNESCO World Heritage 'Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range' (2004) — is the circuit's gravitational center, where the lanterns before the master are said to have burned for twelve centuries.
lore.syncretism: Shikoku's religious landscape is layered rather than replaced. Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines share precincts along the henro, and the island's kami — the mountain powers of Ishizuchi, the sea deities of the whirlpool coast — are read through the honji-suijaku logic as local manifestations of buddhas and bodhisattvas. The pilgrimage itself absorbed folk religion: osettai is a village institution older than any temple guild, and the Daishi is at once a historical monk, an incarnation of a cosmic buddha, and a helpful stranger on the road. In the modern era the henro has been recast for international walkers, secular hikers, and 'power spot' tourists without losing its ritual grammar, and churches and new religions appear among the givers of osettai. Syncretism here is not a single historical event but the island's permanent condition: every age walks the same road and calls the companion by a different name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NAH-goh-yah' — three even syllables, with the middle vowel open and short.
pronunciation.note: Nagoya is Tier 2: plain Hepburn romanisation — no diacritic, no distinctive letter; the restoration marks the name as a proper noun. The gloss 'peaceful ancient house' is a folk etymology that historians treat with caution, but it is the meaning the city itself has always preferred.

domains.title: Castle City of the Chūbu Heartland
domains.subtitle: Commerce, Craft, and Tokugawa Power
domains.lead: Nagoya is Japan's fourth-largest city and a historic center of commerce and craftsmanship. Built around the castle commissioned by Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1610, Nagoya grew into a hub of ceramics, textiles, automotive manufacturing, and trade.
