Its name — 'peaceful ancient house' — reflects a city that has long served as a stable crossroads.

cards.name: Nagoya Castle
cards.desc: The Tokugawa fortress ordered by Ieyasu in 1610 and completed in 1612, crowned by the famous golden shachihoko roof ornaments.

cards.name: Industrial Hub
cards.desc: From cotton weaving to the Toyota Motor Corporation, the Chūkyō zone became one of the three engines of Japanese manufacturing.

cards.name: Culinary Capital
cards.desc: Famous for miso-katsu, tebasaki, kishimen, and the beloved 'morning' coffee custom that arrives with toast and egg.

cards.name: Chūbu Gateway
cards.desc: A strategic point on the Tōkaidō linking eastern and western Japan — the reason the castle exists at all.

symbols.name: Shachihoko
symbols.meaning: The golden tiger-headed carp roof ornaments of Nagoya Castle — water beasts pressed into service as fire insurance, and the city's emblem on everything from manhole covers to baseball caps.

symbols.name: Nagoya Castle keep
symbols.meaning: The fortress that was never attacked in war: a 1612 message in stone, a 1959 concrete reconstruction, and since 2018 a document-faithful wooden Honmaru Palace rebuilt beside it.

symbols.name: Red miso (aka-dashi)
symbols.meaning: The dark, salty miso paste of the region, central to miso-katsu, miso-nikomi udon, and the local conviction that flavor should be deep rather than showy.

symbols.name: Ceramics and cloisonné
symbols.meaning: The long craft tradition of the Seto–Nagoya region — Noritake porcelain, Shippo-yaki cloisonné, and the Owari guild instincts that made 'made in Nagoya' a quiet synonym for quality.

mythology.lead: Nagoya's mythology is more historical than divine: a crossroads named for a 'peaceful ancient house,' a castle built to end the age of war, a conference that settled Japan's succession, and a merchant city that traded the sword for the loom and then for the assembly line.

myths.title: The Peaceful Ancient House
myths.text: The name is older than the castle, and its meaning is a folk etymology the city wears proudly. 名古屋 is traditionally read 'peaceful ancient house' — na from 名, 'name, famous,' goya a softened form of koya, 'old house' — explained by the Nagoya Shrine, an old Owari sanctuary whose grounds lay within what became the castle town. Historians treat the derivation with caution: the same syllables appear in several Owari place names, and medieval documents already know 'Nagoya' as an ordinary locality, not a poetic one. But the etymology's modesty suits the city it names — neither Kyoto's courtly antiquity nor Edo's martial swagger, but a prosperous, unpretentious middle. The temple's framing turns the question around: a 'peaceful ancient house' is precisely what a castle town promises its merchants — safety, continuity, and a roof that outlasts the swords.

myths.title: The Building of Nagoya Castle
myths.text: After Sekigahara (1600) gave Tokugawa Ieyasu the country, he turned to securing its spine. In 1610 he ordered a great castle raised at Nagoya — a site no Japanese ruler had ever fortified — to command the Tōkaidō highways where eastern and western Japan meet, and to house his ninth son, Yoshinao, as founder of the Owari branch. Stone and timbers were floated down from Sunpu and hauled over from the dismantled Kiyosu castle upstream; the great keep was complete by 1612, and Yoshinao entered as first lord of Owari in 1616. The keep's roof carried the city's enduring emblem: a pair of golden shachihoko — tiger-headed carp, water beasts that guard against fire — whose shine announced that this was Tokugawa work. The castle was never attacked in war. Its whole career is the message it was built to send: the new shogunate could raise an unneeded fortress at the center of the country and call it peace.

lore.culturalLegacy: Nagoya's reputation is food first: miso-katsu, tebasaki chicken wings, kishimen flat noodles, and the beloved 'morning' custom in which a coffee order arrives with toast, egg, and ogura toast. The Tokugawa Art Museum, on the castle grounds, holds the Genji Monogatari scrolls and the heirlooms of the Owari house. Toyota Motor Corporation — and with it the whole Chūkyō industrial zone — anchors an economy that still supplies a large share of Japan's exports; Central Japan Airport (Centrair), the 2005 World Exposition site, and the SCMaglev test line through the mountains behind the city all read as the modern descendants of the Tōkaidō junction Ieyasu chose in 1610. The castle, with its rebuilt wooden palace, remains the emblem — a message of peace that has outlasted every war it was built to prevent.
lore.archaeology: The Honmaru Palace of Nagoya Castle survived in measured drawings and photographs until its destruction in 1945; excavations of its buried foundations (2009–2010) allowed a faithful wooden reconstruction, opened in 2018 — one of Japan's most celebrated modern traditional builds — while the 1959 concrete keep awaits its own re-evaluation. Excavation at Kiyosu Castle (2009) uncovered the buried stone bases of Nobunaga-era tenshu. The city's older sacred stratum survives at Atsuta Jingū, the great shrine south of the center that houses the Kusanagi sword and has drawn pilgrims for well over a millennium; the Tokugawa-en garden preserves the Owari lordly residence grounds. And the castle town's grid itself — one of Japan's classic jōkamachi plans — is the largest standing artifact.
lore.syncretism: Nagoya's identity is a three-layer alloy. The first layer is samurai: the Owari Tokugawa, the 'senior branch' (gosanke) held in reserve to supply a shogun should the main line fail, cultivated a deliberate persona of shitsujitsu gōken — sober, sturdy, unshowy — to reassure the shogunate and everyone else. The second layer is merchant: with the stipends gone, the castle town's energies flowed into the chōnindō, the way of the townsman, whose creed of thrift, calculation, and craft made Nagoya famous for quality rather than fashion. The third layer is industrial: Toyota and its satellites made the region synonymous with Japanese manufacturing and its methods. A city that began as a political message became an economic one; the shachihoko on the keep now watch over a supply chain.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-mah-TEH-rah-soo' — the 'r' is a light tap, and the final 'u' is barely voiced.
pronunciation.note: Amaterasu is Tier 2 here: the ASCII form is identical to Hepburn romanization. Her authority is mythological and political, not phonetically distinctive.

domains.title: Sun Goddess of the High Plain
domains.subtitle: Light, Imperial Ancestry, and Cosmic Order
domains.lead: Amaterasu is the central deity of the Japanese pantheon, the sun itself made divine and the ancestral kami of the imperial house. Her realm is Takamagahara, the High Plain of Heaven. Without her light, rice cannot grow, order collapses, and the world sinks into darkness.

cards.name: Sun Sovereign
cards.desc: Ruler of Takamagahara; her light ripens the rice and orders the day.

cards.name: Imperial Ancestor
cards.desc: Grandmother of Ninigi, whose line produced Jimmu, first emperor of Japan.

cards.name: Weaver and Cultivator
cards.desc: She presides over the heavenly weaving hall; Susanoo's outrage there triggered the cave crisis.

cards.name: Withdrawal and Return
cards.desc: Her seclusion in Ama-no-Iwato and the ruse of the mirror remain the pattern of every restored order.

symbols.name: Mirror (yata no kagami)
symbols.meaning: One of the Three Imperial Regalia; the mirror hung outside the cave showed Amaterasu her own light, and its dwelling at Ise is her own

symbols.name: Cave of Heaven (Ama-no-Iwato)
symbols.meaning: The rock-door of her withdrawal; in ritual memory the sealed cave marks every crisis in which order must be coaxed back

symbols.name: Sun-disc
symbols.meaning: The radiant disk she embodies, echoed today in the red circle of the Japanese flag

symbols.name: Magatama beads
symbols.meaning: The curved jewels Izanagi gave her; her own necklace generated the gods of the ukei rite with Susanoo

symbols.name: Shimenawa rope
symbols.meaning: The sacred rope Ame-no-Futodama stretched across the cave mouth — the first boundary between retreat and the common world

mythology.lead: Amaterasu's mythology, told in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, is a theology of light, legitimacy, and the restoration of order after violence. It moves from her birth in purification to her withdrawal from a wounded heaven and her dispatch of the imperial line to earth.

myths.title: From the Left Eye of Izanagi
myths.text: When Izanami died giving birth to the fire god and Izanagi failed to bring her back from Yomi, the grieving creator purified himself in a river. As he washed his face, three sovereign deities were born: Amaterasu from his left eye, Tsukuyomi from his right eye, and Susanoo from his nose (Kojiki 1). Delighted, Izanagi removed his own necklace of magatama and gave it to her, charging her with rule of Takamagahara, the High Plain of Heaven. Her full style, Amaterasu-ōmikami — the Heaven-Illuminating Great August Deity — is written with the very character for sky. The Nihon Shoki preserves several variant birth accounts, a reminder that these texts were compiled at court rather than received as fixed scripture. The myth makes the sun the eldest child of purification: light is what emerges once pollution has been washed away.

myths.title: Susanoo's Rampage in Heaven
myths.text: Susanoo wept so violently at the death of his mother that mountains shook and rivers swelled; when Izanagi expelled him from the land, the storm god climbed to heaven to bid his sister farewell. Wary, Amaterasu went out armed, but Susanoo protested his innocence and proposed an ukei, a test by which the siblings exchanged ornaments and produced divine children (Kojiki 1). No sooner was the pledge sealed than he reversed the ridges of her rice-fields, filled the ditches, and flayed the heavenly piebald horse, hurling its carcass through the roof of her weaving hall. The shock killed her weaving-maiden. Enraged and grieving, Amaterasu withdrew into the rock cave and sealed the door. The myth insists that the gravest danger to cosmic order is not foreign invasion but violence inside the family — the sun itself can be driven out by her own brother.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ise Grand Shrine remains the supreme sanctuary of Shinto, its twenty-year rebuilding unbroken since the seventh century, and the Daijōsai enthronement rite of each new emperor reenacts Ninigi's descent. The red disc of the flag keeps her sign on every public building, and pilgrims stream across the Uji Bridge at New Year. In the countryside, folk religion still addresses her as the guarantor of the harvest sun. Abroad, Ōkami introduced her to millions who will never visit Ise — the newest link in an unbroken chain of sunlight made visible.
lore.archaeology: The Ise Grand Shrine (Mie Prefecture) is Amaterasu's principal dwelling: its Inner Shrine (Kōtai Jingū), traditionally founded in the reign of Suinin (1st century BCE), is rebuilt every twenty years (shikinen-zōtai) on alternating adjacent plots, a rite documented from 690 CE and continued without break. Architectural and documentary study of the precincts — the Uji Bridge, the Shōden, the treasure halls — makes Ise the best-documented ritual complex in Japan, though the mirror itself is never displayed. Heian ritual compendia (Engishiki) and shrine records (Shintōshū) list the annual offerings of cloth and first fruits presented by the court.
lore.syncretism: In the medieval honji-suijaku system Amaterasu was identified with the cosmic Buddha Vairocana (Dainichi Nyorai) — the sun of the Dharma itself — and Buddhist chapels and sutras stood within Ise's precincts until the Meiji separation edicts. State Shinto then stripped away these Buddhist layers, taught the descent of Ninigi as national history, and made her the theological center of imperial ideology; overseas shrines carried her cult into the empire. Her modern reception extends to the video game Ōkami, whose wolf-goddess is drawn from her iconography — evidence that the sun still needs a face.

pronunciation.approximation: 'TSOO-koo-yoh-mee' — the initial 'ts' is crisp, and the final vowel is clear.
pronunciation.note: Tsukuyomi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is the moon god and sibling of the sun goddess Amaterasu.

domains.title: Moon God of the Night
domains.subtitle: Lunar Order, Separation, and Celestial Sibling
domains.lead: Tsukuyomi is the moon kami of Japanese myth, born from Izanagi's right eye when the creator washed away the pollution of Yomi. He rules the night and the counting of months, and his entire narrative turns on a single act of violence that separated him forever from the sun.

cards.name: Moon God
cards.desc: Ruler of the night sky and the lunar calendar that numbers the months.

cards.name: Sibling of Amaterasu
cards.desc: Born with her from Izanagi's purification — the night's twin of the day.

cards.name: Night Ruler
cards.desc: He governs the realm opposite the sun, where nothing ripens.

cards.name: Separated Deity
cards.desc: His killing of Uke-mochi divided him from Amaterasu into day and night.

symbols.name: Moon
symbols.meaning: The luminous body he rules; in court poetry the moon outshines every other image of the sky

symbols.name: Night
symbols.meaning: The dark half of the cosmic day; his estrangement from the sun fixed its boundary

symbols.name: Blade
symbols.meaning: The weapon with which he answered Uke-mochi's feast — purity's fatal fastidiousness

symbols.name: Crescent
symbols.meaning: Waxing and waning; the counting of months that his name may encode

symbols.name: The five grains
symbols.meaning: Rice, millet, beans, wheat, and soy born from Uke-mochi's slain body — food that his night can never ripen

mythology.lead: Tsukuyomi's mythology is the shortest dossier of the three celestial siblings, and the chronicles themselves treat him as an afterthought. What survives is one birth, one killing, and one eternal estrangement — enough to divide the sky.

myths.title: From the Right Eye of Izanagi
myths.text: After his escape from Yomi, Izanagi washed away the pollution of the underworld, and the three great sovereign deities came from his face: Amaterasu from the left eye, Tsukuyomi from the right eye, and Susanoo from the nose (Kojiki 1). Izanagi appointed Amaterasu to rule the day and Tsukuyomi the night, dividing the luminous and dark halves of the world between the siblings. Where Amaterasu received her father's necklace and the highest heaven, Tsukuyomi received no emblem — a first hint of how thin his dossier would remain. His name joins tsuku, the moon, with yomi, read as 'night' or as 'counting,' the deity who numbers the months. The myth establishes the moon as the sun's twin: born in the same instant of purification, ruling the complementary half of the sky.

myths.title: The Feast of Uke-mochi
myths.text: Amaterasu heard of a wondrous goddess of food, Uke-mochi, and sent Tsukuyomi to look upon her. Uke-mochi turned toward the land and from her mouth and body produced a banquet — boiled rice, millet, and every grain (Kojiki 1). Tsukuyomi was revolted: a meal that issued from a body was pollution itself, and he drew his blade and killed her. Amaterasu's anger was immediate and eternal — she declared him an evil god she would never again face, and from that moment the sun and moon kept separate courses. From Uke-mochi's slain body the useful world sprang: silkworms from her head, rice from her eyes, millet from her ears, beans from her nose, wheat and soy from her lower body (Nihon Shoki 1). The myth weighs purity against fecundity: the moon's fastidious blade cuts the night off from the very source of food.

lore.culturalLegacy: The court's tsukimi moon-viewing banquets — still kept at Ise, at shrines, and in every garden with a patch of susuki grass — descend from rites addressed to the moon's power over the harvest calendar. In modern Japan he has been reinvented as the brooding nocturnal counterweight to solar Amaterasu, appearing in anime, manga, and games as the name of illusions and dream-techniques that trap their victims in a private night. Every autumn the full moon of the harvest festival hangs over rooftops exactly where the myth put him: alone, luminous, and apart.
lore.archaeology: Material evidence for Tsukuyomi is correspondingly scarce. His chief sanctuary, the Tsukiyomi-no-miya, stands among the subsidiary shrines of Ise and is renewed with the Grand Shrine's twenty-year rebuilding cycle; a mirror is enshrined there as his body. Heian court records document monthly tsukimi rites — offerings of dumplings, susuki grass, and sake to the harvest moon — and the Engishiki lists him among the kami receiving state offerings. Beyond Ise, independent shrines to Tsukuyomi are rare, which historians of religion read as the material trace of his thin mythology: a deity with no narrative cycle attracted no pilgrimage geography.
lore.syncretism: Tsukuyomi was drawn early into the Buddhist astronomy that mapped the pantheon onto the heavens: in esoteric mandalas the lunar deity appears among the devas as a moon-disc (gachirin), and medieval Shinto-Buddhist thought quietly read the moon kami as Dainichi's reflected light — the moon as borrowed radiance, a natural metaphor for compassion that mirrors its source. In honji-suijaku terms he attracted no major buddha of his own, and his cult shrank as Amaterasu's and Susanoo's grew. His afterlife is more literary than liturgical: the moon of the Man'yōshū and the Kokinshū poems is Tsukuyomi's territory whether named or not.

pronunciation.approximation: 'EE-zah-nah-gee' — the 'g' is hard, and the 'r' of Western transcriptions is absent in Japanese.
pronunciation.note: Izanagi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is one of the two primordial creator kami of Japanese myth.

domains.title: He-Who-Invites
domains.subtitle: Creator of the Islands, Father of the Gods
domains.lead: Izanagi is the male half of the primordial creator pair. With his sister-wife Izanami he stirred the world-ocean with the jeweled spear and raised the islands of Japan; his failed rescue of her from Yomi founded the boundary of death; and his river purification afterward gave birth to the three rulers of heaven, night, and sea — including Amaterasu herself.

cards.name: Creator of Japan
cards.desc: With Izanami, he stirred the ocean with the jeweled spear and raised the eight great islands.

cards.name: Spear of Heaven
cards.desc: Ame-no-Nuboko, the jeweled spear; the brine dripping from its tip became the first island.

cards.name: Father of the Sun
cards.desc: His misogi bath produced Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, and Susanoo.

cards.name: Visitor to Yomi
cards.desc: He descended to the underworld to retrieve Izanami and sealed its door behind him.

symbols.name: Ame-no-Nuboko
symbols.meaning: The jeweled spear given by the heavenly kami; the drip of brine from its tip congealed into Onogoroshima, the first island

symbols.name: Yomotsu-hirasaka
symbols.meaning: The even slope of Yomi's boundary, sealed by the great boulder — the frontier between the living and the dead

symbols.name: Misogi purification
symbols.meaning: The river ritual that cleansed Yomi's pollution and generated the three sovereign kami; the ancestor of every Shinto ablution

symbols.name: The comb
symbols.meaning: Izanagi's comb, whose lit tooth revealed Izanami's decay — knowledge that cannot be unlit

symbols.name: Peaches
symbols.meaning: The fruits he hurled at Yomi's pursuing hags, from which peaches took their power against evil in Japanese folk ritual

mythology.lead: Izanagi's mythology is the creation narrative of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki: the making of the land, the founding of death, and the birth of the gods who rule heaven and earth. It is also the story of a husband who could not bring his wife back — and of what he made instead.

myths.title: The Spear in the Brine
myths.text: When heaven and earth had parted but the land below floated like oil and drifted like a jellyfish, the heavenly kami commanded Izanagi and Izanami to make it solid. Standing upon the Floating Bridge of Heaven, they lowered the jeweled spear Ame-no-Nuboko and stirred; when they drew it up, brine dripped from the tip and piled up, congealing into the island of Onogoroshima (Kojiki 1). Descending, they built a heavenly pillar and a hall eight fathoms long and prepared to beget the land. The image is the Japanese creation at its most elegant: the cosmos is not spoken or fought into being but stirred — order precipitating out of the world-ocean like salt from brine. Everything that follows, from the imperial line to the boundary of death, crystallizes from that single drip.

myths.title: The Ceremony Spoken Ajar
myths.text: To seal their union, Izanagi and Izanami were to circle the heavenly pillar, he from the left and she from the right, meeting on the far side. But Izanami spoke first in greeting — a breach of ritual order — and though they coupled, their first child was Hiruko, the leech-child, boneless and adrift, whom they set loose in a reed boat (Kojiki 1). Consulting the heavenly kami, they learned the error: the man's voice must come first. They redid the circuit in the correct order, and Izanami bore the eight great islands of Japan. The myth encodes a whole ritual theory — words spoken out of sequence pollute outcomes — and plants cosmic law inside the smallest unit of ceremony: who speaks first at the pillar. No other creation story makes grammar itself a generative force.

lore.culturalLegacy: Misogi and its descendants — shrine ablutions, sumo ring-purifications, and the cleansing rites of martial lineages — descend from Izanagi's bath. The creation couple crowns the genealogies recited at shrine festivals, and Onogoroshima tradition ties them to Awaji, whose Izanagi Jingū preserves their legend. Every telling of the cave myth, every enthronement rite, every New-Year first-shrine visit quietly presupposes his cosmology: a world stirred from brine, lost to death, and washed back into light. Modern manga and games retell his descent to Yomi as readily as the Greeks retell Orpheus.
lore.archaeology: The material trail of the creation pair runs through shrine geography rather than monuments. Awaji Island — identified with Onogoroshima in local tradition — keeps their legend at Izanagi Jingū. Taga Taisha in Shiga Prefecture claims the site of Izanagi's retirement palace and preserves the medieval Taga-dera engi recounting the creation. The Kojiki's note that Izanami was buried on Mount Hiba links the myth to the Chūgoku region's ritual landscape. Shrine treasures and picture scrolls across Japan illustrate the spear-stirring and the Yomi pursuit, while the misogi rite itself — documented in the Engishiki's ritual protocols — remains a living layer of the tradition, performed daily at river-mouths and shrines.
lore.syncretism: Izanagi and Izanami were drawn into Buddhist cosmology as the Japanese counterpart of cosmic parentage: in Ryōbu Shinto, Izanagi's stirring of the brine was read alongside the primal vibrations of Dainichi's two mandalas, and medieval Tendai assigned the pair places in its systems of correspondence between kami and buddhas. In the Meiji period, State Shinto elevated their creation narrative into national history, taught in school primers as the literal origin of the islands and the imperial line; after 1945 the myth returned to the status of myth, though the textbooks' version still shapes popular understanding. Abroad, the couple stirring the primordial ocean has become one of the most recognizable images of Japanese mythology.

pronunciation.approximation: 'EE-nah-ree' — the 'r' is a light tap, and all vowels are short.
pronunciation.note: Inari is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. The name's significance is cultic and agricultural, not orthographic.

domains.title: Kami of Rice, Fertility, and Foxes
domains.subtitle: Guardian of the Harvest and Merchant Prosperity
domains.lead: Inari is one of the most widely worshipped kami in Japan: a deity of rice who became, over a thousand years, the patron of fertility, sake, smiths, merchants, and worldly success. The vermillion torii gates and fox statues of Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyōto are among the most iconic images of Japanese religion.

cards.name: Rice and Harvest
cards.desc: Inari governs the rice plant — enshrined as Uka-no-mitama, the spirit of the grain itself.

cards.name: Fox Messengers
cards.desc: Kitsune carry the kami's messages and hold the granary key in their statues' mouths.

cards.name: Merchant Success
cards.desc: From the medieval period, traders, brewers, and smiths prayed to Inari for prosperity.

cards.name: Fushimi Inari
cards.desc: The head shrine in Kyōto, founded in 711 CE, is ringed by mountains of donated torii.

symbols.name: Vermillion torii gates
symbols.meaning: The donated gates climbing Mount Inari — more than ten thousand — each one an invoice of a fulfilled prayer

symbols.name: Fox (kitsune)
symbols.meaning: The paired foxes flanking the shrine: one bears the granary key, one the jewel; red bibs mark their veneration

symbols.name: Rice sheaf
symbols.meaning: Inari's first body — the plant itself, worshipped as Uka-no-mitama before any temple existed

symbols.name: Jewel
symbols.meaning: The wish-granting gem in the fox's mouth; prosperity compressed to a single stone

symbols.name: Fried tofu (abura-age)
symbols.meaning: The offering said to please the fox — hence the sushi that bears Inari's name

mythology.lead: Inari has no single canonical myth cycle in the Kojiki manner. The kami's identity is distributed across a charter legend, a shifting triad of enshrined gods, the fox lore of the medieval period, and the craft legends of the cities — a biography written by worshippers rather than scribes.

myths.title: The Rice-Cake That Flew
myths.text: The Nihon Shoki (Wadō 4, 711 CE) tells how Hata no Irogu, a leader of the immigrant Hata clan, practiced archery on a mountain by setting up a rice-cake as a target. When his arrow struck it, the cake rose into the air as a white bird and flew to the summit, where a radiance appeared. Taking this as a divine sign, Irogu founded a shrine on the spot. Rice-cake, white bird, mountain light: the kami announced itself through its own substance. The Hata were continental immigrants — weavers, engineers, and shrine-builders — and their mountain cult folded the new rice technology into the older kami world. The date makes Inari's shrine among the oldest documented in Japan, and the legend is the charter of what became Fushimi Inari Taisha. It is already the whole theology of Inari — a deity who arrives riding the rice itself.

myths.title: Three Gods, One Kami
myths.text: At its head shrine, Inari is not one deity but three: Uka-no-mitama, the spirit of the rice plant; Satahiko; and Ōmiyanome, the ancestral weaver and food-goddess. Other Inari shrines substitute Toyouke, the goddess of the Ise Grand Shrine's outer precinct, who prepares the food of the gods. Medieval oracles ratified the triad, and the three remain enshrined today. Even the kami's gender never settled: Inari appears as an aged man, a radiant woman, or a fox-mounted deva, depending on the shrine and the century. Scholars read the fluidity as the mark of a genuinely popular cult, indifferent to the tidy genealogies of the court chronicles: Inari names less a person than an office, the power that fills the granary. The many-faced kami mirrors the many fates of rice — seedling, grain, sake, wealth — each a different disguise of one sustenance.

lore.culturalLegacy: Fushimi Inari Taisha, rebuilt after the Ōnin War and crowned with its endless gates, is among the most visited religious sites on earth, and the estimates of thirty thousand Inari shrines across Japan exceed any other deity's. The kami guards restaurants, rice merchants, and corporate headquarters; the sushi named for the fox, inari-zushi, is sold in every convenience store; and the fox-mask of festival stalls is recognizably Inari's. In a secular age, Inari prospers as the most pragmatic divinity in the pantheon: pray, work, and share the result — the god of the harvest became the god of the hustle.
lore.archaeology: Fushimi Inari Taisha in southern Kyōto has been Inari's head shrine since 711 CE. Burned in the Ōnin War (1468) and rebuilt by the late fifteenth century, its main halls, its tunnel-paths of donated torii — over ten thousand strong, dating chiefly from the Edo period onward — and the mountain-top okusha shrines form one of Japan's best-documented cult landscapes. Excavations and shrine records trace the cult's growth from a Hata-clan agricultural shrine to the devotional center of a national commercial network, and the thousands of subsidiary Inari shrines preserve medieval siting patterns at field boundaries and village entrances.
lore.syncretism: Inari is the great syncret of Japanese religion. Medieval Tendai identified the kami with Dakiniten, the fox-riding deva absorbed from Indian tantra, and esoteric lineages placed Inari within mandala systems of the five grains. The Muromachi and Edo periods saw Inari conflated with Benzaiten and with Uka-no-mitama's Buddhist guises; fox-possession cults and Inari mediums blurred the shrine and the street. No figure in Japan tolerated layered identity more gracefully — male or female, one or three, kami or buddha. When the Meiji state ordered the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, Inari shrines quietly stored their Buddhist statuary away; most of it returned within a generation.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAH-chee-mahn' — the 'ch' is crisp, and the final 'n' is a soft closed nasal.
pronunciation.note: Hachiman is Tier 2: the name is plain Hepburn. His importance is institutional and martial, not orthographic.

domains.title: God of War, Archery, and Divine Protection
domains.subtitle: Guardian of the Nation and the Samurai
domains.lead: Hachiman is the kami of war, archery, and protection, worshipped by samurai, peasants, and emperors alike. His symbol — eight banners (hachi-man) — recalls the standards under which the divine child grew to become a warrior patron. He is one of the most widely enshrined kami in Japan, and his cult blurred the boundary between Shinto and Buddhism for over a millennium.

cards.name: War God
cards.desc: Patron of warriors and archers — but of defense, not conquest: the god who protects the realm and those who fight in its name.

cards.name: Eight Banners
cards.desc: His name refers to the eight ritual banners that accompanied the divine birth of the child who became Emperor Ōjin.

cards.name: Divine Protector
cards.desc: Guardian of the nation — invoked from Usa and Iwashimizu as the shield of the throne, and credited with the storm that sank the Mongol fleets.

cards.name: Shinbutsu Synthesis
cards.desc: Worshipped both as a kami and as the Buddhist bodhisattva Hachiman Daibosatsu — the first kami the national chronicles style a bosatsu.

symbols.name: Eight banners
symbols.meaning: The ritual standards from which his name derives — the eight flags of the divine birth

symbols.name: Bow and arrow
symbols.meaning: Attributes of his role as patron of archery and of the disciplined warrior

symbols.name: White dove
symbols.meaning: His messenger, said to descend where his protection rests; the dove still marks his shrine emblems

symbols.name: Helmet and armor
symbols.meaning: The martial regalia of the deified emperor — a god who fights as a soldier, not a force of nature

mythology.lead: Hachiman's mythology is entangled with imperial history: he is most commonly identified as the deified Emperor Ōjin, making him a kami who was once a man — the only great war god of Japan who had served as a soldier. The chronicles give us the emperor; the shrine oracles, the god; and the medieval centuries fused the two into the nation's shield.

myths.title: The Divine Child of the Campaign
myths.text:
Emperor Ōjin, the fifteenth emperor, was born, the Nihon Shoki says, while his mother the empress Jingū carried him through the Korean campaign, the child holding back his own birth until the war was won — the chronicle's way of making the unborn prince a participant in victory. He grew into a ruler remembered for welcoming scholars, artisans and new technologies from the Korean kingdoms, and when he died, tradition holds, he was enshrined at Usa in Kyūshū and became Hachiman, the kami of the eight banners. The identification between the deified emperor and the war god formed gradually across the eighth century; the chronicles give us the man, and the shrine tradition gives us the god (Kojiki, Nihon Shoki, Ōjin and Jingū narratives).

A man-made kami was a new kind of divinity for Japan: not a nature power but an ancestor — which meant that the warrior's death could have a shrine, and the state's wars could have a patron who had once been a soldier himself.

myths.title: The Oracle of the North
myths.text:
The great shrine at Usa in northern Kyūshū became Hachiman's head shrine, and in the eighth century its oracle began to speak into the politics of the capital. In 749 the Shoku Nihongi records, the god was invited from Usa to Nara to lend divine authority to the casting of the Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji; in 764 his oracle denounced the rebel Fujiwara no Nakamaro and threw the prestige of heaven behind the embattled court; by the later eighth century the chronicles were styling him Hachiman Daibosatsu, the Great Bodhisattva Hachiman. A regional war god of Kyūshū had become a constitutional power — consulted, invoked and quoted in the state's own records.

The oracle's career is the quiet history of Japanese religion: kami authority deployed at the exact moments the court needed legitimacy, until protection of the throne became the god's defining office.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hachiman shrines are found throughout Japan, from the head shrine Usa Jingū in Ōita and Iwashimizu Hachimangū south of Kyōto to the great Tsurugaoka Hachimangū at Kamakura — founded by Minamoto no Yoriyoshi in 1063 and moved to its present site by Yoritomo in 1191 as the shrine of the shogunate's own city. He remains the tutelary kami of the Minamoto line and of countless warrior houses, and his September festival at Kamakura is among the grandest shrine rites in the country. Archers invoke him, sumo honors him, and his dove still serves as his messenger on shrine crests, festival floats and military insignia. In the twentieth century his name was borrowed for battleships and war bonds; in the twenty-first he has quietly resumed his older role — the god who protects a nation rather than a war.
lore.archaeology: Usa Jingū in Ōita is Hachiman's head shrine, with a documented history running from the eighth century in shrine records and excavation. Iwashimizu Hachimangū near Kyōto was founded in 860 as the capital's guardian shrine, and its mountain site preserves the medieval pilgrimage routes. Tōdai-ji's Hachiman shrine preserves the Buddhist-Shinto synthesis of the Nara period in situ, and Tsurugaoka Hachimangū at Kamakura — established 1063, relocated 1191 — is the great medieval monument of his cult, its long approach lined to this day with the banners of his name.
lore.syncretism: Hachiman is the archetype of shinbutsu shūgō, the medieval blending of kami and Buddhist cult. As Emperor Ōjin he is human, ancestral and imperial; as Hachiman Daibosatsu he is a bodhisattva — the first kami the national chronicles style a bosatsu — compassionate, universal and warlike at once. This double identity made him indispensable to the samurai state: the Minamoto claimed him as clan ancestor (ujigami) and patron, and the great medieval temples housed his shrines as their guardian chapels. The Meiji separation of Shinto and Buddhism in 1868 forcibly divided what had been one ritual body for a millennium — the bodhisattva title shelved, the shrines reclassified — yet the union survives in popular practice, where a visit to Tsurugaoka Hachimangū is at once a shrine rite and a memory of the Daibosatsu.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BEN-zai-ten' — three syllables; the final 'n' is a soft, closed nasal.
pronunciation.note: Benzaiten is Tier 2: the Japanese form is plain Hepburn. The name is a Sino-Japanese Buddhist import; its distinctiveness lies in cultural history, not in orthography.

domains.title: Goddess of Music, Wealth, and Eloquence
domains.subtitle: One of the Seven Gods of Fortune
domains.lead: Benzaiten is the Japanese transformation of Sarasvatī, the Indian goddess of rivers, speech, and learning. In Japan she became one of the Seven Gods of Fortune (Shichifukujin), patron of music, eloquence, and wealth, and she is worshipped at island shrines, especially Enoshima and Chikubushima, where land and water meet.

cards.name: Biwa Musician
cards.desc: She is depicted playing the lute-like biwa, master of sound and persuasive speech.

cards.name: Seven Gods of Fortune
cards.desc: The only woman among the Shichifukujin, she brings luck to artists and merchants.

cards.name: Island Patron
cards.desc: Her shrines stand on islands and lakeshores, where water, speech, and commerce converge.

cards.name: Serpent Companion
cards.desc: In Japan she is often accompanied by a snake or dragon, guardians of treasure.

symbols.name: Biwa
symbols.meaning: The lute that makes her goddess of music, poetry, and persuasive speech

symbols.name: Snake or dragon
symbols.meaning: A protector of wealth and water, often coiled beneath her image

symbols.name: Jeweled crown
symbols.meaning: Royal ornament marking her as a Buddhist-Taoist deity of fortune

symbols.name: Water and island
symbols.meaning: Her shrines occupy liminal places where sea or lake meets land

mythology.lead: Benzaiten's mythology is a braid of three traditions: the Vedic river-goddess who became the stream of speech, the Buddhist protector who crossed Central Asia and China, and the Japanese fortune-deity who subdued a dragon and took an island for her home.

myths.title: The River Who Became Speech
myths.text: In India, Sarasvatī was first a river and then a goddess. The Ṛgveda (6.61) hymns her in the triple superlative: 'the best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses,' flowing mountain-strong from the heights to the sea. In RV 8.91 the maiden Apala bathes in her waters and rises golden. But the river that received these hymns was already dying — its course drying toward the Rajasthan desert — and as the water failed, the goddess rose in its place: by the time of the late Vedic ritual texts she is speech itself, inspiration, the mother of the Vedas. Her later Buddhist career is foreshadowed in the conversion: a goddess of one drying stream became the patron of everything that flows — language, music, memory — the geography of grammar replacing the geography of water.

myths.title: The Goddess Who Guards the Preachers
myths.text: Buddhism carried Sarasvatī east, and the Lotus Sūtra gave her its highest commission. In the chapter devoted to her, she appears before the assembly with her retinue and vows to protect and nourish all who keep, recite, and preach the sūtra in the 'evil age to come': she will grant them eloquence, memory, and 'the charm of voice' that can win every assembly, and she teaches a dhāraṇī for their safety. The commission is the pivot of her whole biography: the river-goddess who once watered fields becomes the guardian of the text-field — the first link in the chain that ends, centuries later, in a Japanese fortune ship. Read backwards from Enoshima, the chapter explains everything: eloquence as wealth, memory as treasure, and the preacher as the farmer whose crop she keeps.

lore.culturalLegacy: Benzaiten is still working. Enoshima's shrines receive millions of visitors a year; Chikubushima's Hōgonji still crowns its island rock in Lake Biwa; musicians, calligraphers, and business owners keep her as patron. Her image — biwa on her knee, dragon at her feet — recurs in ukiyo-e, on the takarabune prints hung at New Year, and across modern manga and anime as the default face of a Japanese goddess. She is the luck of artists, the one fortune-god whose treasure cannot be hoarded: played or spoken, it doubles. In a country that blesses companies and consecrates instruments, she remains the patron of every career built on a beautiful voice.
lore.archaeology: Benzaiten's principal sanctuaries are her own archaeology. At Enoshima, the Hetsunomiya and Okutsunomiya shrines preserve Edo-period structures above a cave-cult that is older than any of them; the Enoshima engi scroll itself is a primary document of the medieval cult. Chikubushima's Hōgonji, on its sheer rock in Lake Biwa, preserves temple buildings and statuary from the Muromachi period onward. Itsukushima's great torii and sea-stage (12th–13th centuries, periodically rebuilt) mark the Aki shrine where her Munakata identity is worshipped. And the portable arts document her widest diffusion: countless Edo-period woodblock prints, netsuke, and temple statues show Benten with her biwa and coiled serpent — the material record of a fortune-cult that reached into every pocket.
lore.syncretism: Benzaiten is a palimpsest in three scripts. The underlayer is Indian: Sarasvatī, the Vedic river who became the goddess of speech, carried into Buddhism and east along the caravan roads. The middle layer is Chinese: translators rendered her name as Biancaitian, 'Heaven of Eloquent Talent,' and painted her with the pipa of court musicians. The top layer is Japanese: on entering the archipelago she married the sea — identified with the Munakata water-goddess Ichikishimahime (Kojiki, Nihon Shoki), given a snake-dragon for a companion, and seated among the Seven Gods of Fortune as their only woman. The layers never erase one another: a medieval pilgrim at Enoshima could honor a Vedic river, a Buddhist protector, and a Shinto kami in a single bow, and in the Edo period her cult spread through prints and merchant devotion until 'Benten' was simply the name of luck with a woman's face.

steps: Nahuatl was recorded by Spanish and native scribes in Latin alphabets from the sixteenth century onward.
The name is a compound: quetzalli 'precious green feather' + cōātl 'snake'.
Macrons mark long vowels in scholarly Classical Nahuatl orthography.
The Unicode restoration Quetzalcōātl preserves vowel length; there is no indigenous logographic spelling for the personal name.

provenanceSources.title: Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl
Bierhorst, History and Mythology of the Aztecs

pronunciation.approximation: 'ket-SAHL-KOH-wahtl' — the 'tl' at the end is one sound, the 'z' is like 'ts,' and the whispered 'l' in 'zal' is Nahuatl ɬ.
pronunciation.note: Classical Nahuatl had no /u/; qu before e/i is /k/ and cu is /kw/. The long vowels ō and ā are preserved in the PUNICODEX restoration, and the final -tl is a lateral affricate [t͡ɬ], not English 'tuhl.' The [w] glide between ō and ā is common in natural speech but optional. Tier 1: the two macrons preserve reconstructed vowel length. Sources: Andrews Introduction to Classical Nahuatl, Karttunen An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl, Wiktionary Nahuatl.

domains.title: The Feathered Serpent
domains.subtitle: Wind, Wisdom, and the Morning Star
domains.lead:
Quetzalcōātl is the living bridge between heaven and earth, between the iridescent quetzal of the cloud forest and the coiled serpent of the underworld. In Nahuatl thought he moves through every medium: the wind that carries speech, the dawn light of Venus, the ink and paper of the calmecac school, and the breath that animates the craftsman. He is less a storm god than a motion — the intelligent current that makes culture possible.

Unlike his shadow-twin Tezcatlipoca, the Smoking Mirror who rules night, sorcery, and the arbitrary turn of fate, Quetzalcōātl stands for daylight learning, measured speech, and the priestly arts. Where Tezcatlipoca deceives, Quetzalcōātl instructs. Yet the two are inseparable: creation itself required their partnership, and every age ends in their struggle.

cards.name: Wind and Breath
cards.desc: As Ehecatl, the wind, he is the breath that precedes speech and the storm that scatters the old sun; his temple is a cylinder because the wind has no corners.

cards.name: Learning and the Priesthood
cards.desc: Patron of the calmecac, the school for noble youths; he invented the calendar, established fasting and penance, and taught the arts of the feather-worker and goldsmith.

cards.name: Venus, the Morning Star
cards.desc: The planet Venus as Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli, Lord of the Dawn; his return each morning heralds the sun and the renewal of time.

cards.name: Creation and Sustenance
cards.desc: He shaped the Fifth Sun from the bones of the previous age and brought maize out of secrecy so that humankind could eat and flourish.

symbols.name: Feathered serpent
symbols.meaning: The union of sky (quetzal feathers) and earth (serpent); the animate conduit between cosmic levels

symbols.name: Conch shell (tecciztli)
symbols.meaning: The wind-shell blown by Ehecatl; a token of breath, sound, and the east from which Quetzalcōātl departed

symbols.name: Cut shell mask (Ehecatl)
symbols.meaning: The duck-billed mask of the wind manifestation; worn by priests and dancers to become the moving air

symbols.name: Jade and quetzal plumes
symbols.meaning: Signs of preciousness, life, and the verdant east; the quetzal cannot be kept in captivity, so its feathers are gifts of the wild

symbols.name: Venus glyph
symbols.meaning: The morning-star symbol that marks Quetzalcōātl as a lord of time, recurrence, and celestial order

mythology.lead: Quetzalcōātl's myths are not a single linear biography but a shifting constellation of roles: creator, priest-king, culture hero, exiled lord, and promised return. The narratives collected by Sahagún and other early colonial writers preserve the memory of a deity whose generosity and restraint are inseparable from his grief.

myths.title: The Fifth Sun from the Bones of the Old Age
myths.text: After the collapse of the Fourth Sun, the gods required a new humankind. Quetzalcōātl descended into Mictlān, the land of the dead, to ask Mictlantecuhtli for the bones of the previous races. The lord of the dead set a trap: Quetzalcōātl was to circle the underworld four times blowing a conch that had no holes. Quetzalcōātl had worms bore the shell and bees sound it from within, seized the bones, and fled; a quail sent after him startled the god, he stumbled, and the bones broke — which is why people are of different sizes. In Tamoanchan the fragments were ground into meal; the gods bled themselves over it, and from that sacrifice the humans of the Fifth Sun were formed (Leyenda de los Soles). The shattered bones explain why human beings differ in stature, and the dough of our making is theft, accident and the gods’ own blood: creation is a salvage operation, and humankind is its patchwork.

myths.title: The Theft and Gift of Maize
myths.text: Maize, the flesh of humankind, was originally sealed inside Tonacatepetl, the Mountain of Our Sustenance, while the people of the Fifth Sun lived on bitter roots. Quetzalcōātl watched a red ant carrying a single kernel and followed it to the mountain's heart; taking the form of a black ant himself, he carried one grain back to the gods. Moved — and enraged — the gods summoned the lightning, and the mountain split, spilling red, yellow, white and black corns, which the winds carried to the four quarters of the world. In the tellings recorded by Sahagún (Florentine Codex), it is the ant's example that shames the god into cunning: wisdom, the myth insists, begins in watching small things. The four-coloured maize maps onto the four directions, binding Quetzalcōātl's gift to the whole geometry of the cosmos. Civilisation's staple is not a conquest but a found secret — and its first custodian is the clever priest who knows how to follow an ant.

lore.culturalLegacy:
Quetzalcōātl is now inseparable from Mexican national identity. He appears on the flag as the eagle-and-serpent emblem's feathered ancestor, in the names of parks and universities, and in the architecture of museums that evoke his coils. The feathered serpent remains a shorthand for Mesoamerican civilisation itself: learned, stratified, and visually spectacular. Artists from Diego Rivera to contemporary muralists have returned to his image, and the quetzal bird has become an icon of endangered beauty across Central America.

In popular culture he has become a default 'Aztec god' — sometimes reduced to a dragon or a vague sage, sometimes invoked in fantasy games and speculative fiction as a lost-knowledge figure. More responsibly, astronomers and archaeologists continue to use Quetzalcōātl-related alignments — especially at Chichén Itzá, where the equinox shadow crawls down the Castillo pyramid like a serpent — as entry points into the precision of Mesoamerican sky-watching. The name endures wherever the Americas confront their deep past: not as a simple hero, but as a question about knowledge, power, and what it costs to be wise.
lore.archaeology: The earliest monumental feathered serpent appears at Teotihuacan, where the Temple of the Feathered Serpent (c. 200 CE) preserves carved serpent heads amid offerings of sacrificed warriors and sacrificial goods. At Chichén Itzá, the Castillo pyramid stages the equinox descent of a serpent-shadow down its northern stairway, linking the architecture to solar and Venus cycles. Tula (Tollan) supplies the Toltec warrior columns and Atlantean figures associated with the legendary reign of Ce Acatl Topiltzin. Tenochtitlan's Templo Mayor contained dual shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli, but Quetzalcōātl-Ehecatl imagery appears on sculptural reliefs and the round temple of the wind. Painted books such as the Codex Borgia and the Telleriano-Remensis preserve his calendar and ritual associations in post-contact indigenous art.
lore.syncretism:
The feathered-serpent image predates the Nahuatl name by centuries. At Teotihuacan, the so-called Tlaloc-Quetzalcōātl imagery of the Temple of the Feathered Serpent shows a similar composite being, though its precise name and meaning remain disputed. Among the Maya, the counterpart is Kukulkan ('Feathered Serpent' in Yucatec); among the K'iche' Maya, Gucumatz carries the same cosmogonic role. The Mixtec and Zapotec had their own serpent-sky figures, suggesting that the image circulated across language boundaries as a shared Mesoamerican icon.

Within Nahuatl religion, Quetzalcōātl overlaps with Ehecatl, the wind; with Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli, the morning star; and with the aged creator couple Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl. Spanish friars and indigenous writers after the conquest sometimes drew parallels with Christian figures — St. Thomas the apostle, or Christ in his sacrificial and resurrected aspects — but these equations tell us more about colonial translation than about pre-contact belief. Modern New Age and nationalist movements have embraced Quetzalcōātl as a symbol of indigenous wisdom, often smoothing away the deity's darker, more violent partnerships.
lore.originalScriptNote:
The name is composed of two Classical Nahuatl words: quetzalli, the long tail-feather of the resplendent quetzal bird, and cōātl, 'snake' or 'twin.' In colonial Nahuatl orthography the word is often written Quetzalcóatl with an acute accent on the first o; that spelling reflects Spanish convention, not an attested Nahuatl pitch accent. The PUNICODEX restoration uses macrons on ō and ā to mark reconstructed vowel length, the distinctive prosodic feature that makes the name Tier 1.

Classical Nahuatl had no /u/ sound; qu before e/i represents /k/, not /kw/. The letter tz is the affricate /ts/, and final -tl is a single lateral affricate /tɬ/. The lateral fricative ɬ in the middle of the name is the 'whispered l' of Nahuatl, distinct from the English approximant. We write the name in Latin transcription because the original logophonetic script of the Nahua — a tradition of pictographic and glyphic writing now partly lost — does not survive as a fully readable text for this theonym.

variants.note: Widespread Wikipedia rendering with short o; Karttunen and Andrews give the long ō of īpōca (to smoke), so Tēzcatlīpōca is primary

pronunciation.approximation: 'tehs-kaht-lee-POH-kah' — hold the first e and the lee long, with long ō on the stressed penult.
pronunciation.note: Tēzcatlīpōca is Tier 1: the macrons preserve the long vowels (ē, ī, ō) that ASCII flattens, per Karttunen's lexicon. The name compounds tēzcatl 'mirror' and pōca 'smoke' — the god's black glass is literally his name.

domains.title: The Smoking Mirror
domains.subtitle: Night, Sorcery, Strife, and the God-Impersonator
domains.lead: Tēzcatlīpōca is the Aztec night given will: the god of the obsidian mirror in which all things are seen, patron of rulers and sorcerers, tempter and destroyer of his own brother Quetzalcōātl. He is not evil — he is the shadow the world requires, and the Aztecs honored him with their most terrible beauty: the year-long god made flesh.

cards.name: The Mirror
cards.desc: Obsidian polished to black glass: it shows the future, the hidden, and the viewer's true face.

cards.name: The Missing Foot
cards.desc: Torn off by the earth-monster Cipactli in the creation — the mirror smokes where the foot was.

cards.name: The First Sun
cards.desc: He was the sun of the first age — the jaguar sun — devoured with his world when it ended.

cards.name: The Ixiptla
cards.desc: At Toxcatl, a flawless youth lived as the god for a year — then climbed the temple steps to die as him.

symbols.name: The smoking mirror
symbols.meaning: Knowledge of the hidden; the self seen without mercy

symbols.name: The jaguar
symbols.meaning: His nahual — the night's power and the first sun's ferocity

symbols.name: The missing foot
symbols.meaning: The price of creation: what the earth-monster took, and where the obsidian mirror now sits

symbols.name: The black stripe
symbols.meaning: The paint across his face — the night sky worn as war-color

mythology.lead: Tēzcatlīpōca's myths are all contest: with the earth-monster, with Quetzalcōātl, with the proud — he is the force that measures the strong by breaking them.

myths.title: The Foot in the Jaws
myths.text: To make the world, Tēzcatlīpōca and Quetzalcōātl descended to the primordial waters where the caiman-monster Cipactli floated, all mouths, snapping at every god who offered a limb. Tēzcatlīpōca gave his own foot as bait; the jaws closed on it — the sources preserve the detail that his foot, torn off, became the obsidian mirror that smokes — and in the moment the monster held him, the two gods seized her and tore her apart: her back became the earth, her eyes the springs, her mouth the cave from which humankind would emerge (Leyenda de los Soles; cf. Florentine Codex Bk. 7). Every Aztec king thereafter ruled over ground purchased with the god's flesh, and every sorcerer's mirror carried the same debt. The myth defines the god in a single stroke: the one who will pay a body-part to win a world, and who keeps, forever after, the gleaming proof of what it cost.

myths.title: The Jaguar Sun
myths.text: The Leyenda de los Soles counts the ages: the first was Four Jaguar, Nahui Ocēlōtl, whose sun was Tēzcatlīpōca and whose people were giants; the second Four Wind, whose sun was Quetzalcōātl; the third Four Rain, the sun of Tlāloc, ended in fire-rain; the fourth Four Water, the sun of Chalchiuhtlicue, ended in flood. The first age ended by fratricide: Quetzalcōātl struck Tēzcatlīpōca from the sky with a club, and jaguars devoured the giant people of the fallen world. Through the succession of suns the two brothers keep unmaking each other's worlds — the Aztec cosmos is their long quarrel, and the present Fifth Sun, Four Movement, is only the latest armistice, held together by sacrifice. The doctrine is stark: time itself is strife, every order is temporary, and the god of the smoking mirror is the one who reminds the others of it, age after age.

lore.culturalLegacy: 'Smoking mirror' entered the world's vocabulary as the emblem of deceptive appearances. His obsidian mirror in the British Museum — Aztec-made, later owned by the Elizabethan magus John Dee as his scrying glass — is among the most storied objects on earth, linking Tenochtitlan to the court of Elizabeth I. Every account of Aztec civilization, from the earliest friars to the present, must reckon with his Toxcatl: the rite that made beauty, divinity, and death one ceremony. In Mexico his name still brands nightclubs, football chants, and political cartoons — the god of the untouchable shadow, as serviceable to the modern state as to the empire that fed him hearts.
lore.archaeology: His obsidian mirrors survive across collections — the British Museum's Dee mirror foremost — ground from the volcanic glass that Pachuca and Otumba supplied by the ton. The Florentine Codex's account of Toxcatl, illustrated by Nahua artists under Sahagún, is the fullest ritual description from the pre-Columbian world. Templo Mayor excavations found his cult's material traces among the offerings, and the Calendar Stone's jaguar-sun glyph keeps his first age on the empire's central monument. The ixiptla's flutes themselves survive in museum cases — small clay instruments, some broken exactly as the rite demanded.
lore.syncretism: The friars made him the devil — Sahagún's own informants struggle with the comparison — but the colonial fusion was subtler: he survived in Nahua sorcery as lord of the night and the crossroads, and in the dark side of the Day of the Dead. Scholars compare him with the disruptive, sovereignty-testing trickster found from Loki to Eshu: the power that governs by breaking. Modern Mexican letters reclaimed him as the national shadow — Octavio Paz's 'other Mexico,' the inward, night-facing double of every official sun. Guilhem Olivier's monograph made the point academically: to study Tēzcatlīpōca is to study how the Aztec state understood the necessity of its own negation.
lore.originalScriptNote: In Aztec writing the name is a rebus: the smoking mirror itself — the obsidian disc with its scroll of smoke — worn at his temple or replacing his torn-off foot. The codices draw the name rather than spell it: the smoking mirror is both his glyph and his body.

entries.meaning: He who is made of earth

variants.note: Plain ASCII form

pronunciation.approximation: 'TLAH-lok' — start with the Nahuatl lateral affricate 'tl', hold the first 'a' long, and end with a firm 'ok'.
pronunciation.note: Tlāloc is Tier 1: the macron on ā preserves reconstructed Classical Nahuatl vowel length, and the initial tl- is a single distinctive phoneme impossible in English.

domains.title: Lord of Rain and Mountain
domains.subtitle: Water, Lightning, and Agricultural Life
domains.lead: Tlāloc is the ancient god of rain, lightning, and mountain water. His goggle eyes and jaguar fangs mark him as a being from before the Aztec empire, worshipped at Teotihuacan centuries before Tenochtitlan rose. Without his favour, maize withered and the Fifth Sun turned hostile.

cards.name: Tlalocan
cards.desc: His paradise for those who died by water, lightning, or water-borne disease.

cards.name: Mountain Dweller
cards.desc: He lives in caves and snow-capped peaks where clouds are born and rain is stored.

cards.name: Tlaloque
cards.desc: His multitude of assistants, the little rain gods who brew storms in mountain jars.

cards.name: Maize Lord
cards.desc: Rain is the precondition of corn; Tlāloc controls the timing of planting and harvest.

symbols.name: Goggle eyes
symbols.meaning: Attributes of the storm god across Mesoamerica, perhaps clouds or rain-filled sockets.

symbols.name: Jaguar fangs
symbols.meaning: The predatory power of thunder and the dangerous side of fertility.

symbols.name: Jade and blue paint
symbols.meaning: Signs of water, preciousness, and the verdant east.

symbols.name: Water-lily or frog
symbols.meaning: Creatures of standing water, omens of Tlāloc's presence.

mythology.lead: Tlāloc's myths turn on a single terrifying truth: the same rain that feeds can also drown, strike, or rot. He is generous and punitive in equal measure, and the Mexica state answered his moods with its most terrible gifts.

myths.title: The Abduction of Xōchiquetzal
myths.text: When the world was young, Xōchiquetzal — goddess of flowers, of weaving, and of love's delight — was the wife of Tlāloc. The account preserved in the Leyenda de los Soles tells how Tezcatlipoca, the lord of sorcery, desired her and abducted her to his own realm, and the tale spread widely enough to be retold in Ramírez de Fuenleal's Histoyre du Méchique. The marriage matters because it joins Tlāloc's water to the flowers — rain and blossom, the two halves of agricultural desire — and because its violence names a truth the farmers knew intimately. A god who can lose his bride to sorcery is a god whose gifts can be stolen too: the green world and the water world belong together, but nothing holds them together safely. The myth means that fertility is a marriage forever in danger of abduction.

myths.title: The Destruction of the Fourth Sun
myths.text: The Fourth Sun — the age called 4-Water — was the age of Tlāloc's consort Chalchiuhtlicue, Jade-Her-Skirt, and it ended as a water-god's age must: in a flood. The Leyenda de los Soles tells that the sky broke and rain fell for fifty-two years, until the people of that world were changed into fish and only a remnant survived as the seed of the Fifth Sun. The Histoyre du Méchique deepens the tragedy: Chalchiuhtlicue, falsely accused by her husband the sun of adultery, wept blood for fifty-two years, and the weeping drowned the world. The colonial sources disagree in their details, and modern scholars read the whole Sun-cycle as an Aztec theology of impermanence — every world, even a watery one, is born to end. The myth means that Tlāloc's element is never only the gentle rain of the milpa; it is the universal solvent, and the giver of maize keeps the memory of drowning.

lore.culturalLegacy: Tlāloc's most visible afterlife is the colossal monolith that guards the entrance of Mexico's National Museum of Anthropology. His image has also entered national iconography as a symbol of Mexico's indigenous past and its enduring relationship with water. In an era of drought and water scarcity, Tlāloc returns not as a remote antiquity but as a question: what have we forgotten about the sacred economy of rain?
lore.archaeology: The Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan, excavated from 1978 under Eduardo Matos Moctezuma and Leonardo López Luján, anchors Tlāloc's cult: his blue-painted half of the double pyramid and its offering caches of marine animals, coral, shells and greenstone. His worship is far older than the Aztec — goggle-eyed storm gods appear in the Tepantitla and Tlalocan murals of Teotihuacan (c. 450–650 CE) and in Classic-period Maya art as Chac. The colossal andesite monolith of Coatlinchan (Tlaloc's rain-mountain form, c. 13th–16th century), moved to Mexico City's National Museum of Anthropology in 1964, is among the largest pre-Columbian sculptures known; Mount Tlaloc's summit shrine above the Iztaccíhuatl still receives offerings.
lore.syncretism: The goggle-eyed storm god appears across Mesoamerica under different names: Chac among the Maya, Cocijo among the Zapotec, and Dzahui among the Mixtec. Spanish missionaries equated Tlāloc with Saint John the Baptist and with water-related Christian figures, but the pre-contact cult proved tenacious. Even today, offerings of flowers and copal are left at mountain springs and caves in rural Mexico, often without conscious memory of the Aztec deity behind the practice.
lore.originalScriptNote: The etymology is debated. The most widely accepted reading derives Tlāloc from tlālli ('earth') plus a suffix meaning 'he who has the quality of' or 'he who is made of', giving 'he who is made of earth'—a striking name for a water deity, perhaps because rain rises from the earth and returns to it. Classical Nahuatl macrons mark vowel length; Spanish colonial orthography usually omits them. The final -c is the voiceless velar stop [k].

pronunciation.approximation: 'koh-AH-tlee-kweh' — the 'tl' is one crisp sound, and the macrons stretch the o, a, and i into long vowels.
pronunciation.note: Classical Nahuatl vowel length is the key prosodic feature preserved here. The name is transparently composed of cōātl ('snake, serpent') and īcue ('her skirt'), a possessive form of cueitl 'skirt.' The final labiovelar [kwe] is not a diphthong in English terms but a velar stop followed by a labial glide. Tier 1: the three macrons preserve reconstructed long vowels in the first, second, and fourth syllables.

domains.title: Mother of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Earth, Death, and the Serpent Skirt
domains.lead: Cōātlīcue is the terrible mother at the center of the Aztec cosmos, the earth goddess whose skirt is made of woven serpents and whose necklace of human hands and hearts proclaims her appetite. She is not a gentle nurturer: she is the devouring ground that receives the dead and the fertile soil that demands blood to bear again. In her image, creation and destruction wear the same face.

cards.name: Earth and Fertility
cards.desc: She embodies the fertile and unstable earth; her womb births the stars, the moon, and the sun itself.

cards.name: Mother of the Gods
cards.desc: Called Tēteoh īnnān, she is the progenitor of Huitzilopōchtli, Coyolxāuhqui, and the Centzōn Huītznāhua.

cards.name: Devourer of the Dead
cards.desc: The earth receives corpses and transforms them; her gaping maw and clawed feet mark her as death-in-life.

cards.name: Sacrificial Reciprocity
cards.desc: Blood and hearts are the offerings that sustain her; without them the sun cannot rise and the crops cannot grow.

symbols.name: Serpent skirt
symbols.meaning: Her identifying garment of intertwined snakes, symbolizing the living, dangerous, regenerative earth

symbols.name: Necklace of hands and hearts
symbols.meaning: A garland of sacrificial trophies marking her role as receiver of war-dead and tribute

symbols.name: Two serpent heads
symbols.meaning: Her own head is replaced by facing serpent faces, signifying duality and the gaping maw of the earth

symbols.name: Clawed feet
symbols.meaning: Talons that can dig and grasp, identifying her with predatory earth powers and burial

mythology.lead: Cōātlīcue's best-known myth is the birth of the sun god Huitzilopōchtli, a story of cosmic matricide in which one child is chosen and the others are cast into the sky. The narrative is preserved in the Florentine Codex and colonial Nahuatl histories; it fuses divine genealogy with political theology.

myths.title: The Conception and Birth of Huitzilopōchtli
myths.text: While Cōātlīcue was sweeping on the sacred mountain Coatepec — 'Serpent Mountain' — a ball of brilliant feathers drifted down from the sky, and she placed it in her bosom as she swept. By this sign she conceived, and when her pregnancy showed, her daughter Coyolxāuhqui, the Golden Bells, was shamed and enraged; she incited the Centzōn Huītznāhua, the Four Hundred Southerners, her brothers, to storm the mountain and kill their dishonoured mother. Cōātlīcue's unborn child answered for her. At the very moment of the assault, Huitzilopōchtli emerged fully armed from her womb, wielding the fire-serpent xiuhcoatl as his weapon; he struck off Coyolxāuhqui's head, shattered her body, and sent the Four Hundred tumbling across the heavens, where they became the stars. The account is told in Sahagún's Florentine Codex (Book III) and the Anales de Cuauhtitlan. The myth reads as pure cosmogony — the sun, born of earth, annihilates the moon and the stars at the moment of his rising — and as pure statecraft: the Mexica patron god defeats the older celestial powers at his birthplace.

myths.title: Coatepec at the Center of the World
myths.text: The Mexica mapped the birth myth onto their capital with architectural precision. The Great Temple of Tenochtitlan was Coatepec: Huitzilopōchtli's shrine crowned its summit, and at the foot of his stairway lay the great carved disk of Coyolxāuhqui, eleven feet across, her dismembered limbs exactly where the myth said her brother threw them — at the base of the mountain, forever falling. Cōātlīcue's own shrine stood within the precinct, and the Tlaloc temple shared the pyramid's twin summit, binding rain, earth, and war into one axis. Excavations of the Templo Mayor, begun after the Coyolxāuhqui disk's chance discovery in 1978, revealed this choreography stage by stage, each rebuilding of the city re-stating the myth in stone. The foundation narrative thus did double duty: it explained the cosmos — sun over moon, order over rebellion — and it explained Tenochtitlan itself, whose every enemy could be cast in the role of the Four Hundred and cast down the same stairway.

lore.culturalLegacy: The monumental basalt statue of Cōātlīcue unearthed in Mexico City in 1790 — nearly eight feet of serpents, skull, and clawed feet — became one of the defining images of Aztec art and was displayed beside the Calendar Stone and the Stone of Tīzoc; she now stands in the National Museum of Anthropology as an emblem of Mesoamerican sacred power. The Templo Mayor excavations and the Coyolxāuhqui disk made her myth a public story again, taught in Mexican schools and staged in the Zócalo's Aztec dance revivals. In contemporary Mexican and Chicana thought — from the poetry of Cherríe Moraga to Gloria Anzaldúa's writings on the borderlands — Cōātlīcue has been reclaimed as a symbol of indestructible female creativity, the earth that survives conquest and continues to give birth. Artists and activists invoke her when the land itself is the subject: migration, extraction, the wounded ground that will not stop bearing.
lore.archaeology: The most famous image of Cōātlīcue is the 2.5-meter basalt statue discovered near the Cathedral of Mexico City in 1790, now in the National Museum of Anthropology. Excavations at the Templo Mayor have revealed her shrine at the foot of the temple pyramid, the massive Coyolxāuhqui stone disk, and numerous offerings of seashells, coral, and sacrificial remains. The spatial layout of the sacred precinct dramatizes the myth: Coatepec as the temple, Cōātlīcue as its base, and Huitzilopōchtli's shrine above.
lore.syncretism: Cōātlīcue overlaps functionally with Tlāltēcuhtli, the 'Lord of the Earth,' whose toad-like crouching form receives the same dead, and with Tōnantzin, 'Our Mother,' the more diffuse and venerable earth-mother honoured at shrines across the highlands. The Spanish friars read these overlapping female earth powers through the lens of the Virgin Mary, and the basilica of Guadalupe rose at Tepeyac, a site of Tōnantzin's cult — a fusion that the friar Sahagún himself noticed with dismay. Whether Guadalupe is a successful Christian substitution or a pre-contact devotion wearing a new name is still argued; what is certain is that the earth-mother did not leave her mountain. Modern scholars add a further identification: some read the decapitated Cōātlīcue — head replaced by serpents, womb as the earth's mouth — as the night sky or the devouring earth of myth-time, making her the same power the Mexica worshipped under several names and the Spanish could not name at all.

pronunciation.approximation: 'weet-see-loh-POCH-tlee' — the 'tz' is 'ts,' the 'ch' is as in 'church,' and the final -tli is one released sound.
pronunciation.note: The etymology is debated. The most widely accepted analysis takes huītzilin 'hummingbird' + ōpōchtli 'left/south,' joined by the ligature -o-, with a possible interpretation of the hummingbird as the soul of the warrior returning from death. Tier 1: the three macrons preserve the long vowels of huītzilin and ōpōchtli (per Karttunen), distinctive features the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: The Left-Handed Hummingbird
domains.subtitle: Sun, War, and the Mexica Patron
domains.lead: Huītzilōpōchtli is the southern sun in his hummingbird form, the god who led the Mexica out of Aztlān and guided them to the island where Tenochtitlan would rise. He is the warrior's reward and the warrior's demand: the fallen soldier becomes a hummingbird in his paradise, but the sun itself requires human hearts to rise again. In him, tribal patronage, solar theology, and imperial militarism became inseparable.

cards.name: The Sun at Zenith
cards.desc: He is the sun in its rising and midday strength, the southern brilliance that drives away the stars.

cards.name: War and the Warrior's Death
cards.desc: Dead warriors accompanied the rising sun from the east and were reborn as hummingbirds and butterflies; the cihuateteo, women who died in childbirth, escorted the sun toward the west as feared spirits.

cards.name: Tribal Guide
cards.desc: He appeared to the Mexica leaders in dreams and omens, directing the long migration to the promised land.

cards.name: Sacrificial Sustenance
cards.desc: The sun's daily battle against darkness required nourishers of blood and hearts; Huītzilōpōchtli was the hungry sun itself.

symbols.name: Hummingbird
symbols.meaning: The soul of the dead warrior and the swift, iridescent solar radiance of the god

symbols.name: Xiuhcoatl fire-serpent
symbols.meaning: The flaming weapon Huītzilōpōchtli wields against his sister Coyolxāuhqui

symbols.name: Blue hummingbird helmet
symbols.meaning: The warrior regalia identifying the god in Mexica sculpture and pictorial manuscripts

symbols.name: Templo Mayor
symbols.meaning: His shrine at the summit of the Great Temple, paired with Tlāloc's, marked the center of the Mexica cosmos

mythology.lead: Huītzilōpōchtli's mythology is inseparable from the origin story of the Mexica people. He is the divine ancestor who led the migration, chose the site of Tenochtitlan, defeated the lunar forces arrayed against his mother, and buried an enemy's heart beneath the founding sign of the city.

myths.title: The Birth at Coatepec
myths.text: Cōātlīcue, 'She of the Serpent Skirt,' conceived while sweeping the temple on Coatepec, 'Serpent Mountain': a ball of hummingbird feathers drifted down and she tucked it into her waistband. Her daughter Coyolxāuhqui, 'She of the Golden Bells', and her four hundred brothers, the Centzōn Huītznāhua, were shamed by the unexplained pregnancy and attacked their own mother, Coyolxāuhqui leading the charge with bells ringing on her cheeks. As they closed in, Huītzilōpōchtli sprang from Cōātlīcue's womb fully armed, his face painted, his left leg slender, the xiuhcoatl fire-serpent blazing in his hand (Florentine Codex III). He struck off his sister's head and shattered her body at the mountain's foot — her head he hurled into the sky as the moon, her brothers scattering as the stars. The myth reads like a charter for Mexica sovereignty: the new sun is born by dismembering the old night, and the temple where it happened was rebuilt at the center of Tenochtitlan.

myths.title: The Heart of Copil
myths.text: The migration legend has a dark twin. Copil, son of the sorceress Malinalxōchitl, had sworn vengeance on the Mexica for the wrongs done to his mother; he shadowed the wandering tribe and reported its movements to its enemies, so that everywhere it settled it was attacked. Huītzilōpōchtli ordered his priests to seize the spy, and Copil was sacrificed and his heart cut out. By the god's own command the heart was buried in the reeds of Lake Texcoco — and from it grew a great nopal cactus where no cactus should be, an eagle perched upon it devouring a serpent. That was the sign the god had promised generations before, marking the island of Tenochtitlan (Florentine Codex III; Crónica Mexicayotl). The myth ties the founding sign to a buried enemy: the city's emblem grows out of a heart once set against it — a compact image of how Mexica order converted opposition into ground. The Templo Mayor was raised beside that marsh exactly, and its stairway staged the Coatepec battle in stone.

lore.culturalLegacy: Huītzilōpōchtli remains one of the most recognizable figures of Aztec religion, embodied in the Templo Mayor and the Calendar Stone's central solar imagery. In Mexico today he appears in murals, museum branding, and nationalist iconography, often as a symbol of Mexica identity and pre-Columbian grandeur; Mexico City's coat of arms still shows his founding sign, the eagle on the cactus. Critics and Indigenous scholars caution against romanticizing the militarized theology associated with his cult, even as archaeologists continue to reveal the sophistication of the ritual city built in his honor. The 1978 discovery of the Coyolxāuhqui stone re-centered his birth myth in Mexican public life — and the excavated Templo Mayor, at the heart of the modern capital, keeps the question of what his temple cost permanently on the national agenda.
lore.archaeology: Huītzilōpōchtli's principal shrine was the southern half of the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan, excavated extensively from 1978 onward. The Coyolxāuhqui stone disk at the base of the temple stairway depicts his defeated sister and dramatizes the Coatepec myth; the great serpent heads flanking the stairway repeat the sacred mountain's name in stone. The Calendar Stone (Piedra del Sol), although not exclusively solar, is popularly associated with Huītzilōpōchtli's sun cult. Pictorial manuscripts such as the Codex Borbonicus, Codex Telleriano-Remensis, and Codex Azcatitlan preserve his migration myths and calendar festivals. Recent tunnel and offering excavations at the Templo Mayor have recovered caches of sacrificial victims and sacred objects that give his cult a direct, unflinching material record.
lore.syncretism: Huītzilōpōchtli has no close non-Nahua equivalent; he is a specifically Mexica tribal god elevated to solar supremacy. Within Mesoamerica he shares solar-warrior traits with the Maya sun god K'inich Ajaw and with Mixtec and Zapotec martial deities. After the conquest, Spanish writers sometimes identified him with Hercules or with the Christian devil — comparisons shaped more by revulsion at human sacrifice than by theological correspondence. In the colonial period his festivals were suppressed and his temples dismantled, but his birth story survived in the Florentine Codex, copied out by Nahua scribes under Franciscan supervision. Modern nationalist movements have sometimes celebrated Huītzilōpōchtli as a symbol of indigenous resistance, while other interpreters — including Indigenous scholars — emphasize the imperial violence carried out in his name. Both receptions are true to different layers of the source: a tribal patron turned imperial sun.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SHE-peh' — both vowels are short, the stress falls on the first syllable, and the x is never the English 'ks' or 'z' sound.
pronunciation.note: Xipe is Tier 2: the Classical Nahuatl x stands for [ʃ], but the ASCII string 'xipe' already encodes that phoneme, and the restoration 'Xipe' adds only capitalization — no distinctive letter that ASCII loses. The name means 'the flayed one', from xipehua.

domains.title: Xipe
domains.subtitle: Spring
domains.lead: Xipe — Xipe Tōtec, 'Our Lord the Flayed One' — is the Mexica god of spring, agriculture, and renewal whose priests wore the flayed skins of sacrificial captives for twenty days.
