Beneath the terror lay a farming theology: as the maize seed sheds its husk to sprout, so the god sheds his skin to feed the world. He was also patron of goldsmiths and lord of the west.

cards.name: The Flayed Lord
cards.desc: Xipe Tōtec, 'Our Lord the Flayed One': the deity who wears a second skin, honored from the shaft tombs of West Mexico to the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan.

cards.name: Spring
cards.desc: Patron of the planting season; his festival Tlacaxipehualiztli opened the agricultural year, when the maize sheds its husk (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 2).

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: For twenty days his priests, dressed in flayed skins, walked from house to house — the renewal of the earth enacted in the streets.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form; the restoration returns the god's name to scholarly recognition.

symbols.name: Flayed human skin
symbols.meaning: His defining attribute — a second skin knotted at the wrists and ankles, the visible claim that the old covering must die for new life to emerge.

symbols.name: Maize husk
symbols.meaning: The theological key to his cult: the seed cannot germinate until it sheds its sheath, as the god shed his skin to feed humanity.

symbols.name: Temalacatl
symbols.meaning: The round gladiator stone on which captive warriors fought bound during Tlacaxipehualiztli before being sacrificed in his honor.

symbols.name: Pointed cap (copilli)
symbols.meaning: The conical headgear of his image, marking lordship and linking him to the solar-warrior complex of the western sky.

symbols.name: Chicahuaztli
symbols.meaning: The rattle staff he carries in codex imagery, an instrument of fertility whose sound accompanies the ancestral dances.

symbols.name: Knots at the back
symbols.meaning: In sculpture the god's own skin shows beneath the tied cords of the borrowed skin at his back — death worn as a garment.

mythology.lead: Xipe's mythology survives only in fragments: one late creation story, the great festival book of the Florentine Codex, and the uneasy testimony of Spanish friars. Pieced together, they reveal a god whose apparent cruelty is an agricultural theology — the flayed skin is the seed coat, and the death of the husk is the birth of the maize.

myths.title: The Lord Who Fed the World
myths.text: One late account, preserved in the colonial Histoyre du Mechique, tells that after the great flood the earth gave humanity nothing to eat, and the god Xipe Tōtec flayed himself so that people might be fed; for this reason his images are always shown wearing a human skin. Diego de Durán, who watched the rite's last performances in sixteenth-century Mexico, recorded the same conviction: the god had given his own covering for the world's sustenance. The friars were witnessing an agricultural allegory they only half understood. A maize seed cannot sprout until it splits and sheds its husk; the Mexica made that everyday miracle into a deity who wears the shed skin of a man. The myth teaches that feeding others is never costless: the renewal of the world is paid for with a skin.

myths.title: The Festival of the Flaying
myths.text: The Florentine Codex (Book 2) and Durán describe the great feast of the second veintena, roughly February–March: captives taken in war were dedicated at Yopico, the flayed lord's shrine in the Templo Mayor precinct; bound to the round temalacatl stone, they fought gladiatorial combats against seasoned warriors, then were stretched across the sacrificial stone. The priests then flayed the victims and wore their skins for twenty days, knotted at the wrists and ankles, visiting houses and receiving offerings as living images of the god, until the dried skins were laid away. Sahagún's informants named them tototectin, 'the flayed ones.' The rite horrified the friars and obsesses modern readers, but its logic was exact: at the start of the farming year the city reenacted the first flaying, so that what was done to the god might be done to the seed. Shed skin, shed husk, new season.

lore.culturalLegacy: Xipe Tōtec stands at the center of the modern debate over Aztec sacrifice — read by some as the theological heart of a sophisticated agricultural civilization, by others as evidence of state terror (Clendinnen, Townsend). His images anchor museum collections: the monolithic Xipe of the Templo Mayor Museum, wearing his knotted second skin, is among the most reproduced Aztec sculptures. Nahuatl lexicography (Karttunen, Lockhart) keeps his name etymologically alive, and Danza Azteca troupes across Mexico and the United States still perform in the spring season his festival once owned. For better and worse, the Flayed One is now the world's most recognizable emblem of Mexica religion.
lore.archaeology: The earliest material witness to the flayed-skin complex comes from the shaft tombs of West Mexico (Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit, c. 200 BCE–500 CE), whose ceramic figures wear the flayed skins of other men — proof the imagery predates the Aztec state by centuries. At Tenochtitlan, the INAH excavations of the Templo Mayor precinct (from 1978) located Xipe's shrine, Yopico, and its caches; the Templo Mayor Museum preserves a monolithic Xipe Tōtec whose back shows the wearer's own skin beneath the knotted cords of the second skin. The cult's heartland lay among the Yope of the Guerrero coast and in the Puebla region, and the screenfold Codex Borgia (c. 1500) gives the god's fullest painted dossier.
lore.syncretism: The Dominican Diego de Durán, watching Tlacaxipehualiztli in the decades after the Conquest, was struck that the feast fell near Holy Week — the god who wore a flayed skin commemorated at the season when Christians mourned a god who wore a body and lost it. The friars suppressed the rite, yet its imagery proved durable: in the Puebla and Guerrero regions, masked and costumed dance confraternities — ancestors of today's concheros and Danza Azteca — carried the flayed lord's memory in transformed dress. Twentieth-century revival movements such as the Mexicayotl circle reclaimed Xipe Tōtec as a figure of indigenous identity and renewal rather than barbarism. Comparative religion places him among the world's 'dying vegetation' gods, but the Mexica theology was stranger and more precise: not a god who dies like a plant, but a god who peels like a seed.

pronunciation.approximation: 'METZ-tlee' — the stress falls on the first syllable, and 'tl' is a single sound: tongue pressed to the palate, air escaping at the sides.
pronunciation.note: Metztli is Tier 2: the registered form preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter — a mechanical fact, not a judgment. Classical Nahuatl had a long vowel (mētztli), which philological editions mark with a macron; the lexicon's canonical form carries the plain vowels, so the restoration stands at Tier 2.

domains.title: Metztli
domains.subtitle: Moon
domains.lead: Metztli is the Nahuatl moon — the word means both 'moon' and 'month,' so she is the sky's registrar of time. Colonial sources give the moon several faces: the dimmed twin Tecciztecatl, the dismembered Coyolxauhqui, and Metztli herself, the calm counting presence over night, calendar, and the moist arts of healing.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The Nahuatl word names the moon and the month at once — the sky's light and the calendar's unit in a single breath.

cards.name: Moon
cards.desc: The lunar disk governed the eighteen festival months of the veintena year and the night's vigil alike.

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Kept alive in Nahuatl speech, the temazcal sweatbath, and the rabbit the whole world can still see on the moon's face.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Held as a Unicode domain temple so the moon's name keeps its scholarly form rather than a compromise.

symbols.name: The rabbit on the moon
symbols.meaning: The silhouette cast when a rival's too-bright moon was struck by a hurled rabbit; every Nahua child's explanation of the moon's face.

symbols.name: The lunar disk
symbols.meaning: The moon carried on the back of night-lords in codices; the disk itself is the deity's body.

symbols.name: Golden bells (coyolli)
symbols.meaning: The cheek-bells of Coyolxauhqui, 'She of the Golden Bells,' whose broken body is the moon as defeated rival.

symbols.name: The month
symbols.meaning: Metztli means moon and month alike; in Nahuatl the word is the calendar.

symbols.name: Bath steam
symbols.meaning: The vapour of the temazcal — the moon's moist light brought down into the house of healing and birth.

mythology.lead: The stories told of the Nahua moon are stories about light that must be limited: a twin who shines too bright and is struck by a rabbit, a sister dismembered at the serpent mountain, and a calm disk that keeps the months. The sources disagree about names — Tecciztecatl, Coyolxauhqui, Metztli herself — and the disagreement is the theology: one moon, many meanings.

myths.title: The Leap into the Fire
myths.text: At the dawn of the fifth era the gods assembled at Teotihuacan, and darkness still covered the world. Two volunteers offered themselves to become the lights. Nanahuatzin, the pustule-covered, leapt first into the sacred fire without hesitation; Tecciztecatl, the proud and bejewelled, flinched four times before at last following. The Codex Chimalpopoca's Leyenda de los Soles tells what happened: the humble one rose as the sun, and the splendid one rose as the moon, shining as bright as the day. The gods would not endure two equal lights. One of them seized a rabbit and hurled it into Tecciztecatl's face, dimming his splendour and fixing the dark silhouette on his disk. Sahagún's informants repeat the tale in the Florentine Codex (Book VII), where the moon's brightness is cut back precisely because the world needs contrast — day to work, night to fear and dream. The rabbit flew, the moon dimmed, and the celestial order was set. The myth means that in the Nahua cosmos even glory must accept a wound to become useful: the moon is what remains when a radiant rival is struck down to size.

myths.title: The Dismembered Sister
myths.text: On the serpent mountain of Coatepec, Coatlicue was sweeping when a ball of feathers descended upon her; she conceived, and her four hundred sons, led by Coyolxauhqui — 'She of the Golden Bells' — raged at the shame. As she attacked her mother, Huitzilopochtli sprang fully armed from Coatlicue's womb and cut his sister to pieces, hurling her head into the sky. The Leyenda de los Soles and the Florentine Codex (Book III) agree on the essentials, and the Coyolxauhqui Stone, excavated at the Templo Mayor in 1978, shows her broken body with bells on her cheeks — a moon dismembered by a sun. Scholars caution that the sources never simply call Coyolxauhqui 'Metztli'; rather, Nahua thought distributes the moon among several names. For the city that kept the sun's temple, the myth was political theology: the moon's light is the light of a defeated enemy, hung in the sky as a permanent warning. The myth means the moon is remembered violence — the night ruled by what the day dismembered.

lore.culturalLegacy: Metztli survives first in language: in modern Nahuatl, metztli still means both moon and month — one of the oldest living double meanings in the Americas. The twenty day-signs of the tonalpohualli and the eighteen veintena months kept lunar time central to Mexica civic life, and Durán describes whole cities reordering themselves around each new fire and new month. The temazcal — the sweatbath overseen by the lunar healer Temazcalteci — remains in use across Mexico and the diaspora. In popular culture the rabbit on the moon is told to children to this day, and the name circulates in art, poetry, and identity movements that reclaim Nahuatl heritage. The moon in Mexico is not a dead myth but a working word: to say metztli is still to count the month.
lore.archaeology: Material evidence for the Nahua moon is anchored at the Templo Mayor: the Coyolxauhqui Stone (c. 1473, Phase II), a monolith some 3.25 metres across of the dismembered moon goddess, excavated by Eduardo Matos Moctezuma's team in 1978. Lunar deities carry the moon disk on their backs in codices such as the Codex Borgia and the Codex Fejérváry-Mayer. The textual evidence is equally material: Sahagún's Florentine Codex (Books I, III, VI, VII) was compiled 1555–1576 in Nahuatl and Spanish with Nahua elders, and the Codex Chimalpopoca preserves the Leyenda de los Soles — both manuscripts, not folklore collections, and the core witnesses for the leap into the fire and the rabbit hurled to dim the moon.
lore.syncretism: Under Spanish rule the moon's cult did not end but changed costume. The Immaculata stands on a crescent, and the Virgin of Guadalupe keeps lunar imagery in her mantle's folds. Maya parallels — Ix Chel of the Dresden and Madrid codices — kept the same lunar triangle of weaving, healing, and flood that the Nahua sources distribute across Metztli, Temazcalteci, and the moon-rabbit. In the bilingual centuries metztli became the Spanish word's quiet rival: luna names the body, metztli names the reckoning. Modern Nahuatl speakers still say metztli for both moon and month, and Mexican folklore still points out the rabbit on the moon's face. The syncretism is less a conquest than a translation: the Virgin inherits the crescent; the rabbit keeps the disk.

pronunciation.approximation: SHAH-ngoh — low 'sha', then a sharp high 'ngoh' with the final syllable slightly nasal.
pronunciation.note: Ṣàngó is Tier 1: the dot below ṣ and the acute accent on ó are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the acute preserving the high tone of the final syllable. The dot below ṣ marks the historical/orthographic distinction of the Yoruba 's' series.

domains.title: Thunder and Justice
domains.subtitle: Fire, Royalty, and the Drum
domains.lead: Ṣàngó is the thunder-god and the deified fourth king of the Ọ̀yọ́ Empire — the fire that strikes from heaven and the drumbeat that brings the possessed to their feet. His justice is public and swift: the oath-breaker, the thief, and the liar hear him before they see him. In life a warrior-king, in death he became the storm itself.

cards.name: Lightning
cards.desc: He strikes the liar, the thief, and the oath-breaker; his fire is both weapon and verdict.

cards.name: Double-Headed Axe
cards.desc: The ọ̀ṣẹ́ Ṣàngó — the double-axe dance wand, his emblem of royal justice and the power to split heaven and earth.

cards.name: Royal Charisma
cards.desc: He was king before he was god; his worship links divine power to political authority.

cards.name: Drum and Dance
cards.desc: The bàtá drum calls him down; possession by Ṣàngó begins in the shoulders and feet.

symbols.name: Thunderstones (ẹ̀dùn àrá)
symbols.meaning: 'Thunder stones' — prehistoric stone axes kept in his shrines as the thunderbolts he hurled to earth; collecting one is collecting his signature.

symbols.name: Double-headed axe (ọ̀ṣẹ́ Ṣàngó)
symbols.meaning: The emblem of his kingship and his power to render judgment; carved dance wands of it are carried by the possessed.

symbols.name: Bàtá drum
symbols.meaning: The hourglass drum whose pitch bends under the arm — the drum language that summons him and encodes the history of Ọ̀yọ́.

symbols.name: Red and white beads
symbols.meaning: The colours of fire, blood, and royal authority; his initiates wear them in double strands.

mythology.lead: Ṣàngó's mythology moves between the palace and the sky. He is a king who could not govern his own household, a husband of powerful and dangerous wives, and a storm whose justice is as dramatic as its noise.

myths.title: The Fourth Aláàfin of Ọ̀yọ́
myths.text: Ṣàngó was the fourth Aláàfin — king — of Ọ̀yọ́, and the traditions collected by Samuel Johnson (The History of the Yorubas, 1921), checked against the chronicles analysed by Robin Law (The Oyo Empire, 1977), make him a historical ruler later wrapped in divinity. His capital was at Koso, and his cult grew from the worship of a deified king: subsequent Aláàfins ruled as his heirs, and the Ṣàngó festival at Ọ̀yọ́ remains an act of state as much as of religion. The sources disagree about his end — some say he hanged himself in defeat, others that his own fire consumed him and he ascended bodily — and the people of Koso answered the shameful version with a proud folk etymology: Koso, they said, means 'he did not hang'. Whatever happened in history, mythology turned a failed king into an eternal verdict from the sky.

myths.title: The Fire That Consumed the Palace
myths.text: Johnson's chronicle credits Ṣàngó with a fearful sorcery: charms that breathed fire on his enemies. In the most told episode, his own overreaching turned the weapon inward — the fire that burned his foes spread through his palace and his household, and the king who had terrorised Ọ̀yọ́ with thunder-magic died, or fled, by the same element (Johnson 1921; Law 1977 treats the traditions with scholarly reserve). Later Ifá verses and praise-chants amplify the tale into cosmic register: Ṣàngó did not merely wield fire, he was fire, and he left the earth by immolating himself into the storm. The palace fires of the chronicle became, in worship, the lightning of the sky. The legend reads like a parable of charisma — the force that makes a king irresistible is the force that finally consumes him, and only deification survives the burning.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ṣàngó is one of the most recognisable orishas in the African diaspora. His image strides through Caribbean and Latin American art, music, and festival; his bàtá drumming — carried by Cuban santeros to stages worldwide — has fed into jazz, salsa, and contemporary percussion. In Nigeria the Ṣàngó Festival in Ọ̀yọ́ draws thousands each year, and the Aláàfin still keeps ritual ties to the deified founder of his line. Politically, Ṣàngó remains a badge of Yoruba royal authority and cultural pride; spiritually, he embodies the demand that justice be as visible and unavoidable as a thunderclap. His double-headed axe has become an emblem of Afro-Atlantic religion itself, recognisable from Lagos to Havana.
lore.archaeology: The Ṣàngó cult centre at Koso, near Ọ̀yọ́ in present-day Nigeria, preserves the ritual memory of the deified king, and the Ṣàngó festival re-enacts his kingship annually. Prehistoric stone celts — the thunderstones his priests collected as his spent bolts — are held in shrines and museum collections; so are brass double-headed axes, bàtá drums, and the red-and-white bead regalia of his initiates. Diaspora terreiros and ilés conserve his dance wands and thunderstone altars, making Ṣàngó one of the best-documented royal cults in African religious history.
lore.syncretism: In Cuban Santería, Ṣàngó became Changó, one of the most beloved orishas, merged with Santa Bárbara because of her lightning, her tower, and her protection of the faithful — his feast, 4 December, is hers as well. In Brazilian Candomblé he is Xangô, syncretised in the Ketu nation with São Jerônimo, the thunder-voiced doctor of the Church. The diaspora preserved and amplified what Ọ̀yọ́ began: the union of kingship, rhythm, and storm. Where the old empire fell to the Fulani wars of the nineteenth century, its thunder-god reigned on in Havana, Salvador, and Brooklyn — a royal cult that lost its palace and gained an ocean.

variants.note: Plain ASCII form

pronunciation.approximation: 'aw-YAH' — begin low in the chest on 'aw', then rise sharply to 'YAH'.
pronunciation.note: Ọya is Tier 1: the dot below marks a phonemic vowel distinction (open o versus close o) — a diacritic the ASCII form loses. Tonal variation, though crucial to Yoruba meaning, is not registrable in the DNS root zone.

domains.title: Lady of the Winds
domains.subtitle: Storms, Change, and the Cemetery Gate
domains.lead: Ọya is the orixá of wind, lightning, and radical change — the storm that tears down what is finished so that something new can grow. She is the only female warrior to ride into battle beside the thunder-god Ṣàngó, and she guards the threshold between the marketplace and the grave. Her name means 'she tore', and tearing is her ministry.

cards.name: Whirlwind
cards.desc: She arrives as a sudden gust that uproots trees and old assumptions.

cards.name: Warrior Queen
cards.desc: Wife of Ṣàngó and fearless general, she carries a sword and the irukere fly-whisk.

cards.name: Guardian of the Dead
cards.desc: She rules the cemetery gate and guides souls through transformation.

cards.name: Marketplace
cards.desc: Crossroads and markets are her terrain, where chance and commerce meet change.

symbols.name: Irukere (fly-whisk)
symbols.meaning: Her emblem of authority, whisked to summon and direct the winds and to sweep away what is stale.

symbols.name: Sword or machete
symbols.meaning: The blade that cuts away the obsolete and defends the community; swung by her possessed dancers at full speed.

symbols.name: Buffalo horns
symbols.meaning: Her kinship with the buffalo — the storm's brute force joined to maternal ferocity; in some rites the buffalo is her mount.

symbols.name: Nine colours
symbols.meaning: Her necklaces and cloth run to nine colours, especially burgundy and brown — the shades of the storm-lit earth and the graveyard's laterite.

mythology.lead: Ọya's stories are told in Ifá divination, Candomblé praise-songs, and the oral traditions of the Yoruba and their diaspora. She is change embodied, and her myths turn on thresholds — between sky and earth, market and grave, marriage and war.

myths.title: She Who Tore
myths.text: Her very name is her biography: Ọya derives from the verb yà, 'to tear, to split apart' (Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba, 1958). The name is a title of office. In ritual and story she tears whatever has outlived its time — she rips the old cloth of custom when it smothers the living, splits the storm front when the air has stood too still, and opens the ground between the marketplace of the living and the cemetery of the dead. To be mounted by Ọya in possession is to be unmade and remade: devotees whirl, brandish swords, and speak with the tearing voice of the wind. The mythology is exact about its own meaning: transformation is not a gentle persuasion but a rupture, and what refuses to be changed peaceably will be changed violently.

myths.title: The Secret of Lightning
myths.text: Ọya was wife and battlefield companion to Ṣàngó, and the traditions agree that she learned from him what no other orisha was taught — the secret of fire and lightning. Verger (Notes sur le Culte des Orisa et Vodun, 1981) records that when Ṣàngó's fortunes collapsed and he fled his kingdom, Ọya did not flee with him meekly: she tore at the sky with her winds, and some accounts say she cast herself into the river that bears her name, the Niger (Odò Ọya), rather than outlive his disgrace. Other lineages, especially in Cuba, make her the guardian of that disgrace's relics. The sources disagree about her end and do not care to reconcile; what matters is the pattern — she is the only one who shared the thunderer's power and the only one who did not abandon him. Her lightning is inherited, and inheritance is loyalty.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ọya remains one of the most honoured orixás in the African diaspora. She strides through the literature of the Black Atlantic — from Cuban letra del año pronouncements to Brazilian samba-enredo lyrics — as the patroness of the turnaround: the queen who loses the battle and wins the war. Her colours fly at every Candomblé ijexá; her swords flash in the hands of possessed dancers from Salvador to Havana. Feminist and womanist theologians have claimed her as a model of female force that is not domesticated by marriage, motherhood, or mourning. In an age of climate change and social upheaval, Ọya speaks with uncomfortable relevance: the storm is not cruelty — it is the only way the forest clears its own dead wood.
lore.archaeology: Ọya's material traces ride the storm: buffalo horns and iron swords from Candomblé shrines in Bahia, nine-strand bead necklaces in burgundy and brown, and the fly-whisks (irukere) whisked by her initiates, conserved in museum and terreiro collections on both sides of the Atlantic. In Yorubaland her presence is read in the Niger's storm seasons and in market-edge shrines where traders leave offerings against sudden loss — an archaeology of thresholds rather than temples.
lore.syncretism: In the Afro-Atlantic religions Ọya became Iansã in Brazilian Candomblé, syncretised with Saint Barbara and Saint Teresa — saints of lightning, of decisive action, of the fortress under siege. In Cuban Santería she is Oyá, paired with the Virgen de la Candelaria; her nine-coloured cloth and buffalo horns identify her instantly in any botánica. In Haitian Vodou her winds blow through the Gede's cemetery humour, and in New Orleans Voodoo she survives as a spirit of storms and sudden reversals. Wherever Yoruba people were dispersed, Ọya travelled as the orixá of necessary upheaval — her whirlwinds, one might say, crossed the Atlantic itself and have not stopped turning since.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is Yoruba: Ọya. Yoruba is a tonal language; the standard written form uses a dot below ọ to distinguish open [ɔ] from close [o]. The full tonal spelling is Òyá (low tone, then high tone), but tone marks are not registrable in the DNS root zone. The meaning 'she tore' derives from the verb yà. PUNICODEX therefore registers Ọya with the dot below, preserving the distinctive open vowel.

variants.note: Fully tone-marked dictionary form with the initial low tone (Abraham). Written Yoruba routinely omits tone marks.

steps: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality.
The name Ọ̀ṣun is composed of the low-tone /ɔ̀/ prefix plus ṣun, a root associated with the river and the goddess.
The underdot distinguishes /ɔ/ and /ʃ/ from their plain counterparts; tone marks distinguish lexical meaning.
The Unicode restoration Ọ̀ṣun preserves tone and vowel quality; the ASCII form loses both.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-SHOON — start low on 'aw', then rise to a bright, slightly nasal 'SHOON'.
pronunciation.note: Ọṣun is Tier 1: the dots below ọ and ṣ are distinctive features the ASCII form loses. The dot below ọ marks the open [ɔ] vowel.

domains.title: Sweetness of the River
domains.subtitle: Love, Freshwater, and Fertility
domains.lead: Ọṣun is the orixá of the river that bears her name, which flows through Oshogbo in southwestern Nigeria. She rules love that persuades rather than commands, fertility that arrives as pleasure, and the cool freshwater that answers Ṣàngó's fire. When the male orishas tried to build the world without her, their work collapsed until her sweetness completed it.

cards.name: Freshwater
cards.desc: Rivers, streams, and springs are her body; she governs fertility, bathing, and healing.

cards.name: Love and Seduction
cards.desc: Honey, perfume, and gold are her tools; she wins by making herself irresistible.

cards.name: Women's Power
cards.desc: She represents the agency of women in a world that often forgets to ask them.

cards.name: Fertility
cards.desc: Barren women, failing crops, and blocked creativity all come under her care.

symbols.name: Brass fan (àbẹ̀bẹ̀)
symbols.meaning: Her emblem of beauty, cooling breeze, and ceremonial authority; swung at her festivals to cool and summon her.

symbols.name: Honey
symbols.meaning: The sweetness of her words and the bait of her persuasion; offered to her river and placed on the tongues of the possessed.

symbols.name: Yellow beads and gold
symbols.meaning: Her colours, associated with the river's sunlight, brass, and material prosperity.

symbols.name: Peacock
symbols.meaning: A diaspora emblem of her beauty, pride, and watchful eye.

symbols.name: Five (or seventeen) brass bracelets
symbols.meaning: Her gleaming armlets, rattled in dance; the number varies between lineages, each telling of a river bend she governs.

mythology.lead: Ọṣun's stories are told in Ifá verses, river rituals, and the annual Oshogbo festival. They centre on the power of sweetness, the necessity of women's wisdom, and the river as a living goddess.

myths.title: The Creation That Failed Without Her
myths.text: When the orishas set out to organise the world, the men among them — Ọbatalá, Ọ̀gún, Ṣàngó and the rest — took the tasks for themselves and ignored Ọṣun, the only woman in their number. Everything they attempted failed: what they built collapsed, what they planted withered, and their councils came to nothing. At last, alarmed, they asked Olódùmarè what was wrong; the high god told them they had left Ọṣun out. They apologised and invited her in, and she completed with her sweetness what their strength could not finish. The tale, told in oral and Ifá-related sources and made famous in print by the essays collected in Murphy and Sanford's Òṣun across the Waters (2001), is a charter for the necessity of feminine power: a world designed without women is not merely unjust — it does not work.

myths.title: The River Chooses a City
myths.text: Tradition holds that Oshogbo was founded when the river goddess made herself known to the town's first rulers and claimed the grove along her banks as her dwelling. The Òṣun River is not her symbol but her body, and the seventy-odd acres of forest around it — the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2005 — are her palace (Drewal, Yoruba Ritual, 1992; Murphy and Sanford 2001). Every August the Osun-Osogbo Festival carries the king, the priestesses, and thousands of devotees to the river with flowers, coins, and prayers; the grove's twentieth-century sculptures, begun under Susanne Wenger, extended the sanctuary with monumental art. Priestesses of the river, the Iya Osun, keep the grove's shrines and guard its ancient trees. The myth of the choosing river makes a civic claim: Oshogbo exists because Ọṣun consented to live there.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ọṣun is one of the most widely honoured orishas on earth. The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove is a UNESCO World Heritage site, one of the last great sacred forests of the Yoruba; her August festival is among West Africa's largest religious gatherings. Her image flows through Nigerian film, Brazilian Carnival, Cuban Santería altars, and global feminist spirituality — the Nigerian-American novelist and essayists of the diaspora invoke her as a patron of women's authority. The phrase 'honey in the mouth' captures her ethics: that persuasion, beauty, and pleasure are legitimate and necessary forms of power. In an age that splits love from politics, Ọṣun insists they cannot be separated — and that the world built without her will always collapse.
lore.archaeology: The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove is the principal living site: shrines, palaces of the priestesses, and the river itself, enriched in the twentieth century by the monumental sculptures of the New Sacred Art movement associated with Susanne Wenger. Brass àbẹ̀bẹ̀ fans, gold jewellery, and yellow-bead necklaces from Yoruba shrines are conserved in Nigerian and diaspora collections, and the grove's restoration is itself a documented episode in the modern archaeology of African sacred art.
lore.syncretism: In Brazilian Candomblé, Ọṣun became Oxum, the golden orixá of fresh water and wealth, syncretised with Our Lady of the Conception. In Cuban Santería she is Ochún, paired with Our Lady of Charity (La Virgen de la Caridad del Cobre), the patroness of Cuba — a natural identification, for the Virgin is dark-skinned, wears gold, and is found in the water. In Haitian Vodou she overlaps with Ezili, though Ezili carries additional Fon and Kongo inheritances. The diaspora consistently preserves her triad of beauty, money, and the river; where her river could not cross the ocean, her devotees gave her every stream and bathhouse in the New World.

variants.note: Fully tone-marked dictionary form (Abraham). Written Yoruba routinely omits tone marks; the underdots are the obligatory phonemic marks.
English/Wikipedia convention: tone-marked without underdots

The underdot marks the open vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ and the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/; these are the obligatory phonemic marks.
Tone marks (grave low, acute high) are fully written in dictionaries but routinely omitted in everyday Yoruba writing.
The owned Unicode form preserves the underdots and the tone marks the domain could carry; the fully tone-marked dictionary form is documented in the variants and here.

pronunciation.approximation: eh-SHOON — start low on 'eh', rise to a bright, slightly nasal 'SHOON'.
pronunciation.note: Ẹṣu is Tier 1: the dots below ẹ and ṣ are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the dot below ẹ marking the open [ɛ] vowel. The name is often wrongly conflated with the Christian devil; in Yoruba religion he is a necessary divine functionary, not an evil being. Tone conventions for the name vary between dictionaries (Èṣù / Èṣú); written Yoruba routinely omits tones.

domains.title: Guardian of the Crossroads
domains.subtitle: Trickery, Messenger of the Gods, and Opener of Roads
domains.lead: Ẹṣu is the divine linguist and guardian of the crossroads — the orisha who carries sacrifice upward and meaning sideways. He is neither good nor evil in the Christian sense: he is indeterminacy itself, the pun that undoes a contract, the road not taken. No prayer reaches heaven without him, and no promise is safe from him.

cards.name: Crossroads
cards.desc: Every intersection is his altar; every choice is his domain.

cards.name: Divine Messenger
cards.desc: He carries prayers and sacrifices to the orishas and brings their answers back — the postal system of the sacred, and he expects to be paid.

cards.name: Trickster
cards.desc: He exposes hypocrisy and punishes those who forget that language has two edges.

cards.name: Opener of Roads
cards.desc: No enterprise begins safely without his permission; he removes or places obstacles.

symbols.name: Crossroads stone
symbols.meaning: A small cement head or stone placed at doorways and intersections as his dwelling — the most ubiquitous African-diaspora religious icon, and the one most often misidentified by outsiders as diabolical.

symbols.name: Red and black beads
symbols.meaning: The colors of danger, desire, and the boundary between life and death — Ẹṣu dressed as the threshold itself.

symbols.name: Cigar and rum
symbols.meaning: Pleasures of the threshold; he accepts what others deny, which is why the moralizing chroniclers never forgave him.

symbols.name: Phallus or trickster stick
symbols.meaning: Vital force, mischief, and the disruptive energy that starts change — the door that opens because it is pushed.

mythology.lead: Ẹṣu's mythology is a catalogue of tricks, translations, and tests, preserved in the Odu Ifá corpus and recorded in the twentieth century by Bascom, Idowu, and Verger. Every story is an anatomy of a single insight: meaning is unstable, and the god of instability is its only honest guardian.

myths.title: The Two Friends and the Two-Colored Hat
myths.text: Two farmers worked adjoining fields, and they were so close that they swore an oath: whatever fortune came to one would be shared with the other. Ẹṣu, walking between their farms one day, wore a hat that was red on one side and black on the other. After he had passed, the first farmer said: 'Did you see the man in the red hat?' The second answered: 'He wore a black hat.' Each was certain; each called the other a liar; the quarrel rose from words to blows, and the friendship — and the oath — lay in ruins. Then Ẹṣu returned, turned his hat around, and showed them its two faces, and both men saw at once that each had told the truth and each had been wrong. The tale, preserved in the Odu Ifá corpus and recorded by William Bascom (Ifa Divination, 1969), is the trickster's masterpiece of instruction: certainty is the tribute certainty pays to itself, and the man who will not doubt his own eyes can be set at war with his best friend by a piece of headwear.

myths.title: The Messenger Who Must Be Fed First
myths.text: Every Yoruba sacrifice follows one law: Ẹṣu is served first. The teaching is framed as history in the tradition recorded by E. Bolaji Idowu (Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief): when the orishas received their offices from the high god, each asked for a domain — sea, iron, rivers, wind — but Ẹṣu asked for nothing, because his office was already total: he stands between all offices. He is the door. A sacrifice carried to Ọṣun, to Ṣàngó, to any power at all must pass Ẹṣu's post, and a messenger who is not acknowledged stops the letter. Hence the first pinch of every offering is laid at the crossroads, at the foot of the market wall, or before his stones. The theology is exact: communication is not automatic. Between any human intention and any divine hearing stands a medium — neutral, fallible, and owed a fee — and a religion that forgets its postman simply loses its mail.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ẹṣu's legacy is double. On one hand, he is among the most misunderstood African deities in the world, repeatedly equated with Satan by outsiders — a misreading so durable that early scholars of Candomblé were still apologizing for him in print a century after abolition. On the other hand, he is indispensable to Afro-Atlantic religion and a powerful symbol in diaspora literature and philosophy: writers from Léopold Sédar Senghor to Wole Soyinka and Henry Louis Gates Jr. have used Ẹṣu/Esu/Eshu as a figure for signification, translation, and the multiplicity of meaning — Gates's Signifying Monkey makes him the very model of African-American literary criticism. In ritual he remains the first orisha honoured in every ceremony, from Lagos to Havana to Bahia.
lore.archaeology: Ẹṣu is represented materially by small cement or stone heads placed at crossroads, doorways, and market entrances throughout Yorubaland and the diaspora; the oldest documented examples are the sculpted stones photographed by researchers in the early twentieth century, and the doorway heads of Bahia photographed by Verger. Red-and-black bead necklaces, cigars, rum bottles, and phallic staffs fill Candomblé and Santería collections, and the cooking pot (asebere) of Exu sits at the entrance of every terreiro. Colonial and missionary accounts frequently misidentified these figures as diabolical — a misreading itself preserved in the archive.
lore.syncretism: Colonial missionaries and enslavers misunderstood Ẹṣu as the devil, an equation that has caused centuries of distortion — in Brazil his name was bowdlerized in print as 'Exu' and his images destroyed, while in Cuba he was split in two: Eleguá, the child-like road-opener of Santería, and the sterner Exú of the Palo traditions. Yet the diaspora traditions kept what the missionaries could not read: that he is essential, honored first in every ceremony, and never optional. The Yoruba original is not demonic; he is the necessary principle of ambiguity that makes choice, language, and sacrifice possible. In the twentieth century, African and diaspora writers recovered him as a figure of hermeneutics — the god who proves that no message arrives unchanged.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-GOON, low tone on the first syllable, high on the last.
pronunciation.note: Ògún carries Yoruba's tonal low-high melody: ò with the grave (low tone), gún with the acute (high) — the tones are phonemic, and the restoration keeps both exactly as the language requires. The name is bound to the word for iron (irin) in his praise-names: "Ogun, master of iron, the one who clears the road."

domains.title: The Road-Opener
domains.subtitle: Iron, War, Labour, and the First Path through the Forest
domains.lead: Ògún is the orisha of iron and of every road iron opens: the hunter who cleared the primordial forest so the gods could descend, the smith who arms the farmer and the warrior alike, and the patron of every worker who makes a living by metal — from the blacksmith to the surgeon to the driver.

cards.name: The Cutlass
cards.desc: His tool and emblem: the blade that clears the forest path — creation by cutting.

cards.name: The Forge
cards.desc: The smith's fire: iron is his body, and every smithy his shrine.

cards.name: The First Road
cards.desc: He hacked the road through the primal forest that let the orisha reach the earth.

cards.name: The Dog
cards.desc: His companion and sacrifice — the hunter's faithful one, honoured at his festivals.

symbols.name: The cutlass
symbols.meaning: The path-making blade — technology as the opener of ways

symbols.name: The anvil
symbols.meaning: The forge's heart, where his power is hammered into tools

symbols.name: The palm wine
symbols.meaning: His drink — offered by hunters and smiths for coolness and courage

symbols.name: The dog
symbols.meaning: The hunter's companion and the sacrifice his festivals accept — loyalty that follows the road even into the earth

symbols.name: The iron itself
symbols.meaning: His praise-names say it plainly: the metal is the god's body and his dwelling among men

mythology.lead: Ògún's myths are the Yoruba meditation on power: the strength that clears the way for everyone, and the rage that, unmastered, turns on its own town.

myths.title: The First Road
myths.text: When the orisha first sought to descend from heaven to the unfinished earth, the primordial forest stood unbroken and no god could pass — not even the greatest among them, for all their wisdom. Ògún took his cutlass and cut the road through, and the gods followed him down (the tradition preserved by E. B. Idowu in Olódùmarè, 1962, and sung in the Ifá odù Ogunda, ‘Ògún creates’). The detail the storytellers never drop is the technology: where other cosmogonies begin with a word or a combat, the Yoruba world begins with a blade — creation as clearance, being as path. Yet ritual order keeps its own counsel: Èṣù-Ẹlẹ́gbá, not Ògún, is propitiated first in every rite, for the road-opener opens ways that others must keep. The myth encodes an entire philosophy of work: civilisation is something hacked out of chaos, by someone, with a tool — and the hacker is owed his portion forever after.

myths.title: The King of Irè
myths.text: Installed as king of Irè, Ògún came one festival day to find his people silent — the honours due him unperformed (the Irè tradition recorded by Idowu, Olódùmarè). In his rage he drew the sword and cut down his own townsfolk, and the slaughter ended only when he saw his own son among the fallen. Coming to himself, he declared that he would walk no more among men, and sank into the earth — remaining, as the praise-songs say, in the iron itself. Every Ògún festival at Irè replays the king’s coming and going: the worshippers greet him with noise and honour precisely where the myth says silence once killed. The myth does not excuse the rage; it institutionalises the apology — a god whose festival is a town’s vow never again to repeat the silence that set him off.

lore.culturalLegacy: Nigeria's Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka is his most famous devotee: Ògún is the patron of Soyinka's art — the road-maker who is also the destroyer — and the essay "The Fourth Stage" and the novel The Road are his modern liturgy. Ògún state in Nigeria bears his name; his praise-names echo in the foundries and mechanics' yards of every Yoruba city, where a splash of palm wine on the anvil still opens the working day.
lore.archaeology: Yorubaland is one of Africa's oldest iron-working regions: the smelting furnaces of the Nsukka plateau (Lejja) date the craft back over two thousand years, and the guild-smithies of the forest belt kept the ritual side — the first iron of a furnace smelted with prayers to Ògún. His shrines are often the anvil itself; the great festivals of Ire and of Ọndó preserve the masquerades and the dog-sacrifice described in the earliest ethnographies, and the odù Ogunda verses are still divined daily by babaláwo across the Yoruba world.
lore.syncretism: The Middle Passage carried him across the Atlantic, where the iron god found new irons: in Cuban Santería he is Oggún, syncretized with Saint Peter (keeper of the keys — the metal of heaven's gate) or Saint George; in Brazilian Candomblé, Ògún is Saint George of the dragon-slaying spear; in Haitian Vodou he is Ogou Feray, the warrior-loa of the forge and the soldier's flag. The saints changed the face; the iron, the road, and the dog kept the god.
lore.originalScriptNote: Yoruba is written in Latin letters with tone marks — the orthography the restoration preserves: Ò (low tone) and ú (high tone) are the name as spoken. In the Ifá divination corpus his signs live in the odù Ogunda, "Ogun creates," one of the sixteen principal odù: the god written into the divination system itself.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-bah-TAH-LAH — low on 'aw-bah', then high on 'TAH-LAH'.
pronunciation.note: Ọbàtálá is Tier 1: the dot below ọ and the acute accents on the final two syllables are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the acutes preserving high tones. The dot below ọ marks the open [ɔ] vowel, a phonemic distinction essential to Yoruba.

domains.title: King of the White Cloth
domains.subtitle: Creation, Purity, and Peaceful Judgment
domains.lead:
Ọbàtálá is the orixá who shapes humanity. While Olódùmarè breathes the soul into the body, Ọbàtálá is the sculptor who moulds the limbs, the one whose hands first pressed cool clay into human form. He is the eldest of the orishas in many accounts, the patron of white cloth, purity, peace, and the aged. His voice is soft, his judgments slow, and his anger terrible precisely because it is so rare.

He is also the guardian of those whom the world calls imperfect: the disabled, the deformed, the albino. In Yoruba thought, these are not mistakes; they are Ọbàtálá's own children, marked by his hand.

cards.name: Creator of Bodies
cards.desc: He moulds human form from earth; Olódùmarè alone gives it breath.

cards.name: White Cloth
cards.desc: Spotless garments, white beads, and cool water mark his altars and his devotees.

cards.name: Peaceful Judgment
cards.desc: He settles disputes with patience; his curses fall on the unjustly proud.

cards.name: Patron of the Vulnerable
cards.desc: The disabled and the elderly are his special children; harming them offends him directly.

symbols.name: White cloth
symbols.meaning: Purity, coolness, and the veil between the human and the divine.

symbols.name: Snail shell
symbols.meaning: The slow, deliberate pace of Ọbàtálá's wisdom and the spiral of creation.

symbols.name: Ivory or white bead necklace
symbols.meaning: His sacred colour and the wealth of patience.

symbols.name: Calabash of cool water
symbols.meaning: Coolness of temperament; the antidote to hot anger.

mythology.lead: Ọbàtálá's mythology turns on creation, sobriety, and the cost of pride — preserved in the corpus of Ifá divination poetry (odu), in the oral histories of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, and, across the Atlantic, in the liturgies of Candomblé and Santería, where the details shift with each retelling. He is the elder who knows that making life is more difficult than destroying it.

myths.title: The Moulding of Humanity
myths.text: When Olódùmarè, the supreme God, resolved to people the earth, Ọbàtálá — also known as Ọ̀rìṣànlá, 'the great orisha' — took up the making of bodies. From clay given him by Olódùmarè he moulded each human form with care, and Olódùmarè breathed the emí, the living soul, into what his servant's hands had shaped. But one day, working, Ọbàtálá drank too much palm wine, and the figures he shaped that afternoon came out twisted, incomplete, unfinished. Olódùmarè gave them life anyway, and they remain among us — the disabled, the albino, the differently formed. From that day Ọbàtálá forbade palm wine to all who serve him and took these children of the drunken afternoon as his own, to be honored and never mocked. The myth is told across the Ifá corpus and the diaspora; its point is exact — even the maker's failure is gathered into the design, and the people the world calls broken are the ones heaven claims first.

myths.title: The Contest for Ilé-Ifẹ̀
myths.text: Yoruba cosmogony tells that Olódùmarè once charged the orishas with creating solid earth from the primordial waters, giving them a chain, a hen, and a bag of sand for the work. The mission fell to Ọbàtálá, who climbed down the chain — but paused on the way, drank palm wine, fell into sleep, and dropped the bag of sand. Odùduwà, coming after, caught it, scattered the sand upon the waters, and set the hen to scratching: where the hen scratched, the first dry land rose, and on it Odùduwà founded Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the city of origin from which the Yoruba kingdoms descend. The sources disagree on details — some traditions name Ọbàtálá as the intended creator, others give the mission to Odùduwà from the first — and the rivalry between elder orisha and founding king became a standing theme of Ifá poetry. The myth encodes history as well as theology: Ifẹ̀'s supremacy is not brute primacy but a succession debated, remembered, and argued over in verse for a thousand years.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ọbàtálá's influence extends far beyond formal religion. The Yoruba value of ìtẹ̀lọ́rùn — patience, coolness of heart — is modelled on his temperament. In the African diaspora his white garments appear in Candomblé, Santería (Lukumí), and Trinidad Orisha; the feast days of Oxalá are among the most important in the Bahian ritual year. Artists and disability-rights advocates have reclaimed him as a divine patron of bodily difference, while environmental thinkers see in his clay-and-breath creation story an early recognition that matter and spirit are not separate. Every white garment worn at a Candomblé ceremony is his signature still.
lore.archaeology: No temple of Ọbàtálá has been excavated as such; his archaeology is embedded in the urban fabric of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, where excavations in the twentieth century uncovered shrine deposits and the naturalistic terracotta and bronze heads of the twelfth–fifteenth centuries — the art of the city he is credited with founding. What does not survive is the perishable core of his cult: white cloth, offerings of cool water, and palm-wine libations leave no trace in the Yoruba soil. Across the Atlantic, the material record is richer — his white bead necklaces, snail shells, ivory bracelets, and calabashes are conserved in collections of Afro-Brazilian religion in São Paulo and Salvador and in the museums of Afro-Cuban religion in Havana and Matanzas — while the Ifá corpus itself, recited by diviners to this day, preserves the creation narrative in an unbroken oral line older than any of them.
lore.syncretism: In Brazilian Candomblé, Ọbàtálá became Oxalá, often syncretised with Jesus Christ in his role as the white-robed saviour and with the dove as a symbol of peace. In Cuban Santería he remains Obatalá, father of the white beads, and is divided into youthful and aged paths (Obatalá Ayáguna and Obatalá Orishánlá; Oxaguiã and Oxalufã in Brazil). The Catholic overlay preserved his colour and gentleness while translating his mythology into a Christian idiom of purity and creation. In Africa itself, Ọbàtálá stands in a studied complementarity with the thunder-god Ṣàngó and the ferocious Ògún: where they are hot, he is cool; where they cut, he binds. The orishas function less as rivals than as a single temperament distributed across many bodies, and Ọbàtálá holds the body's share.
