pronunciation.approximation: aw-loh-doo-MAH-reh — low 'aw', high 'loh', low 'doo', high 'MAH', low 'reh'.
pronunciation.note: Olódùmarè is Tier 1: the acute accent on ó preserves a high tone and the grave accents on ù and è preserve low tones, distinctive features the ASCII form loses. Tonal distinctions are crucial to Yoruba meaning.

domains.title: Owner of the Universe
domains.subtitle: Supreme Creator, Destiny, and Final Authority
domains.lead: Olódùmarè is the high god of Yoruba religion — the sole creator and owner of heaven, earth, and every breath that moves within them. Remote and self-sufficient, he receives no images and depends on no offerings; the orishas govern the world, but only as his delegates. He assigns destiny and stands beyond all appeal.

cards.name: Supreme Creator
cards.desc: He alone creates ex nihilo; the orishas shape and govern what he has made.

cards.name: Destiny
cards.desc: He assigns àkúnlẹ̀yàn, the destiny chosen by each soul before birth, and ratifies it with the breath of life.

cards.name: Final Authority
cards.desc: No orisha can override his decree; even Ọrúnmìlà interprets rather than changes fate.

cards.name: Transcendence
cards.desc: He needs no temple image; he is worshipped through the sky, the sun, and the breath of life.

symbols.name: The sky (ọ̀run)
symbols.meaning: His visible throne; the firmament is his temple and his garment.

symbols.name: The rainbow-serpent (ọ̀ṣùmàrè)
symbols.meaning: The celestial serpent-arch whose appearance seals the passage between heaven and earth; revered as an orisha in its own right and a sign of Olódùmarè's covenant with the sky.

symbols.name: Cool wind and breath (éémí)
symbols.meaning: The invisible life-force he breathes into the bodies shaped by Ọbatalá; the felt proof of the remote god in every living chest.

symbols.name: White light
symbols.meaning: Pure, imageless presence; Olódùmarè has no anthropomorphic cult statue anywhere in Yorubaland.

mythology.lead: Olódùmarè's mythology is theology: the origin of the world, the distribution of destiny, and the hierarchy between the high god and the orishas who serve him.

myths.title: The Chain from Heaven
myths.text: At the beginning the world was water below and sky above, and Olódùmarè resolved to make a place for life. He charged Ọbatalá (Orishanla) with the task: descend the golden chain from heaven carrying a snail shell filled with sand, a five-toed hen, and a chameleon to test the ground. But at the threshold the trickster Ẹṣù offered Ọbatalá palm wine; he drank, grew drowsy, and slept. His younger brother Odùduwà seized the chain, the shell, and the hen, scattered the sand on the primordial flood, and the hen scratched it into the ridges of the earth (Ifá corpus; retold by E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, 1962). When Ọbatalá awoke and descended, the work was done; humbled, he accepted as his own share the moulding of human bodies from clay. The myth divides creation into command, execution, and embodiment: Olódùmarè wills the world, others build it, and the god whom failure humbled receives the clay of humanity.

myths.title: The Potter Àjàlá and the Unborn Heads
myths.text: Before birth, every soul kneels in heaven to choose a destiny — àkúnlẹ̀yàn, 'that which is chosen kneeling' — from the moulds of Àjàlá, the divine potter of heads (orí). Ifá verses do not flatter the potter: Àjàlá is a drunkard whose wares are badly fired, and some heads are cracked, some crooked, while only the patient find the sound ones. The choice made, Olódùmarè himself ratifies it and breathes the éémí, the life-force, into the chosen head — and because the seal is his, destiny can be softened by sacrifice and wisdom but never revoked (Idowu 1962; Abimbola, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus, 1976). Idowu reads the myth as Yoruba theodicy in miniature: the world is not unjust because Olódùmarè is cruel, but because choosing is the price of being human — and heaven itself keeps a careless potter.

lore.culturalLegacy: Olódùmarè remains the theological centre of Yoruba religion and its diaspora. The idiom 'Olódùmarè willing' structures daily speech, and the doctrine that destiny is chosen but ratified by the high god shapes Yoruba ethics of responsibility and sacrifice. In African philosophy he is a key figure in debates over monotheism and polytheism, destiny and freedom — Idowu's classic study made him a proof that African theology possesses a doctrine of God as rigorous as any. His name echoes through reggae, Afrobeat, and global spirituality as a byword for the supreme source, a standing reminder that African theology has always made room for the One beyond the many.
lore.archaeology: As a transcendent deity without anthropomorphic cult images, Olódùmarè leaves few direct archaeological traces, and that absence is itself the primary evidence of the theology. Sky-oriented prayer sites across Yorubaland — open-air enclosures without idols, oriented to the sunrise — match Idowu's description of a god worshipped through light and breath. His presence is inferred from the cosmological vocabulary of Ifá verses recorded by Bascom and Abimbola and from the white-cloth, empty-throne symbolism placed above orisha altars in Cuban Santería and Brazilian Candomblé houses, where the transcendent Creator is represented precisely by what is absent: an unoccupied seat under the sky.
lore.syncretism: Because Olódùmarè is a remote, imageless high god, he was readily mapped onto the Christian God by enslaved Yoruba people and their descendants. In Cuban Santería and Brazilian Candomblé, Olódumare is identified with the transcendent Creator, while the orishas correspond to saints and angels. In the scholarship this is called parallelismo rather than simple substitution: each orisha kept its own name, colours, and drum while accepting a Catholic 'cover'. The theological structure — one high god above a host of intermediaries — let the Yoruba pantheon survive inside monotheistic frameworks without losing its polytheistic texture, and in recent decades the diaspora has exported the model back to Nigeria itself.

steps: The name is attested in East Slavic chronicles as Дажьбогъ (Dažĭbogŭ) and in the Primary Chronicle.
It is usually analyzed as daždĭ 'rain, gift' + bogŭ 'god', hence 'giving god' or 'rain god'.
The modern Unicode restoration Dažbog uses the caron ž; the medieval Cyrillic spelling includes the reduced jer vowels ь and ъ.
The Cyrillic form is not registrable in .com; the Latin transliteration Dažbog is.

provenanceSources.title: Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor, The Russian Primary Chronicle
Vlasto, The Entry of the Slavs into Christendom
Mallory & Adams, Encyclopedia of Indo-European Culture

pronunciation.approximation: 'DAHZH-bog' — crisp 'dah', then the 'zh' sound of 'measure', and end with 'bog' as in 'god' (which is what the word means).
pronunciation.note: Dažbog is Tier 1: the caron on ž preserves the distinctive Common Slavic fricative, a feature the ASCII form loses. The h in the lexicon's ASCII form is silent, reflecting an older East Slavic spelling convention (Daždbog / Dadzbog) that was later simplified. We do not invent an etymology beyond the attested compound 'giving god'.

domains.title: The Giving God
domains.subtitle: Sun, Wealth, and Fertility in Slavic Tradition
domains.lead: Dažbog is the Slavic sun god, son of the smith-god Svarog, and a giver of wealth and agricultural bounty. His name means 'giving god,' and in the medieval East Slavic sources he is honored alongside Perun, Svarog, and other members of the Kievan pantheon. Although the Christian chroniclers dismissed him as a demon, folk memory preserved him in blessings, oaths, and the figure of Dabog.

cards.name: The Sun
cards.desc: A twelfth-century gloss equates him with Helios; his warmth is the wealth the name promises.

cards.name: Son of Svarog
cards.desc: The Hypatian Chronicle's gloss on Malalas names him son of the heavenly smith Svarog.

cards.name: Giver of Wealth
cards.desc: His name is a grammar of giving: South Slavs still open wishes with 'Dajbog — may God give'.

cards.name: Grandfather of Rus'
cards.desc: The Slovo o polku Igoreve hails the Rus' princes as 'grandsons of Dažbog' — an origin, not just a god.

symbols.name: Sun wheel or disk
symbols.meaning: The solar body with which Dažbog was identified in the learned glosses

symbols.name: Wheat or sheaf
symbols.meaning: The harvest produced by the sun's warmth and the god's generosity

symbols.name: Gold and amber
symbols.meaning: Treasures associated with sunlight and divine wealth

symbols.name: Horse or chariot
symbols.meaning: The solar vehicle common to Indo-European sun-god imagery, inferred rather than attested

mythology.lead: Dažbog is known almost entirely from external, often hostile, sources. The Slavs left no extensive native mythology, so his story must be rebuilt from the chronicle lists, a single learned gloss, one epic phrase, and the grammar of South Slavic blessings — each fragment saying more than it meant to.

myths.title: The Idols on the Hill
myths.text: The Primary Chronicle reports that in 980 Prince Vladimir raised idols on a hill above Kyiv — Perun of wood with silver head and golden moustache, and with him Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh — and that the people of Kyiv were commanded to sacrifice to them. In 988, as the baptism of Rus' began, the idols were dragged to the Dnieper and thrown in, Perun's beaten with sticks as it bobbed downstream. Of Dazhbog himself not a single tale survives — no birth, no adventure, no cult song. What survives is his rank: the chroniclers list him among the six powers of the capital, and their contempt is the measure of how much they had to erase. A god can be important enough to drown and still leave no story; Dažbog's silence is the size of his former noise.

myths.title: Son of Svarog, Called Helios
myths.text: Our second witness is a bookman's footnote. In the Hypatian Chronicle (s.a. 6622/1114), a monk copying a Slavic translation of John Malalas' world chronicle paused where the Greek text spoke of Hephaestus and Helios, and glossed: Svarog — that is Hephaestus — and his son Dažbog, whom they call Helios. In one stroke the gloss supplies a genealogy (son of the heavenly smith), a domain (the sun), and a place in a learned interpretatio Graeca. And it may be nothing more than one twelfth-century copyist's guess. Everything 'known' about Dažbog as sun god hangs on this marginal act of identification, and scholarship has never stopped weighing how much is living cult and how much is Byzantine bookkeeping. The footnote is either the last echo of a real theology or the birthplace of a scholarly ghost — and the two are not easy to tell apart.

lore.culturalLegacy: Dažbog survives most clearly in South Slavic invocations of Dajbog and in place-names and personal names across Slavic-speaking regions — Dajbog's compound still opens every well-wishing sentence in Serbia, unremarked and unbroken. Modern Slavic Rodnovery (Native Faith) movements honor him as a solar and prosperity deity. In linguistics, his name is a textbook example of the Common Slavic compound *dažь bogъ. For scholars of medieval Slavic religion, Dažbog is a crucial but frustratingly elusive figure: important enough to be named by chroniclers and sworn by in epic, yet absent from the rich narrative cycles that preserve Norse or Greek mythology.
lore.archaeology: No archaeological find names Dažbog directly. His attestation depends on the written sources, especially the Primary Chronicle and the Hypatian Malalas gloss, and on the survival of his name in South Slavic folklore. Solar imagery in Slavic folk art — wheel-shaped amulets, spring-sun rituals, roundel embroidery — may indirectly reflect the cult of a solar deity, but none can be securely linked to Dažbog by inscription or context. The destruction of the Kyiv idols in 988 and the thoroughness of Christianization mean that material evidence for the major gods is sparse and ambiguous; for the sun-giver, the word giving outlasted every object it once described.
lore.syncretism: Christian chroniclers explicitly equated Dažbog with the Greek sun god Helios, reflecting both his solar identification and the Byzantine interpretatio Graeca favored in Kievan Rus'. In South Slavic folk religion, Dabog/Dajbog blends with the Christian God while retaining the old 'giving' epithet. Comparisons have been made to the Vedic Savitar and the Roman Sol Invictus, both solar deities associated with bestowal; the Iranian Mithra has been proposed as a distant cousin, though the evidence is speculative. Dažbog illustrates a common pattern: a major pagan god is first demonized by the chronicle, then absorbed into popular Christian speech, and finally resurrected by philology. In modern Slavic Native Faith he is honored again as a solar and prosperity deity — a reconstruction, but one with better folk credentials than most.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BYEH-loh-bohg' — literally 'White God,' the exact mirror of Chernobog, 'Black God.'
pronunciation.note: Belobog is single-tier Tier 2: the name is a transparent compound — bělъ 'white' + bogъ 'god' — and ASCII loses nothing. His existence as a worshiped god is attested only once (Cosmas), which is less than his modern fame assumes; the restoration preserves the name, not a proven cult.

domains.title: Belobog
domains.subtitle: Light
domains.lead: Belobog — the White God of the Slavs, lord of light, good, and fortune — is known from a single medieval chronicle line and a wide scatter of folklore. He is the bright half of the famous Slavic dualism: the good god who stands opposite the Black God of evil.

cards.name: The White God
cards.desc: His very name is his office: bělъ, 'white' — light, brightness, and the good they signify.

cards.name: Good Fortune
cards.desc: In folklore his name attached to the household's luck — the kept wreath and grain that carried prosperity.

cards.name: Counter of the Black God
cards.desc: He exists in structure as much as in story — the bright pole balancing Chernobog's darkness.

cards.name: The Chronicle God
cards.desc: 'Zeloboch' among the demons of Cosmas of Prague — one line, two words, a whole theology.

symbols.name: White (Bělъ)
symbols.meaning: Light itself — the color-word at the root of his name and of Slavic words for dawn and brightness

symbols.name: The Harvest Wreath
symbols.meaning: The last-sheaf wreath called belobog in Polish and Russian folklore, kept till spring to house the field's fortune

symbols.name: The Waxing Light
symbols.meaning: The growing half of the year — the season attributed, in folk reconstruction, to his governance

symbols.name: The Honored Seat
symbols.meaning: The right-hand place at table and hearth — the 'white' side in Slavic custom, opposite the unclean left

mythology.lead: Belobog has no native mythology in the epic sense — no adventures, no genealogy, no cycle. What he has is an attestation, an opposite, and a folklore. His four 'myths' are therefore documents of how a name can carry an entire cosmology on almost no narrative at all.

myths.title: Zeloboch of the Czech Chronicle
myths.text: The only medieval author to name Belobog is Cosmas of Prague, whose Chronica Boemorum (c. 1125, Book I.4) describes the pre-Christian Czechs sacrificing to demons — and lists among them Zeloboch, the chronicler's Latinized rendering of Belobog, alongside gods of the sky, the harvest, and fortune. The sentence is a sneer from a Christian cleric, and its spelling is garbled; yet it proves that around 1100 a 'White God' received offerings in Bohemia. Cosmas is careful to mock the whole catalogue — sky, harvest, and fortune gods jumbled together — which is exactly why scholars mine his scorn for the only list of Czech deities that survives. No myth accompanies the name.No myth accompanies the name. But the attestation does real work: it converts Belobog from a scholarly inference into a historical god, however thinly witnessed — one line carrying the whole bright half of Slavic dualism.

myths.title: Chernobog at Rethra
myths.text: Belobog's structure is completed by his opposite. Helmold of Bosau (Chronica Slavorum I.52, c. 1172) reports that the Slavs acknowledged a god of all evil 'whom they call the Black One' — Chernobog — and modern scholarship assembles the pair: White God and Black God, light and evil, the Slavic dualism (Gieysztor, Mitologia Słowian; Rosik, Białobóg). Later folklore strengthens the pairing: across the Slavic world the year's good and ill fortune are personified as opposed powers, and the White God's wreath is the benign half of that old bookkeeping. Historians rightly cautionHistorians rightly caution that the two attestations come from different peoples, centuries, and authors — no text shows the pair worshiped together. The dualism is thus partly reconstruction. Still, the reconstruction rests on two independent medieval witnesses: wherever the sources reach the Slavic gods, they find darkness named — and naming darkness implies, at least to us, its bright counterpart.

lore.culturalLegacy: Belobog's name lives wherever Slavic says 'white': in Bělehrad — Belgrade, 'the White City' — and in a family of names and words built on the same root. His cultural afterlife, though, belongs to the modern era. He is the emblem of Slavic pre-Christian heritage in schoolbooks, in Romantic poetry, and increasingly in popular culture — fantasy fiction and games have discovered the White God alongside Chernobog, exporting the pair to a global audience that rarely suspects how thin the medieval evidence is. For Slavic neopagans he is an actively worshiped deity of light and prosperity. The folklore core — the kept wreath, the honored right-hand seat, the luck of the household — persists in attenuated custom. A god of one chronicle line thus presides over a modern renaissance, his name a standing reminder that a civilization's bright self-image needs only a few words to survive.
lore.archaeology: There is no archaeology of Belobog: no image, temple, or inscription bearing his name has been found, and no Slavic sanctuary excavated to date can be assigned to him. The great Slavic cult sites belong to other gods — Arkona's temple of Svetovid on Rügen (destroyed 1168, described by Saxo Grammaticus), the debated 'Rethra' of Helmold's Black God — and the famous carved idols (the Zbruch pillar) name no deity at all. Belobog's evidence is documentary (Cosmas, Helmold) and ethnographic (the harvest-wreath records). The absence is not trivial: it means the White God belongs to that large class of ancient deities known only through the words of their adversaries — a god whose temples were wooden, seasonal, and gone.
lore.syncretism: Belobog's closest ancient analogue was noticed early: Iranian dualism, with its opposed Spenta Mainyu and Angra Mainyu, offers the famous parallel, and comparative works (Gieysztor; Eliade's surveys of Balkan and Slavic religion) discuss whether Slavic dualism is inherited Indo-European structure, Iranian contact in the Carpathian centuries, or Christian devil-cult projected backward. The honest answer is that the evidence cannot decide. Christianization certainly re-mapped the pair: Chernobog slid toward the Christian devil, while Belobog's light-office was absorbed by Christ — the harvest wreath survived longest precisely where it could pose as a Christian household charm. In the reverse direction, modern Rodnovery has reabsorbed Christian folk practice into the White God's cult. Belobog is thus a palimpsest: pagan name, Christian overlay, pagan revival — each layer legible.

pronunciation.approximation: 'PER-un' with a rolled r; the name is an agent noun meaning 'Striker'.
pronunciation.note: Tier 2. The restored form Perun preserves no feature the plain ASCII form loses — no diacritic, no distinctive non-ASCII letter — so the temple stands at Tier 2 by the mechanical rule.

domains.title: Perun
domains.subtitle: Thunder
domains.lead: Perun is the thunderer of the Slavs: god of lightning, storm, and the sacred oak, patron of warriors and guarantor of oaths. His name means 'striker.' The East Slavic chronicles place him first among the gods of Kyiv, and folklore kept his axe, his fire, and his wrath alive long after the idols sank in the Dnieper.

cards.name: The Striker
cards.desc: His weapons are the thunderbolt and the throwing axe; lightning is his signature in every early description of the cult.

cards.name: The Sacred Oak
cards.desc: Oaks struck by lightning were his; a perpetual fire burned for him on open hilltop sanctuaries such as Peryn' near Novgorod.

cards.name: Lord of Oaths
cards.desc: The Rus'-Byzantine treaties swore by Perun and Volos; the perjurer's written curse was death by his own weapons.

cards.name: Enemy of Veles
cards.desc: In the reconstructed myth-cycle he pursues the cattle-thief Veles down through the tiers of the world-tree.

symbols.name: Throwing axe / thunderbolt
symbols.meaning: His striking weapon, worn in miniature on amulets and incised on stones across the Slavic world

symbols.name: Oak and perpetual fire
symbols.meaning: The lightning-struck tree and the hilltop flame kept burning in his honor at open-air shrines

symbols.name: Thunderstone (gromovik)
symbols.meaning: Fossil belemnites kept in Slavic households against lightning, understood as his spent arrows

symbols.name: The sacred hill
symbols.meaning: Kyiv's shrine hill and Novgorod's Peryn' — high ground set apart for his unroofed cult

symbols.name: Elijah's fiery chariot
symbols.meaning: The Christian successor-image that inherited his storm: wheels of fire crossing the sky

mythology.lead: The stories of Perun survive mostly at second hand, through the chronicles of his enemies and the reconstructions of modern philologists. From them emerges a thunderer who is at once war-god and covenant-god: he hurls the bolt, he guards the sworn word, and he wages an eternal feud with Veles, lord of the underworld and the herd.

myths.title: The Idols on the Hill
myths.text: The Povest' vremennykh let ('Tale of Bygone Years') reports that Prince Vladimir, before his conversion, set up idols on a hill outside Kyiv: Perun of wood with a head of silver and a moustache of gold, flanked by Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh, and the people were commanded to sacrifice to them. In 988 the idols were beaten with sticks and thrown into the Dnieper, and the chronicler records that the people waded into the river weeping, 'for they had not yet been baptized, but were baptized in the name of Perun.' The detail is priceless: the Church's own founding history admits that Rus' wept for the thunderer as it left him. Conversion was not a serene enlightenment but a national funeral — and Perun was the body. The idol sank; the oath, as the treaty of 944 shows, floated for another half-century.

myths.title: Sworn by Their Own Weapons
myths.text: The text of Prince Igor's treaty with Byzantium, preserved in the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6452/944), embeds the old oath formula verbatim. For the clauses of war and peace the Rus' swear by Perun — and by Volos, the cattle god, for everything touching livestock — and the curse on the perjurer is physical and total: may he be destroyed by his own weapons, unprotected by his own shield, slain by his own sword, shot by his own arrows. The same formula recurs in the treaty of 971, scaled down but recognizable. Here Perun functions exactly as Zeus Horkios does in Hesiod: not a god of stories but the installed enforcer of agreements between peoples. A thunderer who witnesses contracts is a thunderer whose violence has been socialized — order made audible.

lore.culturalLegacy: Perun never left the languages. The word itself became the poetic Slavic name for thunder — Polish piorun is the everyday word for a thunderbolt, and Russian keeps perun in elevated speech — while Lithuanian Perkūnas keeps the cognate alive next door. Folklore preserved his attributes as 'thunderstones,' fossil belemnites (gromovik) hung in houses against lightning, and the epic hero Il'ya Muromets rides in his shadow with a mace that is really a bolt. In the modern period Perun has become an emblem of Slavic identity: he heads the pantheon of Rodnover and Native Faith communities from Ukraine to Poland, lends his name to military units, rockets, and football terraces, and appears wherever the question is asked what a pre-Christian Slavic civilization would have honored. The Church feared him for a reason: of all the Kyiv gods, his name proved the hardest to drown.
lore.archaeology: The clearest material footprint of Perun's cult is Peryn', a rounded hill at the bend of the Volkhov south of Novgorod, excavated by G. Lebedev's team in the 1950s: a circular ritual enclosure with a stone- and clay-lined platform, dated to the tenth–twelfth centuries, on a site whose very name derives from the god. No temple building was found — the open-air precinct fits the chronicle image of a hill shrine — but the enclosure's planned geometry and burnt deposits mark organized, funded cult practice. Across the Slavic world, miniature axe-amulets ('thunder-axes on chains') and axe-mark graffiti are read as Perun's weapon in miniature, though none is inscribed. The Kyiv hill of 988 has never been securely located archaeologically, and the enigmatic four-sided Zbruch idol is more often assigned to Svetovit than to the thunderer. Direct evidence is thin — but Peryn' proves the cult was real.
lore.syncretism: Christianization did not erase Perun; it reassigned him. His functions passed chiefly to the prophet Elijah — Il'ya — whose fiery chariot crosses the sky in Russian folklore, whose day kept the thunderer's weather, and whose icons still stand in village fields against storm and fire. Saint George absorbed something of the dragon-slaying warrior. Byzantine-educated writers performed the usual interpretatio, reading Perun as a Slavic Zeus, while comparative scholarship has added Thor and Indra as cousins through the shared inheritance of the storm-combat myth. In the twentieth century Perun returned openly: Slavic Native Faith movements restored his name, his day, and his hilltop fires, and he now stands — as the chronicles always placed him — first among the gods. Of all the drowned pantheon, he alone kept a national audience.

pronunciation.approximation: 'VEH-les', two quick syllables; the stress falls forward, as in the modern South Slavic reflexes of the name.
pronunciation.note: Tier 2. The restored form Veles preserves no feature the plain ASCII form loses — no diacritic, no distinctive non-ASCII letter — so the temple stands at Tier 2 by the mechanical rule.

domains.title: Veles
domains.subtitle: Cattle
domains.lead: Veles — Volos to the East Slavs — is the god of cattle and wealth, of the underworld's moist depths, and, in the great reconstruction of Ivanov and Toporov, of poetry and magic. Where Perun strikes from above, Veles moves below: through herds, graves, bargains, and song.

cards.name: Lord of Cattle
cards.desc: The chronicles gloss him explicitly: Volos, 'the cattle god' — herders swore their oaths by him alone.

cards.name: The Underworld River
cards.desc: He rules the wet, root-filled depths beneath the world-tree: the realm of the dead and of hidden treasure.

cards.name: God of Poetry
cards.desc: In the reconstructed mythology he is patron of singers and sorcerers; the wandering volkhvy acted in his name.

cards.name: Adversary of Perun
cards.desc: The eternal enemy in the myth-cycle: thief of cattle, storm of wealth, struck down each spring by the thunderer's bolt.

symbols.name: Cattle horns
symbols.meaning: The herds that were his treasure and the sign under which herders and merchants swore

symbols.name: The serpent
symbols.meaning: His disguise in the myth-cycle: low, wet, and close to the earth — the eternal adversary of the eagle

symbols.name: The bear
symbols.meaning: His chthonic animal in the alternating lore of the Slavic year — master of the wilderness beyond the fence

symbols.name: Gusli (harp)
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the singer he protects; in folklore the magic fiddle makes even the forest dance

symbols.name: Wet earth and roots
symbols.meaning: The moist underworld into which he withdraws and from which wealth returns

mythology.lead: Veles has no surviving epic. His dossier is a chronicle oath here, a famine there, and — towering over the fragments — the modern reconstruction by Ivanov and Toporov of the myth-cycle in which he is the thunderer's eternal adversary. Read together, the fragments describe a god of everything that grows, burrows, and accrues out of sight.

myths.title: Sworn by Volos
myths.text: The Rus'-Byzantine treaty of 944, copied into the Primary Chronicle, has left the only verbatim ritual text of pre-Christian Rus'. For the clauses of war the envoys swear by Perun; for everything touching livestock — sale, theft, compensation — they swear by Volos alone, and the curse on the perjurer is total: 'may we be cursed by the god in whom we believe, by Perun and Volos, the furred one... may we not be protected by our shields, may we be slain by our own swords, may we be shot by our own arrows.' A later copyist glossed the unfamiliar name for his readers: 'Volos — that is, the cattle god.' The division of labor is the myth in miniature: the sky-god witnesses between warriors, while the god of herds and wealth underwrites the peasant's entire fortune, animal by animal. Where your property lives, there your god is invoked.

myths.title: The Angry God of Suzdal
myths.text: In the terrible famine year of 1024, the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6532) tells how wandering sorcerers came to Suzdal' and announced the cause of the people's misery: 'It is the god Veles who is angry.' The volkhvy demanded the sacrifice of a youth — a red-haired one, they specified, from a particular kin — and when the killing was done, they ate the body. The bishop of Rostov rode in, arrested the sorcerers, and drowned them in the Volga. The tale is told by Christian enemies, and its details are horrific precisely in order to damn the old religion; yet its center is precious evidence. A generation after the baptism, when the official gods were Perun's rivals long drowned, it was still Veles whose name a prophet reached for when the earth would not feed her children. The underworld god was the one who explained hunger.

lore.culturalLegacy: Veles endures most durably in words: toponyms like Volosovo across the Russian north, the Dalmatian cult of Sveti Vlaho, the devil-haunted velnias of Lithuanian folklore, and the root itself in Slavic speech. Folklore kept his portfolio — treasure guarded by a chthonic serpent, the magic fiddle of the singer who bargains below, oaths sworn over a herd at market. The nineteenth and twentieth centuries were less kind: the so-called Book of Veles, publicized in the 1950s, purports to be a pre-Christian epic of his people and is now universally judged a modern forgery — a tribute, of a crooked kind, to how badly moderns wanted the lost god back. Rodnover communities today honor Veles as lord of wisdom, wealth, and the written word, and his serpent still guards vaults in banks' logos and fantasy novels alike.
lore.archaeology: No temple of Veles has been identified, and his material dossier is thin — fitting for a god of hidden things. The anchor is textual-archaeological: birchbark letters from eleventh–twelfth-century Novgorod address creditors and debtors on Volosova ulica, 'Volos's street', the market quarter — proof that the cult left footprints in urban topography even where no shrine survives. Riverside hoards and water-logged deposits are sometimes laid at the door of the underworld god, but the attribution is unprovable, and no figurine or amulet bears his name. The honest summary is that Veles's archaeology is his absence: the god of concealment kept himself concealed, and the street sign is the whole monument.
lore.syncretism: Veles's Christian afterlife ran through the saints of the herd. In the Balkans he survives in Sveti Vlaho — Saint Blaise — the Dalmatian patron of cattle whose feast ends with animals blessed in his name; in Russia the same role fell to Saint Vlasiy, whose name is simply Veles re-clothed. The divine adversary was absorbed too: the serpent of the myth-cycle slithered into dragon-slayer legends, and Perun's spring victory was reassigned to Saint George and Elijah. Byzantine-educated writers performed interpretatio on the pantheon as a whole, while comparative scholarship drew bolder lines — Toporov's Veles–Varuna, the Norse Óðinn of poetry and the dead, Hermes as god of herds and boundary-crossings — each a hypothesis about what sort of god this was: sovereign of everything the sky does not see. Demonized in the languages (Czech veles gave way to čert for 'devil'), he remained the underworld's landlord in folklore down to the modern era.

pronunciation.approximation: Say "radagast" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Radagast".
pronunciation.note: Radagast is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized name is pure ASCII — no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. The doubled-a spelling is a scholarly convention descending from Thietmar's 'Radigost'; only the capital distinguishes temple from plain text.

domains.title: Radagast
domains.subtitle: Hospitality
domains.lead: Radagast — medieval Radigost — was the chief god of the Redarii, a Slavic people between the Elbe and the Oder, worshipped in a great wooden temple-city called Radgosc. His name ties him to the guest and the glad welcome: he is the god of hospitality, of the open door, of beasts, and of the trust between strangers.

cards.name: The Temple of Radgosc
cards.desc: Thietmar of Merseburg describes the god's vast wooden temple-city, the religious capital of the Elbe Slavs (Chronicon VI.23–25).

cards.name: The God of Guests
cards.desc: His name — Proto-Slavic *radъ-gostь, 'glad guest' or 'he who gladly receives' — makes hospitality itself a divine office.

cards.name: The Oracle
cards.desc: Adam of Bremen reports that Radgosc gave answers to all the Slavic peoples — and even to Christian Saxons.

cards.name: A Fragile Monument
cards.desc: The temple burned around 1068; what survives of Radagast is the witness of three chroniclers and a borrowed wizard.

symbols.name: The bronze doors
symbols.meaning: Adam of Bremen reports the Radgosc temple's bronze doors — the threshold between the god's house and the world.

symbols.name: The hung weapons
symbols.meaning: Shields and spears of the Redarii dedicated on the temple walls, a West Slavic arsenal of vows.

symbols.name: The carved oracle
symbols.meaning: The god's answers cut into wood and carried home by those who consulted him across the north.

symbols.name: The helmeted image
symbols.meaning: The cult statue of Radigost that stood foremost among the temple's many images, in armor befitting a god of the assembly.

symbols.name: The tribal standard
symbols.meaning: The banner kept in the god's house, carried to war only after the oracle had been consulted.

mythology.lead: Radagast is known almost entirely from three medieval chroniclers — Thietmar of Merseburg, Adam of Bremen, and Helmold of Bosau — writing two to four centuries after the god's heyday. No Slavic myth of him survives in his own language; what follows are the historical episodes that medieval writers themselves treated as his legend.

myths.title: Radgosc, the God Among the Lakes
myths.text: Our earliest witness is an enemy. Thietmar of Merseburg, bishop and chronicler, wrote in book VI of his Chronicon (c. 1012–1018) about Riedegost — the Germans called it Radgosc — the chief seat of the Redarii, a Slavic people between the Elbe and the Oder. There stood a vast wooden temple, heaped with the offerings of many tribes, and in it the image of the god who gave the city his name: Radigost. Thietmar wrote with open contempt — he was a soldier of the Church that wanted this cult destroyed — which is precisely why his testimony matters: a propagandist does not invent the power of what he attacks. Radgosc was not a village shrine but a confederate sanctuary, the religious capital of the Elbe Slavs, where tribes that quarreled in peacetime met in the god's shadow. The myth Radagast never got to tell survives as architecture: a god whose legend is a great wooden hall, and whose worship was the politics of a people.

myths.title: Answers Carved in Wood
myths.text: Adam of Bremen, writing his history of the Hamburg church some sixty years later (Gesta Hammaburgensis II.18, c. 1075), adds what Thietmar omits: the oracle. Radgosc, Adam says, was consulted by all the Slavic peoples; the god answered, and the answers were carved and carried home to govern war and settlement alike. His temple had bronze doors and walls hung with weapons — an arsenal of vows. Helmold of Bosau (Chronica Slavorum I.2, c. 1170) supplies the scandalous coda: even Christian Saxons consulted the oracle, crossing the religious frontier the Church was drawing. An oracle crosses borders because necessity does — the god of a single tribe can be refused, but a god who answers the questions everyone must ask cannot. Radagast's carved judgments made him the judge of peoples who shared no language but his: in the eleventh-century north, a Slavic god sat for a while on the throne of uncertainty where every nation seeks counsel.

lore.culturalLegacy: For scholarship, Radagast is the best-attested god of the Polabian Slavs — a whole people's religion compressed into three Latin chronicles. His name keeps surfacing wherever Slavic studies meet popular culture: in Tolkien's wizard, in neopagan rites, in the reconstructed temple at Groß Raden that thousands visit each year. The hospitality he was named for survives in the living Slavic word for guest — gost — and in its cousins across Europe, host and guest, all from the same Indo-European root. Restoring Radagast to Unicode restores a name the Church tried to burn out of memory, and that a philologist's imagination carried to the ends of Middle-earth.
lore.archaeology: No certain site of Radgosc has been identified, and the candidates lie in the lakeland between the Elbe and the Oder — the region of Neubrandenburg in Mecklenburg has been proposed. The open-air museum at Groß Raden (Mecklenburg-Vorpommern) reconstructs a fortified Slavic temple of exactly the type the chroniclers describe, though its identification with Rethra is traditional rather than proven. Excavations at other West Slavic cult centers — Starigard/Oldenburg in Wagria, Brandenburg an der Havel, and the Arkona headland on Rügen — have yielded wooden idols, temple rings, cult standards, and post-built hall sanctuaries of the tenth to twelfth centuries that match the chronicles' picture of a wealthy, wood-built religion. The material record and the written one agree on the essentials: a god housed in a great timber hall, attended by weapons, standards, and an oracle.
lore.syncretism: Medieval writers and modern scholars alike have tried to fold Radagast into wider patterns. Later philology asked whether Radigost was a name or a title, and whether the god of Radgosc was the West Slavic counterpart of Svantevit, the great armed oracle-god of Rügen described by Saxo Grammaticus — the identification is speculation resting mostly on the shared profile of a tribal war-oracle. The chroniclers performed a syncretism in reverse, reading the wooden temple as a demonic parody of the Church's own shrines. In the nineteenth century Grimm's Teutonic Mythology rescued the name for comparative philology; in the twentieth Tolkien naturalized it into English fantasy; and modern Slavic neopaganism now restores Radogost to worship, usually as a god of hospitality, animals, and the road — a reconstruction built, honestly enough, on three hostile chronicles and a borrowed wizard.

entries.domain: King of Mycenae, Commander at Troy

pronunciation.approximation: Say "patroclus" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Patroklos".
pronunciation.note: The ASCII form "patroclus" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Patroklos" preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

domains.title: Patroklos
domains.subtitle: Warrior
domains.lead: Patroklos — “Father’s glory” — is the dearest companion of Achilles and the moral centre of the Iliad: the gentle healer who dons his friend’s armour, turns the Trojan tide, and dies at Hector’s hands, setting in motion the wrath, grief, and reconciliation that close Homer’s poem.

cards.name: Father’s Glory
cards.desc: The name itself: patḗr, ‘father,’ + kléos, ‘glory’ — the reputation a son leaves in his father’s house.

cards.name: The Therápōn
cards.desc: Homer’s own word for Patroklos — Achilles’ honoured companion and equal, prized above every other ally in the camp.

cards.name: Borrowed Armour
cards.desc: The arms of Achilles that Patroklos wears into battle — glory made visible, and doom attached.

cards.name: One Urn of Bones
cards.desc: Achilles laid their mingled ashes in a single golden vessel — a friendship given permanent architecture.

symbols.name: The borrowed armour of Achilles
symbols.meaning: The self that is not his own: wearing it, Patroklos wins Achilles’ glory and attracts Achilles’ death.

symbols.name: Xanthos, the prophetic horse
symbols.meaning: Achilles’ immortal horse that weeps and foretells Patroklos’ fall (Iliad 19.400–424).

symbols.name: The wine-cup
symbols.meaning: Patroklos pours for Achilles and the embassy (Iliad 9.209–217) — the courteous steward of the hero’s table.

symbols.name: The golden double urn
symbols.meaning: The vessel in Achilles’ barrow holding two men’s bones — loyalty outlasting both lives.

symbols.name: The cut lock of hair
symbols.meaning: Achilles’ shorn hair, vowed to the river Spercheios and finally laid on Patroklos’ pyre (Iliad 23.135–153).

mythology.lead: Patroklos speaks almost nothing in the first half of the Iliad except to serve; when he finally speaks at length — weeping beside the ships — he sets the poem’s whole second movement in motion. His story is the epic’s deepest argument: that gentleness, not wrath, is what a hero finally costs the world.

myths.title: Sent Away from Opus
myths.text: Before Troy, Patroklos was an exile. As a boy in Opus he killed a companion, Klysonymos son of Amphidamas, in a quarrel over a game of knuckle-bones, and his father Menoitios sent him away to Phoinix, who in turn sent him on to Peleus at Phthia (Homer, Iliad 23.84–90). There he grew up beside Achilles, and when the fleet mustered, Menoitios charged him with the older friend’s duty: though Achilles is the stronger, Patroklos is the elder, and he must counsel him well (Homer, Iliad 11.780–790). The Iliad’s gentlest warrior thus begins in an accident of violence — a child sent from home for the kind of loss of temper every child knows — and the poem never lets us forget that the healer was once the boy with blood on his hands.

myths.title: Machaon’s Student
myths.text: Wounded men keep finding Patroklos. When the Achaean healers fall one after another, Eurypylus limps to Achilles’ hut with an arrow in his thigh, and it is Patroklos who eases him down, cuts out the barbed point, and bathes the wound with warm water — the gentle hands Homer says he learned from Achilles, who learned them from Cheiron the centaur (Homer, Iliad 11.809–848). The scene is easy to pass over, yet it is the poem’s clearest portrait of him: in a camp organised around killing, Patroklos’s signature act is stitching a stranger back together. Homer has already told us how the story ends; the healer is being prepared, line by line, for the wound that no one in the camp will be able to close — and for the friend who will close his own.

lore.culturalLegacy: Patroklos survives wherever the faithful companion dies to set the hero’s story moving — the template runs from medieval romance to modern fantasy. Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida gives him a sardonic afterlife as Achilles’ pampered favourite. Madeline Miller’s The Song of Achilles (2011) retold the bond as a love story for a modern readership, and the 2004 film Troy made his death the emotional centre of its second act. In scholarship he anchors one of the field’s standing debates — Dover’s austere reading of Homer against the later eroticising tradition — and his name lives in the language itself: the compound patrōia, ‘paternal inheritance,’ keeps his etymon, ‘father’s glory,’ in ordinary Greek speech. The mound Strabo saw by the Hellespont (Geography 13.1.28) is long ploughed flat, but the question his story asks — what is a hero worth when the gentle one dies? — is still open.
lore.archaeology: Patroklos’s witnesses are text and vase, not temple. Strabo (Geography 13.1.28) records the great barrows of the Troad — Achilles, Patroklos, Antilochos — near Sigeion by the Hellespont, on ground modern survey associates with the Besik Bay anchorage used by the Bronze-Age expedition. In art, the fight over his body was a favourite of early painters: the François Vase (Kleitias, c. 570 BCE, Florence) already arranges the funeral games of Patroklos around the golden jar, and black- and red-figure painters of the sixth and fifth centuries return again to the moment Ajax carries the corpse out of the rain of missiles. The gold-and-urn burial Homer describes matches Late Bronze Age bier-and-ossuary practice from the Mycenaean world — the poem’s material memory outliving any single grave.
lore.syncretism: Antiquity argued over what Achilles and Patroklos were to each other. Aeschylus in his lost Myrmidons made the bond explicitly erotic, and Plato’s Phaedrus, in Symposium 179e–180b, held Achilles up as the model of a lover who chose death to avenge his beloved. Aeschines, defending himself in Against Timarchus 142–150, read Homer’s own text as a chaste ideal of heroic friendship and rebuked the erotic reading — the first recorded round of a debate that has never closed. Alexander the Great staged himself in the pair: at Troy he crowned himself from Achilles’ tomb while Hephaestion did homage at Patroklos’, and after Hephaestion’s death he cut his own hair short over Patroklos’ barrow, replaying Achilles’ grief (Plutarch, Alexander 15.8; 72.2). Homer himself never says the word; every later age supplied it for him.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-yahs' — the first syllable is long and carries the ancient pitch rise; the final syllable is open and sustained.
pronunciation.note: The Greek Αἴας contains both stress (acute on the diphthong) and length (long alpha in the diphthong and final syllable), making it a Tier 1 restoration. The Latin-derived English form Ajax is a secondary spelling, not the original Greek.

domains.title: The Bulwark of the Achaeans
domains.subtitle: Warrior, Defender, and Unyielding Will
domains.lead: Aias is the great defensive warrior of the Greek army at Troy. In the Iliad he is second only to Achilles in strength and courage, a tower of bronze and stubbornness who saves the Greek ships from fire, duels Hector to a standstill, and carries the dead Achilles from the field. Where Achilles is speed and wrath, Aias is mass, endurance, and absolute loyalty. His name became a byword for the soldier who holds the line when everything else breaks.

cards.name: The Shield Wall
cards.desc: Aias fights with a towering seven-fold oxhide shield that protects whole companies, not merely himself.

cards.name: Duel with Hector
cards.desc: He meets Hector in single combat and fights him to a draw, proving that defence can match offence.

cards.name: Rescue of Achilles
cards.desc: After Achilles falls, Aias stands over the body and bears Achilles' corpse from the battlefield.

cards.name: Tragic Pride
cards.desc: Denied Achilles' armour, he falls into a madness of shame and takes his own life on the seashore.

symbols.name: Seven-fold oxhide shield
symbols.meaning: The massive tower-shield that makes Aias a living fortress and protects the whole Greek line.

symbols.name: Sword
symbols.meaning: The weapon with which he slays sheep in his madness and then himself in the tragedy of Sophocles.

symbols.name: The ships
symbols.meaning: The beached Greek fleet that Aias defends when the Trojans press it with fire.

symbols.name: The seashore
symbols.meaning: The place of his suicide and burial, where the waves meet the land of Troy.

mythology.lead: The myths of Aias are told in the Iliad, the lost Epic Cycle, and above all in Sophocles' tragedy Aias. They turn on a single quality: the absolute, unbending commitment of the warrior. That quality makes him the Greeks' greatest defender and, when it is slighted, their most terrible casualty.

myths.title: The Defence of the Ships
myths.text: When the Trojans broke the Greek wall and reached the beached ships, fire was set to Protesilaus' vessel, and the whole Achaean cause hung on a deck. There Homer stations Aias: striding from prow to stern behind his seven-fold oxhide shield, a pike twenty-two cubits long, holding the Trojans off while men rallied behind him (Iliad 15.674–746). Earlier, as Hector cut through the ranks, the poet had compared him to a donkey that boys cannot drive from a cornfield — stubborn, scorned, immovable (Iliad 11.558–562). When even Aias must yield at last, he does so grudgingly, calling the retreat a disaster (Iliad 16.101–111). The Defence of the Ships is the Iliad's hymn to the unglamorous virtue: endurance. Achilles wins the poem's glory; Aias saves its army. Homer seems to know that civilizations stand less on brilliance than on the man who refuses, step by bloody step, to move.

myths.title: Duel with Hector
myths.text: Hector challenges the Greeks to single combat, and the lots fall to Telamonian Aias — the biggest man among them, Homer says, save Achilles (Iliad 7.206–312). The duel fills a book: spear-casts stopped on shield and breastplate, a stone that spins Hector like a top, nightfall parting them at last. Neither yields; each wins honor, and they exchange gifts — Hector's sword and scabbard for Aias's scarlet belt. Homer comments in one terrible line: 'bad gifts' — for Aias will one day fall on Hector's sword, and Hector's corpse will be dragged behind Achilles' chariot by the very belt Aias gave. The duel is the Iliad's picture of war's fairness: two men of equal worth meet, measure each other, and part with respect — while the narrator, who knows how both die, lets us feel the courtesy and the doom in a single gesture. Equality is real; so is what comes after.

lore.culturalLegacy: Aias stands at the centre of Western reflection on military honour and mental injury. Sophocles' tragedy is now read as one of the earliest literary explorations of combat trauma and the violence that shame can turn inward. The American Department of Defense has sponsored performances of the play for veterans. The Ajax football club of Amsterdam takes its name and emblem from the hero, and 'Ajax' has been used for military vehicles, ships, and spacecraft. His story reminds us that the strongest defender may be the most vulnerable when honour is denied.
lore.syncretism: Aias was honoured as a hero at Salamis, his father's island, and at Athens, where the festival Aianteia included games in his honour. The Athenians claimed him as their own through his father Telamon's exile there. Roman writers such as Ovid retold his story, and the name Ajax passed into modern culture as a byword for physical might and tragic pride. In the twentieth century it became a brand name for cleaning products and football clubs, a long descent from the Homeric bulwark.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Greek as Αἴας. The first syllable is a long diphthong αι with an acute accent; the final alpha is long. The Latin form Ajax and English Ajax are secondary spellings that mask the original Greek vowel quantities. The PuniCodex restoration Aias recovers the scholarly transliteration of the Greek form and is classified as Tier 1 because both pitch accent and vowel length are preserved.

pronunciation.approximation: ah-PAYP — start with a slight throaty catch, then a sharp double-p closure like the pop of a striking snake.
pronunciation.note: Ꜥpp is Tier-1: the initial Ꜥ is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The doubled p is written but the vowels are supplied by convention; the Greek form Apophis preserves the final -is suffix but the Egyptian root is simply Ꜥpp. The initial Ꜥ marks a pharyngeal or glottal onset now lost.

domains.title: The Serpent of Chaos
domains.subtitle: Darkness, Eclipse, and the Enemy of Ra
domains.lead: Ꜥpp is the giant serpent of primordial chaos, enemy of the sun and of ma'at, who lies in the depths of the Duat and each night attacks the solar barque. His defeat is renewed daily in temple liturgy and underworld books: without Apophis there is no drama of order, and without his defeat there is no dawn.

cards.name: Swallower of the Sun
cards.desc: Each night Apophis coils around the solar barque; eclipses are moments when he nearly succeeds.

cards.name: Enemy of Order
cards.desc: He personifies isfet, the chaos that opposes mꜣꜥt; his defeat is the daily re-creation of the cosmos.

cards.name: Ritual Binding
cards.desc: Priests performed 'The Book of Overthrowing Apophis' to magically knife, burn, and bind him each day.

cards.name: The Underworld River
cards.desc: He haunts the waters of the Duat, the dark mirror of the Nile through which Ra must pass.

symbols.name: Giant coiled serpent
symbols.meaning: The undifferentiated chaos that threatens to return creation to non-being; the largest monster in the Egyptian cosmos

symbols.name: Solar barque under attack
symbols.meaning: The nightly struggle between light and darkness; the boat itself, with its crew of gods and justified dead, is the emblem of order under threat

symbols.name: Knife and flames
symbols.meaning: The weapons of the temple ritual that destroys Apophis's body and scatters his soul

symbols.name: Dark water or eclipse
symbols.meaning: The moments when order seems closest to collapse — the serpent visible in the sun's blackened disk

mythology.lead: Apophis has no temple, no cult, no hymns of praise — he exists to be defeated. Yet his role is essential: he is the adversary against whom the gods and the justified dead fight each night. His mythology is a mythology of cosmic maintenance, in which order is not given but won again and again.

myths.title: The Nocturnal Battle in the Duat
myths.text: In the New Kingdom underworld books — the Amduat, the Book of Gates, and their relatives, painted on the walls of royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings — Ra's barque sails through the twelve hours of night. In the middle hours Apophis waits, a vast serpent coiled in the river of the Duat, sometimes in his menacing form called Rerek. The crew of gods and blessed dead must fight him with spear, rope, and fire: the serpent Mehen encircles the boat as living armor, goddesses of the hours bind the monster, and Seth stands at the prow to spear him as the barque passes. In the Book of Gates the punishment of the damned is staged as their enforced participation in this warfare — the enemies of order are made to row Apophis's own boat. The scene encodes the whole Egyptian theology of night: the sun's journey is not a cruise but a combat patrol, and dawn is the report of a battle won.

myths.title: The Book of Overthrowing Apophis
myths.text: Preserved most fully in the Bremner-Rhind papyrus (British Museum EA 10188) and on temple walls, this liturgical composition instructs the lector priest to fashion a wax figure of Apophis, pierce it with knives, burn it in a fire of bryony, trample the ashes, spit upon them, and recite spells that sever his vertebrae and scatter his body, his name, and his soul. The ritual was performed daily in the great temples of Amun-Ra at Thebes, so that the sun would rise. It is the most elaborate surviving example of Egyptian execration magic, and Robert Ritner's The Mechanics of Ancient Egyptian Magical Practice remains its definitive study. The text is not symbolic theater to its performers: the wax image is the god of chaos, and its destruction in the temple courtyard is one front of the same war fought each night on the barque. The morning exists because someone, every day, did the paperwork of the cosmos.

lore.culturalLegacy: The name Apophis survives in Egyptology as the archetype of the chaos serpent, and the asteroid 99942 Apophis keeps him in the headlines of planetary defense. In fantasy literature, role-playing games, and comics he appears as a world-destroying serpent. For scholars, he remains the sharpest symbol of the Egyptian worldview: order is not a given but a daily achievement, requiring vigilance, ritual, and collective effort — a theology of maintenance rather than conquest, in which the greatest heroism is getting up every morning to defeat the same serpent again.
lore.archaeology: Apophis is depicted across the New Kingdom royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings — most completely in the burial chambers of Seti I, Tutankhamun, and Ramses VI, where the underworld books paint his nightly binding and decapitation. The Bremner-Rhind papyrus (BM EA 10188) preserves the fullest copy of the Book of Overthrowing Apophis, and temple walls at Karnak, Edfu, and Dendera show the daily ritual of destroying his wax image. Execration figures and inscribed red pots found at Thebes, Saqqara, and Mirgissa in Nubia attest the wider practice of magically neutralizing chaos by name and effigy.
lore.syncretism: Apophis has no positive syncretisms; he is the anti-god against whom all order defines itself. The biblical Leviathan and the Gnostic chaos-dragon have often been compared to him, and Coptic tradition transmitted his name (as Apōph) alongside Christian demonology — though the Egyptian figure is cosmic and impersonal, more entropy than devil. In modern astronomy the asteroid 99942 Apophis, a near-Earth object once feared capable of impact, carries his name with exact appropriateness: a serpent whose approach must be calculated and warded off. Popular culture reduces him to a dragon-like villain, but his ancient precision survives: Apophis is not evil in the moral sense — he is the regression to non-being that creation must eternally refuse.
lore.originalScriptNote: The hieroglyphic writing of Ꜥpp joins the head-with-neck (D1) for the initial Ꜥ, the mouth (D21) for p, and the coiled serpent (I14) as determinative — the serpent writing itself. The initial Ꜥ (ayin) is a voiced pharyngeal fricative or glottal stop that English lacks; the doubled p closes the name like a second coil. Vowels are not written and are supplied by convention from the later Greek Ἄποφις.

pronunciation.approximation: 'sah-ʿA' — a hissing 's', then a deep, tightening 'ah' in the throat.
pronunciation.note: sꜥ is a Tier-1 restoration. The sibilant s and pharyngeal ꜥ are both preserved — the ꜥ is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses — making the Unicode form more phonetically informative than plain 'sia'. As with other Egyptian divine names, the vowel is a modern vocalisation convention.

domains.title: Perception, Intellect, Divine Understanding
domains.subtitle: The domain of sꜥ
domains.lead: In the egyptian tradition, sꜥ is the divine faculty of perception — the clear seeing of the heart that precedes every creative word. Paired with Hu, the authoritative tongue, and Heka, magic itself, he stands in the solar barque beside Rꜥ and in the judgement hall as the witness no deception escapes.

cards.name: Memphite Perception
cards.desc: Ptah conceives the gods through the perception of his heart; Sia is the seeing that precedes creative speech.

cards.name: Barque of Re
cards.desc: Sia stands in the solar barque, perceiving and naming the dangers of the Duat during the nocturnal journey.

cards.name: Witness of Weighing
cards.desc: In the Hall of the Two Truths, Sia's perception ensures that no deception escapes the scales of judgment.

cards.name: Divine Intellect
cards.desc: Paired with Hu, the authoritative tongue, Sia makes understanding the twin engine of cosmic and social order.

symbols.name: Papyrus scroll
symbols.meaning: The written record of perception and knowledge, the domain of Sia

symbols.name: Heart (ib)
symbols.meaning: The seat of understanding that Sia personifies

symbols.name: Scribe's palette and reed
symbols.meaning: The tools through which divine intellect is recorded

symbols.name: Ostrich feather of Maat
symbols.meaning: Truth and perception are inseparable in the judgement hall

symbols.name: Thoth's ibis
symbols.meaning: The god of wisdom with whom Sia is closely associated

mythology.lead: Sꜥ has no adventures and no cult centre; he is a personified faculty — perception itself, deified. His 'myths' are therefore texts of doctrine: the Memphite account of creation by heart-perception and tongue-command, the solar books in which he steadies the god's nightly passage, and the judgement where his clear sight stands between the heart and Ammit.

myths.title: Perception in the Heart of Ptah
myths.text: The Shabaka Stone preserves the Memphite Theology, one of Egypt's most sophisticated statements about creation. In this text, Ptah conceives the gods and the world through the perception of his heart and the command of his tongue. Sia is the intellectual seeing that precedes speech: before Ptah says “Let it be,” he understands what is to be. The heart-thought and tongue-command together transform undifferentiated chaos into the articulated cosmos, with Sia as the bridge between silence and creative word.

myths.title: Sia in the Barque of Re
myths.text:
In New Kingdom funerary texts such as the Book of Gates and the Litany of Re, Sia stands in the solar barque as one of the most intimate companions of Rꜥ. His role is to perceive and to name the dangers of the Duat, articulating what the sun-god must confront during the nocturnal journey. Without Sia's understanding, the barque would be blind; without his speech, the guardian demons could not be addressed and pacified.

This imagery made Sia essential to kingship as well. The pharaoh, as Rꜥ's earthly representative, was expected to possess sꜥ in judgment: to see the truth of a matter, to understand its place within Maat, and to speak accordingly. Scribal and instructional literature repeatedly praised the official whose heart was “wide in understanding,” drawing on the same root that the Memphite Theology placed at the center of creation.

lore.culturalLegacy: Sꜥ left no festivals and no temples of his own — his afterlife is conceptual, and it is everywhere. Royal and priestly epithets such as sꜥ-ꜥꜣ, 'great of perception', carried him into titulary and hymn. The scribal ideal he personifies — listen first, understand, then speak — survives as one of the oldest professional ethics on record, quoted still in studies of ancient education. In modern times his name has been revived by scholarship on Egyptian religion and by the Kemetic spiritual movement, for whom he stands for sacred intellect. And in an age that asks whether machines can perceive, the god whose entire being is the act of understanding invites a wry reflection: Egypt deified the faculty three thousand years before anyone tried to engineer it.
lore.archaeology: Sia appears in temple reliefs as a member of Ra's solar barque, notably in the Book of Gates and the tomb of Seti I. The Shabaka Stone preserves the Memphite theology in which divine perception animates creation. New Kingdom royal tombs and sarcophagus texts emphasize understanding (sia) as the prerequisite for justified speech before the gods.
lore.syncretism: In the Late and Ptolemaic Periods the faculties of Sꜥ and Hu were absorbed into the ever-expanding person of Thoth, and the heart-and-tongue theology of the Shabaka Stone reappears in Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride, where Thoth is made heart and tongue of the world-god — Greek logos wearing an ibis head. The Hermetic writings of Roman Egypt pushed the same current further, making divine mind the instrument of creation. Modern Egyptology recovered Sꜥ as a distinct god only in the twentieth century; earlier scholarship, dazzled by Thoth, folded the personified faculty silently into the ibis-god. His truest comparanda are Egyptian: Hu and Heka, his partners in the creative triad, with whom he forms the doctrine that mind, word, and power together sustain Maat.

etymology.derivation: From Egyptian šw, associated with emptiness/dryness and the rising of light/air; the name denotes the god of wind and sunlight.

provenanceSources.title: Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian

pronunciation.approximation: 'SHOO' — drawn out, breathy, like the sound of wind passing through a corridor.
pronunciation.note: Shu is Tier 1 because the Egyptian Šw preserves the caron-marked š — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The name is an onomatopoeic masterpiece: šw sounds like the rush of air it names. Egyptologists debate whether the primary meaning is 'dryness', 'emptiness', or 'he who rises up'; the god contains all three.

domains.title: The Breath Between Worlds
domains.subtitle: Air · Wind · Lions
domains.lead: Šw is the air that separates earth from sky, the breath that brings consciousness, the light that makes visibility possible. In Heliopolitan theology he is the first being to emerge from the creator Atum — not by procreation alone, but by breath, spittle, or sneeze. His eternal labour is to hold the sky-goddess Nut above the earth-god Geb, so that the space of life can exist between them.

cards.name: Air and Breath
cards.desc: Shu is the atmosphere itself — invisible, life-giving, and inseparable from consciousness.

cards.name: Cosmic Separation
cards.desc: With arms raised, Shu lifts Nut away from Geb, creating the interval in which all life dwells.

cards.name: Light
cards.desc: The rays of the sun are called the 'Shu-forms of Re'; Shu makes seeing possible by making space luminous.

cards.name: The Lion
cards.desc: Shu sometimes takes leonine form as a fighter and defender, paired with Tefnut's lioness form.

symbols.name: Ostrich feather
symbols.meaning: Lightness, air, and truth; Shu wears one or more feathers on his head

symbols.name: Raised arms
symbols.meaning: The posture of Shu supporting the sky; the hieroglyph for ka-arms also echoes his life-giving embrace

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: Shu's fighting aspect; the dry, parching wind of the desert

symbols.name: Ankh
symbols.meaning: The breath of life that Shu carries into every nostril

symbols.name: Four supports / Ogdoad
symbols.meaning: The eight Heh-gods who assist Shu in holding up the heavens

mythology.lead: Shu's mythology is cosmogony in motion. He is not a hero who goes on quests; he is the first differentiation of the creator, the void that becomes space, the breath that makes the world inhabitable. Without him, Nut and Geb would remain locked together and no life could arise.

myths.title: Born from Atum
myths.text: In the oldest Egyptian creation account we possess — Pyramid Text Utterance 600, inscribed in the royal pyramids of the late Old Kingdom — the creator Atum stands alone on the primeval hill in the waters of Nun and, without companion, brings forth the first two gods: he sneezes Shu and spits Tefnut, the sacred text says, and the wordplay is the theology. Shu's very name (šw) echoes the sneeze, Tefnut's the spittle; the world begins with the creator's own body discharging itself into differentiation. The Coffin Texts (spells 75–80) expand the scene: Atum, alone in Nun, says he was not built by any builder, and then — 'I sneezed Shu, I spat Tefnut'. Whether by sneeze, spittle, or exhalation, Shu is the moment creation becomes conscious: the first breath the universe ever takes. The myth's joke is profound — the cosmos as a sneeze — and its claim deeper: life begins not with matter but with air, the lightest thing that exists, without which no god, king, or field can live.

myths.title: Shu Lifts the Sky
myths.text: Shu and Tefnut beget the twins Geb (earth) and Nut (sky), but the children are locked in an embrace that leaves no room for life. Shu places himself in the interval and raises Nut above his head, arching her body into the starry vault — the posture the Egyptians gave him forever: kneeling or standing, arms lifted, the cosmic pillar. The image saturates Egyptian religion. It fills royal tombs from the Book of the Dead papyrus of the scribe Nakht (TT52) to the burial chamber of Horemheb (KV57); the Late Period Book of Nut diagrams it as an astronomical treatise; and every temple doorway flanked by heh-pillars and every palace façade propped by figures with raised arms is a frozen Shu. The Ennead of Heliopolis is thus not only a genealogy but a physics: Atum's first act of self-differentiation, perpetually maintained by his firstborn son. Order is not a state but a held pose — and the sky stays up only because someone never puts his arms down.

lore.culturalLegacy: Shu survives wherever we say 'atmosphere' and mean more than weather. The Greeks, meeting the image of a figure bearing heaven, supplied the parallel of Atlas — a comparison every Egyptology handbook repeats — and the sky-bearer motif migrated through Hellenistic and medieval art into the atlantes of Renaissance architecture, carved men holding up what cannot be held. Modern science gave his domain a name and a fragility: the atmosphere is now known to be thin, held, and breakable — Shu's arms, imaged by satellites. Breath-work, meditation, and singing traditions treat every inhalation as a microcosm of his labour: to breathe is to separate inside from outside and to hold, for a moment, the space in which life happens. Few gods have aged so well into metaphor without losing their physics.
lore.archaeology: Shu raising Nut above Geb is painted in the burial chamber of Horemheb (KV57) and on the Book of the Dead papyrus of the scribe Nakht (TT52, Metropolitan Museum). His ostrich feathers crown bronze and stone statuettes from the New Kingdom onward, and the 'Shu-pose' of raised arms develops into the heh-pillars that flank temple doorways. Reliefs at Karnak and in the Osireion at Abydos show him within the Heliopolitan ennead, and faience and stone feathers from his headgear appear among funerary amulets. The motif crosses media with ease — painted, carved, cast — because it is Egyptian cosmology's most portable sentence: someone holds up the sky.
lore.syncretism: The Greeks associated Shu with Atlas, the Titan who holds up the celestial sphere — a comparison of function, not of name, since no Greek rendering of šw is attested; modern scholars repeat the comparison on the same grounds. In Egyptian theology Shu could merge with Re (as the rays of sunlight) and with Onuris, the warrior god. Later solar theology made Shu the son of Re as well as of Atum, smoothing local variants into a single cosmic scheme. The image of a figure supporting the heavens passed from Egypt into Hellenistic and medieval cosmography, influencing depictions of the celestial spheres.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name šw is written with the folded cloth (S29, phonogram š) and the quail-chick (G43, phonogram w), often with the air/light determinatives. The letter š represents a voiceless postalveolar fricative, like English 'sh'. In older transliteration systems the same sound is written ś or sh; the PUNICODEX form follows Gardiner and the Wörterbuch. The long vowel is inferred from Coptic ϣⲟⲩ and from the word's onomatopoeic quality.
