pronunciation.approximation: 'PAHR-vuh-tee' — hold the first 'pahr' and final 'tee' long; the 'v' is light, almost like a 'w'.
pronunciation.note: Pārvatī is Tier 1 because both the initial ā and final ī are long. The name is a transparent feminine derivative of parvata, 'mountain,' specifically the Himalaya.

domains.title: Daughter of the Mountain
domains.subtitle: Mountains, Fertility, Devotion, and Sacred Marriage
domains.lead: Pārvatī is the mountain goddess whose devotion transforms the absolute into a husband. Born of Himavat, the personified Himālaya, she is Satī reborn — destined to wed Śiva and bridge his fierce asceticism and the needs of the world. She is the śakti without whom the great yogin never turns toward creation: through her, the renouncer becomes a householder and the snow-peak a bridal chamber.

cards.name: Tapas and Devotion
cards.desc: She wins Śiva not by beauty alone but by the heat of her own ascetic discipline, matching his severity with hers.

cards.name: Divine Mother
cards.desc: As mother of Gaṇeśa and Skanda/Kārttikeya, she grounds the divine family in domestic love and protective power.

cards.name: Śakti of Śiva
cards.desc: She is the active energy that complements Śiva's stillness; without her, he cannot move toward the world.

cards.name: Mountain and Fertility
cards.desc: Her Himalayan birth links her to snow, purity, and the life-giving rivers that descend from the heights.

symbols.name: Lotus
symbols.meaning: The blue lotus she holds: purity, and devotion unfolding petal by petal rather than arriving at once

symbols.name: Lion or tiger
symbols.meaning: Her vehicle — maternal gentleness riding sovereign ferocity, the same goddess in two gaits

symbols.name: Coral and gold ornaments
symbols.meaning: The adornment of the auspiciously married goddess — she is Gaurī, 'the golden, radiant one'

symbols.name: Two-armed and four-armed forms
symbols.meaning: From the two-armed girl seated beside Śiva to the four-armed goddess with mirror and lotus: her iconography spans housewife to sovereign

symbols.name: The Himalaya
symbols.meaning: Her father and birthplace — the axis of the world and the source of every sacred river that descends from it

mythology.lead: Pārvatī's mythology is the story of a love that refuses to fail. From Satī's death by fire to the reborn goddess's discipline in the snow, her narratives ask how devotion can soften the remotest ascetic — and answer that it does so not by pleading but by becoming equally still, equally burning.

myths.title: The Bride Who Chose the Fire
myths.text: At the great sacrifice of King Dakṣa, the father of the bride made sure that no portion, no honor, was offered to his son-in-law Śiva — the wild, ash-smeared god who had carried off his daughter Satī. Satī argued with her father, and when he would not yield she declared that since the body he had given her had become the instrument of his insult, it could no longer be her dwelling; she entered the sacrificial fire (Śiva Purāṇa, Satī-khaṇḍa; Devībhāgavata Purāṇa 7; the episode is told across many Purāṇas with differing details). Śiva, insane with grief, arrived with his gaṇas, shattered the sacrifice, and began the dance of destruction that could unmake the worlds. Out of Satī's death two things were born: the Śakti Pīṭhas, the seats of the goddess where her body fell, and the resolve of the gods that she must be reborn — as Pārvatī. The myth insists that the goddess does not tolerate being dishonored, even through her own body, and that her death is always strategic, never final.

myths.title: The Penance in the Snow
myths.text: Reborn as the daughter of Himavat, the mountain king, and his queen Menā, the goddess grew up beneath the peaks she had once been. From childhood she was drawn to the meditating Śiva — remote, ash-clad, unmoved — and when her parents despaired, she did what no one expected of a princess: she became an ascetic. In the forests of the Himālaya she performed tapas so severe that the gods began to sweat, and Indra sent the love-god Kāma to interrupt her; Śiva opened his third eye and burned Kāma to ash (Kālidāsa, Kumārasambhava 3–5; Śiva Purāṇa, Pārvatī-khaṇḍa; Matsya Purāṇa 154). Pārvatī did not break her vow; she intensified it, living on air, standing in icy water, until the balance of the universe itself demanded that Śiva notice her. The courting of Śiva is the tradition's answer to a hard question — how does one win the undivided? Not by seduction but by becoming equally undivided: her penance is her proposal.

lore.culturalLegacy: Pārvatī remains a model of the devoted wife, the disciplined yoginī, and the protective mother in Hindu culture. Her marriage to Śiva is re-enacted in countless festivals, dance dramas, and domestic rituals; images of the divine couple (umāmaheśvara) grace temples and home shrines from Nepal to Tamil Nadu. In classical dance, especially Bharatanatyam and Odissi, her narratives are central. Feminist scholars have reclaimed her tapas as an assertion of female spiritual agency, while popular film and television continue to tell her stories to mass audiences. The name Pārvatī is also widely chosen for girls, embodying the ideal of strength cloaked in gentleness.
lore.archaeology: Images of Umā and Pārvatī appear from the Gupta period onward, often as part of the Umāmaheśvara motif showing Śiva in intimate embrace with his consort. Cave temples at Elephanta, Ellora, and Badami include major sculptural groups of the divine couple. Medieval temples across North and South India dedicated to Pārvatī, Gaurī, or the Goddess in her gentle form preserve her iconography as a beautiful, four-armed goddess seated on a lion or tiger. The annual festival of Gaurī/Gaurī Tṛtīyā and local celebrations of her marriage remain important in Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and South India.
lore.syncretism: Pārvatī is inseparable from the broader network of Śiva's consorts and energies. She is Satī reborn, Umā in the Vedas, Gaurī the fair one, and Caṇḍī or Durgā when wrathful. In South India she merges with the Tamil goddess Taṇṇammai; in Bengal and Assam she is identified with the mother goddess. Tantric traditions further multiply her forms, seeing her as the gentle face of the supreme śakti whose fierce aspect is Kālī. The mountain-goddess type has Indo-European echoes — the goddess born of or dwelling on the high peaks — but Pārvatī's specific identity as Śiva's wife and the mother of Gaṇeśa is distinctively Hindu.

entries.meaning: The Black One — the fierce goddess of time and destruction, consort of Śiva (fem. of kāla)

etymology.derivation: From Sanskrit kālī-, feminine of kāla- 'black, dark; time', meaning 'the black one'; by folk etymology she is also 'Goddess of Time'.

steps: Sanskrit Kālī is written काली in Devanagari.
Each aksara combines a consonant with an inherent or explicit vowel.
IAST diacritics preserve length, retroflexion, and aspiration lost in plain ASCII.
The Devanagari form is not used as the primary domain because Indic scripts are not in the .com IDN table.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KAH-lee' — both vowels are long and clear, the first like the 'a' in 'father' held out, the second like 'lee'.
pronunciation.note: Kālī is Tier 1 because both vowels are long (ā, ī), a feature the ASCII 'Kali' loses entirely. The name is a feminine adjective: she is the Black One, the Time-One, the dark beyond gender.

domains.title: Goddess of Time, Destruction, and Empowerment
domains.subtitle: The Black One of the Battlefield and the Cremation Ground
domains.lead: Kālī is the most terrifying and most tender of Hindu goddesses. She appears when the boundary between life and death, order and chaos, becomes thin enough to see through. With black skin, a garland of skulls, and a tongue that laps blood, she is the raw form of śakti — the feminine power that creates by destroying and destroys by creating.

cards.name: Time & Death
cards.desc: As the feminine of kāla, she is time itself — the devourer of minutes, years, and egos.

cards.name: Destruction of Ego
cards.desc: Her sword severs the head of ignorance; her dance grinds the demon of ego beneath her feet.

cards.name: Empowerment
cards.desc: Especially for the marginalized, Kālī is the mother who grants ferocious courage against oppression.

cards.name: Tantric Transgression
cards.desc: She stands outside conventional purity, teaching that the sacred includes what society rejects.

symbols.name: Black skin
symbols.meaning: The color of the void before creation and after destruction; the unmanifest beyond all forms.

symbols.name: Garland of fifty skulls
symbols.meaning: The fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet, showing that she wears language itself as ornament.

symbols.name: Severed head
symbols.meaning: The ego of the demon Raktavīja, or the ego of the practitioner; what must be sacrificed to see truly.

symbols.name: Sword (khaḍga)
symbols.meaning: Discrimination that cuts through illusion.

symbols.name: Tongue extended
symbols.meaning: The moment of shame and awakening; in Bengali tradition, she bites her tongue after stepping on Śiva.

symbols.name: Standing on Śiva
symbols.meaning: Śakti active above Śiva passive; without her energy, the transcendent god is a corpse (śava).

mythology.lead: Kālī enters scripture mid-battle, leaping from Durgā's brow in the seventh chapter of the Devī-Māhātmya, and she never quite leaves. Behind her battlefield births stand older griefs — the death of Satī, the goddess's body scattered across India — and ahead of her stretches the Tantric theology that made her the supreme deity of Bengal and Assam.

myths.title: From the Brow of Durgā
myths.text: In the war against Śumbha and Niśumbha, the demon Raktavīja seemed unkillable: every drop of his blood that touched the ground spawned another warrior as strong as the first, and Caṇḍikā's arrows multiplied him faster than she could cut him down. Then, as the Devī-Māhātmya (ch. 7) tells it, from the forehead of the battling goddess sprang a new being — black as a storm cloud, gaunt, with a sword, a noose, and a skull-topped staff — who opened her mouth and drank. Kālī swallowed the demon's blood as it spilled, catching every drop on her tongue, stretching her jaws across the battlefield, and devouring his freshly-born doubles until Raktavīja stood alone and died. The gods watched in wonder, and the text names her for what she is: the extreme boundary of the goddess, born when the ordinary weaponry of heaven has failed. She is not rage for its own sake but surgical ferocity against entropy: what bleeds without limit must be drunk without limit.

myths.title: The Demon Only a Woman Could Kill
myths.text: The Kālikā Purāṇa, the great scripture of Assamese Śāktism, tells of Dāruka, a demon so favored by his austerities that the gods could not touch him — until a flaw in his boon was found: only a woman could kill him. As he tormented the worlds, Kālī went to war, and the text lingers on her armies, her weapons, and her fury. But the war's strangest moment became its most famous image: in the tumult, Kālī — drunk on battle, tongue out, garlanded with heads — failed to notice that she was dancing on the body of her own husband, Śiva, who had thrown himself beneath her feet to bring the dance to an end (Kālikā Purāṇa; the image becomes the standard icon of Kālī standing upon Śiva). The theology is exact: śakti without consciousness is a rampage, consciousness without śakti is a corpse, and only when energy stands upon awareness is the goddess complete. It is the same doctrine the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra will state in philosophical terms, here told as a battlefield accident that the whole tradition chose never to forget.

lore.culturalLegacy: Kālī's image has traveled far beyond her temples. In Bengal she is the household mother, worshipped at Kālīghāṭ and Dakṣiṇeśwar — where the nineteenth-century saint Ramakrishna wept before her as a child before its mother, reclaiming her from the colonial caricature; in Kerala she appears as Bhadrakālī in blood-offering rituals; in the diaspora she is a symbol of South Asian identity and feminine power. Nineteenth-century missionaries had singled her out as the most degraded of India's deities, and Bengali nationalists answered by making her the wrathful motherland; revolutionary secret societies took her name before the courts did. Western occultists, from the Theosophists to modern Wiccans, have drawn on her iconography, sometimes with scholarly care and sometimes without. Film, comics, and protest art return to her again and again: the black-skinned woman with the sword, the tongue, the unblinking stare. Kālī endures because she refuses to be domesticated. She is the god who looks back.
lore.archaeology: Kālī's archaeological footprint grows in medieval Bengal and the Deccan. Pala-Sena stone and terracotta images from Bengal and Bihar (10th–12th centuries CE) show her with protruding tongue, skull garland, and severed head. The Kālīghāṭ temple in Kolkata and the Dakṣiṇeśwar Kālī temple built by Rani Rashmoni (1855) anchor her modern cult. Kerala's Bhadrakālī temples preserve blood-offering rites, and Nepalese sculptures display her Tantric iconography.
lore.syncretism: Kālī is inseparable from Durgā, Pārvatī, Satī, and the ten Mahāvidyās of Tantra; she is the fierce face of the same goddess who appears as the gentle Gaurī. In Buddhist Tantra, especially in Tibet, she echoes in fierce ḍākinīs and in wrathful forms of Tārā. Southeast Asian goddess cults, from Cham Po Nagar to Javanese Durga, carry her shadow. The colonial and postcolonial West has appropriated her as a feminist and punk icon, often stripping away ritual context. Whether feared, loved, or misunderstood, Kālī remains the boundary where the sacred becomes unbearably real.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Devanagari form is काली. IAST macrons mark both long vowels (ā, ī). The same root produces kāla ('time, black') and Kālā ('the black one'); the feminine ending -ī gives the goddess her name. In Tantric texts she is also called Kālikā (कालिका).

entries.meaning: 'Furrow' — the field-goddess, wife of Rāma and mother of his twin sons

steps: Sanskrit Sītā is written in Devanagari as सीता
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: SEE-taa — both vowels long, even and open.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit sītā carries two long vowels; the restoration Sītā keeps both macrons. Her name means "furrow" — the plough-line of the field from which she rose — making hers the rare theonym that is a farm word before it is a goddess, and the two macrons are the whole of its written dignity.

domains.title: The Daughter of the Furrow
domains.subtitle: Devotion, Exile, Trial, and the Opened Earth
domains.lead: Sītā is the epic of India told from its quiet center: the furrow-born princess whose abduction sets the Rāmāyaṇa in motion, whose fidelity survives fire, and whose final return is not to her husband but to the earth that bore her. She is virtue tested past every reasonable limit — and found whole.

cards.name: The Furrow
cards.desc: King Janaka found her in the plough-line of a sacrificial field — the earth's own child, named for the cut in the soil.

cards.name: The Fire
cards.desc: The agni-parīkṣā: the trial by fire she walked into to prove what everyone watching already knew.

cards.name: The Exile
cards.desc: Fourteen years in the forest, the abduction to Laṅkā, the second exile while pregnant — endurance as biography.

cards.name: The Return
cards.desc: Her answer to the second doubt: the earth opens, and the daughter of the furrow goes home.

symbols.name: The furrow
symbols.meaning: Her name and origin: the ploughed line — fertility, labor, and the earth's patience

symbols.name: The golden deer
symbols.meaning: The lure that crossed her threshold — desire engineered as trap

symbols.name: The fire
symbols.meaning: Proof demanded of the innocent; the trial that should never have been asked

symbols.name: The lotus
symbols.meaning: Her purity in every depiction from temple bronze to Madhubani painting

mythology.lead: The Rāmāyaṇa calls itself Rāma's story, but its moral engine is Sītā: every choice that matters is measured against her.

myths.title: Daughter of the Field
myths.text: King Janaka of Mithilā, ploughing a sacrificial field, struck something that was not stone: an infant in the furrow, whom he named Sītā — "furrow" — and raised as his daughter. Earth-born, not womb-born, the texts insist: her mother is the field itself, and the Rāmāyaṇa's most beloved heroine begins as a gift of agriculture. Her marriage to Rāma follows the bow of Śiva that only he could string.

myths.title: The Golden Deer
myths.text: In the forest of Daṇḍaka, during the fourteen-year exile, the demon Mārīca became a golden deer to draw Rāma from her side, and Rāvaṇa came as a wandering ascetic. She crossed the line — the lakṣmaṇa-rekhā drawn for her protection — only to give alms, and was carried through the sky to Laṅkā. A year in the Aśoka grove, under guard, refusing a king: the epic's center of gravity is her refusal.

lore.culturalLegacy: Sītā is the standard by which Indian womanhood has been both honored and constrained — the "Sītā ideal" of fidelity and endurance, and the modern feminist re-reading that asks why the proving was hers to do. Her festivals (Sītānavamī, Vivāha Panchamī at Janakpur) draw millions; the Madhubani painting tradition of her Mithilā homeland depicts her in every home; Bollywood and television return to her constantly. Every debate on dignity, loyalty, and who owes whom proof in India runs, sooner or later, through the furrow.
lore.archaeology: Janakpur in Nepal's Terai keeps her city: the Janaki Mandir (1911, on older foundations) marks the site tradition calls her birthplace-home, and the Ram-Janaki Vivāha festival re-enacts the wedding annually. Mithilā's painted tradition (Madhubani/Maithil art, from the kohbar wedding-chamber murals) is among the world's oldest continuously practiced narrative arts. The Rāmāyaṇa sites across India and Sri Lanka — the Aśoka Vatika candidates near Nuwara Eliya, the Sītā Amman temple there — form the epic's living pilgrimage map.
lore.syncretism: Across Asia she travels with the epic: Thailand's Sida in the Ramakien, Cambodia's and Laos' Reamker versions, Indonesia's Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa, and the Jain tellings that soften the fire. In Nepal she is Janaki, daughter of Janakpur — the nation claims her birthplace and keeps her festival. The bhakti traditions make her inseparable from Rāma (Sītā-Rāma as one object of worship), and the Śākta readings make her the goddess herself in human trial: the earth-goddess borrowing a biography.

entries.meaning: The third of the Pāṇḍava princes, a son of Indra and Kuntī; the great archer of the Mahābhārata, to whom Kṛṣṇa speaks the Bhagavad-gītā.

pronunciation.approximation: ah-HOO-ruh MAHZ-dah — the first 'a' is long, the 'u' is long and rounded, and the final 'dah' is drawn out.
pronunciation.note: AhuraMazdā is a Tier-1 restoration: the macron on the final ā of Mazdā preserves the long vowel the ASCII form loses. The compound is written as a single word in the PUNICODEX domain to keep the name registrable as one Unicode string, following the project's convention for the Zoroastrian supreme being.

domains.title: Wise Lord of Creation
domains.subtitle: Supreme Creator, Wisdom, Light, and Order
domains.lead: AhuraMazdā is the highest god of Zoroastrianism, the uncreated creator who thinks the cosmos into being and sustains it through truth (aša), good thought, and the Holy Immortals. He is not a storm warrior or a tribal patron but a cosmic architect whose enemy is the lie (druj). In the Gāthās, the oldest Zoroastrian hymns, he speaks directly to the prophet Zarathustra, asking humanity to choose between good purpose and evil.

cards.name: Creator by Thought
cards.desc: The cosmos existed first as his plan: he shaped it in thought (mainyu), then clothed it in matter — creation as a design executed, not an accident.

cards.name: Lord of Aša
cards.desc: Aša — truth, right order, the fitness of things — is his first emanation; fire itself is aša embodied, which is why temples tend it as his visible self.

cards.name: The Amesha Spentas
cards.desc: Vohu Manah (Good Mind), Aša, Khshathra (Sovereignty), Spenta Ārmaiti (Holy Devotion), Haurvatāt (Wholeness), Ameretāt (Immortality) — his attributes become beings.

cards.name: Fire and Light
cards.desc: The atar, sacred fire, is honored as his purest visible sign — purity, energy, and vigilance in one flame, tended five times a day.

symbols.name: Faravahar
symbols.meaning: The winged disk above the fire altar: a guardian figure within the ring of eternity, adopted in modern times as the emblem of Zoroastrian identity — an icon of watchfulness, not an object of worship.

symbols.name: Sacred fire (atar)
symbols.meaning: The temple flame fed five times daily, his purest visible presence; tending it is the community's central act of worship.

symbols.name: The sun
symbols.meaning: 'The eye of AhuraMazdā' in Pahlavi tradition — light as the visible form of truth, hunting the darkness where the lie hides.

symbols.name: The ring of sovereignty
symbols.meaning: The diadem-ring held by the winged figure: the covenant of just rule — kings reign legitimately only under aša.

symbols.name: The barsom (baresman)
symbols.meaning: The bundle of sacred twigs held in prayer, the ritual instrument that concentrates the worshipper's presence before the fire.

mythology.lead: The mythology of AhuraMazdā is not a cycle of adventures but a grand cosmology: the twin spirits at the world's dawn, the creation in seven acts, the golden age of Yima, the first man Gayōmart, and the final renovation (Frashokereti) when evil will be destroyed and the world made perfect. Every human moral choice participates in this cosmic drama.

myths.title: The Choice at the World's Dawn
myths.text: In the Gāthās, the oldest stratum of Zoroastrian scripture, AhuraMazdā is not alone at the beginning. Two spirits stood forth there, twins — Spenta Mainyu, the Holy Creative Spirit, and Angra Mainyu, the Destructive — 'the better and the bad in thought, word, and deed' (Yasna 30.3–5). The two chose differently at the first dawn: one embraced truth (aša), the other the lie (druj), and through that choice the world became an arena where every human being must choose again. AhuraMazdā is lord of the good choice, not its manufacturer — the Gāthās call him 'the father of Good Purpose' (Yasna 45) while the evil spirit acts 'knowing no lord.' Scholars still debate whether this is metaphysical dualism or a dramatized moral one; either way, the myth insists that evil is a real counter-force that goodness must outlast, not an illusion to be explained away.

myths.title: The Seven Creations and the Assault of Ahriman
myths.text: In the Pahlavi Bundahišn, AhuraMazdā creates the world in seven successive acts: first the sky as a round shell, then water, then earth, then plants, then the sole primordial bull, then Gayōmart the first man, and finally fire — 'the life of all creation' (Bundahišn 1–3). Knowing Angra Mainyu would attack, the Wise Lord fixed time at nine thousand years and offered the destroyer a covenant: darkness would be his for half of it. Ahriman's counter-creations answer each good with its poison — drought against water, the wolf against the dog, winter against summer, death against life — and the cosmos becomes a mixed substance from the start: good in essence, wounded in fact. Human labor, tending fire, cattle, fields, and truth, is thus the active repair of creation. The myth means that the world is not a masterpiece to be admired but a workshop to be defended.

lore.culturalLegacy: AhuraMazdā is the enduring name of God in Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest continuously practiced religions, kept alive today by the Parsi communities of India and the Irani Zoroastrians of Yazd and Kerman. His call to good thoughts, good words, good deeds — humata, hukhta, hvarshta — remains the tradition's central ethical formula, recited at every prayer. The Faravahar has become an emblem of Iranian identity well beyond the faith, and Nowruz, the new year feast, still turns on the renewal of creation he began. Zoroastrian patterns of judgment and cosmic renewal shaped the religious imagination of late antiquity; in modern interfaith discourse, AhuraMazdā represents an early vision of a single moral creator who asks for ethical action rather than blood sacrifice.
lore.archaeology: AhuraMazdā is invoked in Achaemenid royal inscriptions at Bisotun (DB), Persepolis, Naqsh-e Rustam (DN inscription), and Susa, usually in the Old Persian form Auramazdā. The reliefs above Darius at Bisotun and the facades at Naqsh-e Rustam show the king before the winged-disk symbol — whether the figure beneath the ring is the god himself or the royal fravaši remains debated. Zoroastrian fire temples (atešgāhs) from Sasanian and later periods, such as the Āteshkadeh of Yazd, preserve the cult of fire as his visible presence, and Avestan manuscripts copied in India and Iran transmit the Gāthās and the liturgical corpus across a thousand years of transmission.
lore.syncretism: Under the Achaemenids, AhuraMazdā (Auramazdā) stood behind nearly every royal inscription, and Greek observers equated him with Zeus — Herodotus speaks of Persian Zeus-worship, and Greco-Bactrian coins naming Zeus-Oromasdes show the identification made visual. Plutarch (De Iside 46–47) preserves the late-antique pairing of Oromazes with Arimanius, light against darkness. One Pahlavi school went further: Zurvanism made him the twin son of Infinite Time, Zurvān — a doctrine the orthodox condemned yet could not fully erase. His deepest legacy is structural: the shared architecture of final judgment, bodily resurrection, and a savior's arrival that Jewish, Christian, and Islamic apocalyptic hold in common with Zoroaster — whether by direct inheritance or convergent hope remains one of the liveliest debates in the study of religion.

steps: Avestan distinguishes the velar nasal ŋ (𐬢) written here in aŋra.
Unicode restoration AngraMainyu simplifies the nasal to n.
The diphthongal ending -iiu is written with two i letters followed by u.
Yasht 10, the hymn to Mithra, preserves this spelling.
The intervocalic -th- of the restoration corresponds to Avestan θ (𐬚).
Unicode restoration Mithra uses the same consonants as the Avestan original.
Written aŋra mainiiu in the Avesta (Gathic nom. aŋrō mainiiuš, Yasna 45.2; Younger form at Vendidad 19.1)
The Younger spelling writes the ending with two i-letters (…mainiiu)
'Ahriman' is the Middle Persian (Pahlavi) development of the same name

pronunciation.approximation: Say "ahriman" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Ahriman".
pronunciation.note: Ahriman is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the form preserves nothing distinctive against ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter; it is the anglicized Middle Persian name of the Younger Avestan Aŋra Mainyu. The Gāthās know the concept (aŋrō mainiiuš, 'the evil spirit') before they know the name.

domains.title: Ahriman
domains.subtitle: Evil
domains.lead: Ahriman is the Evil Spirit of Zoroastrianism — Avestan Aŋra Mainyu, 'destructive mind' — the adversary of the wise lord Ohrmazd. He is not a rival god but the Lie made willful: choice turned against creation. The tradition is emphatic that he creates nothing, can only corrupt, and is destined to lose.

cards.name: The Twin at Dawn
cards.desc: Yasna 30's two spirits, Better and Bad, choose creation and not-being at the world's first dawn — evil begins as a choice, not a birth.

cards.name: The Lie (Druj)
cards.desc: His essence is the Lie — Avestan druj — deception and disorder that rot good choice; the daēvas are his servants.

cards.name: Counter-Creation
cards.desc: Against Ohrmazd's sky, waters, plants, cattle, and man he fashioned opposites: winter, drought, poison, wolves, and death (Bundahišn).

cards.name: The Powerless End
cards.desc: At the Renovation he is bound and defeated, his weapons melted away — eschatology grants evil no Ragnarǫk, only erasure.

symbols.name: The dragon Aži Dahāka
symbols.meaning: The three-mouthed, three-headed, six-eyed dragon he loosed against creation (Yasna 9.8; Yašt 9) — winter and lie made monster

symbols.name: Druj, the Lie
symbols.meaning: Deception as his true weapon — the dark counterpart of Aša, the order and truth that hold the good creation together

symbols.name: The north
symbols.meaning: The direction of his assault on the sky: he broke in from the north, the realm of cold and darkness (Bundahišn)

symbols.name: Winter and drought
symbols.meaning: His counter-creations against sky and water — the killing seasons raised against Ohrmazd's order

symbols.name: Wolves and xrafstars
symbols.meaning: The noxious creatures of his making — predators and vermin set against cattle, the good man's wealth

mythology.lead: Ahriman's mythology is the drama of Zoroastrian dualism: a spirit of destruction who chooses evil at creation's dawn, assaults the sky, counterfeits every good thing, and is finally bound. The fullest account is the Sasanian Bundahišn; the oldest, the Gāthās of Zarathustra.

myths.title: The Two Spirits at the First Dawn
myths.text: The oldest stratum of Zoroastrian scripture is not a battle story but a choice. In Yasna 30.3–5 Zarathustra hymns 'the two spirits in the beginning, the twins renowned as the Better and the Bad in thought, word, and deed... when the two spirits met, they created life and not-life, and settled that at the last the worst existence would be for the followers of the Lie, but the Best Mind for the followers of Truth.' The Bad Spirit — aŋrō mainiiuš — 'chose not-being' in the deed he performed. Later tradition hardened the twinhood into two eternities, but the Gāthās themselves insist on what scandalized later theologians: evil is primordial as a choice, not as a substance. The myth means that good and evil are first of all directions of the will, and every human soul stands where the two spirits once stood.

myths.title: The Assault on the Sky
myths.text: The Sasanian Greater Bundahišn (ch. 1) narrates the attack. Ahriman, in his darkness below, glimpses Ohrmazd's luminous creation and rises, envious, to destroy it. Ohrmazd — knowing the end belongs to him — offers peace: let the two realms keep to themselves for 9,000 years. Ahriman refuses; but at the first recitation of the Ahuna Vairya prayer he is thrown into stupor for three thousand years, from which the demoness Jahi the Whore wakes him with a shout. He smashes through the sky — egg-like boundary of the ordered world — from the north, and his demons pour in after him. Only then does Ohrmazd set creation in motion against him. The myth means that evil's first act is always an invasion of someone else's order: the Lie owns nothing it does not break into.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ahriman never had a cult — no sane theology worships the Lie — yet his legacy is immense. In New Persian ahriman became an ordinary word for devil, and in Zoroastrian liturgy his name is ritually cursed to this day. The intellectual legacy is larger: the mature Western Devil, the 'prince of darkness' of Second Temple and early Christian writing, took much of its profile from the Persian-period encounter with Zoroastrian dualism — cosmic adversary, tempter, lord of a demonic host, destined loser. In modernity, Anquetil du Perron's 1771 translation of the Avesta reintroduced Ahriman to Europe, where he became a fixture of Romantic orientalism and eventually of scholarship — Boyce's Zoroastrians made the religion legible to a general readership. He endures in games and fantasy as the stock arch-fiend, rarely credited. The name thus tracks a long migration: from Gāthāic abstraction to Sasanian adversary to the modern world's default image of absolute evil.
lore.archaeology: There is deliberately no archaeology of Ahriman: a cult of evil would have been unthinkable, and none existed. The material record is the scripture itself — the Avesta survives in manuscripts of a Sasanian archetype, the oldest substantial copy being the British Library's 'Avesta of 1323 CE'. The closest contemporary witness is linguistic rather than iconic: the Old Persian inscriptions of Darius I at Behistun and Persepolis name drauga, 'the Lie', as the cosmic enemy the king's order fights — Ahriman's essence without his name, some three centuries after Zarathustra. Sasanian iconography avoids his image entirely, and no sanctuary, altar, or votive has ever been identified with him. Evil's archaeological footprint is precisely an absence: the one god-shaped hole in Iran's religious landscape.
lore.syncretism: Medieval Zoroastrianism itself generated the most famous heresy about him: Zurvanism, attested in the Denkard's refutations and in Syriac and Armenian reports, made Ohrmazd and Ahriman twin sons of Zurvan, Infinite Time — evil suddenly genealogical rather than chosen, precisely the move orthodox theology refused. Outside Iran, Plutarch (De Iside et Osiride 46–47) reports the Magi and their good and evil daimones, naming the evil one Arimanius; the name turns up again in a Greek magical papyrus (PGM IV), invoked there by sorcery. Manichaeism took the figure into Middle Persian as hrywm'n, a hostile prince of darkness in the Turfan texts, and through late-antique Christian polemic his outline fed the developing theology of Satan — the 'devil as cosmic adversary' of the West owes much of its shape to the Persian-period encounter. The Achaemenid inscriptions are strikingly silent: Darius knows Auramazda and the Lie (drauga), but never the Evil Spirit by name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'IN-tee' — two even syllables with the weight on the first; the vowels are pure, the t light and unaspirated.
pronunciation.note: Inti is Tier 2: the Quechua name carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter, and the capital alone distinguishes the restoration from the ASCII form. What the temple restores is not a sound but a sovereignty — Inti, the Sun, father and ancestor of the Sapa Inca.

domains.title: Inti
domains.subtitle: Sun
domains.lead: Inti is the sun as sovereign: father of the Inca dynasty, patron of Cuzco, and the divine ancestor whose rays fed the terraces that fed an empire. He is the unseen emperor of the Andean sky — never shown as a body, only as gold, light, and the crimson fringe on his son's forehead.

cards.name: The Punchao
cards.desc: The life-sized golden statue of Inti — 'Daytime' — enthroned in the Coricancha, its face and rays of beaten gold, flanked by golden maize and llamas (Cobo, Historia 13.14).

cards.name: Ancestor of the Sapa Inca
cards.desc: Every reigning Inca was the Sun's son; the empire's genealogy, law, and war were obligations owed to a father in the sky.

cards.name: Inti Raymi
cards.desc: The June festival at Cuzco — fasting, night dancing, and offerings on the usnu, when the Sapa Inca drank with his father at the standing sun (Cobo 13.16–17).

cards.name: Solar Agriculture
cards.desc: Terraces, planting calendars, and frost-shrines along the equator — the sun made harvest, and harvest made the empire.

symbols.name: The Punchao idol
symbols.meaning: The great golden statue of Inti kept in the Coricancha: a round face with rays and a ceremonial fringe, tended each morning like a waking king (Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo 13.14).

symbols.name: The Maskaypacha
symbols.meaning: The crimson tassel-fringe worn on the Sapa Inca's forehead, read as the sun's own rays — kingship made visible as light.

symbols.name: Golden maize and llamas
symbols.meaning: Life-sized gold offerings in the Coricancha's garden of the Sun: the staple crop and beast of burden presented to Inti in his own metal.

symbols.name: The gilded eastern wall
symbols.meaning: The sanctuary's eastern wall was a sheet of gold, catching the first light of the June solstice and setting the whole house of the Sun ablaze.

symbols.name: The June solstice
symbols.meaning: The pivot of Inti Raymi: the sun stands still, the emperor stands before it, and the year is renewed by being witnessed.

mythology.lead: Inti's mythology is imperial theology. The sixteenth-century chroniclers — Betanzos, Sarmiento de Gamboa, Murúa, and later Cobo — preserve the state myths that made a mountain people the children of the sun: a creator who sired the daystar, a brother and sister sent to found Cuzco, and a solstice festival that renewed the world each year.

myths.title: Inti, Child of the Creator
myths.text: In the theology the Inca taught at Cuzco, Inti was not the first power. The creator Viracocha — the incomprehensible god behind the world, as the chroniclers struggled to render him — made the sun, the moon, and the stars and set them in heaven as lights for humankind. Inti and his sister-wife Mama Quilla were thus the children of the highest god, commissioned to govern the sky in their father's place (Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica 7; Betanzos, Suma y Narración 2). The genealogy is political architecture: by making Inti a son rather than a source, the Inca placed their own emperor — Inti's son — only two steps below creation itself. When the Sapa Inca stood before the people as the unique son of the Sun, the title carried a whole cosmology in four words. The myth means that empire, in the Andes, was a family business conducted in the language of the sky.

myths.title: The Golden Staff of Manco Cápac
myths.text: The founding myth of Cuzco is a solar errand. Inti and Mama Quilla, grieving that humankind lived without law, cloth, or maize, sent their children — a son, Manco Cápac, and a daughter, Mama Ocllo — from the Island of the Sun in Lake Titicaca, bearing a golden staff. Wherever the staff sank whole into the earth, there they were to raise the city. At the hill called Huanacauri, above the valley of Cuzco, the staff went down, and the siblings taught the gathered people to plough, to weave, and to live under rule (Sarmiento, Historia Indica 11–12; Betanzos 4; Murúa, Historia general del Piru). The myth makes the Inca capital literally planted in the ground by the sun's own metal: Cuzco was not built so much as sown. Every furrow of its terraces repeated the lesson — agriculture, the technology that let the mountains feed an empire, arrived as a gift from Inti's household, and the ruler in Cuzco ruled as the sun's eldest child.

lore.culturalLegacy: Inti's name still circulates as money and memory. Peru's currency from 1985 to 1991 was the inti, and the sol that replaced it remembers the same sun. Cusco's civic emblems carry solar imagery, and the restored Inti Raymi has made the June solstice the city's defining modern feast, performed now in Quechua before an audience of the world. Across Bolivia and Ecuador the sun appears in indigenous political symbolism, and the vocabulary of Inca statehood — Sapa Inca, Coricancha, the sun's own child — remains the standard language of Andean identity. For scholarship, Inti is the paradigm case of religion as statecraft: a god engineered, with extraordinary sophistication, to make empire feel like family.
lore.archaeology: The Coricancha — the Golden Enclosure — survives as foundations: the curved wall with the Twelve-Angled Stone (Hatunrumiyoc street) and the trapezoidal doorways and niches now enclosed by Santo Domingo. Nothing of the gold survives; the chroniclers' inventories (Cobo, Murúa) are its only catalogue. Platform-shrines called usnu at Vilcashuamán and Huánuco Pampa mark the provincial stages of the solar cult. The Island of the Sun in Lake Titicaca preserves Inca shrines at the myth's supposed source, including the sacred rock from which the founding siblings were sent. And at Sacsayhuamán above Cuzco the June sun still rises over the terrace where the modern Inti Raymi is performed — here the archaeology is partly a calendar.
lore.syncretism: The conquest did not end Inti; it translated him. Spanish missionaries deliberately identified the sun with the Christian God, and the great church of Santo Domingo was planted directly on the Coricancha's foundations, its colonial vaults rising around the curved Inca walls that still hold them up. Extirpation campaigns under the viceroyalty hunted the surviving cult, and the last great idols of the old religion were destroyed in the 1570s. Yet the translation ran both ways: in the Andean highlands the sun kept his ancient festival day, and in 1944 the Cusco teacher Faustino Espinoza Navarro staged the first modern Inti Raymi at Sacsayhuamán — a theatrical revival, partly invented, that has grown into one of South America's great public rituals, drawing hundreds of thousands each June. The Inca sun survives less as doctrine than as performance: a name the conquest could not melt, re-lit every solstice above the city he founded.

pronunciation.approximation: Say "viracocha" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Wiraqucha".
pronunciation.note: Wiraqucha is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the restored form is plain ASCII, with no distinctive feature the ASCII alphabet loses. The name compounds Quechua wira, 'fat, grease, foam,' and qucha, 'lake, sea' — Father Murúa glossed it 'lake of fat,' more evocatively 'foam of the sea.' The restoration follows modern Quechua orthography rather than the colonial Spanish spelling Viracocha.

domains.title: Wiraqucha
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: Wiraqucha is the maker of the Inca cosmos: sky father, creator of sun and moon, and the weeping wanderer who once walked the length of the Andes and was never seen again. The chroniclers knew him as the invisible god who made the world and then withdrew from it — and his name still survives in the politest word an Andean elder can offer a stranger: wiraqucha, sir, gentleman, lord.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The name compounds Quechua wira, 'fat, foam,' and qucha, 'lake, sea'; the chroniclers glossed it 'lake of fat,' more evocatively 'foam of the sea.'

cards.name: Creator
cards.desc: Maker of the sun, moon, and stars and of every nation; to the Andes he is Pachayachachic, 'creator of the world.'

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Honored at Titicaca, Tiwanaku, and Cusco; his cult outlived the empire and endures in solstice pilgrimage, shrine, and everyday address.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple; the scholarly restoration Wiraqucha replaces the colonial spelling Viracocha with modern Quechua orthography.

symbols.name: Sea foam of the lake
symbols.meaning: The etymon wira-qucha, 'foam (or fat) of the lake' — the foam from which the name, and the god, emerged

symbols.name: The staff and traveler's bundle
symbols.meaning: He crossed the Andes as a staff-carrying beggar, weeping at springs and prophesying — the god as itinerant stranger

symbols.name: The reed float
symbols.meaning: The totora-reed float that bore the two survivors of the flood — the seed of the remade world

symbols.name: The stone models of Tiwanaku
symbols.meaning: The sculpted prototypes of every nation, from which Wiraqucha shaped humankind at his workshop

symbols.name: The golden image of Cusco
symbols.meaning: The solid-gold statue in the Coricancha, described by Cobo and Murúa and melted down within years of the conquest

mythology.lead: Wiraqucha's mythology reaches us only through the reports of conquered lords to Spanish chroniclers — Betanzos, Cobo, Sarmiento — yet it holds together a coherent cosmic biography: the making of the world, the flood that erased its first people, the shaping of the nations at Tiwanaku, and a final journey westward that ended in disappearance.

myths.title: The Flood of Unu Pachakuti
myths.text: Juan de Betanzos, whose Suma y Narración de los Incas (1551) is the fullest early account, tells that Wiraqucha made the first people at Tiwanaku and gave them the world to keep; but they grew proud and lived without worship, so he resolved to undo them. He sent a great flood — unu pachakuti, a watery overturning of the world — that drowned the first race, the wari, while he himself rose into the sky above Titicaca. Yet he spared two, a man and a woman, calling them from the waters onto a float of totora reeds near the island, and commissioning them as the ancestors of a new humanity. The myth fixes the shape of Andean time: catastrophe and renewal in cycles, a world unmade and remade, with the creator always watching from above. It is also a charter for the lake itself — Titicaca is not scenery but the hinge where the first world ended and the second began.

myths.title: The Making of Nations at Tiwanaku
myths.text: Father Bernabé Cobo's Historia del Nuevo Mundo (Book 13) preserves the imperial version: after the flood, Wiraqucha set to work at Tiwanaku, where he sculpted the forms of all the nations to come — each with its own face, dress, language, songs, and seeds — and brought them to life. When the work was done he dispatched them, calling them out of caves, springs, and rivers to find their homelands: one nation he sent by way of a cave, another along a river's course, and to the Inca ancestors he gave the special charge that would lead them at last to Cusco. Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa's Historia Indica (ch. 6–7) gives the same program and adds the full titulature: Ticci Uiracocha Pachayachachic, 'ancient foundation, creator of the world.' The myth is a map of the Andes read backward — every people is the deliberate work of the same hand, and the Inca are simply the nation that remembered best who made them.

lore.culturalLegacy: Wiraqucha never lost his mountain. Pilgrims still cross to the Island of the Sun and Moon on Titicaca, and each June solstice thousands gather at Tiwanaku to watch the sun rise through the Gate of the Sun — a rite older than any written version of the myth it now frames. In modern Quechua and Aymara, wiraqucha remains an honorific — sir, elder, gentleman — a fragment of the god carried in everyday address. The modern Inti Raymi festival at Sacsayhuamán keeps the creator in public view, and the story of the weeping god who foresaw the bearded strangers is still told as the Andes' own prophecy of the conquest. The empire that carried his name fell in a generation; the name outlived the empire by five centuries and is still a polite word for a stranger on a mountain road.
lore.archaeology: Wiraqucha's archaeology is the archaeology of his stage. Tiwanaku, the great center of the altiplano (c. 500–1000 CE), holds the Kalasasaya platform, the monumental Gateway of the Sun, and the precision-cut blocks of Puma Punku — the ruins later tradition named as his workshop, where the myth says he modeled the nations in stone. On the Island of the Sun and Island of the Moon in Lake Titicaca, Inca pilgrims' shrines — the Chincana labyrinths, the sacred rock, the sanctuary terraces — mark the myth's exact geography, and Copacabana's basilica stands on the shore where the ritual boats once left. In Cusco, the chroniclers describe a solid-gold image of the god in the Coricancha (Cobo; Murúa), melted down within years of 1532. No pre-Columbian inscription names him: the ruins give the stage, and the chronicles give the script.
lore.syncretism: Spanish missionaries moved quickly to identify Wiraqucha with the Christian God: Father Bernabé Cobo reports Andean lords hearing the gospel and concluding that this Dios must be their own Pachayachachic, finally named. The identification stuck — in Andean parishes 'Dios Pachayachachic' is still a natural sentence — and it let the old shrine centers be absorbed rather than erased, most completely at Copacabana on Titicaca's shore, where the basilica of the Virgin stands where pilgrims once took ship for the island shrines. More remarkably, the god's name became a title for the conquerors themselves: from the earliest chronicles onward, viracocha meant a Spaniard, a gentleman, a lord — the word a conquered people used for strangers who arrived dressed, as Betanzos' prophecy said, exactly like their departing god. Even Tiwanaku's sculpted Gateway of the Sun is popularly read as his image, though that identification is a modern antiquarian conjecture — the gate predates the name by centuries.

pronunciation.approximation: 'pa-cha-MA-ma' — four even syllables with the weight on 'MA'; the 'ch' is the same sound as in English 'church,' not 'chase.'
pronunciation.note: Pachamama is Tier 2: the name is written in plain Latin letters, and the ASCII form 'pachamama' loses nothing the restoration could return — no stress mark, diacritic, or distinctive letter is at stake. The capitalised form marks scholarly proper-name status; the tradition itself was an oral one, carried in Quechua and Aymara long before it was ever written.

domains.title: Pachamama
domains.subtitle: Earth
domains.lead: Pachamama is the living earth of the Andes — mother of harvests, herds, and households, the ground that feeds and the ground that opens. Hers is a religion of reciprocity: nothing is taken from the earth without payment returned to it. She is not a goddess of temples alone but of every furrow, kitchen, and burial in the Inca world and beyond.

cards.name: Pacha Mama
cards.desc: The name itself is the doctrine: pacha 'earth, world, time' + mama 'mother' — the earth as parent, in Quechua.

cards.name: Harvest and Fertility
cards.desc: Maize, potatoes, and llama herds depend on her goodwill; a neglected Pachamama withholds, an honored one multiplies.

cards.name: Payment to the Earth
cards.desc: Chicha poured into the soil, coca leaves buried or burned — the pago, the thanks and the debt acknowledged before eating.

cards.name: Earthquakes and Openings
cards.desc: When offended she stirs: the earth trembles, the underworld mouth opens; her anger is the mountain shaking itself.

symbols.name: Coca leaves
symbols.meaning: The divine plant of the Andes (Cobo calls it the most sacred of all); chewed, shared with guests, and burned or buried as her portion of every meal.

symbols.name: Chicha de jora
symbols.meaning: Maize beer poured into the earth as payment before drinking begins; the first swallow belongs to her.

symbols.name: The foot-plough (taklla)
symbols.meaning: Opening the first furrow is a rite, not a chore; the clods are fed before they are planted.

symbols.name: The clay storage jar
symbols.meaning: Household maize and potatoes guarded in her name; abundance is hers on deposit, not the family's to keep.

symbols.name: The open earth of August
symbols.meaning: In her month the earth's mouth is open and hungry; whatever is spilled is received, and the fields are fed.

mythology.lead: Pachamama has no surviving epic. Andean theology lived in ritual, not scripture, and the written record begins only with the conquest, in chronicles already half-Christian. Her 'myths' are therefore creation reports, foundation legends, and — most authentically — the living practice of feeding the earth.

myths.title: The World the Creator Entrusted to Her
myths.text: Pachamama has no surviving epic of her own; the Andean world kept its theology in ritual, and the written record begins only with the Spanish conquest, in chronicles already half-Christian. Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui, in his Relación de antigüedades deste Reyno del Piru (1613), and the Jesuit Bernabé Cobo, in his Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653), tell a creation in which the god Viracocha — he of the staff and the tears — rose from the depths of Lake Titicaca at Tiahuanaco, made the sun, moon, and stars, and fashioned each people from stone before sending them under the earth to their appointed lands. The earth that received this ordered world, the ground beneath every field and city, is Pachamama. She is older than the Inca state and wider than it: the mother in whom pacha — earth, world, time — is made flesh. The myth, such as we have it, says something quietly radical: creation was delegated. Viracocha shaped the world, but he did not stay to farm it; that daily labor belongs to her.

myths.title: The Golden Staff Sinks into Her Ground
myths.text: The founding myth of Cusco is also a myth of her consent. Bernabé Cobo tells that the Sun, Inti, grieving over the savagery of humankind, sent his own children — Manco Cápac and his sister-wife Mama Ocllo — out of Lake Titicaca to find a valley where a golden staff, sunk into the earth, would disappear: a sign of ground blessed enough to found a city. Where the staff sank at last, they raised Cusco, 'the navel of the world.' Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa's Historia Índica (1572) gives the rival version, in which the ancestors emerge not from the lake but from the caves of Pacaritambo; the chroniclers openly disagree, and modern scholarship treats both as legitimating tales of later dynasties. What the versions share is the theology: the land is not conquered but asked. Every foundation, in the Andean telling, is a pact between the traveling children of the Sun and the earth who accepts their weight. Pachamama's acceptance — the swallowing of the staff — is the true founding act; without it, Cusco is only a camp.

lore.culturalLegacy: Pachamama never stopped being worshipped. On the first of August, from Colombia's highlands to Bolivia's altiplano, households still pour chicha into the ground, bury coca, and feast; builders in Lima and La Paz commission ritual specialists to 'pay the earth' before breaking ground. The word itself entered all the languages of the Andes: pachamama is now ordinary Spanish for the living land, and her ethic — ayñi, reciprocity — is quoted in debates about mining, water rights, and climate. Indigenous movements made her a political symbol, and her name in two national constitutions made that symbol law. Few goddesses anywhere have traveled so far while staying home: she is simultaneously a household grandmother, a field spirit, and a constitutional principle.
lore.archaeology: Her material traces are everywhere and marked with nothing: the Andes built few temples to her because the whole cultivated landscape was her body. At Cusco, the Coricancha — the 'golden enclosure' that was the ritual heart of the empire — stood amid terraces and foundation offerings; at Moray, the great concentric agricultural terraces near the Sacred Valley are read by many archaeologists as a ritual-agricultural complex where highland cultigens were adapted under the earth's eye. Qollqas — the circular stone storehouses that grid the hillsides above the Inca road — embody the doctrine of deposit and return: surplus guarded against years of famine. Excavations at Inca administrative centers such as Huánuco Pampa have recovered coca caches, miniature vessels, and guinea-pig offerings consistent with earth-payments, and the peak shrines of the capacocha rites, excavated on volcanoes such as Llullaillaco (1999), belong to her wider mountain family — the apus who hold the high ground while Pachamama keeps the tilled.
lore.syncretism: Colonial Catholicism met Pachamama with the Virgin Mary, and the meeting was less a conquest than an overlay. The Virgin of Copacabana (1583), the Virgin of Candelaria at Puno, and countless village chapels stand on pre-Hispanic wak'as, and Andean feasts were deliberately moved onto Marian dates — so that the August cycle of earth-payments now runs beside the feasts of the Virgin. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century indigenismo recovered her as the emblem of indigenous identity, and in the late twentieth century she became political: Ecuador's 2008 and Bolivia's 2009 constitutions name Pachamama as the bearer of nature's rights, giving the old reciprocity the force of law. In New Age and eco-spiritual circles abroad she has been adopted as a global 'Mother Earth,' sometimes with little sense of her Andean specificity — a reception the tradition itself treats with the tolerant pragmatism of a goddess who accepts all payments.

pronunciation.approximation: 'per-SEUS' — stress the final syllable, and let the eu glide like 'eh-oo' said in one motion.
pronunciation.note: Perseús is Tier 1: the restored acute accent of Greek Περσεύς is a preserved diacritic that the ASCII form perseus flattens entirely. The accent marks the name's true Greek stress — Per-SEUS, not PER-seus — and the lexicon's canonical restoration keeps it.

domains.title: Perseus
domains.subtitle: Hero
domains.lead: Perseus is the Greek hero who slew the Gorgon Medousa and founded the royal line of Mycenae and Argos. Son of Zeus and Danaë, he accomplishes what no god would attempt, armed only with borrowed wonders — mirrored shield, adamantine harpe, cap of Hades, winged sandals — and his name may itself be eastern: "Destroyer, possibly Persian."

cards.name: The Gorgon-Slayer
cards.desc: With Athena's mirrored shield and Hermes' adamantine harpe he took the one head no god dared face — Medousa's.

cards.name: Hero
cards.desc: Central domain: hero, slayer of medousa — sacker of cities, ancestor of Heracles through his son Electryon.

cards.name: Divine Favor
cards.desc: Athena and Hermes equip him; the kibisis holds the head; winged sandals and the cap of Hades carry him beyond Ocean.

cards.name: Founder of Mycenae
cards.desc: From his dynasty — Electryon, Sthenelus, Eurystheus — come Heracles and the Argive royal line.

symbols.name: Harpe (adamantine sickle-sword)
symbols.meaning: The curved blade Hermes gave him for the one stroke at Medousa's neck — a weapon older than the gods' order

symbols.name: Mirrored shield
symbols.meaning: Athena's polished bronze, in which Perseus watched the Gorgon safely — knowledge taken only by reflection

symbols.name: Cap of Hades
symbols.meaning: The helmet of invisibility that hid him from the waking Gorgon sisters and the giants of Seriphos

symbols.name: Kibisis
symbols.meaning: The wallet that holds the severed head without harm — the first container built for a monster

symbols.name: Gorgoneion
symbols.meaning: The apotropaic face itself, set on Athena's aegis, turning enemies to stone at the city's threshold

symbols.name: Winged sandals (talaria)
symbols.meaning: Flight borrowed from Hermes' own feet, carrying the hero beyond Ocean to the world's edge

mythology.lead: Perseus is the Argive hero of the Gorgon-slaying, the rescuer of Andromeda, and the founder of the dynasty that produces Heracles. His cycle, told most fully by Apollodorus and Ovid, turns on oracles, divine equipment, and the terrible double gift of the Gorgon's head.

myths.title: The Shower of Gold
myths.text: Akrisios, king of Argos, went to Delphi to ask the oracle for a son and received instead a death sentence: his daughter Danaë would bear a child who would kill him. He locked Danaë in a brazen chamber sunk underground, but Zeus came upon her as a shower of gold — 'she took the gold into her lap,' as Simonides sang (PMG 543) — passing through bronze with an immortal's ease. When Perseus was born, Akrisios would not kill mother and child outright; he had them sealed in a chest and cast into the sea, which carried them gently to the island of Seriphos. There the fisherman Diktys drew them ashore and gave them his house (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.2.1; cf. Pindar, Pythian 12.12–16). The oracle has already framed the whole of the hero's life: his greatness and his grandfather's death are the same event, waiting years away at a games-ground for a discus to close the circle.

myths.title: The Graiai and the Gear
myths.text: Polydectes, king of Seriphos, desired Danaë and wanted Perseus gone. Feigning a bride-price for Hippodameia, he demanded horses of his whole court; Perseus rashly promised the Gorgon's head instead — and Polydectes held him to it (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.2.3). Athena and Hermes took charge of the impossible errand and led him first to the Graiai, the 'grey ones' who from birth were old women, sisters of the Gorgons, sharing a single eye and a single tooth (Hesiod, Theogony 270–273). Perseus snatched the eye as it passed from face to face and ransomed it for the road to the nymphs; from them he received the kibisis that safely holds the head, the cap of Hades that makes its wearer unseen, and winged sandals; from Hermes the adamantine harpe, from Athena the polished bronze shield (Apollodorus 2.2.3–4; Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.610ff). The quest's real lesson is assembled before the monster is met: this hero wins not by native strength but by holding hostage what others cannot do without — an eye, a tooth, and the world's best equipment.

lore.culturalLegacy: Perseus survives in the sky: Ptolemy placed him among the 48 constellations, and every August the Perseid meteor shower streams from his direction — the hero still throws. The gorgoneion lives on wherever a face is set up to ward off harm, most famously as the Medusa head of the Versace logo. Cinema keeps returning to him — Clash of the Titans (1981, 2010) — and fantasy gaming has made the mirrored-shield tactic a genre convention. But his deepest legacy is genealogical: through Electryon and Alkmene he is the grandfather of Heracles, so the whole of Greek heroic myth, Argonauts included, descends from the boy in the brazen room. Every retelling of the Gorgon-slaying re-asks his question: how do you face what cannot be looked at?
lore.archaeology: Pausanias walked the hero's topography: at Mycenae he saw the Persea, the spring 'where Perseus is said to have washed when he brought back the Gorgon's head' (2.16.6), and at Argos the grave-heroon the Argives claimed for him beside the sanctuary of Hera (2.18.1). The chest of Cypselus at Olympia, described by Pausanias (5.18), carried carved scenes of Perseus and the Gorgons among its archaic reliefs. The monster herself dominates the material record: the west pediment of the temple of Artemis at Corfu (c. 580 BC) displays the largest early Gorgon in Greek art, wide-eyed and tongue-out, the apotropaic face Perseus delivered to Athena. Attic and Argive vase-paintings of the sixth and fifth centuries show the whole cycle — the chest at sea, the decapitation, the petrification of Polydectes' court.
lore.syncretism: Perseus carried an eastern passport from the beginning. Herodotus records that 'the Persians say that Perseus, son of Danaë, was an Assyrian who became a Greek' (7.61), and later tradition made his son by Andromeda, Perses, the eponymous ancestor of the Persian kings — a genealogy Greeks used to explain a familiar name in a foreign country. In Greece itself he never quite became a god: Pausanias saw the grave the Argives showed for him (2.18.1) and the spring at Mycenae where he washed after the slaying (2.16.6), and his cult remained hero-cult — games, tomb, local memory — rather than Olympian worship. His afterlife in art outran his afterlife in cult: the gorgoneion on Athena's aegis became the West's oldest apotropaic emblem, Cellini's bronze Perseus with the Head of Medusa (Loggia dei Lanzi, Florence, 1554) fixed the decapitation group for the Renaissance, and Rubens and Tiepolo re-staged the Andromeda rescue for a Christian Europe that read the sea-monster as evil and the hero as providence.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written Περσεύς in the Greek alphabet, the name carried an acute accent on its final syllable — the mark the restoration Perseús recovers. Hesiod names him at the moment of the monster's death (Theogony 280), Pindar calls him the Gorgon-slayer (Pythian 12), and the accent is the only feature plain-ASCII perseus loses.

pronunciation.approximation: or-FEWS — the stress lands on the last syllable.
pronunciation.note: Greek Ὀρφεύς stresses the final syllable — Orpheús — and the restoration keeps the acute where the tradition puts it. The etymology is debated (perhaps from a root for 'orphan' or the 'darkness' of his descent); the name is older than its explanations, which is exactly right for the singer who is all voice.

domains.title: The Singer of the World
domains.subtitle: Music, Poetry, the Descent, and the Lost Look Back
domains.lead: Orpheús is the archetype of art itself: the Thracian singer whose lyre moved stones and stopped rivers, who went down living into the underworld for his wife, and whose single look back is the West's permanent parable of love and loss.

cards.name: The Lyre
cards.desc: His instrument: the gift of Apóllōn, the sound that made nature stop to listen.

cards.name: The Argonauts
cards.desc: His song steadied the Argo's crew past the Seirḗnes — art as navigation.

cards.name: The Descent
cards.desc: The katabasis for Eurydikē — the only route out of death that music ever opened.

cards.name: The Look Back
cards.desc: The one forbidden glance, at the threshold — and the second, final loss.

symbols.name: The lyre
symbols.meaning: Art as the measure of the world — the cosmos tuned to a string.

symbols.name: The laurel
symbols.meaning: The crown of his prophetic grove at Pieria, where trees learned to move.

symbols.name: The nightingale
symbols.meaning: Song persisting through darkness — the bird of his native Thrace.

symbols.name: The river Hebrus
symbols.meaning: The stream that carried his still-singing head down to the sea and ashore at Lesbos.

symbols.name: The constellation Lyra
symbols.meaning: His lyre set among the stars — the only instrument in the sky.

mythology.lead: Orpheús' myths are all about what music can and cannot do: it charms everything in nature, opens the underworld's doors, and saves nothing except itself. Epic, lyric, and Roman poetry, and finally the mystery-religion that took his name, turn one Thracian singer into the West's permanent anatomy of art, love, and loss.

myths.title: The Song that Moves Stones
myths.text: Genealogy made him art's aristocrat — son of Kalliopē, Muse of epic, by the Thracian king Oeagrus; or, in the version that flatters him more, by Apóllōn himself (Apollodorus 1.3.2). What he did with the inheritance became proverbial. When Orpheús played, the tradition insists, nature suspended its habits: trees unrooted and followed him down from Pieria, rivers halted mid-course, wild beasts lay down with sheep, and the oldest surviving witness, a line of Simonides (fr. 567 PMG), has 'the birds flying above him, the fishes leaping from the blue deep' — repeated almost verbatim by Apollonius Rhodius (Argonautica 1.23–34). The exaggeration is the point. No one claims Orpheús won a war; his was the one power the gods could not do better — harmony, which is to say the world persuaded rather than forced. Greek art never wrote a stronger claim for itself: song is not entertainment but government, over a jurisdiction that includes the stones.

myths.title: The Singer on the Argo
myths.text: Apollonius Rhodius gives the hero's gift its most practical use. On the Argo, Orpheús is not decoration: his lyre sets the rowers' time and stills the quarrels of heroes crowded on one deck (Argonautica 1.494–515, 1.540–546), and — at the passage of the Seirḗnes — his song saves the expedition outright, drowning the death-song in a nobler strain until the lethal shore is past (Argonautica 4.885–919). Pindar had already numbered him among the Argonauts (Pythian 4.176 ff.) as the one indispensable passenger who carried no weapon. The episode is the epic's quiet thesis: the most dangerous stretch of the most dangerous voyage in Greek legend is survived not by a blade but by a string, tuned. Every crew since — rowing, sailing, singing at the oars — has unknowingly rehearsed his passage, and every navy that still pipes its rowers keeps his discipline without his name.

lore.culturalLegacy: 'Orphic' is the word for haunting, entrancing beauty; the lyre constellation (Lyra) is his; and the look-back is literature's most quoted failure — from Virgil to Rilke's Sonnets to Orpheus to Cocteau's Orphée and on through film and musical after film and musical. Every artist who has tried to retrieve something from loss — and failed at the threshold of the work — is his descendant. Music's power to move the world is his biography; its limits are his lesson. Few figures who may never have lived have been so thoroughly employed: the West has used him, for twenty-five centuries, as its permanent rehearsal of the one question art cannot answer — whether the song was worth the wife.
lore.archaeology: The Orphic gold tablets — thin gold leaves buried with initiates from Thessaly to South Italy, instructing the dead ('say: I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven') — are his cult's material archive. Vase-painting shows him in Thracian dress charming the Greeks, then charming the animals, then (a favorite Roman motif) playing to underworld figures; the Piraeus relief of Orpheús charming the animals (Piraeus Museum) and the singer-cult sites at Pangaion mark his geography. On Lesbos, the ancient tradition placed his head's landing at Antissa, where the oracle of the head was remembered into late antiquity.
lore.syncretism: The mystery-religion that took his name — Orphism — made him the patron of the soul's journey: the gold tablets, the cosmic egg, Phánēs, and the map of the afterlife all carry the Orphic brand, though the historical singer and the theology are centuries apart. Christianity read him as a type of Christ — the descent, the harrowing, the charming of the animals — and he appears in that role in early Christian art. The Renaissance made him the emblem of poetry itself, the divine Orpheus who tunes the world's discord into concord. And opera was effectively invented for him: Monteverdi's Orfeo (1607) is the first great opera, and the hundreds that followed — from Gluck to Offenbach — keep re-judging the look back, which is to say they keep re-trying the threshold.

Prince of Ithaca, Son of Odysseus

entries.domain: King of Pherae, Husband of Alcestis

pronunciation.approximation: 'DIE-dah-los' — the first syllable is long and carries the ancient pitch rise; the remaining syllables are short and light.
pronunciation.note: The Greek Δαίδαλος contains both stress (acute on the diphthong) and length (the diphthong αι is long), making it a Tier 1 restoration. The Latin-derived English form Daedalus is a secondary spelling that preserves the consonants but obscures the original Greek vowel quantities.

domains.title: The Cunning Craftsman
domains.subtitle: Inventor, Architect, and Wingsmith
domains.lead: Daidalos is the master craftsman of Greek mythology: the architect of the Labyrinth, the maker of moving statues, and the father of Icarus. His name means 'cunningly wrought' and became a byword for any work so skillful that it seemed alive. He is the first engineer in Western literature, the inventor whose ingenuity saves him and destroys those he loves.

cards.name: The Labyrinth
cards.desc: The maze he built at Knossos to contain the Minotaur — so cunning that its maker could barely find the way out (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.7-9).

cards.name: Wings
cards.desc: The feathered wings he fashioned from wax and twine to escape Crete — the technology that saves the maker and kills his son (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.183-235).

cards.name: Automata
cards.desc: The moving statues he made so lifelike that Plato says they had to be chained down lest they walk away (Meno 97d).

cards.name: Invention
cards.desc: The transforming power of human skill, celebrated and feared by the Greeks — every artifact of his works exactly as designed, and every design costs him something.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: The instruments of escape and the boundary between human and divine — held together by wax, held up by obedience

symbols.name: Wax
symbols.meaning: The material that holds the wings together and melts when the warning fails — technology as a perishable interface between instruction and desire

symbols.name: Labyrinth
symbols.meaning: The architectural puzzle that embodies his cunning and its dangerous consequences — a mind built in stone

symbols.name: Tools
symbols.meaning: The axe, file, and compass of the craftsman who can make anything except a safe life

symbols.name: The thread
symbols.meaning: The clue Ariadne unrolled through the maze — in Hyginus' telling (Fabulae 43) Daedalus' own stratagem — the one invention designed to be undone

symbols.name: The moving statues
symbols.meaning: His animated figures, so lifelike they had to be tethered — the ancient image of art imitating life one step too far

mythology.lead: The myths of Daidalos are preserved in Homer, Apollodorus, Diodorus, and Ovid: a small cycle that celebrates human invention and prices it — envy, exile, and the fall of a son. Every artifact he makes works exactly as designed, and every design costs him something he did not intend to pay.

myths.title: The Nephew He Killed
myths.text: Daedalus' first recorded act is his worst. His sister entrusted her son to his tutelage — the boy is Perdix in Apollodorus (Library 3.15.8), Talos or Calos in Ovid (Metamorphoses 8.236-259) — and the pupil outshone the master: Perdix invented the saw, taking his cue from a fish's spine or a snake's jaw, and then the potter's wheel and the compass. 'Fearing he might outstrip him,' Ovid writes, Daedalus hurled him from the Acropolis; Athena caught the falling boy and changed him into the partridge — perdix — that still flies low, remembering the fall. Daedalus was banished and fled to Crete. The myth plants its theme at the very root of his career: the first great maker of the Greek imagination is also the first to destroy a rival talent, and the tradition never lets him forget it — the partridge flutters through his story like a conscience.

myths.title: The Labyrinth
myths.text: At the court of Minos, Daedalus built the monument that defines him: the Labyrinth, 'a maze with winding paths, confusing and impassable,' designed to imprison the Minotaur — the bull-headed child born of Pasiphaē and the Cretan bull (Apollodorus, Epitome 1.7-9). The maze was so cunning that its maker, Apollodorus says, could barely find the way out. When Theseus came to Crete as tribute, Ariadne fell in love with him and gave him the thread that marked the path through the puzzle — in Hyginus' version (Fabulae 43) the stratagem was Daedalus' own. Plutarch (Theseus 15) preserves the rationalizers' spin: a prison, an ordinary house, a dance-floor — the ancients were already decoding it. The myth's point needs no decoding: the greatest craftsman in Greece builds a structure whose only function is that no one inside it can get out — including, soon enough, its maker.

lore.culturalLegacy: Daedalus is the archetype of the inventor and the artist in one figure — the engineer whose creations work too well. The labyrinth gave European languages its word for any designed confusion; the wings fathered every myth of flight from Icarus to the space program; the moving statues made him the patron, millennia early, of robotics and AI. Modern debates about autonomous systems, from Frankenstein to lethal drones, are his debate: can a maker foresee what his making will do? Homer already knew the answer the tradition keeps giving — the dancing-floor is beautiful, the maze is brilliant, and both outlive the hand that made them.
lore.archaeology: Homer anchors Daedalus in Bronze Age Knossos a thousand years before the classical city-states told his story, and Arthur Evans' excavations (1900-1905) gave the myth a landscape: the palace's corridors, bull-imagery, and wall paintings let moderns walk his labyrinth. Ancient Athens claimed him too — the murder of Perdix was set on the Acropolis — and classical authors (Pliny, Natural History 36.13) credited him with the first true sculpture, 'opening the eyes and separating the limbs.' The Archaic sculptural style of the seventh century BCE is still called 'Daedalic' after him. No secure artifact is his; like the labyrinth, his archaeology is a structure of plausible paths.
lore.syncretism: The Romans absorbed him as Daedalus, and Ovid's Metamorphoses book 8 — the wings, the fall, the nephew — fixed his canonical Latin form; Virgil alludes to the Cretan maze (Aeneid 5.588-591: 'the Cretan labyrinth... Daedalus, pouring his genius into the craft'). The Renaissance made him the emblem of the artist-engineer, from Vasari's lives to the emblem-books; in the twentieth century James Joyce rebuilt him as Stephen Dedalus, the young artist escaping the nets of family, religion, and nation — wings that also melt. Modern engineering borrowed his name without irony (Project Daedalus, the British Interplanetary Society's interstellar probe study). He remains the myth's permanent consultant on invention: every story about technology outrunning its maker is his story retold.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Greek as Δαίδαλος. The first syllable is a long diphthong αι with an acute accent. The plain ASCII daedalus flattens the diphthong into ae and removes the accent. The PuniCodex restoration Daidalos preserves the scholarly transliteration of the Greek form and is classified as Tier 1 because the diphthong is long and accented.
