pronunciation.approximation: 'NARASIMHA' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.
pronunciation.note: Narasiṃha is Tier 1: the anusvāra (ṃ) in siṃha — the nasal mark Sanskrit writes above the letter — is a distinctive feature the ASCII form narasimha deletes outright. The restoration recovers the exact scholarly transliteration.

domains.title: Man-Lion Avatar
domains.subtitle: Man-Lion Avatar
domains.lead: Narasiṃha is Viṣṇu's man-lion avatāra, the fourth descent of the preserver god, who answered a tyrant's loophole-perfect boon with a form neither man nor beast. Worshipped across India as the god of twilight and the guardian of every threshold, he embodies divine ferocity governed by devotion.

cards.name: Man-Lion Avatar
cards.desc: The central domain: Viṣṇu's fourth avatāra — the form no clause of the tyrant's boon could exclude.

cards.name: The Man-Lion
cards.desc: Nara-siṃha, 'man-lion': nara 'man' + siṃha 'lion' — the hybrid the boon never imagined.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Narasiṃha recovers the anusvāra (ṃ) that plain ASCII deletes — the nasal mark the Sanskrit tradition writes.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Attested across the Purāṇic corpus — Bhāgavata 7, Viṣṇu 1.17–20, Narasimha Purāṇa — and in temple epigraphy from the Gupta age onward.

symbols.name: The man-lion form
symbols.meaning: The theriomorphic body that defeats the boon: leonine mane and claws joined to human torso and intelligence.

symbols.name: Claws (nakha)
symbols.meaning: Neither weapon nor hand — the talons that honor the letter of the boon while breaking its intent; the nails themselves are hymned (nakhastuti).

symbols.name: The pillar (stambha)
symbols.meaning: The palace column that conceals the god; in theology, the stambha is the imperishable inner support of all beings.

symbols.name: Twilight (sandhyā)
symbols.meaning: Neither day nor night — the loophole hour at which the law of the boon is honored and destroyed at once.

symbols.name: The serene child
symbols.meaning: Prahlāda standing unafraid beside the killer — devotion as the one power the man-lion will always answer.

symbols.name: Eighteen-armed Ugra form
symbols.meaning: The ferocious iconography of the killing: multiple arms, bulging eyes, mane aflame, the tyrant stretched across the thighs.

mythology.lead: The stories of Narasiṃha tell how Viṣṇu defeated a loophole-perfect boon: neither man nor beast could kill the tyrant, so the god came as both at once — a man-lion bursting from a palace pillar at twilight, on a threshold, with claws. The Purāṇic cycle turns on the devotion of the tyrant's own son.

myths.title: The Boon of Hiraṇyakaśipu
myths.text: Hiraṇyakaśipu, king of the daityas, performed austerities so severe that Brahmā offered him a boon. Suspicious of every loophole, the demon stipulated that he should not die by day or night, indoors or outdoors, on earth or in the sky, by weapon or by hand, by man or beast, by god, demon, or nāga. Granted near-invulnerability, he conquered the three worlds and forbade the very name of Viṣṇu — commanding his own subjects, on pain of death, to worship him alone. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (7.3) makes the stipulation a masterpiece of conditional theology: Hiraṇyakaśipu does not ask for immortality, which Brahmā cannot give, but for a contract so airtight that only the maker of loopholes could breach it. His blasphemy completes his doom, for by banning Viṣṇu's name from his own household he makes his own son — the boy Prahlāda, who loves the banned god from the womb — the hinge on which the entire boon will turn.

myths.title: Prahlāda, the Devotee
myths.text: Prahlāda, the tyrant's son, refused the milk of his father's ideology along with his nurse's milk: asked what he had learned, the boy answered that the best of all teachings is devotion to Viṣṇu. Hiraṇyakaśipu tried to destroy him — poison in his milk, serpents in his bed, mantra-hurled weapons, a mountain dropped on his head, a fire fed by sorcery. Each attempt failed as devotion summoned rescue, and the boy emerged unburned, unbitten, unbroken, reciting the names of the god (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.5–7.8). The text's power lies in the contrast it never softens: the father holds every worldly power — armies, sorcery, a boon from Brahmā himself — and the son holds only a name, and the name keeps winning. Prahlāda became, for later bhakti theology, the type of the devotee whom nothing can finally injure. His serenity in the face of death is the cycle's quiet, indestructible center — the still point around which all of his father's fury breaks.

lore.culturalLegacy: Narasiṃha remains among the most actively worshipped forms of Viṣṇu. Ahobilam's nine shrines and Simhachalam near Visakhapatnam — where the deity is kept under a coat of sandalwood paste renewed annually — anchor major pilgrimage circuits, and Narasimha Jayanti, falling on the full moon of Vaiśākha, celebrates the twilight of the boon. The name itself never left circulation: Narasiṃha, Narasingh, and Narasimhudu serve as given names across India, and new temples — most visibly Yadadri in Telangana — continue to rise around the old story. Modern retellings, from children's comics to cinema, keep returning to the two figures the Purāṇas made unforgettable: the father with the airtight contract, and the son with only a name.
lore.archaeology: The earliest monumental telling of the cycle stands at Udayagiri in Madhya Pradesh: Cave 6 (c. 400–401 CE, reign of Candragupta II) carves Narasiṃha disemboweling Hiraṇyakaśipu across his lap — one of the first dated images of the avatāra, and already iconographically complete. The sixth-century Dāśāvatāra temple at Deogarh adds a canonical panel within a full Viṣṇu program. In the far south, Ahobilam's nine shrines in the Nallamala hills embed the myth in living pilgrimage geography. The Vijayanagara capital at Hampi preserves the colossal monolithic Ugra-Narasimha, seated with the demon's body across his thighs, attributed to the early sixteenth century. Outside India, the Banteay Srei temple at Angkor (c. 967 CE) renders the same disemboweling in pink sandstone, with Prahlāda kneeling calmly beside the violence.
lore.syncretism: Narasiṃha's afterlife is a study in devotional geography. In South India he became a royal deity: the Vijayanagara court identified itself with Viṣṇu's protective avatāras, and the colossal Ugra-Narasimha at Hampi still shows what the identification looked like in stone. Eastward, Khmer sculptors carved the disemboweling of Hiraṇyakaśipu at Banteay Srei (c. 967 CE), proof that the Purāṇic cycle traveled with Sanskrit culture beyond India. Śaiva tradition answered with the Śarabha episode, in which Śiva must subdue the man-lion's unquenchable rage — a counter-telling that kept Narasiṃha at the center of inter-sectarian argument. In Tantric practice his mantra became standard armor against danger; in vernacular bhakti, Prahlāda's story anchored the claim that devotion outlasts every worldly power.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NOO-ah-oo' — stress the first syllable, hold the 'oo' long, soften the middle d toward the 'th' of 'breathe', and finish on a short 'oo'. Modern English speakers usually say 'NOO-uh-duh'.
pronunciation.note: Nuada is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the attested Old Irish form carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter, so plain ASCII loses nothing. The etymology is honestly uncertain: one proposal reads the name as 'cloud-maker', from a root behind Welsh nudd 'mist'; another, argued by Tolkien for the Gaulish Nodens, connects it to a root meaning 'to catch, acquire' — a fisher or hunter — which would suit the sea-and-hounds imagery of the Lydney temple. Neither is settled, and the temple says so.

domains.title: War, King of Tuatha
domains.subtitle: The Silver-Handed King of the Tuatha Dé Danann
domains.lead: Nuada Airgetlám is the first king of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Ireland — the ruler who lost his arm at the First Battle of Mag Tuired, lost his throne to the law that a blemished man cannot be king, and won both back through the physicians' craft: first the silver arm that named him, then the living arm that restored him. His sword from Findias was one of the Four Treasures of his people, and he died at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired at the hands of Balor of the Evil Eye.

cards.name: The Silver Hand
cards.desc: Dian Cécht's silver arm, made with Credne the brazier, moved in every joint — and gave the king his name, Airgetlám.

cards.name: The Sword from Findias
cards.desc: One of the Four Treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann; once it was drawn from its sheath, no one escaped it.

cards.name: Mag Tuired
cards.desc: The plain of the two battles: against the Fir Bolg, where the arm was lost; against the Fomorians, where the king fell.

cards.name: The Unblemished Throne
cards.desc: Irish kingship law held that no man with a blemish could rule; Nuada's wound cost him Tara, and his healing restored him.

symbols.name: The silver arm
symbols.meaning: Wholeness made by craft when nature failed — the prosthesis that kept a king king in all but law

symbols.name: The sword of Nuada
symbols.meaning: The irresistible weapon from the city Findias, one of the Four Treasures brought to Ireland

symbols.name: Tara (Temair)
symbols.meaning: The seat of the kingship of Ireland, which a blemished man could not lawfully hold

symbols.name: The physician's craft
symbols.meaning: Dian Cécht's silver-work and Miach's flesh-work — healing as the instrument of sovereignty

symbols.name: Dog and fisherman (as Nodens)
symbols.meaning: The hound figurines and sea imagery of the Lydney Park temple, where his Gaulish cognate was worshipped

mythology.lead: Nuada's story is the Irish tradition's great parable of kingship and the body: a ruler can be unmade by a single wound and remade by healing, and the law watches both. The record runs from the Lebor Gabála Érenn through the two battles of Mag Tuired, and his Welsh and Gaulish cognates carry the same silver-handed name across the Celtic world.

myths.title: The First Battle of Mag Tuired
myths.text: When the Tuatha Dé Danann came to Ireland, Nuada had been their king for seven years. They demanded the country from the Fir Bolg, and the two peoples met at Mag Tuired in Connacht. In the battle Nuada fought Sreng, champion of the Fir Bolg, and Sreng struck off his right arm at the shoulder — yet the Tuatha Dé Danann won the field, and the Fir Bolg king Eochaid mac Eirc was driven to his death. The victors then offered the defeated a quarter of Ireland, and the Fir Bolg chose Connacht, which their descendants held. The victory that made the Tuatha Dé Danann masters of Ireland thus cost their king the wholeness the kingship required: one champion's sword-stroke bought a kingdom and unmade its king in the same afternoon.

myths.title: The Silver Hand and the Hand of Flesh
myths.text: Because a blemished man could not hold the kingship, Nuada yielded the throne to Bres. The physician Dian Cécht, with Credne the brazier, made him a full arm of silver that moved in every joint — whence his byname Airgetlám, Silver-hand. But Dian Cécht's own son Miach went further: he set the severed arm to the stump and healed it 'joint to joint and vein to vein' in thrice nine days. Jealous that the son had outdone the father, Dian Cécht struck Miach dead; from the young healer's grave grew three hundred and sixty-five herbs, which his sister Airmed sorted by their virtues — and which Dian Cécht scattered, so that their full knowledge died with him. Healing, in this cycle, is never free of the wound of envy.

lore.culturalLegacy: Nuada's afterlife runs through scholarship into fantasy. When R. E. M. and T. V. Wheeler published their excavation of the Nodens temple at Lydney Park in 1932, the young philologist J. R. R. Tolkien contributed the appendix 'The Name Nodens', tracing the god's name to a root of catching and acquiring — a fragment of Tolkien's scholarly life that fans of his fiction still chase. In modern Irish the name survives as Nuadha, and Maynooth University's old arms carried Nuada's sword. In popular culture the silver-handed king rides again as Prince Nuada Silverlance in Hellboy II: The Golden Army (2008), and the motif of the magical prosthetic hand — from A Song of Ice and Fire to Japanese fantasy — descends, knowingly or not, from Airgetlám. Modern Celtic pagans honour Nuada as a god of rightful rule, healing, and sovereignty restored.
lore.archaeology: Nuada is textual in Ireland — no inscription names him there — but his Gaulish cognate has one of the best-excavated cult sites in Roman Britain. At Lydney Park, Gloucestershire, overlooking the Severn estuary, a temple complex of the late third and fourth centuries CE was dedicated to Nodens: the Wheelers' excavations (1928–29, published 1932 with Tolkien's philological appendix) uncovered mosaic floors, inscribed slabs reading DEVO NODENTI and D M NODONTI ('to the god Mars Nodens'), bronze dog figurines, a fisherman plaque, and pins and bracelets left as votives — the material of a healing-and-hunting cult. The famous curse tablet of Silvianus, asking Nodens to withhold health from whoever stole his ring until it was returned 'to the temple of Nodens', was found on the site; a gold ring inscribed SENICIANE VIVAS IN DEO, plausibly the very ring, surfaced at Silchester. On the Irish side, the texts are the evidence: the Second Battle of Mag Tuired survives in the sixteenth-century British Library Harley MS 5280, the First Battle in a single late vellum copy edited by Fraser, and the Lebor Gabála in its medieval recensions.
lore.syncretism: Nuada belongs to one of the clearest pan-Celtic name families. In Welsh he is Nudd and, in full form, Lludd Llaw Eraint — 'Lludd of the Silver Hand' — the king of Britain in Lludd a Llefelys, whose byname renders Airgetlám word for word (llaw 'hand', eraint 'silver'). In Gaulish he is Nodens (also Nodons, Nudens), worshipped at the great temple at Lydney Park in Gloucestershire, where Roman dedicants equated him with Mars and where the imagery — hounds, fishermen, the sea — suggests a healer and hunter as much as a warrior. The Romano-British curse tablet of Silvianus, asking 'Lord Nodens' to deny health to the thief of his ring, shows the god working as an enforcer of justice. Scholars (Mac Cana, Koch) reconstruct a Common Celtic *Noudont- or *Noudo- behind all three, though the root's meaning — 'cloud-maker' or 'catcher, fisher' — remains genuinely debated.
lore.originalScriptNote: The attested Old Irish form is Nuadu (later Nuada), written by medieval Irish scribes in the Insular Latin bookhand of the great vellum codices; in the Ogham letter-row the name would have been notched ᚅᚒᚐᚇᚐ (N-U-A-D-A), though no Ogham stone yet found carries it. Because the name is already plain ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: nuada.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OHN-gus' — one long open 'oh', the ng of 'singer', a hard g, and a short unstressed 'us'. Modern Irish Aonghus and Scottish Aonghas have worn it toward 'AYN-guhs' — the Anglicized Angus.
pronunciation.note: Aengus is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the temple form is plain ASCII, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to rescue. The normalized Old Irish Óengus does carry a fada, but the project follows the unaccented Middle Irish Aengus, and the mechanical rule judges the restored form, not the manuscript one. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the god's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Love, Youth, Poetry
domains.subtitle: The Mac Óc — the Son of the Young, god of Brú na Bóinne
domains.lead: Aengus — Old Irish Óengus, the mac ind Óc, 'son of the young' — is the ever-young god of the Túatha Dé Danann, son of [[dagda|the Dagda]] and Bóand. His power is the strangest in the corpus: not the club or the spear, but the dream, the bargain, and the unaging house. He was born inside a single day, won the greatest mound in Ireland on a grammar quibble, and found his wife in a dream.

cards.name: The Dream
cards.desc: In the Aislinge Óenguso a maiden comes to him in sleep with music; he sickens for love of a woman he has never seen awake, and the dream must be hunted like a quarry.

cards.name: The Swan
cards.desc: Caer Ibormeith lives one year as a girl and one as a swan among thrice fifty swans on Loch Bél Dracon; to win her, Óengus takes the swan-shape himself.

cards.name: Brú na Bóinne
cards.desc: The Brug on the Boyne — síd in Broga, the mound the world calls Newgrange — his Otherworld house, won from the Dagda for 'a day and a night' and kept ever since.

cards.name: The Day and the Night
cards.desc: Asked when he would surrender the mound lent 'for a day and a night', he answered that the whole world is spent in days and nights — and the answer has never been overturned.

symbols.name: Brú na Bóinne
symbols.meaning: The Brug on the Boyne, his unaging house — the síd the tales call síd in Broga and the world calls Newgrange

symbols.name: The swan-shape
symbols.meaning: The form he takes at Samain on Loch Bél Dracon to win Caer Ibormeith — love answered in kind, shape for shape

symbols.name: The dream (aisling)
symbols.meaning: The maiden's nightly visit with her timpán — desire that arrives before its object, and must be pursued into the waking world

symbols.name: The day and the night
symbols.meaning: The quibble that holds the Brug forever — time itself parsed as a loan without a term

symbols.name: The crystal bower
symbols.meaning: The grianán he built at the Brug for Étaín in her fly-shape — shelter given to a hunted woman when no one else could hold her

mythology.lead: Aengus's mythology is a study in winning without fighting. The three great set-pieces — his birth inside a stopped day, his taking of the Brug, and the dream-quest for Caer Ibormeith — are all victories of time: time held still, time parsed, time waited out. The counselor and the host follow: the son whose wit saves his father, and the keeper of the Brug who shelters Étaín when all Ireland has no safer room.

myths.title: The Day the Sun Stood Still
myths.text:
The Dagda desired Bóand, the wife of Elcmar of the Brug, and sent Elcmar away on a day's errand to Bres. To hide what followed, the tale says, the Dagda made the sun stand still: nine months passed, and the world reckoned it a single day — so the child was conceived and born within one day, and Elcmar came home none the wiser. They named the boy Óengus, but the story gave him the name that stuck: mac ind Óc, 'the son of the young', because young was the day that bore him.

The episode fixes the god's signature before he can speak: he is a child of bent time. Bóand, the Boyne itself made goddess, is his mother; the Dagda, the All-Father, his sire; and his first house is the river-bend his father stole a day to give him. The fosterage that followed — with Midir of Brí Léith — placed him among the proudest of the Túatha Dé Danann and set up every tale that came after. A birth concealed inside a stretched day becomes the charter of a god whose entire career will be spent stretching time further.

myths.title: A Day and a Night
myths.text:
When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, Óengus was away fostered with Midir and received nothing. He came home to claim his share, and the Dagda, having no mound left to give, granted him Brú na Bóinne — the Dagda's own house — for a day and a night. When the term was spent and the Dagda asked for his Brug back, Óengus answered that it is in days and nights that the whole world is spent, and so the grant had no end. The All-Father lost the argument, and the greatest mound in Ireland passed to the son who had read the fine print.

The tale is told with a straight face, but its logic is the logic of the síd itself: the Otherworld does not run on mortal clocks. A god born inside a single stretched day is the natural owner of a house held on a day without a term. Irish law prized the exact word; Óengus's first deed makes etymology into real estate, and it never has to be defended with a weapon.

lore.culturalLegacy: No Irish god had a better literary afterlife than the young one. W. B. Yeats made him a byword for longing itself in 'The Song of Wandering Aengus' (1899) — the hazel wand, the fire in the head, the glimmering girl with apple blossom in her hair who called his name and ran — a poem that poured the Aislinge into the bloodstream of modern English verse. James Stephens gave him speaking parts and moods in The Crock of Gold (1912), where Angus Og wanders the Irish countryside being wise and young. In the later Gaelic tradition he never faded: the Fenian tale of Diarmaid and Gráinne keeps him at Brú na Bóinne as Diarmaid's fosterer and protector, and Irish folklore kept the Brug as his house into the modern period. His name took a second, quieter path: worn to Angus, it became one of the most familiar masculine names in Scotland — a theonym hiding in plain sight on every map of Angus and in every roll of Scottish kings. And his address became the most visited prehistoric site in Ireland: Newgrange, where five thousand winters of sun have entered the chamber the tales assigned to the son of the young.
lore.archaeology: Aengus is a textual god — no ogham stone names him and no votive inscription invokes him — but his mythic address is the single most famous piece of prehistoric architecture in Ireland. Brú na Bóinne, the palace of the Boyne, is a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, and the passage tomb of Newgrange (c. 3200 BCE), older than Stonehenge and the pyramids, has been identified with the tales' síd in Broga, Óengus's Brug, since the medieval topographical tradition. The mound's roof-box, which admits the rising sun into the chamber on the mornings around the winter solstice, was excavated and documented by Michael J. O'Kelly (1962–1975), who observed the phenomenon in 1967 — a real alignment behind the mythology of a god born of a stopped sun. The witnesses to the texts are exact: Tochmarc Étaíne is preserved in the twelfth-century Lebor na hUidre and later manuscripts; Aislinge Óenguso survives in the fifteenth-century British Library MS Egerton 1782, the basis of Shaw's edition. For the comparative figure, the material record is Romano-British: altars dedicated to Apollo Maponus from the military north, including the Corbridge series, with the Ravenna Cosmography's locus Maponi completing the map of the Divine Son's cult — comparative evidence, never identification.
lore.syncretism: The comparison the handbooks prefer for Óengus runs to Gaul and Wales rather than to Rome. The Gaulish Maponos, 'the Divine Son' — known from dedications to Apollo Maponus in the Roman north of Britain and from the Ravenna Cosmography's locus Maponi — is the same figure-type: the ever-young son of a greater divine parent. Mac Cana and Sjoestedt set Maponos beside both Óengus and the Welsh Mabon ap Modron, 'Son son of Mother', the hunter-youth of Culhwch ac Olwen whose name is built on the same Proto-Celtic words *makwos, 'son', and *mātīr, 'mother'. The popular handbooks go further and call Óengus 'the Irish Eros'; the medieval texts give a stranger and more specific figure — a god of dream, youth, and cunning whose love-story is won by patience and shape-changing rather than by arrows. The comparisons are structural and instructive; no inscription identifies him, and the identification of Maponos with Mabon is itself a scholarly argument, not a fact.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Óengus, written in the Insular Latin script of the medieval manuscripts, with a síneadh fada marking the long Ó; the Middle Irish spelling Aengus drops the accent, and the temple follows that unaccented form. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the restored form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: aengus.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-dhuv' — one short syllable; let the d soften into the 'th' of 'this' and the final b melt into a light v. Modern Irish badhbh keeps the softening, and English ears often hear the word as something like 'bave'.
pronunciation.note: Badb is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Irish form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the goddess's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Battle, Death, Crow
domains.subtitle: The Scald-Crow of the Battlefield
domains.lead: Badb is the Irish war-goddess whose name is her shape: badb, the scald-crow — the grey-and-black hooded crow that walks the battlefield when the spears have done their work. She is one of the three of war whom the Lebor Gabála calls the daughters of Ernmas — Badb, Macha, and Anand, the Morrígan — and the Táin gives her its most terrible sound: the shriek over the marching hosts that kills men with fear before a blow is struck. She never fights; she foretells, she panics, and she gathers what the battle leaves.

cards.name: Badb Catha
cards.desc: 'Crow of battle' — her standing title in the texts: the bird that haunts the field and the goddess who owns it are one word.

cards.name: The Shriek over the Hosts
cards.desc: At Gáirech and Irgáirech, the Táin says, Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shrieked above the armies until a hundred warriors fell dead of fright.

cards.name: The Ford
cards.desc: The boundary water where the war-goddess stands washing — the Morrígan at the ford of the Unius, the washer of the doomed in the later Gaelic tradition.

cards.name: The Daughters of Ernmas
cards.desc: Badb, Macha, and Anand — the triple face of Irish war, three sisters of one mother whom the sources also call by the single name Morrígan.

symbols.name: The scald-crow
symbols.meaning: The hooded crow, grey and black — her name, her shape, and her retinue on every field

symbols.name: The shriek
symbols.meaning: Panic as a weapon: the sound that kills men with fear before the spear is thrown

symbols.name: The ford
symbols.meaning: The boundary between bank and bank, living and dead — the water where the doomed are read

symbols.name: The triad
symbols.meaning: Badb, Macha, Némain: the three of war, one terror in three voices

symbols.name: The washing of spoils
symbols.meaning: The harness and garments of the soon-dead, rinsed in the ford before the battle that will bloody them

mythology.lead: Badb's dossier is genealogy, sound, and omen rather than adventure: she is the sister in the list, the voice over the army, the bird on the pillar-stone. The Lebor Gabála fixes her family, the Táin fixes her weapon, and the death-tales fix her posture — and the commentators have spent a century and a half working out where she ends and her sisters begin.

myths.title: The Daughters of Ernmas
myths.text:
The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, gives the war-goddesses their pedigree: 'Badb and Macha and Anand, of whom are the Paps of Anu in Luachair, were the three daughters of Ernmas the she-farmer.' The verse recension sings the same family in another key — 'Badb and Macha, greatness of wealth, Morrígu, springs of craftiness, sources of bitter fighting, were the three daughters of Ernmas' — so that the tradition itself is of two minds: sometimes the Morrígan is the third sister, sometimes the single name for all three.

The same book marries her into the house of the war-god. Neit son of Indui, the god of battle, had two wives — Badb and Nemain — and the pedigree records the slaying of the three of them at Ailech by the Fomorians. Cormac's Glossary had already fixed the marriage in the language of record: Neith, the god of battle among the pagan Gael, and Nemon his wife. Badb is never an isolated figure; she is a sister and a wife in a family whose whole business is war.

myths.title: The Shriek over the Hosts
myths.text:
When the men of Ireland march under [[medb|Medb]] for the brown bull of Cooley, the Táin marks the nights of the hosting with the sound of the war-goddesses: 'Badb and Bé Néit and Némain shrieked above them that night in Gáirech and Irgáirech, so that a hundred of their warriors fell dead of fright.' It is the battle's true opening — the killing has begun before a single spear is cast, and its instrument is a voice.

The passage tells you everything about her method. She does not wound; she announces. The shriek over the column is prophecy delivered as noise, the knowledge of the field's end injected into the march at its beginning — and the Irish phrase for the whole business of battlefield terror, badb catha, the crow of battle, is simply her name at work as a common noun.

lore.culturalLegacy: The crow of battle rode the Celtic revival in English dress. W. M. Hennessy's 'The Ancient Irish Goddess of War' (Revue Celtique, 1870) had already gathered the Morrígan material for scholars, and Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired and its war-goddesses to a wide reading public, crow-form and prophecy complete. Modern fantasy and games have made the war-goddess's crow-shape one of the stock images of the genre, and contemporary pagan practice honors Badb among the three of the Morrígan. In the Irish language the word never needed reviving: badhbh has meant the hooded crow all along, and the grey bird on the battlefield needed no gloss for any Irish hearer. Across the water, the Scottish bean nighe kept her folk shape washing at the ford deep into the era of the great folklore collections.
lore.archaeology: Badb is a textual goddess: no ogham stone names her, no votive inscription invokes her, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. Her manuscript witnesses are exact. The Táin Bó Cúailnge survives in its oldest recension in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow (Royal Irish Academy, c. 1100), and in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster; Lebor Gabála Érenn likewise rests on the Book of Leinster and its sister codices; and Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition. The nearest epigraphic witness is continental: the altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicating to Cathubodua, 'battle-crow', is the standing proof that the crow-of-battle compound is old Celtic and not an Irish literary invention — comparative evidence across the water, never an identification.
lore.syncretism: Badb's clearest cross-border witness is Gaulish, and it is exact. An altar from Mieussy in Haute-Savoie dedicates to Cathubodua — *catu-*bodwā, 'battle-crow' — the precise reverse compound of Irish badb catha. Delamarre and Koch treat the two names as one formation across the Celtic languages: the crow of battle named in stone on the continent and in saga in Ireland. The Welsh corpus, by contrast, is silent on her — no figure of the Mabinogi continues the name, and the Brythonic silence is recorded rather than repaired. Typological comparison has set her beside the Norse valkyries, the raven-feeding choosers of the slain; the handbooks note the parallel without claiming descent. Within the lexicon her closest kin are her own sisters, [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]] and [[macha|Macha]], and the war she prophesied binds her to [[dagda|the Dagda]], [[lugh|Lugh]], and [[nuada|Nuadu]].
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Badb — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: badb.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MAHKH-ah' — two short open a's, stress on the first, and let the ch rasp like the end of Scottish 'loch'. Modern Irish keeps the sound: Eamhain Mhacha is said with the same fricative.
pronunciation.note: Macha is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Irish form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the goddess's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: War, Sovereignty, Horses
domains.subtitle: The Woman Who Outran the King's Horses
domains.lead: Macha is the sovereignty figure of the Ulster Cycle: the otherworld woman who came to the door of the widower Cruinniuc and made his house prosper, and who — when her husband boasted at the assembly that she could outrun the king's horses — was brought out pregnant to the racetrack, outran the horses of Conchobar mac Nessa at the finish, gave birth to twins on the field, and laid on the men of Ulster the curse that shapes the whole Táin: in their hour of greatest need, the pangs of childbirth.

cards.name: The Race at the Assembly
cards.desc: Nine months gone, she begged for delay until she had given birth; the Ulaid refused. She raced the king's chariot-horses and beat them at the line.

cards.name: The Debility of the Ulaid
cards.desc: Her curse, the ces noínden: for five days and four nights, in every generation to the ninth, the men of Ulster would lie in the pangs of a woman in labor — whenever the province needed them most.

cards.name: Emain Macha
cards.desc: 'Macha's twins' — the boy and girl born at the finish line named the royal seat of Ulster, the Navan Fort that still stands outside Armagh.

cards.name: Macha Mongrúad
cards.desc: The red-maned queen of the Lebor Gabála who seized the kingship of Ireland in her own right and traced the rampart of Emain with the brooch of her neck.

symbols.name: The king's horses
symbols.meaning: Conchobar's unmatched chariot-pair — the boast that forced the race and the measure she outran

symbols.name: The twins
symbols.meaning: Emain, the boy and girl born on the racetrack — the naming of Ulster's royal seat and the price of its pride

symbols.name: The debility
symbols.meaning: Five days and four nights of a woman's labor-pangs, laid on a warrior people for nine generations — the curse that left Cú Chulainn to fight the Táin alone

symbols.name: The brooch of the queen
symbols.meaning: Macha Mongrúad marked the circuit of Emain with her eo-muin, her neck-brooch — sovereignty drawing the boundary of its own seat

symbols.name: Macha's mast
symbols.meaning: Mesrad Machae, 'Macha's crop' — the Táin's kenning for the severed heads of the slain, the war-goddess's harvest

mythology.lead: Macha's dossier is one great tale and a family of namesakes: the Debility of the Ulstermen gives her the race, the twins, and the curse; the Táin harvests the consequences; the Lebor Gabála remembers her as Nemed's wife and as the red-maned queen; and the genealogies fold her into the three of war beside [[badb|Badb]] and [[morrigan|the Morrígan]].

myths.title: The Woman at Cruinniuc's Door
myths.text:
Cruinniuc mac Agnomain was a rich farmer of the Ulaid, a widower with sons, and one day a woman he had never seen walked into his house, set about the work of it without a word, and lay with him that night. She stayed, and under her hand everything prospered — the house, the cattle, the table — and she told him the one condition of their life together: he must never speak of her, never boast of her. It is the old compact of the otherworld wife, and it held as long as he kept his mouth shut.

The tale that tells this — Noínden Ulad, 'The Debility of the Ulaid', one of the fore-tales of the Táin — is a sovereignty story before it is anything else: the land's own woman comes to the man of the land, and her condition is silence about the source of the plenty. Cruinniuc kept it until the day of the great assembly of the Ulaid, when the talk turned to the king's horses and there was nothing in the world faster.

myths.title: The Race, the Twins, and the Curse
myths.text:
At the assembly Cruinniuc forgot the condition and boasted: his wife could outrun the king's chariot-horses. Conchobar had him seized, and sent for the woman — who was nine months gone with twins. She begged the gathering for delay until she had given birth, 'for a mother bore each of you'; the Ulaid refused. She was set against the horses and raced them, and she beat them at the line — and at the line the pangs took her, and she was delivered of a boy and a girl on the field.

Then she cursed them: as she had been given no mercy in her labor, so the men of Ulster, in their hour of greatest straits, would suffer the pangs of a woman in childbirth — five days and four nights, for nine generations, every man save the boys and the women. And in most recensions she died there. The twins gave the royal seat of Ulster its name: Emain Macha, 'Macha's twins'. It is the most economical curse in Irish literature — one wrong, answered in exact kind, for nine generations.

lore.culturalLegacy: Macha rode the Celtic revival as the first wrong of the Ulster Cycle. Lady Gregory's Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) opens the epic with her — 'The Curse of Macha' — and made the race and the debility the gateway through which two generations of English readers entered the Táin. Thomas Kinsella's The Táin (1969) kept the fore-tale at the head of the epic, and the twinned figures of the wronged woman and the war-goddess have made Macha a standing subject in the study of Celtic sovereignty myth. On the ground, her names never went anywhere: Emain Macha is Navan Fort, one of the royal sites of Ireland and the ceremonial capital of Ulster, and Ard Macha — Armagh, the ecclesiastical primacy of Ireland, founded by Patrick in the fifth century — still carries her name in every address in the county. Modern scholarship from Mac Cana to Koch treats the race as the type-case of the Irish sovereignty goddess, and contemporary Celtic pagan practice honors her among the three of war.
lore.archaeology: Macha is a textual goddess: no ogham stone names her, no votive inscription invokes her, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. Her manuscript witnesses are exact: Noínden Ulad survives in the Yellow Book of Lecan and its sister codices (Hull's edition in Celtica 8 rests on them), the Táin in its oldest recension in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow (c. 1100), and the twelfth-century Book of Leinster, and the Lebor Gabála in the Book of Leinster and its companions. Her mythic address, by contrast, is one of the most instructive monuments in Atlantic Europe: Emain Macha is Navan Fort, Co. Armagh, where Waterman's excavations (1961–71) uncovered beneath the mound a forty-metre timber structure — a ring of great posts around a central oak — that dendrochronology dates to 95 BC, built in a single episode, filled with a stone cairn, burned, and buried under the mound still visible today. A building raised to be unmade is a ritual statement, not a residence; the standing interpretation, Lynn's, is a one-time ceremonial monument at the very seat the Ulster Cycle calls Macha's. No artifact names her; the identification of the fort with Emain Macha rests on the early medieval record, beginning with the annals and the Book of Armagh.
lore.syncretism: Macha's clearest cross-border witness is Welsh, and it is the standard comparison of the handbooks: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] of the First Branch of the Mabinogi, the otherworld woman on the horse no rider can overtake, who — falsely accused and shamed — is sentenced to sit at the horse-block and offer to carry guests on her back like a beast of burden. Mac Cana and Sjoestedt both set the two figures side by side: the sovereignty woman bound to horses, wronged by the men of the court, and made to bear an equine humiliation. Behind both stands the Gaulish horse-goddess Epona, whose altars run from Britain to the Danube — the one Celtic deity with a festival in the Roman calendar — the continental anchor of the comparison, cited as type, never as identity. Within the Irish corpus her structural kin are [[medb|Medb]], the sovereignty queen whose favor makes kings, and her own sisters of war, [[badb|Badb]] and [[morrigan|the Morrígan]], with whom the Lebor Gabála shares a mother.

pronunciation.approximation: 'FEEN' — one syllable; the f is slender and light, the vowel a long ee, the final nn broad against the teeth. 'Fionn mac Cumhaill' runs roughly 'FEEN mak KOO-il'.
pronunciation.note: Fionn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Irish form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The manuscripts write Find, the modern language writes Fionn, and both are Latin letters; the capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input. The hero's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Hunter, Seer, Leader
domains.subtitle: The Salmon of Knowledge, the Burning of Tara, and the Long Chase of the Fianna
domains.lead: Fionn mac Cumhaill is the great captain of the Fianna, the war-band of young hunters and fighters who held the marches of Ireland between the king's peace and the wild: the boy who burned his thumb on the Salmon of Knowledge and swallowed all wisdom with it, the youth who saved Tara from fire on Samain night, and the aging leader who spent sixteen years pursuing Diarmaid and Gráinne across the country he had sworn to protect.

cards.name: The Salmon of Knowledge
cards.desc: An eo fis — the fish that fed on the nuts of the nine hazels over the well of Segais; whoever ate it would know all things.

cards.name: The Thumb of Knowledge
cards.desc: Burned on the salmon's blister and sucked by reflex — afterward Fionn could chew his thumb and the imbas, the great knowledge, would come.

cards.name: The Magic Spear
cards.desc: The birga Fíacha mac Conga put in his hand at Tara: held with its point to the forehead, its enchantment kept a man awake against Aillén's music.

cards.name: Bran and Sceólang
cards.desc: His two great hounds, born of his own transformed kin — the chase made family, and the Fianna's swiftest trackers.

symbols.name: The salmon of knowledge
symbols.meaning: Wisdom caught in a single instant — meant for another, given by chance, and never returned

symbols.name: The thumb
symbols.meaning: Imbas forosnai, the knowledge that illuminates — knowing held in the body, summoned by the bite

symbols.name: The magic spear
symbols.meaning: The discipline to stay awake when the whole court is lulled — vigilance as a weapon

symbols.name: The hounds Bran and Sceólang
symbols.meaning: The bond of hunter and hunted bound into one kinship — the wild running at the leader's heel

symbols.name: Ben Bulben
symbols.meaning: The boar's mountain in Sligo, where the long pursuit of Diarmaid ended and the water slipped through Fionn's fingers

mythology.lead: Fionn's cycle is the fullest hero-corpus Ireland kept: the Boyhood Deeds that make him wise, the Fenian lays and ballads that make him captain, and the two late romances — the pursuit of Diarmaid and the lay of Oisín — that make him tragic.

myths.title: The Boy in the Wild
myths.text: Fionn's father was Cumhall mac Trénmhóir, captain of the Fianna, who abducted Muirne, daughter of the druid Tadg, when her father refused her. Tadg's appeal brought the king's army, and Cumhall fell at the battle of Cnucha to Goll mac Morna, head of the rival Clann Morna. Muirne bore the child in danger and gave him to two women to rear in secret: Bodbmall the druidess and Liath Luachra the warrior-woman, who raised him in the wild places away from his father's enemies. When the boy grew strong he went openly to his grandfather Tadg and exacted the blood-price for Cumhall — the hill of Allen, Almhain, which would become the Fianna's seat. The women they hid him from gave the world the name by which the manuscripts remember him: the boy they raised was named Demne; the name the world would keep was still swimming in the Boyne.

myths.title: The Salmon of Knowledge
myths.text: Demne came to learn poetry from Finn Éces, Finn the poet, who had waited seven years on the Boyne for the salmon of knowledge — the fish that had fed on the nuts of the nine hazels dropping into the well of Segais, so that all the knowledge of the world was in its flesh. When at last the salmon was caught, the poet set the boy to cook it and forbade him to taste any part of it. A blister rose on the fish's skin; Demne pressed it down with his thumb, burned himself, and thrust the thumb into his mouth — and the knowledge was his. Finn Éces asked the boy his name, heard 'Demne', and told him: Finn is your name now, for it was Finn who was prophesied to eat this salmon. The boy ate what remained, and ever after needed only to chew his thumb to know what was hidden.

lore.culturalLegacy: Fionn became, for a century, the most famous Celt in Europe. James Macpherson's Fragments of Ancient Poetry (1760) and Fingal (1762) presented 'Ossian' — Oisín — as the bard of a northern Homer, with Fingal his mighty father; the poems swept the continent, were carried by Napoleon and quoted by Goethe, and set off a running war over their authenticity in which Samuel Johnson demanded the manuscripts and Macpherson never produced them. The Celtic Revival reclaimed the genuine cycle: Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) brought the Fenian tales into modern English, and Irish scholarship — Meyer's Fianaigecht, Murphy's Duanaire Finn, Dooley and Roe's Acallam translation — rebuilt the cycle from its real witnesses. In Ireland the name never faded: Fianna Éireann named the warrior-band after him, the political tradition borrowed Fianna Fáil, 'the war-band of Ireland', Finn is once again a living given name, and Tír na nÓg remains the Irish idiom for youth that outlasts its bargain.
lore.archaeology: Fionn is a textual hero: no ogham stone names him, and his cycle survives in the great Irish codices — the Acallam in the Book of Lismore and its sister manuscripts, the Boyhood Deeds and the Fenian lays across the Laud and Book of Leinster traditions. His landscape, by contrast, is real and visitable. The salmon of knowledge was caught in the Boyne, the river that bends around Brú na Bóinne — the Newgrange passage-tomb complex (c. 3200 BCE) that the myths make the síd of Óengus, Diarmaid's protector. Tara, the royal seat Aillén burned every Samain, is the hill of Teamhair in County Meath, an Iron Age ceremonial complex of earthworks and standing stones. Ben Bulben, where the boar killed Diarmaid, stands over Sligo as the tales describe it. The Fenian cycle is unusual among Irish corpora for how densely it maps onto ground that can still be walked.
lore.syncretism: Fionn's deepest kin are onomastic and Insular. His name descends from Proto-Celtic *windos, 'white, fair', and the handbooks have long set him beside the Welsh Gwyn ap Nudd — 'white son of Nudd', the Otherworld huntsman of Welsh tradition — as two regional developments of a Celtic figure built on the same word: the fair one who rides between this world and the wild. The more famous comparison is with the Norse corpus: like Sigurðr, who tasted the blood of Fáfnir's heart and understood the speech of birds, Fionn receives a whole mode of knowledge through a single accidental taste — the parallel is a commonplace of the comparative literature, though the two traditions grew the motif independently. Within Ireland his nearest mirror is [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], the Ulster Cycle's solitary champion set against Fionn's communal war-band: the two heroes divide the Irish heroic imagination between them.

Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of Find or any Fenian name has been read on them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: fionn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OG-ma' — a short, closed 'o', the g melted toward a soft gargle before the m, stress firmly on the first syllable. The English habit of a hard g, as in 'dogma', is the one sound to avoid.
pronunciation.note: Ogma is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Irish form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the temple form from the input. The lexicon's traditional gloss is 'the grim one', but the etymology is genuinely unsettled: the standard scholarly line derives the name from Proto-Celtic *Ogmios (attested in Gaulish), with a possible further link to Greek ogmos, 'furrow, swath' — a derivation discussed since Vendryes and registered, not decided, by the handbooks (LEIA; Koch, s.v. Ogma).

domains.title: The Honey-Tongued Champion
domains.subtitle: Eloquence, Writing
domains.lead: Ogma is the champion — in trenfer, the strong man — of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the Irish tradition made his strength and his speech one gift: the Auraicept na n-Éces calls him a man well skilled in speech and in poetry, and credits him with the invention of the ogham itself. His Gaulish cognate Ogmios, the old-man Herakles of Lucian's account, drags a willing crowd by golden chains fastened to his tongue: in the Celtic world, eloquence is what the strongest god is for.

cards.name: The Ogham
cards.desc: The notched alphabet of early Ireland, carved along the edge of standing stones — of which the Scholars' Primer says: the father of the ogham is Ogma, the mother of the ogham is the hand or knife of Ogma.

cards.name: Orna, the Speaking Sword
cards.desc: The sword of Tethra, king of the Fomorians, found by Ogma after Mag Tuired — which recounted every deed that had been done with it, as swords did in those days.

cards.name: The Flagstone of Tara
cards.desc: The great stone Ogma hurled to test the stranger at the gate — which Lugh threw back through the rath to its own place, proving the stronger champion had arrived.

cards.name: The Firewood
cards.desc: The champion's portion under the tyranny of Bres: hauling fuel for a usurper's fires, so weakened by hunger that the sea washed over him as he carried it.

symbols.name: The ogham fews
symbols.meaning: The notched letters along the stemline — writing itself, fathered by the champion's hand

symbols.name: Orna, Tethra's sword
symbols.meaning: The weapon that tells its own deeds — even the champion's steel answers to speech

symbols.name: The flagstone of Tara
symbols.meaning: Strength as the doorkeeper's test — the stone only the worthiest arm can move

symbols.name: The firewood bundle
symbols.meaning: The strong man reduced to serf-labor — endurance under the usurper, repaid at Mag Tuired

symbols.name: The golden chains of Ogmios
symbols.meaning: Lucian's Gaulish image of eloquence: men led willingly, ear fastened to tongue

mythology.lead: Ogma's dossier is compact and exact: the Lebor Gabála gives his lineage, Cath Maige Tuired gives his deeds — the serf-labor under Bres, the flagstone test at Lugh's coming, the killing of the Fomorian king's son, and the talking sword — and the learned tradition gives him his strangest honor, the invention of the ogham.

myths.title: The Son of Elatha
myths.text: The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, writes Ogma into the divine genealogy: Ogma son of Elatha, of the line of Delbaeth, and so the brother of the Dagda himself. The surname carries a sting the saga does not hide — the same Elatha, the beautiful Fomorian prince who came as an arbiter to the Túatha Dé, is father of Bres by a Fomorian woman, which makes the champion of the gods the half-brother of the usurper who will set him hauling firewood. When the Túatha Dé Danann came to Ireland out of the four northern cities, Ogma came with them as the champion of the race — in trenfer, the strong man, the standing title the texts give him. His place in the pantheon is therefore double from the first mention: the arm of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the brother of their all-father, with the enemy's blood already in his own house.

myths.title: The Firewood of the Serf-Years
myths.text: When the half-Fomorian Bres was made king and laid the Túatha Dé Danann under tribute, the greatest of them were put to work like serfs — deliberately, for the tribute was calculated to break the mighty. The Dagda was set to building raths, and Ogma — the champion of the whole divine race — was set to hauling firewood for the fortress. The tale does not spare him: so weakened was he by hunger that the sea washed over him as he carried the fuel. The servitude did not blunt him; when the war came he killed the Fomorian king's son with his bare champion's art, and the firewood years became the measure of what was repaid. But the image stands as the tradition's sharpest statement of what Bres' kingship cost: the strong man of the gods, bent double under a usurper's faggots, with the tide at his knees.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ogma's afterlife runs on the two rails his name already laid down: strength and letters. Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried Cath Maige Tuired into English and made the champion of the firewood years part of the revival's reading; the later romantic cycle, in Oidheadh Chloinne Tuireann, made him the father of Tuireann and so grandfather of the three sons whose blood-price Lugh exacted. His larger legacy is the script itself. The four hundred ogham stones of Ireland and Wales became the national patrimony of early Ireland, and with them Ogma's paternity: the medieval claim that the champion fathered the alphabet is quoted wherever the stones are studied. In the twentieth century Robert Graves's The White Goddess (1948) built a whole modern mythology on the ogham letters — a construction of Graves's own, not a medieval doctrine — and carried the script, and with it Ogma's fame, into modern esoteric and Druid practice, where he is honored as the god of eloquence, writing, and the poet's craft. The scholars, meanwhile, kept the older wonder alive: Lucian's chained crowd remains the most-quoted image of Celtic eloquence in the literature.
lore.archaeology: Ogma is a textual god: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and the irony is the corpus's own — the script the medieval scholars fathered on him survives on some four hundred stones of roughly the fourth to seventh centuries, bearing personal names in formulaic genitives, none of them his. His manuscript witnesses are exact: Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition; the Lebor Gabála Érenn is preserved in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster and its sister codices; and the Auraicept na n-Éces, the tract that credits him with the alphabet, comes down in the great late-medieval compilations such as the Book of Ballymote. The nearest material witness to his figure is classical rather than Celtic: Lucian's second-century description of the Gaulish Ogmios, the old Herakles of eloquence, is the continental portrait of the god, and the Gaulish name is otherwise attested on a small number of defixiones (curse tablets) — comparative evidence, never identification.
lore.syncretism: Ogma has the strongest cross-border witness of any Irish god, and it is a classical author's eyewitness account. Lucian of Samosata, writing in the second century CE, describes a picture the Gauls showed him of their Herakles: not the young Greek athlete but a very old man, bald and wrinkled and sun-dark, drawing after him a great crowd of men — each one fastened by the ears to the god's tongue with slender chains of gold and amber, and following willingly, none struggling. The Gauls, Lucian's guide explains, do not give eloquence to Hermes as the Greeks do; they give it to Herakles, because he is the more powerful, and because the hero achieves everything by persuasion — his arrows are words. In the Gaulish tongue, the guide adds, Herakles is called Ogmios. The equation Ogmios = Ogma is the standard comparison of the handbooks — Vendryes' LEIA derives the Irish name from Proto-Celtic *Ogmios, and Mac Cana and Koch print the Lucian passage as the god's continental portrait. It remains comparison rather than identification: the Irish texts never call Ogma old or bald, and the ogham invention is Ireland's own learned myth. The Welsh corpus, meanwhile, is silent — the Mabinogi knows no counterpart, and no scholar has convincingly supplied one.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Ogma — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script of the great codices; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham — the very script the medieval tradition credits Ogma with inventing — survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: ogma.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'a-ROWN' — the aw sounds like the 'ow' of 'town', and the stress falls on the second syllable, the Welsh penult.
pronunciation.note: Arawn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The lexicon's traditional gloss is 'silver-tongued', but the etymology is genuinely unsettled: scholars have proposed a learned borrowing of the biblical Aaron (a suggestion going back to Ifor Williams) as well as native Celtic derivations, and no derivation commands consensus (Koch; GPC, s.v. Arawn).

domains.title: The King of Annwn
domains.subtitle: Otherworld, Annwn
domains.lead: Arawn is the king of Annwn, the Welsh Otherworld: the lord whose white, red-eared hounds bring down a stag in Pwyll's hunting-ground at Glyn Cuch, and whose answer to the insult is the strangest exchange in the Mabinogi — a year and a day in which two kings trade faces, thrones, and beds, so that honor may be tested where no one is watching.

cards.name: The White Hounds
cards.desc: Arawn's pack, shining white with red ears — the colour of the Otherworld, a sight Pwyll had never seen on any hound of his own.

cards.name: The Exchange of Shapes
cards.desc: A year and a day in which Arawn takes Pwyll's form in Dyfed and Pwyll takes Arawn's in Annwn — and neither court suspects.

cards.name: The Ford
cards.desc: The appointed meeting-place where Pwyll must face Hafgan, king of the other realm of Annwn — with one blow and no more.

cards.name: The Untouched Bed
cards.desc: Arawn's queen, the fairest woman Pwyll had ever seen — with whom he shares a bed for a year and never turns his face to her.

symbols.name: The white hounds with red ears
symbols.meaning: The colour of the Otherworld — a hunt that arrives from the far side of the boundary

symbols.name: The exchanged shape
symbols.meaning: Kingship as a trust held for another: the year Arawn's face ruled two realms

symbols.name: The single blow
symbols.meaning: Restraint as the condition of victory — strike once, or not at all

symbols.name: The untouched bed
symbols.meaning: Honor kept in the dark, where no one would ever have known

symbols.name: The ford
symbols.meaning: The meeting-place between realms, where debts are paid and blows are counted

symbols.name: The yearly gifts
symbols.meaning: Friendship renewed in kind — horses, greyhounds, hawks, and treasure

mythology.lead: Arawn's whole dossier is one story, and it is the opening movement of the Mabinogi: the hunting-debt at Glyn Cuch and the year-long exchange that turns an insult into the strongest friendship in Welsh prose. Every word of it is preserved in the First Branch, Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed.

myths.title: The Wrong at Glyn Cuch
myths.text: Pwyll, lord of Dyfed, goes hunting at Glyn Cuch, and there he sees a sight he has never seen: a pack of hounds shining white with red ears bringing down a stag. He drives them off and sets his own hounds on the kill — and the stranger who rides up is Arawn, king of Annwn, and it was his hunt. Arawn names the discourtesy plainly: he will not take revenge, but a man who feeds his hounds on another's kill has wronged him, and Pwyll offers to buy back his friendship at whatever price. Arawn names it. He has a rival, Hafgan, king of the other realm of Annwn, who wars on him without end; let Pwyll take Arawn's shape and his place for a year and a day, and meet Hafgan at the ford at the year's turning. The insult that opens the Mabinogi is small; the answer to it is a year's borrowed life, and the tale means to show what a king is made of when the test is set by his enemy and graded by his wife.

myths.title: The Exchange of Shapes
myths.text: Each king takes the other's form and goes to the other's court, and neither realm suspects. Arawn rules Dyfed so well that there had never been so good a year in it. Pwyll enters Annwn in Arawn's likeness, and that first night he is led to the bed of Arawn's wife — the fairest and most comely woman he had ever seen. He turns his back to her, and he does so every night of the year: he speaks to her with courtesy by day, and in the bed he never once turns his face toward her. The queen never knows. The whole test of the tale is here, in the dark, where no one could have seen the difference — and that is exactly the point. The First Branch argues that honor is what a man does when the only witness is himself, and it stakes the argument on a bed no court could inspect.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Arawn out of the White and Red Books and into English, and the white red-eared hounds entered the stock of Celtic imagery from that day. In the twentieth century the figure found his widest audience inverted: Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain (1964–68) made 'Arawn Death-Lord of Annuvin' the arch-villain of five children's novels, and Disney's The Black Cauldron (1985) kept the dark-lord version on screen — a long way from the most honorable king in Welsh prose, but the reason the name is known worldwide. The Cŵn Annwn meanwhile never left Welsh folklore, still baying as a death-omen in folk memory into the modern period. Modern Druid and pagan practice honours Arawn as lord of the Otherworld and patron of kept faith, and the name survives in Wales as a rare living given name.
lore.archaeology: Arawn is a textual figure: no inscription, votive deposit, or cult site names him, and the epigraphic record of pre-Christian Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — records personal names, not theonyms. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120. The geography of the tale is real: Glyn Cuch, where the insult happens, is identified with the valley of the River Cych on the Pembrokeshire–Carmarthenshire border, inside the Dyfed the story governs. The nearest material echo of the Otherworld hunt is literary: the Book of Taliesin, the manuscript that preserves Preiddeu Annwfn, is a fourteenth-century Welsh codex (NLW Peniarth MS 2).
lore.syncretism: Arawn's comparisons are almost all inward, and the Welsh corpus itself supplies them. His clearest rival for the kingship of the Otherworld is Gwyn ap Nudd, whom Culhwch ac Olwen says God set over the demons of Annwn — a second king of Annwn in a second text, and the folklore gave Gwyn the hounds that the Mabinogi gave Arawn. The structural reading runs deeper: commentators since Mac Cana have read the Annwn adventure as the proving of Pwyll's character before the coming of Rhiannon — the hero tested in honor and restraint in the Otherworld before the Otherworld's queen chooses him in this one. The name itself may be the tale's one foreign guest: Ifor Williams proposed that Arawn is a learned borrowing of the biblical Aaron, carried into Welsh by Latin learning, and the handbooks register the possibility without deciding it. No Gaulish or Irish counterpart of Arawn has ever been convincingly proposed; the exchange-of-kings motif is the Mabinogi's own.
