Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: arawn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/arawn/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: GWID-yon — the gw is a single lip-rounded consonant, the y sounds like the i of 'kin', and the stress falls on the first syllable.
pronunciation.note: Middle Welsh Gwydion (Gwydion uab Dôn) is already written in the Latin alphabet, so the ASCII form loses nothing: the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, since the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops. The etymology is honestly debated: a derivation from the Celtic root *widu- 'wood, forest' has often been proposed (compare Welsh gwydd 'trees', Old Irish fid, Gaulish vidu-), but the connection is not proven and the standard handbooks mark it uncertain.

domains.title: Magic, Poetry, Trickery
domains.subtitle: Enchanter of Gwynedd — illusion, craft, and the fate of Lleu Llaw Gyffes
domains.lead: In the Welsh tradition, Gwydion fab Dôn is the foremost magician of the Mabinogi: master of illusion, disguise, and the hidden name, whose tricks win a war — and whose craft finally puts a broken world back together.

cards.name: The Enchanted Swine
cards.desc: Disguised as a poet, Gwydion conjured illusory stallions, hounds, and shields to trade for Pryderi's otherworld pigs — the first swine in Wales — and started a war with a vanishing herd.

cards.name: Math's Wand
cards.desc: The wand that transformed Gwydion and Gilfaethwy into deer, boars, and wolves for three years — and that later struck Lleu from eagle back into man.

cards.name: The Flower-Maiden
cards.desc: With Math, Gwydion fashioned Blodeuwedd from the flowers of oak, broom, and meadowsweet — a wife made by craft for the man no earthly wife was allowed.

cards.name: The Eagle on the Oak
cards.desc: When Lleu was struck into eagle-shape, Gwydion followed a sow to the oak, sang three englynion to bring him down, and turned vengeance into restoration.

symbols.name: The magic wand
symbols.meaning: Math's wand of transformation — punishment, testing, and restoration carried in a single rod

symbols.name: Oak, broom, and meadowsweet
symbols.meaning: The three flowers from which Blodeuwedd was made by enchantment

symbols.name: The illusory horses and hounds
symbols.meaning: Gwydion's conjured wealth, real for a day and gone by morning — craft as currency

symbols.name: The eagle on the oak
symbols.meaning: Lleu wounded into bird-shape, rotting flesh feeding a sow beneath the tree

symbols.name: The sow
symbols.meaning: The beast Gwydion followed through the valley to find his foster-son

symbols.name: The shoemaker's disguise
symbols.meaning: The craft under which Gwydion tricked Arianrhod into naming her own son

mythology.lead: Gwydion fab Dôn is the enchanter of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Math fab Mathonwy': nephew of Math the king of Gwynedd, brother of Gilfaethwy, and the foremost magician of medieval Welsh literature. He is poet, trickster, foster-father, and avenger in one figure — the man who makes illusions that pass for wealth, who pays for his crimes in animal skins, and who ends the tale as the careful hand that puts a broken world back into shape.

myths.title: The War for the Swine
myths.text:
King Math of Gwynedd could live only with his feet in the lap of a virgin, except in time of war, and the maiden Goewin held that office. When Gilfaethwy desired her, Gwydion devised the remedy: war. He went to Pryderi of Dyfed in the guise of a poet and asked for the swine — the hobeu, the first pigs ever brought to Wales, a gift from Arawn of Annwfn. Refused, he conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, and traded the apparitions for the herd. By the time Pryderi's glamour faded, Gwydion was gone, and Pryderi came north with an army.

While Math marched to meet him, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin. At the peace-talks Pryderi demanded single combat, 'for it was because of me that the hosts came'; at Maenor Penard, the tale says, Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed went home under tribute. The victory is real and so is its cost: Gwydion's finest trick is also his crime, and the Fourth Branch never lets the two be separated.

myths.title: The Punishment of the Brothers
myths.text:
Math's justice is the strangest in the Mabinogi. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand and turned them into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third. Each year their offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — were sent to the court, baptized, and raised.

After the third year Math struck them back into their own shapes: 'You have had punishment enough, and you have been greatly shamed.' The punishment is exact and even-handed — the brothers suffer in the flesh what they did, and when the debt is paid the king takes them back into honour. It is the Fourth Branch's doctrine of justice in miniature: transformation as sentence, restoration as mercy. And it matters that the wand passes finally into Gwydion's own hand: the man punished by shape-shaping becomes the master of it, and the tale watches to see what he does with the power that once unmade him.

lore.culturalLegacy: Gwydion's afterlife runs from Welsh tradition into modern letters. Later Welsh usage named the Milky Way Caer Gwydion, 'Gwydion's fortress' — the enchanter's castle written across the night sky — and the antiquarian bards kept his tree-battle in the poetic canon. In the twentieth century he entered world literature twice over: Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967) rebuilt the Blodeuwedd tragedy as a haunting that repeats itself down the generations of a Welsh valley, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain gave young readers a Prince Gwydion fab Don, heir of Math, drawn directly from the Fourth Branch. Evangeline Walton's retellings of the Mabinogion made his punishment and restoration the moral hinge of her Fourth Branch volume. In scholarship he remains the standard exhibit of the Welsh magician: Ifor Williams's edition, Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi, and Koch's Celtic encyclopedia all treat the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose and Gwydion as its animating intelligence.
lore.archaeology: Gwydion is a textual figure with no pre-Christian material attestation: no inscription, votive object, or image names him. His witnesses are manuscripts — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1400), in which the Fourth Branch survives, and the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth 2, early 14th c.) for Kat Godeu. The tale's geography is walkable real terrain — Gwynedd, Dyfed, Penllyn, the river Cynfael — and a holed stone traditionally pointed out as Llech Ronw, 'Gronw's stone', the slab Lleu's spear pierced, stands in the Cynfael valley; the identification is local tradition rather than proof, but it shows how early and how firmly the story was mapped onto the Welsh landscape.
lore.syncretism: Gwydion is the Welsh trickster-enchanter, and comparative scholarship has set him beside the other shape-changing cunning figures of Europe: Loki, whose disguises and bargains Gwydion's deceptions recall; Hermês, the poet-thief of the Greek pantheon; and Óðinn in his sorcerer's aspect. Mac Cana treats him as one of the great magician-figures of the Celtic world, and the comparison holds at the level of motif — illusion, disguise, the hidden name, the shape-shifting punishment — not of borrowing. The deeper kinship is insular: Irish tradition is full of druidic shape-shifters, and Gwydion's transformations of and by Math belong to a shared Celtic idiom of magic as metamorphosis. Scholars have also long linked the Fourth Branch's otherworld material — Arawn's swine, the phantom fleet — to the mythology of Manawydan and the First and Third Branches.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Gwydion (the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest), and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. The plain-ASCII domain gwydion.com is registered to a third party and held outside the collection; it is watched for release. Until then this temple stands without a domain of its own.

pronunciation.approximation: 'hree-AH-non' — begin with a breathy, whispered r, and put the stress on the middle syllable, the Welsh penult.
pronunciation.note: Rhiannon is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The etymology is a scholarly reconstruction rather than an attested form: Celticists derive the name from Common Celtic *rīgan- 'queen' plus a divine suffix, 'Great Queen', a reading that fits the figure precisely but must be labelled as what it is.

domains.title: The Rider No Horse Can Catch
domains.subtitle: Horses, Sovereignty
domains.lead: Rhiannon is the Great Queen of the Mabinogi: the lady of the Otherworld who rides past Gorsedd Arberth on a pale horse at a slow, even pace that the fastest mounts of Dyfed cannot close — the goddess who chooses her own king, bears a false charge with unbroken dignity, and endures the penance of the horse-collar without bending.

cards.name: Gorsedd Arberth
cards.desc: The mound above Narberth where wonders are seen: whoever sits there receives blows — or sees a marvel. Pwyll saw her ride past.

cards.name: The Uncatchable Pace
cards.desc: She rides a pale horse at a slow, steady walk, and the swiftest riders in Dyfed cannot close the distance — until she is asked to stop.

cards.name: The Birds of Rhiannon
cards.desc: Adar Rhiannon: three birds whose song, though heard far over the sea, is as clear as if they sang beside you — sweeter than any earthly song.

cards.name: The Horse-Block
cards.desc: The marble mounting-block at the gate of Arberth, where she sits out her penance and offers to carry every guest to court on her back.

symbols.name: The pale horse
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty arriving at its own pace — the mount no pursuit can overtake, because the rider alone decides when to stop

symbols.name: The three birds
symbols.meaning: Adar Rhiannon, whose song crosses the boundary between the living and the dead — the Otherworld made audible

symbols.name: The horse-block
symbols.meaning: Dignity under a false sentence: the queen who carries her guests rather than break under the charge she did not earn

symbols.name: The bottomless bag
symbols.meaning: The cleverness that out-plots a forced marriage — Gwawl's undoing, and the game of Badger in the Bag

symbols.name: The collars of asses
symbols.meaning: The enchantment endured in the Third Branch — humiliation worn without surrender, until the spell is undone

mythology.lead: Rhiannon is the strongest female figure in the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and the tales give her a complete arc: the uncatchable rider who chooses her husband, the accused mother who bears her penance, the captive of the enchantment who comes home still a queen. Every word of her story is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts.

myths.title: The Rider on the Pale Horse
myths.text: Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, goes up to Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where a man either suffers blows or sees a wonder, and there he sees a lady in shining gold brocade riding past on a great pale horse — at a slow, even pace. He sends his swiftest rider after her; the faster the pursuit, the farther she draws ahead. Day after day it happens, with Pwyll's own horse and Pwyll himself, until at last he calls out: 'Maiden, for the sake of the man you love best, wait for me.' She stops at once: 'I will wait gladly — and it would have been better for the horse had you asked me that long ago.' She is Rhiannon, daughter of Hefaidd Hên, and she has come of her own will: she is being given to a man she does not want, and she has chosen Pwyll instead.

myths.title: The Bag That Would Not Fill
myths.text: At the wedding feast, Pwyll grants a request before he hears it — and the petitioner is Gwawl fab Clud, the suitor Rhiannon refused, who claims her by the promise. Rhiannon is not dismayed; she devises the counter-plot. A year later Pwyll comes to Gwawl's feast disguised as a beggar, asking only that a certain small bag she has given him be filled with food. The bag cannot be filled: it will never be full, she has told him, unless a true lord treads the food down with his feet and declares that enough has been put in. Gwawl rises and treads it down — and Pwyll draws the bag shut over him, blows his horn, and his war-band falls on the hall. Each man strikes the bag and asks what is in it; 'a badger,' comes the answer, and from that night the Welsh played the game called Badger in the Bag. Gwawl buys his release with sureties and a renounced claim, and Rhiannon marries the man she chose.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Rhiannon out of the Welsh manuscripts and into the English-speaking world, and the Victorian Celtic revival made her one of the best-known figures of Welsh tradition. Evangeline Walton's twentieth-century retellings of the Four Branches kept her before modern readers, and in 1975 Fleetwood Mac's 'Rhiannon' — written by Stevie Nicks, who found the name in a novel and only afterwards learned it belonged to a Welsh goddess — made the name famous worldwide; the given name Rhiannon, already living in Wales, spread across the English-speaking world in the song's wake. In modern Druid and pagan practice she is honoured as a goddess of horses, sovereignty, and endurance under injustice, and scholars of the Mabinogi rank her among the most fully realized women in medieval European literature — a figure whose dignity the prose never once allows to slip.
lore.archaeology: Rhiannon is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the reconstructed *Rīgantonā has no epigraphic attestation anywhere in the Celtic world. Her evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales themselves are dated by debate rather than document, most often to the later eleventh or early twelfth century. The geography of her story is real — Arberth, the court of Dyfed, stands by modern Narberth in Pembrokeshire — but no sanctuary of hers is known. The nearest material horizon is comparative, not hers: the two hundred and more dedications to the Gaulish horse-goddess Epona recovered across the Roman west, against which scholars have long read the rider of Arberth.
lore.syncretism: The great comparative debate pairs Rhiannon with Epona, the Gaulish horse-goddess whose dedications — more than two hundred inscriptions from Britain to the Balkans — make her the best-attested Celtic deity of the Roman west. A queenly rider whose whole story is bound to horses, whose name the handbooks reconstruct as 'Great Queen', looks very like an insular reflex of the mare-goddess; Mac Cana and others have argued the parallel, and Koch registers it as the standard comparison — but no inscription names Rhiannon or *Rīgantonā, and the identification remains typological, not epigraphic. The second frame is sovereignty: Mac Cana reads the First Branch against the Irish pattern in which the land's queen chooses and validates the king, so that Pwyll's marriage to Rhiannon is his investiture as much as his wedding. The third is Macha, the Irish sovereignty figure forced to race the king's horses: horse, humiliation, and queenship cluster around both women, and the handbooks have compared them for a century. None of these parallels is an identity; together they map the kind of goddess the Welsh prose is remembering.

Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: rhiannon.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/rhiannon/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: 'pruh-DEH-ree' — the y is a soft 'uh', the stress falls on 'der' (the Welsh penult), and the final i is a short 'ee'.
pronunciation.note: Pryderi is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The name's etymology is the tale's own: the First Branch names him from Rhiannon's word pryder, 'care, anxiety', spoken when the lost child was restored — an aetiological naming the medieval author builds into the story itself, and the lexicon's gloss 'Care, anxiety' follows the text.

domains.title: The Lord Who Spans the Four Branches
domains.subtitle: Son of Pwyll, King
domains.lead: Pryderi is the hinge of the whole Mabinogi: the only figure who walks through all Four Branches — stolen on the night of his birth and found outside a stable door, named from his mother's lifted anxiety, emptied out of Dyfed by an enchanter's mist, and killed at last in single combat by Gwydion's craft. Son of Pwyll and Rhiannon, lord of Dyfed, he is the king the tales keep taking things from — and the name he carries is the Welsh word for care.

cards.name: The Stable Door
cards.desc: Outside Teyrnon's stable, where a great clawed hand had come for the newborn foal, lay an infant wrapped in silk brocade — the stolen heir of Dyfed.

cards.name: The Naming
cards.desc: Rhiannon looks at the boy and says her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her; from that word the child is named Pryderi.

cards.name: The Golden Bowl
cards.desc: Hanging by chains above a marble fountain in a fortress that was never there before: when Pryderi grasps it, his hands stick, his feet root to the slab, and his voice dies.

cards.name: The First Swine
cards.desc: The hobeu, first pigs ever brought to Wales — Arawn of Annwn's gift to the house of Pwyll — which Gwydion wins with illusory gold and pays for with Pryderi's life.

symbols.name: The silk brocade wrapping
symbols.meaning: Royal blood declaring itself at a stable door — the foundling child whose swaddling says what no witness can

symbols.name: The clawed hand
symbols.meaning: The Otherworld reaching through the window on May-eve — the unseen power that takes foals and princes alike

symbols.name: The golden bowl on its chains
symbols.meaning: Bait that looks like treasure — the trap at the heart of the enchanted fortress, and the cost of touching what is not yours

symbols.name: The gate-hammer about his neck
symbols.meaning: What he wore out of the enchantment — the humiliation of the Third Branch, borne home and buried in silence

symbols.name: The swine of Annwn
symbols.meaning: Otherworld wealth with a geis upon it — not to be sold or given until the herd had doubled — and the war a broken promise bought

symbols.name: The grave at Maen Tywynog
symbols.meaning: The mound above Y Felenrhyd where the slain lord was buried — the one fixed point of a life lived under enchantment

mythology.lead: Pryderi's mythology is unique in Welsh prose: he is the only character who appears in all Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and his life is the thread the whole cycle is strung on. The First Branch gives his birth, theft, and naming; the Second carries him through the Irish war as one of the seven survivors; the Third empties his kingdom and takes him captive; the Fourth kills him. Every word of it is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts.

myths.title: The May-Eve Vanishing
myths.text: Pryderi is born to Pwyll and Rhiannon after the nobles of Dyfed have pressed for an heir, and on the night of his birth the six women set to watch all fall asleep — and the child is gone. Terrified of the blame, the women kill the pups of a hound, smear the blood on Rhiannon's face, lay the bones beside her, and swear she has destroyed her own son; her penance at the horse-block begins, and it will last until the boy comes home. The child, meanwhile, has fallen into the strangest rescue in Welsh prose. Teyrnon Twrf Liant, a lord of Gwent Is Coed by the sea, loses a foal every May-eve; keeping watch over his mare, he sees a great clawed hand reach through the window to seize the newborn foal, and strikes it off with his sword. Outside the door he finds a baby boy wrapped in silk brocade. He and his wife rear the child as their own and call him Gwri Wallt Euryn — Gwri of the Golden Hair.

myths.title: The Naming at Arberth
myths.text: Gwri grows with uncanny speed — at the end of his first year sturdier than a child of three, at two like a boy of six — and year by year he bears the very likeness of Pwyll. When Teyrnon hears of Rhiannon's penance, he knows what he must do, and he and his wife bring the boy to Arberth. The court sees the likeness at once, and Rhiannon says that if this is true, her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her. Pwyll declares that the boy should take his name from the word his mother spoke when the news was brought to her, and so the child is named Pryderi. The penance ends; Teyrnon will take no reward beyond the boy's friendship; and Pryderi is fostered with Pendaran Dyfed until he is of age, when Pwyll gives him the realm.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Pryderi out of the Welsh manuscripts and into English, and the Victorian Celtic revival made the vanished child of the First Branch one of its set-pieces. Twentieth-century scholarship gave him his modern standing: Ifor Williams's edition fixed the standard Welsh text, W. J. Gruffydd's Rhiannon (1953) built its whole argument about the First and Third Branches around the Pryderi complex, and Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi made the boy who spans all four branches the structural key to the cycle. Evangeline Walton's Mabinogion tetralogy retold his theft and naming for modern readers, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain — five novels built openly on the Mabinogi's world — carried the matter of Pryderi's branches to a vast young readership, though the boy himself never appears under his own name. In modern Druid and pagan practice he is honoured as the lost-and-found divine son and the lord who endured the emptied land, and the name survives in scholarship as the standing example of the Mabinogi's own method: a person named, deliberately and explicitly, out of a single spoken word of grief relieved.
lore.archaeology: Pryderi is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names him, and the early inscribed stones of Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — record personal names in funerary formulae, not the heroes of story. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120. The geography of his story is real and walkable: Arberth, the chief court of Dyfed, stands by modern Narberth in Pembrokeshire; Y Felenrhyd, where the fatal combat was fought, lies in the country toward the border of Gwynedd and Dyfed; and the Fourth Branch points to his grave at Maen Tywynog above it. The nearest epigraphic horizon is comparative, not his: the Gaulish Maponos of the Chamalières tablet and the northern British dedications to Apollo Maponus — the divine son whose figure-type the handbooks read him against.
lore.syncretism: Pryderi's great comparative frame is the Celtic divine son. The handbooks set him beside Mabon ap Modron — 'Son son of Mother' — the youth of Culhwch ac Olwen who was taken from his mother Modron when he was three nights old and found again after a search that outlasts every living memory, and behind Mabon the Gaulish Maponos, the 'Divine Son' whom Romano-Celtic dedications pair with Apollo. A child of an Otherworld mother, stolen at birth and restored, whose name carries his story: the figure-type is one, and Mac Cana and Koch both register the comparison — but the names are not cognate, and no scholar claims identity. The second frame is sovereignty-by-loss: like the stricken kings of Irish tradition, Pryderi holds a kingdom that enchantment can empty in a night, and his rescue comes not by his own strength but by Manawydan's patience — the Third Branch's quiet thesis about where a king's real safety lies. Within the corpus his closest kin are his parents [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] and Pwyll Pen Annwn, his stepfather and rescuer [[manawydan|Manawydan]], his benefactor [[arawn|Arawn]] of [[annwn|Annwn]], and his slayer [[gwydion|Gwydion]] — the enchanter whose conjured wealth bought the pigs and, with them, the war.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Pryderi — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: pryderi.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/pryderi/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: 'keh-RID-wen' — every c is hard, the r is rolled, and the stress falls on the middle syllable, the Welsh penult.
pronunciation.note: Ceridwen is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The etymology is a genuine scholarly debate: Ifor Williams derived the name from an original Cyridfen, 'crooked woman', while the traditional analysis reads cerdd 'poetry' + gwen 'fair, blessed'; the handbooks register both rather than settle the question.

domains.title: Inspiration, Transformation
domains.subtitle: The Cauldron of Awen, the Three Drops, the Flight of Shapes
domains.lead: Ceridwen is the keeper of the cauldron of awen — the poetic inspiration of Welsh tradition. From her house by Llyn Tegid she brews a year and a day for the three drops of inspired knowledge, hunts the servant-boy who steals them through every shape in creation, swallows him as a grain of wheat, and gives him back to the world as Taliesin, the greatest poet Wales remembers. The early Welsh sources concur on the essential fact: she is the owner of the cauldron that is the source of poetic inspiration.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Awen
cards.desc: Boiled a year and a day from the books of the feryllt, the alchemist's art, until three drops of inspired knowledge should rise from it.

cards.name: The Three Drops
cards.desc: All the virtue of the brew gathered in three drops — meant for her ugly son, splashed instead on the finger of Gwion Bach, who put it to his lips.

cards.name: The Flight of Shapes
cards.desc: Hare and greyhound, fish and otter, bird and hawk — the pursuit through every form until the grain of wheat meets the high-crested black hen.

cards.name: Llyn Tegid
cards.desc: The lake of Tegid Foel — modern Bala Lake, the largest natural lake in Wales — beside which her household stood and which still keeps her husband's name.

symbols.name: The cauldron
symbols.meaning: Inspiration brewed by art and patience — knowledge as something cooked, not granted

symbols.name: The three drops
symbols.meaning: The whole of awen compressed into an accident — inspiration that chooses its own vessel

symbols.name: The high-crested black hen
symbols.meaning: The final shape of the hunt: the swallowing that is not death but the first cell of a poet

symbols.name: The hide bag
symbols.meaning: The coracle-skin sewn round the unwanted child and given to the sea — rejection that becomes deliverance

symbols.name: The weir on the Dyfi
symbols.meaning: Gwyddno's salmon-weir where the bag comes to rest — the threshold between the hunted boy and the radiant brow

symbols.name: Llyn Tegid
symbols.meaning: The lake that still bears her husband's name — the story's anchor in real Welsh geography

mythology.lead: Ceridwen's whole dossier is a single tale — Hanes Taliesin, the Tale of Taliesin — preserved in sixteenth-century Welsh manuscripts and customarily printed with the Mabinogion, though it is none of the Four Branches. Within that tale she owns its great engine: the cauldron, the hunt, and the rebirth.

myths.title: The Household by Llyn Tegid
myths.text: In the beginning, the tale says, Ceridwen lived beside Llyn Tegid in the land of Penllyn, the wife of Tegid Foel — Tegid the Bald — whose name the lake still carries. They had two children whose fortunes were weighed in opposite scales: a daughter, Creirwy, the fairest maiden in the world, and a son, Morfran, so dark and ill-favoured that he was called Afagddu, Utter Darkness. No god could have made the boy handsome; but Ceridwen was skilled in the arts, and she resolved to give him what nature had refused — knowledge and the gift of poetry, so that his birth might yet be honoured among men of culture. The household is the tale's moral center of gravity: everything that follows — the cauldron, the chase, the sea — is a mother's engineering on behalf of a child the world despised. Welsh tradition never asks whether her favoritism was just; it asks what a mother with power will do, and then follows the answer for a year and a day.

myths.title: The Cauldron of a Year and a Day
myths.text: From the books of the feryllt — the Welsh name for the alchemist's art — Ceridwen compounded a cauldron of Inspiration and Science. It must boil a year and a day, ceaselessly, until three drops of the spirit of inspiration should be won from it. To keep the vigil she set a blind man, Morda, to kindle the fire beneath, and a servant-boy, Gwion Bach, son of Gwreang of Llanfair in Powys, to stir the pot. The design was exact and the patience enormous: everything in the tale that follows is the unmaking of this design by a single splash. A year and a day is not a deadline but a discipline. The tale insists that inspiration, like ale, is a product of time, fire, and someone else's ceaseless labor — and that the brewer who does everything right is already at the mercy of the last hour, when the drops rise and every plan becomes a hope.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest carried the Tale of Taliesin into English in the nineteenth century, appended to her Mabinogion, and the witch of Llyn Tegid entered the English-speaking imagination beside the Four Branches she never belonged to. Patrick K. Ford's edition and translation fixed the tale's modern scholarly form. Robert Graves made her a figure of international consequence: The White Goddess (1948) read Ceridwen's cauldron and her hunt as the grammar of all true poetry, and though Celticists have never accepted Graves's method, his book set her at the centre of twentieth-century writing about the muse. In Wales the awen she brewed never left the tradition — the word still names poetic inspiration at the National Eisteddfod, and modern Druid orders invoke it in her name — while modern paganism worldwide honours her as keeper of the cauldron of transformation. The name itself, rare in the medieval record, has come back into use as a Welsh given name, carried by the only myth in the language in which a goddess's failure becomes a nation's poetry.
lore.archaeology: Ceridwen is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and pre-Christian Wales left no theonymic epigraphy of the continental kind. Her witnesses are manuscripts. The fullest early text of Hanes Taliesin is embedded in the great world-chronicle of Elis Gruffydd, compiled c. 1530–1552 (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, MS 5276D); a second version was copied by the recusant scribe John Jones of Gellilyfdy around 1607. The name itself is older than its tale: medieval Welsh poetry preserves it in spellings such as Kerritwen and Kyrridven, and the triads' editors record that the early sources agree on her one fixed attribute — the cauldron of awen. The geography of the story is real and still legible: Llyn Tegid, her lake, is Bala Lake in Gwynedd, the largest natural lake in Wales, which keeps her husband Tegid Foel's name; and Gwyddno's weir, where the bag comes ashore, stands in the tradition at the Dyfi estuary below his drowned realm. No sanctuary of hers is known, and none is claimed: her monument is the tale itself, and the lake that still carries the name.
lore.syncretism: The strongest cross-border parallels are Irish. The accidental acquisition of a wisdom brewed for another is the plot of the Irish boyhood deeds of Finn mac Cumaill: cooking the salmon of knowledge for his master Finnéces, the boy Finn burns his thumb, puts it in his mouth, and the knowledge intended for the teacher passes to the servant — the same economy of the three drops and the burning finger. The swallowing that becomes rebirth has its Irish twin in Tochmarc Étaíne, where Étaín, transformed into a fly, falls into a cup of wine, is swallowed by the wife of Étar, and is born again into the mortal world. And the cauldron itself is pan-Celtic furniture: [[dagda|the Dagda]]'s cauldron from Murias feeds every company that comes to it, while the Old Irish text The Cauldron of Poesy locates a cauldron of poetry inside every human being. Folklorists — Juliette Wood chief among them — have shown that Hanes Taliesin braids these native strands with international folktale types, above all the magic flight with its transformation chase. The last syncretism is modern: Iolo Morganwg's Barddas set Ceridwen and the awen at the centre of revival Druidry, and modern Druids and pagans honour her as goddess of the cauldron — a reception Ronald Hutton's histories of the revival document and dissect.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Ceridwen — the tale that contains her, Hanes Taliesin, survives in sixteenth-century manuscripts, above all the chronicle of Elis Gruffydd (NLW MS 5276D, c. 1550) and the copy of John Jones of Gellilyfdy (c. 1607), while earlier Welsh poetry attests the name in spellings such as Kerritwen and Kyrridven. Middle and Modern Welsh write the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: ceridwen.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/ceridwen/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AN-oon' — two syllables, stress on the first; the w is sounded as a short 'oo', so the name rhymes with 'cannon' said with Welsh vowels.
pronunciation.note: Annwn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the realm's fame in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Otherworld, Underworld
domains.subtitle: The Deep, the Abyss — realm of the feast and the hunt
domains.lead: Annwn is the Welsh Otherworld of the Mabinogi and the oldest Welsh poetry — a realm of plenty where the feast never fails, ruled in the First Branch by [[arawn|Arawn]], and hunted across by Gwyn ap Nudd, whom God set over the demons of Annwn lest they destroy this world. Its cauldron, borne home from its fortresses at terrible cost, is the oldest quest of Arthurian tradition.

cards.name: The Cauldron of the Head of Annwn
cards.desc: Kindled by the breath of nine maidens, rimmed with pearls, it will not boil a coward's food — the prize of Arthur's voyage in Preiddeu Annwfn.

cards.name: The Hounds of Annwn
cards.desc: Arawn's pack — gleaming white with red ears, the colours the Welsh tradition gives every creature from the Otherworld.

cards.name: Prydwen
cards.desc: Arthur's ship on the voyage to the fortresses of Annwn — three full loads went in; except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.

cards.name: The Hunt of Gwyn ap Nudd
cards.desc: The son of Nudd rides with the hunt of Annwn; in Culhwch ac Olwen, God set him over its demons lest they destroy this world.

symbols.name: The cauldron of Pen Annwn
symbols.meaning: Plenty that will not serve the coward — abundance that answers only to courage

symbols.name: White hounds with red ears
symbols.meaning: The colours of the Otherworld made flesh — beauty that marks the boundary crossed

symbols.name: Caer Sidi and the fortresses
symbols.meaning: The revolving castle and its sister fortresses — the Otherworld as architecture that must be won, not visited

symbols.name: Prydwen
symbols.meaning: Arthur's ship — the voyage into the deep from which only seven returned

symbols.name: The year's exchange
symbols.meaning: Arawn and Pwyll trading shapes and kingdoms — the Otherworld close enough to wear a man's face

mythology.lead: Annwn is named in the very first pages of the Mabinogi and in the most difficult poem of early Welsh tradition. Its dossier is small and immense: a king who trades his shape, a cauldron that will not boil a coward's food, a hunt that keeps the world's demons leashed — and, behind all three, the deep itself.

myths.title: The Year in Annwn
myths.text:
Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, is hunting in Glyn Cuch when he drives a strange pack off a stag — hounds gleaming white, with red ears, the colours of the Otherworld — and feeds his own dogs on the kill. Their master rides up: [[arawn|Arawn]], a king of Annwn, and the offense is real. To make amends Pwyll accepts Arawn's bargain: for a year and a day they will exchange shapes and kingdoms, and at the year's end Pwyll must face Arawn's rival Hafgan — a king who can be killed by a single blow only; strike him twice and by the next day he fights as strongly as before.

Pwyll rules Annwn for the year in Arawn's likeness, in a court of unsurpassed plenty — and each night lies beside Arawn's queen without once touching her. At the appointed ford he strikes Hafgan once, refuses the second blow the wounded king begs for, and Annwn is united under Arawn. When the two kings meet again at Glyn Cuch and resume their own shapes, Arawn learns of the year's chastity and the friendship is sealed with gifts of horses, greyhounds, hawks, and gold. From that day Pwyll was called not Pwyll Prince of Dyfed but Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll, Head of Annwn.

myths.title: The Spoils of Annwn
myths.text:
The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwfn', preserved in the fourteenth-century Book of Taliesin and spoken in the poet's own voice, is the oldest surviving account of an Arthurian Otherworld raid. Arthur sails in his ship Prydwen against the fortresses of the deep — Caer Sidi, Caer Pedryfan, Caer Wydyr, and the rest — and the refrain tolls after each: 'except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.' Three full loads of Prydwen went into Annwn; seven men came back.

The prize is the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — kindled by the breath of nine maidens, its rim set about with pearls, and marked by the rule the Welsh tradition fixes on Otherworld vessels: it will not boil the food of a coward. The poem is elliptical, proud, and mournful at once — the poet stands apart from the swordsmen who went in and never came out — but its facts became permanent: the Otherworld has a cauldron, Arthur went to get it, and almost no one returned.

lore.culturalLegacy: Preiddeu Annwfn stands at the head of the Arthurian tradition: the raid on the Otherworld fortresses is older than every romance of the Grail, and scholars from Loomis onward have read the quest for the Head of Annwn's cauldron — a vessel of plenty that tests the worthy — as the Grail story's deepest Welsh root. The name kept working in Welsh: Annwn remains the living word for the Otherworld, and the white red-eared hounds became the Cŵn Annwn of later Welsh folklore, the pack whose crying in the night sky foretells a death. Gwyn ap Nudd rode out of the texts into modern Druidry and pagan practice as the great huntsman and psychopomp of the Welsh tradition, and Glastonbury Tor — crowned now by the stump of St Michael's tower — still carries his court in the popular imagination. Restoring Annwn in Unicode costs nothing and fixes something: the canonical spelling of the deep, held against the drift of anglicized spellings like Annwvyn and Annwyn.
lore.archaeology: Annwn is a wholly textual realm: no inscription invokes it, and the Romano-British epigraphy of Wales is silent on the Otherworld by name. Its manuscript witnesses, however, are exact. The Mabinogi survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1400), the two great codices of medieval Welsh prose; Preiddeu Annwfn is preserved uniquely in the Book of Taliesin (National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century); and Culhwch ac Olwen comes down in a White Book fragment and the full Red Book text. The one site the tradition ties to Annwn is Glastonbury Tor, Gwyn ap Nudd's seat in Buchedd Collen: excavations on the Tor in the 1960s found sub-Roman and early medieval occupation beneath the ruins of St Michael's church — real archaeology on the hill, though none of it speaks to the Otherworld, whose only true location is the text.
lore.syncretism: Annwn's clearest kin are Irish: the síd of the Túatha Dé Danann, where the feast likewise never fails — the Dagda's cauldron of Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standing comparison for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and Mac Cana sets the two vessels side by side as one Celtic figure-type. The Irish Otherworld of the immrama and echtrai — Mag Mell, Emain Ablach, lands 'without grief, without sorrow, without death' — matches Annwn's profile point for point: plenty, beauty, and the suspension of age and sickness. Yet the Brythonic tradition is not a copy of the Gaelic one: no Irish text knows the name Annwn, and the Welsh corpus built its Otherworld on its own geography — the ford at Glyn Cuch, the revolving fortresses of the Taliesin poem, the Tor at Glastonbury. The Christian redactors left the structure intact while re-labelling its inhabitants: by Buchedd Collen, Gwyn ap Nudd's splendid court could be dismissed as a demonic glamour without surrendering one detail of the feast.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh has been written in the Latin alphabet throughout its manuscript history, and the normalized form Annwn is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. The manuscripts spell the name Annwfn (Middle Welsh f writes the voiced [v]); the modern normalized spelling is Annwn. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: annwn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: EKH-ooshkya — stress the first syllable, let the ch rasp as in 'loch', and run the second word tight: the whole compound is one breath, horse and water together.
pronunciation.note: Eachuisge is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Gaelic compound is written in plain Latin letters — no diacritic and no distinctive character for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone marks the temple form; the creature's standing in the folklore record is beside the point. The hyphens of the dictionaries (each-uisge) are a grammatical courtesy, not a registrable form.

domains.title: The Water Horse of the Lochs
domains.subtitle: The Perfect Stallion, the Adhesive Back, and the Liver That Floated Ashore
domains.lead: Eachuisge — the each-uisge, the water horse — is the most dangerous being in the Highland Otherworld: a shape-shifter that haunts the lochs and sea-lochs of Gaelic Scotland, wearing the shape of a flawless stallion at the water's edge. Mount him and your hands stick fast to his hide; the loch does the rest. The Lowland kelpie haunts rivers and is content to drown you — the each-uisge devours.

cards.name: The Loch
cards.desc: His true country: the deep freshwater lochs and sea-lochs of the Highlands, where he waits beneath the surface.

cards.name: The Perfect Stallion
cards.desc: His chosen lure: a beautiful horse standing tame by the shore, offered to any traveler in a hurry.

cards.name: The Adhesive Back
cards.desc: Once mounted, the rider cannot dismount: the hide holds the hand like pitch, and the horse runs for the water.

cards.name: The Handsome Stranger
cards.desc: His other shape: a fine young man by the shore — betrayed, the tales say, by the water-weed in his hair.

symbols.name: The flawless stallion
symbols.meaning: The too-perfect gift at the water's edge — beauty as bait, offered where the ground runs out

symbols.name: The adhesive hide
symbols.meaning: The choice that cannot be unmade: once mounted, the mount decides

symbols.name: The liver on the shore
symbols.meaning: The one thing the loch gives back — the Highland record's grimmest detail, and its proof that this horse devours

symbols.name: The weed in the stranger's hair
symbols.meaning: The tell the shape cannot shed: water keeps its mark on whatever walks out of it

mythology.lead: The each-uisge has no medieval manuscript behind him: his mythology is oral, and its primary witnesses are the great nineteenth-century field collections of the Highlands — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland. The tales agree on the essentials with the consistency of a warning passed from shore to shore.

myths.title: The Rider Taken
myths.text: The core of every telling is the same. A traveler on the shore of a loch finds a beautiful horse standing idle — fine beyond any horse in the parish, saddled by luck, or so it seems. He mounts; the horse is smooth and willing; and then the rider finds his hands fast to the hide, stuck as if with bird-lime, and the horse's head already turned toward the water. The loch takes them both. In the grimmest tellings the loch gives the rider back in pieces — the tradition is exact about this: the each-uisge devours the whole body, and what floats ashore is the liver alone. That detail is the Highland folklore's way of drawing the line between its own water horse and the Lowland kelpie, which drowns but does not eat.

myths.title: The Boy Who Cut Off His Finger
myths.text: The best-known of the warning-tales gives the creature a longer game. A fine horse appears to children playing by a loch, and one by one they climb its back — and the back lengthens to take them, seat after seat, until all are mounted save one wary boy, who will only touch the hide with a finger. The horse springs for the water with its load of children, and the boy, stuck by that single finger, does the one thing left: he cuts the finger off and escapes. The loch gives back the others the next day, piecemeal. The collectors recorded the tale across the Highlands, and Briggs notes it among the each-uisge's defining episodes: the compound's lesson compressed into a single image — touch with everything and you lose everything; touch with a finger and a finger pays for the lesson.

lore.culturalLegacy: The each-uisge entered print through the great Victorian field collections — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–62) and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900) — and it never left. Katharine Briggs's Encyclopedia of Fairies fixed its modern profile as the fiercest of the British water-horses, and MacKillop's Dictionary of Celtic Mythology carried it into the standard Celtic reference shelf. Burns had already put the Lowland cousin into verse — the 'water-kelpie' of the Address to the Deil — and the whole water-horse tradition stands behind the Highlands' most famous modern legend: commentators have long read the loch-monster lore of the twentieth century against this older record of horses in the water. Andy Scott's Kelpies at Falkirk (2013), the thirty-meter horse-head sculptures on the Forth and Clyde Canal, are the tradition's monumental afterlife — kelpies by name, but the image they make permanent is the each-uisge's own: the horse rising out of Scottish water. In Gaelic itself the compound never went anywhere: each-uisge still means the water horse, and the warning it carries is older than any collection that preserves it.
lore.archaeology: The each-uisge has no material witness, and the record must be exact about what that means: no inscription names him, no manuscript illuminates him, and no medieval codex preserves his tales, because he belongs to oral tradition rather than to the literary cycles. His primary evidence is the nineteenth-century field collection — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–62), gathered from Gaelic-speaking informants across the western Highlands and Islands, and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900), the fullest single dossier of the water horse's habits. Carmichael's Carmina Gadelica records the same Highland world in its charms and invocations. The landscape itself is the rest of the evidence: the deep freshwater lochs and sea-lochs of the west are the named settings of the tales, and the water-horse complex they belong to is one of the most widely attested figure-types in northern European folklore — a fact the comparatists established from the collections, not from the ground.
lore.syncretism: The each-uisge is the Highland head of a family that runs the length of the Celtic coasts and beyond. His closest cousin is the Lowland Scots kelpie, which haunts rivers rather than lochs and is generally the milder power — drowning without devouring; the two are kindred, not cognate, for the words are unrelated. The Northern Isles keep their own: Shetland's nuggle or njogel, and Orkney's nuckelavee, a far worse thing — a skinless fusion of man and horse that must be distinguished from the shape-shifting water horse proper. The Isle of Man has the cabbyl-ushtey, Wales the ceffyl dŵr, and Ireland the each-uisce and the shape-shifting [[pooka|Púca]], which takes horse-shape among its many forms. The tradition is older than the collections: [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]]'s horse Aonbharr, which runs over land and sea alike, shows the medieval Irish imagination already at work on the horse that owns both elements. Beyond the Celtic world the type recurs — the Scandinavian bäckahäst and the nøkk among them — and the handbooks treat the whole complex as one of the most widespread figure-types of northern European water-lore: the horse as the beautiful face of drowning.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is the ordinary Gaelic common-noun compound each-uisge, 'water horse', written in the Latin alphabet Gaelic has used since the early medieval period — normalized here as Eachuisge for the temple form. There is no older monumental attestation: the figure belongs to oral tradition, and its primary record is the nineteenth-century field collection, not the manuscript codex. The compound is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the restoration changes nothing but the capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: eachuisge.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'EE-zah-nah-mee' — four even syllables, with a soft final vowel.
pronunciation.note: Izanami is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. She is the primordial mother whose death gave birth to the underworld.

domains.title: She-Who-Invites
domains.subtitle: Creator Goddess, Mother of Kami, Queen of Yomi
domains.lead: Izanami is the female half of the primordial creator pair and the first being to die. Her body became the landscape of the underworld, and her exchange of curses with Izanagi across the sealed slope set the arithmetic of mortality. She is both the mother of the gods and the fearsome queen of Yomi.

cards.name: Creator Goddess
cards.desc: With Izanagi, she stirred the ocean with the jeweled spear and bore the eight great islands.

cards.name: Mother of Kami
cards.desc: She gave birth to the elemental gods, the land, the sea, and the winds.

cards.name: Death in Childbirth
cards.desc: She died bearing the fire god Kagutsuchi; her dying body birthed the thunders.

cards.name: Queen of Yomi
cards.desc: Beyond the boulder she rules the dead and sends the thunders forth.

symbols.name: The comb
symbols.meaning: Her own comb's tooth, lit by Izanagi, revealed her decay — the light that ended their marriage

symbols.name: Boulder of Yomotsu-hirasaka
symbols.meaning: The stone she cannot cross; the sealed door between the living and the dead

symbols.name: Fire (Kagutsuchi)
symbols.meaning: The child that killed her — and the ancestor of every hearth

symbols.name: The eight thunders
symbols.meaning: Yakusanoikazuchi, born from her head, breast, belly, loins, hands, and feet — her honor guard in Yomi

symbols.name: Mount Hiba
symbols.meaning: Her burial place in the land of Kibi, where the myth touches real geography

mythology.lead: Izanami's mythology is central to Japanese understandings of creation, death, and the boundary between the living and the dead — and it never forgives her for speaking first at the pillar.

myths.title: She Who Stirred the Brine
myths.text: The heavenly kami gave the command to the pair, but it was Izanami who set her hand on the spear. Standing upon the Floating Bridge of Heaven, she and Izanagi lowered the jeweled Ame-no-Nuboko into the formless ocean and stirred; the brine dripping from its tip congealed into Onogoroshima, and upon that first island the couple founded their union and their hall (Kojiki 1). The chronicles, even while making her the mother of everything, mark her as the one who stepped outside the ritual order — she spoke the first greeting at the pillar — and who suffered for it. Everything that follows, islands, gods, death, night, proceeds from her equal hand on the spear. The creation is a marriage as much as a manufacture: the world begins in a couple's shared labor, and its first law is how they address each other.

myths.title: Hiruko, the Leech-Child
myths.text: When the couple circled the heavenly pillar to greet each other and beget, Izanami spoke first; their firstborn, Hiruko, was a boneless child who could not stand even at the age of three, and they set him adrift in a reed boat (Kojiki 1). Consulting the heavenly kami, they learned the error — the man's voice must come first — and repeated the rite in the proper order; Izanami then bore the eight great islands and the gods of wind, river, sea, and mountain. Modern readers have reclaimed Hiruko as a poignant emblem, the 'sun-child' as the name can be parsed, the disabled firstborn of the gods; some traditions even drifted to connect the drifting child with Ebisu. But the chronicle records him only as the price of a word out of place. For Izanami the myth is a double wound: blamed for the error, she is then consumed bearing the children that redeem it.

lore.culturalLegacy: Izanami is the most re-imagined figure of the Japanese pantheon: tragic mother in one reading, vengeful corpse-queen in another, and — in modern manga, anime, and games — a glamorous embodiment of death's authority. The drifting Hiruko of the chronicles was later rationalized as Ebisu, the laughing god of fishermen, giving her first failure a strange afterlife as another deity's fortune. Place-names and shrines anchor her legend around Awaji and the Kibi region, and Taga Taisha in Shiga honors the pair. The curse and counter-curse of Yomotsu-hirasaka remain the mythic charter for Japanese funeral grief: the dead take a thousand; the living answer with fifteen hundred.
lore.archaeology: Izanami's cult geography clusters where the myth's geography points. Taga Taisha (Shiga Prefecture) venerates the creation pair and preserves the medieval Taga-dera engi recounting her story. On Awaji Island, Izanagi Jingū serves the pair's legend at the traditional site of Onogoroshima. Mount Hiba in the Chūgoku region — named in the Kojiki as her burial place — anchors the myth in real landscape, and the ancient ritual sites around it have been linked to early underworld cult. The Engishiki lists shrines receiving state offerings for Izanami, confirming that by the tenth century the official cult acknowledged the dead goddess alongside the living one.
lore.syncretism: Izanami's Buddhist reception was quieter than her consort's: as queen of Yomi she was overlaid on images of the underworld's judges and on the earth deities of esoteric cosmology, and in some medieval systems Yomi itself was mapped onto the realm of hungry ghosts. Her gendered fate — the first mother, the first corpse — made her a natural figure for funerary reflection, though no stable buddhological identification took hold. In the Meiji restoration of 'pure' Shinto she was presented as the foremother of the nation; after 1945 her story returned to the libraries of myth. Folklore studies of the period found her scattered cult strongest in the San'in and Kibi regions, close to the geography the chronicles assign her.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NEE-nee-gee' — light, even syllables; the 'g' is hard.
pronunciation.note: Ninigi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn with no distinctive feature for the ASCII form to lose. He is the heavenly grandson sent to rule the terrestrial world.

domains.title: The August Rice Spirit
domains.subtitle: Heavenly Grandson and Bearer of the Regalia
domains.lead: Ninigi is the grandson of Amaterasu, sent from heaven to rule the terrestrial world and establish the imperial line. He descended to Takachiho in Kyūshū bearing the Three Sacred Regalia — the mirror, the sword, and the jewel — and his great-grandson became Emperor Jimmu, the legendary first emperor of Japan.

cards.name: Bearer of the Regalia
cards.desc: He carried the mirror Yata, the sword Kusanagi, and the jewel Yasakani from heaven to earth — the warrant of every later throne.

cards.name: Heavenly Descent
cards.desc: Amaterasu sent him to rule the land of reed plains — the tenson kōrin, the founding descent of Japanese sovereignty.

cards.name: Imperial Ancestor
cards.desc: His line produced Hoori, Ugayafukiaezu, and Jimmu — four generations from heaven to Kashihara.

cards.name: Rice Spirit
cards.desc: His name's final character, 芸, ties him to rice and skill — agricultural sovereignty in a single syllable.

symbols.name: Three Sacred Regalia
symbols.meaning: The mirror, sword, and jewel that legitimize imperial rule

symbols.name: Rice
symbols.meaning: The agricultural foundation of his name and authority

symbols.name: Takachiho
symbols.meaning: The Kyūshū peak where he descended from heaven

symbols.name: Heavenly robe
symbols.meaning: The divine garments that accompanied his descent

mythology.lead: Ninigi's mythology is the bridge between the heavenly realm of Amaterasu and the earthly rule of the emperors: four scenes — the descent, the negotiated surrender of the land, the ordeal by fire that proved his wife's fidelity, and the genealogy that produced Jimmu — suffice to carry three regalia and a nation from the Floating Bridge of Heaven to Kashihara.

myths.title: The Descent from Heaven
myths.text: When Amaterasu resolved that the land of reed plains should be governed from heaven, she chose not her son but her grandson. She gave Ninigi the Three Sacred Regalia — the mirror Yata, the sword Kusanagi that Susanoo had won from the eight-forked serpent, and the curved jewel Yasakani — and sent him down, escorted by the deities Ame-no-koyane and Futodama, from the Floating Bridge of Heaven to Takachiho in Kyūshū. The Kojiki (Book I) frames the descent as a transfer of title: heaven holds sovereignty, and the earth must receive it. One detail sharpens the stakes. As Ninigi left, Amaterasu told him the mirror was to be worshipped as her own spirit — the warrant of his rule was simultaneously her presence. A thousand generations of imperial ideology condensed into a single instruction: the emperor rules because he carries what Ninigi carried. The myth means that legitimacy, in the Japanese telling, is a thing handed down, not taken.

myths.title: Ōkuninushi's Withdrawal
myths.text: The earth, however, was occupied. Its master, the great kami Ōkuninushi, had built and governed the land — some say he had won it by ordeal and war — and heaven's envoy could not simply take it. The Kojiki (Book I) tells how Ninigi pressed the matter through negotiation rather than battle, with pressure from the celestial host. Ōkuninushi consulted his sons; his wise son Kotoshironushi, recognising heaven's claim, withdrew of his own accord and is still honored at Mount Miwa. His father then set his price: a great sanctuary built for him at Kizuki in Izumo — the origin of the shrine now called Izumo Ōyashiro — and the keeping of the land's hidden, numinous affairs. In one stroke the myth explains two of Japan's greatest shrines and establishes a template of Japanese statecraft: conquest by diplomacy, and the defeated party honored, not erased. The Nihon Shoki gives variant versions, but the pattern holds. The myth's deepest meaning may be that sovereignty is best taken by leaving the former holder something greater than his loss.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ninigi's legacy is carried by objects and places rather than temples. The Three Sacred Regalia he bore — mirror, sword, jewel — remain the symbols of imperial legitimacy, presented at each accession though never publicly displayed. Takachiho in Miyazaki Prefecture, his traditional landing place, draws pilgrims and visitors to the Ama-no-Iwato shrine and the gorge of the descent; Kashihara Jingū in Nara marks where his great-grandson Jimmu is said to have acceded. The Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720) preserve his story as the hinge between gods and emperors. In a Japan that no longer claims divine descent, Ninigi endures as the mythological explanation of why the islands were long thought to belong to one unbroken line.
lore.archaeology: No artifact can be tied to Ninigi himself, but the geography of his myth is mapped in standing shrines. Takachiho in Miyazaki Prefecture keeps the sites of the descent — the Ama-no-Iwato ('Cave of Heaven') shrine and the sheer gorge where, by tradition, he first set foot on earth. Izumo Ōyashiro in Shimane, rebuilt in its monumental ancient form, marks the sanctuary Ōkuninushi demanded as the price of withdrawing; excavations in 2000 uncovered pillar bases suggesting an ancient structure of unprecedented height. Kashihara Jingū in Nara stands at the foot of Unebi-yama, the traditional accession site of Jimmu, Ninigi's great-grandson. The regalia he carried are kept at Ise (the mirror), Atsuta (the sword), and the palace (the jewel) — none ever displayed or archaeologically examined. Ninigi's material record is thus a landscape of shrines rather than a museum of objects.
lore.syncretism: Ninigi was never a popularly worshipped god, and that absence is itself revealing. His role was absorbed into two institutions: the imperial house, which descends from him, and State Shinto, which taught his descent as the founding act of the Japanese nation. In the Meiji period the tenson kōrin became civic doctrine, and Jimmu's traditional accession date anchored the national holiday Kigensetsu. After 1945 the emperor's divinity was renounced, and Ninigi settled back into mythology — taught in schools, visited at Takachiho, but rarely prayed to. Buddhism, meanwhile, largely ignored him: he is one of the few major kami without a Buddhist avatar (honji). His syncretic afterlife is thus mostly political memory — the story a state told about where its authority came from.

pronunciation.approximation: 'RAH-ee-jeen' — the 'r' is a light tap, and the final 'n' is a soft nasal.
pronunciation.note: Raijin is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is the thunder god, often paired with Fūjin at temple gates; the script has no diacritic the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: God of Thunder and Lightning
domains.subtitle: Storms, Drums, and Temple Guardianship
domains.lead: Raijin is the thunder god of Japan, a fierce, demon-like kami who beats drums to create thunder and hurls lightning bolts. He is the counterpart of Fūjin, the wind god, and the two are often depicted together at the gates of Buddhist temples, where their terrifying forms ward off evil. Beneath the demon mask lives one of Japan's oldest powers: thunder, the voice of the dead world breaking into ours.

cards.name: Thunder Drummer
cards.desc: He beats drums set around his body to produce thunder; the number of rings on the drums counts the storm's strength.

cards.name: Lightning Hurling
cards.desc: He casts lightning in the shape of arrows or writhing thunder-snakes from the storm clouds.

cards.name: Fūjin's Companion
cards.desc: Paired with the wind god in temple art and architecture for more than a thousand years.

cards.name: Demon Guardian
cards.desc: His fierce form protects temples from harmful influences; as one of the Twelve Devas he guards the Dharma itself.

symbols.name: Thunder drums
symbols.meaning: The ring of drums around his body; each beat of thunder is a drumstroke, and the rings on the drumheads count them

symbols.name: Lightning bolts
symbols.meaning: The arrows or thunder-snakes (raiki) he casts from the clouds

symbols.name: Demon face
symbols.meaning: His fierce oni expression — the standard visual grammar of Japanese protective deities, whose ugliness is a shield

symbols.name: Storm clouds
symbols.meaning: The dark clouds from which he emerges, drawn as a floating island of thunder

mythology.lead: Raijin's mythology is a palimpsest: the thunder kami of the Kojiki, the Buddhist guardian of esoteric temple art, the storm god of the Mongol-invasion legend, and the bogey of nursery warnings — four layers of one drumbeat. The sources are layered and partly at odds, and each layer tells us what thunder meant to a different Japan.

myths.title: Thunder Born of the Dead Goddess
myths.text: In the Kojiki, Izanami dies from the burns of the fire god Kagutsuchi, and her grieving husband Izanagi pursues her into Yomi, the land of the dead. When he breaks his promise not to look, he sees her body corrupted; in her fury Izanami sends the yakusa no ikazuchi — the eight thunder spirits — in pursuit, together with the hags of Yomi. The text explains that these thunderers were born from the filth of Izanami's dying body. Izanagi escapes at the Even Pass of Yomotsu Hirasaka and seals the way with a boulder. Thunder, then, is older than the cleanly born gods: it issues from death itself, from the corruption of the beloved. Fūjin, by contrast, is born later, from Izanagi's breath during his river purification — wind as the breath of the purified, thunder as the voice of the dead. The later Buddhist painters gave this archaic terror his demon drums and his cloud-island, but the Kojiki keeps the older truth: the storm speaks with the voice of the world we have lost.

myths.title: Guardian of the Dharma
myths.text: With the arrival of esoteric Buddhism, the thunder power was enrolled in the defenses of the Dharma. From the Heian period, Raijin appears among the Jūni-ten, the Twelve Devas who guard the four directions and the zenith and nadir of the mandala, and with Fūjin he comes to stand at temple gatehouses — the pair most famously at the great Nioh-mon gates of Zen temples, where their sculpted forms confront visitors with the storm itself. His drumbeats scatter demons; his lightning burns away obstacles; his ugliness is itself a weapon, since in Buddhist iconography the fierce faces (the same grammar as the Nioh guardians) are shields that frighten evil before it can enter. Native kami and Buddhist guardian are not rivals here but one figure read twice: the Kojiki's thunderer and the mandala's defender are the same sound heard through two theologies. Japan's thunder god guards the gate because thunder has always guarded the boundary between worlds.

lore.culturalLegacy: Raijin remains one of Japan's most visually striking deities. His most famous portrait, Tawaraya Sōtatsu's Fūjin-Raijin-zu screens (early seventeenth century, now a National Treasure at Kennin-ji in Kyoto), is a canonical image of Japanese art, endlessly reproduced. The Kaminarimon — 'Thunder Gate' — of Sensō-ji in Asakusa has guarded the temple approach since 942, its great red lantern one of Tokyo's landmarks. He drums his way through ukiyo-e, manga, anime, and video games as the archetype of overwhelming natural power, and the old folk instruction to cover one's navel in a storm is still spoken to Japanese children. Few gods so terrifying in appearance live so comfortably in a modern city.
lore.archaeology: Raijin's material record is pictorial and architectural rather than inscriptional. The supreme witness is Tawaraya Sōtatsu's Fūjin-Raijin-zu (early seventeenth century, ink and color on paper, National Treasure, Kennin-ji, Kyoto), which fixed the modern image of the drum-ringed thunderer. The Kaminarimon ('Thunder Gate') of Sensō-ji, Asakusa, first built in 942 and rebuilt in 1960 after the 1865 fire, enshrines Fūjin and Raijin statues above its famous lantern. Sets of the Twelve Devas (Jūni-ten) at esoteric temples such as Tō-ji in Kyoto preserve Heian-period sculptural lineages of the thunder guardian, and Hokusai's manga sketches spread his likeness to every corner of Japan.
lore.syncretism: Raijin descends from Indian Indra through the Buddhist Taishakuten, but he is no simple borrowing: the Kojiki's thunder spirits born of Izanami's body are native and older, and the mature Raijin is the fusion of both lines. In esoteric Buddhism he serves among the Twelve Devas, and his permanent pairing with Fūjin expresses the Japanese reading of storms as coupled powers — wind and thunder — rather than as one god's attribute. The medieval kamikaze legend added a third layer, national salvation; the nursery warning a fourth, domestic discipline. Each tradition kept the same figure because each needed the same thing: a way to say that the storm is not random.
