steps: The name is written with two kanji: 風 'wind' + 神 'god'.
Hepburn romanization Fūjin uses a macron to mark the long vowel /ɯː/.
The compound appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki as one of the kami born from Izanagi's purification.
The Unicode restoration Fūjin preserves vowel length; the kanji form is not used as a domain because CJK scripts are not supported in the .com IDN table.

pronunciation.approximation: 'FOO-jin' — the first syllable is long and breezy, with lips almost touching for the 'f'; the final 'jin' is quick with a soft 'j'.
pronunciation.note: Fūjin is Tier 1 because the initial ū is long. The name is a straightforward Sino-Japanese compound: 風 (fū, 'wind') + 神 (jin, 'god/spirit'). He is typically paired with Raijin, the thunder god, in Japanese temple and popular art.

domains.title: God of the Wind
domains.subtitle: Storms, Breath, Destruction, and Renewal
domains.lead:
Fūjin is the wind made wild. In Japanese art he appears as a fierce demon, hair streaming, clad in a leopard-skin loincloth, carrying a vast bag of winds on his shoulders. When he opens it, gales tear through forests, scatter roofs, and flatten fields; when he closes it, the air grows still. He is one of the oldest kami in the Japanese pantheon, a destructive force that is also necessary for pollination, dispersal of seeds, and the cleansing of stale air.

He is the brother or counterpart of Raijin, the thunder god, and the two are often depicted together at temple gates, where their terrifying presence keeps danger away from sacred ground.

cards.name: Bag of Winds
cards.desc: He carries a great sack slung over his shoulders; opening it releases the winds of the world.

cards.name: Demon Guardian
cards.desc: His fierce face and muscular body mark him as one of the powerful oni-like kami who protect temples.

cards.name: Companion of Raijin
cards.desc: He is paired with the thunder god at temple gates and in screen paintings, storm and wind as twin forces.

cards.name: Cosmic Breath
cards.desc: Beyond destruction, wind is the breath that moves pollen, carries clouds, and clears the air for new growth.

symbols.name: Wind bag (fūtaku)
symbols.meaning: The sack from which all winds are released, his most distinctive attribute

symbols.name: Leopard skin
symbols.meaning: His wild garment, marking him as a powerful, untamed kami

symbols.name: Green or red skin
symbols.meaning: His demonic complexion, shared with other fierce protective deities

symbols.name: Streaming hair
symbols.meaning: The visual sign of wind in motion, often rendered with exaggerated dynamism

symbols.name: Temple gate pairing with Raijin
symbols.meaning: The fūjin-raijin-zu motif that protects Buddhist temples from harmful influences

mythology.lead: Fūjin's mythology is grounded in the creation narratives of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, in esoteric Buddhist iconography, and in the visual tradition of Japanese screen painting. He is both a primordial force and a temple guardian — and, in national memory, the wind itself that twice saved Japan.

myths.title: The Birth of the Wind Kami
myths.text: The wind kami are older than the name Fūjin. In the Kojiki's birth-of-the-kami sequence, the wind god Shina-tsu-hiko (志那都比古) and his partner Shina-tsu-hime are born as Izanagi and Izanami take stock of the elemental kami of the new-made land; the Nihon Shoki preserves the lovelier etiology — Izanagi, looking out over the country he had made, found it wrapped in morning mist, breathed, and blew the fog away, and that first breath became the wind god. The thunder kami have a harsher nativity: when the fire god Kagutsuchi burned his mother Izanami to death, Izanagi cut him down, and from the sword's blood were born the thunder gods, among them Takemikazuchi — born, like storm's own electricity, from the catastrophe of fire itself. The demonic figure called Fūjin — leopard skin, wind-bag, streaming hair — is the later, Buddhist-inflected portrait of these older kami of the moving air.

myths.title: The Cave and the Returning Winds
myths.text:
When Amaterasu hid herself in the heavenly rock-cave (Ama-no-Iwato), the world did not merely lose its light — it lost its motion: the kami assembled in the dark, and the very winds of heaven stilled with everything else. The ritual comedy by which the goddess was lured back — the cock, the mirror, Ame-no-Uzume's dance on an upturned tub — is therefore also a weather-myth: when the cave door opened, light returned with wind, rain, and the movement of all things (Kojiki; Aston's Nihongi).

The medieval tradition that paired Fūjin with Raijin at temple gates read this old story into architecture: wind and thunder stand together at the threshold because both are signs that the hidden has come back out. A temple gate with Fūjin on one side and Raijin on the other is a frozen Ama-no-Iwato — kept open.

lore.culturalLegacy: Fūjin remains one of Japan's most recognizable kami. Tawaraya Sōtatsu's celebrated Wind-and-Thunder folding screen (early 17th century), preserved at Kennin-ji in Kyōto, is a national treasure and an icon of Japanese art; Kanō Tan'yū's depictions at Sanjūsangen-dō are nearly as famous. Temples still display the pair at gates and in festival processions, and Fūjin appears in manga, anime, video games, and advertising as a symbol of overwhelming natural force. The word kamikaze — the 'divine wind' of 1274 and 1281 — is his modern inheritance, both as miracle and as warning. The Unicode restoration Fūjin preserves the long vowel that distinguishes this divine name from the ordinary homographs fujin (婦人 'women'; 夫人 'wife').
lore.archaeology: Fūjin is best known from Japanese painting and sculpture rather than from archaeological contexts alone. The oldest surviving depictions appear in Heian- and Kamakura-period Buddhist iconography, where he serves as a guardian deity. The most famous visual testimony is the pair of folding screens by Tawaraya Sōtatsu (early 17th century), preserved at Kennin-ji temple in Kyōto, which depict Fūjin and Raijin in gold-leaf clouds. Temple sculptures and ema (votive plaques) across Japan preserve popular representations of the wind god, while the textual record in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki anchors his mythological origins in the creation age.
lore.syncretism: Fūjin descends from the Chinese wind deity Fengshen, transmitted to Japan along with Buddhism and continental iconography. He also resembles wind gods across Eurasia, from the Greek Boreas and the Vedic Vāta to the Central Asian wind demons depicted on Silk Road textiles. In Japan, however, he became thoroughly domesticated as a kami, paired with Raijin and rendered in a distinctive visual style by artists such as Tawaraya Sōtatsu and Ogata Kōrin. The Japanese fascination with storms — wind, rain, thunder, lightning — produced one of the most dynamic bodies of religious painting in East Asia, with Fūjin and Raijin at its center.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KAHN-nohn' — the first 'n' is a soft nasal; the final syllable closes gently.
pronunciation.note: Kannon is Tier 2: the Japanese form loses the long ā and special ś of the Sanskrit. The name's power is devotional and artistic, not orthographic.

domains.title: Perceiver of the World's Cries
domains.subtitle: Compassion, Mercy, and Salvation
domains.lead: Kannon is the Japanese form of Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of infinite compassion. Kannon hears the cries of all beings and responds in whatever form is needed — male or female, one-faced or thousand-armed, gentle or wrathful — and anchors pilgrimage circuits from Kyōto's Kiyomizu-dera to the island sanctuaries of the coast.

cards.name: Compassionate Listener
cards.desc: Kannon's defining act is to hear; the name itself means 'perceiver of sounds.'

cards.name: Thousand-Armed Form
cards.desc: Senju Kannon wields a thousand arms, each with an eye, to save countless beings.

cards.name: Eleven-Headed Form
cards.desc: Juichimen Kannon surveys suffering from every direction at once.

cards.name: Pilgrimage Patron
cards.desc: Kannon temples anchor the Saikoku and Bandō pilgrimage circuits walked for a millennium.

symbols.name: Lotus seat
symbols.meaning: Purity rising unstained from the mud of samsara; the throne of every Kannon image

symbols.name: Water vase
symbols.meaning: The vase of compassion, holding the healing waters poured over the afflicted

symbols.name: Willow branch
symbols.meaning: The sprinkler of the medicine-Kannon's rites, touching the sick with blessed water

symbols.name: Thousand eyes
symbols.meaning: The eyes set in Senju Kannon's thousand palms — hand and sight united, help that sees

symbols.name: Amida in the crown
symbols.meaning: The small image of Amida in the headdress, marking Kannon as attendant of the Buddha of the Western Paradise

mythology.lead: Kannon's mythology is drawn from Indian sūtras, Chinese legend, and Japanese temple tradition. Every layer restates one vow: to postpone buddhahood until every cry in the world has been heard.

myths.title: The Universal Gate
myths.text: Chapter 25 of the Lotus Sūtra, 'The Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva' — rendered into Chinese by Kumārajīva in 406 CE and chanted across East Asia ever since — promises that whoever calls the bodhisattva's name with a whole heart will be heard. Travelers threatened by fire, flood, yakṣas, executioners, demons, or fetters will find that 'he immediately observes the sound of their cries and frees them.' To those who seek deliverance, the chapter says, the bodhisattva appears accordingly — as a buddha, a warrior, a merchant, a child, even a goddess of wealth. The core miracle is not power but attention: the bodhisattva's defining act is to hear. In the Japanese reading of the name — Kannon, perceiver of sounds — the whole cult is compressed into a single verb.

myths.title: Descending into Avīci
myths.text: The Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra gives the bodhisattva his most strenuous adventure. Avalokiteśvara descends into Avīci, the hell of unbroken torment, and the heat of the hells cools beneath him; he preaches to the hungry ghosts until their needle-throats open and nectar flows. From this same sūtra comes the six-syllable mantra oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ — 'the jewel in the lotus' — which the text exalts above all others. Tibetan religion built its most famous lay practice — the mani wheels and the carved mantra-walls — around these very syllables, and Japanese esoteric lineages embedded them in rites of their own. In Japan the sūtra's hell-rescue fused with local tales of the bodhisattva saving fishers and sailors, seeding the sea-Kannon of the coasts. Compassion here is not a sentiment but a journey downward: the bodhisattva does not wait for sufferers to climb but goes to the lowest place in the cosmos and stays until it changes temperature.

lore.culturalLegacy: The thirty-three-temple Saikoku and Bandō pilgrimage circuits — walked by emperors, warlords, and modern retirees alike — bind Kannon temples into a devotional geography spanning the Kansai and Kantō regions. The 1,001 gilded Kannons of Sanjūsangen-dō in Kyōto, completed in the thirteenth century, remain one of the great spectacles of Buddhist art. After disasters — the 1923 earthquake, 1995, 2011 — Kannon halls became public rooms of mourning, and in manga and anime the thousand arms have become a visual shorthand for overwhelming, many-tasked compassion.
lore.archaeology: Kannon's material presence is among the richest in Japan. Sanjūsangen-dō (Rengeō-in, Kyōto) preserves 1,001 Kamakura-period Kannon statues arrayed around the central thousand-armed image, regilded after centuries of fire. Hase-dera in Kamakura guards its nine-meter gilded Kannon — by tradition carved in 721 and the temple's reason for being — while Kiyomizu-dera's 1633 stage structure, built without nails, still cantilevers over the Otowa valley. The Saikoku and Bandō circuits anchor dozens more temples with Heian and Kamakura images, votive tablets, and pilgrim registers, whose records let scholars trace the cult's expansion from aristocratic chapel to mass devotion.
lore.syncretism: Kannon's absorptive power made the bodhisattva Japan's great religious bridge. Under honji-suijaku the deity was read as the compassionate trace of Amida or of Dainichi; kami of waterfalls, childbirth, and the sea attached themselves to Kannon temples, which often enshrine a Benzaiten or a local kami in the same precinct. Hidden Christians of the Edo period pressed the Virgin Mary into service as 'Maria Kannon,' carving statues with a covert cross. Zen lineages kept the Heart Sūtra's closing mantra — 'gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond' — which tradition assigns to Avalokiteśvara's own insight at the apex of the Prajñāpāramitā. Few figures in world religion have worn so many faces so gracefully.

variants.note: Plain ASCII form

steps: Sanskrit Kṣitigarbha ('Earth Treasury' or 'Earth Womb') was translated into Chinese as 地藏 (Dìzàng).
Japanese borrowed the compound as 地蔵, read in Sino-Japanese as Jizō.
Hepburn romanisation writes the long vowel with a macron: Jizō.
The ASCII form jizo loses the length mark, collapsing the distinction between short and long ō.
The Unicode restoration Jizō is registrable in .com; the kanji form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

provenanceSources.title: Buswell & Lopez, The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism
Nelson, The Original Modern Reader's Japanese-English Character Dictionary

pronunciation.approximation: 'JEE-zoh' — the first syllable is like 'jee', the second is a long, drawn 'zoh'.
pronunciation.note: Jizō is Tier 1: the macron on ō marks the long vowel of the Japanese reading. The full Sanskrit name would require retroflex and aspirated consonants not registrable in the DNS root zone.

domains.title: Earth Treasury Bodhisattva
domains.subtitle: Guardian of Children, Travelers, and the Dead
domains.lead: Jizō is the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha as known and loved in Japan: a gentle monk-like figure who refuses buddhahood until all beings, especially those in hell and the spirits of dead children, are saved. His statues stand by roadsides, cemeteries, and temples, clothed in red bibs and caps offered by grieving parents.

cards.name: Guardian of Children
cards.desc: He protects children, including mizuko, the spirits of miscarried and aborted foetuses.

cards.name: Savior of Hell-beings
cards.desc: He descends into the hell realms to rescue those tormented by their karma.

cards.name: Patron of Travelers
cards.desc: Roadside Jizō guide and protect those on journeys, both living and dead.

cards.name: Bodhisattva Vow
cards.desc: He postpones his own enlightenment until every hell is emptied.

symbols.name: Staff (khakkhara)
symbols.meaning: The ringing staff that warns small creatures underfoot and opens the gates of hell.

symbols.name: Wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi)
symbols.meaning: The gem that grants all needs and dispels the darkness of the six realms.

symbols.name: Red bib or cap
symbols.meaning: Offerings by parents for the protection of their children in the afterlife — the folk garment of Sai no Kawara.

symbols.name: Lotus seat
symbols.meaning: Purity within the muddy world of suffering.

mythology.lead: Jizō's mythology blends Indian scripture, Chinese translation, and Japanese folk belief. He is one of the most actively worshipped Buddhist figures in Japan — a bodhisattva whose statues outnumber his temples.

myths.title: The Original Vow
myths.text: The Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Sūtra recounts that in a previous life the bodhisattva was a Brahmin maiden whose mother had slandered the Dharma. After her mother's death, the daughter made vast offerings at a temple and was transported in vision to hell, where a guardian demon told her the offerings had not yet redeemed her mother. Moved by the suffering around her, she vowed before the Buddha to save all beings in the hell realms, life after life, until not a single one remained. The sūtra frames this as an intercessory chain — the Buddha entrusts the helpless, in the long night between one buddha's passing and the next's arrival, to Kṣitigarbha's keeping. The myth's engine is refusal: heaven has no vacancy so long as hell has a single prisoner, and the bodhisattva is content to wait.

myths.title: Sai no Kawara
myths.text: On the banks of Sai no Kawara, the stony riverbed where dead children must labor, the little souls pile stones as penance for having caused their parents grief — and each night demons scatter their work. Jizō comes in the guise of a wandering monk, hides the children in the sleeves of his robe, and comforts them until their karma is spent. The red bibs and caps set on his statues are gifts intended to warm these child-spirits, since the dead feel the cold. The tale first flowers in the medieval picture scrolls and story collections, where the riverbed's naked little laborers are shown weeping over their scattered stones — and Jizō arrives with his staff ringing. It is the sentimental heart of Japanese Buddhism: hell is real, labor is endless, and yet someone keeps coming down to the riverbed, night after night, to hold the children until morning.

lore.culturalLegacy: Jizō is everywhere in Japan: thousands of stone statues line mountain paths, village boundaries, and temple precincts. The practice of mizuko kuyō — memorial rites for foetal and infant deaths — centres on him, making him a focus of modern debates about abortion, grief, and maternal responsibility. Contemporary artists and writers return to Jizō as an emblem of patient, non-judgmental compassion, and his red-bibbed image has become one of the most recognized symbols of Japanese religion worldwide.
lore.archaeology: Kṣitigarbha's Chinese bodhimaṇḍa is Mount Jiuhua in Anhui, where the Silla monk Jin Qiaojue (696–794) practiced and was posthumously venerated as Dizang's incarnation; the mountain's temple city and his preserved body remain a major pilgrimage destination. In Japan the documented cult begins in the Heian period — court records describe Kṣitigarbha rites performed during the Jōgan-era epidemics — while the great expansion is Kamakura: roadside stone Jizō were set up along the Tōkaidō and other travel routes as traffic, danger, and infant mortality demanded a traveler-saint. Thousands of those weathered, bibbed stones survive from that era.
lore.syncretism: Kṣitigarbha entered China from India and absorbed functions of local earth gods and tomb guardians. In Japan he merged with the kami of roads and boundaries (Sae no Kami / Dōsojin) and with popular protectors of children; roadside stone Jizō often stand where the older phallic boundary gods stood. He is also syncretised with the Christian St. Christopher in some hidden-Christian communities, two wayfarer-saints guarding the same dangerous roads. The result is a uniquely Japanese figure: a Buddhist bodhisattva who feels, to many worshippers, like a local spirit who has simply always been there.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Japanese name 地蔵 is read Jizō, from Middle Chinese 地藏 Dìzàng, which translates the Sanskrit Kṣitigarbha. 地 (ji) means 'earth' and 藏 (zō) means 'storehouse' or 'womb'. The macron on ō marks the long vowel of the Japanese reading. The full Sanskrit would require retroflex ṣ, aspirated bh, and other characters not registrable in the DNS root zone, so PUNICODEX uses the Japanese form.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-mee-dah' — three even syllables, with the middle vowel bright and short.
pronunciation.note: Amida is Tier 2: the Japanese form loses the long ā and aspirated bh of the Sanskrit, so it preserves nothing ASCII cannot already write. The name's power is devotional, not orthographic.

domains.title: Buddha of Immeasurable Light
domains.subtitle: Pure Land, Faith, and the Promise of Rebirth
domains.lead: Amida is the Japanese face of Amitābha, the Buddha whose immeasurable light built a pure land in the west. For over a thousand years his name has been Japan's most repeated prayer — Namu Amida Butsu — and the promise behind it is radical: even those crushed by karma they cannot undo can be born in his Pure Land and attain enlightenment.

cards.name: Immeasurable Light
cards.desc: His name — Amida, from Sanskrit Amitābha — is itself the first teaching: light with no edge, dissolving the karma-darkness of beings.

cards.name: Pure Land (Sukhāvatī)
cards.desc: The Land of Bliss in the west: jeweled ponds and gold trees, where birth in a lotus guarantees the path to Buddhahood.

cards.name: Name as Vow
cards.desc: Hōnen (Senchakushū, 1198) and Shinran (Kyōgyōshinshō) taught that a single recitation, taken on faith, is the working of the vow itself.

cards.name: Welcoming Descent
cards.desc: Raigō painting: Amida descends on clouds with Kannon and Seishi — the deathbed vision of medieval Japan, from temple murals to death registers.

symbols.name: The Amida triad
symbols.meaning: Amida flanked by Kannon (Avalokiteśvara) and Seishi (Mahāsthāmaprāpta) — compassion and wisdom attending every descent

symbols.name: The nenbutsu rosary (juzu)
symbols.meaning: Beads counting Namu Amida Butsu; worn on the wrist of every Pure Land devotee since Hōnen's day

symbols.name: The western direction
symbols.meaning: He faces west — toward the setting sun and toward Sukhāvatī; the dying were laid with their heads west to meet his coming

symbols.name: The mudrā of welcome
symbols.meaning: The raised hand in raigō images, palm open — the gesture of one arriving to receive, not to judge

symbols.name: Halos of light
symbols.meaning: Radiant aureoles of immeasurable light — in Amida's case the body itself is the sermon

symbols.name: Lotus seat
symbols.meaning: Purity and transcendence; the faithful are reborn in Sukhāvatī's lotuses

mythology.lead: Amida's mythology runs from the Indian vows of Dharmākara through Chinese translation into Japan's nenbutsu movement: the radical teaching that calling the Buddha's name with faith is itself the path. His stories are devotional rather than epic — vows, recitations, and descents — and they reshaped how Japan faced death.

myths.title: The Forty-Eight Vows of Dharmākara
myths.text: In the Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra the Buddha tells how, in an inconceivably remote past, the monk Dharmākara knelt before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and set himself a task no being had dared: to survey every Buddha-field in the ten directions, gather the best of each, and build from them a single land where no one who trusted him would fail to reach enlightenment. After five aeons of contemplation he pronounced forty-eight vows. The eighteenth — the Primal Vow (hongan) — promises that anyone who, with sincere entrusting, desires rebirth in his land and calls his name even ten times will be born there. Dharmākara then practiced for countless kalpas until the vows stood fulfilled, and he became Amida, whose Sukhāvatī lies to the west like a shore beyond every storm. The sūtra's logic is startling: enlightenment is not climbed but received, because someone else finished the climbing first.

myths.title: Hōnen Selects the Single Practice
myths.text: By the twelfth century the Tendai establishment taught that every practice could lead to awakening — and therefore, argued the monk Hōnen, none was being done wholeheartedly by ordinary people mired in the latter days of the Dharma. In 1198 he set down his answer in the Senchakushū: select the one practice the Buddha himself had promised would suffice — the nenbutsu, the calling of Amida's name, Namu Amida Butsu — and let every other good act adorn it rather than compete with it. His disciples carried the teaching from the capital to the fishing villages, until peasants and soldiers who had never read a sūtra were reciting the Buddha's name in fields and on battlefields. The authorities proscribed the movement in 1207 and exiled Hōnen, but the nenbutsu had already escaped every gate: the single practice made the highest path the commonest road.

lore.culturalLegacy: Amida's name is among the most recited phrases in Japanese religious history; Namu Amida Butsu appears in literature and film as prayer, thanksgiving, and resigned acceptance alike. His architecture marks the country — Hōryūji, Byōdōin's Phoenix Hall on the ten-yen coin, Zenkōji with its never-displayed hidden image — and his images mark its deaths: raigō paintings and deathbed name-registers survive by the thousand. Jōdo and Jōdo Shinshū remain among Japan's largest Buddhist schools, and the nenbutsu still rings out each New Year. Restoring the name as Amida keeps the Japanese form — devotional, democratic, and distinctly un-Sanskrit — exactly as a thousand years of chanters pronounced it.
lore.archaeology: Byōdōin at Uji (1053 CE) is Japan's most famous Amida temple, its Phoenix Hall built as a built image of Sukhāvatī and its Amida by Jōchō setting the standard for Heian-period sculpture; both hall and image appear on the ten-yen coin. Chūsonji's Konjiki-dō — the gilded Hall of the Golden Hue at Hiraizumi (1124 CE) — stages the Pure Land in gold leaf and mother-of-pearl. Zenkōji in Nagano preserves the hidden Amida triad brought from the continent in the seventh century, and Kamakura's Great Buddha at Kōtoku-in (cast 1252, some eleven meters of bronze) gave Amida the open sea for a backdrop, while the Eikanbetsu tradition gives its face an eternal eastern gaze.
lore.syncretism: Amida is Japan's pronunciation of Amitābha, the Buddha venerated across Asia: Ēmítuó in China, Amit'a in Korea, A-di-đà in Vietnam. Japan's distinctive contribution was not a new doctrine but a new social reach — Hōnen and Shinran made the nenbutsu the practice of farmers, fishermen, warriors, and outcastes, so Amida became a household word rather than a monastic preserve. Japanese popular religion then braided him into older patterns: the warrior-kami Hachiman was declared a bodhisattva who protects devotees of the nenbutsu, medieval honji-suijaku thought read local deities as traces of Amida, and the dying were laid facing west — toward both the setting sun and the Pure Land. In China the complementary synthesis ran through the lay societies founded at Lushan in 402 CE, and in Tibet Amitābha presides over the red Buddha-family and the phowa practice that transfers consciousness to Sukhāvatī at death: one vow, received on three continents.

pronunciation.approximation: 'FOO-jee' — the first syllable is breezy, with lips nearly touching; the second is quick.
pronunciation.note: Fuji is Tier 2: the name is plain Hepburn. Its sanctity derives from its visual dominance and long religious history, not from distinctive orthography.

domains.title: Sacred Mountain of Japan
domains.subtitle: Volcano, Pilgrimage, and National Symbol
domains.lead: Fuji is more than a mountain. For over a thousand years it has been a volcano kami, a Buddhist mandala, and the defining image of Japan — a nearly perfect cone rising alone above the clouds, watched from every road. Pilgrims climb it, poets praise it, and artists have made its snow-capped form one of the most reproduced images on earth.

cards.name: Volcano Deity
cards.desc: As a living volcano, Fuji has been feared and worshipped as a source of both destruction and fertility.

cards.name: Pilgrimage Peak
cards.desc: For centuries pilgrims climbed to the summit, where shrines and lodges marked the path.

cards.name: National Symbol
cards.desc: Its image identifies Japan in art, currency, passports, and global imagination.

cards.name: Artistic Muse
cards.desc: Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views made Fuji an icon of world art.

symbols.name: Snow-capped cone
symbols.meaning: The visual form that has made Fuji a universal symbol of Japan — perfect geometry over restless fire

symbols.name: Torii and shrine markers
symbols.meaning: The network of Sengen shrines, of which Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha is the head, that manages the mountain's cult

symbols.name: Crater and rising sun
symbols.meaning: The summit caldera and the dawn viewed from it — the goraikō, the honored arrival of the sun, central to pilgrimage

symbols.name: Pilgrim's staff
symbols.meaning: The walking stick and stamped robe of those who climbed the sacred slopes, from Fuji-kō confraternities to today

mythology.lead: Fuji generates story because it cannot be ignored: a volcano that sleeps for centuries at a time, a goddess of fire hidden under snow, and an image so constant that a whole civilization has measured its seasons, its festivals, and its art against one unchanging silhouette.

myths.title: The Name and Its Power
myths.text: Folk etymology explains the name as fushi, 'without equal,' or fuji, 'inexhaustible' — both appropriate to a mountain with no rival on the horizon. In the early chronicles the peak's deity was treated as female, a kami of fire, and in the medieval period she was identified with Sengen (Asama-no-kami) and with Konohanasakuya-hime, the blossom princess of the Kojiki, whose marriage to the heavenly grandson Ninigi bound heaven's line to the earth. When Fuji smoked or rumbled, the interpretation was immediate: the goddess of the volcano was stirring, and the province looked to its Sengen shrines. The shrine cult kept the mountain's divinity local and specific — not an abstraction like 'nature,' but a named power with festivals, priests, and a genealogy reaching back to the age of the gods. The mountain's own name became the nation's shorthand for what is highest, purest, and most alone.

myths.title: Fuji as Lotus Mandala
myths.text: In the medieval imagination Fuji was not climbed so much as entered. Buddhist exegetes mapped the mountain as a lotus mandala, its ridges the lotus petals, its crater the heart of the world; ascending it was circumambulation and pilgrimage at once. In the sixteenth century the ascetic Hasegawa Kakugyō is credited with founding the Fuji-kō confraternities, and by the Edo period tens of thousands of pilgrims climbed in white robes reciting sutras, carrying miniature shrines up the stations and building fujizuka — small replica Fujis — in the cities, so that those who could not travel could still 'climb' the mountain. Some confraternities worshipped the crater itself as the Pure Land. The practice reveals the mountain's genius as an image: Fuji is endlessly reproducible, and every reproduction is still Fuji — a mandala you can ascend with your feet, a paradise with a weather problem.

lore.culturalLegacy: Fuji was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2013 — 'Fujisan, sacred place and source of artistic inspiration' — and remains Japan's most photographed and climbed mountain, some three hundred thousand climbers each summer ascending through the night to greet the goraikō, the honored arrival of the sunrise. Its image sits on banknotes and passports and in a hundred million phone galleries; school songs still teach children that it is the noblest mountain in the world. The pilgrimage endures in secular costume — the white robes are rental gear now, the sutras are headlamps — but the shape of the act is unchanged: to reach the summit before dawn and watch the sun rise out of the Pacific, as pilgrims have done since the mountain was a goddess.
lore.archaeology: Fuji is ringed by Sengen shrines, of which Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha in Fujinomiya — its present main hall a 1604 Tokugawa rebuilding — is the head of the cult. The 2013 World Heritage listing protects twenty-five component sites: Yamamiya and Murayama Sengen shrines on the old pilgrim approaches, the Yoshida and Subashiri trailheads with their station lodges and boundary markers, the lava tree-molds of Aokigahara's Sea of Trees, and the summit crater with its own Sengen sanctuary. The Hōei eruption of 1707 left a cinder cone on the flank and tephra beds as far as Edo, recorded in contemporary paintings and official memoranda. Every summer's climbers walk, step for step, a route fixed by the Fuji-kō confraternities four centuries ago.
lore.syncretism: Fuji is a palimpsest of religious traditions. Shinto's Sengen shrines honor the mountain's volcanic kami — under the honji suijaku logic of the medieval centuries, a local kami read as the trace of a universal Buddha. Buddhist Fuji-kō confraternities climbed the mountain as a living mandala; Shugendō mountain ascetics used its slopes for training; and medieval exegetes mapped its ridges onto a lotus. The Meiji state, separating Shinto from Buddhism, promoted Fuji as a national emblem — the purest form of Japan itself — and the image followed the armies abroad and the recovery at home. After more than three centuries of dormancy, the 1707 Hōei eruption reminded the capital that the sacred mountain is still alive: the goddess under the snow has never signed a truce.

pronunciation.approximation: 'EE-seh' — two light, even syllables.
pronunciation.note: Ise is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. Its significance is cultic and geographic, not orthographic.

domains.title: Sacred City of the Imperial Kami
domains.subtitle: Shrine, Pilgrimage, and the Heart of Shinto
domains.lead: Ise is not merely a place; it is the spiritual center of Shinto and the home of Amaterasu, the sun goddess and ancestor of the imperial house. For more than a thousand years, the Ise Grand Shrine has been rebuilt every twenty years in an unbroken cycle of renewal, making Ise a city where architecture, nature, and divine presence are continuously reborn.

cards.name: Ise Grand Shrine
cards.desc: The most sacred Shinto complex, rebuilt every twenty years in the shikinen-zōtai tradition.

cards.name: Amaterasu's Dwelling
cards.desc: The Inner Shrine houses the mirror, one of the Three Imperial Regalia.

cards.name: Pilgrimage Center
cards.desc: For centuries pilgrims traveled the Ise-kaidō to visit the shrines.

cards.name: Renewal Architecture
cards.desc: The shrines are rebuilt from new cypress in a cycle of death and rebirth.

symbols.name: Mirror
symbols.meaning: The yata no kagami, one of the Three Imperial Regalia, enshrined at Ise

symbols.name: Cypress (hinoki)
symbols.meaning: The wood from which the shrine buildings are rebuilt every twenty years

symbols.name: Uji Bridge
symbols.meaning: The bridge over the Isuzu River marking the boundary to the sacred precinct

symbols.name: Shikinen-zōtai
symbols.meaning: The twenty-year rebuilding cycle that renews the shrine and its implements

mythology.lead: Ise's mythology is inseparable from the mythology of Amaterasu and the imperial house. The city exists because the sun goddess needed a dwelling worthy of her.

myths.title: Amaterasu Comes to Ise
myths.text: According to tradition, the imperial princess Yamatohime-no-mikoto traveled for twenty years searching for a permanent dwelling for Amaterasu. She finally received an oracle at Ise, where the goddess declared her love for the place. The Inner Shrine was established there, and the imperial house has maintained it ever since.

myths.title: The Twenty-Year Rebuilding
myths.text: The shikinen-zōtai tradition requires that the shrine buildings be reconstructed on adjacent plots every twenty years. The old structures are dismantled, and their timber is distributed to branch shrines. This cycle ensures that the architecture remains fresh and that the skills of sacred carpentry are passed down through generations.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ise remains the most sacred destination in Shinto. The Ise-Shima region hosts the G7 summit's shrine visit; the rebuilding ceremonies draw national attention; and the phrase 'Ise ni ichido wa' ('to Ise at least once') still expresses a cultural aspiration. The simple, raised-floor architecture of Ise has influenced modern Japanese design and the global image of Shinto.
lore.archaeology: The Ise Grand Shrine complex includes the Inner Shrine (Kōtai Jingū), Outer Shrine (Gekū), and numerous auxiliary shrines. Archaeological investigations have clarified the shifting locations of successive rebuilding plots and the ancient use of the Isuzu River for ritual purification. The nearby Sengu Museum preserves building models and ritual implements from past rebuildings.
lore.syncretism: Ise has both resisted and absorbed outside influences. It remained the symbolic center of State Shinto in the modern period, yet its rituals and architecture preserve ancient Japanese forms. Buddhist influence was deliberately excluded from the Inner Shrine for long periods, making Ise a stronghold of 'pure' Shinto ideology — even as the broader Shinto tradition was itself shaped by Buddhist and continental models.
