pronunciation.approximation: 'TAH-kah-chee-hoh' — the 'ch' is crisp, and all vowels are short.
pronunciation.note: Takachiho is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. Its significance is mythological and scenic rather than orthographic.

domains.title: The Place Where Heaven Descended
domains.subtitle: Myth, Gorge, and Sacred Rice
domains.lead: Takachiho is a town and gorge in the mountains of Kyūshū, famous as the place where Ninigi descended from heaven to begin the rule of the terrestrial world. Its name, 'High Thousand Ears of Grain,' evokes a landscape of tall rice and misty peaks where the divine once touched the earth.

cards.name: Heavenly Descent
cards.desc: Ninigi landed here with the Three Sacred Regalia.

cards.name: Takachiho Gorge
cards.desc: A dramatic volcanic gorge and waterfall, central to local myth.

cards.name: Kagura
cards.desc: The town preserves performances of the Ama-no-Iwato dance.

cards.name: Rice Country
cards.desc: The 'thousand ears' of the name refer to abundant rice.

symbols.name: Takachiho Gorge
symbols.meaning: The scenic canyon associated with the descent myth

symbols.name: Manai Falls
symbols.meaning: The waterfall within the gorge, a sacred natural feature

symbols.name: Kagura masks
symbols.meaning: The masks used in performances of the Amaterasu cave myth

symbols.name: Rice ears
symbols.meaning: The agricultural abundance evoked by the name

mythology.lead: Takachiho's 'mythology' is a convergence of scripture, landscape, and performance. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki agree that Ninigi, grandson of Amaterasu, descended at the peak of Takachiho in the land of Hyūga; the town that bears the name claims the story as its own and keeps it alive each winter in the all-night kagura dances that reenact the cave of heaven.

myths.title: The Descent at the Peak of Takachiho
myths.text: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki agree on the itinerary: when Amaterasu resolved that her grandson Ninigi should rule the visible world, she sent him down from the Plain of High Heaven at the head of a divine escort, bearing the mirror, sword, and curved jewel that became the Three Sacred Regalia. Both texts name the landing place Takachiho no mine — the peak of Takachiho — in the land of Himuka, present-day Miyazaki Prefecture (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, Age of the Gods). Ninigi wed the blossom-princess Konohanasakuya-hime, and from the line of their son Hoori came the first emperor, Jimmu. The tradition is the charter of Japanese kingship, and it plants that charter on a real mountain in Kyūshū. What Takachiho means is therefore not merely 'where the gods came down' but where heaven first accepted a Japanese address — the point where the divine genealogy touches soil that can still be walked.

myths.title: The Cave of Heaven
myths.text: The classical texts do not say where the Rock Cave of Heaven stood. The Kojiki tells how Amaterasu, frightened by her brother Susanoo's rampage, sealed herself inside Ama-no-Iwato and plunged the world into darkness, until the goddess Uzume's bawdy dance on an overturned tub drew the gods' laughter and lured the sun back out (Kojiki, Age of the Gods). Local tradition in Takachiho locates the cave on the Iwato River gorge, where Ama-no-Iwato Shrine keeps the memory — the sacred rope, the crowing rooster, the mirror hung on the sakaki tree. Scholars note that the identification is devotional rather than textual: many places in Japan claim the cave, and the sources are silent. But the gorge gives the story a theatrical setting, a narrow chasm where sunlight and shadow trade places across the water. The myth's engine is social: order is restored not by force but by laughter, performance, and a community coaxing its sun back into view.

lore.culturalLegacy: Takachiho is one of Kyūshū's signature destinations — the gorge with its rental rowboats beneath the basalt columns, the Manai Falls, and the nightly kagura at the shrine. The town's name has become shorthand in Japan for the moment when myth touches ground: school textbooks repeat the descent, and the phrase 'Takachiho of heaven' echoes through tourism copy and local pride. The winter yokagura, designated an Important Intangible Folk-Cultural Property in 1978, keeps thirty-three villages dancing through the coldest months, and the rice of the district still trades on the 'thousand ears' in the name. For many Japanese visitors, Takachiho is the closest thing to a pilgrimage they will make: a place where the national story can be entered by boat, on foot, and by lamplight.
lore.archaeology: Takachiho Gorge is a volcanic landscape formed by the eruptions of Mount Aso, which filled the old river valley with basalt; the Gokase River cut back down through it, leaving the columned walls and the seventeen-metre Manai Falls. The town's ritual architecture records the myth it performs: Ama-no-Iwato Shrine, at the head of the Iwato River gorge, keeps the cave precinct with its sacred rope and sakaki; Takachiho Shrine anchors the town's central cult; and each village preserves a kagura-den (kagura hall) or designated performance ground where the night dances are staged from November to February. The shrine buildings are Edo-period and later reconstructions in the standard style, but the performance spaces, the gorge paths, and the falls themselves are the primary 'site' — a landscape whose geology and whose mythology tell the same story of something vast coming down.
lore.syncretism: Takachiho is a palimpsest of Japanese religious history. The descent myth is imperial and Shinto in its present form, yet the mountain district long lay within the world of Shugendō ascetics, who trained among its peaks and gorges; the cave shrine and the kagura coexist with Buddhist-founded institutions in the town. In the Meiji period the narrative was pressed into service of emperor-centred nationalism, and the 'descent of the grandson' became a station in the state's cult calendar. After 1945 the town quietly re-centred itself on local folklore: the gorge, the shrine, and the dances became heritage rather than ideology. The result is a characteristically Japanese syncretism in which imperial scripture, mountain asceticism, agricultural ritual, and modern tourism occupy the same valley without apparent strain.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KOO-mah-noh' — three even syllables, with the first vowel soft and back.
pronunciation.note: Kumano is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. Its significance is geographic, ritual, and symbolic rather than orthographic.

domains.title: Sacred Land of the Kumano Sanzan
domains.subtitle: Mountains, Pilgrimage, and Imperial Protection
domains.lead: Kumano is a mountainous region on the Kii Peninsula that has been sacred for over a thousand years. Its three great shrines — the Kumano Sanzan — drew emperors, aristocrats, and commoners on pilgrimage along the Kumano Kodō. Kumano is a place where dense forest, rushing rivers, and waterfalls create a landscape felt to be inhabited by powerful kami and Buddhas.

cards.name: Kumano Sanzan
cards.desc: The three shrines of Hongū, Hayatama, and Nachi form a unified sacred complex.

cards.name: Kumano Kodō
cards.desc: Ancient pilgrimage routes, now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

cards.name: Nachi Falls
cards.desc: Japan's tallest waterfall, worshipped as the dwelling of a kami.

cards.name: Imperial Pilgrimage
cards.desc: Emperors and retired emperors made repeated pilgrimages to Kumano.

symbols.name: Three-legged crow (Yatagarasu)
symbols.meaning: The divine guide who led Emperor Jimmu through the mountains

symbols.name: Nachi Falls
symbols.meaning: The sacred waterfall and the deity of water and longevity

symbols.name: Cedar forest
symbols.meaning: The ancient trees through which pilgrims walked

symbols.name: Stone markers and oji
symbols.meaning: The sub-shrines and markers along the Kumano Kodō

mythology.lead: Kumano's mythology blends imperial foundation legend, mountain asceticism, and the medieval fusion of kami and Buddha. Its sources are chronicle, mandala, and ritual text rather than epic, and its stories are walked as much as told: the crow who guided an emperor, the hermits who heard sermons in waterfalls, and the retired sovereigns who came on foot to meet them.

myths.title: Yatagarasu and Emperor Jimmu
myths.text: When Emperor Jimmu, the first emperor of the chronicles, led his eastern expedition into the mountains of Kumano, his army lost its way among the peaks. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki tell that the heavenly gods sent Yatagarasu, a great three-legged crow, to guide him: it flew before the host as a living arrow, and Jimmu emerged from the mountains to claim Yamato. The tale plants the imperial founding inside Kumano's forests and makes the crow — black, solar, three-footed — the sign of divine guidance through wilderness. A thousand years later the mountain shrines still claimed that protection: emperors did not command Kumano, they visited it, and the crow they had followed remained the region's emblem. Guidance through trackless country is Kumano's first gift, and Japan still uses it — the three-legged crow stands on the crest of the national football association.

myths.title: Mountain Asceticism
myths.text: Kumano became the greatest mountain center of Japan's ascetic tradition, Shugendō. Its legendary founder, En no Gyōja, was said to have wandered the Kii peaks in the seventh century working miracles; by the Heian period the yamabushi — 'those who lie down in the mountains' — walked the Kumano Kodō in straw sandals, performed cold-water ablutions beneath Nachi's falls, and sought visions in the cedar dark. They understood the mountains not as scenery but as a mandala: every peak a deity, every waterfall a sermon. The sources for this layer are late and hagiographic, but the practice they describe is real and documented for over a millennium: to enter Kumano was to enter a realm where the boundary between the human and the divine wore thin, and discipline was the price of crossing it.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Kumano Kodō and Kii mountain shrines were designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2004. Modern pilgrims continue to walk the ancient routes, and Kumano remains a powerful symbol of spiritual journey in Japan. The three-legged crow appears on the logo of the Japan Football Association, tracing its lineage back to Jimmu's guide.
lore.archaeology: The Kumano Sanzan (Kumano Hongū Taisha, Kumano Hayatama Taisha, Kumano Nachi Taisha) and the Kumano Kodō pilgrimage routes preserve a landscape of shrines, stone pavements, ritual sites, and Nachi Falls. Archaeological and architectural study documents the region's importance from the Heian period onward.
lore.syncretism: Kumano is a classic case of shinbutsu shūgō, the medieval fusion of Shinto and Buddhism. The Kumano shrines housed Buddhist temples, and the kami were identified with Buddhist divinities. The region also absorbed Shugendō practices, making it a threefold meeting ground of kami worship, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. The Meiji separation of Shinto and Buddhism stripped away the Buddhist layers, but the landscape retains its hybrid memory.

pronunciation.approximation: 'EH-bee-soo' — light, even syllables; the final 'u' is barely voiced.
pronunciation.note: Ebisu is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. His name may derive from a word for 'foreigner' or 'straggler,' reflecting his origins as a deity associated with outsiders and the sea.

domains.title: God of Fishermen, Commerce, and Honest Luck
domains.subtitle: The Smiling God of Daily Prosperity
domains.lead: Ebisu is the most approachable of Japan's fortune gods. With his fishing rod in one hand and a sea bream (tai) under the other arm, he smiles at merchants, fishermen, and anyone who earns a living by honest work. He is the only native Japanese member of the Seven Gods of Fortune (Shichifukujin).

cards.name: Fisherman God
cards.desc: Patron of those who draw wealth from the sea, especially fishers and seafood merchants.

cards.name: God of Commerce
cards.desc: Protector of markets, shops, and fair dealing in everyday trade.

cards.name: Shichifukujin
cards.desc: The only native kami among the Seven Gods of Fortune.

cards.name: Sea Bream
cards.desc: The tai fish is auspicious because its name puns on 'medetai' (auspicious).

symbols.name: Fishing rod
symbols.meaning: His attribute as a fisher of fortune and daily sustenance

symbols.name: Sea bream (tai)
symbols.meaning: An auspicious fish whose name puns on 'medetai' (joyous, auspicious)

symbols.name: Tall hat
symbols.meaning: Courtly headwear marking his elevated status among fortune gods

symbols.name: Smiling face
symbols.meaning: His kindly expression makes him the most approachable of the Shichifukujin

mythology.lead: Ebisu has no single founding myth. He grew from several older figures — the castaway child Hiruko, the oracular Kotoshironushi, and deities of the foreign sea — into the cheerful merchant god of the Edo period. The sources disagree about which ancestor is truly his; the smile, the fishing rod, and the sea bream are the tradition's own answer.

myths.title: Hiruko, the Leech Child
myths.text: The Kojiki tells that when Izanagi and Izanami first coupled, their child Hiruko was born 'without bones', like a leech or a premature thing; at three he could not yet stand. The dismayed parents set him adrift in a boat of reeds and let the sea decide. He survived — and later tradition, above all at Nishinomiya Shrine near Kōbe, identified the foundling with Ebisu: the child the gods abandoned who became the god of those who make their own living from the water. The chronicles themselves never call Hiruko 'Ebisu'; the identification is medieval and early-modern tradition, and scholars treat it as a genealogy of meaning rather than a datum. Its content is exact: Ebisu is the outsider who prospers — the stranger, the latecomer, the one the palace forgot.

myths.title: Kotoshironushi and the Yielding of the Land
myths.text: Another line of descent runs through Kotoshironushi, son of Ōkuninushi, the great god of the land. When the heavenly grandchild's envoys demanded that the earth be yielded, Ōkuninushi deferred to his son's counsel: Kotoshironushi answered on his father's behalf and then withdrew to the sea, or hid his body, leaving the land to the new line (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki). He was a god of oracles, of fishing, and of the boundary between the human settlement and the deep water; he is still enshrined at Shirayama-hime in Kaga and at Miho in Izumo, shrines that keep exactly the oracle-and-fishing profile the Ebisu cult later borrowed. Several shrine genealogies — and much popular etymology — have since folded him into Ebisu, which is why the fortune god carries a fishing rod rather than a purse. The merger makes theological sense: the god who surrendered territory and kept the sea became the patron of everyone who draws wealth from outside the city's walls.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ebisu is everywhere in Japanese commercial life: shop signs, menus, bank logos, New Year prints, and the great January crush at Osaka's Imamiya Ebisu and Kobe's Nishinomiya shrines. The Yebisu Beer brand (Sapporo, launched 1890) took both its name and its logo from the god, making his face one of the most reproduced in modern Japan. Railway stations, shopping districts, and baseball crowds invoke him; the shopkeeper balancing the day's ledger still murmurs 'Ebisu-sama.' He remains what the Edo townspeople made him: the patron of the ordinary miracle by which honest work becomes daily bread.
lore.archaeology: Ebisu is a cultic and commercial figure rather than an excavated one; his material record is the vast folk-art corpus of the Edo and Meiji periods. Votive tablets (ema) from Osaka and the fishing ports of the Inland Sea show the rod, the bream, and the tall court cap; woodblock New Year prints (nishiki-e) fixed his smiling face in the national imagination. The Tōka Ebisu festival at Imamiya Ebisu Shrine preserves the full apparatus of merchant devotion — lucky straw, fuku-musume, gold-leaf charms — as a living tradition centuries deep. The Kojiki's Hiruko narrative has no archaeological correlate; the god's 'evidence' is the continuing rite itself, performed each January in the lanes where the merchants still set out their first scales of the year.
lore.syncretism: Ebisu is the great combiner of Japanese religion. His roots are the Kojiki figures Hiruko and Kotoshironushi; his body is the medieval cult of the 'foreign' sea gods; his career is pure Edo merchant culture; and his congregation is the imported circle of the Shichifukujin, the Seven Gods of Fortune — six of whom arrived from China and India by way of Buddhism, while Ebisu alone is native. He is conventionally paired with Daikokuten as the twin patrons of prosperity, and the two sometimes appear as a single double-faced image. In the medieval Tendai scheme the Seven Gods were read as protective manifestations of the Lotus Sutra, Ebisu included. No other Japanese deity so neatly braids indigenous kami cult, Buddhist imports, and the everyday economics of the town.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OH-koo-nee-NOO-shee' — five even morae; the long Ō is a doubled plain O, never an English diphthong; 'shi' is the soft Japanese sibilant.
pronunciation.note: Tier-1: the restoration Ōkuninushi preserves the long vowel (macron Ō) that the ASCII Okuninushi erases — the very feature that marks Ō- 'great' as distinct from a plain o-. One preserved feature, mechanically verifiable: a single-tier Tier-1 name.

domains.title: The Lord of the Reed-Plain
domains.subtitle: Nation-Building & Marriage
domains.lead: Ōkuninushi — the Great Land-Master — is the earthly sovereign of Japanese myth: heir of Susanoo, who built wild Izumo into a nation with the dwarf-god Sukunabikona and codified medicine, agriculture and the rites of marriage. His was the visible world — Ashihara no Nakatsukuni, the Central Land of Reed-Plains — until he ceded it to the heavenly line of Amaterasu in what the chronicles call kuni-yuzuri, the transfer of the land.

cards.name: Land-Building
cards.desc: With the dwarf god Sukunabikona he “made the land”, binding the borders of the Reed-Plain in the Kojiki’s land-building cycle.

cards.name: Marriage & Alliance
cards.desc: He survives Susanoo’s underworld trials to win Suseri-hime and takes the Yakami bride, sealing rule through union (Kojiki).

cards.name: Medicine & Spellcraft
cards.desc: Remembered as a healer: with Sukunabikona he teaches the medicines and incantations that cure both men and beasts.

cards.name: Kuni-yuzuri — The Transfer of the Land
cards.desc: He cedes the Reed-Plain to Amaterasu's line on terms — a grand shrine and perpetual worship — in the myth-treaty that gave Japanese its word for peaceful abdication (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki).

symbols.name: White hare of Inaba
symbols.meaning: His first patient and his prophet: the flayed hare of Cape Keta whose healing proved Ōkuninushi's medicine and foretold his marriage to Yakami-hime; emblem of the province of Inaba.

symbols.name: The great shimenawa
symbols.meaning: The colossal sacred rope hung across the halls of Izumo-taisha — among the largest in Japan — marking the boundary of his enshrined presence.

symbols.name: Susanoo's sword, bow and lute
symbols.meaning: The regalia of lordship he carried out of Ne-no-Kuni with Susanoo's blessing — the storm-god's own charter for his rule over the land.

symbols.name: The tiny boat of Sukunabikona
symbols.meaning: The skiff of Metaplexis pod-husks (ama-no-kagami-no-fune) and the moth-skin cloak of the dwarf-god, emblem of the small partner in nation-building.

symbols.name: Herbs and the mortar
symbols.meaning: The pharmacology he and Sukunabikona devised for gods and men — beginning with the remedy of fresh water and katami (cattail) pollen prescribed for the hare.

symbols.name: The high pillars of Izumo
symbols.meaning: The towering hall promised at the kuni-yuzuri, to be raised with pillars 'high as the heaven of the gods' — his eternal seat after the surrender of the land.

mythology.lead: Ōkuninushi's cycle, preserved in the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720), is the longest and most novelistic narrative in Japanese myth — a story of escape, ordeal, sovereignty and renunciation at the meeting-point of earth and heaven. Every stage of it, from the healed hare to the final treaty, teaches one art of rule.

myths.title: The White Hare of Inaba
myths.text: In the Kojiki (Book I), a hare from the isle of Oki tricks the wani sea-beasts into forming a bridge, is flayed for the deception, and meets the eighty cruel brothers of Ōnamuji, who mockingly prescribe a bath in salt sea-water — agony for its wounds. The youngest brother, Ōnamuji (later Ōkuninushi), advises instead a rinse in fresh river water and a roll in the pollen of katami, the cattail rush; the hare is healed. Grateful, the hare prophesies that Ōnamuji — not his eighty brothers — will win the hand of the princess Yakami-hime of Inaba. It is the first medical prescription in Japanese myth, and the deed that marks the future land-master out from his rivals: where the brothers offer cruelty disguised as counsel, the youngest offers the right remedy and wins a prophet for his pains.

myths.title: The Trials of Ne-no-Kuni
myths.text: Fleeing his brothers' repeated attempts to kill him, Ōnamuji descends to Ne-no-Kuni, the root-land of Susanoo, as the Kojiki (Book I) relates. There he loves Susanoo's daughter Suseribime, and the storm-god tests him: a night in a hall of snakes, a night in a hall of centipedes and wasps — each survived through Suseribime's protective scarves — and a burning meadow where a mouse leads him to safety underground and retrieves the arrow Susanoo had fired. When Ōnamuji at last washes the great god's hair and steals away with Suseribime, Susanoo's sword, bow and heavenly lute, the pursuing god yields and proclaims him Ōkuninushi-no-kami, Great Land-Master, bidding him drive out his brothers and rule the land. The trials invert the heroic pattern: the hero wins not by strength but by endurance, courtesy, and a mouse's friendship — the virtues of a healer, not a berserker.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ōkuninushi still anchors the Izumo region of Shimane, where Izumo-taisha draws millions of pilgrims and couples across Japan pray to him as the nation's great matchmaker of en-musubi. The white hare of Inaba endures as the emblem of Tottori prefecture; his son Kotoshironushi presides over the great pilgrimage shrine of Kotohira in Shikoku; and his name survives in the Daikokuten of household luck and the Seven Gods of Fortune. The word kuni-yuzuri itself remains the standard Japanese term for the peaceful cession of sovereignty — a god's abdication absorbed whole into the political vocabulary of the nation.
lore.archaeology: Izumo-taisha (Taisha-machi, Izumo, Shimane) is among the oldest and grandest shrines of Japan; the present main hall dates to 1744, but excavations in 2000 uncovered massive clustered pillar bases confirming medieval records of a towering earlier hall — the 'high pillars' the kuni-yuzuri myth demands. The region's cultic antiquity is independently attested by the 1984 Kojindani discovery, a ritual cache of 358 bronze swords, the largest single find of its kind in Japan.
lore.syncretism: Japan's gods met no Roman pantheon; Ōkuninushi's later travels ran through Buddhism instead. Through the folk reading Daikoku-sama of the characters 大国, he was identified with Daikokuten, the Japanese form of Mahākāla, becoming the smiling god of wealth and the household hearth — one of the Seven Gods of Fortune. At Izumo the older identity survived intact: there he remains the great matchmaker of en-musubi, the binding of marriage fates, and in the month the rest of Japan calls Kannazuki, 'the godless month', Izumo calls it Kami-ari-zuki — 'the month the gods are here', when the eight million kami convene at his shrine.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SAH-roo-tah-hee-koh' — the 'r' is a light tap, and all vowels are short.
pronunciation.note: Sarutahiko is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is the kami who guided Ninigi's descent and who stands at boundaries.

domains.title: Monkey-Field Prince
domains.subtitle: Guide of the Heavenly Descent, Guardian of Crossroads
domains.lead: Sarutahiko is the kami who stands at the boundary between heaven and earth. When Ninigi descended from Takamagahara, Sarutahiko blocked the way until Ame-no-Uzume persuaded him to become the guide. With his long nose, glaring eyes, and red face, he became the model for the taikomochi and tenjin figures of Japanese folk performance and the patron of those who stand at thresholds.

cards.name: Guide of Ninigi
cards.desc: He led Ninigi's descent from heaven to earth.

cards.name: Crossroads Guardian
cards.desc: He protects boundaries, paths, and transitions.

cards.name: Husband of Uzume
cards.desc: Ame-no-Uzume married him after negotiating the heavenly descent.

cards.name: Folk Performer
cards.desc: His appearance influenced comedic and ceremonial performers.

symbols.name: Long nose
symbols.meaning: His most distinctive feature, symbolizing spiritual perception

symbols.name: Red face
symbols.meaning: The color of power and boundary-crossing deities

symbols.name: Jeweled spear
symbols.meaning: The weapon he brandished when blocking Ninigi's path

symbols.name: Crossroads
symbols.meaning: The thresholds he guards

mythology.lead: Sarutahiko's mythology is compact but complete in its own way: the earth-born kami who blocks the heavenly descent and becomes its guide; the husband of the dancing goddess; a drowned god whose spirit is still named at Ise. Around these Kojiki and Nihon Shoki episodes, folk religion built a vast afterlife of crossroads, masks, and martial arts.

myths.title: The Blockade at the Floating Bridge
myths.text: When Ninigi no Mikoto, grandson of Amaterasu, prepared to descend from Takamagahara to rule the Central Land of Reed-Plains, an awesome figure stood at the eight-fold crossroads at the earthward end of the Floating Bridge of Heaven. The Kojiki describes Sarutahiko with a long nose, a red and shining face, eyes like eight-span mirrors, and a beard that hung down; the Nihon Shoki variant measures him more exactly — a nose of seven hand-spans, a height over seven feet, eyes red like mirrors — and says the heavenly envoys sent to negotiate all stood back in fear. Only Ame-no-Uzume, goddess of dawn, mirth, and dance, stepped forward. She spoke to him boldly and well, and the gatekeeper was won: he asked who was coming and offered himself as guide. No force moved him and no god outranked him; what opened the road was speech. The myth's meaning is a charter of legitimacy: heaven's claim to the land passes through an earthly gatekeeper's consent — rule is negotiated at the threshold, not imposed from the sky.

myths.title: The Marriage That Founded a Line
myths.text: After the descent was accomplished, Ame-no-Uzume married Sarutahiko, and the Kojiki draws the genealogical consequence: Uzume is the ancestress of the Sarume — the “monkey-women” — the order of female ritual dancers of the Yamato court, whose sacred performances are the root from which kagura, and in part the comic spirit of Noh, descend. The marriage folds the unruly leader of the earthly kami into the celestial order without domesticating him: he remains the red-faced giant, she remains the dancer who out-talked him, and together they become the founding couple of Japanese sacred performance. Structurally the pairing is exact — the goddess who moves between worlds weds the god who guards the crossing — and politically it is shrewd: the oldest indigenous power of the archipelago is not defeated by Ninigi's line but married into it. The myth remembers that Japan's ritual arts were born at a boundary, from a negotiation.

lore.culturalLegacy: Sarutahiko is worshipped at Tsubaki Grand Shrine and other shrines associated with guidance and performance. His image influences Japanese masks, festival costumes, and the design of tenjin figures. He remains the kami you call upon when standing at a threshold.
lore.archaeology: Sarutahiko's cult geography is unusually legible. Tsubaki Grand Shrine at Suzuka in Mie Prefecture, set at the foot of Mount Nyūdō, is the head shrine of his cult, first among some two thousand branch shrines; Sarutahiko Jinja stands by the Isuzu River at Ise, beside the river of his drowning, and Ōasahiko Shrine in Tokushima is another ancient seat. Images of the god — the red shining face, hanging beard, long nose — survive in shrine statuary, festival regalia, and the masks of the Menkake Gyōretsu procession still performed at Kamakura's Tsurugaoka Hachimangū, a medieval rite whose masks are preserved as temple treasures. No inscription from the archaic period names him; his earliest witnesses are the Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720) manuscripts themselves.
lore.syncretism: Sarutahiko is an earthly kami who becomes an ally of the heavenly order. His long nose and red face connect him to other boundary figures in Japanese folk religion, and his marriage to Ame-no-Uzume unites two of the most dynamic kami in the pantheon. He is also venerated in Shugendō as a guide for mountain ascetics.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KAH-goo-tsoo-chee' — the 'tsu' is crisp, and the final 'chi' is like 'chee'.
pronunciation.note: Kagutsuchi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is the volatile fire god whose birth marks the beginning of death in the world.

domains.title: God of Fire and Volcanic Force
domains.subtitle: Creation, Destruction, and the Origin of Death
domains.lead: Kagutsuchi is the fire god whose birth burned his mother Izanami to death, introducing mortality into the mythic world. He is creation and destruction in one figure: the flame that forges and the flame that consumes. After his death at the hands of Izanagi, his scattered body became the volcanoes and hot springs of Japan.

cards.name: Birth of Fire
cards.desc: His birth from Izanami introduced both fire and death into the world.

cards.name: Slain by Izanagi
cards.desc: Izanagi avenged Izanami's death by cutting Kagutsuchi into pieces with the Totsuka-no-Tsurugi.

cards.name: Volcano God
cards.desc: His dismembered body became the volcanoes and geothermal springs of the land.

cards.name: Forge and Hearth
cards.desc: Fire for cooking, warmth, and metalwork descends from his power.

symbols.name: Flame
symbols.meaning: The elemental fire he embodies — the one power in the house that must never be insulted.

symbols.name: The Totsuka-no-Tsurugi
symbols.meaning: The 'ten-handled sword of the brine' with which the grieving Izanagi cut him down.

symbols.name: Volcano
symbols.meaning: His dismembered body became the mountains and steaming springs of Japan.

symbols.name: Forge
symbols.meaning: Hearth and smithy — the domesticated half of his double nature.

mythology.lead: Kagutsuchi's mythology is brief and absolute: a birth that kills, a death that multiplies life, and a legacy of fire that Japan's volcanoes still preach. The Kojiki spends little more than a page on him — yet that page is the hinge of the whole cosmogony, for it is at his birth that the creator goddess dies and the world divides into the living and the dead.

myths.title: The Burning Birth
myths.text: After the islands were born, Izanami bore the last child of the creation — the fire kami Kagutsuchi — and his birth burned her. The Kojiki (I.8) tells it with terrible economy: the fire from the child's body scorched her, and from the agony of the wound the dying goddess brought forth still more kami — Kanayamabiko and Kanayamabime, the kami of metal, from her vomit; Haniyasubiko and Haniyasubime, the kami of clay and pottery, from her feces; and Midorikonomikami from her urine. Then, her body spent, Izanami died. She who had borne the islands and the thirty-odd kami of the land was destroyed by her final child: creation consuming its maker is the first law the new world teaches, and the fire god learned it in the only way a newborn can — by being it.

myths.title: The Blade of Grief
myths.text: Izanagi's grief turned to rage — 'Why must I lose my beloved for this one child?' — and drawing the Totsuka-no-Tsurugi, the ten-handled sword of the brine, he cut the fire kami down. What fell from the blade was life. From the blood on its point came Iwasaku and Nesaku, the 'stone-cutting' kami; from the blood on its hilt came Mizuhanome, the goddess of water who quenches fire; and from the severed body came the mountain kami whose peaks still steam along the Japanese chain (Kojiki I.9). The Nihon Shoki preserves variant versions of the same burning-birth and gives the child the parallel names Homusubi and Hi-no-Kagutsuchi. Kagutsuchi thus dies the only death in the cosmogony struck by a god's own hand — and the dismemberment, like the birth, manufactures gods: fire destroys, and destruction is revealed as one of generation's ordinary forms.

lore.culturalLegacy: Kagutsuchi survives wherever Japan's volcanoes are in the news — the country that monitors its peaks for eruption is, in the old language, watching over the scattered body of a god. His name circulates widely in modern fantasy and games as a volcanic or destructive kami, sometimes flattened into a monster, though the original story is more tragic than fearsome: a child destroyed for being born what he was. The geothermal energy industry has quietly theologized him in reverse, tapping the heat his body left in the mountains as power. And at every hearth and every forge the oldest layer of his cult persists without shrines — the simple, ancient caution that fire is a guest who must be fed, watched, and never insulted. His is the only major Japanese cult whose temple is a kitchen.
lore.archaeology: Kagutsuchi left no temples, inscriptions, or cult images — the evidence for him is textual and geological. The textual witness is the eighth-century manuscript tradition of the Kojiki (712 CE) and the Nihon Shoki (720 CE), whose compilers fixed the story; the Shinpukuji-bon and the Urabe recension are its principal witnesses. The 'archaeology' of his body is the archipelago itself: the volcanic chain from Fuji to Aso to Sakurajima, with its crater shrines and steam vents, and the hot-spring country the Kojiki already reads as the fire kami's remains. And beneath the myth lie the oldest controlled fires on earth: the hearths of Jōmon pit-dwellings (from c. 14,000 BCE), where a culture learned to keep the exact double attitude the myth prescribes — fire fed daily, and feared daily. That hearths older than any shrine in Japan still govern his cult is the most honest monument he has.
lore.syncretism: Comparisons come readily — Hephaistos and Vulcan as smith-fire, Agni as the god born who must be handled with care, Prometheus as the power that costs its bearer everything — but Kagutsuchi's closest relatives are his own siblings and victims: Izanami, whom his birth killed, and the metal and clay kami born from her dying body, who made his fire usable. Within Japan his identity overlapped with the folk hearth deity Kōjin and with the volcano kami of the great peaks; Buddhist Japan did not canonically adopt him, but shrine and temple practice alike made offerings to the hearth fire. His theology stays pointedly Japanese: not a forge-god of artisans nor a fire-thief of the gods, but the tragedy of fire itself — the child whose birth introduced death into the world and whose dismembered body is the landscape. Where other traditions send fire to humanity as a gift or a theft, Japan keeps it at home as a birth, and mourns it.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written 迦具土 — phonetic man'yōgana whose characters ('add', 'tool', 'soil') were chosen for sound, not sense. Later tradition sometimes writes the fire deity with the more transparent 火産霊 (Homusubi, 'fire-producing spirit').

entries.meaning: Hawaiian god symbolized by the squid or by the octopus, typically associated with Kāne

variants.note: Owned stylized form with conventional long-vowel marks; Pukui & Elbert and UH Mānoa write Kanaloa without kahakō

pronunciation.approximation: 'kah-NAH-loh-ah' — both 'a' vowels are long, and the name flows like a slow wave.
pronunciation.note: Kānāloa keeps the Hawaiian macrons that mark vowel length — a phonemic feature of the language, and one the ASCII form loses. The lexicon nevertheless classifies the name Tier 2: the macron marks quantity, and the name carries no distinctive non-Latin letter or mark such as the glottal ʻokina (which would have changed the consonants themselves). The rhythm of the long vowels is the name's dignity, but by the mechanical rule it stays Tier 2.

domains.title: Lord of the Vast Ocean
domains.subtitle: Sea, Underworld, and Healing
domains.lead: Kānāloa is the Hawaiian god of the deep ocean, the underworld, and healing. He is the companion and sometimes rival of Kāne, the creator; while Kāne governs fresh water and life, Kānāloa rules the salt sea and the mysteries beneath it. He is associated with the octopus, whose arms reach in all directions like ocean currents.

cards.name: Vast Ocean
cards.desc: The Pacific itself is his body, source of food, travel, and the unknown.

cards.name: Underworld
cards.desc: He receives the dead into the dark realm beneath land and sea.

cards.name: Healer
cards.desc: Kānāloa and Kāne together discovered medicinal plants and healing arts.

cards.name: Octopus Kin
cards.desc: The heʻe (octopus) is his animal, shape-shifting and intelligent.

symbols.name: Octopus (heʻe)
symbols.meaning: The many-armed creature of the deep, Kānāloa's kin or avatar.

symbols.name: Ocean waves
symbols.meaning: The visible movement of his vast body.

symbols.name: Kava plant
symbols.meaning: A plant of ritual and healing associated with him.

symbols.name: Dark depths
symbols.meaning: The mysterious underworld where souls and sea creatures dwell.

mythology.lead: Hawaiian myths present Kānāloa as a complementary power to Kāne, the creator. Their partnership structures much of traditional cosmology: one god of fresh water and daylight, one of salt sea and depth, together covering the whole of the living world.

myths.title: Kāne and Kānāloa
myths.text: In Hawaiian cosmogony, Kāne and Kānāloa are paired creator gods. Beckwith's Hawaiian Mythology preserves the tradition that the two traveled together across the primordial ocean, striking the earth with their staffs to open springs of fresh water — Kāne's gift of life in the midst of Kānāloa's salt realm — and calling forth the plants and creatures of the islands. Kāne is the fresh water and the sunlight; Kānāloa is the salt sea that surrounds and sustains the land. Their partnership is not hierarchy but dynamic balance: no island exists without both the spring and the surrounding ocean, and the two gods are invoked together so often that the pairing itself became a formula of blessing. The myth encodes an ecological truth the Hawaiians lived by — life on an island is a negotiation between land and sea, and neither partner can be dispensed with.

myths.title: The Discovery of Medicine
myths.text: The healing tradition, recorded by Kamakau and Malo, begins with Kānāloa himself falling ill, and no remedy in the world able to help him. Kāne prayed and was shown the healing plants of the forest and shore; after Kānāloa was cured, the two gods shared this knowledge with humankind, establishing the practice of lāʻau lapaʻau, traditional Hawaiian herbal medicine, and ordaining the kahuna lāʻau lapaʻau who guarded the recipes — which plant for fever, which for broken bone, which for the sickness of the soul — as a sacred trust handed down within families. Illness and cure both belong to Kānāloa's watery realm — the same depths that take life also restore it. The story makes the underworld-god the founder of medicine: only the power that rules decay understands how to reverse it.

lore.culturalLegacy: Kānāloa's name survives in Hawaiian place names, in the scientific names of deep-sea creatures, and in the cultural revival movements that seek to restore indigenous relationships with the ocean. He is invoked in debates over marine conservation, deep-sea mining, and the rights of native Hawaiians to their waters. The octopus, his kin, has become an emblem of intelligent, adaptable life in the Pacific.
lore.syncretism: Kānāloa is clearly related to the pan-Polynesian Tangaroa / Taʻaroa, the great sea deity of the Māori, Tahitians, and Cook Islands — the consonant correspondences (Hawaiian k- against Polynesian t-) are among the cleanest in comparative Polynesian linguistics. In Hawaiian tradition, however, he is less a creator-from-void and more a partner of Kāne, a god of depth and healing. Christian missionaries sometimes identified him with Satan because of his underworld associations, but this identification distorts a figure who was primarily beneficent. Modern Hawaiian cultural revival has reclaimed Kānāloa as a symbol of oceanic sovereignty and ecological wisdom.
lore.originalScriptNote: Hawaiian had no indigenous writing system before European contact. The name is written in the Latin alphabet introduced by missionaries, with macrons added by modern scholars to mark long vowels. Kānāloa is composed of ka (article or intensifier) + nā (plural or intensifier) + loa ('long, vast, far'), together evoking vastness. PUNICODEX preserves both macrons because vowel length is phonemic in Hawaiian and the feature that gives the restored name its dignity, even though the mechanical tier rule keeps the name Tier 2.

entries.meaning: Hawaiian deity, associated with fertility, agriculture, rainfall, music and peace

pronunciation.approximation: 'LOH-noh' — two clean open syllables, the weight on the first; no diphthong, no swallowed ending.
pronunciation.note: Lono is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Hawaiian name is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter. Nor is there an older spelling for Unicode to recover: Hawaiian was unwritten until mission scribes fixed the alphabet in the 1820s. The restoration honors the name as the pan-Polynesian Rongo's Hawaiian form.

domains.title: Lono
domains.subtitle: Agriculture
domains.lead: Lono is the Hawaiian god of fertility, agriculture, rainfall, music, and peace — the deity of the Makahiki season, when war was forbidden and the feathered image of the long god made its circuit of every island collecting tribute. His name is the ordinary Hawaiian word for news and tidings, as if the arriving god were good news himself.

cards.name: The Makahiki Circuit
cards.desc: The akua loa — the long, feathered image of Lono — was carried counterclockwise around each island for four months of peace, games, and tribute (Malo, Hawaiian Antiquities, ch. 33).

cards.name: Rain and Cultivation
cards.desc: His cloudburst watered the dry leeward fields; under his star the people planted ʻuala, sweet potato, and the year turned from war to husbandry.

cards.name: The Peace of Lono
cards.desc: During Lono's months the temples closed to war and the aliʻi gathered the Makahiki tax — a season when law was the god's own itinerary.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple; a pre-literate name first written by mission scribes in the 1820s, restored here to Polynesian dignity.

symbols.name: The akua Lono
symbols.meaning: The long feathered image carried around the island in the Makahiki circuit — the god made portable, travelling to receive his tribute.

symbols.name: The Pleiades (Makaliʻi)
symbols.meaning: Whose heliacal rising opened the Makahiki season — Lono returned with the star-cluster the sailors also steered by.

symbols.name: Rain over the leeward fields
symbols.meaning: His cloudburst on the dry Kona side of the islands — the storm that answered drought and began the planting year.

symbols.name: The sweet potato (ʻuala)
symbols.meaning: The dryland crop of Lono's months, planted as the god came round — agriculture performed as liturgy.

symbols.name: The sacrificial pig (puaʻa)
symbols.meaning: The offering laid at each ahupuaʻa boundary platform as the image passed — the tax paid in flesh to the god of peace.

mythology.lead: Lono's stories are Hawaiʻi's seasonal memory: a chief who lost his wife and sailed away to Kahiki promising return, and a god who returns every year as the Makahiki — the months when rain, games, and taxation replace war. When Cook sailed into Kealakekua Bay during the festival, the myth was already waiting for him.

myths.title: Lono and Kaikilani
myths.text: Among the chiefly legends preserved by Kamakau and Beckwith, Lono-i-ka-makahiki is a chief of Kaʻawaloa in the Kona district of Hawaiʻi island, whose story became the god's. His wife is the beautiful Kaikilani; a jealous rival fabricates reports of her infidelity, and Lono — believing the lie — kills her, learning the truth too late (Kamakau, Ruling Chiefs of Hawaiʻi). Maddened by grief, he wanders the island, boxing and wrestling his way around the coast, until he boards a canoe at Kealakekua and sails for Kahiki, promising to return. The people say the Makahiki is that return: the god comes back each year when the Pleiades rise, and the season of his circuit is the season of peace. Beckwith's variant (Hawaiian Mythology, ch. 15) reshapes the tale within Pele's circle — a reminder that the legend grew in more than one telling, and that its fixed point is the departure and the promise, not any single version of the crime.

myths.title: The Circuit of the Long God
myths.text: The Makahiki, the Hawaiian New Year festival, is Lono's season and his biography performed. When the Pleiades (Makaliʻi) appeared at sunset, the temples closed to war and the image of the long god (akua loa) — a tall staff hung with feathered emblems — was carried around each island counterclockwise, district by district (Malo, Hawaiian Antiquities, ch. 33; Kamakau, The Works of the People of Old). At every ahupuaʻa boundary the procession halted at the ahu platform, where a pig was offered and the ruling chief's collectors gathered the Makahiki tribute, the hoʻokupu that funded the court's year. Boxing, surfing, and spear-dancing filled the days, and ordinary disputes were set aside until the god had passed. For four months, taxation itself was liturgy: the god circled the land, and the land's wealth circled with him. When the image was lifted back into the temple at the season's end, war could resume — the myth's own answer to what holds a kingdom together when no enemy threatens.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Makahiki never fully died. In the Hawaiian renaissance that began in the 1970s it returned as school festivals, games leagues, and island-wide circuits of the akua images; today Hawaiian immersion schools open their year with it, and the festival's sports — wrestling, surfing, spear-throwing — have league lives of their own. Kealakekua Bay is a state historical park, and a white obelisk at Kaʻawaloa marks where the god-story and the captain's log collided. In 1976 the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa made Lono's return literal, sailing to Tahiti and back by traditional navigation — Kahiki proven reachable, the promise kept by human hands. Lono remains a common Hawaiian given name, and the god's peace still names the season when a year, not a war, can begin.
lore.archaeology: The material trace of Lono is the Makahiki landscape itself. Hikiau heiau at Kealakekua Bay — the platform where Cook was received as the returned god — survives as a restored temple complex above the bay, beside the older Mailekini heiau, while the Cook monument obelisk stands at Kaʻawaloa across the water. Along the old circuits, ahu — small offering platforms at ahupuaʻa boundaries — mark where the akua image halted and the tribute was laid. No pre-contact temple can be securely assigned to Lono alone: Hawaiian heiau served shifting dedications, and his worship was mobile by design, carried around the island on poles rather than fixed in stone. The archaeology is therefore the route, not the shrine — a procession that left platforms every few miles around every inhabited island.
lore.syncretism: Across Polynesia, Lono's kin rule the cultivated foods: Māori Rongo — hidden guardian of the kūmara and god of peace, one of the children of Rangi and Papa — Marquesan ʻOno, Tahitian Roʻo, and Rarotongan Rongo are all reflexes of the same eastern-Pacific theonym whose Hawaiian form arrives by the regular sound change (Beckwith, ch. 4; Craig, s.v. Rongo). In Aotearoa, Rongo is invoked to make peace; in Hawaiʻi, Lono's four months did the same work. The mission century overlaid the pattern: Christian preachers found in Lono's annual return a ready-made parable of the second coming, and Hawaiian converts could hear the Makahiki itself as prophecy. Modern scholarship has made Lono a battleground of another kind — the Sahlins–Obeyesekere debate over Cook's apotheosis is, at bottom, a debate over whether gods can still walk in when the calendar says they should.
lore.originalScriptNote: Hawaiian was an unwritten language until the 1820s, when mission scribes fixed the alphabet, so the name has no older orthography for Unicode to recover — Lono is itself the first spelling. The philological record is the sound change instead: pan-Polynesian *Rongo becomes Hawaiian Lono by the regular shift of *R to l, with the second *g dropping, leaving a name that Hawaiian speakers heard as both the ancient god and their own word for tidings.

pronunciation.approximation: 'hee-EE-ah-kah' — four light syllables, the second long and stressed; give the doubled i a tiny catch in the throat (the ʻokina).
pronunciation.note: Hiiaka is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter to recover. The fuller Hawaiian spelling Hiʻiaka carries both the ʻokina, a true consonant the ASCII erases, and the long ī. The temple keeps the normalized restoration and shows the fuller form in the lore.

domains.title: Hiiaka
domains.subtitle: Hula
domains.lead: Hiiaka is the youngest sister of the volcano-goddess Pele: patroness of the hula, guardian of the hālau hula where the dance is taught, and a healer whose chants restore the dying. Her story — an oath, a quest, and a betrayal between sisters — is the great romance of the Hawaiian Pele cycle.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The restoration Hiiaka names the goddess Hawaiʻi's dancers invoke before any performance begins.

cards.name: Hula
cards.desc: She is patroness of the hālau hula and keeper of the mele and dances taught to her friend Hopoe at Puna.

cards.name: Healing Chant
cards.desc: Her repertoire includes the chants (mele oli) that raise the dying — the power she finally spends on Lohiʻau.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The fuller Hawaiian form is Hiʻiaka, with ʻokina and long ī; the normalized Hiiaka keeps the name registrable.

symbols.name: The egg at ʻĀinahou
symbols.meaning: Her first form, found on Kauaʻi and warmed in Pele's bosom until the goddess hatched — the birth the name Hiʻiaka ('carried at the bosom') remembers

symbols.name: The pāʻū hula
symbols.meaning: The dancer's skirt, emblem of her office as patroness of the hula schools

symbols.name: The ʻōhiʻa lehua
symbols.meaning: The red blossom of Puna beneath which her friend Hopoe danced — the groves she swore to protect

symbols.name: Mele oli
symbols.meaning: The unaccompanied chant through which her healing power works, restoring breath and life

symbols.name: The kupua's path
symbols.meaning: The road across the islands she fought along — passes guarded by moʻo serpents that she cleared for every traveler after

mythology.lead: Hiiaka's mythology is the longest continuous narrative in Hawaiian tradition: the Pele cycle, preserved in chant and family memory, in which the youngest volcano-goddess crosses every island on her sister's errand and comes home to a betrayal that splits the heavens' first family in two.

myths.title: The Egg at ʻĀinahou
myths.text:
Pele's migration legend carries the volcano family westward from Kahiki — the Hawaiian name for Tahiti — until the goddess finds her home in the pit of Kīlauea. Beckwith's digest of the tradition (Hawaiian Mythology, 'The Pele cycle') preserves the birth of her youngest sister: at ʻĀinahou on Kauaʻi, Pele discovers an egg and takes it into her bosom to keep it warm; from the egg hatches the goddess whose name, Hiʻiaka, is traditionally explained as 'carried in the bosom' (Hawaiian hiʻi, to hold a child close; Pukui & Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary).

The myth makes kinship the first fact of Hiʻiaka's being: she exists because Pele carried her, and her whole career will replay that carrying as loyalty, as errand, and finally as grievance.

myths.title: The Quest for Lohiʻau
myths.text:
Sleeping in the crater at Kīlauea, Pele sees in a dream the young chief Lohiʻau of Kauaʻi and falls in love with his image. Because she cannot leave her volcanic work without peril, she binds her youngest sister by an oath: Hiʻiaka must cross the islands, find Lohiʻau, and bring him back within forty days — and Hiʻiaka in turn binds Pele to guard her sacred lehua groves and her beloved friend Hopoe until she returns (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Emerson's Pele and Hiiaka, 1915, is the classic literary retelling of the cycle).

The journey becomes the longest road in Hawaiian myth: Hiʻiaka battles the moʻo monsters that bar the passes, wins kupua allies of her own, and at last finds Lohiʻau dead of longing — and slays the serpent who killed him, passing her pāʻū over his body until he breathes again. The quest myth turns the islands into a single moral geography: every valley crossed is a test of the oath, and love in this family is always love at the end of a long and dangerous errand.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hālau hula across Hawaiʻi still open their practice with chants to Pele and Hiʻiaka, and the Merrie Monarch Festival's hula competition, founded in 1964 and held each spring in Hilo — the very coast of the sisters' battle — is the visible heart of her cult today. Place memory keeps her close: ʻĀinahou on Kauaʻi where the egg lay, the groves and shores of Puna where Hopoe danced. In the Hawaiian renaissance her name has returned to concert stages, children's books, and mele, and to the recovery of the ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi in which her chants were always sung.
lore.archaeology: Pre-contact Hawaiʻi had no writing, so Hiʻiaka's evidence is cultic and ethnographic rather than epigraphic. The material center of her family's worship is the pit of Kīlauea: nineteenth-century observers (Emerson, Westervelt) and native historians (Kamakau, Malo) record offerings of ʻōhelo berries and lehua blossom at Halemaʻumaʻu, where the Pele family was believed to dwell. The chants of the cycle were preserved in the memory of the hālau and committed to manuscript in the nineteenth century; Emerson's Pele and Hiiaka (1915) drew directly on that living tradition. Heiau dedicated to the Pele family along the Puna and Kaʻū coasts, many now reduced to stone platforms, mark the old geography of the cycle's events.
lore.syncretism: The Pele cycle in which Hiʻiaka moves is itself a layered composition: Hawaiian tradition remembers the family's arrival from Kahiki (Tahiti), and Beckwith read the migration of the volcano deities against Tahitian parallels, while the offices of hula and healing chant root the goddess in religion older than any remembered voyage. Nineteenth-century Christianity nearly silenced the cycle: missionaries suppressed the hula after the 1820s, and the chants survived only inside the hālau lineages and a few manuscripts, of which Emerson's Pele and Hiiaka (1915) is the great published monument. The modern Hawaiian renaissance returned both the dance and its goddess to public honor.
lore.originalScriptNote: Pre-contact Hawaiʻi had no writing; the name comes down in the Latin-based Hawaiian orthography developed after the 1820s. The fuller traditional spelling is Hiʻiaka, with ʻokina (glottal stop) marking the consonant between the vowels and kahakō (macron) marking the long ī; the canonical temple restoration is the normalized form Hiiaka.

entries.meaning: male fertility deity in Hawaiian mythology

pronunciation.approximation: 'kah-mah-POO-ah-ah' — five light syllables; stress on the pu, and let the final a-a sound as two separate vowels.
pronunciation.note: Kamapua'a is the Hawaiian pig-god of O'ahu; the lexicon keeps the older missionary-era spelling, in which the ʻokina is unwritten. No vowel length marks the name: Tier 2, a display fact only. His name is his biography — kama 'child,' pua'a 'pig' — and his myth makes both halves true.

domains.title: Kamapuaa
domains.subtitle: Pig God
domains.lead: Kamapua'a is the pig-god of O'ahu — shape-shifter, ravager of plantations, master of rain and flood, and the only suitor who ever beat Pele at her own element. He is agriculture's wild side: the animal that roots up the garden, and the storm that waters it.

cards.name: The Shape-Shifter
cards.desc: Man and hog and fog: he changed form at will, and his tusk-furrows became the valleys of O'ahu's Ko'olau range.

cards.name: The Hog of Kaliuwa'a
cards.desc: Born in the sheer valley of Kaliuwa'a — Sacred Falls — to the goddess Hina; the cliffs are still his birthplace.

cards.name: Lord of Cultivars
cards.desc: He stole and spread the garden's wealth — taro, yam, gourd — and finally bargained Pele's lava away from the farms.

cards.name: The Flood That Courted Fire
cards.desc: He wooed Pele with rain until her fires hissed; their marriage joined storm and volcano in treaty.

symbols.name: The boar's tusk
symbols.meaning: His tusks furrowed the valleys; pig-tooth ornaments (niho pua'a) worn by chiefs carried his mana.

symbols.name: Kaliuwa'a — Sacred Falls
symbols.meaning: The sheer-walled valley of his birth, closed to entry under old custom — a sanctuary the myth still owns.

symbols.name: The rain
symbols.meaning: His element of courtship and war: he came to Pele as fog, rain, and thunderstorm, and water is how he wins.

symbols.name: The spring
symbols.meaning: Where his tusks struck the rock, fresh water broke forth — the wild hog as water-bringer.

symbols.name: The cultivated field
symbols.meaning: The garden he ravaged and then defended: his cycle ends as god of agriculture, not only of its destruction.

mythology.lead: Kamapua'a's cycle, best preserved in the O'ahu traditions Beckwith summarized and Westervelt printed, is a trickster epic with a strange ending: the ravager marries the destroyer, and the islands get a farm treaty.

myths.title: The Child of the Cliffs
myths.text: Kamapua'a was born in Kaliuwa'a, the sheer valley of the Ko'olau range on O'ahu — the valley the Hawaiians call Sacred Falls — to the goddess Hina. From the first he was double: a child who was also a hog, fair-faced as a young chief, yet able to swell into an enormous boar whose bristles swept the ferns. He grew among the cliff country of the windward coast, and the cycle follows him as he raids the coastal plantations — pulling up taro and yam, devouring or carrying off the stored wealth of the district — while the farmers' traps and the chiefs' hunters fail against an animal that is also a man. (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Gods and Ghosts.) The myth's heart is in the name itself: kama, child; pua'a, pig — the beloved and the pest as one being, as any farmer who has watched a feral boar in the taro already knows.

myths.title: The Chiefs Who Could Not Catch a God
myths.text: The raids brought the hunt. The chiefs of the coast — in the longer versions led by 'Olopana, lord of the district — pursued the sacred hog into the mountains with spears, ropes, and traps, and Kamapua'a made fools of every formation: he vanished into fog, doubled back as a handsome stranger who ate at the pursuers' own fires by night, and was the boar again bursting their cordons by day. The versions collected in the nineteenth century delight in these escapes — the hog bleeding one moment into mist, the next a man laughing on the cliff — and they end the same way: the hunters quit, and the hog keeps the mountain. (Fornander, An Account of the Polynesian Race; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology.) What reads as a folk tale of an uncatchable pig is a charter: the uplands belong to the wild thing, and human order stops at the tree-line.

lore.culturalLegacy: Kamapua'a's legacy runs from the museum case to the dinner table. Pig remains dominate Hawaiian faunal assemblages from the earliest settlement layers — the pig was the islanders' principal meat and most prestigious offering, which is why a pig-god could carry chiefly mana. Pig-tusk ornaments, documented by Kamakau and preserved in the earliest contact-period collections in London and Honolulu, attest his prestige in chiefly dress. Sacred Falls — Kaliuwa'a — was closed to visitors after fatalities in the 1990s and remains kapu, a closure many Hawaiians frame as the valley reasserting his tapu. Taro farmers invoke him wryly: taro is his stolen treasure that became the staff of life. And the courtship cycle is performed still — the flood wooing the fire is one of the great set-pieces of Hawaiian storytelling, a comic epic that ends, unusually for a trickster, in a working marriage.
lore.archaeology: Kamapua'a's material traces are modest but real. Pig bones dominate Hawaiian faunal assemblages from the earliest settlement layers — the pig was the islanders' principal meat and most prestigious sacrifice, which is why a pig-god could carry chiefly mana. Pig-tusk ornaments (niho pua'a), worn as anklets and necklaces by the ali'i, are well represented in contact-period museum collections. Kaliuwa'a, the sheer valley of his birth, shows no monumental works — Hawaiian gods kept open-air shrines — but its waterfalls, pools, and cliff walls were the sanctuary itself, and its modern closure to the public has made it again what the myth says it always was: his valley, closed.
lore.syncretism: Kamapua'a is Hawaiian to the bone — the pig has no pan-Polynesian divine twin of quite his kind, though the boar figures everywhere in island myth and tabu — and his nearest relations are local: his mother Hina, the great Polynesian goddess the Hawaiians multiplied into a dozen local Hinas, and his wife-rival Pele, whose cycle absorbs his. The nineteenth century treated him as a curiosity, and the early tale-collectors printed him as a marvel-story; Beckwith restored him to seriousness as the agricultural meaning of the pig. In the modern renaissance he is claimed as the god of the Hawaiian rainforest and of the feral pig problem alike — the axis between conservation and subsistence hunting — and his name rides canoes, taro brands, and hālau. If Pele is the volcano that owns the land, Kamapua'a is the garden that owns its pest.
