pronunciation.approximation: 'poh-lee-AH-hoo' — stress on the third syllable; every vowel is sounded separately.
pronunciation.note: Poliahu is single-tier Tier 2: the restoration carries no macron or ʻokina, so ASCII loses nothing the canonical form preserves. The lexicon gloss 'Cloaked bosom' follows the standard dictionary parsing (poli + ahu) given in Pukui & Elbert.

domains.title: Poliahu
domains.subtitle: Snow
domains.lead: Poliahu is the Hawaiian goddess of snow — the beautiful and powerful mistress of Mauna Kea's summit, whose white mantle crowns the highest mountain in the Pacific and whose duel with the volcano goddess Pele for possession of the mountain is one of Hawai'i's most beloved and most retold legends.

cards.name: Mistress of Mauna Kea
cards.desc: She dwells on the summit of the White Mountain, wrapping its peak in snow and mist.

cards.name: The Snow Mantle
cards.desc: Her cloak of snow — beauty that can fall as hail and blizzard when she is angered.

cards.name: Rival of Pele
cards.desc: She met Pele in the legendary hōlua sled race and drove the fire goddess back with snow and hail.

cards.name: Guardian of the Heights
cards.desc: Lake Waiau and the summit region are her household — the sacred cold at the island's crown.

symbols.name: The Snow Mantle (Kahiko)
symbols.meaning: Her garment of snow spread over Mauna Kea — the 'cloaked bosom' of her name

symbols.name: The Hōlua Sled
symbols.meaning: Her racing sled from the great contest with Pele — beauty in swift, sure motion

symbols.name: Lake Waiau
symbols.meaning: The sacred summit lake, home of her sister Waiau — one of Hawai'i's most revered waters

symbols.name: The Summit Shrines (Ahu)
symbols.meaning: The stone shrines of Mauna Kea's peak, built within her sight over a thousand years

symbols.name: Hail and Mist
symbols.meaning: Her two tempers — the soft mist of welcome and the stinging hail of her anger

mythology.lead: Poliahu's mythology is preserved chiefly in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Hawaiian-language and Hawaiian-authored texts — above all Emma Nakuina's Hawaii, Its People, Their Legends (1904), synthesized in Beckwith's Hawaiian Mythology (1970). Its centerpiece is the great contest of snow and fire for the mountain, a duel that Hawaiians read in the island's very lava flows and snowfields to this day.

myths.title: The Stranger on the Mountain
myths.text: On the slopes of Mauna Kea, Poliahu and her snow-sister friends were challenged to a hōlua sled race by a beautiful stranger. The stranger lost — and flung off her disguise: she was Pele, goddess of volcanoes, and she erupted in fire down the mountainside (Nakuina, Hawaii, Its People, Their Legends, 1904; retold in Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology, 1970, and Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, 1916). Poliahu rose to her full height and answered with snow and hail, beating the flames back. The race ran on the great hōlua slide of the mountain's flank, whose stone track can still be traced — the legend pins its scene to a course its first audience knew. The battle of the two goddesses scarred the mountainThe battle of the two goddesses scarred the mountain — fire trenches, snowfields — and the legend still reads the landscape: every cinder and snowbank on Mauna Kea is a stroke of that duel.

myths.title: The Household of the Peak
myths.text: Poliahu does not keep the summit alone. Her companions are her sisters — Lilinoe, who rules the mountain's mists, Waiau, who dwells in the sacred lake that bears her name, and Kahoupokane — together the cold maidens of the high mountain (Nakuina 1904; Beckwith 1970). Waiau's water lies nearly four thousand meters above the sea and never truly warms; tradition held it cold and pure as the goddess herself, and chiefs drank of it only after ceremony. Lake Waiau, among the highest lakes in Oceania,Lake Waiau, among the highest lakes in Oceania, was kapu — its water reserved for the highest chiefs and for the goddess's own uses. The mythology does the work of a natural history: it distributes the summit's phenomena — snow, mist, lake, wind — among a family, making the mountain a household rather than a heap of rock.

lore.culturalLegacy: Poliahu's cult center was the summit itself: Lake Waiau, still sacred, and the dozens of stone shrines that crown the mountain. Offerings of lei and hoʻokupu continue at the lake in the present day, and her name is taught in Hawaiian-medium schools as part of the island's own natural history. In the broader culture she is the personification of Mauna Kea's snow — the sight of the white peak above tropical Hilo remains, for many Hawaiians, her visible presence. Her legend cycle anchors a children's and school literature in Hawaiian, and her duel with Pele is the standard telling through which Hawaiians explain the island's two volcanoes-in-character. Since the telescope protests, her name has appeared on signs, chants, and banners across the world — a snow goddess become an emblem of a people's claim to their own mountain.
lore.archaeology: Mauna Kea's summit preserves one of the most remarkable ritual landscapes in Polynesia. Archaeological surveys (notably Patrick McCoy's work from the 1970s–80s) documented well over a hundred stone shrines (ahu) above 13,000 feet, platforms, burials, and marker cairns clustering around the summit and Lake Waiau — a sacred precinct used for roughly a millennium before Western contact. The mountain's slopes hold the great Keanakākoʻi adze quarry, where Hawaiians knapped summit basalt into tools across many centuries, its workshops marked by vast scatters of flakes and preforms. Lake Waiau itself was a kapu water source, its sediments holding a continuous record of human presence. No image of Poliahu is known — the shrines are her portrait: a mountain-top kept like a heiau, its snow the goddess's own visible temple.
lore.syncretism: Christianization in Hawaiʻi suppressed the goddess cults, but Poliahu survived in a characteristic Hawaiian mode: through the Hawaiian-language newspapers of the nineteenth century and through authors such as Emma Nakuina — a Hawaiian woman writing in English in 1904 — who preserved the legends while Victorian ethnographers were flattening them. In the twentieth century, a modern form of identification emerged: Poliahu became the patroness of Mauna Kea's defense. During the protests against telescope construction on the summit — most visibly the 2014–2019 movement against the Thirty Meter Telescope — kiaʻi (guardians) invoked her name and her snow: the mountain, they argued, is her body and her home, and science must kneel at the summit as at a temple. The goddess of the snow mantle thus became a contemporary standard-bearer for Hawaiian sovereignty over sacred land.

availability.details: RDAP registered; DNS resolves, no HTTP

pronunciation.approximation: Say "haumiatiketike" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Haumiatiketike".
pronunciation.note: Haumia-tiketike is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Māori spelling writes the name without macrons, so no diacritic or distinctive letter is lost against plain ASCII — only the capital distinguishes the temple form. The hyphenated scholarly form Haumia-tiketike is traditional (Grey 1855; White), not a phonetic restoration.

domains.title: Haumiatiketike
domains.subtitle: Wild Food
domains.lead: Haumia-tiketike is the Māori god of uncultivated food — the bracken fernroot (aruhe) dug from the wild with a digging stick, the foil to his brother Rongo's planted kūmara. A child of Rangi and Papa, he hid within the earth-mother's body when the world was divided and never left it: wild food belongs to Papa herself, and cannot be owned, only gathered.

cards.name: Fernroot (Aruhe)
cards.desc: His plant: the bracken fern (Pteridium esculentum), whose starchy rhizomes were dug, beaten, washed, and steamed into a staple of pre-European Aotearoa.

cards.name: Child of Rangi and Papa
cards.desc: One of the children of the sky-father and earth-mother; brother of Tāne, Tangaroa, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, and Rongo (Grey, Polynesian Mythology ch. 1).

cards.name: Sheltered in the Earth
cards.desc: When his brother Tāne pried the parents apart, Haumia hid in Papa's bosom and stayed — the wild food that grows unseen within the mother.

cards.name: The Digging Stick (Kō)
cards.desc: The foot-driven spade of his harvest: fernroot was dug, never planted — the difference between Haumia's wild plenty and Rongo's cultivated gardens.

symbols.name: The bracken frond
symbols.meaning: Pteridium esculentum — the wild fern whose starchy rhizome fed the people when the kūmara crop failed

symbols.name: The digging stick (kō)
symbols.meaning: The foot-driven spade for unearthing fernroot — gathering rather than planting, the sign of uncultivated food

symbols.name: The earth-mother's bosom
symbols.meaning: Papa's body, where Haumia hid when the world was separated — wild food as the earth's own gift

symbols.name: The earth oven (hāngī, umu tī)
symbols.meaning: The steaming pit that leached and cooked the bitter fernroot into a staple — the 'fern oven' of tradition

symbols.name: The uncultivated ground
symbols.meaning: Fern country — the bracken clearings of the bush edge, territory no fence enclosed and no hand had sown

mythology.lead: Haumia-tiketike's stories are chapters of the Māori creation cycle: the separation of sky and earth, the war among the children, and the settlement of the food quest. His single decisive act is a refusal — to leave the earth-mother's body — and from that refusal the wild food of Aotearoa takes its sanctity.

myths.title: Child of the Sky and the Earth
myths.text: In the Māori creation cycle recorded by George Grey in Polynesian Mythology (1855) and in the fuller recensions of John White's Ancient History of the Māori, the sky-father Rangi and the earth-mother Papa lay locked in an embrace that left no room for light or life. Their children — Tāne, Tangaroa, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo-māui, Haumia-tiketike and the rest — grew cramped in the darkness between them. Among them Haumia was the quiet one, the god whose portion was to be everything the forest floor offered without planting. When at last the brothers voted on whether the parents should be separated, Haumia stood with Tāne: the world must be divided so that light, food, and people could come into it. The genealogy is short and absolute: every wild root dug in Aotearoa descends from this moment, when the children of the dark chose to break their parents' embrace and make room for a harvest.

myths.title: Hidden in the Earth-Mother
myths.text: Tāne thrust his parents apart, raising the sky on his shoulders and pressing the earth down, and the world took its shape. But the separation left some children with nowhere to go. Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, raged at what had been done and turned on his brothers; Tāne and Tangaroa fled to the forests and the sea. Rongo-māui took refuge inside the body of Papa, and Haumia-tiketike went with him — into the earth-mother's bosom, where the two brothers have remained ever since (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, 'The children of Heaven and Earth'). The story explains the Māori food world with an elegant symmetry: Rongo, who hid in the earth, is the god of the kūmara that must be planted; Haumia, who hid with him, is the god of the fernroot that is only gathered. What the mother shelters she does not surrender to the cultivator.

lore.culturalLegacy: Haumia's legacy is written into the New Zealand landscape and its food memory. Aruhe, fernroot, was the staple that carried Māori communities through winters and crop failures for centuries; the bracken clearings the digging parties made became, in places, the only open ground in the bush. The knowledge of gathering — where the fern grew thickest, how long to steam it — formed part of the mātauranga handed down within hapū, and it has returned in the modern revival of traditional foods and foraging. The digging stick (kō) he presided over survives in museum collections and in proverb: wild food is the food no one can fence, sell, or tax. Orbell's Concise Encyclopedia and Māori-medium teaching keep his name current, and the distinction he embodies — planted versus gathered — remains one of the most elegant classificatory ideas in any Polynesian pantheon.
lore.archaeology: No image or named shrine of Haumia survives — his was a cult of practice, not of temples. The material record is indirect but abundant: archaeobotanical studies of starch residues on prehistoric stone tools from sites across Aotearoa confirm that bracken fernroot was a dietary staple from the earliest settlement, and earth-oven (hāngī / umu tī) cooking features — fire-cracked stones in pits — are among the most common archaeological features on pre-European sites. Hardwood digging sticks (kō) survive in museum collections, their blades polished by generations of use. The archaeological signature of Haumia is, fittingly, everywhere and nowhere: not a temple to the god, but a landscape of fern country opened, dug, and steamed in his name.
lore.syncretism: Within Polynesia, Haumia's closest relations are his own brothers. Rongo(-māui) — in Hawai'i Lono, in the Cook Islands Rongo — rules cultivated food and agriculture, and the two are sometimes treated as aspects of one god of vegetation; Margaret Orbell notes that in some recensions Haumia barely appears apart from Rongo. The wider Polynesian pattern is consistent: Tangaroa of the sea, Tāne of the forest, Rongo of the garden, Haumia of the wild ground. No Greco-Roman equivalent maps cleanly onto him — even Demeter presides over cultivated grain and never descends into the distinction the Māori make between what is planted and what is gathered. The most instructive comparison is structural: Haumia, like the Greek deities of the wildwood, sanctifies the food that lies outside the fence. In the modern revival of mātauranga Māori he has been recovered as the emblem of the uncultivated larder — the fern country that fed Aotearoa before agriculture and still feeds its imagination.

pronunciation.approximation: 'FEE-roh' — the wh is an f-sound in most modern Māori, and the r is trilled.
pronunciation.note: Whiro is single-tier Tier 2: ASCII preserves everything the Māori name requires; the digraph wh already encodes the f-sound to those who know Māori orthography. His epithet -te-tipua marks him as a tipua, a goblin-like being — a class, not a compliment.

domains.title: Whiro
domains.subtitle: Darkness
domains.lead: Whiro is the Māori personification of darkness, evil, and death — the adversary of Tāne and the lord of the night-world. He sends sickness, commands the reptiles of the night, and, in the oldest accounts, wars against every ascent toward light, knowledge, and life.

cards.name: Lord of Darkness
cards.desc: He rules the Pō, the realm of night and the dead that lies beneath and behind the world of light.

cards.name: Enemy of Tāne
cards.desc: He battles Tāne at every ascent — the cosmic rival who must be defeated for knowledge to come down.

cards.name: Sender of Sickness
cards.desc: Disease is his assault; the tohunga's art was, in origin, the war against his influences.

cards.name: Father of the Lizards
cards.desc: He is styled ancestor of the ngarara, the reptiles — the creatures Māori tradition reads as his embodied kin.

symbols.name: The Lizard (Moko/Ngarara)
symbols.meaning: His embodied kin — reptiles were feared as carriers of his malign influence (hence 'the lizard of death')

symbols.name: The Night (Pō)
symbols.meaning: His domain — the darkness that preceded light and that receives the dead

symbols.name: The War-Party of Spirits
symbols.meaning: The host of atua he leads against the worlds of light, named in accounts of Tāne's battles

symbols.name: Sickness (Mate)
symbols.meaning: The weapon he hurls — illness conceived as an invading atua to be fought and expelled

symbols.name: The Underworld Path
symbols.meaning: The descent to Rarohenga over which, in some traditions, he holds final power

mythology.lead: Whiro's mythology is an antagonist's dossier — he exists in the Māori corpus chiefly as the power Tāne and the tohunga must overcome. The sources are nineteenth-century records of oral tradition (Grey 1855; White 1887–90; Best 1925), and they agree on his office while differing on his genealogy and extent.

myths.title: The War Over the Baskets of Knowledge
myths.text: In the great myth preserved by George Grey (Polynesian Mythology, 1855; Nga Mahi a nga Tupuna), Tāne ascends through the layered heavens to obtain the three baskets of knowledge (ngā kete o te wānanga) for humankind. Whiro — Whiro-te-tipua — marshals the powers of darkness against the ascent, and the myth is explicitly a war: each heaven is contested, and Tāne prevails only with the aid of the winds and ancestor-gods above. Grey's text, dictated by Māori experts in the 1850s, is our fullest witness; the Tūhoe versions add that the battle-lines were drawn anew in each heaven as Tāne climbed. The variant accounts collected by Elsdon BestThe variant accounts collected by Elsdon Best (Tūhoe, 1925) and John White (Ancient History of the Maori) fill in different battle-lines. Whatever the version, the structure is fixed: knowledge descends only through victory over darkness, and darkness is a person who resents the delivery.

myths.title: Whiro and the Descent to Pō
myths.text: Māori eschatology sends the dead (ngā mate) to the underworld of Rarohenga, in the keeping of the goddess Hine-nui-te-pō. Within that realm the sources assign Whiro a dreadful office: Best (Tūhoe, 1925) records that Whiro consumes the dead — the final extinction that awaits those who pass fully into his night — while other authorities make the underworld a guarded, not devoured, existence. Best records how carefully the dying were guarded: kin kept vigil so the soul's journey began rightly, for a misstep on the path meant falling among the powers that answered to Whiro rather than to the ancestors. The disagreement is itself instructive:The disagreement is itself instructive: Māori tradition was not systematic about its dark gods. What holds across the accounts is the direction of dread: after death lies a jurisdiction Whiro administers, and his administration is nothing to hope for.

lore.culturalLegacy: Whiro was never worshiped — he had no marae, no priesthood, no offering; his 'cult' is a vocabulary of avoidance and exorcism. His legacy runs through language and practice instead: the fear of lizards as omens, the ritual cautions of the night, and the entire therapeutic tradition of the tohunga, whose first question — which atua did this? — assumes his world. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries Whiro has become a figure of the Māori cultural renaissance: a dignified, fully Māori face for the dark side of existence, used in health frameworks that treat illness within a Māori cosmology (te ao Māori models of wellbeing explicitly name and counter the atua of affliction). A god nobody prayed to thus shapes how a people still prays for health — his lasting temple is the rite that casts him out.
lore.archaeology: As with most Māori atua, there is no material representation of Whiro: Māori religion was aniconic, and no carving, amulet, or structure is identified with him — the dread of his likeness would itself have been a contradiction. The relevant archaeology is contextual: the carved meeting houses whose pou (posts) embody ancestors of light, set against the prohibitions and ritual zones around burial caves and urupā, where his jurisdiction was strongest. Traditional Māori rock art and tattoo (tā moko) employ curvilinear forms sometimes read as reptilian, but attributing them to Whiro exceeds the evidence. The 'sites' of Whiro are instead the documented places of night practice — the sickbed, the burial ground, the lizard-haunted gully — mapped for us by Best's ethnography rather than by excavation.
lore.syncretism: The missionaries who translated Māori cosmology reached immediately for their own devil — and George Grey's English Polynesian Mythology (1855) already frames Whiro as a 'personification of evil' in Victorian moral vocabulary, a reading modern scholarship (Orbell; Craig) treats as an over-Christianization of a more ambivalent figure. Whiro is darkness and death, but Māori tradition also treats night as generative — the Pō is where spirits dwell and from which thought ascends — so his 'evil' is an office in a balanced cosmos, not a fallen angel's rebellion. In the modern renaissance, Whiro has been reclaimed as exactly that: a necessary power, appearing as an antagonist in Māori-language fiction, film, and graphic narrative where a culture works out its relationship to sickness, night, and fear on its own terms rather than Christianity's.

pronunciation.approximation: 'tah-ah-ROH-ah' — keep all four vowels pure, tap the r lightly, and let the middle syllable catch on a gentle glottal stop.
pronunciation.note: Ta'aroa is the Tahitian form of Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa, the name carried across the triangle as Tangaloa, Tangaroa, and Kanaloa. The catalog restoration keeps the older missionary-era spelling used by Henry and Ellis, in which the Tahitian glottal stop is unwritten — a sound DNS cannot carry. Tier 2: no vowel length marks the name; the loss is a display fact, not a judgment of rank.

domains.title: Taaroa
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: In the old religion of Tahiti, Taaroa is not one god among many but the ground of all divinity — the self-existent one who dwelt alone in the primal darkness, burst the shell of his own being to make sky and earth, and fathered or simply is every other god. The first missionary scholars recorded his cosmogony with respect verging on awe.

cards.name: The Unbegotten
cards.desc: Ta'aroa has no father and no mother: the accounts insist he was never made, because before him there was nothing that could make him.

cards.name: Maker of Sky and Earth
cards.desc: He broke his world-shell: the upper half became the sky, the lower half the earth, and the space between them the living world.

cards.name: Father of the Gods
cards.desc: In the fuller tellings he fashioned the other great gods — Tane, Rono, Tū, 'Oro — and set each over a domain of the world.

cards.name: The Distant One
cards.desc: When creation was finished he withdrew to the highest heaven; every prayer began and ended with his name.

symbols.name: The world-shell
symbols.meaning: The egg-like shell in which Ta'aroa crouched alone in the darkness; when he broke it, sky rose from the upper half and earth spread from the lower (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).

symbols.name: The spiral
symbols.meaning: The ʻōro spiral of growth by which creation proceeds outward from a point — the geometry the priests saw in the unfolding world and in the sacred hair of the gods.

symbols.name: The primal darkness (Te Pō)
symbols.meaning: The night in which Ta'aroa existed alone before anything else; creation is not the defeat of darkness but its self-opening.

symbols.name: The opening invocation
symbols.meaning: Every Tahitian prayer and chant began with Ta'aroa's name and closed with it — the priests named him 'the god of gods' before any other name was spoken (Henry, Ancient Tahiti).

symbols.name: The raised stones of the marae
symbols.meaning: The open-air temple platforms of Tahiti with their carved god-houses (ʻōroʻō); his cult was administered by the highest priesthood of the islands.

mythology.lead: Taaroa's mythology is a cosmogony in the strict sense — an account of how anything at all came to be. The Tahitian priests told it to the first missionaries, and it survives in two nineteenth-century witnesses: the narrative taken down by the missionary John Davies and the longer version preserved by Teuira Henry from the scholars of Papeari.

myths.title: Before There Was Anything
myths.text: The old scholars of Tahiti told the missionary John Davies — and Teuira Henry heard it again two generations later — that before there was sky, sea, land, light, or any other being, Taaroa was. He had no father and no mother, for nothing existed before him that could beget him; his cult name Ta'aroa-'onohi-'ote-na'i-'atu means 'Ta'aroa, the self-existing, the origin of all things.' He dwelt in the primal darkness called Te Pō, wrapped in his own shell like a chick in the egg, calling into the void — and no one answered, because there was no one else to answer. The whole of the world-to-come lay folded inside him, as the tree lies folded in its seed, and the first act of the cosmos was that loneliness outgrew its shell. (Davies' account, preserved in Ellis, Polynesian Researches I; Henry, Ancient Tahiti 336–338.) The myth makes the first moment of existence a soliloquy: creation begins as a being who has no one else to speak to, speaking himself into company.

myths.title: Sky from the Upper Half, Earth from the Lower
myths.text: Weary of confinement, Ta'aroa broke his shell open. The upper half of it he raised high above him and made the sky; the lower half he spread out beneath him and made the earth. From himself he brought forth the sea, the springs, the rocks and sands, the trees and plants, the fish and birds, and the land animals — the whole inventory of the world drawn, item by item, out of his own being, nothing borrowed and nothing left over. In Henry's version he then turned to its government, which is where the third myth begins. (Henry, Ancient Tahiti 336–349; Ellis, Polynesian Researches I.) The image is precise and strange: the cosmos is not built from outside materials but hatched — the world as the broken shell of a god who could no longer bear to be alone.

lore.culturalLegacy: Taaroa's direct cult ended in the early nineteenth century, but his name never left Tahiti. It lives in the great marae the Polynesian nations are rebuilding: Taputapuātea on Ra'iatea, dedicated to his son 'Oro, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2017 and re-consecrated by delegations from across the triangle. The cosmogony recorded by Henry remains a foundational text of Polynesian studies, taught wherever the old religion is taken seriously as theology rather than curiosity. Contemporary Tahitian dancers and orators invoke Ta'aroa as the name of origins in the renaissance of ʻōrero and ori Tahiti. And because the creation chant opens every traditional ceremony with his name, 'Ta'aroa' has become the shorthand Polynesians reach for when they want to say: this is where we begin.
lore.archaeology: No temple of Ta'aroa survives intact — the LMS converts dismantled the marae — but the stone platforms do: hundreds of paved marae with their upright back slabs (unu) and stepped god-houses (ʻōroʻō) dot the Society Islands, most famously the great complex of Taputapuātea at 'Ōpōa, Ra'iatea (UNESCO World Heritage, 2017). The restored valley marae of 'Ārahurahu in Papeari preserves the setting Henry's informants described. Carved tiki figures attest the anthropomorphic image of the gods: the celebrated figure A'a, from Rurutu in the Austral Islands (British Museum), a deity studded with thirty small figures, is widely read as the creator teeming with the gods and people he brought forth.
lore.syncretism: When the London Missionary Society reached Tahiti in 1797, the first catechists did not find a clutter of squabbling idols — they found a supreme god whose creation narrative sounded uncomfortably like Genesis, and they said so in their journals. Tahitian scholars who worked with them, the deacons of the mission schools, readily compared Ta'aroa to Jehovah, a comparison that eased conversion and ultimately doomed the cult: the great marae were abandoned within a generation, the god-houses burned or left to rot. Ta'aroa survived in the cult of his son 'Oro, whose war-god religion absorbed the national priesthood. In the western islands his own name lived on as Tangaloa, creator of Tonga and Samoa; in Aotearoa it had already become Tangaroa, lord of the sea; in Hawai'i, Kanaloa, god of the deep. One god, three more names, many biographies — the comparative method's favorite case.

pronunciation.approximation: 'tah-ngah-LO-ah' — stress falls on the third syllable, and the g is a soft 'ng,' never a hard English g.
pronunciation.note: Tagaloa is single-tier Tier 2: the restoration adds no feature that plain ASCII loses — no diacritic and no distinctive atomic letter — under the mechanical tier rule. The name's dignity is carried by its meaning, 'The Lord,' and by the scholarly consensus behind the restoration (Tregear, Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary; Craig 1989).

domains.title: Tagaloa
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: Tagaloa is the supreme creator god of the Samoan islands, lord of the layered heavens who looked down on the empty sea and made the land. He is the maker of islands, the father of gods and chiefs, and the dweller in the highest sky — the figure around whom Samoan cosmology turns.

cards.name: Creator of the Isles
cards.desc: He threw down the vine and stone from which the Samoan islands were formed, founding the world itself.

cards.name: Lord of the Heavens
cards.desc: He dwells in Lani-uli, the highest of the layered heavens, above wind, rain, and the soaring birds.

cards.name: Father of Sina
cards.desc: His daughter Sina, mother of chiefs, anchors the island's greatest cycle of stories.

cards.name: Ocean's Lord
cards.desc: Across Polynesia his name is the sea's: Tangaroa in Aotearoa, Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Kanaloa in Hawai'i.

symbols.name: The Vine of the Isles
symbols.meaning: The heavenly vine Tagaloa let down into the sea, whose parts became the islands of Samoa

symbols.name: The Layered Heavens
symbols.meaning: Lani-uli and the descending storeys of the sky, his dwelling above all clouds

symbols.name: The Coconut Palm
symbols.meaning: Born from the body of the eel Tuna in the Sina cycle that belongs to Tagaloa's household

symbols.name: The Star-Path
symbols.meaning: In the wayfinding revival, the ocean road by which his dispersed namesakes are rejoined

mythology.lead: Tagaloa's mythology is cosmogony in the strict sense — stories of how land, people, and rank came to be. It survives not in epic but in creation chants recorded by nineteenth-century missionaries and ethnographers, whose accounts disagree in detail but agree that the world began when the Lord of the Heavens acted upon the sea.

myths.title: The Vine Let Down into the Sea
myths.text: In the beginning Tagaloa dwelt alone in Lani-uli, the highest heaven, and beneath him lay only the boundless sea. He let down into the waters a vine from the sky; where its parts touched the surface, the islands of Samoa rose. On the largest he set the first settlement, and from the sky he watched over it. The fullest form of this creation account was recorded by the missionary J. B. Stair in Old Samoa (1897) and compared with related versions by Augustin Krämer in The Samoa Islands (1902); George Turner had published a shorter form in Nineteen Years in Polynesia (1861). Manu'a, the island group of the myth's first landing, is still styled the 'beginning of Samoa' in formal oratory, and the creation chant remained the deep charter for its paramount titles. The story is the charter of Samoan identity:The story is the charter of Samoan identity: the homeland is not discovered but made — thrown down from heaven and rooted in the sea.

myths.title: Sina and the Eel
myths.text: Tagaloa's daughter Sina came down to the pool of Mata o le Alelo to bathe, where a great eel, Tuna, confessed its love. When the eel was killed at Sina's command, she buried its head, and from it grew the first coconut palm — its two eyes, mouth, and body still showing on the nut. The tale was recorded across Polynesia (Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, 1876; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology, 1970, §§ on the coconut cycle) and became the most retold of all Samoan stories. In Samoa the cycle carries a chiefly resonance as well: Sina's name became a byword for beauty in proverb, and her bathing pool, Mata o le Alelo, was pointed out to visitors into the twentieth century. The myth answers a child's questionThe myth answers a child's question — why does the coconut look like a face? — and binds the staple tree of island life to the death of an impossible love.

lore.culturalLegacy: Tagaloa's most durable legacy is genealogical. Samoan orators trace chiefly lines (gafa) to divine ancestors of his household, and the sacred honorifics of chiefly oratory still invoke the sky's lordship. His daughter Sina gave her name to one of the most widespread of all Polynesian story-cycles — found from Samoa to Mangaia to Hawaii — and the proverbial Sina remains a figure of beauty and longing in Samoan speech. The god's name lives quietly in the landscape: villages, titles, and the old name Savai'i-region traditions. Since the 1970s the Pacific-wide voyaging renaissance has restored Tagaloa–Tangaroa–Kanaloa to active cultural memory: the canoe is again read as the sea-god's vehicle, and the navigator's art, once missionized into silence, is once more taught as his inheritance.
lore.archaeology: No cult image of Tagaloa is known — Samoan religion, like Polynesian religion generally, was essentially aniconic, and its temples were open-air malae and stone platforms rather than statue houses. The material landscape nevertheless preserves his world: Pulemelei mound on Savai'i, the largest prehistoric monument in Polynesia (roughly 60 × 50 m, dated by some researchers to the first millennium CE), served as a ceremonial platform, though which god it served is beyond proof. Scattered stone platforms, star mounds for pigeon-snaring (tia seu lupe), and chiefly burial sites across 'Upolu and Savai'i map the sacred geography the myths describe. The 'archaeology' of Tagaloa himself is documentary: the creation accounts recorded by Turner (1861), Stair (1897), Krämer (1902), and in the Journal of the Polynesian Society remain the primary evidence.
lore.syncretism: Christian missionaries arriving in Samoa in the 1830s found Tagaloa the principal rival of their God and absorbed rather than destroyed him: his title 'Atua' became the generic word for the Christian deity, and his mythology was pushed into folklore, where it survived. The pan-Polynesian evidence suggests an older unity: Tangaroa of Aotearoa, Ta'aroa of Tahiti, and Kanaloa of Hawai'i are cognate names with divergent portfolios, a pattern linguists explain by the settlement of the Pacific out of the Samoa–Tonga region (Tregear's comparative dictionary; Craig 1989). In Hawai'i, Kanaloa survives as the twin and companion of Kāne, the two wandering the islands together as culture-bringers — a pairing that arguably preserves Tagaloa's original creative role. In the twentieth century the Polynesian Voyaging Society's revival of long-distance navigation deliberately re-enshrined these sea-gods: Hōkūleʻa's ocean road was, in the crews' own framing, Tangaroa's and Kanaloa's road again.

pronunciation.approximation: 'nah-fah-NOO-ah' — stress falls on the penultimate syllable as in all Sāmoan words; every syllable is open and clean.
pronunciation.note: Nafanua is Tier 2: the restoration differs from the ASCII form only in capitalization — no diacritic, length mark, or distinctive letter is lost. Sāmoan stress falls predictably on the penultimate syllable, so no accent is required to recover the spoken name.

domains.title: Nafanua
domains.subtitle: War
domains.lead: Nafanua is the Sāmoan war goddess 'hidden in the earth': daughter of the underworld king Saveasi'uleo, she rose from the ground at Falealupo to overthrow tyrannical chiefs, took the malo — the rule of the districts — for herself, and prophesied the governments that would come after her. She is war waged for the oppressed, prophecy spoken from below, and salvation arriving from the most unlikely place.

cards.name: Righteous War
cards.desc: She led the people of Falealupo against chiefs whose demands of pigs and kava had become tyranny, striking them down with her war club.

cards.name: Prophecy
cards.desc: She foretold that rule would come to Samoa from the west and that only a remnant would remain — words later read as foretelling the missionaries and the colonial government.

cards.name: Hidden in the Earth
cards.desc: Her name is her biography: the child of a buried shame, raised beneath the soil of Falealupo, unknown until the moment she rose.

cards.name: Salvation of the Malo
cards.desc: The defeated chiefs ceded the malo, the government, to her — the woman no chief had thought to fear.

symbols.name: The war club Televave
symbols.meaning: 'Blows in different directions' — the weapon Nafanua carried out of the earth at Falealupo

symbols.name: The earth-mound of Falealupo
symbols.meaning: The hidden place at the western tip of Savai'i where she lived beneath the soil before her rising

symbols.name: The cup of water
symbols.meaning: The small mercy a village woman offered the hidden stranger — the act that armed the rebellion

symbols.name: The malo
symbols.meaning: The rule or government of the districts, ceded to Nafanua after the victory and the object of her prophecy

symbols.name: The pig and the kava
symbols.meaning: The tribute the chiefs demanded from every household, and the refusal that sparked the war

mythology.lead: Nafanua's cycle, recorded from Sāmoan oral tradition in the nineteenth century, is Samoa's great story of concealed power: a goddess hidden in the earth, a people crushed by tribute, and a victory that made a woman the ruler and prophet of the islands.

myths.title: The Tattoo Voyage of Taema and Tilafaiga
myths.text: Before Nafanua's story begins, the sources tell of her mother Tilafaiga and her twin Taema. Born joined at the back, the girls were cut apart at 'Aopo on Savai'i with the obsidian teeth of the Fijian king Tui Fiti. Sent to Fiji to fetch a gift for their father, the underworld king Saveasi'uleo, they returned with the tattoo instruments — and, laughing, reversed the words of the song that told which sex should bear the marks, so that in Samoa it was the women who were tattooed first. In the recorded genealogies (Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago, 1884; Stair, Old Samoa, 1897) this voyage of the twins explains the origin of Sāmoan tattooing, and it frames everything that follows: Nafanua's drama of concealment and emergence belongs to a family that already moves between worlds — Samoa, Fiji, and Pulotu, the land of the dead. The myth reads Samoa's geography of kinship as a single story.

myths.title: Nafanua, 'Hidden in the Earth'
myths.text: Nafanua was the child of Tilafaiga and her own father Saveasi'uleo — a union the tradition does not hide and does not excuse. Because of it, the infant was spirited away and hidden in the earth at Falealupo, at the western tip of Savai'i; her very name is her biography, glossed in the early records as 'hidden in the earth' (Stair 1897; cf. fanua, 'land, earth'). She grew beneath the ground, fed in secret, known to the village only as a rumor. The detail is theological as much as narrative: Samoa's savior is not born in a chiefly house but underground, the child of a shame that had to be buried. When the chiefs' tyranny later breaks over the district, it is precisely the person the earth was hiding who rises out of it. The myth of her concealment makes Nafanua the standing answer to disgrace — what a family buries, the land remembers.

lore.culturalLegacy: Nafanua endures in Samoa as the patroness of just rebellion and the archetype of the woman who rules. The village of Falealupo on Savai'i keeps her story on its own ground — the site of the earth that hid her and the battlefield that raised her — and Sāmoan orators still invoke her in speeches about legitimate government, the malo. Her tale is told in Sāmoan schools and retold in English-language collections of Pacific mythology; 'Nafanua' has become a girl's name in the islands and the diaspora, carrying the goddess's dignity into ordinary life. In scholarship she anchors the classic study of the Sāmoan myth cycle (Mead, 1930), and to folklorists she stands with Pele of Hawaii and Ina of the Cook Islands as proof that the Pacific remembered female sovereignty long before modern politics rediscovered it.
lore.archaeology: Nafanua's world survives in place rather than on stone: Sāmoan tradition is unwritten, and her witnesses are the living village of Falealupo at the western tip of Savai'i and the district's malae, the ceremonial grounds where her story is still told. The monumental landscape of Savai'i — above all the Pulemelei stone platform, the largest ancient structure in Polynesia, built and rebuilt between roughly 1100 and 1600 CE — records the chiefly world her myth remembers: tribute, work-parties, and the concentration of authority she broke. The earliest written records of her cycle are the nineteenth-century manuscripts of missionaries and administrators (Turner 1884; Stair 1897), and Margaret Mead's 1930 monograph preserves the cycle as it was told in village councils. There are no inscriptions and no images — her archaeology is a village, a battlefield, and a remembered pit in the earth.
lore.syncretism: When the London Missionary Society's teachers landed in the 1830s, Sāmoan orators already had a frame ready for them: Nafanua's prophecy of a government from the west, recorded decades earlier by Stair, was reinterpreted in village talk as foretelling the new faith and the new order arriving across the sea. The tradition was never flattened into Christianity — she remains a goddess, not a saint — but her prophecy gave the conversion an indigenous grammar of expectation, letting Samoa receive the missionaries as the fulfillment of its own story rather than a rupture. In the twentieth century her cycle entered scholarship through Margaret Mead's Social Organization of Manu'a (1930), and her name passed into oratory about lawful resistance to unjust rule. Modern retellings in Sāmoan schools and by the custodians of Falealupo keep the cycle alive, and she has become an emblem of Pacific women's leadership.

pronunciation.approximation: Say 'makemake' with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration 'Makemake'.
pronunciation.note: Makemake is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the restored form is plain ASCII — no diacritic or distinctive letter for DNS to lose — so the temple form differs from the input only by the capital. The restoration restores dignity, not sound.

domains.title: Makemake
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: Makemake is the creator god of Rapa Nui — Easter Island: father of fertility, lord of the seabirds, and the hidden face behind the island's birdman cult. His carved eyes watch from the stone village of Orongo, where each spring a contest chose the tangata manu, the man who bore the god's sign for a year.

cards.name: Tangata Manu
cards.desc: The birdman of the Orongo contest — the year's chosen lord, raised by Makemake's sign: the first sooty-tern egg brought unbroken from Motu Nui.

cards.name: Creator of Rapa Nui
cards.desc: Head of the island's recorded pantheon: maker of humankind, father of fertility, lord of the manu, the birds on which the island's life depended.

cards.name: Orongo
cards.desc: The stone village on the rim of the Rano Kau crater, where hundreds of petroglyphs carry Makemake's enormous staring face.

cards.name: Tapati Rapa Nui
cards.desc: The island's annual festival, where the birdman legend is staged again — the tradition's living return after the nineteenth-century silence.

symbols.name: The sooty tern's egg
symbols.meaning: The unbroken egg carried from Motu Nui by the swimmer: Makemake's annual sign, the seed of the birdman's year of sacred rule.

symbols.name: The wide-eyed face
symbols.meaning: Makemake's carved visage at Orongo, eyes hugely enlarged: the god as watcher — seeing and knowing everything that happens below, the lexicon's gloss made stone.

symbols.name: Frigatebird (manu)
symbols.meaning: The great sea-bird of the contest islets; manu, 'bird', is the root of tangata manu, the birdman himself, and of the god's lordship over the flocks.

symbols.name: Rano Kau crater
symbols.meaning: The great volcanic bowl above Orongo whose rim is the ceremonial stage of the birdman cult — the island's sacred theater, open to the sea.

symbols.name: Aku aku
symbols.meaning: The guardian spirits of the caves in the recorded lore — attendants of Makemake's hidden realm, keepers of what the island buried.

mythology.lead: Makemake is the creator god of Rapa Nui (Easter Island): father of fertility, lord of the seabirds, and the hidden face behind the island's birdman cult. The sources are late — the tradition was recorded in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, after the population's collapse — and they must be read as the memory of a wounded tradition.

myths.title: The Creator in the Chants
myths.text: When the first ethnographers asked the islanders who made the world, the answer was Makemake. Alfred Métraux, working on Rapa Nui in 1934–35, recorded chants in which Makemake appears at the beginning of things as the great god, the maker of humankind, attended by the aku aku, the guardian spirits of the caves; Katherine Routledge heard related accounts during the Mana expedition of 1914–15. The surviving material is fragmentary — Peruvian slave raids and smallpox had shattered the population in the 1860s, carrying off the initiated experts, and much of the theology survived in the mouths of a handful of elders. In the recorded lore Makemake stands at the head of the pantheon, paired with the sea-god Tangaroa. What can be said with confidence is this: on the most isolated inhabited island on earth, creation was not a distant cosmic event but a local one, governed by a god whose staring face was carved into the living stone of the island itself.

myths.title: The Birdman Contest
myths.text: Each spring the men of Rapa Nui gathered at Orongo, the stone village on the rim of the Rano Kau crater, to compete for the title of tangata manu — the birdman. Swimmers called hopu descended the sea cliffs and crossed shark-filled water to the islet of Motu Nui, there to await the sooty tern's first egg of the season. The sponsor whose hopu returned first with an unbroken egg won: he was shaved, painted red and black, given the egg to wear against his body, and seated for a year in sacred seclusion as Makemake's chosen — the year's lord of fertility, whose fortune was read in the fortunes of land and sea. Métraux reconstructed the full ritual cycle from informants' testimony, and Routledge saw the last performances in 1914. The contest means that on an island without kingship, legitimacy came not from conquest but from a god-given sign: the birdman's egg was the island's crown, and Makemake alone conferred it.

lore.culturalLegacy: The birdman's egg became the island's flag: the Tapati Rapa Nui festival, held each February, stages canoe races and dance competitions in which the old birdman legend is the centerpiece, and the winner's crown echoes the tangata manu's year of rule. Orongo, restored as a ceremonial village, anchors the UNESCO-listed Rapa Nui National Park. In 2008 the International Astronomical Union named the dwarf planet Makemake — one of the largest objects in the Kuiper belt — after the god, explicitly honoring Easter Island's cultural heritage. Meanwhile the Rapa Nui language, once nearly extinct, is taught again in island schools, and with it the old names return to living mouths. A tradition recorded from the last survivors of a catastrophe has become the founding charter of a cultural renaissance.
lore.archaeology: The material evidence is concentrated at Orongo, the ceremonial village on the Rano Kau crater rim: some fifty stone houses and over a thousand petroglyphs, including the wide-eyed Makemake faces and birdman figures documented by Routledge (1914–15) and catalogued by Georgia Lee (1992). Several carved slabs were removed to museums in the 1970s after weathering and vandalism; the village was consolidated under William Mulloy's restoration program. The islets of Motu Nui, Motu Iti and Motu Kao Kao below the cliffs preserve the contest's arena; Rano Raraku's quarry and the ahu platforms (notably Ahu Tongariki) form the wider sacred landscape. The Rapa Nui National Park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995.
lore.syncretism: Makemake had no classical syncretism — there was no neighboring pantheon on the loneliest island in the world. His transformation came with catastrophe: after the Peruvian slave raids and epidemics of the 1860s, the survivors embraced Catholicism, and the creator god was absorbed into the image of the Christian God or quietly retired to the petroglyphs. Comparison with other Polynesian traditions remains the useful lens: Tahiti's Ta'aroa and the wide Tangaroa-complex of the eastern Pacific give the intellectual frame for understanding how a high creator-god sits above a crowd of specialist spirits and ancestor-deities. In the modern world the identification has run in reverse — the dwarf planet Makemake, named in 2008 after the Easter Island god, has carried the name of a Polynesian creator into every astronomy textbook, a rare case of a colonial-era suppressed deity colonizing the heavens.

pronunciation.ipaLabel: Approximate Old East Slavic phonemic rendering
pronunciation.approximation: 'svah-ROHG' — stress on the second syllable, hard g as in English 'god.'
pronunciation.note: Svarog is single-tier Tier 2: the ASCII form loses no distinctive letter, since the Cyrillic Сварогъ transliterates without diacritics. His name is usually connected to the root svar- 'radiance, bright sky,' though the etymology remains debated (Gieysztor, Mitologia Słowian).

domains.title: Svarog
domains.subtitle: Sky
domains.lead: Svarog is the elusive Slavic god of the sky, fire, and smithing — known almost entirely from a handful of early Russian and Western chronicle notices that name him, compare him to a smith, and make him father of the sun. He is the Slavs' heaven-forge: the god at whose anvil the daylight was made.

cards.name: The Sky-Smith
cards.desc: The Izbornik of 1073 names him beside the forge-god comparison — heaven's smith, working in radiance.

cards.name: Father of Dažbog
cards.desc: The Primary Chronicle makes him father of Dažbog, the Giving God — the sun as the smith's son.

cards.name: Lord of the Fire
cards.desc: As Svarožič he descends to the hearth — the divine fire that must be fed and kept pure.

cards.name: The Named One
cards.desc: Rare among Slavic gods, he is textually attested — a god pagans and preachers both had to name.

symbols.name: The Forge
symbols.meaning: Heaven as smithy — the place where light and daylight were hammered out

symbols.name: The Tongs
symbols.meaning: The smith's tool, emblem of his craft and of handled, controllable fire

symbols.name: The Sun-Disk
symbols.meaning: His finished work — the Primary Chronicle makes Dažbog, the sun, his son

symbols.name: The Anvil-Stone
symbols.meaning: The fixed point of the sky on which the world-shaping blows fall

symbols.name: Sacred Fire
symbols.meaning: The hearth flame addressed as Svarožič — the god scaled to every home

mythology.lead: Svarog has no surviving epic and no surviving cult — his entire dossier is a few chronicle lines, a gloss, and a name. The mythology below is therefore an archaeology of attestations: each 'myth' is a document, read as closely as the evidence allows, with the tradition's silence stated plainly.

myths.title: Named in the Izbornik of 1073
myths.text: The earliest notice of Svarog comes not from a pagan shrine but from a court book. The Svyatoslav Izbornik of 1073 — a miscellany compiled for Prince Svyatoslav of Kiev — pauses over the Slavic gods to say: 'There is a god named Svarog', and in the surrounding passage draws the comparison with the smith-god Hephaestus, whose forge was read as an image of heaven's fire. The compiler's source was probably a South Slavic manual translated for Duke Svyatoslav's court, which would make the notice the fossil of a lost Slavic mythographic handbook. The sentence is three words in Old Russian,The sentence is three words in Old Russian, yet it proves that in eleventh-century Rus', a century and a half after official conversion, learned men still needed to name and explain the old sky-smith. The attestation tells us less what Svarog did than how stubbornly he survived — a god preserved in the margin of a Christian book.

myths.title: Svarog and the Birth of Dažbog
myths.text: The Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let), in its anti-pagan sermon, records the genealogy plainly: 'from him was born Dažbog' — the Giving God, the sun — a line preserved in the Laurentian and Hypatian codices (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor, trans.). Dažbog in turn gave his name to the Rus' themselves in the chronicler's bitter pun — 'Dažbog's grandchildren,' a folk memory the sermon meant to shame into silence. With it comes the whole logicWith it comes the whole logic of the sky-smith: what a smith fathers is a made light, a produced radiance, and Dažbog's very name ('the giver') reads like the boast of a successful forge. Scholars caution that the chronicler's sermon is polemic, not ethnography. Even so, the fragment preserves a genuine Indo-European intuition in Slavic dress: the sun is not a body but a work — hammered out, handed down, and called a gift.

lore.culturalLegacy: Svarog's modern presence is out of all proportion to his ancient evidence. He is the Slavic god schoolchildren meet first — the smith of the sky in every compendium of Slavic mythology — and his name has become a byword for the lost pre-Christian heritage of Eastern Europe. Rodnover communities keep his festivals; blacksmiths and metalworkers claim his patronage; and in literature from Słowacki onward he stands as the emblem of a Slavic cosmos that conversion only partially erased. The Primary Chronicle line about Dažbog ensured his survival in another way: every retelling of Russian origins must reckon with him. A god of whom three medieval sentences survive now carries a civilization's memory of its own forge — perhaps a fitting tribute to the smith of lights.
lore.archaeology: There is, strictly speaking, no archaeology of Svarog — no image, temple, amulet, or inscription bearing his name has ever been found, and the famous monumental idols of the Slavs (the Zbruch idol, the Svetovid of Arkona, the Prillwitz figures) belong to other gods. The Slavic smith-god is a documentary phenomenon: three medieval texts and their later copies. This absence is itself instructive. Baltic and Scandinavian pagans left cult objects; the early Slavs, converting earlier and building in wood, left almost none — so the chronicles, compiled by their enemies and converts, are the sole excavation. Every claim about Svarog's worship should be weighed against that silence.
lore.syncretism: Svarog's afterlife is a study in resurrection. After the chronicle notices fell silent, he slept for seven centuries — until the Slavic national revivals of the nineteenth century reforged him. Juliusz Słowacki reached for him in Polish Romantic verse (most famously in Beniowski), and comparative mythologists of the era, seeing the forge-and-sun logic, set him beside Hephaestus and Vulcan. In the twentieth century the identification hardened in schoolbook mythology; in the twenty-first, Rodnovery — the Slavic neopagan movement — restored him to actual worship, with Svarog as smith of heaven and patron of crafts. Every layer must be labeled: attested god in the eleventh century, literary construction in the nineteenth, living deity today. Modern scholarship (Gieysztor; Ivanits) keeps the layers distinct — and notes that a god can be reconstructed honestly, provided the reconstruction admits what it is.

pronunciation.approximation: 'STREE-bog', rolled r, stress forward; the second half of the name literally means 'god'.
pronunciation.note: Tier 2. The restored form Stribog preserves no feature the plain ASCII form loses — no diacritic, no distinctive non-ASCII letter — so the temple stands at Tier 2 by the mechanical rule. The gloss 'father of winds' is traditional; the name's deeper etymology is not settled.

domains.title: Stribog
domains.subtitle: Winds
domains.lead: Stribog is the wind-god of the Kyiv pantheon, sixth of the six idols cast into the Dnieper in 988. His name's second element is the word for 'god'; its first is opaque — but the epic tradition calls the winds his grandsons, and that one formula is the whole of his surviving theology.

cards.name: The Winds
cards.desc: His domain by every ancient inference: the moving air that brings thaw, storm, and war-weather.

cards.name: Grandfather of Winds
cards.desc: The Slovo o polku Igoreve calls the winds 'grandsons of Stribog' — a complete genealogy in one phrase.

cards.name: Sixth of the Six
cards.desc: Listed among the idols of Kyiv in the Primary Chronicle: Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, Mokosh.

cards.name: The Opaque Name
cards.desc: No other god's name so resists analysis; its first element is an open problem of Slavic philology.

symbols.name: Wind and weather
symbols.meaning: The element itself, which the epic makes his family: the winds do what grandsons do

symbols.name: Storm cloud and squall
symbols.meaning: The war-weather of the Slovo — the black sky under which Igor's campaign marched

symbols.name: The steppe horizon
symbols.meaning: Kyiv's winds came off the open steppe; his one vivid scene is a steppe wind rising from the sea

symbols.name: The moving air of thaw
symbols.meaning: The spring winds that break the river ice — function inferred from his wind-kin, not attested

mythology.lead: The sources for Stribog are two lines long: a place in the chronicle's list of drowned idols, and a genealogy in the nation's greatest poem. Everything else — his character, his rites, his season — is inference, and this entry says so wherever inference is doing the work.

myths.title: The Idols in the Dnieper
myths.text: When Vladimir's baptism swept the old pantheon into the Dnieper in 988, the Primary Chronicle preserved the full list of the drowned: Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh. No anecdote attaches to Stribog — no oath, no sorcerer, no gloss, no weeping crowd. Of the six he is the most silent: not first like Perun, not glossed like Dažbog, not folk-remembered like Mokosh. Yet the chronicler's list is itself a kind of myth — the orderly procession of gods into the river, each name checked off as it sinks, is the Christian founding story of Rus', and Stribog's place in that procession is the entire record of his worship. A god can be a major power and still leave no story; the river took his narrative along with his statue, and the list is the wake.

myths.title: The Grandsons of Stribog
myths.text: The single vivid sentence about Stribog stands in the Slovo o polku Igoreve (c. 1185), the greatest work of Old Rus' literature. As Igor's doomed army rides out against the Polovtsians, the poet summons the omens, and the winds rise on cue: 'Then the winds, Stribog's grandsons, blew from the sea' — a squall driving the dust and the portents before it. The phrase is a fossil of theology. Where a monk would write 'God sent a storm,' the epic poet instinctively reaches for kinship: the winds are not Stribog's subjects or his weapons but his grandsons, doing what grandsons do — arriving uninvited, raising a racket, unmistakably of the family. Two centuries after the idols sank, the grammar of the old pantheon still blew through the language like weather that knows its own name.

lore.culturalLegacy: Stribog's legacy is almost entirely onomastic and literary. The Slovo's phrase 'Stribog's grandsons' entered every anthology of Old Rus' literature and every schoolroom, so that his name survives more widely read than those of gods with far richer cults. Modern paganism adopted him enthusiastically but thinly: he appears in Rodnover calendars and in fantasy fiction, games, and brand names, usually as a generic wind or storm patron — attributes supplied by authors, not sources. For linguists he remains a standing exhibit in seminars on Slavic theonymy, a name whose opaque first element defeats each new generation of etymologists. If Perun is the god who would not die and Veles the god who would not stay hidden, Stribog is the god who never quite existed in the record — a place kept for the wind in the pantheon's seating plan, honored now mostly by being quoted correctly.
lore.archaeology: No artifact, building, image, or inscription can be tied to Stribog. Unlike Perun's Peryn' enclosure or Veles's Novgorod street, the wind-god left no footprint in the ground, and the destruction of 988 swept away whatever shrine the Kyiv hill may have held. Wind and storm imagery on medieval jewelry and amulets — whirlwind stamps, storm-bird pendants — is sometimes laid at his door, but the attributions are decorative rather than demonstrated, and nothing bears his name. The Slovo's 'grandsons of Stribog' remains his only monument: a line of verse that has outlasted every temple in the pantheon, copied in more than a hundred manuscripts of the national epic and read aloud in classrooms eight centuries after the last wind was officially his.
lore.syncretism: Stribog attracted no Christian successor — no saint took the winds from him the way Elijah took Perun's storm — and Byzantine writers had no classical slot for a wind-god, so no interpretatio rescued him either. His afterlife is purely literary and comparative. Comparative mythology seats him beside the Vedic Vāyu, master of the winds, and beside the Greek winds as a brood rather than a person — Aeolus managing his bag of quarrelsome grandchildren. In the twentieth century Rodnover calendars promoted him as a god of winds and weather, roles extrapolated from the Slovo formula; fantasy fiction and games drift him as a stock 'old Slavic' name. The most honest syncretism is the one the poet performed unwittingly: naming the winds a family. That is how a polytheist sky is actually experienced — every gust somebody's relative, every storm a household arriving.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SEE-mar-gl' — three quick syllables; a Slavic tongue shaped the foreign name until it could be declined.
pronunciation.note: Tier 2. The restored form Simargl preserves no feature the plain ASCII form loses; the temple stands at Tier 2. The name's Iranian origin is among the most secure facts about this figure.

domains.title: Simargl
domains.subtitle: Winged Guardian
domains.lead: Simargl is the strangest god in the Kyiv pantheon: a name borrowed from the Iranian Simurgh, worn smooth by Slavic tongues, standing sixth among Vladimir's idols in 988 with no story, no oath, and no gloss to say what he did. Scholars have made him a guardian of seeds and plant life by inference; the sources themselves are silent.

cards.name: The Idols
cards.desc: One of the six gods of Kyiv drowned in the Dnieper in 988, listed without comment by the Primary Chronicle.

cards.name: Iranian Wings
cards.desc: His name is the Simurgh of Persian epic — a loan carried north by steppe contact, like amber carried by rivers.

cards.name: Guardian of Seeds?
cards.desc: Rybakov's influential hypothesis made him protector of sown fields — a reconstruction, not an attestation.

cards.name: The Silent One
cards.desc: No oath, gloss, festival, or folk name survives — the least documented god of the six.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: From the Simurgh lineage: the composite winged guardian of Iranian iconography, adapted to Slavic soil

symbols.name: Grain and seed
symbols.meaning: Under Rybakov's hypothesis, the sprouting seed he guards against the chthonic adversary

symbols.name: Lion's paws, dog's head
symbols.meaning: The Simurgh's composite body — part dog, part lion, part bird — carried inside the loanword's meaning

symbols.name: Fire on the hill
symbols.meaning: The 980 sacrifices on Kyiv's hill included him; whatever received the offering, flame was its medium

mythology.lead: Simargl has no mythology in the ordinary sense — no tale was ever told about him. He exists as a single line in a chronicle, a name of Iranian ancestry, and a century of scholarly argument about what a winged guardian was doing in a Slavic pantheon.

myths.title: The Idols in the Dnieper
myths.text: In 988 the Primary Chronicle's procession of drowned gods includes, between Stribog and Mokosh, a name no Slavic tongue built: Simargl. The chronicler lists him without curiosity, one idol among six, but modern scholarship has never been able to leave him alone — because his name betrays a long journey, from the Iranian Simurgh, through the speech of steppe peoples who traded and raided along the Black Sea, into the capital of Christianizing Rus'. A pantheon is a nation's self-portrait; Kyiv's included a god borrowed from Persia's. The chronicle line is the whole dossier: no oath, no gloss, no sorcerer, no saint. One drowning, recorded by the enemies who arranged it — and a foreign accent still audible in the name as it went under. No later source ever asked who had carried him there; only modern scholarship heard the accent at all.

myths.title: A Name from Persia
myths.text: The Simurgh of Iranian tradition is one of the oldest great birds of world mythology. In the Avesta she roosts in the branches of the sacred tree; across Sogdian and Sasanian art she spreads composite wings over the Tree of Life; and in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh she rears the hero Zal and guides his son Rostam through every impossible task — part dog, part lion, part bird, and wholly wise. How her name crossed into Slavic as Simargl is the ordinary work of steppe history: Alanic- and Sarmatian-speaking peoples of the north Pontic steppe served as carriers, and a worn-down Simurgh entered East Slavic speech generations before a chronicler wrote it down. The borrowing tells its own myth: a god can be an import, and a pantheon a port — Kyiv's sky had been in conversation with Persia's for centuries before either had a church.

lore.culturalLegacy: Simargl's legacy divides in two. Among Iranists he is a footnote in the biography of the Simurgh — evidence of how far the great bird's name flew, from Avestan hymns to a chronicle on the Dnieper. Among Slavists and the wider public he is the patron of gardens and sown fields, a role created almost entirely by Rybakov's twentieth-century reconstruction and embraced with enthusiasm by Rodnover communities, children's encyclopedias, and fantasy games, where winged guardians named Simargl recur from Minsk to the app stores. The historical god is a lesson in how reception manufactures memory: two lines of real evidence, a century of confident elaboration, and a deity who now feels as anciently Slavic as Perun — though his wings were grown on the Iranian plateau and only molted into Slavic on the way north.
lore.archaeology: No material evidence names or securely depicts Simargl. Candidates have been proposed — winged figures on medieval pendants, Tree-of-Life motifs on jewelry, the enigmatic four-sided Zbruch idol, more often assigned to Svetovit — but none carries an inscription, and the Iranian visual language he would have borrowed is precisely what Christian-era Rus' did not carve. The Kyiv hill of 988 has yielded no shrine deposit attributable to him. His 'archaeology' is therefore the archaeology of the steppe itself: Sarmatian and Alanic grave goods of the north Pontic region, with their Iranian animal-style art, supply the cultural bridge his name implies. The absence is itself informative — a vegetation-guardian's cult may have been domestic and unmonumental, kept in fields and storehouses rather than on hills, and such gods leave whorls, not walls.
lore.syncretism: Simargl is syncretism made flesh — or rather, made loanword. His entire existence in Rus' is the product of an intercultural translation: the Simurgh, grandmother-figure of Persian epic and guardian of the sacred tree, re-emerging on the Dnieper as a minor idol with a clipped name. Iranian studies have tracked his relatives across Sogdian silver, Sasanian stucco, and the Shahnameh; Slavic studies have tracked the reception — a name absorbed, declinable, and finally drowned. The Christian centuries had no use for him and no saint took his place, which is why no folk-fossil survives to compare with Dajbog or Sveti Vlaho. In the modern era the borrowing has run in reverse: fantasy fiction and Slavic Native Faith re-export Simargl toward his Iranian cousins, sometimes literally reuniting him with the Simurgh in games and novels — a reminder that gods, like names, travel, and the border between borrowing and genealogy is where most pantheons actually live.

pronunciation.approximation: Say "lada" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Lada".
pronunciation.note: Lada is Tier 2: the ASCII form 'lada' is already the full Latin spelling, and the restoration adds nothing distinctive that DNS would lose. What the record lacks is not diacritics but early attestations — every source naming Lada postdates Christianization by centuries.

domains.title: Lada
domains.subtitle: Love
domains.lead: Lada is the Slavic goddess of love, harmony, and spring — or perhaps a folk-song cry that the chroniclers turned into a goddess. Every written source naming her is late: medieval glosses, a Renaissance school play, and spring refrains sung on Jurjevo (St George's Day). Her divine status is debated; her presence in the song tradition is not.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The name rides on Slavic *ladъ, 'order, harmony, concord' — love conceived as the harmonizing force, not mere desire.

cards.name: Love
cards.desc: Stryjkowski's Kronika (1582) names her the Slavic goddess of love; folk tradition keeps her in wedding songs as the beloved 'lado'.

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Her oldest witnesses are alive: the refrain 'Lado!' still rings through Đurđevdan / Jurjevo round-dances in the Balkans each May.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

symbols.name: The spring round dance (kolo)
symbols.meaning: Lado is sung inside the circle dance that opens the grazing season on Jurjevo — the goddess lives in the choreography, not the statue.

symbols.name: Jurjevo / Đurđevdan (St George's Day)
symbols.meaning: The spring feast whose songs carry her name, absorbed into folk Christianity as St George's day, 6 May.

symbols.name: Lel and Polel
symbols.meaning: The twin companions named beside her in the Roksana play and the chronicles — love flanked by play and youth.

symbols.name: Green branches (zelenika)
symbols.meaning: The green oak bough ritually cut for Jurjevo and carried to the pasture — the spring rite's portable sacred tree.

symbols.name: *ladъ — harmony
symbols.meaning: Her name's root: concord, good order, the reconciliation of lovers — love as cosmic harmony made audible.

mythology.lead: No medieval Slavic text tells a myth of Lada. What survives is a trail of witnesses — a funeral play, a chronicler's glosses, Renaissance mythography, and living spring songs — from which scholarship must carefully separate memory from invention. Her 'mythology' is therefore the history of how a song-cry became a goddess, and an honest temple must tell it that way.

myths.title: The Refrain in the Round Dance
myths.text:
The oldest trace of Lada is not a story about her but a word sung in her place. In the spring round-dances of the South Slavs on Jurjevo — St George's Day, 6 May, when the grazing season opens — the cry Lado! punctuates the melody: greeting, praise, chorus, or the goddess herself, the sources never say. Young people cut the green oak, the zelenika, dance around it, and carry it to the pasture; nineteenth-century ethnographers among Croats, Serbs, and the Balkan Roma recorded the songs with the refrain intact. Farther north the same word softens into endearment: in Polish and Ukrainian wedding songs ladko and lado mean simply 'dear one.' The earliest stratum of the evidence is thus not narrative but music.

If Lada was ever a full goddess, her first body was a song — which is why she has survived every empire that buried her chroniclers.

myths.title: Lada, Lel, and Polel on the Stage
myths.text:
The first text to list Lada among the gods is a joke at her expense. The Kraków school drama Pogrzeb świętej Roksany ('The Funeral of St. Roxane'), composed around 1500 and printed in 1535, brings together three students — a German, a Czech, and a Pole — to argue over whose hero deserves burial. The Pole defends his own ancestors: our gods, he insists, were Lada, Lel, and Polel, and our songs still remember them. The comedy mocks him for clinging to heathenry; but mockery preserves what reverence forgot, and the schoolboy's boast is now our earliest catalogue of Slavic divine names. The sources disagree even here: the play pairs Lada with Lel and Polel, while later writers split the twins differently and added genealogies no one attests.

A goddess remembered in ridicule is still remembered — the play is less evidence of cult than of a name refusing, two centuries after conversion, to disappear.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lada's cult centers are songs, not ruins: Jurjevo and Đurđevdan round-dances in Croatia, Serbia, and Bosnia; the Roma Ederlezi, when spring is ritually opened with the green oak; Kupala's fires on St John's Eve in Poland, Belarus, and Ukraine — a sister spring festival whose own antiquity is equally debated. Her name fared better in the dictionary than in the temple: Polish ład 'order, tidiness', Czech lad 'harmony, proportion', and the adjective ladný 'graceful' all descend from the same *ladъ that scholars hear in her name — love as concord made audible. Romanticism painted her on salon canvases; Slavic Native Faith circles hail her today at wedding rites and spring gatherings. No inscription marks her grave because none marks her birth: Lada lives wherever Slavic speakers still sing lado over a bride or a green branch.
lore.archaeology: No material object can be assigned to Lada, and the catalogue says so plainly: no pre-Christian inscription, figurine, or cult site names her, and the so-called Slavic idols — the Zbruch figure and its kin — depict no identifiable goddess of love. Her 'archaeology' is the archaeology of performance: green-oak branches (zelenika) ritually cut and carried to pasture on Jurjevo, round-dance grounds, and the ritual calendar of Đurđevdan. The written witnesses are manuscripts, not monuments: Długosz's Annales in the Komasius copy (16th century), the 1535 print of Pogrzeb świętej Roksany, and Stryjkowski's Kronika (1582). A goddess whose entire dossier is paper, wax, and song must be honored differently from one with temples — her material record is a living spring.
lore.syncretism: Later ages never found a Roman Lada to match her to, so they invented one: Długosz and Stryjkowski gloss her as Venus, Kromer as a love-goddess, and the equation stuck — every early-modern portrait of Lada is Venus in Slavic dress. The honest parallels are structural: the Greek Horai, guardians of spring's order, and the Latvian Laima, who apportions luck and love, fill her functional niche in neighbouring traditions, though no borrowing can be shown. Folk Christianity absorbed her feast without noticing her: Jurjevo became Đurđevdan, St George's Day, and the Balkan Roma keep the same spring festival as Ederlezi. The twentieth century added a final layer: Rodnovery, the modern Slavic Native Faith, enthrones Lada as a supreme goddess of love and cosmic harmony — a reconstruction built, openly and defiantly, on the refrains and the chroniclers alike.
