pronunciation.approximation: mar-ZAH-nah — the stress falls on the second syllable, and the double n is held longer than English allows.
pronunciation.note: Marzanna is Tier 2: the Polish name is plain ASCII, and no diacritic or distinctive letter distinguishes the restoration from the domain form. What the capitalized restoration restores is not orthography but standing — the scholarly citation of a living Slavic goddess.

domains.title: Marzanna
domains.subtitle: Winter
domains.lead: Marzanna is the Slavic goddess of winter, frost, and death — the withering power whose departure is celebrated each spring. Her name belongs to the cold family of Polish marznąć, 'to freeze,' and her kinship with the nightmare-hag mora ties her to the dying of the year itself. Every March her effigy is drowned so the world can thaw.

cards.name: Winter's Rule
cards.desc: From autumn to early spring she governs the frozen months: fields locked in frost, rivers stilled, the sun weak and low.

cards.name: Death and the Dying Year
cards.desc: Her domain includes the death of the old year — the withered hag whose reign must end before anything can grow.

cards.name: The Drowning Rite
cards.desc: Each spring, in Zielone Świątki ('Green Week'), her straw effigy is carried out and drowned — driving winter from the village.

cards.name: The Morana Family
cards.desc: Under the names Morana, Morena, and Mara she is honored across Poland, the Czech lands, Slovakia, and the Balkans.

symbols.name: The straw effigy
symbols.meaning: The braided doll of rags and straw drowned in the river — the goddess made portable, so the village itself could carry her out.

symbols.name: The river
symbols.meaning: The running water that receives her each spring; drowning is not execution but return.

symbols.name: Green boughs (gaik)
symbols.meaning: The green branches brought back from the drowning — proof that life returns the moment she leaves.

symbols.name: Frost
symbols.meaning: Her visible body on window glass and ploughed earth — the signature she leaves on the world.

symbols.name: The last ice
symbols.meaning: The final snowdrift at the village edge, where the effigy is sometimes burned instead of drowned — the season's funeral pyre.

mythology.lead: Marzanna is a goddess of ritual, not text: no Slavic epic survives to tell her story, so her mythology lives in the calendar — in the spring drownings, the dirges for drowned maidens, and the folk etymologies that name her Frost or Nightmare. The sources are ethnographic and late; the feeling they preserve is very old.

myths.title: Death to the Winter Queen
myths.text: Every spring, in the week the church calendar calls Zielone Świątki ('Green Week'), villages across Poland carry Marzanna out of the settlement: a doll of straw and rags dressed as a woman, crowned, shawled, and splashed with water as she goes. The procession winds to the river or the last snowdrift, where the effigy is beaten, burned, or — most often — thrown into the current and held under until she drowns. The children sing that Marzanna is dead, and they carry home green boughs, the gaik, to prove that life has returned with her going. Jan Máchal described the rite for the Mythology of All Races survey in 1918, and Polish ethnography has recorded it without a break into the twenty-first century. The myth built into the ritual is stark and unsentimental: winter is a goddess, and the year cannot turn until she is dead. The village does not mourn her. It drowns her.

myths.title: The Lament for Kostroma
myths.text: North of Poland the mourning falls on a different name. In the cycle assembled by A. N. Afanasyev and printed by Máchal (Slavic Mythology, 1918), Russian girls sing spring dirges for Kostroma, a maiden of the rites. In one legend she is the daughter of the Polotsk prince Samo; walking on the Volga's bank she fell asleep, the water-nymphs came and braided her hair, played with her — and drowned her. Her death was mourned like a calamity, with funeral songs, and the mourning ended by burying a straw effigy in her place. Afanasyev argued that the dirges preserve a dying vegetation goddess behind the maiden, a reading later scholars have accepted with caution: the songs are genuine folklore, the goddess is inference. Whether Kostroma is Marzanna under another name is exactly the kind of question the fragmentary Slavic record cannot settle. The grief, at least, is real — and it is the grief due to the dying of the year.

lore.culturalLegacy: The drowning of Marzanna is not folklore embalmed in a book; it is a living custom. Every March, Polish schoolchildren still braid her effigy, march it to the river, and throw it in — television covers it, ethnologists measure it, and the rite stands on the Polish national register of intangible cultural heritage. Her wider family stays busy: Morana is drowned in the Czech lands and Slovakia each spring, and Rusalka week in early summer belongs to the same watery calendar of female spirits. In language she survives on both sides of her disputed etymology — in 'nightmare,' if the mora school is right, and in the very word for freezing, if the frost school is. And in the new Slavic paganism she has come fully back: not a demon to be exorcised each spring, but a goddess to be addressed — winter, death, and return, honored in her own right.
lore.archaeology: Marzanna left no temples, statues, or inscriptions — the early Slavs built in wood and wrote little — so her material record is the rite itself. Ethnographic museums in Warsaw and Kraków hold collections of the drowned effigies, rescued from rivers by curators: straw women in shawls, each one a winter actually ended. The written evidence is mostly hostile: medieval Polish church synods repeatedly condemned the drowning and the songs that went with it, which lets us track the custom backward through the condemnations for centuries. Archaeology adds only indirect light — early-medieval Slavic river cult sites with votive deposits are known — but the rite's continuity needs no dig: it has eyewitnesses, from 16th-century clergy complaining about it to news crews filming it this March.
lore.syncretism: Christianity did not erase Marzanna; it rescheduled her. The drowning migrated to Zielone Świątki, the 'Green Week' after Pentecost, so that a pagan death-rite could wear the church's calendar, and medieval Polish synodal statutes thunder against the custom for centuries — the surest proof it never died. Her identity also split along her etymologies: where the frost reading dominated she remained a personified winter; where the mora reading survived she shaded into the night-hag, the rusalka's colder cousin, and into the whole Slavic company of female spirits of death and water. Modernity returned her to dignity: the drowning of Marzanna entered Poland's national register of intangible cultural heritage in the twenty-first century, and Slavic neopaganism (Rodnovery) now worships her openly as a goddess of winter, death, and the rebirth that only her departure makes possible.

pronunciation.approximation: Say 'mo-RAH-nah' in the Polish fashion, or 'MO-rah-nah' in the Czech and Slovak; all three syllables are open and plain.
pronunciation.note: Morana is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the name is plain Latin script with no distinctive diacritic or letter for ASCII to lose. The restoration adds only the capital and the dignity of a citation form.

domains.title: Morana
domains.subtitle: Winter
domains.lead: Morana (Morena, Mara, Marzanna) is the Slavic goddess of winter and death — the cold season and the mortality it threatens made into a single female figure. Where she walks, the ground freezes; where her effigy is drowned and burned, the thaw begins. She is among the few Slavic divinities whose name and rite survive in attestation from the Middle Ages to the present day.

cards.name: The Name That Means Death
cards.desc: Every Slavic form of her name descends from Proto-Slavic *morà — 'death, pestilence, nightmare' — the old word-family of dying that Greek μόρος and Latin mors also inherited.

cards.name: Winter in Person
cards.desc: She is the season itself: Czech and Slovak children still carry Morena's effigy to the water on 30 April, while in Poland the drowning of Marzanna closes the winter half of the year.

cards.name: A Rite That Never Died
cards.desc: No Slavic goddess has a better-attested continuous ritual: the straw effigy drowned or burned at winter's end is described in writing from the sixteenth century and performed to this day.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

symbols.name: The straw effigy
symbols.meaning: The doll of straw and rags dressed as a woman, ritually drowned or burned at winter's end — attested in Polish sources since the sixteenth century

symbols.name: Frozen water
symbols.meaning: Her signature element: the locked rivers and iced-over wells that bind the countryside until she is drowned in turn

symbols.name: The last sheaf
symbols.meaning: In harvest custom the final sheaf of grain was bound into a female figure and kept until spring — the field's own 'death' doll

symbols.name: The night-hag (mora)
symbols.meaning: The demon that crushes sleepers shares her name and her root *morà — plague, nightmare, and death in one word

symbols.name: The spring bonfire
symbols.meaning: The fire that consumes her effigy, releasing the new season and closing the year's account with winter

mythology.lead: Slavic paganism wrote almost nothing down, so Morana's mythology survives as a rite, a name, and a constellation of village customs across Poland, Bohemia, Moravia, Slovakia, and the Balkans — read together, they amount to a complete theology of winter's death and spring's return, kept alive by practice rather than by any book.

myths.title: A Goddess between the Lines
myths.text: Morana reaches us obliquely, through the margins of other people's books. Her earliest written trace is a fifteenth-century Latin–Polish school glossary, the so-called Medulla Grammatice, where the Latin word mors — 'death' — is glossed with the Polish morana; schoolboys were being taught the goddess's name as the plain word for dying. Sixteenth-century writers then describe the rite itself: Marcin Siennik complains of peasants who fashion a straw woman at winter's end and drown or burn her in the name of Marzanna, and Maciej Stryjkowski's chronicle records the custom in the villages of Mazovia. No epic survives in which Morana acts, and no chronicler retells her deeds. What survives is a name, a meaning, and a crowd of village rituals that kept both alive. The myth tells us how this tradition stored its goddess: not in pages, but in practice — in a rite repeated so faithfully that five centuries of theologians could not kill it.

myths.title: The Drowning of Marzanna
myths.text: On the fourth Sunday of Lent — or on the spring equinox in the older reckoning — the village takes a figure of straw and rags dressed as a woman and carries it in procession to the riverbank: Morana's Polish ritual self, Marzanna. The girls who carry her sing farewells to winter; then the effigy is doused with water, drowned, and often burned where it lies. Her Moravian and Slovak cousins carry the Morena doll out on 30 April and throw it into the stream while the children cry that Morena should carry winter out of the village with her. The Church denounced the custom for centuries as a pagan survival; Communist-era ethnography filed it under folklore; neither suppressed it, and after 1989 the rite returned openly to Polish schools. Today children across Poland still drown and burn Marzanna every spring. The rite enacts the year's great transaction: winter is not begged to leave — it is killed, and spring arrives as the corpse sinks.

lore.culturalLegacy: Morana is the rare pagan goddess who never left. Polish schoolchildren still drown Marzanna on the fourth Sunday of Lent in a custom older than the schools; Czech and Slovak villages still carry Morena to the stream at the end of April; Slovene spring songs still remember Morana's expulsion in verse. In the living languages her name became ordinary vocabulary — zmora, mòra, the nightmare — and Romantic poetry adopted 'Morana' as a poetic word for winter itself. Modern fantasy, games, and Rodnovery liturgy have given her the temples history withheld. For Slavic cultures she performs a service few mythologies preserve so vividly: she lets winter be mourned like a person, and killed like one.
lore.archaeology: No temple, statue, or inscription of Morana is known: Slavic paganism built perishable shrines and wrote almost nothing, and the goddess's pre-Christian material trace is effectively nil. Her real archaeology is ethnographic. The rite of drowning the effigy is documented in writing from the sixteenth century onward — Siennik, Stryjkowski, and the complaints of church synods — and was then recorded in detail by nineteenth- and twentieth-century ethnographers across Poland, Moravia, Slovakia, and Slovenia: the straw doll, the procession, the riverbank, the songs. The surviving artifacts are humble and contemporary: the effigies themselves, photographed and collected by regional ethnographic museums, and the festival riverbanks still used each spring. Where other goddesses left ruins, Morana left a custom.
lore.syncretism: Living between Catholic Poland and Orthodox Russia, Morana was reinterpreted by every regime that met her. The medieval Church read the drowned effigy as a Lenten allegory of sin drowned in baptismal water and tolerated the rite once it was moved onto the fourth Sunday of Lent; Reformation-era moralists simply condemned it. Nineteenth-century Romantic nationalism made her a figure of the eternal Slavic soul, while sober philologists connected her to the same word-family as Greek Moros and Latin Mors. She is often paired with the Baltic goddess Māra, who presides over earth, birth, and death in Latvian folk religion; the resemblance is real but the names are not cognate, and the comparison is typological rather than genealogical. Under communism the rite was folklorized; since 1989, Rodnovery groups have reclaimed Morana as a sovereign goddess of the dark half of the year. Each age rewrites her, and the drowning continues.

pronunciation.note: Zmeygorynych is Tier 2: the name is plain ASCII, and its Russian form Змей Горыныч is Cyrillic, outside the Latin restoration system — the transliteration loses no distinctive feature the ASCII alphabet could keep. The placeholder earlier note claiming the ASCII form was 'a DNS compromise' missed that the lexicon assigns Tier 2 mechanically.

domains.title: Zmey Gorynych
domains.subtitle: Three-Headed Dragon
domains.lead: Zmey Gorynych is the fire-breathing, three-headed dragon of the Russian byliny — terror of the Sorochinsky mountains, abductor of princesses, and the nemesis of the hero Dobrynya Nikitich. His name joins zmei, the Slavic dragon, with Gorynych, 'of the mountain': the serpent made into geography.

cards.name: Fire from Three Heads
cards.desc: Each head spits flame; the bylina says his breath scorched the mountains black and burnt the hero's clothing to ash.

cards.name: The Sorochinsky Mountains
cards.desc: His lair beyond the serpent's river — the ridge Dobrynya's mother forbade her son ever to ride toward.

cards.name: Princess Zabava
cards.desc: Prince Vladimir's niece, carried off twice — the abduction that forced the hero to break his oath and finish the fight.

cards.name: The Slayer's Oath
cards.desc: Dobrynya swore on his sword to let the beaten dragon live; mercy once given became the dragon's second chance — and the hero's second battle.

symbols.name: Three fire-breathing heads
symbols.meaning: The bylina numbers them three, each mouth a furnace — appetite that multiplies faster than it can be cut down

symbols.name: The Sorochinsky mountains
symbols.meaning: The named lair of the bylina world — the untamed margin beyond the river where heroes are told not to ride

symbols.name: The wet women's hat (mokryi golvnik)
symbols.meaning: The soaked cap Dobrynya holds against the flame — soaked wool, not steel, defeats dragonfire

symbols.name: The burnt neck-stumps
symbols.meaning: A zmei's severed heads grow back unless the stumps are burned — victory must be made irreversible

symbols.name: The serpent's river
symbols.meaning: The boundary where Dobrynya's horse stumbled — the omen-line between the hero's world and the dragon's

mythology.lead: The crown of the Dobrynya cycle: how a hero's mercy gave the dragon a second life, and how the second battle was won by a wet hat, not a sword. The byliny are oral epic, recorded from living singers in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

myths.title: Dobrynya Rides to the Mountains
myths.text: In the bylina of Dobrynya Nikitich and Zmey Gorynych, recorded by the nineteenth-century collectors of the Kireevsky circle, the hero's mother warns him never to ride to the Sorochinsky mountains, for the fire-breathing serpent holds them. The young hero rides anyway. From a dark cloud the dragon descends with three heads, and fire pours from each mouth. They fight for three days — Dobrynya's arrows spent, his clothing burnt, the earth scorched black around them. At last the dragon begs for mercy: let me go, brave Dobrynya, and I will never again carry off Christian people. The hero remembers his mother's teaching — she who spared the serpent brought grief upon herself — but he sheathes his sword and lets the dragon go. The bylina's first lesson is mercy; its second, still to come, is what mercy costs when it is spent on a dragon.

myths.title: The Second Battle and the Wet Hat
myths.text: The dragon keeps neither his word nor his fear. He seizes Zabava, niece of Prince Vladimir, and carries her to his mountain. Dobrynya rides after him, but at the serpent's river his horse stumbles and refuses the water — an omen he cannot ignore. The second battle is worse than the first: flame no shield can face. Dobrynya survives by his mother's counsel — he soaks his women's hat in the river and fights beneath the dripping hood, the wet wool hissing where the fire strikes it. When the dragon weakens, Dobrynya cuts off all three heads, then gathers the severed stumps and burns them, for a zmei's heads grow back if they are allowed to rejoin; finally he bathes in the dragon's blood and returns Zabava to her uncle's hall. The detail every singer kept is the wet hat: the weapon that wins the second battle is not steel but preparation — soaked wool against dragonfire, and the patience to finish what mercy left unfinished.

lore.culturalLegacy: The byliny are still sung — by folk ensembles in the Russian north and by animators in Moscow — and Zmey Gorynych remains their star monster. His name is the Russian byword for any three-headed menace, from political caricature to sports mascots; 'Gorynych' alone summons the whole image of fire, mountains, and tribute. The 2006 animated feature Dobrynya Nikitich and Zmey Gorynych introduced him to children three generations removed from the last village singers, and Ptushko's 1956 dragon puppet is studied as a landmark of practical-effects cinema. In the global fantasy mainstream he is now the default Slavic dragon — three heads, mountain lair, maidens' tribute — read back into novels and games by writers who never heard a bylina performed. The song outlived the singers; the dragon, characteristically, outlived the song.
lore.archaeology: No monument names Zmey Gorynych; the evidence is textual and pictorial rather than excavated. The dragon lives first in manuscripts — Kirsha Danilov's mid-eighteenth-century collection, the Kireevsky recordings of the 1860s, and the later Gil'ferding expedition collections from the Russian north. He lives second in the folk image: lubok woodcuts of the dragon fight sold at fairs from the seventeenth century onward, and the iconographic type of St George and the Dragon, which popular art quietly converted into Dobrynya's battle. Medieval Russian church sculpture and manuscript margins supply the serpent of Genesis and the dragon of the Apocalypse — the visual stock from which the bylina's Gorynych was assembled. The most vivid material witness is the most recent: the towering three-headed puppet built for Aleksandr Ptushko's film Ilya Muromets (1956), still the most-seen Gorynych ever made.
lore.syncretism: Scholars read the bylina dragon through two overlays. The older stratum is pagan: the Slavic zmei descends from Proto-Slavic *zmьjь, kin to Vedic ahí and Avestan aži, the great serpents of Indo-Iranian myth, and some hear in Dobrynya's duel a faint memory of the storm god's war on the chthonic snake. The visible stratum is Christian: after the baptism of Rus the zmei absorbed the devil's portfolio — fire, the wilderness, the carrying-off of Christians — and folklorists showed how closely the duel tracks the iconography of St George and the Dragon, the saint's spring feast of Yuri's Day folded into the ritual year. In the Soviet century the dragon was nationalized into a fairy-tale villain, and Aleksandr Ptushko's 1956 film Ilya Muromets gave him his definitive pop-culture body, a towering three-headed puppet. In the internet age Gorynych became an ironic self-emblem of Russia: three heads, one fire, famously hard to kill. The layers never replaced one another; the dragon simply grew a new head each century and kept all the old ones.

pronunciation.approximation: SHOH-lotl, long ō on both syllables.
pronunciation.note: Xōlōtl carries two long ō vowels, both preserved in the restoration; the final -tl is Nahuatl's signature consonant cluster, released laterally — the sound every visitor learns on the name of the axolotl, the water-monster that shares his name and, in myth, his skin.

domains.title: The Twin in the Dark
domains.subtitle: Venus's Evening Star, the Dog-Guide, and the Last Transformation
domains.lead: Xōlōtl is the twin who goes down with the sun: brother of Quetzalcōātl, guide of the dead across the underworld's river, and the god who turned himself into maize, maguey, and finally the axolotl rather than be sacrificed. He is the Aztec soul's ferryman — and the lake that still bears his name.

cards.name: The Dog
cards.desc: His animal: the guide that leads the dead across the ninefold river of Mictlān.

cards.name: The Evening Star
cards.desc: Venus at dusk — his station, twin to his brother's morning star.

cards.name: The Axolotl
cards.desc: His final disguise: the water-monster of Xochimilco, gilled and smiling, that shares his name.

cards.name: The Empty Sockets
cards.desc: The codices show him weeping his eyes out at the gods' sacrifice — grief itself, dog-eared.

symbols.name: The dog ears
symbols.meaning: His constant feature in every codex — the faithful guide's mark

symbols.name: The conch and crossbones
symbols.meaning: His lordship of death's roads, shared with Mictlāntēcutli

symbols.name: The maize stalk
symbols.meaning: His first transformation — the god hiding in the staff of life

mythology.lead: Xōlōtl's myths run on twoness: twin of the morning star, guide of the dying sun, the god who is always the second of a pair — and always the one who goes down into the dark.

myths.title: Across the Nine Waters
myths.text: The Aztec dead journeyed four years through Mictlān's nine levels, and at the deep river it was the dog — Xōlōtl's creature — who swam them across: a soul whose family had mistreated dogs in life found no ferryman, while one buried with his red dog had a guide already in the grave (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, trans. Anderson & Dibble — the funeral rites of the dead's journey). The funeral rite killed a dog 'the color of fire' and laid it with the dead to carry its master home. Among the world's psychopomps, he is the only one who comes as a pet — the escort you raised from a pup, not a paid professional of the crossing, and the myth's quiet claim is that loyalty outlasts the life that earned it.

myths.title: The God Who Hid
myths.text: At the creation of the fifth sun the gods gathered at Teotihuacan to sacrifice themselves and set the new sun moving (Leyenda de los Soles, Codex Chimalpopoca). Xōlōtl refused to die: he fled, weeping so hard his eyes fell from their sockets, and hid — as the twin-stalked maize, as the doubled maguey, and at last as the axolotl in the lake. They found him even there, and he died like the rest. The myth is the Aztec anatomy of the price of survival — and of the god who begged to live and serves death anyway: the one who ran is precisely the one the dead meet at the river, as if the underworld drafted its guide from the only god who had tried, with everything he had, to stay on this side of it.

lore.culturalLegacy: The axolotl — Ambystoma mexicanum, the salamander that never grows up, regenerating limbs and heart — took his name into every biology classroom on earth; its survival in Xochimilco's canals is now a national project. The xoloitzcuintli dog is Mexico's national breed, and Dante's Divine Comedy has, in the Mexican imagination, a local answer: the Xolo that carries you across. Frida Kahlo painted her xolos; the 2018 animated films gave him to the world's children.
lore.archaeology: Colima's ceramic dogs — plump, tumored, dancing, two thousand years old — are the west-Mexican ancestors of his cult, buried in shaft tombs to guide their masters. Aztec dog-effigy vessels and the Florentine Codex's account of the funeral dog detail the central-Mexican rite. Xochimilco's chinampa system — the floating gardens where the last wild axolotls hold on — is a UNESCO World Heritage site, the god's water-form's last stronghold, guarded by canals older than the Aztec state.
lore.syncretism: The friars identified him with the devil's lesser angels, but the people kept him closer to a saint of the road: the dog that guards the grave and guides the traveller survived in Mexican folk custom, and the hairless xoloitzcuintli — the national dog, named from his name — was never exorcised. Scholars pair him with every underworld canine from Cerberus to Anubis, and the Maya twins' underworld journey in the Popol Vuh runs on his same road. The axolotl, his water-form, became Mexico's ambassador-species: the smiling face of conservation itself.
lore.originalScriptNote: The codices write him as what he is: the dog-headed god, often shown twisted in transformation — half into maize, half into the water-beast — with the twin's ball-court and the Venus star in his glyphic entourage. The name and the animal (xōlōtl, "water monster," the axolotl) are one word: the god hiding inside his own spelling.

variants.note: Plain ASCII form

pronunciation.approximation: 'eets-pah-PAHL-ohtl' — the name crackles like obsidian breaking; hold the second 'a' and the final 'o' long.
pronunciation.note: The macrons on ā and ō mark reconstructed long vowels, making the restoration Tier 1. The name is onomatopoeic and lethal: a butterfly made of razor-sharp obsidian.

domains.title: Obsidian Butterfly
domains.subtitle: Stars, Tamoanchan, and the Cihuateteo
domains.lead: Itzpapālōtl is one of the most fearsome goddesses of the Nahua cosmos: a butterfly with wings of obsidian blades, mistress of Tamoanchan, and mother of the Cihuateteo. She is beauty that cuts, maternity that devours, and the star-demon who descends when the sun is darkened.

cards.name: Obsidian Wings
cards.desc: Her wings are edged with itztli, the black volcanic glass used for sacrifice and mirrors.

cards.name: Tamoanchan
cards.desc: The paradise of origins, where the gods created the first humans from ground bones.

cards.name: Mother of Cihuateteo
cards.desc: Women who died in childbirth became warrior spirits under her command, dangerous to the living.

cards.name: Eclipse Star
cards.desc: As a Tzitzimitl she leads star-demons against the sun, threatening cosmic collapse.

symbols.name: Obsidian butterfly
symbols.meaning: The union of delicate beauty and sacrificial cutting power.

symbols.name: Knife-edged wings
symbols.meaning: Instruments of war and childbirth, both forms of tearing that bring life or death.

symbols.name: Jaguar claws
symbols.meaning: Her taloned hands link her to the night hunters of the Mesoamerican forest.

symbols.name: Star headdress
symbols.meaning: Her identity as a Tzitzimitl, a stellar power that descends during eclipses.

mythology.lead: Itzpapālōtl belongs to the dangerous borderlands: between paradise and underworld, birth and death, daylight and eclipse. Her myths are preserved in fragments of the Florentine Codex, the Borgia-group codices, and late alphabetic histories — and where the evidence is late, the entry says so.

myths.title: The Lady of Tamoanchan
myths.text: Tamoanchan is the paradise of origins in Nahua thought — a lush mountain of flowers beyond the human world, where the gods dwelt and where humanity was fashioned (López Austin, Tamoanchan, Tlalocan). Itzpapālōtl rules there as guardian and terror at once: in the codices she appears with obsidian-bladed wings and taloned jaguar claws, mistress of a beauty that cuts the hand that touches it. The Florentine Codex treats her as one of the formidable powers of the upper world, and the name itself — ītztli, 'obsidian', joined to papālōtl, 'butterfly' (Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl) — is a theological statement: the loveliest thing in the air, built from the sharpest thing in the earth. In her, paradise and its danger are one flower.

myths.title: The Butterfly Who Led the Chichimecs
myths.text: Later alphabetic sources attach Itzpapālōtl to the Chichimec ancestors of the Mexica. The Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas (c. 1540) names an obsidian butterfly among the wonder-beings of the migration age, and the Anales de Cuauhtitlan preserves the wider lore of the Chichimecs' star-guided wanderings out of Chicomoztoc, the Seven Caves. The evidence is late and fragmentary — friars wrote down what their informants said, and the Borgia-group codices show her sign without narrating her story — so the tradition should be cited with caution. But the association fits her astronomy: a people guided through the dark north by a star-demon. She is migration itself made divine — fragile as a butterfly, cutting as flint, leading the nameless toward an empire.

lore.culturalLegacy: Itzpapālōtl survives where Mesoamerican antiquity meets contemporary creativity. Her obsidian-butterfly form has inspired jewelry, tattoos, graphic novels, and installations that explore the beauty of the lethal. She is also a touchstone in studies of Nahua gender: the Cihuateteo show that childbirth was a battlefield as honoured as the warrior's, and that the dead women who fell in it were not victims but powers.
lore.archaeology: No temple or inscription names Itzpapālōtl; her witnesses are the screenfold codices. Codex Borgia (c. 15th c., Puebla–Tlaxcala region) shows her repeatedly: a butterfly being with obsidian-tipped wings, taloned hands, and starry regalia, presiding over the ritual deer-hunt sequence and the Venus almanacs. Codex Laud and the Tonalamatl Aubin carry her day-sign associations, and the divinatory manuscripts give her sign, Tecpatl (flint), to births beneath her patronage. The Great Temple precinct itself yielded the physical vocabulary of her imagery: obsidian blades and mirrors by the tens of thousands in the Templo Mayor offerings, the sacrificial material her name fuses with the butterfly. Post-conquest alphabetic witnesses — Sahagún’s Florentine Codex (1570s) and the Historia de los Mexicanos — complete the record from indigenous informants.
lore.syncretism: Colonial friars associated Itzpapālōtl with demons of the air and witches, flattening her complex identity into a Satanic figure. Modern scholars and artists have reclaimed her as an emblem of feminine ferocity, the dangerous side of motherhood, and the ecological violence of volcanic landscapes. Her image appears in Mexican feminist art and in celebrations of Día de los Muertos as a skeletal butterfly.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is composed of ītztli ('obsidian') and papālōtl ('butterfly'). Classical Nahuatl used macrons to mark vowel length, now reconstructed from colonial sources and comparative Uto-Aztecan evidence. The final -tl is a single lateral affricate. There is no surviving pre-contact alphabetic text of the name; it is known from alphabetic Nahuatl manuscripts produced under Spanish supervision, above all the Florentine Codex.

pronunciation.approximation: 'TLAH-lteh-KWEH-tlee' — begin with the single 'tl' sound, hold the first and second vowels long, and treat the final -tl as one release.
pronunciation.note: The name is a straightforward compound of tlālli ('earth') and tēcuhtli ('lord'). The honorific suffix is not gender-exclusive in Nahuatl; Tlāltēcuhtli is depicted as both male and female, and sometimes as a toad-like being. Tier 1: the macrons on ā and ē preserve reconstructed vowel length.

domains.title: Lord of the Earth
domains.subtitle: Chthonic Power and Cosmic Sustenance
domains.lead: Tlāltēcuhtli is the living earth beneath the feet of the Fifth Sun, the monster-toad whose body became the world and whose gaping mouth swallows the sun each evening. Unlike the sky gods who demand attention with thunder and light, Tlāltēcuhtli works in silence: receiving the dead, pushing up crops, and reminding mortals that every step is taken on a conscious being.

cards.name: The Earth as Body
cards.desc: Mountains rise from Tlāltēcuhtli's back; rivers flow from its folds; caves are its open mouth.

cards.name: Receiver of the Dead
cards.desc: The sun descends into Tlāltēcuhtli's jaws at sunset; corpses return to the earth that fed them.

cards.name: Agricultural Generosity
cards.desc: Maize, beans, squash, and cotton rise from its body; offerings of blood ensure the earth's continued fruitfulness.

cards.name: Devourer and Transformer
cards.desc: The earth consumes and renews; Tlāltēcuhtli is both tomb and womb, endings and beginnings.

symbols.name: Crouching toad
symbols.meaning: The common posture of Tlāltēcuhtli images, expressing the earth as a low, wide, waiting creature

symbols.name: Gaping jaws
symbols.meaning: The mouth that receives the setting sun and the bodies of the dead

symbols.name: Curved fangs and claws
symbols.meaning: Predatory features that mark the earth's power to destroy as well as nourish

symbols.name: Blood-red coloring
symbols.meaning: Aztec depictions often paint Tlāltēcuhtli red, the color of vitality and sacrifice

mythology.lead: Tlāltēcuhtli appears in several Mesoamerican creation accounts as the earth monster who must be defeated and dismembered before the present world can exist. The most detailed Nahuatl version survives in the Histoyre du Méchique, a sixteenth-century colonial manuscript; the Leyenda de los Soles and the Florentine Codex supply parallel doctrines. These sources are fragmentary and written after the conquest — the tradition itself says so, and this temple reports them as such.

myths.title: The Dismemberment of the Earth Monster
myths.text: Our fullest Nahua creation account survives in a sixteenth-century French manuscript, the Histoyre du Méchique (associated with the cosmographer André Thevet) — colonial, fragmentary, and precious for exactly that reason. It tells that the gods Quetzalcōātl and Tēzcatlīpōca, seeing a great monster in the form of a caiman called Tlāltēcuhtli floating on the primordial waters, transformed themselves into two great serpents and seized her, one by the right hand and foot, one by the left, and tore her in two. From one half they made the earth, from the other the sky; from her hair they made trees, plants, and flowers, from her eyes wells and springs, from her nose rivers and valleys, from her shoulders mountains. The victim did not die quietly: she cried out in the night for the hearts of men, and the gods consented to feed her. The Leyenda de los Soles tells a parallel creation. The myth's meaning is contract, not conquest: the world exists because a being was broken, and it keeps existing only while the debt of flesh is paid.

myths.title: The Sun's Nightly Journey
myths.text: The Florentine Codex — the encyclopedia compiled under Bernardino de Sahagún from Nahua elders in the 1540s–1570s — describes the sun's nightly passage in the plainest physical terms: at evening the sun enters the gaping mouth of the earth in the west, passes through the body of Tlāltēcuhtli, and is delivered again at dawn in the east. To the sources this is no metaphor: the earth has a mouth, jaws, and hunger, and the day itself is a meal it cannot be allowed to refuse. Nahuatl vocabulary underwrites the image — the earth is tlālli, and Tlāltēcuhtli is that land made lord. The doctrine that night is the sun passing through a body made every evening an act of digestion and every morning a birth: in this cosmology time does not flow above the world but through it, and the calendar keeps its count in the gut of the ground.

lore.culturalLegacy: Tlāltēcuhtli entered global consciousness through the vivid monolith discovered during the Templo Mayor excavations in Mexico City — a massive red-painted stone slab showing the crouching, fanged earth lord. The image has become a staple of museum exhibitions on Aztec cosmology and a touchstone for discussions of ecological reciprocity in pre-Columbian thought. Contemporary Mesoamericanist artists and environmental writers invoke Tlāltēcuhtli to express the idea of the earth as a living, conscious, and hungry body.
lore.archaeology: The most spectacular find is the monolithic Tlāltēcuhtli sculpture uncovered in 2006 near the Templo Mayor, measuring more than 4 meters on a side and preserving red and yellow pigment. Templo Mayor excavations have located Tlāltēcuhtli shrines, offering caches, and sculptural reliefs showing the sun entering the earth's mouth. Postclassic and early colonial pictorial manuscripts such as the Codex Borgia and Codex Magliabechiano preserve ritual and iconographic details of the earth lord.
lore.syncretism: Tlāltēcuhtli overlaps with Cōātlīcue, Tōnantzin, and other female earth figures in Nahuatl religion; the gender and precise identity of the earth lord were fluid across regions and periods. In Maya traditions the cognate figure is often the crocodilian earth monster whose body supports the sky. Colonial Christian writers interpreted the earth devourer as a demonic figure, but the persistence of earth shrines and offerings suggests a deeper continuity of chthonic devotion, folded after the conquest into reverence for the land itself and, in the modern period, into an indigenous ecological theology that reads the earth as a living, conscious body.

variants.note: Fully tone-marked dictionary form with the initial low tone (Abraham). Written Yoruba routinely omits tone marks.

steps: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality.
The underdot marks the open vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ and the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/; these are the obligatory phonemic marks.
Tone marks (grave low, acute high) are fully written in dictionaries but routinely omitted in everyday Yoruba writing.
The owned Unicode form preserves the underdots and the tone marks the domain could carry; the fully tone-marked dictionary form is documented in the variants and here.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-ROON-mee-LAH — low 'aw', high 'ROON', then low 'mee-LAH'.
pronunciation.note: Ọrúnmìlà is Tier 1: the dot below ọ and the acute and grave accents that preserve Yoruba tones are distinctive features the ASCII form loses. The dot below ọ marks the open [ɔ] vowel.

domains.title: Witness at Creation
domains.subtitle: Wisdom, Divination, and the Ifá Corpus
domains.lead: Ọrúnmìlà is the orixá of wisdom and the patron of Ifá, the divination system that reads human destiny against the patterns of the cosmos. Present at creation, he alone remembers how the world was founded. Kings consult him before they act; his priests, the babalawos, speak for him through sixteen palm nuts.

cards.name: Ifá Divination
cards.desc: Sixteen palm nuts and the divination chain reveal the odù that governs a situation.

cards.name: Sacred Knowledge
cards.desc: He remembers the verses, medicines, and sacrifices that restore cosmic balance.

cards.name: Witness of Creation
cards.desc: Only he saw the world being made; therefore only he can interpret its deepest laws.

cards.name: Babalawo
cards.desc: The father of secrets — the title of the priests who speak for him in divination.

symbols.name: Ikin palm nuts
symbols.meaning: The sixteen sacred nuts used in Ifá divination; they hold the signatures of the odù.

symbols.name: Ọpẹ̀lẹ̀ divination chain
symbols.meaning: The chain of eight half-shells that provides quicker access to Ifá wisdom.

symbols.name: Green and yellow beads
symbols.meaning: His sacred colours, associated with palm leaves, knowledge, and mature wisdom.

symbols.name: Staff of wisdom
symbols.meaning: The iron staff that grounds his authority and marks the babalawo in ceremony.

mythology.lead: Ọrúnmìlà's mythology lives in the thousands of Ifá verses (òdù Ifá) that record his journeys, judgments, and interventions — wisdom's biography told as scripture.

myths.title: The Witness at the Foundation of the World
myths.text: According to Ifá tradition, Ọrúnmìlà was the only orixá present when Olódùmarè created the earth. He observed the placing of the rivers, the rising of the mountains, and the distribution of destinies, and the corpus never stops drawing authority from that attendance (Abimbola, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus, 1976; Bascom, Ifa Divination, 1969). The other orishas received domains; Ọrúnmìlà received the memory of everything. Because he witnessed the beginning, he can trace any present trouble back to its origin and prescribe the sacrifice that will set it right. The Ifá verses return to this scene whenever authority is questioned, and it has silenced sceptics for centuries. The myth defines knowledge as witnessing rather than power: the one who watched the world being made became the one to whom the world turns when it forgets what it is for.

myths.title: Àgbọnnìrègún, the Medicine That Never Fails
myths.text: Before descending to earth, Ọrúnmìlà received from Olódùmarè the gift called àgbọnnìrègún — the sixteen sacred palm nuts and the science of reading them, glossed in the corpus as 'the medicine that never fails' (Bascom 1969; Idowu, 1962). The myth has a practical moral: the other orishas came down with powers over fire, water, and iron, but Ọrúnmìlà came down with a method. Wherever he travelled — and the verses send him wandering through every kind of settlement — he could answer any question put to him by casting the nuts and reciting the odù that fell. That is why the nuts are addressed with the respect due a founder, and why their loss ends a priest's career. The story makes divination a deliberate endowment, not an improvisation: heaven equipped its witness with the one tool the world would never stop needing.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ọrúnmìlà's legacy is the Ifá corpus itself — one of the largest bodies of African sacred poetry, inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity as the 'Ifa divination system'. His influence reaches into literature, psychology, and ethics: the idea that wisdom is not possession but practice, that destiny can be read but must be met with sacrifice, and that the future is a conversation rather than a sentence. Contemporary African philosophers and diaspora theologians return to him as a model of disciplined, compassionate knowledge — the sage whose authority rests entirely on having paid attention when the world was made.
lore.archaeology: The Ifá corpus is preserved orally and in manuscript form across Yoruba-speaking regions, with material evidence in the divination kit itself: carved palm nuts (ikin), brass ọpẹ̀lẹ̀ chains, and wooden divination trays (ọpọ́n Ifá) whose rims bear the face of Ẹṣù. Bascom's mid-century recordings and Abimbola's transcriptions fixed tens of thousands of verses in writing for the first time. Diaspora collections hold beaded necklaces, iron staffs, and the palm-nut pouches of working babalawos in Havana and Bahia — instruments of a scripture whose primary medium remains the trained and consecrated memory.
lore.syncretism: Ọrúnmìlà travelled to the Americas as the patron of Ifá and the apex of Santería's religious hierarchy. In Cuba, babalawos of the Regla de Ifá initiate through a ceremony that makes them 'godfathers' of the oracle itself, and Catholic syncretism sometimes pairs him with Saint Francis of Assisi, whose humility and poverty invited the identification. In Brazil he is Orunmilá, less publicly prominent than in Cuba but foundational to the Casas de Ifá that preserve the palm-nut casting beside the cowrie oracle. In both countries the figure who witnessed creation ended up witnessing another creation: a religion reassembled in exile, with himself as its librarian.

entries.meaning: The hunter — orisha of the hunt, the forest, and deliberate strategy (standard Yoruba Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì; Cuban Ochosi, Brazilian Oxóssi)

variants.note: Standard Yoruba orthography, fully tone-marked

steps: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality.
The name Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì is the standard orthography of the hunter orisha known in Brazil as Oxóssi.
The underdots distinguish /ɔ/ and /ʃ/ from their plain counterparts; tone marks carry lexical tone (low–high–low–low).
The Unicode restoration Ọṣọọsì preserves the underdots and the final low tone; the ASCII form loses all of them.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-shaw-AW-sih — the dotted ọ is the open 'aw' of 'law'; ṣ is 'sh'; the tones run low-high-low-low.
pronunciation.note: The name in standard Yoruba orthography is Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì, fully tone-marked; the owned form Ọṣọọsì keeps the underdotted vowels (ọ, the open o) and the long double-o while following the diaspora convention that leaves tone marks implicit — the spelling carried across the Santería and Candomblé worlds. Abraham's Dictionary of Modern Yoruba lists him as the god of hunters; the etymology is debated, though the ọ̀ṣọ́ element suggests swiftness. Tier-1 by rule: the underdots and the ṣ are distinctive letters the ASCII "Ochosi" cannot carry.

domains.title: The Single Arrow
domains.subtitle: The Hunt, the Forest, and the Justice of the Patient Shot
domains.lead: Ọṣọọsì is the hunter orisha: lord of the forest, master of the bow, and patron of strategy — the one whose praise-poems say he kills with a single arrow, because he has learned what every hunter must learn: wait.

cards.name: The Single Arrow
cards.desc: One shaft, never wasted: his oríkì hail the hunter who does not need to shoot twice.

cards.name: The Bow (Ofá)
cards.desc: His emblem across three continents — the hunter's bow, carved on his shrines and sung in his names.

cards.name: The Forest (Igbó)
cards.desc: His cathedral and his larder: the deep bush where game, medicine, and danger all live.

cards.name: Justice
cards.desc: In the diaspora he stands with the accused: the orisha of right judgment and the patient case.

symbols.name: The bow and arrow
symbols.meaning: Skill married to patience: the whole doctrine of the hunt in one image

symbols.name: The forest
symbols.meaning: The realm of the provider — game, leaves, and the tests that make a tracker

symbols.name: The single shot
symbols.meaning: Strategy as worship: preparation so complete that one attempt suffices

mythology.lead: Ọṣọọsì's mythology lives in praise-poetry and divination verse — the oríkì that greet him, the Ifá corpus that ranks him among the orisha, and the itan, the sacred stories of the diaspora houses that still tell of the one arrow.

myths.title: The Hunter Who Kills Once
myths.text: His praise-poems are the hunt distilled: the oríkì greet Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì as the hunter who kills with a single arrow — the archer whose patience is so complete that the forest gives him what it denies the noisy and the hasty. In the Candomblé houses of Brazil the same idea opens his festivals: Oxóssi, rei das matas, king of the forest, the provider whose one shot feeds the whole town. The oríkì tradition is not ornament here; it is the liturgy of competence.

myths.title: The Orisha of the Odù
myths.text: In the Ifá divination corpus — the 256 odù and their thousands of memorized verses — the divine hunter walks as provider and strategist: the orisha who knows the paths of the bush as the babaláwo knows the paths of the palm nuts. Bascom's fieldwork in Ife and among Cuban practitioners recorded his place in the diviners' world; Idowu's theology of the orisha sets him among the ministers Olódùmarè appointed over creation's wild half. Wherever Ifá is consulted, the forest has a spokesman.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ọṣọọsì is a living god, not a memory: his festivals still fill the terreiros of Bahia, his initiates still receive the Guerreros in Havana and Miami, and his oríkì are still sung in the tonal Yoruba that the written restoration tries to honor. The single arrow has become the tradition's own emblem of Afro-diasporic resilience — patience, precision, and provision against every odds. The spelling Ọṣọọsì keeps the marked vowels of the language the praise-poems were made in.
lore.archaeology: The hunter orisha's record is oral and liturgical rather than monumental: his corpus is the Ifá verse tradition, the oríkì preserved by praise-singers, and the ethnographies of Abraham, Idowu, Bascom, and Verger. His material culture is real but perishable — bows, iron implements, and forest shrines — and his oldest durable monuments are the diaspora's: the terreiros of Bahia, some a century and more old, the casa-templos of Havana, and the January streets of Rio on São Sebastião's day.
lore.syncretism: The diaspora rebuilt him with local materials and never lost the pattern. Cuba gave him the Guerreros and the courtroom; Brazil gave him São Sebastião's feast-day and the caboclos of Umbanda; Trinidad, Haiti, and the United States received the Lukumí lineages intact. Scholars from Bascom to Verger mapped the route: the Ketu nation's Oxóssi, the Oyo-heritage hunter, and the Yoruba Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì of Abraham's dictionary are one figure wearing three orthographies. His closest cousins abroad are the other divine hunters — but none of them shoots only once.

pronunciation.approximation: ah-gah-NYOO — start low on 'ah', stay low on 'gah', then rise sharply to 'NYOO'.
pronunciation.note: Aganjú is Tier 1: the acute accent on ú preserves the high tone of the final syllable, a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The dot below is absent from the lexical form because the stem vowel is plain /a/, not open /ɔ/ or /ɛ/.

domains.title: Lord of the Volcano
domains.subtitle: Wilderness, Desert, and Terrestrial Fire
domains.lead:
Aganjú is the orixá of the uninhabited places: volcanic earth, desert scrub, and the molten core beneath the mountain. Unlike Ṣàngó, whose fire crackles in the sky, Aganjú's fire moves slowly through stone. He is the son of Odùduwà and Ọbatalá in many accounts, the giant whose strides once shook the earth and whose breath still steams from fissures in the ground.

In Afro-Atlantic ritual he appears as Aggayú Solá, the bearer of the world, a deity so tall that rivers reach only his ankles. To invoke him is to acknowledge that civilization rests on forces older and more patient than human law.

cards.name: Volcanic Earth
cards.desc: Magma, lava fields, and earthquakes are his body; he is the planet's slow, burning voice.

cards.name: Desert Wilderness
cards.desc: The uninhabited plain where no farm can take root; the place beyond the town's edge.

cards.name: World-Bearer
cards.desc: In the diaspora he becomes the giant who supports the earth on his shoulders.

cards.name: Terrible Strength
cards.desc: Force without malice; the power that does not negotiate because it does not need to.

symbols.name: Volcanic stone
symbols.meaning: His seat and his bones; cooled lava is placed on altars to ground his presence.

symbols.name: Palm frond fan
symbols.meaning: Used to cool and direct his immense heat during ritual possession.

symbols.name: Red and brown beads
symbols.meaning: The colors of iron-rich earth, dried blood, and scorched clay.

symbols.name: Giant's staff
symbols.meaning: The walking stick of the world-bearer, marking his stride across deserts.

mythology.lead: Aganjú's myths are less numerous than those of Ọṣun or Ṣàngó, but they centre on a single theme: the earth as a living, burning body that carries human life without belonging to it. Where other orishas crowd the town and its markets, Aganjú's dossier is written at the boundary — volcano, desert, quarry — and in the diaspora's discovery that the wilderness god was carrying the world all along.

myths.title: Son of Odùduwà and Ọbatalá
myths.text: Aganjú's birth is a statement of his character: he arrives from the union of the two powers that divide the Yoruba cosmos. In many lineages he is counted a son of Odùduwà, the royal ancestor who founded the earth's cities, and of Ọbatalá, the white-clothed sculptor of human bodies; the genealogies vary — oral tradition keeps several versions, and no single Ifá corpus settles the question. What the variants agree on is the outcome. This child of kingship and craft refuses both inheritances and chooses the uncultivated bush, the lava field, the place no farm can claim. Where Ọbatalá shapes and Odùduwà rules, Aganjú simply burns and bears. Divination verses recorded by Bascom and others keep him at the world's edge, immense and mostly silent, invoked when the earth itself must be addressed — droughts, eruptions, the cracking of foundations. The myth means that every order rests on an unowned force it cannot command: the volcano is the family member the palace never invited home.

myths.title: The King Who Became the Volcano
myths.text: A second tradition makes Aganjú not a god from birth but a king who became one. Samuel Johnson's History of the Yorubas (1921), the great early record of Oyo tradition, preserves the memory of an Aláàfin — a king of the old Ọ̀yọ́ empire — remembered as Aganjú, whose rule ended in apotheosis: his name passed to the orisha of the wilderness, and the royal cult and the wilderness cult folded into one figure. Johnson is a single, late, colonial-era source, and modern scholarship treats the deified-king account cautiously — it may be a rationalization, or a genuinely remembered apotheosis of the kind Yoruba kingship often produced. But the tradition matters even if it is embroidery, because it explains why Aganjú carries both a king's gravity and a volcano's indifference to law. The myth means that the wilderness god may once have worn a crown — and that a king too fierce for the palace could still find a temple.

lore.culturalLegacy: Aganjú remains one of the less domesticated orixás. He is not the god of the marketplace or the bedroom; he is the god of what lies beneath and beyond. In an age of ecological awareness, his mythology reads like a warning: the ground we build on is alive, slow, and capable of overwhelming any city. His colors — red, brown, and iron — appear in Candomblé and Santería altars, and his giant stride survives in the heavy, deliberate dance of his possessed devotees.
lore.archaeology: Direct archaeological attestation of Aganjú is sparse because Yoruba orixá cults were transmitted orally and through ritual objects rather than temple inscriptions. In Yorubaland, volcanic-stone implements, iron slag from early smelting, and boundary markers in uncultivated bush mark the zones over which such wilderness orishas preside. The diaspora, by contrast, keeps a dense material record: the assentamento — the stone-and-metal altar of Candomblé houses — regularly includes volcanic and iron-bearing stones for Aganjú, his palm-frond fan, and beadwork in his red and brown colors. Cuban ilé-orishá shelves hold similar offerings, and chalk-drawn firmas diagram his volcano in Lucumí practice. The orisha who owns uncarved wilderness lives on in carved, kept, and beaded objects.
lore.syncretism: In Brazilian Candomblé, Aganjú is syncretised with Saint Christopher, the giant who carries the Christ child across water. In Cuban Santería he becomes Aggayú Solá, often paired with the thunder-god Ṣàngó as complementary powers of sky-fire and earth-fire. The identification with Saint Christopher preserves the theme of colossal bearing strength, while the pairing with Ṣàngó maps the volcanic interior onto the stormy sky. Christianity gave him a new face but kept his scale.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-bah-loo-ah-YEH — low on the first three syllables, then high on 'YEH'.
pronunciation.note: Ọbalúayé is Tier 1: the dot below ọ and the acute accents on ú and é are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the acutes preserving high tones, while grave accents would mark low tones. The dot below ọ distinguishes open [ɔ] from close [o].

domains.title: Father of the World
domains.subtitle: Disease, Healing, and the Earth
domains.lead: Ọbalúayé is the orixá who both strikes and heals. He governs infectious disease — above all smallpox — and the earth that receives the body after death. The hand that sends sickness can also lift it, and those who survive what he sends become his healers. In the diaspora he walks as an old man on crutches, wrapped in burlap, with two dogs at his side.

cards.name: Disease and Pestilence
cards.desc: Smallpox, leprosy, and epidemic illness walk in his shadow — he is the scourge no wall keeps out.

cards.name: Healing
cards.desc: The same hand that sends illness can remove it; his priests are herbalists, and his broom sweeps sickness from the house.

cards.name: Earth and the Grave
cards.desc: He rules the soil that receives the dead and the smallest beings that break the body down.

cards.name: Survival
cards.desc: Those who survive his illness often become his children for life — survival itself is the initiation.

symbols.name: Crutches
symbols.meaning: His diaspora attribute, marking lameness and the limit of the human body.

symbols.name: Burlap or sackcloth
symbols.meaning: Poverty, humility, and the rough texture of illness and recovery.

symbols.name: Two dogs
symbols.meaning: His messengers and guardians at the boundary of sickness and health.

symbols.name: Earth-coloured beads
symbols.meaning: Brown, black, and purple beads that link him to soil and burial.

symbols.name: The ritual broom
symbols.meaning: The broom that sweeps a house clean of sickness — his oldest instrument of healing.

mythology.lead: Ọbalúayé's mythology is not a heroic cycle but an oral canon — Yoruba praise poetry carried across the Atlantic and kept in patakís, the teaching stories of Santería and Candomblé. The versions disagree in detail and agree in meaning: affliction is real, the earth sends it, and survival rightly borne becomes holiness.

myths.title: The King Cast Down
myths.text: In the most widely told patakís of the Cuban canon, Babalú-Ayé was not always a beggar. He was a king — some say the proudest of the orixás — who grew contemptuous of the sick, or hoarded the secrets of healing, until Olodumare's judgment fell on him: sores from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, and exile from every door. Only the dogs stayed, licking his wounds, and in their rough tenderness lay the first medicine. Cast out, he walked the earth as the poorest of the poor, and the humiliation remade him: the god who had despised affliction became its master and its cure. His modern collectors — Mason in Four New World Yoruba Rituals, Murphy in Santería: African Spirits in America — record versions that differ in detail; all agree on the moral: the healer must know the body from inside affliction, and pride is the first disease he treats.

myths.title: The Dogs and the Hidden Path
myths.text: Dogs belong to Ọbalúayé on both continents because they live at the boundary he owns — between the village and the bush, the healthy and the sick, the living and the earth that takes them. In Yoruba teaching the dog runs ahead on paths men cannot see; in diaspora patakís it is the dog who leads the sufferer to the stream where the healing leaves grow, or who carries the message between the sick person's door and the orixá's. His devotees keep the image literally: two dogs stand beside the old man on crutches in every altar figure, and dog imagery runs through his beadwork and his cloth. The myth encodes the practical work of healing in an epidemic age — one must follow signs that do not speak in human language, keep low to the ground, and trust the guide that never strays far from the earth that sends both the sickness and the herb.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ọbalúayé's legacy is the theology of illness. In Yoruba and Afro-Atlantic thought, sickness is not mere biological accident; it is a message, a punishment, or a calling, and those who survive smallpox — or the modern afflictions that have inherited his domain — often dedicate their survival to him. The old man's image governed the public meaning of disease in the Americas for centuries: the sick were not hidden but displayed, at the crossroads, on crutches, wrapped in sackcloth, with dogs. In the age of global pandemics his mythology has gained uncomfortable new resonance: the earth still sends plagues, the boundary between health and sickness is still thinner than medicine admits, and the crowds at El Rincón each December are, among other things, the largest annual public acknowledgment anywhere that we are all, sooner or later, his.
lore.archaeology: Ọbalúayé left no inscriptions and no ancient monuments — his material culture is the living altar. In Cuba, the casa-templo and the home altar keep his figure: the old man in burlap on crutches, flanked by dogs, ringed with gourds of grain and bundles of his herbs; the great pilgrimage church of San Lázaro at El Rincón, Santiago de las Vegas, receives his votive offerings by the thousand each December. In Bahia, Candomblé ilé shrines preserve the cowrie strings, earth-colored beads, and consecrated brooms of Obaluaiê, documented by ethnographers since the nineteenth century and by Verger's surveys. Behind the diaspora altar stands the West African substrate: the shrines and guarded groves of the smallpox deity described by Idowu and Bascom, suppressed under colonial medicine, surviving in the secrecy his theology always claimed as its own. His oldest 'excavation site' is the epidemic graveyard itself.
lore.syncretism: In Brazil he became Obaluaiê or Omolu, syncretised with São Lázaro and São Roque — the Catholic saints of sores and plague, whose images (Lazarus covered in ulcers at the rich man's gate, Roch displaying the sore on his thigh) mapped almost perfectly onto the orixá. In Cuba he is Babalú Ayé under the cloak of San Lázaro, and across the wider diaspora he keeps the same two saintly disguises. The mapping was not camouflage alone: it was translation. Catholic hagiography already told his essential story — the despised sick man at the gate who is closer to God than the healthy — and the African canon simply read the saints as another telling of the king cast down. His modern afterlife is global: his earth-colored beads appear wherever the Yoruba diaspora sings, and each December his pilgrim crowds at El Rincón outdraw nearly every other feast in the Americas.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BYE-ah-meh' — stress the first syllable, keep the vowels open, and avoid turning the final vowel into a long English 'ee'.
pronunciation.note: The name Baiame is a romanization of an oral tradition; no single original script exists. PuniCodex renders it as Baiame, capitalizing the conventional scholarly citation form. Because the restoration does not add a diacritic or distinctive letter absent from the ASCII form, the name is Tier 2. The spoken name and the mythic role remain intact; the ASCII string is a DNS convenience, not an ancient spelling.

domains.title: Sky Father and Maker
domains.subtitle: Creator, Law-Giver, and Ancestor
domains.lead: Baiame is the great creator and Sky Father of several Aboriginal nations of south-eastern Australia, above all the Wiradjuri and the Gamilaraay/Euahlayi. He made the land, the animals, and the people, and then gave them the laws, kinship systems, and initiation ceremonies by which they still live. After the work of creation he withdrew to the sky, where he remains as a remote but watchful ancestor, his presence felt in the Milky Way, in the flight of the emu, and in the sound of the bullroarer at initiation.

cards.name: Creator of Land and Life
cards.desc: Baiame shaped the mountains, rivers, and plains, and made the first people and animals. Creation is not a single event but an ongoing relationship with country.

cards.name: Sky Dwelling
cards.desc: After creation Baiame returned to the sky. His camp is sometimes identified with the dark patches and stars of the Milky Way, especially the Emu in the Sky.

cards.name: Law and Initiation
cards.desc: He gave the first laws, the kinship rules, and the initiation ceremonies that turn boys into men. The bullroarer is sounded in his name.

cards.name: Great Ancestor
cards.desc: Baiame is not worshipped in the everyday sense; he is remembered as the founding ancestor whose actions set the moral and social order of the world.

symbols.name: The Emu in the Sky
symbols.meaning: The dark constellation of the Milky Way, a celestial marker of Baiame's camp and of the emu he created

symbols.name: Bullroarer
symbols.meaning: A sacred sound-maker used in men's initiation; its voice is associated with Baiame and his son Daramulum

symbols.name: Stone arrangements and bora rings
symbols.meaning: Earth-and-stone ceremonial sites where initiation and law are enacted under Baiame's authority

symbols.name: Stone axes
symbols.meaning: Often linked to Baiame as tools of creation and as sacred objects exchanged across southeast Australia

mythology.lead: Baiame's mythology is preserved in the oral traditions of the Wiradjuri, Gamilaraay, and neighbouring nations. The stories are not free-floating entertainment: they are title deeds to country, instruction manuals for law, and maps of the sky. What follows are widely reported themes; local elders hold the authoritative versions of each nation's stories.

myths.title: The Making of the World
myths.text:
In the beginning Baiame shaped the land. He formed the hills and rivers, planted the trees, and made the animals. Then he made the first people and gave them their languages, their countries, and the laws by which they should live — the earliest ethnographers of the Euahlayi, above all K. Langloh Parker in The Euahlayi Tribe (1905), record the Baayami of creation as the maker whose work is the country itself. Every mountain, waterhole, and plain became a reminder of his creative act, and every clan received the responsibility to care for the part of country made for it (Parker 1905; Berndt and Berndt 1964).

Creation here is not a finished product handed over but a continuing arrangement: the world is a country made by an ancestor and entrusted to his descendants, and the deed of trust is the story itself.

myths.title: The Retreat to the Sky
myths.text:
When the work of creation was finished, Baiame rose into the sky and made his camp there. From that distant place he watches over the world he made — remote, but not absent, his presence announced by the dark lanes of the Milky Way, which are said to be his camp or the tracks of the emu he placed there, and by the stars themselves, the campfires of the ancestors who went before. The early recorders of the southeast (Parker; Elkin 1938) heard the same withdrawal in many nations: the Sky Father who made the world does not govern it day by day, because the law he gave does that work for him.

The withdrawal is the gift: a maker who stayed would be a ruler, but a maker who leaves behind law becomes an ancestor. Distance is how the Sky Father turns creation into inheritance.

lore.culturalLegacy: Baiame remains a powerful symbol of Aboriginal sovereignty over country and culture. His name appears in place names, in rock art and stencil sites, and in contemporary Aboriginal art and literature. The Emu in the Sky is now widely recognised as one of the best-known Aboriginal astronomical traditions. At the same time, Aboriginal custodians have rightly insisted that Baiame's sacred aspects — especially those connected with men's law and initiation — are not open-source material for casual adaptation. PuniCodex presents only the publicly documented, scholarly record and directs readers to AIATSIS and to the relevant Aboriginal communities for authoritative teachings.
lore.archaeology: The material record of Baiame-related belief includes stone arrangements, bora (initiation) grounds, rock engravings, and rock shelters across the Wiradjuri and Gamilaraay countries of New South Wales. Notable sites include Baiame Cave near Milbrodale in the Hunter Valley, which contains a large painted figure sometimes identified with Baiame, and numerous carved and painted emus that reference the Emu in the Sky. These sites are protected under Aboriginal cultural-heritage law and are best understood in consultation with the traditional custodians.
lore.syncretism: Early colonial observers sometimes compared Baiame to the Christian God, and some recorded traditions show signs of post-contact reinterpretation. Modern scholarship, led by Berndt and Berndt and by AIATSIS, treats Baiame as a specifically Aboriginal Sky Father whose identity is tied to country, kinship, and initiation rather than to any universal deity. He is not interchangeable with the biblical creator, and each nation retains its own protocols for how his name and stories may be used.
lore.originalScriptNote: Baiame belongs to an oral tradition that had no pre-contact writing system. The name first enters the written record in nineteenth-century ethnographies. PuniCodex therefore restores it as Baiame, the conventional capitalized romanization, rather than as an 'original script' in the strict sense. The ASCII form baiame is a practical DNS compromise; the restored form is the scholarly citation form used in Australian Indigenous studies.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BUN-jil' — stress the first syllable; the 'j' is the 'j' of 'jump', and the final vowel is short like the 'i' in 'kit'.
pronunciation.note: The name Bunjil is a conventional Latin transcription of an Aboriginal theonym. The PuniCodex restoration capitalises the first letter, giving the standard proper-name form. Because no diacritic or distinctive letter is added, the ASCII string 'bunjil' already encodes the conventional spelling; the name is therefore Tier 2.

domains.title: Creator Eaglehawk
domains.subtitle: Sky Ancestor, Law-Giver, and Moiety Founder
domains.lead: Bunjil is the wedge-tailed eaglehawk made ancestor of the Kulin nations of central Victoria. In the Dreaming he shaped the mountains, rivers, plants, animals, and the laws by which people should live. He is one of two moiety ancestors, paired with Waang the crow, and after his work on earth he was lifted into the sky, where he remains as the star Altair.

cards.name: Creator of Country
cards.desc: He shaped the land, water, flora, and fauna of south-eastern Australia, and established the order of the living world.

cards.name: Sky Ancestor
cards.desc: After creation he ascended to the sky and became the star Altair; his two wives became the black swans beside him.

cards.name: Law-Giver
cards.desc: He gave the Kulin peoples their social and ecological laws, including the obligation to care for Country and each other.

cards.name: Moiety Founder
cards.desc: As the eaglehawk ancestor he heads one of the Kulin moieties, balanced by Waang the crow on the other side.

symbols.name: Wedge-tailed eagle
symbols.meaning: The living form of Bunjil and the largest bird of prey in Australia; a sign of creative power and watchful authority

symbols.name: Spear
symbols.meaning: The instrument with which Bunjil commanded the rising sea to stop, and a mark of law-giving authority

symbols.name: Black swan
symbols.meaning: Bunjil's two wives, who became the stars flanking Altair after his ascent

symbols.name: Rainbow
symbols.meaning: His son Binbeal, the rainbow spirit, who continues the creative lineage in the sky

mythology.lead: Bunjil's stories belong to the Dreaming of the Kulin nations — the Woiwurrung, Boonwurrung, Wathaurong, and their neighbors — recorded by A. W. Howitt, Aldo Massola, and the communities themselves. They explain how Country was made, how law was given, and how the creator withdrew into the sky so that he might continue to watch over the world.

myths.title: Shaping the Land and the Law
myths.text: In the Dreaming, Bunjil travelled across what is now central Victoria and shaped Country into its living form: he raised the mountains, traced the courses of the rivers, named the plants and animals, and taught each where it belonged. Then he did what a mere landscape-maker would not: he gave law. The Kulin peoples remember him establishing the rules of kinship and marriage, the obligations between clans, and the duties each people owes to its Country — seasonal burning, careful taking, respect for the places where spirit beings remain. His two wives, the black swans, and his son Binbeal the rainbow accompanied the work. Crucially, the stories insist that Country and law were made together: the mountains are not scenery but scripture, and the river's bends are not geography but instruction. (Howitt 1904; Massola 1968) The tradition encodes a complete environmental philosophy — creation, tenure, and responsibility in a single narrative.

myths.title: The Sea That Would Not Stop Rising
myths.text: In the telling recorded from Boonwurrung elder Carolyn Briggs, the Kulin nations fell into conflict and began to neglect family and Country, and the sea rose in anger and would not stop. The people gathered and asked Bunjil to intervene. He agreed — but on a condition: they must change their ways and return to the law. He walked to the water's edge, raised his spear, and commanded the sea to stop, and the sea stopped. (Briggs, 'Boon Wurrung Story', Yarra Healing 2000) The story is told as a moral charter, but it carries what may be a far older memory: at the end of the last Ice Age, rising seas flooded the Bassian Plain and cut Tasmania from the mainland — an inundation the ancestors of the Kulin peoples witnessed over generations, and which Australia's oral traditions are now famous for preserving with geological accuracy. The myth's force lies in its bargain: the sea keeps its bounds only while the people keep their obligations — a covenant, not a one-time miracle.

lore.culturalLegacy: Bunjil remains a powerful and public symbol of Aboriginal Victoria. Bunjil's Shelter in the Black Range Scenic Reserve is a protected cultural site and a focus of education and careful tourism. Melbourne's skyline carries his name and form: Bruce Armstrong's monumental eagle sculpture Bunjil (2002) rises from Wurundjeri Way in the Docklands, and Bunjil Place in Narre Warren carries the name into the suburbs. For the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung, Boonwurrung, and other Kulin communities, Bunjil is not only an ancestral figure but a living authority in Welcome to Country ceremonies, land-care work, language revival, and the ongoing negotiation of recognition and reconciliation — the creator whose law still describes how Country should be held.
lore.archaeology: The principal material site associated with Bunjil is Bunjil's Shelter, a rock-art shelter in the Black Range Scenic Reserve within Gariwerd (the Grampians region), Victoria, where a red-ochre painting depicts the creator figure flanked by two dingoes. The site is protected under the Aboriginal Heritage Act 2006 and is managed with Traditional Owner input. Textual witnesses include A. W. Howitt's ethnographic notes, Aldo Massola's 1968 compilation of south-eastern traditions, and contemporary community publications by Kulin educators and language custodians — together forming an unusually well-documented record of a living tradition.
lore.syncretism: Bunjil is not a solitary deity but one half of a Kulin social and cosmological pair. The eaglehawk moiety, headed by Bunjil, is balanced by the crow moiety, headed by Waang — a pairing that structures kinship, marriage, and ritual obligation across the Kulin nations, so that every person belongs to one ancestor's side and marries into the other. Different clans preserve different episodes: the Woiwurrung stress the sky ascent and Altair, the Boonwurrung remember the rising sea, and the peoples of Gariweld keep the place-based accounts tied to Bunjil's Shelter. In the colonial period the name was recorded under many spellings — Winjeel, Wingeel, Pundjel, Bunjel — reflecting dialect variation and the difficulty of rendering Kulin phonology in English orthography; several survive in Victorian place names.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Kulin languages were traditionally oral, and Bunjil has no original alphabetic script. The name survives in Latin transcription made by early settlers and anthropologists. PuniCodex therefore treats Bunjil as the scholarly citation form and bunjil as the DNS compromise. The restoration adds only the capital initial; the absence of diacritics or special letters places the name in Tier 2, not because the figure is less significant, but because the ASCII form already carries the conventional spelling.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DARR-uh-MOO-lum' — four even syllables, stress on the first, with the soft 'oo' of 'book' in the third and fourth syllables.
pronunciation.note: The name is Tier 2 in the PuniCodex system: the ASCII string 'daramulum' already encodes the same phonemic material. The restoration capitalizes the initial letter to mark a proper name, but no stress mark, length mark, or distinctive letter is added.

domains.title: Sky Hero of the Bora
domains.subtitle: Initiation, Law, and the Emu in the Sky
domains.lead: Daramulum is the one-legged son of Baiame, sky father and creator of the Aboriginal nations of south-eastern Australia. He presides over the bora, the initiation ground where boys become men and the Law is handed down, and he lives on in the sky — his emu-shaped body traced in the dark dust-lanes of the Milky Way as a seasonal clock for ceremony and hunt.

cards.name: Sky Hero
cards.desc: Son of Baiame and a power of the upper world; his camp is said to lie in the sky, especially among the stars of the Milky Way.

cards.name: Keeper of the Bora
cards.desc: Guardian of the bora ring and the initiation ceremonies through which Law, identity, and adult responsibility are transmitted.

cards.name: Emu in the Sky
cards.desc: His one-legged form is identified with the dark emu traced in the Milky Way, a seasonal clock and sacred map.

cards.name: Son of Baiame
cards.desc: The principal male descendant of the creator-sky father, acting as his agent in teaching, judging, and protecting the Law.

symbols.name: Boomerang
symbols.meaning: Emblem of initiation and the lawful exchange between earth and sky; also a weapon associated with Daramulum's authority over the bora ground.

symbols.name: Emu
symbols.meaning: His one-legged or emu-footed form; the dark emu in the Milky Way is read as his celestial body or his watching sign.
