pronunciation.note: Haurvatāt is Tier-1: the macron on the long final ā is a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. As an Amesha Spenta, her name is an abstract noun meaning 'wholeness' or 'health,' personified as a divine being.

domains.title: Wholeness and Health
domains.subtitle: Water, Integrity, and the Amesha Spenta
domains.lead: Haurvatāt is the Amesha Spenta of wholeness, health, and water in Zoroastrianism. Her name means 'every-ness' or 'completeness': she guards what is unbroken, undiminished, and life-giving. Waters — rivers, springs, rain, and the sea — are her domain, and health is her gift to those who live in harmony with Aša. With Amərətāt she forms a pair that promises the body and the earth restored.

cards.name: Guardian of Waters
cards.desc: Rivers, springs, rain, and the sea are sacred because they manifest Haurvatāt's wholeness — the second of the seven creations.

cards.name: Health and Integrity
cards.desc: Her name names the state of being complete, sound, and free from the wounds of the lie.

cards.name: Pair with Amərətāt
cards.desc: Wholeness and immortality are invoked together in every Yasna as the gifts that sustain body and soul.

cards.name: Purity of Water
cards.desc: Polluting water is a serious sin because it violates her domain and the cosmic order — the seed of Zoroastrian environmental law.

symbols.name: Water vessel or spring
symbols.meaning: The sacred waters that embody Haurvatāt's wholeness

symbols.name: Circle or ring
symbols.meaning: Completeness, integrity, and the unbroken cycle of health

symbols.name: Pairing with Amərətāt
symbols.meaning: The twin promise of health and eternal life in Zoroastrian devotion

symbols.name: Pure flowing water
symbols.meaning: The element most closely identified with her presence and blessing

symbols.name: The covered well
symbols.meaning: The purity rule made architecture: wells sealed from contamination, washing done downstream

mythology.lead: Haurvatāt, like the other Amesha Spentas, does not have a long heroic mythology. Her importance lies in cosmology, ritual, and law: she is the divine principle that makes water pure, bodies whole, and the cosmos complete. Her myths are the myths of creation, purity, and final restoration — and of the legislation that still guards every well.

myths.title: The Creation of Water
myths.text: Second among the seven good creations is water, and the Bundaahišn gives it the full cosmic résumé: the gathered seas, the rivers running to the great lake of Vourukaša, the springs 'which never fail' (Bundaahišn 1, 3, 7). Its custodian is Haurvatāt — 'every-ness, completeness' — wholeness as a divine person, and by derivation the purity of her element; Ahriman answers with brine and bitter springs, poisoned wells, and the withholding of rain. The myth is the charter of Zoroastrian water law: since water is a creation entrusted to an Immortal, to foul a river is sacrilege rather than littering, and the duty to protect it binds layperson and priest alike. Her invocations name her simply 'wholeness and health' — the two words every sickroom still borrows. Wholeness begins upstream — a religion whose second commandment is, in effect, keep the waters clean.

myths.title: Water in the Yasna
myths.text: The Yasna joins her domain to her sister's: water for the haoma, plant for the pressing, word for the consecration (Yasna 9–11). In the litanies of the Aban Gāh — the watch of the waters in the daily round — the officiant addresses the waters themselves: 'we sacrifice to the good waters, to the waters of the springs' (Yasna 63–69). The chalice of the Yasna is washed with elaborate care; nothing impure may touch it, and the leftover water is returned to the earth with a blessing rather than poured away casually. The rite makes a small, portable sea in which the congregation's sip binds each worshipper to the completeness the goddess guards. Even the drawing of water became liturgical: the vessel is addressed, the source is thanked, the surplus is blessed back. To drink the consecrated draught is to taste the wholeness she guards, one careful sip at a time.

lore.culturalLegacy: Haurvatāt remains central to Zoroastrian ethics of environmental purity, especially the protection of water from contamination. Her name survives in the Zoroastrian calendar and in prayers to the Amesha Spentas. In modern ecological readings of the tradition, Haurvatāt is invoked as the sacred dimension of clean water and holistic health. She reminds us that wholeness is not a private state but a cosmic condition that depends on how we treat the waters we share.
lore.archaeology: Haurvatāt is invoked in Avestan liturgical texts and in Sasanian inscriptions and seals naming the Amesha Spentas. Zoroastrian water rituals, including offerings at springs and the careful protection of wells, preserve her domain in practice — the covered well and the downstream washing-place are her oldest surviving 'temples.' Manuscript illuminations and temple art associate her with flowing water and the paradisal garden, and archaeological sites near ancient water sources often show the material culture of these purification practices.
lore.syncretism: Haurvatāt is paired with Amərətāt in Zoroastrian worship and cosmology; their names passed into Middle Persian as Hordād and Amurdād and are preserved in the Zoroastrian calendar. The abstract noun haurvatāt is cognate with Vedic Sanskrit sarvatāt, 'all-ness,' showing the deep Indo-Iranian roots of the concept. In Greek and Roman contexts, the Amesha Spentas were sometimes compared to abstract virtues or to nymphs and water deities, though these comparisons are loose.

Both medial vowels are schwa ə (𐬆).
The ending -tāt uses long ā (𐬁) before final t (𐬙).

pronunciation.approximation: ah-muh-ruh-TAHT — the middle syllables are light and quick, while the final 'tah' is long and emphatic.
pronunciation.note: Amərətāt is Tier-1: the macron on the long final ā is a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. As one of the Amesha Spentas, her name is an abstract noun meaning 'immortality' personified.

domains.title: Immortality in Bloom
domains.subtitle: Plants, Longevity, and the Amesha Spenta
domains.lead: Amərətāt is the Amesha Spenta of immortality and plants in Zoroastrianism. She embodies the divine promise that the soul endures and that the earth's vegetation sustains life. Where her sister Haurvatāt guards water and wholeness, Amərətāt guards the plant kingdom and the final victory over death. She is the green hope at the heart of Zoroastrian cosmology.

cards.name: Guardian of Plants
cards.desc: Every tree, herb, and grain falls under her protection as the divine patron of vegetation — the fourth of the seven creations.

cards.name: Immortality
cards.desc: Her name means 'non-death'; she is the spiritual force that promises life beyond death, sealed by the white haoma.

cards.name: Pair with Haurvatāt
cards.desc: She and Haurvatāt (wholeness/health) are invoked together in every Yasna as the complementary gifts of body and eternity.

cards.name: The Final Renovation
cards.desc: At Frashokereti, Amərətāt's domain will flourish in a world without death or decay.

symbols.name: Tree or branch
symbols.meaning: Vegetation, growth, and the plant kingdom under her guardianship

symbols.name: Fruit or grain
symbols.meaning: The sustenance that links earthly agriculture to divine immortality

symbols.name: Watered garden
symbols.meaning: The paradise-like setting where plants and water together manifest wholeness

symbols.name: Pairing with Haurvatāt
symbols.meaning: The two Amesha Spentas together symbolize health and eternal life

symbols.name: The white haoma
symbols.meaning: The paradisal plant of the renovation, her sacrament of endless life (Bundahišn 30)

mythology.lead: Amərətāt does not have a long narrative mythology of her own; her stories are the cosmogony's fourth chapter, the Yasna's nightly rite, and the eschatology's final meal. As one of the seven Holy Immortals she helps govern the created world — and the war over her domain, the green one, is the war we call agriculture.

myths.title: The Creation of Plants
myths.text: Zoroastrian cosmogony counts seven good creations, and the fourth is the green one: plants, urwarō, fashioned by Ahura Mazdā as the roof of the food chain — beneath sky, water, and earth, above cattle and man (Bundaahišn 1, 3). To this creation he appoints Amərətāt, 'non-death-ness', her name locking the root mar-, 'to die', behind a private prefix. Ahriman's reply is the counter-creation of decay — drought, frost, locust, and blight — so that the struggle between growth and rot becomes a cosmic front on which every farmer is a soldier. The pairing is exact and the lesson practical. The calendar keeps the assignment: the fifth day of every month and the month of Amurdād still bear her name. To plant, water, and weed is to fight on the right side of a cosmic war — gardening is the original act of religion.

myths.title: The Bodies of the Righteous
myths.text: At Frashogard the resurrection bodies will need more than spirit — they will need the food of immortality, and the texts supply it: the white haoma, the paradisal plant of the renovation, offered to the risen so that they shall not die again (Bundaahišn 30; Zātspram 35). Amərətāt's gift is realized through her sister-domains: the pressed plant of Haoma's rite, the pure water of Haurvatāt's, the consecrated fire of Ašavahišta's — the whole ecology of the seven creations serving one meal. Immortality in this scheme is not an escape from matter but matter's perfection: the same bodies, finally unwound from decay. The image stayed with the tradition's artists, who fill manuscript margins with paradisal gardens for precisely this scene. The resurrection meal is a garden and a spring — eternal life arrives as ecology restored.

lore.culturalLegacy: Amərətāt remains a focus of Zoroastrian devotion as the divine guardian of vegetation and the promise of eternal life. Her name survives in the Zoroastrian calendar and in the prayers offered to the Amesha Spentas. In ecological readings of Zoroastrianism, Amərətāt is invoked as the sacred dimension of plant life and the religious duty to protect the earth's green cover. She is a reminder that immortality in this tradition is not escape from the world but the world's final healing.
lore.archaeology: Amərətāt is invoked in Avestan liturgical texts and in Sasanian-era inscriptions and seals that name the Amesha Spentas. Zoroastrian ritual vessels, fire temples, and manuscript illuminations associate her with vegetation and the paradisal garden. The haoma rite, though now performed with substitutes in many communities, preserves the plant-offering at the center of her domain.
lore.syncretism: Amərətāt is one of a pair with Haurvatāt, and the two are often worshipped together as guardians of water/plants and health/immortality. Their names passed into Middle Persian as Amurdād and Hordād, and they are still commemorated in the Zoroastrian calendar. The Greek concept of ambrosia is closer than a loose parallel: Greek ambrotos, 'immortal', and ambrosia descend from the same Proto-Indo-European privative formation *n̥-mr̥-to-, 'undying', built on the root *mer-, 'to die' — the very root that, with the Iranian abstract suffix -tāt, produces Amərətāt; Sanskrit amṛta is the same formation again.

domains.title: The Immaculate Waters
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Healing, and Wisdom
domains.lead: Anāhitā is the great Yazata of the Avestan pantheon, the goddess of the life-giving waters, and one of the most widely worshipped deities of ancient Iran. She is called Aredvi Sura Anāhitā — the moist, strong, undefiled — and her realm runs from the mythical river that surrounds the world to the springs that nourish fields, wombs, and kings.

cards.name: Lady of the Waters
cards.desc: The Avestan Yasht 5 hymns her as the source of all rivers, the force that makes the cosmos fertile and clean.

cards.name: Fertility and Royalty
cards.desc: Kings pray to her for legitimacy, warriors for victory, women for safe childbirth, and farmers for abundant crops.

cards.name: Star of the Waters
cards.desc: She is linked to the planet Venus in later tradition — the bright star that rises from and governs the waters.

cards.name: Golden Splendor
cards.desc: The hymn describes her clothing of gold, her crown, her earrings, and her necklaces — a figure of Iranian royal magnificence.

symbols.name: Running water
symbols.meaning: The river, spring, or canal that is her body and her blessing

symbols.name: Lotus
symbols.meaning: The flower that rises from the water, a later emblem of her purity and fertility

symbols.name: Star (Venus)
symbols.meaning: The celestial body identified with Anāhitā in Sasanian and later Zoroastrian tradition

symbols.name: Golden dress and crown
symbols.meaning: The royal insignia described in Yasht 5, marking her as patron of legitimate kingship

mythology.lead: Anāhitā's mythology flows through the fifth Yašt — the great hymn that names her the mighty river of the world and lists the kings, heroes, and empires that sought her favor — and onward into Achaemenid inscriptions, Sasanian star-lore, and the temples of Armenia. She is a goddess of water who became a goddess of empire, and finally a morning star.

myths.title: The River That Girds the World
myths.text: Aredvi Sura Anāhitā is first a river — the great, the far-famed — rising on Mount Hara and pouring into the sea Vourukaša, whence all the waters of the world are distributed (Yašt 5.3–5). Her hymn is the fifth of the Avestan hymns, recited still in the liturgy of the waters, and it moves between cosmic geography and personal petition: the same goddess who girdles the world with a mythical stream also makes the womb fertile and gives easy childbirth (Yašt 5.2). The hymn's theology is hydrological: to praise Anāhitā is to acknowledge that every canal, spring, and cloud is one circulation. Between these poles the hymn ranges for over a hundred stanzas, and its very length is a theology: no praise of the waters can be too long. The goddess is the water cycle personified — and her immaculate name is an ecological creed, since her worshippers vow to keep her element clean.

myths.title: The Beaver Mantle and the Chariot of Storms
myths.text: Yašt 5 describes her coming to sacrifice on a chariot drawn by four horses — wind, rain, cloud, and sleet (5.16) — splendid in gold, bright and tall, with white arms (5.123–125). Most striking is her mantle: thirty beaver skins, taken from four-year-old beavers, worn so that the seed and evil eye of the daevas cannot touch her body (5.126–129). Modern readers often misread the passage as luxury; the hymn's logic is purity, not wealth — every element of her dress is armor against defilement, and the worship she accepts begins with purification rites (yaozdāθra) performed before sacrifice. The detail fascinated antiquity: classical writers echo these lines when they describe the dress of Persian noblewomen at her festivals. Anāhitā's golden splendor is a visual theology of integrity — beauty as the radiance of what cannot be stained.

lore.culturalLegacy: Anāhitā's name lived on in Iranian languages as Anāhīd, a popular female name and a poetic word for the planet Venus. The pre-Islamic Iranian new year, Nawrōz, preserved water-rituals that honored her. In modern Zoroastrian practice, the veneration of water and the divine feminine continues, and Anāhitā remains one of the best-known Yazatas outside the tradition. Her temples at Kangāvar and Bīšāpūr are among the most impressive surviving monuments of Sasanian religion. Restoring Anāhitā recovers the long vowels and stress that distinguish the Avestan goddess from the flattened modern name.
lore.archaeology: Major temples dedicated to Anāhitā have been identified at Kangāvar (often identified with the temple of Artemis/Anāhitā mentioned by Isidore of Charax), Bīšāpūr, and Takht-e Soleymān. Sasanian and Kushano-Sasanian coinage depicts her with mural crown, lotus, and lions. Achaemenid inscriptions from Susa and Hamadan name her alongside Ahura Mazdā and Mithra, confirming her place in the official cult of the empire.
lore.syncretism: Anāhitā absorbed and was absorbed by neighboring goddesses. In Armenia she was identified with the indigenous goddess Nana or Nanē, and with the Greek Artemis and Tyche. The Seleucid and Parthian periods saw her portrayed in Hellenistic dress with a mural crown, tympanum, and lions — the visual vocabulary of the Syrian goddess Atargatis. Some scholars compare her functions to those of the Mesopotamian Ishtar/Inanna and the Indic Sarasvatī, though these are typological parallels, not direct borrowings. She is best understood as an Iranian development of the ancient Near Eastern goddess of water, fertility, and sovereignty.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MAH-mah KEE-lyah' — the chroniclers' 'Mama Quilla'; in modern Quechua orthography Mama Killa.
pronunciation.note: Mama Quilla is single-tier Tier 2: ASCII loses nothing — the q-to-k of Quechua orthography and the palatal ll are conventions the plain spelling already implies. Her name is a plain description: 'Mother Moon.'

domains.title: Mama Quilla
domains.subtitle: Moon
domains.lead: Mama Quilla — Mother Moon — is the Inca goddess of the moon, sister and wife of the Sun, mother of the dynasty's founders, and keeper of the calendar. Silver was her metal, the night her realm, and the Coya — the queen — her living image on earth.

cards.name: Mother Moon
cards.desc: The moon as mother — her name itself, and her office over fertility, women, and the night.

cards.name: Keeper of Time
cards.desc: She governed the lunar months and festival calendar — the waxing and waning that set the empire's rhythm.

cards.name: Sister-Wife of the Sun
cards.desc: Wed to Inti, her brother — the paired lights of sky, with gold for him and silver for her.

cards.name: Mother of the Founders
cards.desc: From her and Inti came Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, sent to found Cuzco and the Inca line.

symbols.name: Silver
symbols.meaning: Her metal — her shrine in the Coricancha was sheathed in silver facing the Sun's gold

symbols.name: The Crescent (Killa)
symbols.meaning: The waxing moon, the favorable phase — the very word quilla means both 'moon' and 'month'

symbols.name: The Lunar Calendar
symbols.meaning: Her arithmetic: the twelve (or thirteen) lunar months that timed festivals, planting, and war

symbols.name: The Mirror of the Coya
symbols.meaning: The queen, her earthly counterpart, who bore the moon's title and diadem

symbols.name: The Eclipse
symbols.meaning: The jaguar's attack on the moon — the omen that emptied plazas and filled the night with noise

mythology.lead: Mama Quilla's mythology comes through the colonial chroniclers — Cobo above all — who recorded a functioning state theology: the moon as mother, wife, and calendar. The tradition offers genealogy rather than epic, and it is richest where the moon meets the people — in the founding legend, the eclipse rites, and the silver shrine.

myths.title: Sister-Wife of the Sun
myths.text: The chroniclers — Cobo (Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Book 13) most fully, Polo de Ondegardo and Murúa in agreement — make Mama Quilla the sister and wife of Inti, the Sun. The pairing is cosmic administration: two lights of opposite temper and opposite metal, gold and silver, day-side and night-side, ruling the sky as the emperor and Coya ruled the earth. The Coya embodied the correspondence on earth: her title, her silver ornaments, and her seat beside the emperor all repeated the sky's arrangement at court scale, as the chroniclers noted with visible discomfort. The sibling-marriage, startling to Europeans,The sibling-marriage, startling to Europeans, marked the gods as the model of the dynasty's own endogamy — the Inca married his sister the Coya as Inti married the Moon. The theology reads like a constitution written in sky: what is highest in heaven licenses what is highest on earth.

myths.title: Mother of Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo
myths.text: From the union of Sun and Moon came Manco Cápac and his sister-wife Mama Ocllo, who were sent from the cave of origin to find the place where a golden staff would sink into the ground — the valley of Cuzco (Cobo, Book 13; the parallel accounts of Murúa and the Sarmiento de Gamboa tradition). There they taught the people to plant, weave, and worship, and there the Inca dynasty began. Later empire converted the genealogy into policy: marriages among kin kept the founding blood undiluted, so the moon's marriage quietly licensed the palace's. Mama Quilla is thus not a background figureMama Quilla is thus not a background figure but the dynasty's own mother: every emperor's claim ran through her, and the Coya her daughters-in-line embodied her office. The myth is political at its root — a capital city justified as a family homestead of the moon.

lore.culturalLegacy: Mama Quilla's most durable legacy is lexical: killa/quilla, 'moon,' is also the Quechua word for 'month' — her cycles are still how millions count time, and the lunar-timed agricultural calendar remains the skeleton of Andean ritual life. Her festival, Killa Raymi or Coya Raymi (the 'moon festival,' associated with women and with September in the modern revival), is celebrated again in Ecuador and Peru as a festival of femininity and planting. The silver moon survives in the crafts: Quechua and Aymara artisans still make the crescent-disc pendants that descend from her shrine imagery. And in Cuzco's living calendar — Inti Raymi on the June solstice, with the Coya at the Sun's side — the sister-wife of the Sun remains the model of the queen: her title passed into the Spanish viceroyalty's own court etiquette.
lore.archaeology: The physical center of her cult was the Coricancha in Cuzco, whose curved western wall still stands beneath the Santo Domingo convent; excavations and the chroniclers' descriptions fix the moon chapel opposite the sun's — silver-clad, with her silver image facing the Punchao (the sun's golden boy-idol). The Spanish melted her silver into bullion, but the temple's plan survives in the foundations. Beyond Cuzco, moon imagery — crescents and full-moon discs — appears on colonial-era qirus (ritual cups) and in textiles that kept pre-conquest canons. Eclipse and moon observations are embedded in the architecture of state ritual sites such as the Coricancha itself, aligned to both solar and lunar standstills as modern archaeoastronomy (e.g., work associated with Dearborn and others at Cuzco) has argued.
lore.syncretism: Under Spanish rule, Mama Quilla's moon was quietly reassigned to the Virgin Mary — a mapping prepared by the Virgin's own lunar iconography (the woman clothed with the sun, the moon beneath her feet) and welcomed in Andean devotion, where Marian feasts absorbed the timing of the old lunar rites. The conversion was rarely clean: eclipse rituals survived under the surface, and the moon-festival season persists in the festival calendar of Cuzco's Corpus Christi. In the twentieth century the process reversed — the indigenous movement reclaimed the moon for Mama Quilla, and modern Killa Raymi celebrations in Ecuador and Peru explicitly restore the goddess to her festival, pairing her again with Inti in the revived Inti Raymi pageants. Andean religion here shows its characteristic resilience: the moon changed name for four centuries without changing office.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ma-ma-KOO-cha' — the pitch peaks on the third syllable, the qu is a deep, throaty k, and the ch is as in 'church'.
pronunciation.note: Mamaqucha is Tier 2: the restoration adds no diacritic or distinctive letter, because Quechua orthography needs none — the name is transparently mama 'mother' plus qucha 'lake, sea'. What the temple preserves is not a mark but a meaning: the sea addressed as mother.

domains.title: Mamaqucha
domains.subtitle: Mother Sea
domains.lead: Mamaqucha — Quechua mama, 'mother', and qucha, 'lake, sea' — is the Andean sea as mother: mother of fishes, horizon of the Inca world, the one great power their mountain religion never fully mastered. Coastal peoples made offerings where desert meets surf; the Inca themselves met her only late, and named her with the kinship word they gave the earth.

cards.name: Mother of Fishes
cards.desc: The sea as progenitor of marine life — fish are her children, and the coast's peoples addressed her as 'mother' when casting nets (Cobo, Historia 13).

cards.name: The Boundless Waters
cards.desc: The Pacific as the western horizon of Tahuantinsuyu: venerated from the shore, crossed only late, and never absorbed into the mountain cults.

cards.name: Coastal Shrines
cards.desc: Seaside huacas received offerings along the desert littoral; the great oracle of Pachacamac faced the ocean its maker had filled with fish (Cieza de León, Crónica ch. 5).

cards.name: The Unmastered Realm
cards.desc: Apus ruled peaks and springs within the ceque system; Mamaqucha stood outside it — the empire's one unincorporated power (Bauer, Sacred Landscape).

symbols.name: The mother-name
symbols.meaning: mama + qucha — the sea addressed with a kinship term, as Pachamama is the earth addressed as mother.

symbols.name: Fish
symbols.meaning: Her children and the coast's staple food; the sea's bounty is a mother's milk.

symbols.name: The balsa raft
symbols.meaning: The ocean-going craft of Andean mariners; the royal voyage tradition makes it the bridge to the mother sea.

symbols.name: The western horizon
symbols.meaning: The sea as sunset, rain-cloud, and the unknown islands of empire-era story.

mythology.lead: The record of Mamaqucha is honest about its thinness: Andean peoples venerated the sea, but the highland Inca met the ocean late, and no great epic of hers survives. What we have is attested in colonial chronicles — and where those chronicles disagree or romanticize, this temple says so.

myths.title: The Sea That Feeds
myths.text: Along the desert coast, where river valleys reach the Pacific, Andean peoples venerated the sea as a mother. Bernabé Cobo, writing in the seventeenth century from earlier sources, describes how the seashore itself was sacred: offerings were made where the surf breaks, because the sea was the mother of fishes, the source of the coast's food. The name says the theology plainly — mama, mother, plus qucha, lake or sea, a word that names every highland lake, so the ocean was conceived as the greatest of lakes, the mother of waters. This was no abstract personification: fishermen lived from her bounty and addressed her with the kinship term before casting their nets. Later devotion gave the idiom to the Virgin — Mamacha Candelaria of Puno — but the grammar of it, mother by the water, is far older than the church.

myths.title: The Maker Who Filled the Sea
myths.text: The Huarochirí Manuscript, recorded from Quechua speakers around 1608, tells of the coastal maker Pacha Kamaq, 'Creator of the World', whose great shrine stood in the Lurín valley above the sea. In the flood that ended an earlier humanity, the creator punished the unworthy and then made the fish — populating the ocean as a pasture. Cieza de León, touring the coast in 1547, marveled at Pachacamac's oracle, consulted by pilgrims from across the Andes, and at its temple commanding the waters below. The sea of Mamaqucha and the shrine of Pachacamac belong to one geography: the maker above the valley, the mother-water below. The myth encodes a coastal theology older than the Inca state, in which creation and ocean are a matched pair, and the narrow desert coast mediates between them.

lore.culturalLegacy: Mamaqucha never stopped being spoken. Quechua-speaking communities across Peru still call the ocean mama qucha, and the word qucha rides in the names of uncounted lakes. The Mamacha Candelaria festival of Puno keeps the mother-by-the-water idiom at the center of Andean public religion, with dancers, barges, and a procession over the lake itself. Coastal communities from Chimbote to Ilo keep sea-side rituals in which offerings are still cast into the surf. And the name survives in scholarship as the standard example of Andean hydro-theology — the sea, like the mountains, addressed by kinship rather than distance. Restoring Mamaqucha as a name returns the Pacific to the grammar of family it had before the empire that failed to master it.
lore.archaeology: No temple of Mamaqucha as such is known, and the sea-cult has left no secure iconography. What the coast has is Pachacamac: the vast adobe temple complex of the Lurín valley, occupied from the first millennium CE and expanded under the Inca, whose painted walls and plazas were still being described by Cieza in 1547. Seaside offerings documented ethnohistorically leave few durable traces — textiles, food, and shell disperse in the surf — but the maritime technology is material enough: balsa-raft traditions of the Ecuadorian and northern Peruvian coasts, confirmed archaeologically by navigation between the coast and offshore islands, gave the royal voyage legends their plausibility. The Chimú and earlier coastal societies left sea imagery in metal and mural; the Inca left the coast's greatest shrine enlarged. The mother sea herself was worshipped, fittingly, at the point where everything she gives washes back.
lore.syncretism: Colonial Catholicism did not replace Mamaqucha so much as re-house her. The Virgin of Candelaria, Mamacha Candelaria, is the 'Mother' of Puno, the city on the shore of Lake Titicaca — the great lake addressed by the very word qucha; her February festival is among the largest in the Andes. Coastal devotion took similar paths: fishermen's religion folded the old mother-of-waters into saints' calendars, and north-coastal folklore kept sea-maiden figures who marry or drown mortal men, the mamá del mar motif recorded by twentieth-century ethnographers. Afro-Andean coastal cults along the Pacific later added Yemayá-style ocean motherhood, though that current comes from Brazil rather than deep antiquity. The syncretic pattern is stable: wherever Andean or Andean-descended communities face a large water, the water becomes a mother again.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ee-LYAH-pah' — stress on the middle syllable; the Spanish chroniclers wrote the name Catuilla or Katoylla.
pronunciation.note: Illapa is single-tier Tier 2: the restoration carries no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII loses. The Spanish double-l spelling in older sources encodes a palatal sound that the ASCII 'll' already signals to Spanish-literate readers.

domains.title: Illapa
domains.subtitle: Thunder
domains.lead: Illapa is the Inca god of thunder, lightning, and war — the storm warrior whose sling-stones are the thunderbolts. He drew the rain from the celestial river and hurled it earthward, patron of soldiers and of every field that waited for rain.

cards.name: Lord of Thunder
cards.desc: Armed with sling and mace, bright-clothed, he walks the sky; his flashing forehead is the lightning.

cards.name: Bringer of Rain
cards.desc: He draws water from the Milky Way's celestial river and releases it as the storms that fill the fields.

cards.name: Patron of Warriors
cards.desc: The war god of the empire; captives and maize beer were poured to him before battle.

cards.name: Master of Omens
cards.desc: A lightning strike read the future: ground hit by his bolt became a shrine, and his rainbow was feared.

symbols.name: The Sling
symbols.meaning: His thunderbolt-thrower; the whirl of his sling is the rolling of thunder across the sky

symbols.name: The Thunderstone
symbols.meaning: Prehistoric worked stones (piedras de rayo) believed to be his spent missiles, kept as heirlooms

symbols.name: The Mace
symbols.meaning: His war-club, marking his office as patron of Inca armies

symbols.name: The Celestial River
symbols.meaning: The Milky Way (Mayu), his reservoir — the water he slings down as rain

symbols.name: The Rainbow (K'uychi)
symbols.meaning: His dread bow, an omen serpent crawling on the earth, to be placated, never touched

mythology.lead: Illapa's mythology comes to us almost entirely through colonial chroniclers writing after the conquest — Cobo, Polo de Ondegardo, Murúa — whose accounts agree on the god's person and differ on detail. What they preserve is a fully formed storm theology: a warrior in the sky with a household, a water supply, and weapons.

myths.title: The Man in the Sky
myths.text: Bernabé Cobo (Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Book 13, c. 1653) describes Illapa as a man dressed in shining clothing, carrying a sling and a mace; when he whirls the sling, the flash of lightning leaps from him, and the crack of the stone's release is the thunder. Other chroniclers — Polo de Ondegardo in the 1550s, Martín de Murúa later — add that his temples and fields near Cuzco received the first chicha of the harvest. No pre-conquest narrative of his deeds survives; the Inca seem to have honored him through description and offering rather than epic. Polo adds that the thunderer's season opened when the Pleiades returned to the dawn sky — the whole agricultural year answered to his cue. The image nonetheless is complete:The image nonetheless is complete: the storm is a soldier on patrol, armed and fed by the people below.

myths.title: Sisters Stored Among the Stars
myths.text: Cobo records that Illapa kept his kinswomen — his sisters — in the sky as constellations, and that when the earth needed rain he drew water from the celestial river, the Milky Way, and slung it down. Urton stresses that this celestial economy still orders Quechua weather talk: streams in the sky are watched filling as the rains approach, and the dark cloud-constellations are read as the very animals of the old star lore. The astral geography of the Andes is precise:The astral geography of the Andes is precise: dark-cloud constellations (the fox, the llama, the toad) drink from the Mayu's stream, and modern Quechua speakers still read weather in their positions (Urton, Inca Myths, 1999). Whether or not every detail is pre-Hispanic, the theology is coherent: rain is a family business — a brother in the sky working a reservoir kept by his sisters.

lore.culturalLegacy: Illapa's name is his principal monument: illapa — thunder — is everyday Quechua from Ecuador to Bolivia, a linguistic fossil of the empire's sky. The material cult continues in the apachetas still raised at passes, in thunderstones kept as family heirlooms, and in the offerings left where lightning has struck. In Cuzco's festival calendar, the revived Inti Raymi and the rain-linked rites of the agricultural year keep a place for the storm. For historians, Illapa anchors a larger legacy: he is the clearest case of how the Inca organized nature into an administration — a pantheon that ran like a bureaucracy of sky, weather, and war, each office with its priesthood, its fields, and its liturgy (Rowe 1946; D'Altroy 2002). The thunder god is the empire's artillery, still audible.
lore.archaeology: No temple of Illapa has been securely identified, and his aniconic, sky-directed cult left few images. The archaeological record is instead one of place: cairn fields (apachetas) along the Qhapaq Ñan road system, mountain-top shrines (huacas) where offerings accompanied weather rites, and fields struck by lightning that became enduring places of offering — practice documented by Polo de Ondegardo in the sixteenth century and confirmed ethnographically ever since. Prehistoric stone tools ('thunderstones') circulate in modern Andean households as identified relics of his bolts. Cobo and Murúa describe his cult buildings in the Cuzco region — small, field-endowed shrines rather than monumental temples — but none has been excavated under his name.
lore.syncretism: Under Spanish rule, Illapa's storm office was quietly reassigned. Andean converts mapped the thunderer onto Santiago (St. James), whose horse's hooves became the new thunder — a pairing documented across colonial Andean religion, in which the saint's festivals answered the old storm rituals. Yet the god himself was never fully displaced: illapa remains the ordinary Quechua word for thunder, so every storm in the Andes still speaks his name. In the twentieth century, indigenist movements and Quechua-language media restored the god to public dignity — school texts, festival pageants, and the Killa Raymi and Inti Raymi revivals place the storm god back among the honored. The word's survival is itself the syncretism's measure: Christianity borrowed his sky, but kept his vocabulary.

pronunciation.approximation: SOO-pie — two syllables, stress on the first; the '-ay' is the 'y' of 'fly'.
pronunciation.note: Supay is Tier 2: the Quechua name carries no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII loses; only the capital distinguishes the restored form. Its pre-conquest meaning was 'spirit'; the modern sense 'devil' is a colonial redefinition, not an original one.

domains.title: Supay
domains.subtitle: Underworld
domains.lead: Supay is the lord of uku pacha, the inner world beneath the Andes — the domain of the dead, of cave-dwelling spirits, and of the mineral wealth the earth conceals. No temple bore his name; he was propitiated, not praised. Under Spanish rule the name was reforged: supay became the Quechua word for 'devil', and the lord of the inner world survives today as the miners' Tío.

cards.name: Lord of Uku Pacha
cards.desc: Master of the inner world beneath the earth where the dead dwell and the ore veins run (Polo de Ondegardo 1571; Cobo, Historia 13.10).

cards.name: Master of the Supaykuna
cards.desc: The dangerous spirits — the supaykuna — who send illness and haunt caves and crossroads; offerings kept them from taking the living.

cards.name: The Caves of Tambillos
cards.desc: Caverns near Huarochirí where the people said the supay dwelt; the Huarochirí manuscript records the rites paid there.

cards.name: The Miners' Tío
cards.desc: In the colonial mines, above all Potosí, miners fed the underground lord coca, alcohol, and cigarettes under the alias El Tío.

symbols.name: Cave mouth or mine shaft
symbols.meaning: The visible entrance to uku pacha; every shaft sunk into the earth is a doorway into Supay's jurisdiction

symbols.name: Coca and chicha
symbols.meaning: The standard offerings that made the underground lord generous toward the living who disturbed his realm

symbols.name: Funerary goods
symbols.meaning: Food, tools, and treasure interred with the dead as provision for the journey down to Supay's household

symbols.name: The horned devil figure
symbols.meaning: The post-conquest iconography in which the extirpation campaigns re-imagined Supay as the Christian Devil

mythology.lead: No Inca myth cycle of Supay survives on its own terms. Everything we know comes through colonial chroniclers, Quechua-language manuscripts, and the living memory of Andean communities — the record of a lord of the inner world who was propitiated, feared, demonized, and finally renamed, yet never quite dethroned.

myths.title: Lord of Uku Pacha
myths.text: The earliest European witness is the corregidor Polo de Ondegardo, whose 1571 report De los errores y supersticiones de los indios explains Inca cosmology as three stacked worlds: hanaq pacha, the upper world; kay pacha, this present world; and uku pacha, the inner world within the earth. The dead descended to uku pacha, Polo reports, and there remained in the power of the being they called Supay. Bernabé Cobo repeats the scheme a century later (Historia del Nuevo Mundo 13.10), adding that the dead were furnished with food, tools, and treasure for the journey down. Nowhere in these accounts is Supay a god of a temple or a priesthood: he is the one who holds the dead, and the offerings made at funerals are essentially payments that keep him from reaching further into the world of the living. The Inca underworld was not a place of punishment but of retention, and Supay was its jailer as much as its king. The belief encodes a sober arithmetic: every death adds to his household, so the living must forever feed the boundary between the worlds.

myths.title: The Caves of Tambillos
myths.text: The Quechua-language Huarochirí manuscript, recorded by the extirpator Francisco de Ávila in the first years of the seventeenth century (trans. Salomon & Urioste, 1991), treats supay not as a single lord but as a class of dangerous beings — the supaykuna — who dwell in caves, springs, hills, and crossroads and send illness to those who offend them. The most famous haunt is the cavern of Tambillos, near San Pedro de Huarochirí, where the people made offerings of coca and maize beer so that the spirits of the rock would not take their children. Scholars have long debated whether the chroniclers' single 'Supay, lord of the inner world' is a Spanish simplification of this older, plural spirit-world, or whether the supaykuna were always understood as the lord's subjects. The manuscript itself does not resolve the question; it simply shows communities negotiating, offering, and appeasing. Whatever the hierarchy, the logic is constant: the earth's interior is populated, and it must be paid. Supay's power was never worshipped from a temple — it was managed at the cave mouth, one offering at a time.

lore.culturalLegacy: Supay remains embedded in Andean language itself: to this day supay means devil in Quechua and Aymara, a living fossil of the extirpation campaigns. In the mining regions of Bolivia the Tío effigies are still fed and still feared, and the Diablada festivals stage his masked dance before crowds of thousands. For scholarship, Supay is a key witness to how colonialism rewrote indigenous cosmology — studied by Taussig, Platt, and Duviols as the paradigmatic case of a deity demonized, renamed, and secretly retained. The name also circulates in global culture: Andean diaspora communities, museum exhibitions on Inca religion, and contemporary indigenous revival movements all return to the older, pre-Christian meaning of the word — spirit, not devil — as part of recovering what the extirpations tried to erase.
lore.archaeology: No temple of Supay is known — he was propitiated at cave mouths, springs, graves, and mine faces rather than in built sanctuaries. The material record is therefore indirect: the rock shelters and cave shrines of the Huarochirí region, including Tambillos, where colonial extirpation records describe offerings of coca and maize beer; colonial-era dictionaries and confessionals that fixed supay as 'devil' (González Holguín 1608; Bertonio 1612); the Tío effigies and their offerings still maintained at Potosí and Olmillos; and the abundant documentary archive of the extirpation campaigns (Arriaga 1621; Duviols). The evidence honestly shows a cult of place rather than of monuments.
lore.syncretism: Supay's entire afterlife is a history of forced translations. The conquering church mapped him onto Satan, and the mapping was so successful that modern Quechua and Aymara use supay as the ordinary word for devil. Yet the older figure survived the translation in the mines, where El Tío — the Uncle — continues the uku pacha lord's contract with those who take wealth from below. Scholars such as Taussig (1980) and Tristan Platt have read this double life as the emblem of colonial capitalism: the indigenous underworld lord re-employed as the owner of the silver that fed Europe. The Diablada dance traditions of Oruro and the miner rites at Potosí keep both identities visible at once — Christian devil masks performing unmistakably pre-Christian obligations.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OOR-kah-wah-ree' — four light syllables; the 'g' is only the glide w and the final y a short 'ee'. Stress placement is not recorded: the initial stress follows modern Quechua habit and is a convention, not a fact.
pronunciation.note: Urcaguary is Tier 2: the restored form carries no diacritic or distinctive letter beyond the capital, and the pre-conquest pronunciation is irrecoverable — even the stress is a modern convention. The catalog's gloss ‘He of the underground’ follows the reading of the name from Quechua urqu and quri; both are ordinary living words, which is why the figure's title and domain are one.

domains.title: Urcaguary
domains.subtitle: Underworld Jewels
domains.lead: Urcaguary is the Inca guardian of what lies beneath the mountains: gold, silver, emeralds and the other precious things sealed in the earth. The figure is known only through the colonial chronicle tradition and later folklore, and the sources are late, brief and partly modern — but they agree on the core: the underground hoard has a watcher, and it is not a vault, it is a god.

cards.name: Guardian of the Hoard
cards.desc: Beneath the mountains Urcaguary keeps the metals and gems of the inner earth; the traditional description hangs gold chains and precious stones from the serpent's tail.

cards.name: The Serpent with a Deer's Head
cards.desc: The figure takes the body of a serpent and the head of a taruka, the Andean deer — wealth that watches and thinks like a mountain animal.

cards.name: He of the Underground
cards.desc: The name reads from Quechua urqu, ‘within the earth’, and quri, ‘gold’: the title is the domain, and the domain is the treasury.

cards.name: The Treasure That Judges
cards.desc: The hoard belongs to the guardian, not the miner: in the moral economy of the Andean mine, gold is taken only as tribute, never as theft.

symbols.name: Gold chains
symbols.meaning: Hung from the serpent's tail in the chroniclers' descriptions — wealth worn as the guardian's own ornament

symbols.name: Emeralds and precious stones
symbols.meaning: The green gems of the Andes stored in the subterranean house the serpent keeps

symbols.name: The taruka (Andean deer) head
symbols.meaning: The alert head he wears: the deer of the high puna, watchful and unreachable

symbols.name: The serpent body
symbols.meaning: The winding form that coils through the veins of ore inside the mountains

symbols.name: The mountain vault
symbols.meaning: Every sealed vein and hidden pocket of ore is a door of his treasury

mythology.lead: Urcaguary has no surviving epic. The sources are late, brief and partly modern, and honesty requires saying so plainly. What the tradition preserves is a portrait rather than a cycle: a serpent-bodied watcher below the mountains, a theology of treasure, and a mining etiquette that is still practiced in the Andes.

myths.title: A God Seen Through Colonial Eyes
myths.text:
Everything securely known about Urcaguary descends from the chroniclers writing after the conquest — above all Martín de Murúa, whose Historia general del Piru (1616) catalogues the gods of the Andes, and Bernabé Cobo, whose Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653) preserves the most orderly account of the Inca huacas. In their pages Urcaguary appears as the deity of metals, jewels and the other precious things hidden underground — a figure who presided over ore-rich mountains and mining shrines, but whose cult left no standing temple and whose myths were never written down in Quechua. The colonial writers worked decades after the religion they described had been outlawed, from informants under missionary pressure, so their catalogues are triage documents as much as testimonies.

Read that way, Urcaguary is half-known by necessity: a god glimpsed through the gap between destroyed shrines and Spanish notebooks. The temple built here is therefore a temple over an archive, not over a ruin.

myths.title: The Serpent in the Veins of Gold
myths.text:
Later tradition gives the figure a body. Urcaguary is pictured as a great serpent with the head of a taruka, the Andean deer, gold chains and precious stones linked along the tail, dwelling beneath the mountains in the uku pacha, the world within the earth. The deer's head is explained as a mark of the guardian's way of thinking — alert, swift, impossible to catch — and in the same layer of folklore the guardian serpent of the depths, Hurkaway, is identified with Urcaguary: the snake that coils through the ore veins is the treasure's own watchman made visible.

The image is exact theology in zoological form. A vault guards wealth with walls; a serpent guards it with intention. The Andes buried their treasure in the most guarded shape the animal world offers.

lore.culturalLegacy: The etiquette Urcaguary presides over is alive: Andean miners still offer coca, alcohol and smoke to the mountain and to the Tío of the workings before blasting, a rite documented ethnographically from Potosí across Bolivia and Peru for over a century. In folklore collections the name circulates as the guardian of hidden treasure — the tesoros ocultos whose gold turns to leaves in the hands of the unworthy, a pan-Andean motif his serpent keeps. In the museums of Cuzco and Lima the legacy is an absence: the gold and silver he hypothetically guarded, described at length by Cobo and Murúa, was melted into ingots within decades of the conquest, and his treasury survives only as chronicle. For Quechua language revival the name's elements remain living words — urqu, the mountain, and quri, gold — so the god's title is still pronounceable as a sentence of modern Quechua.
lore.archaeology: No temple, cult statue or offering securely attributable to Urcaguary survives; the figure's archaeology is textual. The chronicles describe the golden effigies and huancas of the Coricancha and of provincial shrines — works seized and melted between 1533 and the 1570s, known today only through Cobo, Murúa and Cieza de León. Mining archaeology supplies the milieu: pre-Hispanic workings at Potosí's Cerro Rico and across the central Andes, stone hammers, ore-processing floors and shaft burials that kept the mountain's dead close to its metal. Andean art gives the iconography of his form without the name — serpents and deer crowd Moche and Inca metalwork and rock art — but no piece can be assigned to this deity with confidence.
lore.syncretism: Urcaguary's afterlife is a history of translations. Colonial missionaries folded the spirits of the uku pacha into Christian demonology — Supay, lord of the inner world, became the very word for devil in Quechua — while the miners kept the old courtesies under new names. The serpent body invited comparison with the amaru, the sacred Andean serpent of water, earth and the underworld, and in regional folklore the two guardians of the deep merge and separate: sometimes the amaru carries the treasure, sometimes Urcaguary carries the amaru's shape. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century compilations detached the figure from cult context entirely, presenting it as a ‘god of treasure’ in the European fairy-hoard sense, and modern summaries go further still, calling the gender ambiguous — a flattening the chronicles, which say little either way, cannot support. Read through all three layers, Urcaguary is best understood as the Inca theology of subterranean wealth caught mid-translation into European categories.

pronunciation.approximation: Say "ekkeko" — two open syllables with a light glottal catch between the double k in the Aymara-influenced pronunciation; stress falls on the penult.
pronunciation.note: The ASCII form "ekkeko" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Ekkeko" preserves the name's scholarly dignity. The name's own etymology is uncertain: the gloss 'dwarf' rests on a proposed Aymara derivation (ikiqu) that handbooks record as plausible rather than proven. The entry is Tier 2: the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops.

domains.title: Ekkeko
domains.subtitle: Luck
domains.lead: Ekkeko is the Andean god of luck and abundance: a smiling little man bowed under a pack holding everything a household could wish for. His mythology is young as myths go — a colonial chronicler's notice, a founding legend printed in 1904, and a January fair where all of La Paz buys its dreams in miniature — but it rests on burden-carrier figurines far older than the name.

cards.name: God of Plenty
cards.desc: The loaded pack on his back carries every good thing a household can hope for: grain, coin, houses, health, and a lit pipe besides.

cards.name: The Alasitas Fair
cards.desc: Every 24 January the streets of La Paz fill with miniatures of everything people want, bought, blessed, and set on his altar to be grown into reality.

cards.name: Household Idol
cards.desc: Bernabé Cobo described how Andean families kept his little image by the hearth, loading it with tiny packs and offerings so prosperity would stay in the house.

cards.name: Consort of Coya
cards.desc: In the legend recorded in 1904, Ekeko fed his beloved Coya from his own flesh during a famine; her faithful search restored him as the little clay god.

symbols.name: The loaded pack
symbols.meaning: The bundle of goods on his back — every modest desire of the household, abundance compressed into one bowed, patient burden.

symbols.name: Clay figurine
symbols.meaning: Pre-Columbian Tiwanaku figures of burden-carriers are the archaeological ancestors of the modern Ekeko images.

symbols.name: Miniatures (alasitas)
symbols.meaning: The tiny objects of the fair — money, houses, cars, diplomas — wishes bought small so the god can grow them large.

symbols.name: The ritual offering cloth
symbols.meaning: The mesa laden with sugar figurines, seeds, and breads set before the idol on his feast day.

symbols.name: The pipe
symbols.meaning: The little clay pipe of folk images, an emblem of contentment and the unhurried ease of a well-fed house.

mythology.lead: Ekeko's mythology is unusual: nearly all of it is modern. A colonial Jesuit notices the household idol in 1653; a founding legend is printed in 1904; the January fair of Alasitas keeps the cult alive in the streets of La Paz. Beneath all of it lie burden-carrier figurines from Tiwanaku, a thousand years older than the name.

myths.title: Ekeko and Coya in the Famine
myths.text: The best-known story of Ekeko is surprisingly recent: it was printed in 1904 by the Bolivian writer Antonio Díaz Villamil in his Exaltación de la Alasita. In the time of drought, when the storehouses stood empty, the little man Ekeko fed his beloved Coya from his own flesh, cutting pieces from his body so that she would not starve. When the rains finally returned, Coya searched the hills for him and found only a small clay figure bowed under an enormous load. She recognized her lover in the idol, carried it home, and set it on the household altar; from that day, abundance never left her house. Scholars treat the legend as modern folklore rather than pre-Columbian scripture — and say so openly — yet it explains everything the ritual actually does: the little body, the heavy pack, the beloved who keeps him. The myth reads Ekeko as love converted into provision.

myths.title: The Little God Cobo Saw
myths.text: Bernabé Cobo, writing his Historia del Nuevo Mundo in 1653, is the earliest secure witness. Among the household devotions of the Andean people he describes a small idol called Equeco, revered as a god of wealth and contentment: his image was a little figure loaded with packs and bundles, set up in the house and offered food, so that he would keep the family supplied with the small goods of life — food, clothing, coin. Cobo's Equeco is no state god of the Sun's rank but a humble domestic numen, carried and coddled by ordinary households. That a Jesuit chronicler should pause over so modest a deity is itself testimony to how thoroughly the little god had entered daily life. The passage anchors Ekeko in the colonial record and shows what he was always for: not empire or war, but the prosperity of the kitchen and the storeroom.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ekeko is today a national emblem of Bolivia, printed on lottery tickets, staged in civic pageants, and set on altars in houses that no longer remember the famine legend. The Alasitas fair has travelled with Bolivian migration — to Buenos Aires, Santiago, and the Peruvian highlands, where Puno keeps its own January fair — so the little god now presides over diaspora longing as much as over household luck. Twentieth-century letters and art reworked the Díaz Villamil legend into schoolbooks, murals, and popular song. UNESCO recognition fixed the fair on the world stage. Through it all the image barely changes: a small smiling man under a heavy pack, the patron of everyone who wants ordinary things — a roof, a wage, a full table — and asks for them the Andean way, in miniature first.
lore.syncretism: Ekeko is a study in colonial layering. His name and image passed into Spanish as Ekeko or Equeco; his consort bears Coya, the title of the Inca empress; and his fair was folded into Catholic time — the January date in La Paz is bound up with the feast of Our Lady of Peace, and priests bless the miniature purchases even as the Church has periodically denounced the whole commerce as idolatry. The blessing is the syncretism in one gesture: sacrament and ch'alla sprinkling the same little car. Under the colonial surface the substrate is older — Aymara marketplace piety and the burden-carrier imagery of Tiwanaku — so that the 'little god' condenses three strata: pre-Columbian figurine, colonial household saint, and republican national emblem.

pronunciation.approximation: wa-MA-ni — three even syllables, the middle one weighted; every vowel pure and Spanish-like.
pronunciation.note: Tier 2: the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter — the distinction lies in scholarship and meaning, not orthography. The chronicles and modern Quechua sources agree on the mountain-sense; the older gloss 'falcon' (waman) survives in place-names and surnames.

domains.title: Wamani
domains.subtitle: Sacred Mountain
domains.lead: Wamani is the Andean sacred mountain made person: the tutelary peak of a province, ancestor of its people, and keeper of the springs that descend from its snowfields. In the Inca world every region had its wamani, and the covenant between community and mountain — offerings for water, harvest, and protection — remains alive in Andean religion today.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The name joins Quechua waman, 'falcon,' to the mountain-sense recorded by the chroniclers — the falcon that watches from the peak.

cards.name: Sacred Mountain
cards.desc: The apu of a province: snowfield, spring, and ancestor in one body — the vertical axis of Andean religion.

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Qoyllur Rit'i pilgrims still dance before the glacier of Sinakara each June; the covenant with the mountain has never lapsed.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Kept at the registrable form while the temple explains the restoration and the falcon-meaning the plain form conceals.

symbols.name: Snowfield and spring
symbols.meaning: The glacial melt that feeds the terraces below — water is the wamani's first gift and the reason for his cult

symbols.name: The falcon (waman)
symbols.meaning: The older sense of the name: the raptor that quarters the peaks — from it come Wamanga (Ayacucho) and Guamán Poma

symbols.name: Coca and chicha
symbols.meaning: The covenant's currency: coca leaves and maize beer laid on the stone platforms for the mountain's favor

symbols.name: The paqarina
symbols.meaning: The emergence-place where ancestors rose from the earth; each wamani is someone's birthplace in the genealogies

symbols.name: The ukuku
symbols.meaning: The bear-dancer of Qoyllur Rit'i who climbs the glacier and carries the star-snow down to bless the fields

mythology.lead: Wamani has no epic cycle: Andean mountain religion lives in ritual, pilgrimage, and origin story rather than narrative text. What survives — from the colonial chronicles, the temple origin legends, and a living cult at Qoyllur Rit'i — reads as one long covenant between people and peak; the four 'myths' below are its chapters.

myths.title: The Mountain that Gives Birth
myths.text: Every Andean community once knew which mountain it came from. The colonial chronicles — Cobo's Historia del Nuevo Mundo (Book 13), Sarmiento de Gamboa's Historia Indica, and the now-lost Cusco paintings they copied — record a landscape dense with paqarina, 'emergence places,' from which founding ancestors rose to establish the ayllu. The Inca told the type-tale at the greatest scale: their own forebears, the four Ayar siblings, emerged from the cave of Pacaritambo and traveled ridge by ridge until the golden rod sank at Huanacauri, the hill that chose Cusco. A wamani is this story in the singular: one peak, one people, one bloodline running from snowfield to village. The mountain is not scenery behind the genealogy; it is the first ancestor and the final grave, and the covenant — people tend the mountain, the mountain feeds the people — is the oldest contract in the Andes.

myths.title: Water for Offerings
myths.text: The wamani's side of the covenant is water: from the snowfields the apu sends the springs that fill the terraces, and the people's side is the offering — coca leaves and maize beer poured on stone platforms, llamas driven to high pasture, prayers spoken to the peak by name. Cobo watched the rites; modern ethnography (Flores Ochoa) records their grammar: an offering is not a purchase but a greeting, the same exchange of coca and goodwill with which one honors an elder. Neglect brings drought, hail, and sickness — the mountain, like any elder, is patient but not forever. Brian Bauer (The Sacred Landscape of the Inca) calls this reciprocity the operating system of the Inca state. The covenant makes hydrology a religion: the aquifer has a face, the watershed a will, and the annual offering the family's standing appointment with both.

lore.culturalLegacy: The covenant still runs. Qoyllur Rit'i draws tens of thousands of pilgrims every June; coca is still offered to the apus before planting; and in modern Quechua wamani itself has widened from one mountain to a whole people or nation — Peru wamani, 'the land of Peru.' The mountain-deities entered the colonial church as saints and virgins and came out the other side still mountains. And in the Andean diaspora — miners, market vendors, students abroad — the first libation still goes to the Pachamama and the apu of wherever you happen to be standing: the wamani's greatest miracle is portability, a god who moves with his people.
lore.archaeology: The wamani's evidence is the mountain itself. The great capacocha shrines have yielded the most spectacular finds in Andean archaeology: the three Llullaillaco children (excavated 1999 by Reinhard and Ceruti; Museum of High-Altitude Archaeology, Salta), the Ampato mummy ('Juanita,' found 1995), and more than a hundred high-altitude sites from Argentina to Ecuador. At Cusco, the Inca capital's ritual landscape — documented building by building in Bernabé Cobo's Book 13 before the colonial city erased it — was a mapped constellation of apus, anchored by the Coricancha's golden garden and the intihuatana stone. Machu Picchu's planners sited its sacred district by the same rule: the city is a wamani-cult in masonry, every window and altar answering a named peak.
lore.syncretism: The extirpators did their worst. From 1610 the colonial Church ran campaigns — Diego de Arriaga's manual of 1621 prescribed them — to unmask and destroy huacas, and the wamanis of the rites were beaten, burned, and forcibly 'baptized.' What survived, survived by translation: the mountain became a saint's hill, the cave-shrine a Virgin's chapel, and at Qoyllur Rit'i the glacier apu of Sinakara now shares his sanctuary with a rock painted as the crucified Christ. Scholars of the pilgrimage (Sallnow, Pilgrims of the Andes; Flores Ochoa) warn against calling this a disguise: the rites' logic — reciprocity with the living landscape — is pre-Columbian, and the Catholic overlay functions less as mask than as a second language the mountain was given, and never asked for.

steps: Anima is a Latin noun meaning "breath, air, soul, life force".
Its original script is the Latin alphabet; it is not attested in Greek letters.
The PuniCodex restoration Anima is identical to the ASCII form because the classical spelling uses no diacritics.
provenanceSources: Plato’s Latin reception in Cicero and Apuleius

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-nih-mah' — stress the first syllable; the middle vowel is short and light.
pronunciation.note: Anima is a Latin word, not a Greek proper name. It has no indigenous alphabetic 'original script' other than the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form anima is already the Latin spelling; the restoration capitalises the proper-noun form as a scholarly citation. Because no distinctive diacritic or special letter is added, the entry is Tier 2.

domains.title: The Breath that Becomes Soul
domains.subtitle: Soul, Breath, and Life Force
domains.lead: Anima is the Latin word for breath, air, and — by extension — the soul or life-force that animates a living body. It names one of the most ancient equations in Western thought: that the difference between a corpse and a living person is the presence of breath. From this simple observation Latin developed a rich vocabulary of animation, soul, and spirit that still shapes modern psychology, religion, and biology.

cards.name: Breath
cards.desc: The literal meaning of anima: the air drawn in and expelled by living creatures.

cards.name: Soul
cards.desc: In philosophy and theology anima becomes the immaterial principle that gives life and, later, the rational soul.

cards.name: Life Force
cards.desc: The active power that distinguishes the living from the dead, the moving from the still.

cards.name: Inspiration
cards.desc: Literally 'breathing in' — the moment when life, ideas, or the divine enter the self.

symbols.name: Breath or wind
symbols.meaning: The invisible current that enters at birth and departs at death.

symbols.name: Bird
symbols.meaning: A widespread symbol for the soul as something light, winged, and capable of leaving the body.

symbols.name: Blood or pulse
symbols.meaning: The physiological sign that anima is at work in the living body.

symbols.name: Flame
symbols.meaning: The small fire of individual life, easily extinguished and often identified with the soul's spark.

symbols.name: The World-Soul (anima mundi)
symbols.meaning: The breath of the cosmos itself — the Stoic and Platonic doctrine that the universe is a living being, its body the world and its soul the divine air.

symbols.name: The departing breath
symbols.meaning: The final exhalation at death — the moment anima leaves the body, caught by artists as the last visible vapor of a person.

mythology.lead: Anima is not a mythological character in the Greek or Roman sense; it is a concept that acquired a long philosophical and theological history. Its 'mythology' is therefore the story of how breath became soul, and how soul became one of the foundation stones of Western psychology.

myths.title: The Breath of Life
myths.text: In Classical Latin anima first names the air itself: the breeze in the trees, the breath in the lungs. Cicero uses the word for the vital spirit that ties soul to body (Tusculanae disputationes 1), but the word's great theorist is the materialist Lucretius. In De rerum natura 3 he argues that the soul is a bodily thing — a subtle compound of heat, air, and wind, fine as smoke — dispersed and destroyed when the body dies. To understand the soul correctly, for Lucretius, is to be cured of the fear of death: no afterlife, no punishment, only rest. The Latin word thus begins as physiology and becomes philosophy in a single step. Western psychology starts here — not with a ghost in a machine, but with weather inside the body, measurable in warmth and breath.

myths.title: The Rational Soul
myths.text: Early Latin Christianity adopted anima as the standard rendering of Greek psychē, and the word's career turned theological. Tertullian devoted a treatise to it (De anima); Augustine's De quantitate animae asks, in dialogue, what the soul's 'magnitude' can be; Boethius made the soul the hinge of the Consolation of Philosophy. The scholastics completed the fusion: following Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas calls the soul the body's form — 'the first principle of life in things which live in our world' (Summa Theologiae I.75.1) — and the Council of Vienne (1312) defined as doctrine that the rational soul is truly, of itself, the form of the human body. The breath-word ended up carrying the heaviest load in Christian metaphysics, while never quite losing its breeze: between clinic and creed, anima kept both meanings at once.

lore.culturalLegacy: Anima is one of the most quietly influential words in Western languages. It underlies 'animal' (a being that has breath), 'animate' (to give life), 'animation' (the illusion of life in images), and 'animism' (the attribution of soul to natural objects). In Jungian psychology the anima is a central archetype, and in contemporary spirituality it names the feminine soul-principle. The word's persistence shows that the ancient equation of breath with life has never really been replaced.
lore.archaeology: A concept has no tombs, but it has manuscripts, and the material trail of anima is among the most dramatic in Latin literature. Lucretius' De rerum natura — the greatest ancient book of the soul's materiality — survives through a single early medieval lineage, crowned by the ninth-century codex Oblongus (Leiden, Bibliotheek der Rijksuniversiteit, Vossianus Latinus F 30); the poem's recovery in 1417, when Poggio Bracciolini's agents pulled a copy from a German monastery shelf, detonated the Renaissance debate over atom and soul. Augustine's De quantitate animae and the scholastic summae travelled in hundreds of copies across medieval Europe. Jung's twentieth-century revival rests on printed editions and the working library at Küsnacht — archaeology of a different kind.
lore.syncretism: The Latin anima overlaps with Greek psychē, Hebrew nephesh, Sanskrit ātman, and Greek pneuma. All of these terms begin with breath or wind and develop into concepts of soul, spirit, or self. In medieval philosophy anima became the bridge between Aristotelian biology and Christian theology, a development that shaped European thought until the early modern period. In modern psychology it survives as Jung's anima and as the root of 'animation,' the art of giving apparent life to images.
lore.originalScriptNote: Anima is a Latin word. It has no 'original script' in the sense of Greek or cuneiform; its canonical form is the Latin spelling anima. The ASCII form anima already represents the Latin spelling exactly. The restoration Anima is therefore the capitalised proper-noun citation form, not a phonetic recovery. The appropriate label is 'Scholarly Transliteration' or simply 'Latin'.

steps: The term is a Latin common noun and philosophical concept, not a theonym in the strict sense.
PuniCodex treats it under the Greek pantheon bucket by convention, but its original script is the Latin alphabet.
The restored form Animus preserves the classical spelling; the ASCII form animus is identical because no diacritics are required.
provenanceSources: Cicero, De Natura Deorum and Tusculanae Disputationes

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-nih-moos' — stress the first syllable; the final vowel is short and rounded.
pronunciation.note: Animus is a Latin word, not a Greek proper name. It has no indigenous alphabetic 'original script' other than the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form animus is already the Latin spelling; the restoration capitalises the proper-noun form as a scholarly citation. Because no distinctive diacritic or special letter is added, the entry is Tier 2.

domains.title: Mind, Spirit, and Courage
domains.subtitle: The Active Power of the Soul
domains.lead: Animus is the Latin word for mind, spirit, courage, and sometimes fierce anger. It names the active, directing part of the person: the faculty that thinks, decides, resists, and fights. Where anima is breath and life, animus is will and consciousness. Roman ethics placed great weight on the animus as the seat of virtue, and the word survives in English as a sign of both spiritedness and settled hostility.

cards.name: Mind
cards.desc: The rational faculty that deliberates, remembers, and plans.

cards.name: Spirit
cards.desc: The animating energy of character and resolve.

cards.name: Courage
cards.desc: The quality that enables a person to face danger without yielding.

cards.name: Wrath
cards.desc: Animus can also mean fierce temper — the same energy turned destructive.

symbols.name: Heart
symbols.meaning: The seat of courage and emotional resolve in Roman and modern symbolism.

symbols.name: Sword
symbols.meaning: The instrument of courage and the willingness to act with force.

symbols.name: Flame
symbols.meaning: The fire of spirit, ambition, and anger that drives action.

symbols.name: Brow or forehead
symbols.meaning: The visible place of mind and determination, where animus shows on the face.

mythology.lead: Animus is not a mythological character but a concept that runs through Roman literature, rhetoric, and ethics. Its 'mythology' is the story of how Latin speakers imagined the active self: the mind that commands, the spirit that endures, and the anger that destroys.

myths.title: The Seat of Courage
myths.text:
For Roman writers the animus is the source of virtus, the courage that makes a citizen worth the state. Cicero calls the animus divine — a fragment of the gods' own fire dwelling in the human breast, to be cultivated as our best part (Tusculan Disputations 1.64–66) — and Livy makes the point with a story: Horatius Cocles, holding the bridge alone against Etruria, cries that every man must sooner or later die, and those who die for their country are blessed (Ab Urbe Condita 2.10). The word runs through the whole ethic: magnanimus, great-souled; fortis animo, brave in mind; abicere animum, to throw away one's spirit — the one unforgivable loss.

Roman heroism is interior before it is physical: the legion's discipline was an animus trained in common.

myths.title: The Ruling Faculty
myths.text:
Roman Stoics identified the animus with the hēgemonikon, the ruling part of the soul, and made its governance the whole of philosophy. Seneca's treatise On Anger anatomizes the animus inflamed: wrath, he says, is a brief madness, and the wise man cures it as a doctor cures fever, before it becomes habit (De Ira 1.1–4). Marcus Aurelius, emperor and diarist, began his mornings reminding his ruling faculty what it was and what work lay before it (Meditations 2.1–2). The passions were diseases of the animus; reason its hygiene; tranquility its health. The prize of this medicine was freedom — the only kind Rome could not grant by law: an animus dependent on nothing external, therefore afraid of nothing external.

The Stoic wager is that the will, properly governed, is the one province fortune can never invade.

lore.culturalLegacy: Animus survives in English as both a technical term and an everyday word. 'Animate,' 'animation,' and 'animal' derive from anima, but 'animus,' 'magnanimous,' 'pusillanimous,' and 'animosity' preserve the masculine, spirited sense. In Jungian psychology the animus is a major archetype, and in law and rhetoric 'animus' still names intention or state of mind. The word's career shows how Roman concepts of mind and courage continue to shape Western languages and thought.
lore.archaeology: No altar to Animus is known — the word never had a cult — but the concept has a material footprint. Polybius, explaining Roman power to Greeks, describes the aristocratic funeral: the corpse arrayed in the forum with actors wearing the wax portrait-masks (imagines) of every ancestor, each mask a stored animus brought back to embody the dead (Histories 6.53–54). The Roman portrait tradition — the veristic busts of the Republic and thousands of funerary inscriptions commending the animus to the gods — is the largest surviving archive of the idea. Roman coins personified virtus and fides; what they struck in bronze was the disciplined animus itself, made payable.
lore.syncretism: The Latin animus maps onto Greek thymos (spiritedness), nous (mind), and psychē (soul). Roman Stoicism absorbed Greek psychology and gave it a distinctly Roman emphasis on duty, endurance, and public virtue. In modern English 'animus' has narrowed to mean hostility or ill will, but the broader Latin sense survives in words such as animate, magnanimous, and animosity. The word is a bridge between ancient ethics and modern psychology.
lore.originalScriptNote: Animus is a Latin word. It has no 'original script' in the sense of Greek or cuneiform; its canonical form is the Latin spelling animus. The ASCII form animus already represents the Latin spelling exactly. The restoration Animus is therefore the capitalised proper-noun citation form, not a phonetic recovery. The appropriate label is 'Scholarly Transliteration' or simply 'Latin'.

steps: Gravitas is a Latin abstract noun denoting weight, seriousness, and dignity.
The original script is the Latin alphabet; the concept is Roman, not Greek.
The PuniCodex restoration Gravitas preserves the classical spelling.

pronunciation.approximation: 'GRAH-wih-tahs' — three syllables, the first stressed and grounded, the ending short and definite; no diphthongs, no drift.
pronunciation.note: Gravitas is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the form is plain Latin letters with no diacritic or distinctive character, so the restoration capitalizes and nothing more. The word needs no ornament; it coined the concept it names.

domains.title: Gravitas
domains.subtitle: Weight
domains.lead: Gravitas is the Roman virtue of weight: the seriousness of bearing, word, and office that made a citizen worth listening to. From gravis, 'heavy,' it names the quality by which speech, gait, and judgment press down on a matter — and by which a person becomes someone the republic can safely trust with power.

cards.name: The Weighted Word
cards.desc: Cicero's ideal orator speaks with weight: authority comes not from volume but from the bearing behind the sentence (De Oratore; Orator).

cards.name: Cincinnatus at the Plough
cards.desc: Livy's dictator took emergency power, saved the army, and gave the power back — gravitas as power carried without hunger (Livy 3.26–29).

cards.name: The Composed Face
cards.desc: Aeneas 'feigns hope on his face and presses his grief deep in his heart' (Virgil, Aeneid 1.209) — the inner weight that steadies others in ruin.

cards.name: Against Levitas
cards.desc: Gravitas is defined by its opposite: levitas, lightness — the fickleness the old Romans blamed when luxury rotted the state (Sallust, Catiline 3–13).

symbols.name: The toga
symbols.meaning: The heavy woollen garment of the citizen engaged in public business — its very drape part of the office it announces

symbols.name: The fasces
symbols.meaning: The magistrate's bundle of rods carried by attendants: public power, physically borne, whose weight the bearer must carry with dignity

symbols.name: The plough
symbols.meaning: Cincinnatus' four-acre farm on the far bank of the Tiber — the ground to which true weight returns when office is done (Livy 3.26)

symbols.name: The set jaw
symbols.meaning: Aeneas' composure before his shattered crews — grief pressed down in the heart so that hope can be shown on the face (Aeneid 1.209)

symbols.name: The surveyor's plumb-line
