pronunciation.approximation: WOO-SHING — 'wu' dips low and rises (or stays low in fast speech), and 'xing' rises like 'sheen' with a rising tone.
pronunciation.note: 五行 (Wǔxíng) denotes the 'Five Phases' or 'Five Agents'—wood, fire, earth, metal, and water—the cyclical modes of transformation in Chinese cosmology, medicine, and feng shui. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading in this philosophical context is wǔ (Tone 3) + xíng (Tone 2), as given by the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and the Hanyu Pinyin scheme. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 五 as *C.ŋˤaʔ (GSR 0058a) and 行 in the sense 'walk, conduct' as *C.[g]raŋ (GSR 0748a). The Unicode restoration Wǔxíng preserves the citation tones; note that 行 is disyllabically distinguished from the reading háng ('row, profession').

domains.title: The Five Phases
domains.subtitle: Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water
domains.lead:
Wǔxíng is often mistranslated as 'five elements,' but xíng means movement, conduct, or phase. Wood, fire, earth, metal, and water are not static substances but dynamic processes: wood grows, fire flames, earth ripens, metal contracts, water descends. Together they form a grammar of transformation that Chinese thinkers applied to seasons, organs, emotions, dynasties, and military strategy.

The system works through two main cycles: the generating cycle (wood feeds fire, fire makes earth, earth bears metal, metal carries water, water nourishes wood) and the controlling cycle (wood parts earth, earth absorbs water, water quenches fire, fire melts metal, metal chops wood).

cards.name: Generation Cycle
cards.desc: Each phase gives birth to the next in a circle of mutual nourishment and support.

cards.name: Control Cycle
cards.desc: Each phase checks another, preventing any one process from running to destructive excess.

cards.name: Correspondence System
cards.desc: Every phase maps to a direction, season, color, organ, emotion, taste, and musical note.

cards.name: Cosmic Calendar
cards.desc: The phases organize the year: wood/spring, fire/summer, earth/late summer, metal/autumn, water/winter.

symbols.name: Wood
symbols.meaning: Growth, spring, the east, the liver, the color green/blue, the wind

symbols.name: Fire
symbols.meaning: Flaming, summer, the south, the heart, the color red, heat

symbols.name: Earth
symbols.meaning: Ripening, late summer, the center, the spleen, the color yellow, dampness

symbols.name: Metal
symbols.meaning: Contracting, autumn, the west, the lungs, the color white, dryness

symbols.name: Water
symbols.meaning: Descending, winter, the north, the kidneys, the color black/dark, cold

mythology.lead: Wǔxíng has no divine biography — it is a cosmology, not a theogony — but its intellectual history is dramatic. It began as a description of natural processes in the Shangshu, became a theory of dynastic legitimacy under Zou Yan, and ended as the diagnostic grammar of Traditional Chinese Medicine, where it still orders diagnosis today.

myths.title: The Great Plan
myths.text: The Hongfan ('Great Plan') chapter of the Shangshu presents the five materials as the first of the Nine Categories revealed to Yu the Great — the cosmic charter through which Heaven's order was transmitted to the founder of the Xia. Water, fire, wood, metal, and earth are listed with their natures: water soaks and descends, fire blazes and ascends, wood bends and straightens, metal yields and can be changed, earth receives sowing and yields harvests (Shangshu, Hongfan). This is the earliest systematic statement of Wǔxíng cosmology, and its setting matters as much as its content: the phases are handed down in the same breath as the laws of government, because in early Chinese thought there was no separating how nature behaves from how rule must behave. The myth's core meaning is that transformation is lawful — and law, understood deeply enough, is a description of transformation.

myths.title: The Yin-Yang and Five Phases School
myths.text: The philosopher Zou Yan (c. 305–240 BCE) of Qi turned the five phases into an engine of history. Sima Qian, who appends his biography to those of Mencius and Xunzi in the Shiji (ch. 74), records the doctrine: each dynasty rules by the virtue of one phase, and Heaven signals the coming transfer with omens — the Yellow Emperor possessed the virtue of earth, the Xia of wood, the Shang of metal, the Zhou of fire — so that each new house commands the phase that conquers its predecessor's. Conquest, not election, is the mechanism of legitimacy: the Qin claimed water (and the color black) to douse Zhou fire, and two centuries of Han debate argued whether the Han ruled by earth or by fire. Xunzi's school dismissed Zou Yan's talk of heaven as grandiose, but the emperors kept the theory for a simple reason — it made revolution look like meteorology. The myth means that cosmic legitimacy is a technology: whoever reads the phases correctly can crown a conquest as a season.

lore.culturalLegacy: Wǔxíng is the hidden scaffolding of much that looks merely 'Chinese' on the surface. The five flavors, five colors, five notes, five grains, and five directions all derive from it. Traditional Chinese Medicine diagnoses in its terms; feng shui designs spaces by it; Xingyiquan organizes its five basic fists around it; Chinese astrology assigns each year an element. The system even colored imperial ritual: the Yellow Emperor claimed earth, the Qin chose black water to overcome Zhou red fire. Today Wǔxíng survives in video-game elemental mechanics, wellness branding, and martial-arts school names — sometimes faithfully, often trivially. Its deepest legacy is a habit of mind: the tendency to see nature not as a collection of things but as a field of interactive processes.
lore.archaeology: The textual foundation of Wǔxíng appears in the Shangshu's Hongfan chapter, transmitted through Warring States and Han manuscript traditions. The Mawangdui tomb library (sealed 168 BCE, excavated 1973) preserves early medical manuscripts that apply the five phases to diagnosis and treatment, while the Huangdi Neijing became the canonical medical synthesis. Han dynasty lacquerware, bronze mirrors, and tomb murals display the color-direction correspondences of the five phases. Unlike a deity, Wǔxíng has no temple, but its logic is inscribed across the material culture of state ritual, medicine, and calendrical science.
lore.syncretism: Wǔxíng was sometimes compared by Western observers to the Greek four elements, but the comparison is misleading. The Greek elements are building blocks of substance; the Chinese phases are patterns of change. A closer Indian analogue is the pañca mahābhūta, though the correspondences differ. Wǔxíng entered Japan as gogyō and Korea as ohaeng, shaping East Asian medicine, astrology, and martial arts. In modern times, Wǔxíng has been invoked — and sometimes distorted — in management theory, martial-arts branding, and popular spirituality, often reduced to a color-coded personality test. The medical tradition, however, continues to use the five phases as a sophisticated heuristic for pattern differentiation.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 五行; traditional and simplified forms are identical. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading in the philosophical sense is Wǔxíng (Tone 3 + Tone 2), per Hanyu Pinyin and the Unihan Database. Note that 行 has a separate reading háng ('row, profession'); here it means 'movement, conduct, phase.' The registrable form preserves the tone marks; the characters are displayed in the Original Script card. Baxter & Sagart reconstruct 五 as *C.ŋˤaʔ and 行 in the sense 'walk, conduct' as *C.[g]raŋ.

pronunciation.approximation: foo-shee, rising tone on fu, high level on xi.
pronunciation.note: Fúxī 伏羲 carries the rising tone on fú and the high level tone on xī in Mandarin; older romanizations write Fu-hsi. The first graph 伏 suggests "to subdue, to prostrate," the second 羲 a sacrificial term — a name older than its etymologies, borne by the first of the Three August Ones. The older romanization Fu-hsi records the same syllables; pinyin's x is the alveolo-palatal fricative of modern Mandarin.

domains.title: The First Teacher
domains.subtitle: The Eight Trigrams, the Net, and the Marriage on the Mountain
domains.lead: Fúxī is where Chinese civilization says it learned to think: the sage-king who looked up at the heavens, down at the earth, and at the markings on birds and beasts — and abstracted the eight trigrams, the first writing of pattern itself.

cards.name: The Eight Trigrams
cards.desc: Bāguà: broken and unbroken lines in threes — the binary alphabet of the Yìjīng, attributed to his observation.

cards.name: The Net
cards.desc: He taught the people to knot cords into nets — fishing, hunting, and the technology of the snare.

cards.name: The Serpent Bodies
cards.desc: Han art shows him and Nǚwā as serpents intertwined — the primal pair, measuring square and compass in hand.

cards.name: Marriage
cards.desc: He instituted the rites of marriage and the bride-price of deer skins — order after the flood.

symbols.name: The trigrams
symbols.meaning: Pattern abstracted from nature — the seed of all Chinese correlative thought

symbols.name: The carpenter's square
symbols.meaning: His emblem in Han art: the earth-measurer's tool (Nǚwā holds the compass of heaven)

symbols.name: The dragon-horse
symbols.meaning: The creature from the Yellow River whose markings revealed the diagram

mythology.lead: Fúxī's myths are all acts of notation: he does not fight or flee — he observes, abstracts, and teaches. He is the culture-bringer as draftsman.

myths.title: Reading the World
myths.text: The Yìjīng's Great Treatise records the founding act: Fúxī looked up and contemplated the images of heaven, looked down and contemplated the patterns of earth, contemplated the markings of birds and beasts and the order of the near at hand — and from all three made the eight trigrams, "to comprehend the powers of the spirits and to classify the natures of the ten thousand things." Writing, mathematics, and divination begin as one gesture of attention.

myths.title: The Dragon-Horse's Map
myths.text: Later tradition gives the revelation a courier: a dragon-horse rose from the Yellow River bearing on its back the Hétú, the River Chart — the arrangement of numbers and marks from which Fúxī drew the trigrams. Paired with the Luò River Writing that inspired the Great Plan, the Chart made the Yellow River itself the first text of Chinese civilization.

lore.culturalLegacy: Every reading of the Yìjīng — the book that shaped Confucian statecraft, Daoist alchemy, and Leibniz's binary arithmetic — begins with his act of looking. The eight trigrams appear on the flag of South Korea; the River Chart structures a millennium of cosmological diagrams; and "Fúxī" remains the standard icon for the inventor-ancestor in Chinese cultural memory, the answer to the question of where pattern-thinking began.
lore.archaeology: The Wu Liang shrine reliefs (2nd century CE, Shandong) show Fúxī and Nǚwā with serpent bodies entwined, square and compass raised — the canonical image, replicated across Han tomb art from Sichuan to Xinjiang (the famous Astana cemetery banner). The myth's textual archaeology runs from the Zhuangzi and Xunzi mentions to the Tang's flood-cycle records: a steady accretion from sage-king to cosmic progenitor, all preserved in the transmitted classics.
lore.syncretism: He heads most lists of the Three August Ones (Sānhuáng), paired inseparably with Nǚwā — their intertwined serpent forms in Han art echoing, scholars note, the union of measure and generation. Daoist tradition absorbed him as a revealer of the trigrams to the immortal lineages; Confucian tradition kept him as the first historian of pattern. The serpent-pair iconography has been compared by art historians with intertwined pairs from Egypt to India — diffusion debated, the resemblance celebrated.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 伏羲: fú (subdue; the man-radical with the hound) plus xī (the ancient graph for sacrificial breath). The compound is attested from Warring States texts onward — the name predates any agreed reading of it, which is itself a mark of antiquity.

pronunciation.approximation: nyoo-wah, low-dipping tone on Nǚ, high level on Wā.
pronunciation.note: Nǚwā 女娲 bears the third tone on nǚ — the vowel ü written with its two dots, which the restoration keeps and plain ASCII drops. Wā is the level-toned archaic graph for this goddess alone: a character invented for her name, used for nothing else in the language. The ü is the front rounded vowel — the sound French writes u — which plain ASCII loses to plain u.

domains.title: The Mender of Heaven
domains.subtitle: The Five-Colored Stones, the Clay, and the First People
domains.lead: Nǚwā is the great repairer: the goddess who melted five-colored stones to patch the broken sky, cut off the giant turtle's legs to prop the corners of the world, and — on a quieter day — knelt by the Yellow River and made the first human beings out of mud.

cards.name: The Five-Colored Stones
cards.desc: Melted and poured into the sky's wound — the world's first and greatest repair, one stone left over (the seed of Dream of the Red Chamber).

cards.name: The Serpent Body
cards.desc: Her form in Han art: human head, serpent body — earth's maker in earth's image, twined with Fúxī.

cards.name: The Rope of Mud
cards.desc: The rich she shaped by hand, the poor she flung from a rope — humanity's two fortunes, told without flinching.

cards.name: The Marriage Rites
cards.desc: She prayed to become the matchmaker and instituted marriage — society's first legislator, outsourcing creation to love.

symbols.name: The five colors
symbols.meaning: The five phases (wood, fire, earth, metal, water) — the sky rebuilt in cosmic order

symbols.name: The compass
symbols.meaning: Her emblem in Han art, paired with Fúxī's square — heaven's measure in her hand

symbols.name: The turtle's legs
symbols.meaning: The four pillars she cut and set — sacrifice repurposed as architecture

symbols.name: The rope of mud
symbols.meaning: Her tool of mass creation — and the myth's blunt explanation of why fortunes differ

symbols.name: The stone she did not use
symbols.meaning: The one stone left over after the mending — the stone that becomes the jade of Dream of the Red Chamber and the book itself

mythology.lead: Nǚwā's myths answer the two great questions — where people came from, and why the sky holds — and a third the tradition added later: what happens when the whole human race must begin again. They are told in the earliest strata of Chinese myth and never improved upon.

myths.title: The Mending of the Sky
myths.text: The Huáinánzǐ (ch. 6, the Lanming xun, c. 139 BCE) tells it in the grammar of catastrophe: in high antiquity the four pillars snapped and the nine provinces split; fire blazed unquenched, waters rose undrained; fierce beasts devoured the people and birds of prey seized the old and weak. Then Nǚwā acted, and the text lists her works like an engineer's report: she smelted stones of five colors to patch the azure sky; cut the legs from the great turtle to set the four pillars true; slew the black dragon to deliver Jì province; and heaped reed-ashes to dam the flooding waters. Then — and only then — 'the people of the four quarters could set foot on the land again', and the cunning beasts went quiet. Nothing in the passage is creation from nothing: heaven is mended with worked matter, propped with sacrifice, and drained with humble ash. The oldest Chinese creation story is a repair manual, and its author is a goddess with a craftsman's hands.

myths.title: People of Yellow Earth
myths.text: The gentler myth survives in quotation from Ying Shao's Fengsu Tongyi (c. 195 CE): when sky and earth had opened and there were not yet people, Nǚwā knelt by the Yellow River and shaped human beings from yellow clay. The work delighted but wearied her — so she trailed a rope through the mud and flung the drops loose, and the drops too became people. The handmade figures became the rich and noble; the rope-flung drops, the poor and common — China's oldest surviving reflection on how inequality began, set inside its tenderest creation story. Note what the myth refuses to do: it does not blame the poor for their fortune or flatter the rich for theirs. Both were made by the same hands in the same afternoon; the difference is only which instrument touched them. Two thousand years before the word existed, the tradition was teaching that class is an accident of the tool.

lore.culturalLegacy: Her stones became literature: the great novel Dream of the Red Chamber (Hónglóu mèng) opens with the one stone Nǚwā rejected for the sky — the stone that becomes the hero's jade and the book itself. 'Nǚwā mends the sky' is the standing idiom for heroic repair; engineers, surgeons, and diplomats are all praised with it. Temples to her survive across North China — Shexian's cliff-hanging Wahuang Palace in Hebei is the grandest — where she is still prayed to for children. Her name entered the language twice over: as Wāhuáng, the August Wa, and in the everyday compliment of the mender of any broken thing.
lore.archaeology: The Wahuang Palace at Shexian — pavilions chained to a cliff above the Zhang River, founded in the Northern Qi dynasty (6th century) — is her principal surviving sanctuary and one of China's architectural marvels. Han pictorial stones pair her with Fúxī from Shandong to Sichuan; the Astana cemetery silk banner carried the image to the Silk Road's far end. Her myth's textual strata are mapped from the Huáinánzǐ (139 BCE) backward into Warring States fragments and forward into the Tang flood-cycle accounts.
lore.syncretism: She pairs with Fúxī as sister-wife in the Han synthesis — their intertwined serpent bodies, compass and square in hand, form the canonical image of cosmic order on tomb stones from Shandong to Sichuan — and she absorbs older creation figures as the myth spread south and north. Daoist tradition adopted her without difficulty: a goddess who mends heaven and authorizes marriage fits a canon of celestial bureaucracy. Modern readers note her kinship with every world-mother from Gaia to the Navajo Changing Woman, but the Chinese tradition keeps her distinct signature: she is not just a mother but a repairer, the goddess of maintenance. And the novel Dream of the Red Chamber completed her canonization in literature, making the one stone she rejected for the sky the seed of China's greatest book.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 女娲: nǚ (woman) plus wā — a graph so specific to her that dictionaries list almost no other word under it. The ü of the restoration is the sound itself; without it, the name is another word.

pronunciation.approximation: SHYEHN — a high, level tone held steady, with a light 'sh' that touches the palate.
pronunciation.note: 仙 denotes a transcendent being in Daoism, distinct from ordinary gods (shén) and from Buddhist arhats or bodhisattvas. The character combines 人 (person) with 山 (mountain), suggesting one who withdraws to the heights. The Pinyin restoration Xiān preserves the high level tone.

domains.title: The Immortal
domains.subtitle: Transcendence, Daoist Practice, and Celestial Freedom
domains.lead:
Xiān is the Chinese immortal: a human being who has refined body and spirit until death no longer applies. Unlike the gods of popular religion, who receive offerings and grant petitions, the xiān has escaped the bureaucracy of heaven and earth. He or she dwells in mountains, rides clouds or cranes, and appears unpredictably to those who have cultivated the Dao.

The path to becoming xiān is not faith but practice: meditation, breath control, diet, alchemy, and moral discipline. Immortality is an achievement, not a gift.

cards.name: Longevity
cards.desc: The xiān has overcome ageing and death through disciplined transformation of the body.

cards.name: Mountain Dwelling
cards.desc: Immortals withdraw to peaks and grottoes where the qi is pure and the world is far.

cards.name: Internal Alchemy
cards.desc: Neidan refines the three treasures — jīng, qì, shén — into an immortal embryo.

cards.name: Freedom from Bureaucracy
cards.desc: Unlike gods bound by celestial office, the xiān wanders freely between realms.

symbols.name: Crane
symbols.meaning: The mount and companion of immortals; a thousand-year lifespan.

symbols.name: Peach of immortality
symbols.meaning: The fruit of the Queen Mother of the West's garden, ripening every three thousand years.

symbols.name: Gourd
symbols.meaning: The bottle that holds elixirs, medicines, and the boundless space of the Dao.

symbols.name: Clouds and mist
symbols.meaning: The medium through which immortals travel and the boundary between mortal and transcendent realms.

mythology.lead: Xiān mythology is a vast gallery of individual adepts, each with a distinctive method of transcendence — and a long argument, running from the Zhuāngzǐ to the Míng novel, about what exactly escapes when a human being escapes death.

myths.title: The Divine Person of Mount Gūshè
myths.text: The xiān blueprint is drawn before the word has fully settled. In the first chapter of the Zhuāngzǐ the philosopher describes the shénrén, the divine person of Mount Gūshè: skin like frost and snow, gentle as a maiden, who does not eat the five grains but sucks the wind and drinks the dew, mounts the clouds and mist, rides the flying dragon, and roams beyond the four seas (Zhuāngzǐ, ch. 1). Nothing here requires doctrine — no elixir, no scripture, no school. The figure simply is what perfect alignment with the Dào looks like from outside: weightless, unhurried, ungovernable. Later Daoism would attach the label xiān to precisely this silhouette and then spend two thousand years working out the mechanics of achieving it. The myth’s power lies in its refusal to explain itself: transcendence first appears in Chinese literature not as a promise but as a description, offered in passing, of a person the world cannot hold.

myths.title: The First Hagiographies
myths.text: The Hàn scholar Liú Xiàng — or the circle writing in his name — assembled the Lièxiàn zhuàn, Biographies of Exemplary Immortals: the tradition’s founding hagiography, some seventy lives of the transcendent. Its gallery is startlingly democratic. Chìsōngzǐ, Master Redpine, rain-master to the god-king Shénnóng, who entered the fire and ascended; Wángzi Qiáo, the crown prince who abandoned his throne to play the shēng mouth-organ on a mountain, and who was last seen riding a white crane skyward; woodcutters, courtiers, silkworm-tenders — each perfected by an idiosyncratic path (Lièxiàn zhuàn, Hàn dynasty). The collection fixed the genre’s grammar — birth omen, eccentric practice, wondrous departure — that every later Daoist hagiography would reuse. Its quiet revolution was sociological: the gods had always taken offerings, but immortality, it turned out, could be earned by almost anyone, including people history would otherwise never have recorded.

lore.culturalLegacy: Xiān permeate Chinese culture. They appear in landscape painting as tiny figures on misty peaks, in New Year prints carrying peaches and gourds, and in countless novels, operas, and films. The aspiration to longevity shapes Chinese medicine, diet, and exercise practices such as tai chi and qigong. The word xiān is also used for extraordinary people: a great cook is a 'food immortal,' a beautiful woman a 'fairy.' In global spirituality, the xiān offers an alternative to Western heaven: not a reward after death but a transformation of life itself, achieved through sustained practice.
lore.archaeology: The xiān tradition is attested in Warring States and Han dynasty texts, tomb art showing feathered immortals ascending to heaven, and the Mawangdui tomb manuscripts on longevity and breath cultivation. Medieval Daoist caves and temple murals depict the Eight Immortals and other transcendent figures. Alchemists' stoves, elixir recipes, and neidan manuals survive in the Daozang and in archaeological contexts from the Han through the Song dynasties.
lore.syncretism: The xiān tradition absorbed many influences. Indigenous Chinese quest for longevity merged with shamanic flight, alchemical experimentation, and Buddhist meditation techniques. The figure of the wandering immortal influenced Chan Buddhism, Confucian self-cultivation, and Chinese poetry and painting. In popular religion, local spirits and historical figures were posthumously enrolled as xiān. The West knows the xiān chiefly through the Eight Immortals and martial-arts films, where they appear as eccentric sages with superhuman powers. Modern Daoist lineages continue to practice neidan in pursuit of the same goal.

pronunciation.approximation: MAH-tsoo — level tone, then a dip-and-rise.
pronunciation.note: Māzǔ 媽祖 — "Maternal Ancestor" — carries the first tone on mā and the dipping third tone on zǔ; the restoration keeps both tone marks. Her personal name was Lín Mòniáng ("Silent Maiden"), but the world prays to the title: Grandmother of the sea. The third tone on zǔ dips and rises — the small valley in the name that Mandarin speakers sing without noticing.

domains.title: The Mother of the Sea
domains.subtitle: Sailors, Storms, and the Red Lantern
domains.lead: Māzǔ is the most-worshipped sea goddess on earth: the fisherman's daughter who became the guardian of everyone who works the water, whose temples line every coast of the Chinese world, and whose red lanterns guide sailors home through a thousand years of storms. The historical Lín Mòniáng of Meizhou Island was deified not by doctrine but by rescue — and the rescues never stopped.

cards.name: The Sailors' Guardian
cards.desc: The goddess of everyone who goes to sea — the busiest answering voice on the water.

cards.name: The Red Lantern
cards.desc: Her signal in the storm — the light sailors pray to see.

cards.name: The Two Generals
cards.desc: Qiānlǐyǎn and Shùnfēng'ěr — her thousand-mile eyes and wind-sharp ears.

cards.name: Meizhou
cards.desc: Her island home off Fujian — the Nazareth of the sea-faith.

symbols.name: The red robe
symbols.meaning: Her temple color — protection worn bright against the grey sea

symbols.name: The lantern
symbols.meaning: The guide-light of the storm-tossed

symbols.name: The two generals
symbols.meaning: Sight and hearing deified — vigilance in both directions

mythology.lead: Māzǔ's myth is a life, not a legend-cycle: the historical Lín Mòniáng of 10th-century Meizhou, whose silence, visions, and early death became the sea's own religion — a canon written not in scripture but in rescue-stories kept at harbors, and crowned by twelve centuries of imperial gratitude.

myths.title: The Silent Girl of Meizhou
myths.text: The historical Lín Mòniáng was born on Meizhou Island, off the Fujian coast, in 960 CE, as the Five Dynasties gave way to the Song — and the tradition remembers that she did not cry at birth, which is why the world calls her the Silent Maiden. She learned the sea on her father's fishing junk, stood watch on the cliffs in her red dress, and was said to fall into trances in which her spirit walked the waves beside foundering ships, guiding them home. The legend insists she died at twenty-eight, in 987, ascending bodily from the island's peak on a ribbon of incense smoke; other tellings say she drowned searching for her father's lost boat in a typhoon. The sources are late — the miracle collections were compiled centuries afterward — so the facts inside the legend cannot be audited. But the outline is stable, and it is the whole theology: a daughter who never stopped watching the water.

myths.title: From Daughter to Empress of Heaven
myths.text: The titles came as the rescues accumulated. The Song court's first recognition was modest — after the diplomat Lù Yùndì's storm-battered embassy to Korea came safely home in 1122–23, the Huizong emperor granted her island temple the plaque Shùnjì, "Facilitating Succor" (1123). The Southern Song made her Consort (1155) and then raised her again (1190); Kublai Khan's Yuan made her Heavenly Consort, Tiānfēi, in 1278, after her winds saw the grain fleets safely to Dàdū; Zhèng Hè thanked her on ocean-facing steles before his voyages; and the Kangxi emperor, after her waves helped Shi Lang's fleet take Taiwan in 1683, raised her at last to Tiānhòu — Empress of Heaven (1684). The ladder is a ledger. Every rank commemorates a storm survived, and the imperial bureaucracy kept promoting the fisherman's daughter until she outranked every other god in the register.

lore.culturalLegacy: Her temples number in the thousands — over 1,500 in Taiwan alone; her birthday (23rd of the 3rd lunar month) shuts down the island's coasts; her Dajia procession is a national institution watched by millions more online. Fishermen, sailors, the navy, and migrants all claim her: the goddess who was once a girl watching the sea is now the sea's own government, elected annually by the crowds who walk behind her statue.
lore.archaeology: The Meizhou Ancestral Temple on her home island — rebuilt repeatedly from the Song original, crowded with imperial plaques — is her Nazareth; the Dajia Jenn Lann Temple and Taipei's grand Tianhou temples are her living capitals. Macau's A-Ma Temple (15th c., older than the Portuguese) marks her oldest colonial-era shore, and the Mazu statues of the Taiwan Strait's temples document eight centuries of her iconography.
lore.syncretism: She absorbs the coast's other sea-powers: associated with Guānyīn (who is sometimes her patron in the legends), honored in Daoist and Buddhist temples alike, and worshipped as Tin Hau in Hong Kong and A-Ma in Macau — whose very name, some say, comes from her ("A-Ma-Gau," Bay of A-Ma). The diaspora carried her to every Chinese port from San Francisco to Sydney: wherever junks and container ships anchor, her shrine overlooks the harbor.

entries.domain: War, Justice, Nephew of Jade Emperor

pronunciation.approximation: NUH-jah — the first syllable rises like a question, the second stays high and level; keep the 'zh' retroflex, tongue curled back, closer to 'dr' than to 'j'.
pronunciation.note: 哪吒 is the settled transcription of a name that entered Chinese through Buddhist transmission from Sanskrit Nalakūvara, son of the guardian king Vaiśravaṇa. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Nézhā: 吒 zhā (Tone 1) is the value recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard dictionaries, while 哪 carries here its special proper-name reading né (Tone 2), preserved only in this name and recorded as such in the standard dictionaries (Xiandai Hanyu Cidian, Hanyu Da Cidian); its ordinary interrogative reading is nǎ (Tone 3), the value given under kMandarin in the Unihan Database. Because the name is a medieval transcription of a foreign theonym rather than a native Chinese word, Old Chinese reconstruction does not apply.

domains.title: The Lotus-Born Rebel
domains.subtitle: Filial Sacrifice, Divine Weaponry, Unconquerable Youth
domains.lead: Nézhā is the child who would not stay born: third son of the garrison commander Li Jing, armed by the immortal Taiyi Zhenren with ring, sash, spear, and wind-fire wheels — and destined to repay the debt of his own body to his parents in the most harrowing act of filial sacrifice in Chinese myth, before heaven rebuilt him from lotus.

cards.name: The Universe Ring
cards.desc: Qiánkūnquān, the golden ring of heaven and earth, first of the weapons Taiyi Zhenren bestowed — a cosmic bracelet that strikes with the weight of the world it names.

cards.name: The Eastern Sea
cards.desc: Bathing in the sea, Nézhā stirred the waters with his sash until the Dragon King's palace shook — the act that killed Āo Bǐng and set the cycle of debt and sacrifice in motion.

cards.name: The Lotus Rebirth
cards.desc: His soul rebuilt from lotus roots and blossoms by Taiyi Zhenren, Nézhā returns in a body owing flesh to no parent — purity, renewal, and freedom from the debt of birth.

cards.name: The Wind Fire Wheels
cards.desc: Fēnghuǒlún, the paired wheels of wind and flame beneath his feet — the mount that carries the celestial vanguard faster than storm across the three realms.

symbols.name: Universe Ring (乾坤圈)
symbols.meaning: Cosmic sovereignty in miniature — heaven and earth bound into a single striking weapon

symbols.name: Red Armillary Sash (混天綾)
symbols.meaning: The seven-chi silk that churns seas and binds foes; the instrument of the East Sea upheaval

symbols.name: Fire-Tipped Spear (火尖槍)
symbols.meaning: Martial fire and unrelenting advance, the spear of the vanguard who never retreats

symbols.name: Wind Fire Wheels (風火輪)
symbols.meaning: Unstoppable motion — the storm itself harnessed as a vehicle for the young marshal

symbols.name: Lotus (蓮花)
symbols.meaning: Rebirth without debt: purity rising from the water, a body remade beyond blood and bone

mythology.lead: The Nézhā cycle is the great Chinese myth of the filial rebel — a story in which the most radical act of disobedience and the most extreme act of filial piety turn out to be the same act. Its canonical form was fixed by the Ming dynasty's two great novels, the Investiture of the Gods and Journey to the West; its oldest motifs are Buddhist, carried into China along the Silk Road.

myths.title: The Flesh Ball
myths.text: In the Investiture of the Gods (ch. 12), Lady Yin, wife of the garrison commander Li Jing, has carried her third child for three years and six months when the birth finally comes — and what emerges is not an infant but a ball of flesh, glowing like a lantern. Certain he faces a demon, Li Jing strikes it with his sword, and the ball splits: inside stands a boy already able to walk and speak. The immortal Taiyi Zhenren arrives to claim the child as his destined disciple, names him Nézhā, and arms him beyond all reason — the Universe Ring (Qiánkūnquān) and the seven-chi Red Armillary Sash (Hùntiānlíng). The boy grows at supernatural speed; at seven he is already the terror of the riverbanks, his two treasures humming with borrowed cosmic power. The wrongness of the birth is the myth's point. Nézhā enters the world not owed to ordinary nature — a disciple sent down from above, whose "parents" receive him rather than make him.

myths.title: The Dragon King's Third Son
myths.text: Bathing one summer day in the Nine-Bend River where it meets the East Sea, the seven-year-old dips his Red Armillary Sash into the water — and the cosmic instrument does what it is for: it churns the sea until the crystal palace of the Dragon King Āo Guǎng trembles on its foundations (Fēngshén Yǎnyì, ch. 12–13). Āo Guǎng sends his yaksha enforcer Lǐ Gèn to seize the offender; Nézhā kills him with a single cast of the Universe Ring. Then the third prince, Āo Bǐng, rises from the waves on his beast of the deep, and Nézhā kills him too, stripping out his sinews to make a belt. A child has bloodied the oldest bureaucracy in heaven — the ancient administration of the waters — and the Dragon King, robbed of an heir, will have justice or drown Chéntāngguān. The myth stages a collision it never resolves: ungovernable youth against an institution that mistakes its palace for the world.

lore.culturalLegacy: No Chinese deity has had a stronger twenty-first century. Nézhā's cult thrives in Taiwan and the diaspora, where the Marshal of the Central Altar dances in temple processions — in recent decades to electronic music, the 'techno Nézhā' of modern festival culture. On screen, the 2019 animated feature Ne Zha became the highest-grossing animated film in Chinese history, its defiant reading of the myth — fate is a rumor the child refuses — resonating with a generation; Ne Zha 2 (2025) went further, breaking global box-office records for animation. The rebel child who returned his body to his parents has become, arguably, the most popular Chinese deity of the modern era: an emblem of youth that will not be told what it owes.
lore.archaeology: Nézhā is a textual rather than an archaeological figure, and his attestation history tracks the Buddhist transmission itself. The name first appears in Tang-dynasty Buddhist translations as 那吒 (Nata), a transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, son of the guardian king Vaiśravaṇa, whose cult flourished in Tang China and whose iconography — armor, spear, and reliquary pagoda — later passed to Nézhā's literary father, Li Jing. By the Song dynasty the flesh-and-bone-returning motif was current in Chan literature, and Yuan-era drama gave the child a stage life. The canonical narrative was fixed in the Ming novels: the Investiture of the Gods supplied the full cycle from flesh ball to lotus rebirth, and Journey to the West installed him as a marshal of the celestial court. Material attestation is chiefly cultic — temple statuary of the Marshal of the Central Altar, a wheel-riding, ring-bearing youth, across southeastern China, Taiwan, and the diaspora.
lore.syncretism: Nézhā is himself a product of transmission: the name enters Chinese through Buddhism as a transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, a son of the guardian king Vaiśravaṇa, and the earliest Chinese forms (那吒, read closer to Nata) preserve that foreign sound. As the figure was naturalized, the genealogy was rewritten — his father became the historical-flavored general Li Jing, who absorbed Vaiśravaṇa's iconography wholesale and became the pagoda-bearing Heavenly King (托塔天王) of the Chinese celestial court. Taoism then claimed the child outright: under the title Zhōngtán Yuánshuài, Marshal of the Central Altar, Nézhā became one of the most vividly worshipped protectors in the Chinese ritual pantheon. The figure traveled with the Chinese world — to Korea, Vietnam, and Japan (where he is Nataku) — but it is in the Sinitic ritual tradition, and above all in the temples and processions of Taiwan and the southeastern diaspora, that the lotus-born marshal remains a living god rather than a literary memory.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 哪吒, identical in traditional and simplified Chinese. Pinyin Nézhā combines the special proper-name reading né (Tone 2) of 哪 — preserved only in this name, the ordinary interrogative reading being nǎ — with 吒 zhā (Tone 1), as recorded in the standard dictionaries and the Unihan Database. The name is a medieval transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, so no Old Chinese reconstruction applies. The tone-marked restoration Nézhā maps directly to the registrable domain form: the display keeps both diacritics (é and ā, both registrable IDN characters), and no apostrophe is required anywhere in the name.

entries.meaning: The Moon goddess who drank the elixir of immortality

pronunciation.approximation: CHAHNG-UH — both syllables rise in tone, as in a questioning intonation; 'ch' is an aspirated retroflex with the tongue curled back, and 'é' is close to the vowel of 'her' with the r removed.
pronunciation.note: 嫦娥 denotes the Chinese goddess of the moon. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Chángé — cháng (Tone 2) and é (Tone 2) — as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard Mandarin dictionaries. The goddess's earlier name was 姮娥 Héng'é; under the Han it was altered to Chángé to observe the naming taboo on the personal name of Emperor Wen (Liú Héng 劉恆), the graph 常 cháng ('constant') replacing the tabooed homophone 姮 héng. The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Chángé preserves the citation rising tone on both syllables; in connected speech the contour may be compressed, but the lexical tones remain Tone 2.

domains.title: Goddess of the Cold Moon
domains.subtitle: Immortality, Exile, Reunion
domains.lead: Chángé is the woman who swallowed forever and paid for it with the earth. Wife of the archer Hòuyì, she came into possession of the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West — and drank it. Whether to keep it from a treacherous disciple or out of her own longing, the sources divide; what they agree on is the result: she rose through the night until the moon received her, and there she remains, in the Guǎnghán Palace — the Palace of Vast Cold.

cards.name: The Moon
cards.desc: Her dwelling and her domain; the full moon of Mid-Autumn is read as her face, brightest and roundest when mortal eyes seek reunion.

cards.name: The Archer Hòuyì
cards.desc: Her husband, who shot down nine of the ten suns and received the elixir of immortality from Xīwángmǔ — the gift that divided them forever.

cards.name: The Palace of Vast Cold
cards.desc: The Guǎnghán Palace (廣寒宮), her luminous and solitary court on the moon, shared with the Jade Rabbit and the woodcutter Wú Gāng.

cards.name: Reunion under the Full Moon
cards.desc: The Mid-Autumn Festival (中秋節): mooncakes, moon-gazing, and the gathering of families — the night her separation sanctifies mortal togetherness.

symbols.name: The full moon
symbols.meaning: Her dwelling and her face; completeness, distance, and the reunion it mirrors

symbols.name: The Jade Rabbit
symbols.meaning: Her companion (玉兔), who pounds the elixir of immortality with mortar and pestle — labor without end in her service

symbols.name: Mortar and pestle
symbols.meaning: The ceaseless preparation of the elixir she carried to heaven

symbols.name: The cassia tree
symbols.meaning: The self-healing tree Wú Gāng chops forever beside her palace — punishment and persistence in a single image

symbols.name: The mooncake
symbols.meaning: The round pastry of Mid-Autumn, cut and shared as an edible likeness of the moon she rules

mythology.lead: Chángé's story is short and inexhaustible: one ascent, endlessly retold. The early sources preserve a bare skeleton — an elixir, a flight, a moon — and two thousand years of poets, painters, and festival-goers have hung their longing on it.

myths.title: The Elixir of Immortality
myths.text: The core myth, fixed in the Lǎnmíng xùn 覽冥訓 chapter of the Huáinánzǐ (c. 139 BCE), begins with the archer Hòuyì, who had shot down nine of the ten suns and so received from Xīwángmǔ, Queen Mother of the West, the elixir of immortality. Chángé took it and floated up to the moon, where she became its goddess. The sources divide on her motive: in some versions she drinks to keep the elixir from Féngméng, Hòuyì's treacherous disciple; in others she drinks out of her own longing for deathlessness. Scholarship preserves both strands rather than adjudicating between them — the myth holds theft and sacrifice in suspension, and it is precisely the undecidability that has kept two thousand years of readers arguing on her behalf or against it — the earliest Chinese debate about a woman's motives that is still open.

myths.title: From Héng'é to Chángé
myths.text: The goddess was originally 姮娥 Héng'é. Under the Han, her name was altered to avoid the naming taboo on the personal name of Emperor Wen, Liú Héng 劉恆: the graph 姮 was replaced by the synonymous 常, and Héng'é became Chángé. It is a rare case where imperial censorship is legible inside a divine name itself — a goddess renamed so that a mortal emperor's name could remain unspoken. The change also shows how the myth lived inside institutions rather than outside them: not a fossil preserved in a book, but a name people actually said, and therefore a name the court could edit. Every modern recitation of 'Chángé' quietly repeats a two-millennium-old act of deference — the goddess has been carrying an emperor's taboo on her own identity ever since.

lore.culturalLegacy: Chángé has been China's shorthand for beautiful distance since the poets claimed her. Sū Shì's Mid-Autumn lyric closes with the wish that, though a thousand miles apart, we may share chánjuān 嬋娟 — the lovely one, the moon, her. The Mid-Autumn Festival remains one of the great holidays of the Chinese world, and the mooncake its edible emblem. In 2020 the animated film Over the Moon carried her to global audiences as a pop-diva goddess still waiting for Hòuyì. Most remarkably, she has gone back: China's lunar exploration program is named for her, and the probes Chángé 1 through 6 (2007–2024) orbited the moon, landed on it, achieved the first landing on its far side (Chángé 4), and returned samples to earth (Chángé 5 and 6). No other deity in this lexicon has been so literally restored to her own heaven.
lore.archaeology: The flight to the moon is attested remarkably early. An early version of the story circulated in the Guǐcáng (歸藏), a divination text known from medieval quotations and from Qin-dynasty bamboo slips excavated at Wangjiatai in Hubei (tomb closed c. 3rd century BCE), in which Héng'é takes the elixir and ascends. The Huáinánzǐ (c. 139 BCE) gives the first full surviving account. Pictorial evidence is nearly as old: the painted silk funeral banner from Mawangdui Tomb 1 (sealed 168 BCE) depicts the moon disk with its toad and rabbit, and Han pictorial stones — notably from the Nanyang region — show Chángé in flight toward the moon, her robes streaming. Later dynasties rendered her on mirrors, ceramics, and festival prints, and moon-gazing scenes became a staple of Ming and Qing painting.
lore.syncretism: The rabbit in the moon is older than any single nation's telling of it. Buddhist tradition carried the śaśajātaka — the tale of the rabbit who offered itself as food and was set in the moon as a reward — from India into East Asia, and scholars commonly link the Chinese moon rabbit to this transmission, though the Jade Rabbit's elixir-pounding is China's own elaboration. Taoist religion absorbed Chángé into its celestial bureaucracy, where she is often identified with the sovereign of the yin luminary (太陰). Japan received the moon rabbit without the elixir: there he pounds mochi instead, and the autumn moon-viewing custom (tsukimi) echoes Mid-Autumn without keeping its goddess. Korea's harvest festival Chuseok and Vietnam's Tết Trung Thu share the same full-moon night of cakes, lanterns, and family gathering — the festival traveled further than the myth, and in each harbor took local form.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 嫦娥, written identically in traditional and simplified Chinese; the earlier form of the name is 姮娥, altered under the Han naming taboo on Emperor Wen's personal name. Pinyin Chángé (Tone 2 + Tone 2) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries. The apostrophe is part of standard Hanyu Pinyin orthography, separating the two syllables so the name cannot be misread as a single syllable or wrongly divided; the display form Chángé keeps it, while the registrable domain label drops it, since IDN labels cannot contain an apostrophe — the tone-marked vowels alone carry the restoration into the domain system.

entries.meaning: The divine archer who shot down nine suns

pronunciation.approximation: HOH-yee — two crisp syllables, each spoken with a sharp falling tone, like a decisive command: 'HOE! YEE!'
pronunciation.note: 后羿 names the divine archer: 后 is an archaic title meaning 'lord, sovereign' (not the later sense 'empress', for which 皇后 is used), and 羿 is the archer's given name. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Hòuyì (both syllables Tone 4), as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard Mandarin dictionaries. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese reading of 羿 as *N-ŋ(r)ik-s. The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Hòuyì preserves the citation falling tone of both syllables; in connected speech the contour may be compressed, but the lexical tones remain Tone 4.

domains.title: Archer of the Nine Fallen Suns
domains.subtitle: Precision, Deliverance, the Spared Light
domains.lead:
Hòuyì is the divine archer of Chinese myth, the hero who stood between heaven's excess and the earth's survival. In the age of the sage-emperor Yáo, the ten suns — three-legged crows, sons of Dìjùn and the sun-mother Xīhé — rose all at once instead of taking their appointed turns. Rivers dried, crops failed, and monsters crawled out of the scorched wilderness. Hòuyì drew his great bow and shot nine suns from the sky, sparing one so that day and night, sowing and harvest, could keep their order.

His story is a hinge between worlds: the same bow that cleared the earth of monsters also won him the elixir of immortality from Xīwángmǔ, the Queen Mother of the West — the elixir his wife Chángé would ultimately take, fleeing to the moon. The archer who saved the earth lost heaven, and Chinese myth has never stopped telling both halves of that story.

cards.name: The Divine Bow
cards.desc: The great bow and its arrows are heaven's instruments of correction — not conquest, but the precise removal of what has grown excessive.

cards.name: The Ten Suns
cards.desc: Ten three-legged crow-suns, sons of Dìjùn and Xīhé, once took turns crossing the sky; their simultaneous rising nearly ended the world.

cards.name: Slayer of Monsters
cards.desc: With the suns subdued, Yi cleared the earth of the beasts the drought had unleashed: Yàyǔ, Záochǐ, Jiǔyīng, Dàfēng, the serpent Xiūshé, and the boar Fēngxī.

cards.name: The Elixir
cards.desc: Xīwángmǔ's gift of immortality, earned by the archer's service — and lost when Chángé drank it and rose to the cold palace of the moon.

symbols.name: The great bow and arrows
symbols.meaning: Heaven-sent precision; the power to correct cosmic disorder without destroying the cosmos

symbols.name: The three-legged crow
symbols.meaning: The true form of each sun; nine were shot down, and the tenth still crosses the sky

symbols.name: The Fusang tree
symbols.meaning: The cosmic mulberry at the eastern edge of the world where the ten suns roosted between journeys

symbols.name: The elixir of immortality
symbols.meaning: Xīwángmǔ's reward and the pivot of loss — the gift that carried Chángé to the moon

symbols.name: The spared sun
symbols.meaning: Measured judgment; the hero preserves the order he restores rather than abolishing it

mythology.lead: The cycle of Hòuyì is the great Chinese myth of cosmic correction: a heaven that gives too much, an earth that suffers for it, and one archer whose arrows restore the mean. Its episodes run from the scorched world of the ten suns to the cold moon where his wife still dwells — and to the darker coda in which the master dies by his student's hand.

myths.title: The Shooting of the Nine Suns
myths.text: In the reign of Emperor Yáo, the ten suns — three-legged crows roosting in the Fusang tree, sons of Dìjùn and the sun-mother Xīhé — abandoned their orderly rotation and rose together. The earth burned: rivers dried, crops withered, and the people starved. Yáo called on Hòuyì, the divine archer, who climbed to the heights and loosed his arrows. One by one nine suns fell from the sky in their crow forms, and the tenth — spared at Yáo's prayer, or the archer's own measure — resumed its solitary, lawful journey. The myth is told across the Shān Hǎi Jīng tradition, given its fullest early form in the Huáinánzǐ (139 BCE), and interrogated with wonderful skepticism in the Chǔ Cí poem Tiān Wèn ('Why did Yì shoot down the suns? Why did the crows shed their feathers?'). The myth teaches that the world can be saved not by abolishing light but by restoring its measure — and that one well-aimed arrow can outweigh a cosmos of excess.

myths.title: The Clearing of the Monsters
myths.text: The drought had loosed terrors on the world, and the Huáinánzǐ lists the archer's second labor in its characteristic catalogue: he slew Yàyǔ, the man-eating beast of the wilds; Záochǐ in the waters of Chouhua; Jiǔyīng, the nine-headed monster of the Xiong river; the great wind-bird Dàfēng in the marshes of Qingqiu; the giant serpent Xiūshé at Lake Dongting; and the monstrous boar Fēngxī in the mulberry groves of Sanglin. When the last beast fell, 'the people of all within the seas rejoiced, and the ten thousand things came to life.' Only then could the people plow in peace. The second labor teaches that the hero's work is never finished with the wonder: after the miracle, the ordinary world must still be made safe for ordinary life — and Chinese myth, unusually, gives us the inventory. Cosmic correction, the list insists, is mostly administration.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hòuyì never left the Chinese imagination. The shooting of the suns is among the first myths Chinese children learn, retold in primers, animated films, and television dramas, and the Chángé sequel anchors the Mid-Autumn Festival, when families gaze at the moon where the archer's wife is said to dwell. Modern China has written the pair onto the sky itself: the national lunar exploration program is named Chángé, and its missions are spoken of as the moon goddess finally receiving visitors — a deliberate bridal of myth and engineering. The idiom of 'shooting the suns' survives as a metaphor for cutting down excess and correcting what has grown monstrous. In art, from Han dynasty tomb reliefs to contemporary illustration, the archer drawing his bow against a wheel of suns remains one of the most recognizable images in the Chinese visual canon.
lore.archaeology: Hòuyì's deeds are textual before they are pictorial. The earliest witnesses are Warring States literature: the Shān Hǎi Jīng preserves the ten-suns framework and the suns' parentage, the Chǔ Cí poem Tiān Wèn (c. 4th–3rd century BCE) interrogates Yì's shooting of the suns and his tangled fate, and the Mèngzǐ records the Féngméng betrayal. The fullest surviving narrative is the Huáinánzǐ (139 BCE), which sets the archer in Emperor Yáo's reign and catalogs the slain monsters. In Han dynasty art the cycle became a staple of funerary iconography: tomb reliefs and painted stones at sites such as the Wu Liang shrines (Shandong, 2nd century CE) show the archer drawing against crow-bearing suns, while Mawangdui funerary art (168 BCE) depicts the solar crow and the moon's toad-and-hare company that would gather around Chángé. Han mirrors and later pictorial stones continued the imagery, fixing the bow, the crows, and the moon as the archer's permanent attributes.
lore.syncretism: Hòuyì's myth traveled with Chinese civilization itself. In Japan the story of the archer and the ten suns was known through Chinese texts and pictorial art, where it informed depictions of solar catastrophe alongside native Amaterasu lore; Korea received the cycle through the same classical canon, and its own founding archer figure Jumong — whose very name is glossed as 'skilled archer' — shows how deeply the archer-hero type resonated on the peninsula. Vietnamese tradition likewise absorbed the ten-suns narrative through Chinese literature. Within China, Taoist tradition folded Yì into its cosmology of solar regulation and immortality elixirs, while the Queen Mother of the West, his benefactor, rose to become one of the highest deities of the Taoist pantheon. Scholars have long noted the parallel with other great archers — Apollo's plague-bringing arrows in Greece, Rama's bow in India — but the Chinese version is distinctive: the archer's target is not a rival god but disorder itself.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 后羿, identical in traditional and simplified Chinese (the character 后 'sovereign' must not be confused with 後 'after', which simplifies to 后 — in the archer's name it is the archaic title, 'lord'). Pinyin Hòuyì (both syllables Tone 4) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries. The registrable Unicode restoration uses the tone-marked Pinyin Hòuyì rather than the hanzi because PUNICODEX renders the original characters in the temple's 'Original Script' card while keeping the domain label pronounceable and internationally registrable; the name carries no apostrophe, so the display form and the domain form differ only in the tone marks. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese reading of 羿 as *N-ŋ(r)ik-s.

etymology.derivation: Sūn (猴) the monkey clan name; Wù (悟) 'awakened'; Kōng (空) 'emptiness' — the name given by the Buddhist Patriarch Subhūti in Journey to the West.

pronunciation.approximation: SOON-oo-KOHNG — first syllable high and level like a held note, middle syllable falling away sharply, last high and level again; the 'o' of kōng is like the 'oo' in 'book'.
pronunciation.note: Sūnwùkōng is Tier 1 because the tone-marked restoration preserves a distinctive feature ASCII loses: the citation tones of all three syllables (ū, ù, ō). The name is native Chinese — sūn "grandchild", wù "awakening", kōng "emptiness", glossed in the novel itself as "Monkey awakened to emptiness" — so unlike a transcription such as Nézhā, the full Mandarin tonal reading applies, recorded in the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and standard dictionaries.

domains.title: Monkey King
domains.subtitle: Monkey King, Chaos, Enlightenment
domains.lead: Sūnwùkōng, the Monkey King, is chaos with a crown: born from stone, armed from the sea floor, appointed Great Sage Equal to Heaven by his own proclamation, and finally harnessed as the guardian of the scripture pilgrimage — the untamed mind that Buddhism learned to employ.

cards.name: The Stone Egg
cards.desc: Born from an immortal stone egg on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, nourished by sun, moon, and the essence of creation — a monkey owing nothing to any parent.

cards.name: The Compliant Gold-Banded Staff
cards.desc: The Rúyì Jīngū Bàng, a 13,500-catty iron pillar that once pinned the seas; to the Monkey King it shrinks to a needle behind the ear and grows to a pillar that props up heaven.

cards.name: Havoc in Heaven
cards.desc: Insulted with the stable-boy title Bìmǎwēn, he storms out of heaven, proclaims himself Qítiān Dàshèng, and defeats the celestial host until Laozi's furnace forges his fiery golden eyes.

cards.name: The Victorious Fighting Buddha
cards.desc: Bound to the monk Tripitaka by the golden fillet and the headache spell, he fights through eighty-one tribulations and receives the most martial of the Buddha's titles at the journey's end.

symbols.name: Rúyì Jīngū Bàng (如意金箍棒)
symbols.meaning: The compliant staff — the sea's own measure, once used to pin the floods, carried off from the East Sea treasury; a cosmic instrument reduced to a personal weapon

symbols.name: The golden fillet (緊箍兒)
symbols.meaning: The band Tripitaka tightens with a spell — the will, harnessed: the novel's whole argument that the mind's power is safe only under a vow

symbols.name: Jīndǒuyún, the cloud-somersault
symbols.meaning: 108,000 li in a single flip — the speed of an ungoverned mind, which can outrun every army and not outrun one palm

symbols.name: The fiery golden eyes (火眼金睛)
symbols.meaning: Forged in Laozi's eight-trigram furnace — eyes that see through every disguise and illusion, heaven's punishment turned into the pilgrim's greatest gift

symbols.name: The peaches and the pills
symbols.meaning: Stolen longevity — the Peaches of Immortality and Laozi's elixir pills, the wages of the Heavenly revolt, digested into a body heaven cannot process

symbols.name: Five Phases Mountain (五行山)
symbols.meaning: The Buddha's hand made landscape — five hundred years of imprisonment under a wall of stone, the weight of consequence for the wager the monkey could not imagine losing

mythology.lead: The Monkey King's story is China's great comic epic of self-mastery: born from a stone egg, tutored in the arts of immortality, at war with heaven itself — then bound to a monk and set on a road that turns the cosmic delinquent into a Buddha. Every age has read its own rebellion in him.

myths.title: Born from the Stone Egg
myths.text: The novel opens at the beginning of its world-within-a-world: on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, an immortal stone egg, left over from the creation and nourished by the essence of sun, moon, heaven, and earth, one day splits in the wind. From it steps a stone monkey, who at once bows to the four directions — and the beams of light that shoot from his golden eyes startle the Jade Emperor on his distant throne (Journey to the West, ch. 1). The new-made monkey leads his tribe through the waterfall curtain into the Water-Curtain Cave, and the discovery wins him a crown: Handsome Monkey King. He is born twice over — from stone, and from the water's test — owing nothing to any parent, court, or god. The book's whole psychology is in that birth: the Monkey King is the self-made self, and heaven will spend a hundred chapters trying to make it answerable.

myths.title: Striking Out the Names of Death
myths.text: The first grief of the Monkey King's life is an old monkey's death, and it sends him on the novel's first quest: to learn the secret of escaping mortality. For eight or nine years he wanders — across seas, through markets, in the guise of a scholar — until he reaches Mount Lingtai and the cave of the Patriarch Subodhi, who takes him as a disciple, names him Wùkōng, "Awakened to Emptiness," and teaches him the two arts that will make him famous and impossible: the seventy-two transformations and the cloud-somersault, 108,000 li in a single flip (ch. 1–2). Even death cannot keep him. When the soul-snatchers of the underworld drag him down while he sleeps, he bullies the Ten Kings of Hell, seizes the Registers of Death, and strikes out his own name and every monkey’s in the tribe (ch. 3). The episode fixes his character forever — faced with the one law no creature escapes, his answer is not repentance but erasure.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Monkey King is arguably the most retold character in Chinese history. The 1592 Shidetang edition fixed the novel; Peking opera made havoc-in-heaven a signature sequence; the 1986 CCTV television series became one of the most-watched dramas ever aired in the Chinese-speaking world, rebroadcast every summer since. The diaspora carried him into global pop culture — Japan's Son Goku, and through it the Dragon Ball franchise — and the 2024 video game Black Myth: Wukong carried him to the top of world sales charts, a Ming-dynasty pilgrim headlining a global entertainment industry. Meanwhile he never ceased to be a god: the cult of Qítiān Dàshèng persists in Fujian and Taiwan, where his temples, mediums, and festival troupes treat the Great Sage as a living, oath-binding power. The rebel has two afterlives, and neither cancels the other.
lore.archaeology: Wùkōng's material record tracks the novel's. The earliest narrative stratum is the Song Poetic Tale of Tripitaka's Pilgrimage; the Ming zaju play was preserved in part through the Yongle Encyclopedia; and the 1592 Shidetang woodblock edition of Journey to the West is the earliest extant complete text. The cult beneath the literature is older than the novel: a Song-dated stone shrine at Baoshan, Shunchang County, Fujian, dedicated to Qítiān Dàshèng and his brother Tōngtiān Dàshèng, is among the earliest material evidence of the Great Sage's worship — decades, at least, before the novel fixed his story. Qítiān Dàshèng temples remain active across Fujian and Taiwan, where the Great Sage's spirit-medium rites are among the most dramatic survivals of Chinese popular religion.
lore.syncretism: Sūnwùkōng is a palimpsest, and scholarship has mapped his layers. At the bottom lies the historical pilgrimage: the monk Xuánzàng's journey to India (629–645 CE) and its biography, the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions. Over it the storytellers laid a monkey-disciple motif that appears by the Song in the Poetic Tale of Tripitaka's Pilgrimage and in the Yuan-Ming zaju play attributed to Yang Jingxian — and beneath that, some argue, the Tang tale of the water-monster Wuzhiqi, chained by Yu the Great (Li Gongzuo, Guwuyue jing). The Indian Hanuman has been proposed as a source since the twentieth century; the case is suggestive but contested, and most scholarship now treats Wùkōng as a largely indigenous synthesis dressed in Buddhist pilgrimage clothes. Daoist readers then recast the whole novel as inner alchemy: Wùkōng is the xīnyuán, the monkey of the mind, whose harnessing is the work of cultivation. The figure travelled onward as Son Goku in Japan, Tôn Ngộ Không in Vietnam, and Seoyugi's pilgrim in Korea.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 孫悟空 in traditional Chinese, 孙悟空 simplified. Sūn 孫 is the surname ("grandchild, descendant"); wù 悟 is "awakening, enlightenment"; kōng 空 is "emptiness, the void" — the Buddhist technical term. The novel glosses the full name as the monkey awakened to emptiness. The tone-marked restoration Sūnwùkōng keeps all three citation tones (sūn Tone 1, wù Tone 4, kōng Tone 1); no apostrophe is needed, as the segmentation sūn·wù·kōng is unambiguous.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KHEH-rōn' — long ē, long ō, the pitch rising on the first syllable
pronunciation.note: Tier 1: the Greek original Χείρων carries both stress (the acute on ει) and long vowels (ει and ω). The restored form Cheírōn preserves both marks — the accent and the macron — that plain ASCII 'Cheiron' erases.

domains.title: The Most Just of Centaurs
domains.subtitle: Wisdom · Teaching · Heroes
domains.lead: Cheírōn is the exception among the wild κένταυροι: the immortal son of Kronos who dwells in a cave on Mount Pelion and turns raw princes into heroes. Where his kin are drunkards and rapine, Homer calls him δικαιότατος Κενταύρων — the most just of centaurs. He is the teacher: medicine for Asklepios, the lyre and the remedies for Achilles, the whole heroic craft for Iason and Herakles.

cards.name: The Tutor's Craft
cards.desc: He reared Achilles, Iásōn, and Asklepios on Mount Pēlion — 'the most just of the Centaurs' (Iliad 11.832).

cards.name: The Healing Hand
cards.desc: He taught Asklepios the art of drugs, and was himself struck by Herakles' hydra-venomed arrow that no healing art could cure.

cards.name: The Hunter's Art
cards.desc: From him the heroes learned the chase itself — tracking, coursing, and spear-work in the mountain wilds.

cards.name: The Incurable Wound
cards.desc: Herakles' stray arrow, dipped in the Lernaean hydra's venom, struck his knee — the healer whom no remedy could heal (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4).

symbols.name: The Pelian Ash Spear
symbols.meaning: The great spear of ash wood that Cheírōn cut on Pelion's peak and gave to Peleus at his wedding — the same spear Achilles alone could wield (Iliad 16.143–144). The teacher's gift that arms the hero.

symbols.name: The Cave on Mount Pelion
symbols.meaning: His dwelling and school, the legendary academy of heroes; the gods themselves feasted there at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis (Pindar, Pythian 3.86–95).

symbols.name: The Lyre
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the education he gave Achilles, who in Iliad 9 (186–189) is found in his hut singing the glories of heroes to the lyre.

symbols.name: Herbs and Remedies (φάρμακα)
symbols.meaning: The healing lore he taught Asklepios and gave to Peleus's line; Achilles treats wounds with remedies 'that Cheiron gave his father' (Iliad 4.219, 11.831–832).

symbols.name: The Hydra-Poisoned Arrow
symbols.meaning: Herakles's stray arrow, dipped in the Lernaean hydra's venom, that struck his knee and gave the immortal an unhealable wound (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4).

symbols.name: The Stars
symbols.meaning: Zeus set him in the sky — remembered as Centaurus or Sagittarius — after he surrendered his immortality and died (Ovid, Fasti 5.379–414; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38).

mythology.lead: Cheírōn stands at the hinge of two orders: Titan-born yet honored by the Olympians, beast-bodied yet the very image of wisdom. His myths are the myths of transmission — what one generation hands to the next.

myths.title: Son of Kronos and Philyra
myths.text: Kronos lay with the Oceanid Philyra in the shape of a horse, and from that union was born a child of double nature — half god, half horse (Apollodorus, Library 1.2.4). Pindar names him 'the son of Philyra and Kronos', making Cheírōn the half-brother of Zeus and Poseidon (Pythian 4.102–115) — an older generation's blood serving the new order. Philyra, ashamed of her foal, begged to be changed into anything else and became a linden tree, under which the infant was found and reared by Apollo and Artemis; from them he drew the arts he would spend eternity handing on. The myth's double nature runs deeper than the body: the wisest of teachers begins as the child of deception and rejection, and his school in the cave on Pelion is founded by the one centaur whom the gods did not exile from their company.

myths.title: Tutor of the Heroes
myths.text: Pindar gives the roll of his pupils: in his cave Cheírōn reared Iason, gentle-handed Asklepios whom he taught the craft of remedies, and Achilles, whom he fed on the marrow of lions and wild boars to make him fierce (Nemean 3.43–58). Homer twice seals the bond: Achilles treats wounds with remedies 'that Cheiron gave to his father in friendship' (Iliad 4.218–219), and is the man 'whom Cheiron taught, the most just of the centaurs' — dikaiotatos Kentaurōn (Iliad 11.831–832). Actaeon and Herakles also passed through his tutelage. When the Argo sailed, the centaur came down from Pelion to see her off and give the Argonauts his blessing for the voyage (Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.553–558). And in Pindar's grief for the sick Hieron, the poet's deepest wish is that Cheírōn still lived in his cave, that another healer might rise from Pelion and sail to Sicily (Pythian 3.1–7). The school had an address, and the whole Greek world knew it.

lore.culturalLegacy: His name lives in the sky: the minor planet 2060 Chiron, discovered in 1977 between Saturn and Uranus, was named for him and gave its class of objects — the centaurs, bodies orbiting among the giant planets — their collective name. Modern astrology adopted him as the emblem of the wounded healer, the one whose incurable hurt becomes the source of healing for others. Ancient herbalists named the plant centaury (κενταύριον) after the centaurs' healing lore. And the old association of his name with χείρ, the hand, echoes — by the word's own root, not by his name's — in 'surgery', from χειρουργία, 'hand-work.'
lore.archaeology: No great temple of Cheírōn is known; he is a daimonic tutor, not an Olympian with a state cult, though a cave above Portaria on Mount Pelion is traditionally identified as the Cheironeion, his school. His real monument is the art: Attic black- and red-figure vases repeatedly show Peleus handing the infant Achilles into the centaur's arms, and Roman sarcophagi of the 2nd–3rd c. CE show him teaching the lyre — the 'education of Achilles' among the most copied sarcophagus compositions of the empire. The sculpted centauromachies — the Olympia west pediment and the Parthenon south metopes — preserve the wild centaur type against which his justice was defined.
lore.syncretism: Rome changed Cheírōn least of all the Greek figures: he keeps his name as Chiron in Latin, too singular to be merged with any Italian power. What Rome absorbed was his catasterism — Latin poets and star-cataloguers fixed him in the sky, debating whether the Centaurus or the Sagittarius was his (Ovid, Fasti 5; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38). In later tradition he remains the named exception among his kind: Dante makes him chief of the centaurs who guard the violent in Inferno 12 — still 'Chiron, who nursed Achilles,' still teaching, still assigning duties to his infernal pupils. The word 'centaur' traveled into every European language, but Cheírōn travels as himself, the one monster whom civilization quotes.

etymology.derivation: Sanskrit Śakti, from the root śak 'to be able, to have power'; the dynamic feminine energy of the divine.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SHAKTI' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.
pronunciation.note: Śakti is Tier 1: the palatal ś — the sibilant IAST writes Ś, the sound English flattens to 'sh' — is a distinctive diacritic-bearing letter that the ASCII form loses. The word itself is the abstract of √śak, 'to be able': the name of power, marked as Sanskrit by the very letter that carries its meaning.

domains.title: Power
domains.subtitle: Power, Energy, Divine Feminine
domains.lead: Śakti is power itself: the energy without which the god is a lifeless body — śiva without śakti is a corpse. She is the active power of the divine personified as the goddess: consort of Śiva in the Purāṇas, the Devī who slays the buffalo-demon in the Devīmāhātmya, and the coiled force of Kuṇḍalinī in Tantra.

cards.name: Śakti, the Active Power
cards.desc: The name means power, ability, energy — the operative might of a deity personified as his consort (Monier-Williams, s.v.).

cards.name: Devīmāhātmya
cards.desc: In the Caṇḍī (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 81–93) the gods' combined śaktis blaze forth as the Devī who destroys Mahiṣāsura.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The palatal Ś — IAST's ś, the sound English writes 'sh' — is recovered from the ASCII flattening, letter by letter.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Devanagari शक्ति — attested from the Ṛgveda's śacī-, 'might', onward as śakti, 'power, ability, energy'.

symbols.name: The kuṇḍalinī serpent
symbols.meaning: Coiled at the base of the spine — the latent śakti that Tantra raises through the cakras to unite with Śiva at the crown

symbols.name: The triśūla (trident)
symbols.meaning: Śiva's weapon as energy — the three powers of will, knowledge, and action (icchā, jñāna, kriyā) personified

symbols.name: The śrīcakra
symbols.meaning: The nine-interlocked-triangle diagram of Śrīvidyā — śakti worshipped as pure geometry, the goddess as the map of her own power

symbols.name: The sword of the Devī
symbols.meaning: The blade with which Caṇḍikā beheads Mahiṣāsura — divine power as the weapon the gods only hold because she wields it

symbols.name: The lotus (padma)
symbols.meaning: The unfolding seat of the goddess — energy rising, petal by petal, toward the thousand-petalled crown

mythology.lead: Śakti is both a theological principle and a goddess with a story. The Veda knows her as śacī, the might of Indra; the Purāṇas give her a body, a husband, and a battlefield; the Tantras make her the equal — in places the superior — of the god she empowers.

myths.title: Śacī, the Might Before the Goddess
myths.text: Before Śakti had temples she had a word. The Ṛgveda uses śacī-, 'might, help, assistance,' for the power that makes Indra the conqueror of Vṛtra, and already personifies it: Indra is śacīpati, 'lord of śacī,' and his consort bears the name Śacī/Indrāṇī — celebrated in RV 10.86, where Indrāṇī boasts she is greater than all the wives of the gods. The abstract noun never quite loses its abstractness: Śakti the goddess grows directly out of śakti the grammatical fact, the capacity to act. The interpretive core of later Śākta theology is already visible in the Vedic idiom — a god's power is not his possession but his partner. What the Veda states as a linguistic intuition, that might is feminine and stands beside the god as his wife, the Purāṇas will raise into a cosmos.

myths.title: The Power of All the Gods
myths.text: The Devīmāhātmya (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 81–93) stages the supreme demonstration. When the buffalo-demon Mahiṣa overthrows the gods, they gather and pour forth their śaktis — a flame-mass of energy issues from Śiva, from Viṣṇu, from Indra, from each — and the blazes converge into female form: the ten-armed Devī, 'the śakti of all, whose form is the power of all beings.' Riding a lion, armed with every god's own weapon, she battles Mahiṣa across nine days and nights, cuts off the buffalo head, and pins the demon with her spear as he emerges in human form; the gods hymn her as the power behind their power — 'only in you do we triumph.' The text's claim is the charter of Śākta religion: the goddess is not one deity among many but the energy by which every deity acts, and without her the pantheon stands unarmed.

lore.culturalLegacy: Śakti is the foundation of Śākta Hinduism, one of the four major devotional streams, centered on the Devī in her forms as Durgā, Kālī, Lalitā, and Tripurasundarī. Her festivals are among the largest on earth: Durgā-pūjā builds the goddess a whole temporary city each autumn, and Navarātri's nine nights re-enact the Devīmāhātmya battle. The Tantric lineages — Śrīvidyā still transmitted in initiations, the kuṇḍalinī vocabulary of haṭha-yoga — exported the concept globally: 'shakti' entered English as a loanword for spiritual energy in the nineteenth century through the Theosophists and through Vivekananda's Vedānta. Every yoga class that promises to 'raise your energy' is teaching Śakti's doctrine of the coiled serpent under another name.
lore.archaeology: Śakti's material record is the long history of goddess worship in South Asia. Kuṣāṇa-period Mathura (1st–3rd c. CE) yields early sculpted Devī and mother-goddess figures; Gupta and post-Gupta temples across Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, and Bengal install Durgā in her Mahiṣāsura-mardinī form, the Devīmāhātmya's battle rendered in stone. Copper and gold śrīcakra yantras, the Kālī images of Bengal, and the living pīṭhas — Kāmākhyā in Assam raised over the goddess's yoni, Kālīghāṭ in Kolkata — mark the tradition's sacred geography. The Devīmāhātmya itself survives in palm-leaf and paper manuscripts from the medieval period, the witnesses behind its modern critical edition.
lore.syncretism: Buddhism absorbed śakti as readily as it debated it. Vajrayāna pairs every male buddha with a female consort — Prajñā as the śakti of Upāya, wisdom as the power of compassion — and elevates Tārā, Vajrayoginī, and the ḍākinīs to powers the male figures cannot act without, a structural debt to Śākta theology the tantras do not conceal. In Purāṇic Hinduism, śakti became the umbrella for the great goddesses: Lakṣmī as Viṣṇu's energy, Pārvatī as Śiva's, Sarasvatī as Brahmā's — while the Devīmāhātmya and Devī Purāṇa went further, making the Devī the supreme power of which the gods are instruments. Medieval Europe met the idea through Jesuit accounts of the 'shaktis' of Śiva; modern yoga and global wellness vocabulary adopted the word wholesale, often stripped of the theology that insists she is not a mood but the motor of the divine.

entries.meaning: 'Lord of Creatures' — the creator and progenitor ranked above or among the Vedic gods

etymology.derivation: Sanskrit tatpuruṣa compound prajā- 'offspring, creatures' + pati- 'lord, master', meaning 'Lord of Creatures'.
