symbols.meaning: The quest accomplished by cunning — and Arthur's mocking englyn that ended the fellowship

symbols.name: Cei Hir, 'the Tall'
symbols.meaning: Tall as the tallest tree in the forest when it pleased him — stature as the visible sign of the older, larger hero

mythology.lead: Kai's mythology lives in the oldest stratum of Welsh Arthurian tradition: Culhwch ac Olwen gives him the tale's largest dossier after Arthur himself, and the fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur remembers exploits the prose never told. The later Latin and French traditions kept the man and quietly spent the magic.

myths.title: The First Companion
myths.text: When Culhwch comes to Arthur's court to win Olwen daughter of Ysbaddaden Chief Giant, Arthur grants him help, and the first companion named is Cei son of Cynyr. The warrior-list fixes his peculiarities in one breath: nine nights and nine days he could be under water; nine nights and nine days he could go without sleep; a wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal. Cei the Tall — when it pleased him he could make himself as tall as the tallest tree in the forest. And the list adds the attribute the whole fellowship depended on: when the rain was heaviest, whatever he carried in his hand stayed dry for a handbreadth above and below, so great was his heat; and when the cold was hardest on his companions, he was fuel to them to light their fire. The list also preserves his mother's prophecy that his heart would be cold — the oldest trace of the coldness the later romances turned to mockery.

myths.title: The Salmon and the Sword
myths.text: Two of the hardest anoethau — the 'things hard to get' that Ysbaddaden sets as the bride-price — fall to Cei. To free Mabon son of Modron from his prison at Caer Loyw, the company follows the oldest animals to the Salmon of Llyn Llyw, and Cei and Bedwyr ride up the Severn on the salmon's shoulders; while Arthur's men assault the fort from the front, Cei carries Mabon away on the salmon's back. And when Arthur's band comes to the hall of Wrnach the giant, whose sword is needed to hunt the boar Twrch Trwyth — no guest had ever left that hall alive — Cei claims to be a master polisher of swords. Admitted, he burnishes the giant's blade, asks to hold it to test the work, and strikes Wrnach's head off with his own sword; the company destroys the fortress. The wonder-hero's greatest feats in the tale are won with a craftsman's hands, not a charge of horse — a hint of how the tradition will later make him the man who keeps the tools, not the one who swings them.

lore.culturalLegacy: The steward outlived the giant-killer. Malory's Sir Kay — the foster-brother who claims he drew the sword from the stone, confesses, and is made seneschal at Arthur's coronation — fixed the English image: blunt, envious, brave enough, and indispensable to the household. Chrétien's Keu had already made him the court's satirist, and the romances of every language kept that register. T. H. White's The Sword in the Stone made Kay the human counterweight to the Wart, the brother who gets the crown's shadow instead of the crown. In Welsh the name never left: Cai remains a living given name, and the Mabinogion's Cei Hir is still the tall man of the oldest Arthurian tale. Modern scholarship treats the arc from wonder-hero to comic steward as one of the great case-studies in how the Arthurian legend domesticated its oldest figures.
lore.archaeology: Kai is a literary figure: no inscription, ogham stone, or Romano-British dedication names him, and Welsh tradition generally left texts rather than cult monuments for its heroes. His manuscript witnesses are exact and early. The dialogue poem Pa Gur survives in the Black Book of Carmarthen (c. 1250), the oldest substantial manuscript of Welsh verse; Culhwch ac Olwen survives in a fragmentary copy in the White Book of Rhydderch (Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and complete in the Red Book of Hergest (Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1425); and the Otherworld-raid poem Preiddeu Annwn, the companion witness to this stratum, is preserved in the Book of Taliesin (Peniarth 2, early 14th c.). Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) and Lifris of Llancarfan's Vita Cadoci (c. 1100) carry the Latin attestations. The places of the tales — Caer Loyw on the Severn, the Anglesey of Cath Palug — remain on the map, but the tall man himself left nothing in stone.
lore.syncretism: Kai is less a figure who absorbed other gods than one whom each retelling rewrote. The Welsh stratum gives a wonder-hero: the tall, fire-handed, sleepless companion whose attributes belong to the oldest legendary stock of Britain. Geoffrey of Monmouth euhemerizes him into Caius dapifer, a duke and steward of recognizable twelfth-century type; Chrétien de Troyes turns the steward's sharpness into Keu's venomous tongue, the court's mocker who is always wrong; and Malory resolves the long arc into Sir Kay, Arthur's foster-brother — loyal, loud, and forever outmatched. Scholars have long paired him with Bedwyr, his constant companion in Culhwch ac Olwen, as the two oldest members of Arthur's band; and Mac Cana and others note that the tale-patterns around the pair — the raid on a giant's stronghold, the hunt of the enchanted boar — have close Irish analogues, though no Irish cycle preserves Cei himself. The transformation of the tall man into the seneschal is the tradition's own syncretism: one name, four costumes, and the office outlasting the magic.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Cei, with the spelling variants Kei and Kai — plain Latin letters in Insular script, c. 12th–14th c. CE, in the Black Book of Carmarthen, the White Book of Rhydderch, and the Red Book of Hergest. No diacritic and no distinctive letter is involved: the normalized form is already ASCII, and the restoration Kai differs from the input only by its capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: kai.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DOHN' — one syllable, one long pure 'oh' held steady, like English 'dawn' with the vowel kept clean and simple.
pronunciation.note: Don is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the temple follows the Middle Welsh manuscript spelling Don — three plain ASCII letters, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Modern Welsh scholarship writes Dôn with a circumflex, but that mark is a modern length-sign, not a letter the manuscripts carry; the normalized temple form preserves it only in the pronunciation record, not the spelling. The etymology is honestly uncertain: derivation from Common Celtic *dēwā 'goddess' — the root the Welsh still hear in Dyfrdwy, the Dee — is the traditional reading, while a river-name origin is also argued; the handbooks mark the question open.

domains.title: Mother of Gods
domains.subtitle: Plant Dôn — the children named for the mother
domains.lead: Dôn is the matriarch of the Mabinogi's magical house: sister of Math fab Mathonwy, lord of Gwynedd, and mother of the great kindred the Welsh tradition called Plant Dôn, the Children of Dôn — Gwydion the enchanter, Gilfaethwy his brother, Arianrhod of the star-castle, Gofannon the smith, and Amaethon the ploughman. She is the only major figure of the Four Branches who never speaks, acts, or appears: the whole of the Fourth Branch happens among her children and her brother, and she is present only in the names they carry — uab Dôn, son of Dôn; uerch Dôn, daughter of Dôn.

cards.name: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy
cards.desc: The sister-sons at Math's court: Gwydion the enchanter, 'the best teller of tales in the world', and Gilfaethwy his brother — named, always, as sons of Dôn.

cards.name: Arianrhod ferch Dôn
cards.desc: The daughter proposed for Math's footholder, tested by the wand, mother of Dylan and Lleu — and the proudest, most wounded figure of the Fourth Branch.

cards.name: Gofannon and Amaethon
cards.desc: The craftsman-sons of Culhwch ac Olwen: Gofannon the smith and Amaethon the ploughman, without whom the giant's impossible tasks cannot be done.

cards.name: Plant Dôn
cards.desc: The Children of Dôn — the Welsh divine kindred named for its mother, the standing parallel to Ireland's Túatha Dé Danann.

symbols.name: The matronymic (uab Dôn)
symbols.meaning: 'Son of Dôn' — the mother-name standing at the head of every child's name, her whole presence in the text

symbols.name: Math's wand
symbols.meaning: Her brother's instrument of testing and transformation, laid across her children's fates — the power of the uncle's house over the mother's

symbols.name: Plough and anvil
symbols.meaning: Amaethon's plough and Gofannon's smithy — the crafts of cultivation and making that her sons carry into the oldest tale

symbols.name: The Dee (Dyfrdwy)
symbols.meaning: The river the Welsh still call 'the goddess' — *Dēwā, the name's closest living relative, flowing through the real landscape

symbols.name: The star-castles
symbols.meaning: Caer Arianrhod and Caer Gwydion — her daughter's and her son's halls written into the Welsh night sky by later tradition

mythology.lead: Dôn has no myth of her own — no tale, no speech, no deed the sources record. What she has is a family, and the family is the mythology: the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi unfolds among her children and her brother Math, and the oldest Arthurian tale cannot finish its tasks without two more of her sons. Every witness names her the same way — as the mother in the matronymic — and the Welsh tradition built its northern divine house around exactly that: Plant Dôn, the Children of Dôn.

myths.title: The Sister-Sons at Math's Court
myths.text:
The Fourth Branch opens at the court of Math fab Mathonwy, lord of Gwynedd — who cannot live unless his feet rest in a virgin's lap, except when war is in the land — and it introduces the great men of that court by their mother's name: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy, sons of Dôn, Math's own sister-sons, his nephews and his company. Gwydion is 'the best teller of tales in the world'. It is these two who set the branch's whole tragedy in motion: Gilfaethwy desires Goewin, the maiden of the foothold, and Gwydion engineers the remedy — a war against Pryderi of Dyfed, bought with conjured stallions, hounds, and shields that vanish after a day, so that the king marches south and the rape can happen.

Through all of it — the war, the crime, the three years of animal-shape punishment — the mother never appears. Dôn is present in the text exactly as a name inside other names: uab Dôn, son of Dôn, the matronymic the tale attaches to her children every time it introduces them. The most consequential family in Welsh prose walks the stage under her name, and she never once walks it herself.

myths.title: Arianrhod ferch Dôn and the Wand
myths.text:
When Math needs a new footholder after Goewin, Gwydion proposes his own sister: 'Seek for you a maiden... here is Arianrhod daughter of Dôn.' The maiden is summoned and asked if she is a virgin; she answers that she does not know but believes she is. Math makes her step over his magic wand, and as she steps she drops a fine yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who at once makes for the sea and takes the sea's nature, Dylan Eil Ton, son of the wave — and, all but unnoticed, 'something small' that only Gwydion marks, wraps in a cloth, and hides in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest comes the boy who will be Lleu.

Arianrhod, shamed before the whole court, refuses the boy and lays upon him the three tynghedau — the fated destinies — that he shall have no name until she names him, no arms until she arms him, and no wife of any race then on earth. The rest of the branch is Gwydion undoing his sister's curses by craft. Dôn's daughter is the Fourth Branch's proudest and most wounded figure — and Dôn is present, once again, only in the patronymic: uerch Dôn, daughter of Dôn.

lore.culturalLegacy: Dôn rode into English on the same wagon as the rest of the Mabinogi: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation (1838–49) first carried the Fourth Branch into print, and the antiquarian mythography that followed made Plant Dôn the standard label for the northern divine kindred — the house of Gwydion, set beside the house of Llŷr, in every Victorian account of the Welsh gods. Twentieth-century scholarship fixed her place with precision: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) established the text, Mac Cana's The Mabinogi read the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of Welsh prose, and the great encyclopedias — Koch's Celtic Culture and MacKillop's Dictionary — gave the matriarch her standing head-words, Danu comparison and all. Her widest modern audience came through a children's classic: Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain (1964–68) made 'the Sons of Don' the ruling house of Prydain, with Math son of Mathonwy and Prince Gwydion at Caer Dathyl — her name on the throne of the best-loved Welsh-derived fantasy ever written. Modern Druid and pagan practice honours her as the Welsh mother-goddess and mother of the magical line, and the Welsh sky keeps her children's names: Caer Gwydion, the Milky Way, and Caer Arianrhod among the stars.
lore.archaeology: Dôn is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the epigraphic record of early Wales — the Latin and ogham memorial stones catalogued by Nash-Williams — records personal names in funerary formulae, not theonyms. Her evidence is manuscript evidence. The Fourth Branch survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1420), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; Culhwch ac Olwen is preserved in the same two codices; the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century) holds Kat Godeu. The tales' date of composition is debated, most often placed in the later eleventh or twelfth century. The geography of her house is real — Gwynedd and Arfon in the north-west of Wales, where Math's court and Arianrhod's castle stand in the tale — but no sanctuary of hers is known. The closest thing to a material trace of the name is a river: Dyfrdwy, the Welsh name of the Dee, continues Common Celtic *Dēwā, 'the goddess', and keeps the matriarch's name-element flowing through the landscape to this day.
lore.syncretism: Dôn's great comparison is Irish, and it is as old as modern Celtic studies: [[danu|Danu]] (or Dana), the equally shadowy mother after whom the Túatha Dé Danann — the peoples of the goddess Danu — are named. A Welsh divine kindred called the Children of Dôn and an Irish one called the peoples of Danu look like two faces of one inheritance, and MacKillop and Koch both register the comparison as standard. But it is a comparison, not an equation: no Welsh text identifies the two names, and the philology is genuinely disputed. The traditional reading derives Dôn from Common Celtic *dēwā, 'goddess' — the very word the Welsh language keeps in Dyfrdwy, its name for the River Dee — while a river-name origin, matching the continental Dānuvius (Danube) and the English Don, is also argued; the handbooks leave the question open rather than resolve it. Inside the Welsh corpus her closest kin are the tradition's other mothers and queens: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], the Great Queen of Dyfed, and, in later genealogical speculation, her pairing with [[beli|Beli Mawr]] as father of her children — a marriage the genealogies assert and the Mabinogi never mentions. Her husbandless, speechless sovereignty has no exact parallel anywhere in Celtic literature: she is the matriarch reduced to pure name.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Don — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1375–1420), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Modern Welsh orthography writes Dôn with a circumflex, but that mark is a modern length-sign for the long vowel, not a letter any manuscript carries; the project therefore follows the manuscript form, and the name stands in Tier 2 by the mechanical rule — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, nothing for ASCII to lose. Because the name is pure ASCII — and also an ordinary English word and river-name — its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: don.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/don/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: BEL-ee — two syllables, stress on the first; the e is the open e of 'bed', never the long ay of 'bailey'.
pronunciation.note: Middle Welsh Beli (Beli mawr uab Manogan, 'Beli the Great, son of Manogan') is already written in the Latin alphabet, so the ASCII form loses nothing: the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, since the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops. The traditional gloss 'bright, shining' reaches the name through its long-proposed connection with the Celtic god Belenos — conventionally derived from the root *bhel-, 'to shine' — but the etymology of Belenos itself is debated, and the handbooks record the link as a possibility, not a proof.

domains.title: The Root of the Pedigrees
domains.subtitle: The Island of Britain, the Four Sons, and the Question of the Bright One
domains.lead: Beli mawr — Beli the Great, son of Manogan — is the deep ancestor of British kingship: the king of the Island of Britain whom the Mabinogion sets at the head of its dynasties, father of Lludd, Caswallawn, Nynniaw, and Llefelys, and the name to which the medieval Welsh royal pedigrees climb. Behind the king, scholarship has long glimpsed a god — the continental Belenos, the 'bright, shining' one — but the texts give us the ancestor, and the ancestor is what the record can defend.

cards.name: The Island of Britain
cards.desc: Beli's realm in Lludd a Llefelys: the whole island, 'the crown of London' its seat — the deep past of a single British kingship.

cards.name: The Four Sons
cards.desc: Lludd, Caswallawn, Nynniaw — and, 'as the story tells', a fourth, Llefelys: the branches of the house the whole tradition descends from.

cards.name: The Pedigree
cards.desc: The Harleian genealogies carry the royal houses of Wales back to Beli Mawr — the name at the root of the British family trees.

cards.name: The Bright One
cards.desc: The proposed god behind the king: Belenos, 'bright, shining' — the continental name Tertullian and the Aquileia altars attest, linked to Beli by a long scholarly tradition.

symbols.name: The Island of Britain
symbols.meaning: The single realm Beli held and his sons inherited — kingship imagined whole before it was ever divided

symbols.name: The family tree
symbols.meaning: The pedigrees of the Welsh dynasties growing back to one root — ancestry as the ground of legitimacy

symbols.name: The veil of illusion
symbols.meaning: Caswallawn's invisible cloak in Branwen — the house of Beli taking the crown unseen

symbols.name: The walled city
symbols.meaning: Lludd's rebuilding of London — Lud's town, the memory of the dynasty fixed in stone and street-names

symbols.name: The sun's brightness
symbols.meaning: The traditional gloss of the name — 'bright, shining' — carried from the Belenos inscriptions into the Welsh ancestor

mythology.lead: Beli has no adventure of his own: his story is his house. The Mabinogion knows him as the dead king whose four sons inherit Britain, France, and the quarrels of the next generation; the pedigrees know him as the root; and Geoffrey of Monmouth knows him as Heli, father of the builder of London.

myths.title: The Four Sons of Beli
myths.text:
The tale of Lludd and Llefelys opens with the settlement of the island: Beli the Great, son of Manogan, was king of this island, and he had three sons — Lludd, Caswallawn, and Nynniaw — and, as the story tells, a fourth son called Llefelys. When Beli died, the kingdom of the Island of Britain fell to Lludd as the eldest, and Lludd ruled it prosperously, rebuilding the walls of London and living there for most of the year. Llefelys, the youngest, went to France, won the love of the old king's only daughter, and inherited that kingdom in his turn.

What follows — the three plagues that fall on Britain, and Llefelys's counsel from the middle of the Channel — belongs to the sons' temples. Beli's part is finished in the opening lines, and that is precisely his function: he is the point from which legitimacy flows, the dead father whose reign makes his sons' divided world one family.

myths.title: Caswallawn's Veil
myths.text:
The Second Branch remembers Beli's house at the moment it takes the crown. While Brân the Blessed marched into Ireland to avenge Branwen, he left seven men as regents in Britain, his son Caradog at their head. Caswallawn son of Beli marched against them wearing a veil of illusion, so that no one could see him — only his sword killing. He slew the seven, and Caradog died of a broken heart at the sight of the slaughter and the knowledge of who held the island now.

Caswallawn son of Beli became king in London. The branch never explains or excuses the usurpation; it simply registers that while the children of Llŷr spent themselves overseas, the children of Beli took the island — the two great houses of Welsh tradition passing the crown between them without a battle anyone could see.

lore.culturalLegacy: Beli's afterlife is genealogical before it is literary. The medieval pedigrees made descent from Beli Mawr the deepest claim a British dynasty could print, and the convention outlived the Middle Ages: Tudor and Stuart antiquaries, eager to trace the crown to British and Trojan roots, found Beli waiting at the root of the trees Geoffrey had Latinized. Through Geoffrey's Heli he fathered the legend of London itself — Lud's town, Lud's gate, the name written into the city's streets — and through his son Cassibelaunus he stands two generations above Shakespeare's Cymbeline, whose Britain is still Beli's island. In modern Wales the name persists quietly: Beli remains a Welsh personal name, and Beli Mawr keeps his place in the national memory as the grandfather of kings. Modern Celtic pagan and Druid practice honors the ancestral Belenos beside him, keeping the old question — king or bright god — alive rather than answered.
lore.archaeology: Beli is a textual figure: no inscription, image, or votive object from Britain names him, and no cult site is his. His witnesses are codices — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410) for the Mabinogion tales, and British Library Harley MS 3859 (c. 1100) for the genealogies that root the Welsh dynasties in him. The material evidence belongs to his proposed continental cognate: the dedications Belino Augusto sacrum from Aquileia and the eastern Alps are real stones with a real theonym — the strongest archaeological fact in the whole dossier, and the reason the 'bright, shining' gloss will not go away. Comparative evidence only: no altar can be read as addressed to the Welsh ancestor-king himself.
lore.syncretism: Beli's whole cross-cultural argument is the Belenos question. The continental god is attested from Aquileia to Noricum, glossed by the ancients as a Celtic Apollo, and derived by tradition from *bhel-, 'to shine'. Welsh Beli Mawr matches the name nearly perfectly, and from O'Rahilly onward scholars have set the Irish ancestor-god Bile beside both, proposing a single Celtic 'bright one' dimmed into three literatures as three ancestors. Mac Cana and Koch record the comparison; neither certifies it. The distinction worth keeping is Geoffrey's other Belinus — the son of Dunvallo, brother of Brennius — a different figure who shares nothing with Beli Mawr but the name. Within the Welsh corpus, Beli's closest kin are the other fountainheads of dynasty: [[don|Dôn]], mother of the Children of Dôn, and Llŷr, father of the house of Llŷr, whose sons Brân and [[manawydan|Manawydan]] lose the island's crown to Beli's son Caswallawn in the Second Branch.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Beli (Beli mawr uab Manogan) in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: beli.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

availability.details: RDAP registered; DNS resolves, no HTTP

pronunciation.approximation: MAATH — a long, open 'ah', held like the a of 'father', closing on the soft voiceless th of English 'thin'. One syllable; the whole weight of the name sits on the length of the vowel and the hush at the end.
pronunciation.note: Middle Welsh Math (Math uab Mathonwy) is already written in the Latin alphabet, so the ASCII form loses nothing: the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, since the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops. The standard etymology derives the name from Proto-Celtic *matu- 'bear' — compare Old Irish math 'bear' (attested in the compound mathgamain), the Irish name Mathgen borne by the seer of the Túatha Dé Danann, and Gaulish Matugenos 'bear-born'. The father's name, Mathonwy, is built on the same root, and the handbooks treat the bear-derivation as the best-supported reading.

domains.title: Magic, Kingship
domains.subtitle: The domain of Math
domains.lead: Math fab Mathonwy is the king at the still centre of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi: lord of Gwynedd, master of the magic wand, uncle of Gwydion and Gilfaethwy. His kingship runs on the strangest condition in Welsh literature — he cannot live unless his feet rest in a virgin's lap, save when war calls him out — and the whole plot of his branch is what happens when two nephews read that condition like a statute and use it against him.

cards.name: The Wand of Office
cards.desc: Math's hutlath — the magic wand that tested Arianrhod, turned his nephews into beasts for three years, and helped fashion a woman out of flowers.

cards.name: The Footholder's Geas
cards.desc: The strange condition of his kingship: Math could not live except with his feet in the lap of a virgin, unless the turmoil of war released him.

cards.name: The Threefold Sentence
cards.desc: His justice wore animal skins: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy spent a year each as deer, boars, and wolves — and their beast-children were baptized at his court.

cards.name: The Flower Bride
cards.desc: With Gwydion he took oak, broom, and meadowsweet and made Blodeuwedd — the wife no earthly race could supply for the nephew fated to have none.

symbols.name: The magic wand (hutlath)
symbols.meaning: The rod of transformation and testing — proof, punishment, and creation carried in one length of wood

symbols.name: The virgin's lap
symbols.meaning: The footholder's office — the geas that bound the king's life to an untouched maiden, save in time of war

symbols.name: Goewin ferch Pebin
symbols.meaning: The footholder of Dôl Pebin in Arfon, wronged in the king's own house and made his queen in redress

symbols.name: The swine of Annwfn
symbols.meaning: The otherworld herd whose engineered theft gave Gwydion his war — the first pigs in Wales, and the pretext that broke the geas

symbols.name: Hyddwn, Hychddwn, and Bleiddwn
symbols.meaning: Stag, pig, and wolf — the three beast-sons of the punished brothers, restored to human shape and baptized

symbols.name: Oak, broom, and meadowsweet
symbols.meaning: The three flowers Math and Gwydion wove into Blodeuwedd, the bride made by craft

mythology.lead: Math fab Mathonwy is the king at the still centre of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi — the branch that bears his name: lord of Gwynedd, master of the magic wand, uncle of Gwydion and Gilfaethwy. His rule hangs on the strangest condition in Welsh literature — he cannot live except with his feet in a virgin's lap, unless war calls him out — and around that geas the whole plot turns: the theft of the swine, the wrong to Goewin, the justice of the three animal years, and the making of a bride from flowers.

myths.title: The Geas of the Footholder
myths.text:
Math son of Mathonwy was lord over Gwynedd, and the tale's first fact about him is the condition of his life: except when the turmoil of war prevented it, he could not live unless his feet lay in the lap of a virgin. The office of footholder went to Goewin daughter of Pebin of Dôl Pebin in Arfon, the fairest maiden of her generation; and while Math kept the lap, his sister's sons Gwydion and Gilfaethwy ruled the realm in his stead.

The arrangement is neither joke nor luxury: it is the Fourth Branch's picture of sacral kingship, a rule whose life is bound by taboo. When Gilfaethwy sickened with desire for Goewin, Gwydion read the geas like a statute. The king may leave the lap for one thing only — war. Therefore there would be a war.

myths.title: The War for the Swine
myths.text:
Pryderi of Dyfed held the hobeu, the swine sent him from Annwfn by its king Arawn — the first pigs ever brought to Wales. Gwydion went south in the guise of a poet, conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, traded the day's glamour for the herd, and was gone before the illusion faded. Pryderi mustered and came north, and Math led Gwynedd out to meet him — out of the lap, exactly as the condition required.

At the parley Pryderi demanded single combat, for it was because of him that the hosts had come; at the maenor of Penardd Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed gave hostages and went home under tribute. But while Math marched, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin in the king's own chamber. The war had only ever been the key, and the lap the lock.

lore.culturalLegacy: Math's afterlife is quieter than his nephews', but the Fourth Branch carried him far. In the twentieth century the branch was remade twice over: Evangeline Walton's The Virgin and the Swine (1936) retells his story as a tragedy of old religion and new, with the geas and the three animal years as its moral engine, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain made Math son of Mathonwy the aged High King of Prydain for a generation of young readers — the geas laid aside, the grave authority kept. Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967) drew its haunting from the Blodeuwedd strand that Math's wand set in motion, the branch repeating itself down the generations of a Welsh valley. In scholarship he stands at the centre of the Mabinogi industry: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi fixed the text, Sioned Davies's Oxford translation carries it to the world's readers, and Mac Cana's and Koch's handbooks treat the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose, with the footholder geas among the most-discussed cruxes in Celtic studies.
lore.archaeology: Math is a textual figure with no pre-Christian material attestation: no inscription, votive object, or image names him. His witnesses are manuscripts — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1400), the two codices in which the Fourth Branch survives. The epigraphic witness belongs to the root rather than the man: Gaulish personal names such as Matugenos, 'bear-born', attest the *matu- element in the onomastics of the continental Celts. The tale's own geography is real Gwynedd terrain — Dôl Pebin in Arfon, where Goewin's father held his land — and the branch's southern war-road runs to the maenor of Penardd, where Pryderi fell.
lore.syncretism: Math is the Welsh reflex of a pan-Celtic institution: the sacral king whose rule is bound by taboo. Irish tradition gives the condition its clearest grammar — the gessi of kings, the network of prohibitions whose slow breaking dooms Conaire Mór in Togail Bruidne Da Derga — and Math's footholder geas is the same machinery in Welsh dress, a kingship valid only while its condition holds. Mac Cana reads the Children of Dôn as the Welsh counterpart of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the name itself crosses the water on its own root: Cath Maige Tuired names Mathgen as the seer of the Túatha Dé Danann, and Gaulish epigraphy attests Matugenos — both 'bear-born', from the *matu- that names the king and his father. Within the Mabinogi the root echoes across the branches: [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the Irish king of the Second Branch, carries the same Math- element. His closest kin are the members of his own house — his sister [[don|Dôn]]'s children, above all [[gwydion|Gwydion]], whose plots the geas licences and whose punishments the king's wand performs — and the co-made bride [[blodeuwedd|Blodeuwedd]], his one act of creation.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Math (Math uab Mathonwy), in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. The plain-ASCII domain math.com is registered to a third party and held outside the collection; it is watched for release. Until then this temple stands without a domain of its own.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KOH-toh-shee-roh-noo-shee' — the 'r' is a light tap, and the final vowels are soft.
pronunciation.note: Kotoshironushi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is a son of Ōkuninushi and a key figure in the transfer of the land to Amaterasu's descendants.

domains.title: Lord Who Substitutes
domains.subtitle: Oracle, Fishing, and the Transfer of the Land
domains.lead: Kotoshironushi is the son of Ōkuninushi who, according to the Kojiki, surrendered the central land of reed plains to the heavenly descendants of Amaterasu. A god of oracles and fishing, he withdrew to the sea and became identified in later tradition with the fortune god Ebisu.

cards.name: Land Transfer
cards.desc: His counsel ceded the land of reed plains to the heavenly grandchildren — the surrender that founded imperial rule without a war of extermination.

cards.name: Oracle God
cards.desc: His name means “lord who substitutes”: the voice that speaks the divine will when the god himself is hidden.

cards.name: Fishing Deity
cards.desc: A grandson of the sea deity Ōwatatsumi, he withdrew toward the water and became patron of its catches.

cards.name: Ebisu Link
cards.desc: Nishinomiya’s Ebisu — rod and red tai in hand — is his smiling later face, the only purely Japanese god among the Seven Gods of Fortune.

symbols.name: Fishing rod
symbols.meaning: The attribute he carries as Ebisu, god of the catch — the tool by which fortune is drawn from the sea

symbols.name: Sea bream (tai)
symbols.meaning: The auspicious fish whose name puns on medetai, “auspicious”; Ebisu’s perpetual catch

symbols.name: Oracle implements
symbols.meaning: The divination tools of the Miwa tradition — the “substituted” voice of the hidden god

symbols.name: Kakuremi (the hiding)
symbols.meaning: His withdrawal into concealment after the cession — the survival strategy of the defeated old order

mythology.lead: Kotoshironushi’s mythology is brief but pivotal: as a son of Ōkuninushi, ruler of the earthly kami, he advised the peaceful cession of the land to the heavenly line of Amaterasu and then withdrew from the world. His “hiding” let the imperial succession begin without the annihilation of the old order, and later ages gathered his memory into Ebisu, the beloved god of fishermen and merchants.

myths.title: The Cession of the Land
myths.text: Amaterasu resolved that her grandson Ninigi should rule the central land of reed plains, and sent the warrior god Takemikazuchi to compel its ruler, Ōnamuchi — Ōkuninushi — to yield. Ōkuninushi’s son Takeminakata answered the embassy with defiance, was defeated in a trial of strength, and fled across the sea to Suwa. Then the Kojiki slows for the decisive interview: Ōkuninushi asked his son Kotoshironushi what should be done. Kotoshironushi answered that the land should be given up to the heavenly grandchildren, and — his counsel accepted — he withdrew into concealment, kakuremi, and “the land was then at peace.” His mother, the Kojiki adds, was Hayaakitsuhime, a daughter of the sea deity Ōwatatsumi, which is why his disappearance ran seaward. By choosing counsel over resistance, one son of the old order ended a war that his brother’s arms could not have won — and the mythology marks the cost exactly: the surrendering god simply vanishes from the story he made possible.

myths.title: The God Who Hides
myths.text: The Nihon Shoki’s parallel account deepens both the withdrawal and the genealogy: it names Kotoshironushi’s mother a child of the sea deity, binding him to Watatsumi’s watery realm, and dwells on the hiding itself — the kakuremi by which the god of the old dispensation removes himself so that the new one can begin. Japanese scholarship has long read the “hiding kami” as the mythic signature of cults that withdrew from the political centre: deities who lost the argument survived by retreating into oracles, mountains, and the sea, keeping a voice precisely by surrendering a throne. The theme recurs across the early chronicles — gods who conceal themselves and must be lured, cajoled, or divined back into relationship with the court. Kotoshironushi is the purest case: he is the patron of every defeated thing that refuses to die, and his entire myth is an exit that turned out to be a survival.

lore.culturalLegacy: Kotoshironushi is rarely worshipped under his own name today, but his legacy is everywhere in January: Ebisu, his smiling later form, presides over the first business of the year at shrines from Nishinomiya to Osaka’s Imamiya. The Tōka Ebisu festival draws millions of merchants and fishermen who buy lucky bamboo to invite prosperity into the new year. In the national myth, he is remembered as the son whose counsel spared the country a war of extermination — the voice of peaceful succession on which the imperial line’s legitimacy partly rests. And at Ōmiwa, before Mount Miwa, one of Japan’s oldest sanctuaries keeps the older stratum of his story: a god who hides, and speaks.
lore.archaeology: Ōmiwa Jinja in Sakurai, Nara prefecture — among the oldest shrine sites in Japan — faces Mount Miwa directly, the mountain itself revered as the shintai, the divine body of the god; no main hall stands between worshipper and peak. The site’s antiquity is supported by third-century Chinese chronicles, which attest the political prominence of the Yamato region’s great shrine cults, and by the dense concentration of kofun burial mounds in the Miwa area. At the other pole of his myth, Suwa in Nagano preserves the Takeminakata cult that the land-transfer story left behind. Nishinomiya Shrine’s Ebisu identification took its present form in the early modern period, but the shrine claims older precedent, and the Tōka Ebisu rite is documented from the Edo period onward.
lore.syncretism: Kotoshironushi is a nodal figure connecting the land-transfer myth, the oracle cults of Miwa, and the later Ebisu tradition. He represents the old order’s willing surrender and the sea’s continuing bounty, and his identification with Ebisu — ratified at Nishinomiya and celebrated across Japan at Tōka Ebisu — is one of the clearest cases of mythological condensation in Japanese folk religion. Within the Seven Gods of Fortune he keeps company with deities of Buddhist, Daoist, and Hindu origin, yet remains the only member with a purely native genealogy. Some scholars have further proposed identifying him with Ōmononushi, the serpent-kami of Miwa, which would bind the surrender myth directly to Japan’s oldest oracle shrine; the identification remains a hypothesis, but it shows how completely the hidden god was absorbed into the living cult.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OH-moh-noh-noo-shee' — even syllables, with soft final vowels.
pronunciation.note: Omononushi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is an ancient mountain deity associated with Miwa and the land-transfer myth.

domains.title: Great Thing Lord of Mount Miwa
domains.subtitle: Mountain, Oracle, and Sacred Snake
domains.lead: Ōmononushi is the mysterious kami of Mount Miwa, one of the oldest and most enigmatic deities in Japan. He is associated with snakes, oracles, and the transfer of the land to Amaterasu's descendants. Unlike most kami, he had no image and was worshipped in the form of the mountain itself.

cards.name: Mountain God
cards.desc: He is identified with Mount Miwa itself; Ōmiwa Shrine has no inner sanctuary because the peak is the kami's body.

cards.name: Snake Deity
cards.desc: He comes to Ikutamayori as a serpent in the Kojiki, and snake offerings of sake attend his Miwa cult.

cards.name: Oracle Kami
cards.desc: His consent to the land-transfer was given by oracle — sovereignty in Japan changes hands by consultation, not conquest.

cards.name: Land Transfer
cards.desc: He is the voice that yields the land to the heavenly descendants, binding the Miwa line to the imperial house.

symbols.name: Mount Miwa
symbols.meaning: The mountain itself, worshipped as the kami's body — his true shintai

symbols.name: Snake
symbols.meaning: The form in which Ōmononushi appears in the Ikutamayori legend — the sacred without a face

symbols.name: Sake
symbols.meaning: Offered to the serpent-kami; Ōmononushi is patron of the brewers of Miwa, honored with sugitama cedar balls

symbols.name: The Miwa-torii
symbols.meaning: The unique three-pillared torii through which worshippers face the peak directly — architecture that frames a god who is geology

mythology.lead: Ōmononushi's mythology is preserved in strange, archaic tales of snakes, possession, and oracles — the Kojiki's strangest marriage, the constitution of Japan's sovereignty, and a shrine with no god-house, because the mountain is the god.

myths.title: The Serpent Husband of Ikutamayori
myths.text:
A maiden named Ikutamayori was visited each night by a beautiful man who came unseen. When she bore his child, her parents demanded to know the father. She had him leave a needle threaded with red silk in the hem of his garment; in the morning she followed the thread, and it led to the foot of Mount Miwa and vanished into a cave — where the visitor declared himself: he was Ōmononushi, the great lord of the mountain, and he appeared in serpent form. The child of this union was Kotoshironushi, the god who would one day counsel the peaceful surrender of the land to the heavenly grandson (Kojiki; cf. Nihon Shoki, Aston's translation).

The tale binds three things into one knot — mountain, snake, and the Miwa priestly line, whose descent from the kami's human bride it exists to explain.

myths.title: The Oracle of the Land
myths.text:
When the heavenly emissary Takemikazuchi descended to demand the land from the earthly god Ōnamuji (Ōkuninushi), Ōnamuji consulted his children. Kotoshironushi, away at Cape Miwa, answered that resistance to the heavenly grandson was hopeless — and then all eyes turned to the mountain. Ōmononushi was consulted, and his oracle settled the matter: 'Let the land be given over in peace,' he declared; the land was yielded, and he withdrew into a hidden realm, promising that his favor would attend his proper worship. The Nihon Shoki tells the same event differently, folding the mountain god into Ōnamuji himself: Ōnamuji, it says, is also called Ōmononushi (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, tr. Aston, I).

Here the god is pure voice: sovereignty changes hands in Japan not by conquest but by consultation — and the mountain kami's consent is the constitution.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ōmiwa Shrine still stands where the myth says it must: at the foot of Mount Miwa, without a main hall, prayer aimed at the peak. The surrounding district remains sacred geography — Isonokami, one of Japan's oldest shrines, close by, and the great early kofun of Hashihaka on the horizon. Miwa sake is still brewed under the god's patronage, and brewers across Japan hang sugitama cedar balls in his honor. The mountain appears in Nara-period poetry, and the Miwa-torii's third pillar is studied wherever shrine architecture is taught. For modern Shinto, Ōmononushi is the standing proof that the kami need not be anthropomorphic: his 'image' is a modest ridge of green rock and cedar, and on clear mornings the faithful still bow toward it before entering the shrine.
lore.archaeology: The Engishiki shrine register (927 CE) already lists Ōmiwa among the great sanctuaries, and the site's archaeology is deep: excavations around Miwa have yielded ritual deposits and prestige objects — bronze mirrors, swords, and beads — from the Yayoi-to-Kofun transition, indicating a sanctuary of unusual antiquity at the mountain's foot, and the great keyhole tomb Hashihaka nearby marks the district as an early center of power. No honden has ever stood at Ōmiwa; worship runs toward the peak through the unique Miwa-torii, whose third central pillar frames the mountain as the true sanctuary. The 'artifact' of this god is thus geological and botanical at once — bedrock, cedar, and the spring-water sake that the shrine has brewed since the rite began.
lore.syncretism: Ōmononushi never left Shinto, but he was folded into it from two directions. The Nihon Shoki already identifies him with Ōkuninushi — the local Miwa kami gathered into the imperial land-myth — and medieval honji suijaku doctrine went further: Mount Miwa's deity, as Miwa Daimyōjin, was given the Buddhist original ground of Śākyamuni Buddha, and Miwa mandalas picture the mountain with Buddhist cosmography laid over it. Under the mountain, ascetics of the Shugendō tradition practiced until the modern period, treating the peak itself as the object of cult. The serpent, the sake, and the oracle — archaic, local, and oracular — are precisely the features a centralizing mythology needed to absorb rather than erase: Ōmononushi survives because he was useful, first to the court that took his oracle, then to the Buddhism that crowned him, then to the brewers who still hang cedar balls for him.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SOO-koo-nah-hee-koh-nah' — light, even syllables; the final vowels are soft.
pronunciation.note: Sukunahikona is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is a small but powerful kami who assisted Ōkuninushi in shaping the land.

domains.title: Renowned Little Prince
domains.subtitle: Healer, Sake-Maker, and Shaper of the Land
domains.lead: Sukunahikona is a tiny kami with enormous power. Floating to Japan in a boat of bark, he met Ōkuninushi and helped him pacify and cultivate the land. He taught the arts of healing and sake-making, and he became a protector against smallpox and illness. His small size makes him a deity of the overlooked and the underestimated.

cards.name: Tiny Helper
cards.desc: The Kojiki calls him a kami 'small in body'; in his bark boat he crossed the sea and became Ōnamuchi's indispensable companion.

cards.name: Healer
cards.desc: He taught the curing of disease, and later centuries invoked him against smallpox and epidemic.

cards.name: Sake God
cards.desc: He taught the brewing of sake, the offering that mediates between humans and kami.

cards.name: Land Shaper
cards.desc: With Ōnamuchi he pacified the land, set boundaries, and made the world fit for people.

symbols.name: Bark boat
symbols.meaning: The tiny muku-bark vessel in which he arrived from across the sea

symbols.name: Sake jar
symbols.meaning: His gift of brewing to humanity

symbols.name: Medicine
symbols.meaning: His role as a healer, especially against smallpox

symbols.name: Small stature
symbols.meaning: The sign that great power can come in small forms

mythology.lead: Sukunahikona's dossier is small but perfectly formed: the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720) tell how a kami no bigger than a child crossed the sea in a bark boat, partnered the great Ōkuninushi, taught medicine and sake, and sailed away to the Everlasting Land. The lesson the sources keep pressing: size and power are not the same thing.

myths.title: The Little Prince from Across the Sea
myths.text: The Kojiki ('Records of Ancient Matters', 712) tells how Ōnamuchi — the god later called Ōkuninushi, 'Great Renowned Lord' — stood on a beach in Izumo when a strange little boat came gliding over the sea. In it sat a kami small in body, and his boat was woven of muku bark. Ōnamuchi asked his name, and the small one answered: he was the son of Kamimusubi, one of the three creation deities, and his name was Sukunahikona, the Little Renowned Prince. Then came the exchange that defines the whole partnership: Ōnamuchi, who had struggled alone to make the wild land fit for people, asked, in effect, whether anyone would be his companion in that work — and Sukunahikona answered that this was why he had come. The meeting is the myth's thesis: the great lord had strength without knowledge, and the little prince had knowledge without strength; the land needed both. The Nihon Shoki ('Chronicles of Japan', 720) tells a parallel version with details of its own. (Kojiki, trans. Philippi, 1968; Nihon Shoki, trans. Aston, 1896.)

myths.title: Shaping the Land Together
myths.text: Together the two set about the work the Kojiki calls making and pacifying the land. Ōnamuchi brought the authority — he had survived Susanoo's trials by fire and serpent and the malice of his eighty brothers — and Sukunahikona brought knowledge: the two traveled the islands fixing boundaries, subduing hostile kami, and settling where rivers, rocks, and forests would belong to people. The Kojiki gives the partnership no single set-piece battle; its point is duration — the long, unglamorous labour of turning wilderness into a country. When the work was done, the land had shrines where none had been and fields where none had grown. Later ages read the pair as a charter for Japanese rule: sovereignty as collaboration between visible majesty and hidden craft, the great lord above and the little prince below — a division of labour the Kojiki quietly credits with everything that made Japan habitable.

lore.culturalLegacy: Sukunahikona's cult is still alive where his story ended in trade. Sukunahikona Jinja in the Horie district of Ōsaka — the old medicine wholesale quarter — is affectionately known as 'Sukunahiko-san' and draws prayers for health; its famous Fukumusume mascot dolls are ceremonially burned each New Year as scapegoat figures, carrying away illness with the flames. Sake brewers have claimed him as patron across Japan, and pharmaceutical companies invoke his name in branding. In modern retellings and games he recurs as the archetypal tiny-but-mighty spirit. The afterlife suits the myth: a deity who did his greatest work as a helper rather than a king is remembered in workshops, breweries, and pharmacies rather than on thrones.
lore.archaeology: No excavated sanctuary can be securely assigned to Sukunahikona; his presence is textual and cultic. The witnesses are the manuscripts: the Kojiki survives in the Shinpukuji manuscript of 1371–72 and later copies, the Nihon Shoki in twelfth-century and later codices — the oldest stratum of Japanese prose. On the ground, Sukunahikona Jinja in Ōsaka's Horie district preserves his living cult amid the warehouses of the old medicine market, a rare case of a shrine and the trade it protects growing up together. Offerings of model sake barrels at brewing shrines across Japan extend the evidence from paper to practice.
lore.syncretism: Sukunahikona sits at several crossroads of Japanese religious history. In local tradition he has often been paired or identified with Ebisu, the laughing god of fishermen and fortune, since both arrive from across the sea and stand cheerfully outside the pantheon's hierarchy; shrines in the Kansai region have conflated the two. Medieval honji-suijaku interpreters, mapping kami onto buddhas, naturally aligned a healing deity with Yakushi, the Medicine Buddha — an association his later epidemiological cult made almost inevitable. Comparativists note the type: the tiny helper who equips the hero is as old as the Kojiki and as wide as Eurasia. But his specific portfolio — medicine, sake, and the conversion of a raw land into an inhabited one — is distinctively Japanese, and his partnership with Ōkuninushi anchors him permanently in the Izumo cycle.

pronunciation.approximation: 'TAH-jee-kah-rah-oh' — the 'j' is soft, and the 'r' is a light tap.
pronunciation.note: Tajikarao is Tier 2: Hepburn romanization preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter, so nothing distinctive is lost against the ASCII form. Within the myth he is pure function — the strong hand that acts once cunning has done its work — and his name says exactly what he does.

domains.title: Strong-Handed Man
domains.subtitle: Strength, Caves, and the Restoration of Light
domains.lead: Tajikarao (Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-kami) is the kami of raw physical strength in the Japanese pantheon, remembered for a single decisive act: when the sun goddess Amaterasu withdrew into the Ama-no-Iwato rock-cave and plunged the world into darkness, it was Tajikarao who seized her hand and pulled the light back out. His name means 'Strong-Handed Man', and his cult gathers at Togakushi — 'the hidden door' — where tradition says the cave's rock-door landed.

cards.name: Cave Opener
cards.desc: He seized Amaterasu's wrist and hauled her from the Ama-no-Iwato cave as she leaned out (Kojiki).

cards.name: God of Strength
cards.desc: The personification of chikara, 'strength' — the second graph (力) of his own name.

cards.name: Cave Deity
cards.desc: Patron of caves, thresholds, and the breaking of seals; honored in the mountains of Togakushi in Shinano.

cards.name: Restorer of Order
cards.desc: His one act ended the cosmic darkness and returned the sun to the Plain of High Heaven.

symbols.name: Strong hands
symbols.meaning: The attribute his name encodes and the instrument of every deed attributed to him

symbols.name: The rock-door
symbols.meaning: The stone slab he tore from the cave mouth; tradition places its landing at Togakushi, 'the hidden door'

symbols.name: Sunlight
symbols.meaning: What returned to the world the instant his grip closed on the sun goddess's wrist

symbols.name: Mountains
symbols.meaning: The cave-country of the kami, where strength and silence meet

mythology.lead: Tajikarao's mythology is a single great scene — the Ama-no-Iwato, the Heavenly Rock-Cave — yet it is among the most retold scenes in Japanese religion. When Amaterasu hid herself and night swallowed the world, the eight hundred myriad kami tried persuasion, dance, and mirrors; only when the strong-handed kami acted did the sun return. His entire dossier is those few seconds at the cave mouth (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki).

myths.title: The Sun Withdraws into the Rock
myths.text: The crisis begins with Susanoo's rampage. The storm god, granted leave from heaven, trampled down the ridges of Amaterasu's rice-paddies, filled in her irrigation ditches, and finally flayed the heavenly piebald colt and hurled its carcass through the roof of the sacred weaving-hall, so that a weaving-maiden, struck by the flying shuttle, died at her loom (Kojiki). Amaterasu, in grief and fear, 'went into the Rock-Cave of Heaven and fastened its Rock-Door'. At once the Plain of High Heaven went dark and the Central Land of Reed-Plains — Japan itself — fell into long night; the eight hundred myriad kami wailed, and calamitous deities swarmed like summer flies. The myth's architecture is precise: the sun's absence is not night but negation — nothing in the world works until the goddess is brought back out.

myths.title: The Laughter at the Cave Door
myths.text: The assembled kami answered with misdirection. The goddess Ame-no-Uzume bound up her sleeves with a heavenly vine, took a bundle of sasaki grass for a headdress, overturned a tub before the cave, and stamped out a lewd, rattling dance upon it, baring herself to the roaring laughter of the whole assembly. Amaterasu, hearing the uproar, wondered how the gods could make merry while the world lay dark. When she cracked the Rock-Door to ask, Ame-no-Uzume answered that a goddess greater than she had come — and the kami had already hung the polished mirror Yata-no-Kagami and the curved jewel on the branches of a sakaki tree beside the door, while Ame-no-Koyane intoned the first ritual words. The mirror did the persuading; the dance bought it a crack of light. Cunning opens the door a finger's width — no more.

lore.culturalLegacy: Tajikarao's living monument is Togakushi. The shrine complex above Nagano, approached by an avenue of centuries-old cedars, draws pilgrims and hikers to the Oku-sha and worshippers seeking strength and favorable outcomes to its Middle Shrine; the mountains acquired a second, separate fame in the medieval period as the legendary home of the Togakure-ryū ninja tradition — the 'hidden door' serving concealment as well as revelation. Beyond the shrine, he survives wherever the cave myth is told: in classical kagura repertoires, in school textbooks, and in a steady stream of anime, manga, and games that borrow the Ama-no-Iwato scene and, with it, the strong hand that ends it. Athletes and competitors occasionally invoke him as a kami of chikara, raw power. His name remains what it was in the Kojiki: a byword for the moment deliberation ends and someone finally pulls.
lore.archaeology: No excavated site attests Tajikarao himself from the Kofun period or earlier; his evidence is cultic and textual. The clearest material anchor is Amanoiwato-jinja above the Takachiho Gorge in Miyazaki Prefecture, where the cave of the myth is identified and a worship-hall faces the cliff across the gorge. His principal shrine, the Middle Shrine (Chū-sha) of Togakushi in Nagano, stands within a complex whose documented history runs from the mid-ninth century, when the Tendai temple Togakushi-san was founded on the mountain; the present shrine buildings are early modern, and the famous cryptomeria avenue to the Oku-sha was planted in the medieval period. Kagura masks and votive tablets depicting the cave scene, from the early modern period onward, are held in shrine collections across western Japan.
lore.syncretism: Tajikarao resists syncretism precisely because his role is so pure: he is the strong arm inside a theology of coordinated function. In the Ama-no-Iwato assembly every kami performs one office — Uzume the dance, Futotama the rope, Koyane the words, Tajikarao the hand — a picture of the kami as functionaries in a cosmic administration that Shinto reflection has read ever since as a model of communal harmony (wa). Buddhism, which absorbed so many kami as guardians and avatars, found little to work with in a god of one deed; he has no avatar and no second career. The cave scene, however, travelled without him: it is re-enacted in kagura across the country, painted on shrine votive panels, and taught to every Japanese schoolchild, so that his five seconds of action are among the most-watched moments in the national mythology. Comparativists set the disappearing-sun motif beside eclipse and solstice myths worldwide; the Japanese version is distinctive in that the sun hides from wounded pride, not from a cosmic enemy, and is recovered by theatre plus muscle.

pronunciation.approximation: 'TOH-yoh-tah-mah' — four even syllables, with the second beginning with a soft 'y'.
pronunciation.note: Toyotama is Tier 2: plain Hepburn romanisation, preserving no diacritic or distinctive letter. She is the sea princess and mother of the imperial ancestor Ugayafukiaezu.

domains.title: Abundant Jewel Princess
domains.subtitle: Sea, Transformation, and the Mother of Emperors
domains.lead: Toyotama is the daughter of the sea god Ryūjin and the wife of Hoori. Her name, 'Abundant Jewel,' evokes the treasures of the undersea palace. She is the mother of Ugayafukiaezu, making her an ancestor of Emperor Jimmu and a bridge between the ocean depths and the imperial line.

cards.name: Sea Princess
cards.desc: Daughter of Ryūjin and jewel of the undersea palace.

cards.name: Wife of Hoori
cards.desc: She married the descendant of Ninigi and bore his son.

cards.name: Mother of Ugayafukiaezu
cards.desc: Her son continued the line to Emperor Jimmu.

cards.name: Shape-Shifter
cards.desc: Her true form was the sea-dragon she hid from Hoori's eyes.

symbols.name: Jewel
symbols.meaning: The abundance and treasure of the sea, enshrined in her name

symbols.name: Sea palace (Ryūgū)
symbols.meaning: The undersea realm where she was born and to which she returned

symbols.name: The wani (sea-dragon)
symbols.meaning: Her true form, seen by Hoori when he broke his promise

symbols.name: Cormorant-feather thatch
symbols.meaning: The birth-hut she sealed with cormorant feathers — the garment between forms

mythology.lead: Toyotama's cycle, told in the Kojiki's Hoori narrative, is the story of a sea princess who marries into the land — and of the promise whose breaking closes the road between the realms forever. She is at once bride, mother, and exile: the ocean's gift to the imperial genealogy, and its loss.

myths.title: The Bride of the Sea Palace
myths.text: Hoori — Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto, the hunter prince — came to the seashore weeping over a lost fishhook and a broken brotherhood. Guided by the old man of the sea, Shihotsuchi, he descended to the palace of Watatsumi, the dragon god of the depths. The palace walls were fish-scaled, its lanes alive with every creature of the sea, and the god received the prince with ceremony, presenting him to his daughter Toyotama-hime: 'I give you this maiden; dwell in our midst as long as heaven endures.' For three years Hoori lived in the sea palace, and there he recovered the hook, mastered his elder brother Hoderi, and won his bride (Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto; trans. Philippi). The marriage is the myth's hinge: the land's prince, powerless on land, is made whole by the sea's alliance — an oceanic bride as the seal between the hunting shore and the deep.

myths.title: The Vow at the Birth-Hut
myths.text: When Toyotama was with child, she told Hoori: 'In our country, when our kind give birth, we do so in our true form; do not look.' She built a parturition hut, sealed its entry, and withdrew. But longing overcame the prince: he stole to the hut and peered inside, and there he saw no woman but a great eight-fathom sea-dragon — a wani, sea-serpent or crocodile — coiling about the child. Ashamed to be seen in her true shape, Toyotama abandoned the newborn, left the hut, and returned to her father's palace; and the road between the sea and the land, she declared, was closed, because he had broken his promise (Kojiki). The sources preserve the detail without comment, and its force needs none: in the economy of this myth the gaze is the one theft the sea cannot forgive. What Hoori took by looking, the lineage paid for in a mother lost.

lore.culturalLegacy: Toyotama's legacy is dynastic before it is cultic: every emperor of Japan descends from her through Jimmu, so her name is woven into the state's founding genealogy. Her landscape is the Hyūga coast of Miyazaki — Aoshima, reached at low tide by its own sandbar, keeps the legend of the birth-hut, and Cape Kasasa and the Horikiri pass are pointed out as the myth's stations. The Ryūgū-palace motif she inhabits saturates Japanese art and story, from Noh and fairytales to modern film and anime, and 'Toyo-tama' was adopted by one of the twentieth century's great industrial houses — a modern reuse of the 'abundant jewel'. Her story endures because it is the founding genealogy's most human page: a marriage across worlds, a broken trust, a child raised between shore and sea.
lore.archaeology: Toyotama has no excavated sanctuary and no inscription names her; her witnesses are books. The Kojiki was compiled in 712 and the Nihon Shoki in 720, and the Kojiki's oldest complete manuscript, the Shinpukuji-bon of 1371–72, still transmits the Hoori narrative. The myth's geography, however, is walked rather than read: the Miyazaki coast — Aoshima's tide-washed island shrine, the Cape Kasasa lookout, the Horikiri pass — preserves the story as local topography. Inland, at Kashihara in Nara prefecture, Kashihara Jingū marks the site of Jimmu's palace and throne, the terrestrial terminus of the sea-borne genealogy she began. Her material record, in short, is the map of Japan's founding geography.
lore.syncretism: Toyotama belongs to one of the oldest families of tales in East Asia: the supernatural bride whose true form must not be seen — the Japanese cousin of the Chinese dragon-palace romances and of the hagoromo 'feather-robe' cycle, in which a wife recovers her stolen robe and leaves her human family. Buddhist Japan read her father's palace through the nāga lens: the fish-scaled halls of the deep are the sea-serpents' treasure house, and Ryūjin's daughter moves between the two cosmologies without friction. In the medieval Shinto-Buddhist synthesis she is simply a kami of rank, fixed in the imperial genealogy she founded. Modern Japan keeps her as the archetype of the bride from the sea — beautiful, powerful, and gone — and the Ryūgū palace she left behind remains the nation's favourite undersea legend, retold in Noh, in the otogi-zōshi fairytales, and on screen.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OO-gah-yah-foo-kee-ah-eh-zoo' — many light syllables; the 'f' is soft, made with both lips.
pronunciation.note: Ugayafukiaezu is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. His strange name refers to a birth hut thatched with cormorant feathers and left unfinished. He is the immediate father of Emperor Jimmu.

domains.title: Cormorant Thatching Unfinished
domains.subtitle: Father of Jimmu and Link Between Sea and Land
domains.lead: Ugayafukiaezu is one of the most strangely named figures in Japanese myth. His name describes the unfinished thatched hut, covered with cormorant feathers, in which he was born. As the son of Hoori and the sea princess Toyotama, and the father of Emperor Jimmu, he is the final link between the ocean depths and the imperial line.

cards.name: Father of Jimmu
cards.desc: His fourth son, Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko, won the succession and founded the Yamato line as Emperor Jimmu (Kojiki I).

cards.name: Sea-Land Bridge
cards.desc: Son of Hoori the land-hunter and Toyotama-bime, daughter of the sea god Watatsumi — the marriage that joined coast and deep.

cards.name: Unfinished Birth Hut
cards.desc: His name glosses the cormorant-feather thatch of the Kojiki's birth hut — and the roof never finished (鵜草葺不合).

cards.name: Imperial Ancestor
cards.desc: The last link of the divine genealogy: through him the regalia line descends to the historic emperors (Nihon Shoki, books 1–3).

symbols.name: Cormorant feathers
symbols.meaning: The black plumage of the diving bird that the Kojiki makes the roof of his birth hut (ugaya)

symbols.name: Thatching
symbols.meaning: fukiaezu — 'not yet completed': the unfinished roof read directly as his name

symbols.name: Sea and land
symbols.meaning: His double heritage: the tide-jewel deep of Watatsumi's house and the hills of his father Hoori

symbols.name: Bow and fishhook
symbols.meaning: The paternal gear of Hoori's line — the hunter's bow against the sea's hooked line

mythology.lead: Ugayafukiaezu's mythology is the final chapter of the Hoori–Toyotama cycle and the prologue to the reign of Jimmu: one night on a seashore, one unfinished roof, one farewell poem, and a lineage that steps out of the hut into history.

myths.title: The Cormorant-Feather Hut
myths.text: The Kojiki (age of gods) tells how the sea princess Toyotama-bime, daughter of Watatsumi the sea god, came up from the deep to bear the child of the land-hunter Hoori. On the seashore she built a hut and thatched its roof with cormorant feathers, and as her hour came she warned her husband: do not look inside. Hoori waited, but when the cry came he could not hold back; he peered through the wall and saw his wife transformed into a great sea-creature — the Kojiki says an eight-fathom shark — coiled in labor. Toyotama knew herself shamed. She left the newborn where he lay, in the hut whose cormorant thatch had never been finished, and the compilers give the child his name from the shelter itself: Ugayafukiaezu, 'Cormorant-Thatching-Unfinished'. The scene survives because a roof was never completed: a goddess of the sea delivering on land, and a lineage beginning in the gap between the elements.

myths.title: The Farewell Song
myths.text: Before she returned to the sea, Toyotama spoke the poem the Kojiki preserves as one of its most celebrated archaic songs: had you not shamed me, I would have come and gone by the sea-road, and for ever eased the way of the ships; but now that you have looked, the crossing will be hard — the precise wording varies in translation, but Philippi's rendering keeps its reproach intact. She left the child in the care of her younger sister Tamayori — 'Good Jewel' — who came up out of the water to suckle him. In a text crowded with genealogies, the poem is the rare moment the myth turns elegy: a mother who could have made the sea a road for her son instead leaves him a song — and the imperial line inherits, with its treasures, a story about the price of looking.

lore.culturalLegacy: His legacy runs through the one institution he made possible. As Jimmu's father, Ugayafukiaezu stands in the imperial genealogy, and Japan's National Foundation Day (11 February) marks the legendary accession of the son born in the unfinished hut. The birth-hut custom behind his name outlived the myth in practice: ethnographers recorded ubuya seclusion into the modern period, especially in the Izu Islands and the northeast. In scholarship his name is a permanent puzzle — every handbook of Japanese myth pauses over the cormorant feathers — and in popular culture the Jimmu cycle, Yatagarasu and all, returns in anime, manga, and school texts as the nation's prologue. The strange name does the work: a lineage that begins under an unfinished roof can never be accused of having begun too comfortably.
lore.archaeology: Ugayafukiaezu has no independent material cult; the evidence is textual and funerary. The Kojiki survives through the Shinpukuji manuscript line (supplemented by the 1371–72 date-bearing copies), and the Nihon Shoki through Heian-period manuscript traditions. The imperial mausoleum his line supposedly founded is real as a site: at Kashihara in Nara prefecture the Imperial Household Agency tends Unebi-yama no ushitora no sumi no misasagi, the kofun-style tomb attributed to Jimmu, the son whose birth the hut story explains — a large early-period enclosure, undisturbed by archaeology and unprovenanced to any historical person. Birth huts (ubuya) themselves, the custom behind the myth, persisted in parts of Japan into the twentieth century and were documented by ethnographers — the closest the earth comes to the cormorant-thatched roof.
lore.syncretism: Ugayafukiaezu has no cult and no shrine — his whole existence is genealogical, and his meaning is that of the custom his name preserves. Japanese ethnographers documented birth huts, ubuya, in which mothers delivered and secluded themselves, persisting in parts of the country into the twentieth century; the Kojiki's cormorant-feather hut is read against this custom as its mythic charter. Medieval Buddhist exegetes folded the age-of-gods narratives into the honji suijaku framework, treating the kami's doings as local manifestations of cosmic Buddha-activity, while Edo-period nativists of the Kokugaku school — Motoori Norinaga above all — pored over the strange compounds of the divine genealogy as evidence of an authentically Japanese antiquity. Each tradition found in the unfinished roof what it needed: ritualists a birth custom, monks a parable of manifestation, nativists a pure native word.
lore.originalScriptNote: The age-of-gods names are written in kanji that gloss rather than transcribe. The full ceremonial form is 鵜草葺不合命 (Ugayafukiaezu-no-mikoto), with the honorific 命 (mikoto): 鵜 “cormorant,” 草 “grass, reed,” 葺 “to thatch,” 不合 “not joined, unfinished.” The characters record the Kojiki's own explanation of the name, not a phonetic spelling; medieval manuscripts abbreviate the compound variously, and its reading has been debated since the earliest commentaries.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HOH-deh-ree' — the 'r' is a light tap, and all vowels are short and clear.
pronunciation.note: Hoderi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is a minor but structurally important figure in the imperial genealogy.

domains.title: Fire-Shining Prince of the Sea
domains.subtitle: Fisherman, Elder Brother, and Tragic Heir
domains.lead: Hoderi is the elder son of the heavenly grandson Ninigi and the blossom princess Konohana-Sakuya-hime. His name means 'Fire-Shining,' and he was gifted with the fishhook that made him master of the sea. His story turns on the rivalry with his younger brother Hoori, a conflict that costs him his birthright and sets the imperial line on a new path.

cards.name: Master of the Sea
cards.desc: He received the fishhook and was meant to rule the waters.

cards.name: Elder Brother
cards.desc: Firstborn of Ninigi, but destined to lose precedence to Hoori.

cards.name: Tragic Competitor
cards.desc: His attempts to best Hoori end in the loss of his hook and his inheritance.

cards.name: Ancestral Figure
cards.desc: Ancestor of the Hayato, a people of southern Kyūshū.

symbols.name: Fishhook
symbols.meaning: The gift from Ninigi that gave him dominion over the sea

symbols.name: Fire
symbols.meaning: His name associates him with shining heat and the brilliance of the sun

symbols.name: Sea
symbols.meaning: The realm he was to master, contrasted with Hoori's mountains and fields

symbols.name: Bow
symbols.meaning: The weapon by which he and Hoori disputed precedence

mythology.lead: Hoderi's story in the Kojiki is a tale of sibling rivalry, the exchange of gifts, and the transfer of sovereignty from the sea to the land. He is the elder son, the firstborn of Ninigi, destined to be bypassed — and Japan's two oldest histories tell his falling-short with different temperaments, and the difference is itself instructive.

myths.title: The Exchange of Gifts
myths.text: When Ninigi's sons grew up, he divided the world's livelihood between them: to Hoderi, the elder, he gave the fishhook that rules the sea; to Hoori, the younger, the bow and arrow that rule the mountains (Kojiki, age of the gods). Hoori proposed that they exchange — he would try the sea, Hoderi the chase — and Hoderi agreed. But the sea resisted the stranger: Hoori fished for days and caught nothing, and in a fury he flung the precious hook into the waves. Hoderi's response was absolute: he would sooner lose a kingdom than his hook, and he demanded its return on pain of their brotherhood itself. Cornered, Hoori walked into the sea to answer for the loss. The exchange looks innocent but is the hinge of the whole cycle: a fisherman's tool, lost and owed, becomes the lever that moves sovereignty from elder to younger, from sea to land.

myths.title: Hoori's Triumph
myths.text: Beneath the waves Hoori found not punishment but fortune: the palace of the sea god Watatsumi, and marriage to the god's daughter Toyotama-hime. From the sea's depths he sent the lost hook back to land — recovered, in the Kojiki's wry detail, from the throat of a sea bream — bearing a curse that turned against its owner: whatever it touched would fail and wither. Struck by the curse, Hoderi saw his stores dwindle and his luck collapse, until he came barefoot to his younger brother, begging terms. Hoori took the submission and the precedence; Hoderi gave him his daughter and his allegiance, and the elder line bent to the younger. The myth's meaning is economical and severe: legitimacy in the age of the gods does not follow birth order but the flow of fortune, and the sea, for all its plenty, could not hold the future that was gathering on the land.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hoderi is little known outside scholarly and ritual contexts, but his story underlies one of the key narratives of Japanese origins: the transfer of legitimacy from sea to land, from elder to younger, and the inclusion of older peoples within the imperial frame. His name survives in Kojiki retellings, in schoolbook summaries of the age of the gods, and in the quiet pride of communities in southern Kyūshū whose traditions remember the Hayato. For modern readers he is the necessary counterweight to the imperial success story — the elder brother whose loss makes the victory legible, and whose descendants' service reminds us that Japanese identity was assembled, not simply inherited.
lore.archaeology: Hoderi has no independent archaeological attestation — no shrine, image, or inscription names him — and his importance is textual and genealogical, preserved in the Kojiki's account of the imperial lineage and in the Nihon Shoki's parallel version. The historical echo of his myth is the documentary record of the Hayato themselves: the early chronicles (Shoku Nihongi and its predecessors) register Hayato delegations, military service, and ritual office at court from the eighth century, and southern Kyūshū place names and burial remains attest the ancient populations the genealogy claims as his children. The 'evidence' for Hoderi is thus a people remembered, not a stone inscribed.
lore.syncretism: Hoderi is primarily a genealogical figure, and his afterlife is interpretive. Shinto scholarship has long read him as the mythic signature of the sea peoples and older lineages of southern Japan folded into the Yamato order — his 'Fire-Shining' name suggests a solar brilliance eclipsed by the mountain brother's steady fire. The myth's structure invites comparison with other younger-son-victories in the imperial line (Ninigi himself was passed over for rule of heaven in favor of the narrative's landward mission), making Hoderi one link in a chain where sovereignty repeatedly detours around seniority. Buddhist and Confucian readers of later centuries found in him a lesson in the submission of fortune to virtue; modern folklorists find an ethnographic memory. He absorbed no foreign cult — the traffic ran the other way, his story naturalizing an absorbed people.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HOH-ree' — hold the first syllable long; the 'r' is a light tap.
pronunciation.note: Hoori is Tier 2 in this restoration: the long ō is not represented, so the ASCII form is identical to Hepburn. He is a pivotal ancestor in the imperial genealogy.

domains.title: Fire-Subduing Prince and Imperial Ancestor
domains.subtitle: Hunter, Sea-Voyager, and Founder of the Royal Line
domains.lead: Hoori is the younger son of Ninigi and Konohana-Sakuya-hime, the husband of the sea princess Toyotama, and the great-grandfather of Japan's first emperor, Jimmu. His name, 'Fire-Subduing,' marks him as the brother who overcame Hoderi's fire and whose line would rule the land.

cards.name: Master of the Mountains
cards.desc: He received the bow and became a hunter of the highlands.

cards.name: Husband of Toyotama
