Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: Say 'amoghasiddhi' with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration 'Amoghasiddhi'.
pronunciation.note: The ASCII form 'amoghasiddhi' is a DNS compromise; the restoration 'Amoghasiddhi' preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

domains.title: Amoghasiddhi
domains.subtitle: Infallible Success
domains.lead: Amoghasiddhi — 'Unfailing Accomplishment' — is the fifth of the Five Meditation Buddhas (Dhyānibuddhas), lord of the karma family and sovereign of the mandala's northern quarter. Where his companions preside over insight, anger, pride, and desire, he presides over action itself: the wisdom that completes what is begun. His raised palm answers fear; his green body, the color of ripening, promises that no honest effort is wasted.

cards.name: The Karma Family
cards.desc: Lord of the karma family and bearer of all-accomplishing wisdom — the knowledge that finishes what is begun.

cards.name: The North and the Green
cards.desc: He occupies the northern quarter of the mandala, body the color of dusk-lit emerald, his element the wind that carries the deed.

cards.name: The Gesture of Fearlessness
cards.desc: His right hand raised in abhaya mudrā — the open palm that answers fear with the promise that no effort is wasted.

cards.name: Envy Transmuted
cards.desc: The affliction of envy — frozen, comparative, sterile — becomes under his gaze the energy of benevolent action for others.

symbols.name: The double vajra (viśvavajra)
symbols.meaning: The crossed thunderbolt stamped on his throne base — unshakeable means, doubled for the four directions, the karma family's seal.

symbols.name: The abhaya mudrā
symbols.meaning: The raised right hand, palm outward: fearlessness offered as a teaching, not brandished as a triumph.

symbols.name: The garuḍa throne-bearers
symbols.meaning: The sovereign birds that carry his seat in the iconographic manuals — emblems of power subdued and enlisted.

symbols.name: Green
symbols.meaning: His body-color in the five-Buddha system: the hue of ripening action, of autumn and of deeds coming to fruit.

symbols.name: The wind (vāyu)
symbols.meaning: His element — movement and transmission, the deed carried outward to its object; he is the least static of the five.

symbols.name: Samayatārā and Viśvapāṇi
symbols.meaning: His consort, the Green Tārā, and his bodhisattva Viśvapāṇi, 'he whose hand is everywhere' — pledge and method made persons.

mythology.lead: Amoghasiddhi has no biographical myths — he was never born, never walked the earth, never died. He belongs to the tantric synthesis of the early medieval period, when Mahāyāna Buddhism organized its meditation Buddhas into a mandala of five. His stories are the ritual and iconographic programs that grew around his name from the eighth century on, above all in the Sarva-tathāgata-tattva-saṅgraha, the root tantra of the system.

myths.title: The Fifth from the One
myths.text: The Sarva-tathāgata-tattva-saṅgraha — 'The Compendium of the Reality of All the Thus-Gones' — is the great tantra of the late eighth century from which the five-Buddha system descends. It organizes the Buddhas as a mandala: Vairocana at the center, and four Jinas in the quarters — Akṣobhya east, Ratnasambhava south, Amitābha west, Amoghasiddhi north. Each rules a family (kula) and transmutes a poison into its mirror-virtue: anger becomes mirror-like wisdom, pride becomes equality, desire becomes discernment, and, for Amoghasiddhi, envy becomes all-accomplishing wisdom (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna). Note what his name does that the others' do not: while Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Amitābha are described by what they are — unshakable, jewel-born, infinite light — Amoghasiddhi is described by what he does. The name is the system's only promise: it does not fail.

myths.title: The Subduing of Maheśvara
myths.text: The tantra stages its founding drama in the karma family's own theater. The worldly gods, led by Maheśvara — Śiva enthroned on Mount Meru with his consort and his host — defy the Buddha's law and oppress the beings under their rule. Vajrapāṇi, first among the karma-family beings, descends to the summit, binds Maheśvara with his noose, and tramples him underfoot; and where a lesser story would end in destruction, this one ends in conscription — the conquered god accepts initiation and becomes a guardian of the very mandala that broke him (STTS; Snellgrove, Indo-Tibetan Buddhism, reads the episode as the tantric appropriation of Śiva). It is a theological conquest, not a defeat: the powers of the older religion are neither destroyed nor tolerated but converted into doorkeepers. The karma family's first recorded action is the transformation of an enemy into a function.

lore.culturalLegacy: Amoghasiddhi's legacy is liturgical rather than narrative, and vast in that register. He presides over the top registers of countless Nepalese paubha paintings and Tibetan thangkas, where his image is among the most standardized in Himalayan art — green, right hand raised, seated on a throne borne by garuḍas. In Japan the esoteric schools chant his mantra within the Kongōkai mandala rites performed at Tō-ji and Kōya-san since the ninth century, and Fukūjōju remains a familiar presence in temple statuary from Nara to Kamakura. His doctrine survives as a compact psychology: envy — the conviction that others accomplish while I do not — is transmuted into all-accomplishing action, because karma performed for others cannot fail. In contemporary dharma centers his name is invoked less often than Tārā's, but it answers a question hers does not: whether the effort itself is worth anything. His name is the vow that it is.
lore.archaeology: There are no ancient temples of Amoghasiddhi, no inscriptions naming him, no early coins: he appears first in manuscript and image. Palm-leaf copies of the Sarva-tathāgata-tattva-saṅgraha survive among the Newar Buddhist manuscripts of the Kathmandu Valley, and his figure becomes canonical in paubha painting from the twelfth century and in Tibetan thangkas from the thirteenth, where the five Buddhas crown the registers of monastery murals across the Himalaya. In East Asia the ninth-century Tō-ji mandala scrolls preserve him as Fukūjōju in the Kongōkai, among the oldest monumental images of the system. His material record is therefore neither a site nor a relic but a genre — the painted mandala, portable and reproducible, in which the north never lacks its green Buddha.
lore.syncretism: Amoghasiddhi's closest relative is Śiva, in a relationship of deliberate supersession: the root tantra has Vajrapāṇi of the karma family subdue Maheśvara on Mount Meru and trample him into the mandala as its guardian — conquest written as conversion. In East Asia the five-Buddha mandala traveled with esoteric Buddhism: in the Shingon school of Japan, Amoghasiddhi appears as Fukūjōju Nyorai, the 'Tathāgata of Infallible Success', enthroned in the north of the Diamond-Realm mandala preserved in the ninth-century scrolls of Tō-ji. His consort Samayatārā is simply the Green Tārā absorbed into the five-Buddha family scheme, so that the most beloved goddess of Tibetan devotion is also, doctrinally, his wisdom made feminine. Modern Western reception has been quieter than for his companions: he is known chiefly through museum galleries and meditation literature, where his name circulates as a compact promise — that accomplishment pursued without vanity does not fail.

entries.meaning: 'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will return as the future Buddha

steps: Sanskrit Maitreya is written in Devanagari as मैत्रेय
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: 'MIGH-tray-yuh' — stress forward on the diphthong; the name is built on maitrī, 'loving-kindness,' so it should sound warm, not martial.
pronunciation.note: Tier 2: 'Maitreya' is the ASCII-canonical form, with no diacritic-bearing feature lost in plain spelling — the name's restoration lies in its meaning (maitrī, loving-kindness) rather than its letters. Pāli Metteyya preserves the same sounds.

domains.title: Maitreya
domains.subtitle: The Benevolent One — Bodhisattva of the Age to Come
domains.lead: Maitreya is the Buddha of the future — now a bodhisattva enthroned in Tuṣita heaven, waiting for the Dharma's decline to run its course. His name is his program: maitrī, loving-kindness, the first of the four immeasurables — a promise that the wheel, having turned down, will turn up again.

cards.name: The Future Buddha
cards.desc: The prophecy of DN 26: after the Dharma's long decline and renewal, Metteyya will awaken when lifespans reach eighty thousand years.

cards.name: Maitrī, Loving-Kindness
cards.desc: The name made doctrine — the first of the four brahmavihāras, boundless friendliness toward all beings.

cards.name: Tuṣita Heaven
cards.desc: The realm of delight where he waits — and where Śākyamuni waited before his own final birth.

cards.name: The Descent at Ketumatī
cards.desc: The Maitreyavyākaraṇa names his future city, his royal patron Saṅkha, and the tree under which he will wake.

symbols.name: The stūpa in the crown
symbols.meaning: Gandhāran iconography crowns him with a small stūpa — Śākyamuni's relic-shrine marking Maitreya as the appointed successor

symbols.name: The water flask (kamaṇḍalu)
symbols.meaning: The āmra-ghataka of the princely ascetic — the elixir of the future age, medicine for a world whose Dharma has faded

symbols.name: The wheel of Dharma
symbols.meaning: Set beneath his feet on Kushan reliefs — the teaching he will turn again, three assemblies strong

symbols.name: The nāga-puṣpikā tree
symbols.meaning: The tree under which he will awaken in one night at Ketumatī — the future's Bodhi tree, named in the prophecy

symbols.name: The cloth sack (Budai)
symbols.meaning: His Chinese transformation: the laughing monk with his sack of sweets, the future Buddha as abundance and belly-laugh

mythology.lead: Maitreya's mythology is unique in the Buddhist world: it is scheduled but unfulfilled — prophecy rather than biography. The canon names him, the Mahāyāna sūtras detail his future career, and Asia's art made him the most visible future the ancient world ever gave a face.

myths.title: Metteyya at the End of the Decline
myths.text: The oldest prophecy of the future Buddha stands in the Cakkavattisihanāda Sutta (DN 26): after the wheel-turning king Daḷhanemi, greed returns, human life shrinks to ten years — and then, slowly, morality climbs back until people live eighty thousand years. In that age a Buddha named Metteyya will arise, fully awakened, attended by thousands, holding three great assemblies beneath a pavilion — and the wheel will turn a fourth time in this eon. Later Pāli texts place him now in Tuṣita heaven, where Śākyamuni himself waited before his final birth. The myth is the Buddhist answer to a hard fact — every Buddha's teaching decays — and its answer is not despair but schedule: the wheel turns down and up again, and the next teacher is already named, already enthroned, already waiting.

myths.title: The Descent at Ketumatī
myths.text: The Sanskrit tradition gives the future a city and a plot. The Maitreyavyākaraṇa — transmitted within the Divyāvadāna and translated repeatedly into Chinese and Tibetan — describes Maitreya's birth in splendid Ketumatī, when the wheel-turning king Saṅkha rules, lifespans run to eighty thousand years, and the Dharma has been forgotten. Born to the brahmin Subrahma, he will leave his palace by the four gates, meet an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a renunciant — the very sights that unseated Śākyamuni — and awaken beneath a nāga-puṣpikā tree in a single night. The sūtra's sharpest promise is addressed to its hearers: those who receive this prophecy will meet Maitreya face to face. The myth makes eschatology personal — salvation not as catastrophe but as a scheduled appointment with a named teacher, and a ticket any listener can hold.

lore.culturalLegacy: No Buddhist figure is more painted. The colossal Maitreya niches of Bamiyan — one of the two great Buddhas was identified with him — dominated the Silk Road until their destruction in 2001; the third phase of Borobudur and the cave temples of Bingling and Maijishan climb toward his heaven. The Anāgatavaṃsa kept his cult alive in Sri Lanka, and Burmese and Thai Buddhism still recite the prophecy of his coming. In East Asia, Budai-Maitreya smiles from restaurant windows and temple gates, and the word for his sack of plenty entered the language of New Year greetings. The laughing form is the deeper truth of the name: a future guaranteed not by wrath but by friendliness — maitrī itself, scheduled to arrive.
lore.archaeology: Maitreya is among the earliest bodhisattvas imaged in stone. Kuṣāṇa-period Gandhāra (2nd–3rd c. CE) gives him his classic type: princely jewelry, stūpa-in-crown, water flask, the wheel at his feet; Mathurā workshops add the dharma-cakra-mudrā preaching pose. The colossi scale up along the Silk Road — the 55-meter Bamiyan east niche (6th–7th c., destroyed 2001) and the 27-meter Maitreya of Bingling Si's cave 171. In China the earliest datable Maitreya image (the gilt bronze of 443 CE in the Asian Art Museum tradition) and the great Northern Wei votive steles mark the cult's imperial sponsorship. Inscriptions from Swat to Khotan name him Metr — the future Buddha already receiving donations in his own lifetime's echo.
lore.syncretism: Maitreya's reception is the strangest career of any bodhisattva. In India he absorbed the iconography of a future world-ruler — crowned, princely, seated European-style with pendant legs, a god of the age to come. Central Asian Islam met him on the cave walls of Dunhuang and kept his silhouette in manuscript illumination. China fused him with the folk saint Budai and made the laughing fat monk his universal form; Korea and Japan inherited both the regal Maitreza/Miroku of the temples and the round-bellied Hotei of the gate. In Japan, Miroku became the focus of sundered-age hope — the mappō centuries looked to him as the one who comes when Śākyamuni's law has faded. Modern scholarship (Sponberg & Hardacre's Maitreya, the Future Buddha) treats him as the closest Buddhism came to a messiah: not a savior from outside history, but its next chapter.

steps: Sanskrit Mañjuśrī is written in Devanagari as मञ्जुश्री
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: mun-joo-SHREE — the ñ is the nasal of 'canyon'; śrī is one syllable, the 'sh' softened.
pronunciation.note: Mañjuśrī is a compound: mañju, 'gentle, sweet, lovely,' + śrī, 'glory, splendor' (Monier-Williams) — 'the Gentle Glory.' His other names are a litany of the same music: Mañjughoṣa, 'Gentle Voice'; Vāgīśvara, 'Lord of Speech.' The restoration keeps the palatal ñ, the ś, and the long ī; the ASCII 'Manjushri' loses all three. Tier-1 by rule: three distinctive letters preserved.

domains.title: The Gentle Glory
domains.subtitle: The Flaming Sword, the Book on the Lotus, and the Mountain of Five Terraces
domains.lead: Mañjuśrī is the bodhisattva of transcendent wisdom: the ever-youthful prince who raises the flaming sword that cuts ignorance and bears the book of the Perfection of Wisdom on a blue lotus — the mind of every Buddha made visible as a sixteen-year-old with a blade.

cards.name: The Flaming Sword
cards.desc: The khadga that does not wound but severs: ignorance cut at the root, wisdom flaming at the edge.

cards.name: The Book on the Lotus
cards.desc: The Prajñāpāramitā volume resting on a blue utpala — the text the sword serves.

cards.name: The Lion Mount
cards.desc: He rides the lion of the teaching — wisdom's roar that no argument withstands.

cards.name: A Ra Pa Tsa Na
cards.desc: Oṃ A Ra Pa Tsa Na Dhīḥ — the Arapacana syllabary as mantra, recited across the Himalaya for a sharp mind.

symbols.name: The flaming sword
symbols.meaning: Discrimination that liberates: the cut that ends confusion, not the one that starts it

symbols.name: The blue lotus and the book
symbols.meaning: Wisdom as a text to be carried and a flower that opens by itself

symbols.name: The seed syllable Dhīḥ
symbols.meaning: The sound of insight itself, traced on children's tongues in the Himalaya

symbols.name: The lion mount
symbols.meaning: The vehicle of the teaching: majesty that roars once and settles every dispute

symbols.name: The sixteen-year-old form
symbols.meaning: Wisdom is not the slow deposit of years but the freshness of a mind that has not agreed to be confused

mythology.lead: Mañjuśrī's mythology is the biography of wisdom itself: he appears wherever the sūtras need the hardest question asked — and answered without a flicker. He debates laymen and nāga girls, drains lakes with a sword-stroke, teaches from a mountain that became China's greatest pilgrimage, and sends pilgrims out to find the truth for themselves.

myths.title: The Debate of Non-Duality
myths.text: When the layman Vimalakīrti feigned illness to draw the Buddha's disciples into dialogue, every bodhisattva found an excuse not to visit — each remembered being corrected by him once. Mañjuśrī alone went, leading the whole assembly, and their exchange crowns the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa (ch. 9, 'Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality'). Thirty bodhisattvas define non-duality by dissolving paired opposites — motion and rest, self and being, bondage and release — each more subtly than the last. Mañjuśrī declares that all their words are themselves dualistic, and that he has nothing to say. Vimalakīrti answers with silence, and Mañjuśrī pronounces the silence itself the teaching: 'Good sirs, this is truly the entrance into non-duality.' It is the most famous consultation in Buddhist literature — the wisdom bodhisattva certifying that the highest truth declines to be phrased.

myths.title: The Nāga King's Daughter
myths.text: In the twelfth chapter of Kumārajīva's Lotus Sūtra — the Devadatta chapter — Mañjuśrī returns from the nāga palace beneath the sea, where he had preached the Lotus, and reports that the dragon king's daughter, eight years old, has already attained the highest awakening. The elder Śāriputra objects on every ground his age could supply: a female body, a child, an animal's realm — surely the bodhisattva path cannot be completed so fast, in such a vessel. The girl appears, offers a precious jewel to the Buddha, and completes the path before the whole assembly; the sūtra lets her achievement answer the objection rather than argue it. Mañjuśrī's role is the chapter's quiet engine — he carries the teaching where it was never expected to go, into a palace under the sea. The myth is his brief for the universality of awakening: wisdom, taught well, does not check credentials.

lore.culturalLegacy: Mañjuśrī is the patron saint of students across half the world: Himalayan children still have the syllable Dhīḥ traced on their tongues for a quick mind, and his Arapacana mantra is murmured before examinations from Ladakh to Lhasa. His iconography — sword in the right hand, book on the lotus at the left — is the universal Buddhist shorthand for the two halves of wisdom, cutting and knowing. Mount Wutai, his earthly seat, is a UNESCO landscape where a dozen languages still call on Wénshū. In Japan, Monju presides over the school-examination season, his name invoked in June by students at temples from Tokyo to Kamakura. The restoration Mañjuśrī keeps the palatals and the long vowel of a name that, in every language it entered, never stopped meaning a sharp and gentle mind.
lore.archaeology: His mountain is the monument: Wǔtái shān preserves the Nanchan temple hall (782 CE) and the Foguang temple's East Hall (857 CE) — the two oldest surviving timber buildings in China — on the terraces pilgrims have climbed for fifteen centuries. The Kathmandu valley keeps his founding stroke in stone and water: the Chobhar gorge through which the lake drained, and the Svayambhū stūpa on its hill. His certain images emerge in the early centuries CE and multiply along the Silk Road; by the Pāla period the sword-and-book type was fixed, and it has not changed since. In Japan, Monju's seat at the temple Tōdai-ji — where the great Vairocana was dedicated in 752 — marks how closely wisdom bodhisattva and cosmic Buddha were paired in the Nara mind.
lore.syncretism: He is the most portable of the great bodhisattvas: Wénshū in China, Monju in Japan, 'Jam dpal in Tibet. In Tibet his cult became inseparable from scholarship itself — Tsongkhapa venerated as his emanation, and the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti, 'Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī,' recited as the daily liturgy of the monasteries (Wayman's translation made the text a classic in the West). With Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi he forms the lords of the three families — wisdom, compassion, and power — the triad painted over a thousand Himalayan doorways. His sword-and-book traveled the sea routes as well: his images stand in the temples of Buddhist Java. And in China the identification ran both ways — Wenshu was held to appear to worthy students as a humble stranger, testing them with a question before vanishing.

entries.meaning: 'Universal Beneficence' — the Bodhisattva of practice, rider of the white elephant

steps: Sanskrit Samantabhadra is written in Devanagari as समन्तभद्र
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: 'suh-MUN-tuh-bhud-ruh' — the bh is aspirated like 'b-hud' in one breath; the name runs even and calm, like the practice it names.
pronunciation.note: Samantabhadra is samanta, 'on all sides, universal,' + bhadra, 'good, auspicious' (Monier-Williams) — 'Universal Good.' Tier 2 by rule: the owned restoration 'Samantabhadra' preserves nothing that plain ASCII 'samantabhadra' loses — no diacritics, no distinctive atomic letters. The name's distinction is lexical, not orthographic: it means the good that has no edges.

domains.title: Samantabhadra
domains.subtitle: Universal Good
domains.lead: Samantabhadra is the bodhisattva of practice: if Mañjuśrī wields the sword of wisdom, Samantabhadra is the goodness that actually walks — his ten great vows (homage, offering, confession, rejoicing, dedication...) are the Mahāyāna's complete curriculum of the heart, recited daily from Wutai to Lhasa.

cards.name: The Ten Great Vows
cards.desc: Homage, praise, offering, confession, rejoicing, requesting the teaching, beseeching buddhas to remain, imitation, dedication, transfer — the Avataṃsaka's whole practice in ten lines.

cards.name: The Six-Tusked White Elephant
cards.desc: His mount, fragrant and steadfast: practice that carries all beings without hurry or display.

cards.name: The King of Prayers
cards.desc: The Bhadracarī-praṇidhāna — 'Vows of Good Conduct' — closing the Avataṃsaka and opening every Tibetan monastery's day.

cards.name: Mount Emei's Patron
cards.desc: Pǔxián's earthly seat, one of China's four sacred Buddhist mountains — where his bronze elephant has stood since 980 CE.

symbols.name: The six-tusked white elephant
symbols.meaning: The vehicle of practice: strength that never hurries, six tusks for the six pāramitās

symbols.name: The wish-fulfilling jewel
symbols.meaning: The cintāmaṇi he holds: the good whose granting never depletes it

symbols.name: The sun and moon on his lotus seat
symbols.meaning: His throne supports a lotus bearing the sun disc — practice illuminated at every hour

symbols.name: The golden-hued body
symbols.meaning: Like a mountain at dawn: the color of the golden light that fills the Avataṃsaka's cosmos

symbols.name: Kun tu bzang po with consort
symbols.meaning: In the Nyingma tradition, the primordial Buddha in union with Samantabhadrī — good as the ground of being itself

mythology.lead: Samantabhadra's mythology is the biography of goodness as a discipline. He closes the two greatest Mahāyāna sūtras with vows rather than visions, becomes Tibet's primordial Buddha without ever leaving his elephant, and turns a Sichuan peak into the most walked bodhimaṇḍa in China. His stories are quiet — and deliberately so.

myths.title: The Ten Great Vows
myths.text: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra closes with his testament, the Bhadracarī-praṇidhāna or Vows of Good Conduct: homage to all buddhas as numerous as atoms, praise of their virtues, offerings as vast as space, confession of faults, rejoicing in others' merit, requesting the wheel of Dharma be turned, beseeching buddhas not to pass into nirvāṇa, constant imitation of their deeds, dedication of all merit, and its transfer to all beings — whatever good I have done, may all beings share it. The prayer is appended to the great sūtra in its Chinese recensions and has never left the tradition's daily life: Tibetan monasteries chant it at the close of every session, and East Asian liturgy still folds its verses into repentance rites. Ten lines carry the entire Mahāyāna practice — the myth's point is that goodness, fully articulated, turns out to be this short and this inexhaustible.

myths.title: The Vow of the Lotus
myths.text: The Lotus Sūtra ends not with the Buddha but with a visitor. Its twenty-eighth chapter brings Samantabhadra from the eastern land, riding a great white elephant with six tusks, each tusk bearing seven lotuses, each lotus a radiant Buddha, surrounded by an entourage streaming across the sky — and he vows before the assembly to protect anyone who keeps, reads, or teaches the Lotus in the latter age, sending his fragrant elephant and his retinue to guard them, even laying his hand on their heads in blessing. To forgetful minds he grants dhāraṇīs — spells of retention — so the sūtra survives its readers. The closing chapter is the sūtra handing itself to practice: wisdom (the Lotus's teaching) sealed by goodness (the bodhisattva who promises to carry it). A scripture that ends in a vow is telling you how it intends to be read — not admired, but kept.

lore.culturalLegacy: Samantabhadra's legacy is the most recited prayer in the Mahāyāna world: the Bhadracarī, his ten vows, closes the day's practice in monasteries from Dharamsala to Kyoto, and its verses — just as Samantabhadra practiced, so may I — are the template of Buddhist dedication across Asia. Mount Emei, his seat, is a UNESCO-listed sacred landscape climbed by pilgrims for two thousand years, its ten-thousand-year temple guarding his bronze elephant. In Japan, Fugen presides over the Lotus Sūtra's protection cult; in Tibet, Kun tu bzang po opens the Dzogchen teachings as the name of the mind's own nature. The restoration Samantabhadra needs no diacritics to carry its meaning — the name itself is the sentence: good, on all sides, without exception.
lore.archaeology: His bronze at Wannian Temple on Mount Emei — Pǔxián riding an elephant, cast 980 CE under Song Taizu, some sixty-two tonnes of it — is among the largest and oldest surviving bronze Buddhist images in China, and the temple's founding legend reaches back to a Han-era sighting on the same slopes. The mountain's Golden Summit temples, rebuilt through the centuries, still anchor a living pilgrimage. At Dunhuang, ninth- and tenth-century mural fragments and banner paintings of the Avataṃsaka's assemblies preserve his early iconography, and the Tibetan manuscript caches of the same caves include early copies of the Kunjed Gyalpo — the primordial Buddha's text traveling the Silk Road in his name.
lore.syncretism: Across East Asia he is the third of the great bodhisattva triad — with Avalokiteśvara (compassion) and Mañjuśrī (wisdom) — the trio enthroned beside Śākyamuni in countless Chinese halls: the heart, the head, and the hands. Japan received Fugen with the same triad logic, and medieval honji-suijaku thought read him as the Buddhist truth behind several kami. Tibet's reception was the boldest: the Nyingma school made Kun tu bzang po the primordial Buddha, the dharmakāya personified, so that the bodhisattva of good conduct became the very ground of enlightenment — practice revealed as the nature of mind itself. The two identities never merged, and the tradition sees no contradiction: the elephant-rider is what the All-Good One looks like when he consents to have a form.

entries.meaning: The Earth-Womb — bodhisattva of the great vow to empty the hells (kṣiti 'earth' + garbha 'womb')
entries.domain: Earth Womb, Savior of Hell Beings

pronunciation.approximation: kshih-tih-GUR-bhuh — the kṣ is one conjunct sound; the bh is aspirated.
pronunciation.note: Kṣitigarbha is kṣiti, "earth" (from √kṣi, "to dwell, abide" — Monier-Williams), + garbha, "womb, inner chamber, treasury": "the Earth-Womb," the earth as the storehouse that holds and hides all treasure. East Asia translated rather than transliterated: Chinese Dìzàng, "Earth-Store," Japanese Jizō. The restoration's whole distinctiveness is carried by one letter — the retroflex ṣ inside the kṣ conjunct — which the ASCII "Ksitigarbha" writes but cannot show. Tier-1 by rule.

domains.title: The Earth-Womb
domains.subtitle: The Great Vow, the Six-Ringed Staff, and the Hells Emptied One Being at a Time
domains.lead: Kṣitigarbha is the bodhisattva of the greatest vow ever sworn: not to attain Buddhahood until the hells are emptied — the monk-robed guardian of the dead, the traveler, and the child, who accepted the loneliest commission in Buddhism: to fill the age between one Buddha's passing and the next one's coming.

cards.name: The Great Vow
cards.desc: "Until the hells are empty, I shall not become a Buddha" — the pledge that defines him.

cards.name: The Khakkhara
cards.desc: The six-ringed monk's staff: its jingle warns the small creatures, and its point opens the gates of hell.

cards.name: The Wish-Fulfilling Jewel
cards.desc: The cintāmaṇi in his hand: the light he carries into the darkest of the six realms.

cards.name: The Six Jizō
cards.desc: One for each realm of rebirth: the six forms in which he patrols the whole wheel of existence.

symbols.name: The monk's robe and shaven head
symbols.meaning: The only great bodhisattva who refuses princely ornament: humility as the uniform of the vow

symbols.name: The staff of six rings
symbols.meaning: The sound of mercy approaching: the rings ring so beings may step aside, and hell's doors not stay shut

symbols.name: The red bib
symbols.meaning: The cloth mothers tie on roadside Jizō: the grief and gratitude of the living made visible

symbols.name: The wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi)
symbols.meaning: The luminous pearl in his hand — the light of merit he carries into the darkest realm; in Japanese iconography he raises it to brighten the road of the dead

symbols.name: Dìtīng, the truth-hearing beast
symbols.meaning: The lion-like mount crouched at Dìzàng's throne (諦聽, 'hears the true'), said to distinguish truth from falsehood — judgment's ear made animal

mythology.lead: Kṣitigarbha's mythology is the story of a vow repeated across lifetimes — a brahmin daughter, a king — each life renewing the same impossible promise.

myths.title: The Commission in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven
myths.text: The Sūtra of the Past Vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva (Taishō 412) is set in the heaven of the Thirty-Three, whither Śākyamuni ascended to preach for the sake of his mother before his passing. There the Buddha recounts Kṣitigarbha's long record of vows — in one former life a king who promised to save every deluded being before accepting awakening, while a fellow king chose the shorter road to Buddhahood — and then delivers the commission: in the dark age between Śākyamuni's parinirvāṇa and Maitreya's arrival, when no Buddha walks the world, Kṣitigarbha is to stand in the gap and answer for all beings. The sūtra's most quoted line is the vow itself: until the hells are empty, he shall not become a Buddha; only when every being is saved will he accept awakening. The Sanskrit original is lost; the text survives chiefly in Chinese and Tibetan — and its promise survived everything.

myths.title: The Brahmin Daughter
myths.text: The sūtra's most beloved past life is a daughter's. A pious brahmin girl's mother died slandering the Dharma, and the daughter, selling all she had to make offerings, was granted a vision of the Avīci hell — where she learned that her merit had already lifted her mother toward heaven. Seeing the legions of the damned who had no daughter to save them, she vowed to deliver them all: the vow was born of filial piety and outgrew the family in a single act. In East Asia this story fused his cult with the Ghost Festival itself, the season of the dead, when the gates between the realms are said to stand open. It is the Mahāyāna's most efficient piece of narrative engineering: one girl's grief for her mother generalized into a bodhisattva's grief for everyone — filial piety enlarged until it became universal compassion.

lore.culturalLegacy: Kṣitigarbha is the working religion of grief in East Asia: the mizuko kuyō services in which Japanese parents memorialize lost pregnancies are held before him; the bibbed stone Jizō is Japan's commonest roadside sight; and Dìzàng's temples anchor the Chinese underworld's moral map. His vow has become the Mahāyāna's most quoted sentence — the standard against which every other pledge of compassion is measured — and his monk's robe the proof that the highest bodhisattva need not look like a king.
lore.archaeology: His surviving landscape is vast. Jiuhuashan's temple-mountain, with the flesh-body hall of the Silla prince, remains an active pilgrimage city. The Dunhuang caves and the Library Cave's banners preserve paintings of Dìzàng enthroned among the Ten Kings of hell — the earliest great cycle of his iconography, now chiefly in the British Museum and the Musée Guimet. Japan's material record is the stone Jizō itself: uncounted thousands of carved figures at village edges, crossroads, and temple yards, from medieval stelae to today's bibbed statues — the densest distribution of any Buddhist image in the archipelago, each one a small, weathered keeping of the vow.
lore.syncretism: East Asia rebuilt him in its own image without touching the vow: China seated him over the Ten Kings of the underworld bureaucracy and wove him into the Ghost Festival's calendar; Korea's Jijang shares the Jiuhua inheritance; Japan fused Jizō with the roadside protector-deities of the old highways and the cult of dead children. Tibet received him as Sa yi snying po among the eight great bodhisattvas, though without the underworld portfolio. Comparatists place him among the great psychopomps — but note the difference: he does not guide the dead out; he goes in and stays until the last one leaves.

entries.meaning: The Vajra-Bearer — wielder of the thunderbolt, protector of the Buddha (vajra + pāṇi 'in the hand')

pronunciation.approximation: vuj-ruh-PAH-nih — the j is as in 'jam'; the ṇ is the retroflex n; the ā of pāṇi is long.
pronunciation.note: Vajrapāṇi is a bahuvrīhi: vajra, "thunderbolt, diamond," + pāṇi, "hand" (Monier-Williams) — "the one with the vajra in hand." The name is older than Buddhism: Monier-Williams lists it first as an epithet of Indra, the thunderbolt-wielder, and the lexicon preserves that gloss. Buddhism transferred the weapon and the title to the Buddha's own protector. The restoration keeps the long ā and the retroflex ṇ; the ASCII "Vajrapani" flattens both. Tier-1 by rule.

domains.title: The Vajra-Bearer
domains.subtitle: The Buddha's Shadow, the Lord of Secrets, and the Power of the Three Families
domains.lead: Vajrapāṇi is the power of the Buddhas in person: the thunderbolt-bearer who walks at the Buddha's shoulder in the earliest Gandhāran panels, the enforcer who once held a blazing club over a liar's head in the Pāli canon, and the Lord of Secrets to whom the tantras themselves were entrusted.

cards.name: The Vajra
cards.desc: Thunderbolt and diamond in one implement: the irresistible force that is also the unbreakable thing.

cards.name: The Buddha's Shadow
cards.desc: In Gandhāran art he stands beside the Buddha at every step — the first bodyguard of the Dharma.

cards.name: The Lord of Secrets
cards.desc: Guhyakādhipati: the keeper and compiler of the tantras, the power behind the esoteric throne.

cards.name: The Three Protectors
cards.desc: With Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara — power beside wisdom and compassion, the lords of the three families.

symbols.name: The vajra
symbols.meaning: The weapon that gives Vajrayāna its very name: the diamond vehicle is his vehicle

symbols.name: The wrathful stance
symbols.meaning: Pratyālīḍha, the warrior's lunge: compassion with its patience spent

symbols.name: The serpent ornaments
symbols.meaning: The nāga girdle of the wrathful form: the powers of the deep enlisted as jewelry

symbols.name: The blazing club
symbols.meaning: The ayoguḷa of the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, raised but never swung — deterrence as the highest use of force

symbols.name: The blue-black body
symbols.meaning: Nīlambaradhara, the Blue-Clad: the wrathful color of the vajra family, wrath that is fidelity in another register

mythology.lead: Vajrapāṇi's mythology runs from the Pāli canon to the highest tantras without a break: the same thunderbolt, passed from Indra's hand to the Buddha's bodyguard to the Lord of Secrets. Every stage of the career adds an office — enforcer, guardian, archivist — and none ever retires the last.

myths.title: The Yakkha with the Blazing Club
myths.text:
His earliest certain appearance is already dramatic. In the Dīgha Nikāya's Ambaṭṭha Sutta, the proud young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, come to examine the Buddha, twice evades the Buddha's direct question about his ancestry. The Buddha warns him: refuse a third time, and your head will split into seven pieces on the spot. And there, in the air above the youth's head, appears the yakkha Vajirapāṇi, holding aloft a great blazing iron club — an ayoguḷa, a bolt of iron — burning, glowing, ready. Ambaṭṭha glances up, sees it, and answers. The scene then turns inside out: the Buddha reveals that the Kaṇhāyan lineage Ambaṭṭha is so proud of descends, by the brahmins' own genealogy, from a slave-girl of the very Sakyans the young man has been insulting — the thunderbolt merely opens the door to the humiliation that does the real work.

The episode is the whole doctrine in miniature. The thunderbolt exists not to strike but to make truth the easier choice; it is raised, blazing, where it can be seen, and the text never once says it was swung. In the only sūtta where a yakkha enforces debate-manners, Buddhism defined its relationship to force: present, luminous, and permanently unspent.

myths.title: Heracles at the Buddha's Side
myths.text:
When Gandhāran sculptors of the early centuries CE carved the Buddha's life in grey schist for the monasteries of the Peshawar valley — Takht-i-Bahi, Sahri Bahlol, the whole stūpa belt of the northwest — they faced a casting problem: the Buddha himself could not be shown acting in the old way, yet his scenes needed a protagonist. For the miracles and the confrontations they used a muscular attendant at the Master's shoulder, sometimes bearded, sometimes wearing the lion-skin: the Greek Heracles, imported whole from the art their patrons had grown up with, his club exchanged for a vajra. In the panels of the Buddha's bathing, the snakes' protection, the conversion of the Kāśyapas, it is this Heracles-body that acts while the Buddha stands composed — Vajrapāṇi in the dress of the strongest man the Mediterranean could imagine.

It is the most candid syncretism in ancient art: the thunderbolt-bearer wearing another culture's power, because power was the job description. Within a few centuries the Heracles-body would be refined away into the princely bodhisattva the Mahāyāna preferred, but the Gandhāran panels preserve the moment when the Buddha's bodyguard was literally the strongest figure in someone else's pantheon, hired by iconography.

lore.culturalLegacy: Vajrapāṇi gave the third turning of Buddhism its very name: Vajrayāna, the diamond-thunderbolt vehicle, is the way of his implement. The paired Niō still loom in the gates of Japanese temples; the wrathful krodha protectors of Himalayan art inherit his stance, his serpents, and his color; and the three-lords triad remains the standard threshold of Tibetan sacred painting. In Tibet his mantra-function is so basic that wrathful deities are addressed in his person, and Mongolian and Buryat Buddhism inherited the blue figure whole. His is the oldest continuously employed job in Buddhist art: someone has to hold the thunderbolt. Every school agrees on the job description even where they redraw the uniform — guardian at the shoulder in Gandhāra, archivist of the tantras in the monasteries, door-god in Japan and Korea, ferocious blue lord on the Himalayan walls — five costumes, one office, twenty centuries of employment.
lore.archaeology: His material record begins with Gandhāra: schist panels of the second and third centuries CE — now divided among Peshawar, Lahore, the British Museum, and the Musée Guimet — show the Heracles-bodied attendant at the Buddha's shoulder, the first datable images of a bodhisattva-protector. The type traveled: the paired gate-guardians descend from him — the Niō or Heng-Ha pairs of Japan and the Korean Geumgang yeoksa, mouths open and closed, culminating in the Nandaimon colossi of Tōdai-ji (1203, Unkei and Kaikei workshops). Himalayan art fixed his wrathful blue form by the Pāla period, and the three-lords triad became the standard threshold of Tibetan sacred painting. In the Swat valley, pilgrims were still being shown the cleft of the Apalāla legend into modern times.
lore.syncretism: His lineage is a relay of weapons: Indra's vajra — the name is first Indra's epithet, as Monier-Williams records — passed to the Buddha's yakkha enforcer, then to the bodhisattva of power; and in East Asia the single figure split into the paired gate-guardians of every great temple: the Kongōrikishi or Niō of Japan, mouths open and closed, the alpha and omega of the spoken world, whose colossi at Tōdai-ji's Nandaimon (1203, Unkei and Kaikei) are national treasures. The Heracles parallel runs in both directions: as the Greeks lent him a body in Gandhāra, so scholarship reads him as the Buddha's answer to every culture's strong-armed sky-god — Zeus's bolt, Indra's club, Þórr's hammer — reassigned from storm to awakening. The comparison is functional rather than historical, but it is the comparison every borderland of the old world kept making: one pantheon after another met the Buddha and reached for its strongest figure to walk beside him.

entries.meaning: She who saves — the goddess of compassion and liberation in Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna Buddhism, the Savioress who ferries beings across the ocean of saṃsāra.

pronunciation.note: Tier 2: 'Asanga' is ASCII-canonical in spelling; the restoration restores the name's meaning — a- + saṅga, 'without attachment' — which is also the psychological thesis of the Yogācāra school he founded.

domains.title: Asanga
domains.subtitle: Without Attachment — Founder of Yogācāra, the Practice of Mind Only
domains.lead: Asanga (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the founder of Yogācāra, the Buddhist school that analyzed consciousness itself — the ālayavijñāna store-mind, the three natures, the construction of the world by perception — and the man who, by tradition, received the future Buddha Maitreya's five treatises on a visit to Tuṣita heaven.

cards.name: Yogācāra
cards.desc: The 'practice of yoga' school — Abhidharma rewritten as psychology: suffering located in the structure of consciousness itself.

cards.name: The Vision of Maitreya
cards.desc: Twelve years of retreat, a dying dog, and transport to Tuṣita heaven — where the future Buddha dictated the five great treatises.

cards.name: The Two Brothers
cards.desc: He and his half-brother Vasubandhu wrote half the Indian Mahāyāna — the gentle ambush that converted the greatest critic of the Mahāyāna.

cards.name: Mind-Only
cards.desc: The world as construction of consciousness — 'mind-only,' his opponents' nickname, became the school's thesis and modern cognitive science's ancestor.

symbols.name: The wounded dog
symbols.meaning: The dying dog whose maggots he moved with his tongue — the act of compassion that revealed Maitreya, and the founding parable of Yogācāra: insight comes through the heart, not the head

symbols.name: Maitreya's tower
symbols.meaning: Tuṣita heaven, where the five treatises were received — Yogācāra's scriptural charter is literally from the future

symbols.name: The mirror
symbols.meaning: The school's favorite image in later East Asian art — perception like a mirror: images arise, none stick; Asanga's name, 'without attachment,' is the mirror wiped clean

symbols.name: The storehouse (ālaya)
symbols.meaning: The ālayavijñāna, the warehouse consciousness where seeds of karma sleep and sprout — his school's most influential and most argued concept

symbols.name: The three natures
symbols.meaning: Imagined, dependent, perfected — Asanga's map of how the mind builds its world and how it sees through the building

mythology.lead: Asanga's mythology is the hagiography of a psychologist: the vision that founded his school came through compassion for a dog, and his school's charter texts were, by tradition, dictated by the future Buddha — scholarship's verdict is that Asanga wrote them himself, which changes nothing about the parable.

myths.title: Two Brothers, One Teaching
myths.text: Asanga and his younger half-brother Vasubandhu — arguably the two most consequential Buddhist philosophers after Nāgārjuna — were born, the story runs (Xuanzang preserves it in his Great Tang Records of the Western Regions), to a brahmin of Kauśika lineage; their mother, the legend adds, resolved that one son should master the Mahāyāna and the other its rival, the analytical Abhidharma of Kaśmīr. Vasubandhu became the encyclopedist of the Abhidharmakośa; Asanga wandered and meditated until he founded Yogācāra. Then the elder brother executed the gentlest ambush in the history of ideas: feigning a mortal illness, he had disciples read him a Mahāyāna sūtra and plant objections that only the Mahāyāna could answer — until the great critic recanted on the spot and joined the school he had spent his career refuting. Vasubandhu's conversion doubled the school's firepower: the Viṃśikā and Trimśikā became its core. The myth explains a real fact: half of the Indian Mahāyāna was written by one family — brotherly love as the engine of a philosophical revolution.

myths.title: Twelve Years, a Wounded Dog, and Maitreya
myths.text: The founding vision of Yogācāra is a story about compassion first. Asanga, the tradition says (Xuanzang; the Tibetan historians Bu ston and Tāranātha repeat it), spent twelve years in solitary retreat awaiting a vision of the future Buddha Maitreya — and saw nothing. Despairing on his way down the mountain, he met a dog dying in the road, its open wounds alive with maggots; to save both creature and worms he cut flesh from his own thigh and reached to lift the maggots with his tongue. The dog vanished: it was Maitreya. The bodhisattva then carried Asanga bodily to Tuṣita heaven, where he received the five great treatises — Abhisamayālaṃkāra, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, Madhyāntavibhāga, Dharmadharmatāvibhāga, Ratnagotravibhāga. Modern scholarship — Frauwallner most forcefully — argues Asanga wrote them himself. The interpretive point survives either way: a philosophy of mind founded by a man whose breakthrough came through the gut — the dying dog was the last rung of the ladder.

lore.culturalLegacy: Asanga's legacy is institutional and conceptual at once. Nālandā, where his lineage taught for seven centuries, is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the name of India's modern flagship university; the Tibetan monastic curriculum still opens philosophy with his Abhisamayālaṃkāra, memorized line by line across every shedra from Lhasa to Mundgod. In East Asia the Faxiang/Hossō line, though small, preserved his texts when India lost them — Xuanzang's rescue of the manuscripts is itself one of the great stories of civilization's luggage. And the concepts migrated far beyond Buddhism: the store-consciousness anticipates the unconscious, the three natures prefigure constructivist accounts of perception, and 'mind-only' is quoted in contemporary philosophy of mind and machine-learning debates alike. A man whose name means 'without attachment' ended up attached to everything.
lore.archaeology: Asanga left no monument of his own, and his century left few datable ones — the 4th–5th-century Buddhist world of northern India is known mostly through the pilgrim accounts (Faxian, then Xuanzang) and the great monastic cities they describe. Nālandā, excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India from 1915 and now a UNESCO site, preserves the excavated grid of his school's eventual home: eleven monasteries and six temples in brick, the sarai and the stūpas. The Ajanta caves' later viharas (5th–6th c.) show the scholastic monasticism his movement filled — rows of cells, lecture halls, painted jātakas. His true artifacts are textual: the five Maitreya treatises survive in hundreds of Sanskrit fragments and complete Tibetan and Chinese translations, their colophons still arguing about who wrote them — which is, for a school about the construction of authorship, exactly right.
lore.syncretism: Yogācāra's fate was absorption: too useful to defeat, it was eaten by its rivals. In India, the great synthesis of the 8th century married Asanga's psychology to Nāgārjuna's emptiness — Śāntarakṣita's Madhyāmakālaṃkāra declared the two schools two doors into one house, a verdict all later Indian Buddhism accepted. In East Asia, Yogācāra merged with Huayan's cosmos and Tiantai's Lotus hermeneutics, surviving explicitly only in Japan's Hossō school while secretly structuring everything else. In Tibet, Asanga is 'the two brothers' half of every curriculum — the Abhisamayālaṃkāra is the master commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā that Nāgārjuna supposedly rescued from the sea. The modern meeting is stranger: William James and the Yogācārins now read each other — 'pure experience' and 'mind-only' are neighbors across a century, and the ālayavijñāna reappears in cognitive science as 'predictive processing.' The school named 'practice' became, in the end, the theory everyone practices against.

entries.meaning: The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school

pronunciation.approximation: Say "vasubandhu" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Vasubandhu".
pronunciation.note: The ASCII form "vasubandhu" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Vasubandhu" preserves the name's scholarly dignity. Sanskrit is not a stress-accent language like Greek; the name is a transparent compound of vasu ('wealth, good') + bandhu ('kinsman, friend') — 'Kinsman of Wealth' — so there is no distinctive accent or long-vowel mark for a restoration to recover, and the lexicon classifies the name Tier 2. What the capitals restore is recognition, not phonology.

domains.title: Vasubandhu
domains.subtitle: Abhidharma
domains.lead: Vasubandhu is the great systematizer of Buddhist philosophy: author of the Abhidharmakośa, the encyclopedia of Abhidharma that every later school had to answer, and, with his half-brother Asaṅga, co-founder of the Yogācāra, the 'Mind-Only' school that reshaped Mahāyāna thought from India to Japan.

cards.name: The Kośa Verse
cards.desc: Six hundred verses of Abhidharmakośa kārikā summarizing the entire Sarvāstivāda analysis of mind, matter, and liberation.

cards.name: Abhidharma
cards.desc: His auto-commentary made the Kośa the standard curriculum: studied in Nālandā, debated in Tibet, translated in China by Xuanzang.

cards.name: Yogācāra
cards.desc: The Twenty and Thirty Verses argue the world is 'mind-only' — the doctrine his Kośa-era Sautrāntika readers found hardest to accept.

cards.name: The Conversion
cards.desc: Legend says his brother Asaṅga sent him a begging letter: compassion, not argument, turned the Kośa's author toward the Mahāyāna.

symbols.name: The Kośa stanza
symbols.meaning: A verse (kārikā) whose eight-syllable lines hold whole Abhidharma treatises — scholarship compressed into memorable sound

symbols.name: The begging bowl
symbols.meaning: The monk's only equipment; Vasubandhu remained a bhikṣu all his life even while moving courts and schools

symbols.name: The letter from Asaṅga
symbols.meaning: In the Tibetan biographies, the note that converted him — affection and mortality doing what doctrine could not

symbols.name: Treasury (kośa)
symbols.meaning: The storehouse metaphor of the Abhidharmakośa: every dharma catalogued like treasure in a vault, each with its own nature

mythology.lead: Vasubandhu was a historical philosopher, not a mythological figure — a monk of Puruṣapura (Peshawar) who, the early Tibetan biographies say, wrote the Abhidharmakośa as a Sarvāstivādin critic and then embraced the Yogācāra Mahāyāna of his half-brother Asaṅga. His 'myths' are the legends his tradition grew around a real life.

myths.title: Three Years in Seclusion
myths.text: The Tibetan biographies recount that Vasubandhu withdrew into seclusion to master the Abhidharma of the Kashmir Sarvāstivādins, and emerged with the Abhidharmakośa — six hundred verses (kārikā) of flawless eight-syllable metre that summarized the entire system. When the Kashmir masters admired the verses but missed their own subtlety, he added an auto-commentary (bhāṣya) of his own in which, tradition says, he quietly refuted them. The Kośa became what it remains: the one Abhidharma text every later school — Theravāda, Mahāyāna, and the Tibetan lineages — had to study, debate, or answer, translated in its entirety into Chinese by Xuanzang and memorized in fragments by generations of monks from Kashmir to Kyoto. Its author's own allegiance was already drifting as he wrote: the commentary, tradition says, shows the Sautrāntika reservations that would later make his conversion credible. To condense a library into verse, and the verse into a single lifetime, is the legend's whole point: scholarship can be a kind of asceticism.

myths.title: The Begging Letter of Asaṅga
myths.text: Vasubandhu had mocked the Mahāyāna as a corruption of the Buddha's teaching, calling its scriptures fabrications. His elder half-brother Asaṅga, already a great Yogācāra teacher, sent him no rebuttal — only a note reporting that he was dying, and begging Vasubandhu to recite the Mahāyāna sūtras for him. Struck by the affection of the request, Vasubandhu read them, found them profound, and entered the Mahāyāna himself. The story is hagiography — no Indian source records it independently — yet it encodes the tradition's own account of its greatest conversion: Vasubandhu did not abandon analysis for devotion. He turned the same razor-sharp mind to the 'mind-only' philosophy, composing the Twenty Verses (Viṁśikā) and the Thirty Verses (Triṁśikā) that define the Yogācāra, and the two halves of his career became one continuous argument about how carefully the world must be taken apart before it can be seen whole.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Abhidharmakośa never went out of use: it has been memorized, commented, and debated continuously for some fifteen centuries, from Nālandā to the great Tibetan commentarial traditions (Prajñākaramati's and Yaśomitra's subcommentaries in Sanskrit; Sthiramati's in the mind-only line). Its author is honored as a patriarch in China and Japan, and Tibetan debate courtyards still open with his verses. In the modern academy Vasubandhu anchors the study of Buddhist philosophy — his Viṁśikā is a standard text in courses on philosophy of mind, cited in debates about idealism and representation. A brahmin-born monk of Gandhāra thus became one of the most-read authors in human history, his name a byword for the possibility that analysis itself can be a path to compassion.
lore.archaeology: Vasubandhu left no shrine — his witnesses are manuscripts. Fragments of the Abhidharmakośa survive in Central Asian Sanskrit finds, and the complete tradition rides on Xuanzang's Chinese translation (Taishō 1558) and the later Tibetan canon (Toh. 4089–90). Gandhāra, his homeland, is one of the richest archaeological regions of the Buddhist world: the monastery and stupa complexes around Peshawar — where the biographies place his birth — have yielded the oldest datable Buddha images (c. 1st–3rd c. CE). At Nālandā, the university whose ruins still stand in Bihar, his Kośa was a founding text; the debate-court culture his legend describes is the same institution archaeology reveals. The colophons of the Dunhuang and Gilgit manuscript finds carry his name as authority across the Silk Road.
lore.syncretism: Vasubandhu's legacy is the creation of a pan-Asian scholastic commons. In China, Xuanzang's pilgrimage was undertaken substantially to resolve disputes over the Kośa, and his massive translation of 649–660 CE made Vasubandhu the doctrinal backbone of the Faxiang (Consciousness-Only) school. In Japan the Hossō school of Nara claimed him as its patriarch, while the Kyoto lineages of the future would read his Viṁśikā as the foundation of 'mind-only' meditations. In Tibet every monastery curriculum begins with the Kośa. Modern comparative philosophy — from Thich Nhat Hanh's engaged Buddhism to analytic treatments of idealism — still frames its questions in his vocabulary. He is perhaps the only ancient philosopher whose works are simultaneously a living liturgy, a graduate textbook, and a modern research programme.

entries.meaning: 'Awakening-being' — one who vows Buddhahood for the sake of all beings

steps: Sanskrit Bodhisattva is written in Devanagari as बोधिसत्त्व
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: 'BOH-dhi-sut-tuh' — stress on BOH; the dh is a voiced breath; the final va is a soft 'wuh.'
pronunciation.note: Tier 2: 'Bodhisattva' is ASCII-canonical in spelling. The scholarly restoration adds the knowledge the spelling hides — the long ā of sattva and the compound's meaning: not 'enlightenment-being' in the abstract but a being whose essence is a specific, nameable awakening.

domains.title: Bodhisattva
domains.subtitle: The Awakening-Being — the Vow That Refuses the Exit
domains.lead: A bodhisattva is a being who has vowed awakening for the sake of all beings — and who, by that vow, defers the exit: not final nirvāṇa while a single being remains unliberated. The Mahāyāna made the word its founding institution: the bridge from one man's awakening to a vocation open to everyone.

cards.name: The Vow
cards.desc: Praṇidhāna — 'may I not sit on awakening's seat until every being is freed' — the founding act of the bodhisattva career.

cards.name: The Ten Stages
cards.desc: The Daśabhūmikasūtra's bhūmis — from Joyful to Dharma-Cloud — enlightenment surveyed as a climbable landscape.

cards.name: The Perfections
cards.desc: The six pāramitās — giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, wisdom — the curriculum every vow must pass through.

cards.name: The Exemplars
cards.desc: Avalokiteśvara hearing the world's cries, Kṣitigarbha vowing the hells be emptied — compassion walking in person.

symbols.name: The lotus
symbols.meaning: Untouched by the mud it grows from — the bodhisattva in the world but not of its stain; also Padmasambhava's birthplace, the word made landscape

symbols.name: The sword of wisdom
symbols.meaning: Mañjuśrī's blade cutting through ignorance — insight wielded not for oneself but to clear the road for others

symbols.name: The water flask and willow
symbols.meaning: Guanyin's healing emblems — the nectar of compassion poured drop by drop onto specific suffering

symbols.name: The moon in water
symbols.meaning: The bodhisattva's presence as reflection — appearing to beings in whatever form frees them, without ever leaving the empty sky

symbols.name: The staff that shakes the six realms
symbols.meaning: Kṣitigarbha's iron khakkhara — its rings wake the dead; his vow keeps him in hell's doorway until it is empty

mythology.lead: The bodhisattva is the Mahāyāna's answer to its own founder's stunning success: if one man woke, the door was never locked. Its mythology runs from the Pāli canon's bodhisatta — Gotama's pre-awakening selves — to cosmic vows that hold the door open for everyone else.

myths.title: An Awakening-Being, Not Yet a Buddha
myths.text: The word is a compound: bodhi, awakening, plus sattva, being — "one whose essence is awakening." In the Pāli canon bodhisatta is a technical term for the Buddha before his awakening: the Nidānakathā and the Mahāpadāna Sutta (DN 14) use it of Gotama's past lives, from the bodhisatta enthroned in Tuṣita down to the last birth at Lumbinī. The Mahāyāna inverted the lens: the bodhisattva is no longer the road one man walked but a vocation open to all — one who deliberately defers final nirvāṇa until the grass of beings is dry, in the Sanskrit formula of the Kāraṇḍavyūha. The compound thus carries an entire schism in six syllables: the earlier tradition's biography against the later tradition's program. An awakening-being is the answer of a religion to its own founder's success: if one man woke, the door was never locked.

myths.title: The Promise That Builds a Bridge
myths.text: Everything begins with a vow. The Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra — the final book of the Avataṃsaka — sends the pilgrim Sudhana through fifty-three teachers and ends inside Maitreya's tower, where past vows stand visible as architecture, each floor a former life; the praṇidhāna, "may I not sit on awakening's seat until every being is freed," is the bodhisattva's founding act. Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra (8th c.) gives the vow its classic liturgy: "For as long as space endures, and for as long as beings remain, may I too abide, to dispel the misery of the world." The jātakas test the vow against the body itself — Prince Śibi giving his eyes to the hawk (Jātaka 499), Vessantara giving away his wife and children (Jātaka 547). The mythic kernel: a promise made not to a god but to the uncountable future — compassion as a contract written across lifetimes, signed before any power existed that could enforce it.

lore.culturalLegacy: The bodhisattva is the most painted figure in Buddhist art after the Buddha himself — Guanyin's white-robed thousand-armed forms fill the caves of Dunhuang and the museums of the world; Samantabhadra rides his elephant across China's sacred mountains; Jizō's red-bibbed statues line every Japanese roadside, guardian of dead children. The vow's four lines — beings are numberless, I vow to free them; delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them — open every sesshin on earth. In the West the word entered the language through the Beats and the Engaged Buddhism of Thich Nhat Hanh, who translated the vow into antiwar action: the bodhisattva, he wrote, is one who postpones nirvana "to help suffering beings." A term coined to describe one man's past lives now names anyone who refuses to be free alone.
lore.archaeology: The bodhisattva's archaeology begins where the Buddha's ends. Aniconic reliefs at Bharhut and Sanchi already show the bodhisatta of the jātakas — the Vessantara and Śibi legends carved in the 2nd–1st c. BCE — while the great anthropomorphic bodhisattvas arrive with the Kuṣāṇas: the Maitreya of Gandhāra with his flask, Avalokiteśvara beside Amitābha's triad. The caves of Ajanta (5th–6th c.) give the career its narrative walls — the jātaka cycles painted as the bodhisattva's résumé. Along the Silk Road the type multiplies: the crowned Guanyin of the Tang, the eleven-headed Kannon of Nara's Hōryūji. The figure is, in the end, archaeology of an idea: art keeps finding new bodies for a being who has, by definition, promised not to stop being born.
lore.syncretism: The bodhisattva was Buddhism's great export. In China the male Avalokiteśvara became Guanyin, the most beloved goddess of East Asia — a transformation paralleled in Japan's Kannon and Korea's Gwan-eum, each culture finding in the vow the compassion it needed. Hinduism quietly adopted the figure: the Laṅkāvatāra-era Nārāyaṇa passages echo the Nārāyaṇa of the epics, and bodhisattva-like figures such as Hanumān in later bhakti are hard to imagine without the model. The Jesuits meeting Tibetan Buddhism classified the bodhisattvas as "Buddhist saints"; Romantic scholarship made them "altruistic saints of the East"; modern chaplaincy and engaged Buddhism have made the vow itself — beings are numberless, I vow to free them — a secular covenant recited in zendos, cathedrals, and hospitals. The word outgrew its religion and became a description of a human possibility: awakening on behalf of others.

entries.meaning: an Arhat or superior divinity with the Jainas

pronunciation.approximation: 'UHR-hut' — short vowels throughout; the h is a voiced breath between the syllables, and the final t is pure dental, not English 't'.
pronunciation.note: Tier 2: 'Arhat' is ASCII-canonical, with nothing lost in plain spelling; the restoration's weight is semantic — the title literally means 'worthy of gifts,' holiness as a completed and inspectable task.

domains.title: Arhat
domains.subtitle: The Worthy One — Perfection as a Finished Task
domains.lead: The arhat is the ideal of early Buddhism made flesh: one who has destroyed the taints, done what had to be done, and laid down the burden — freedom achieved in this life, by this person, without a god's intervention. The Theragāthā lets the finished saints speak for themselves.

cards.name: Worthy of Gifts
cards.desc: The literal sense — āhūneyyo, 'worthy of offerings,' the field of merit for gods and men alike.

cards.name: The Task Complete
cards.desc: The canonical formula: 'done is what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the goal' — the end of need itself.

cards.name: The Four Stages
cards.desc: Stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat — the graduated ladder to the deathless, rung by rung.

cards.name: The Sixteen Lohans
cards.desc: In China the arhat ideal became an immortal garrison — sixteen great disciples commanded to guard the Dharma until Maitreya comes.

symbols.name: The begging bowl
symbols.meaning: The arhat's only possession — and the reason the laity feed him: the worthy one is a field of merit, and a donation ripens

symbols.name: The crutch and long eyebrows
symbols.meaning: The lohans' immortal attributes in Chinese art — longevity so extreme it needs support, and sight so deep it overgrows

symbols.name: The flame of the taints extinguished
symbols.meaning: Nirvāṇa as a fire gone out — the arhat is the one whose fuel (rāga, dosa, moha) is spent; nothing more burns

symbols.name: The lion's roar of assurance
symbols.meaning: The arhat's declaration 'there is no more coming to any state of being' — certainty spoken from completion, not faith

symbols.name: The assembly of elders
symbols.meaning: Sāriputta and Moggallāna flanking the Buddha — wisdom and powers as the twin pillars of the arhat ideal

mythology.lead: The arhat has no biography because the arhat is a hundred biographies — the finished saints of the Theragāthā and Therīgāthā, the chief disciples of the canon, and in China a band of sixteen immortals commanded to wait out the ages for the next Buddha.

myths.title: Worthy of Gifts
myths.text: Arhat comes from √arh, "to deserve, to be worthy," with the participle -at — "the worthy one," one deserving of the alms of gods and men. The Buddha claimed it as his own foremost title: in the canonical litany he is arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, "arahant, fully self-awakened" — a claim whose audacity the Udāna records being tested in his lifetime, when rivals demanded he prove it. The commentarial definition sharpens the word into a checklist: one who has destroyed the taints (āsava), lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, and knows "there is no more of this." The Jaina tradition uses the same word in parallel: its twenty-four tīrthaṅkaras are arhats, worthy ones who ford the flood of rebirth. The mythic weight of a title: Buddhism made holiness a completed task, not a birth — and gave it a word anyone could check.

myths.title: Sāriputta and Moggallāna
myths.text: The Buddha named his two greatest arahants in the Etadagga verses (AN 1): Sāriputta, foremost in great wisdom — the Dhamma's marshal, who could unfold a single line into a hundred meanings and who, questioned on his deathbed in the Sāriputta Sutta (SN 47.19), replied only that there was nowhere he had ever clung; and Moggallāna, foremost in psychic powers, who humbled Brahmā's pride by shaking the Vejayanta palace with a toe (DN 11, Kevaṭṭa Sutta). Both were murdered — Moggallāna beaten to death by brigands — the Buddha predicting that the pair would die as the twin sāla trees fall. The Theragāthā lets the arahants speak in their own voices: "Cut down the whole forest of craving, not just one tree; from the jungle of craving, fear is born." The ideal is given a human face twice — the thinker and the wonder-worker — and both faces end in the one death arahants cannot refuse.

lore.culturalLegacy: The arhat's afterlife is the afterlife of the Theragāthā — a book of verses by the first saints, still chanted in Pāli lands, among the oldest autobiographies in the world. Chinese temples fill halls with lohan: the Five Hundred Arhats of Beijing's Biyun Si and the sixteen of Hangzhou's Jingshan Si are national treasures; Guanxiu's originals survive in Japan, designated national treasures there too. In Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia the arhat remains the living summit of the path — every forest monastery's kammaṭṭhāna tradition claims the title's ladder, rung by rung. And in the modern West, where "saint" had grown vague, "arhat" arrived with its etymology intact: the worthy one — holiness defined as a task you can finish.
lore.archaeology: The arhat's archaeology is the archaeology of the aniconic saṅgha. The Bharhut and Sanchi reliefs (2nd–1st c. BCE) show the great disciples flanking the empty throne — identifiable by label in Brahmi inscriptions: Sāriputa, Mogalāna, Maha Kāsava. The earliest anthropomorphic saṅgha images come from Gandhāra and Mathurā (1st–3rd c. CE): monks in patched robes, each with his attribute. The lohans' gallery in Chinese art is documented from the Tang — Guanxiu's sixteen (c. 891–901) survive in the Tokyo Seikado and Imperial Household collections — and the Five Hundred Lohans halls of the Song and Ming (Jingshan, Biyun, Baoguang monasteries) preserve the type at monumental scale. In Pāli lands, the arhat leaves no relic-cults of his own by design: the finished one, the tradition says, leaves nothing to enshrine but the teaching.
lore.syncretism: The Jaina sister-tradition used the same title in parallel: every tīrthaṅkara is an arhat, and the two śramaṇa movements argued over who deserved the word — evidence that it belonged to the age, not to one sect. Mahāyāna sūtras, building the rival bodhisattva ideal, chastised the arhat's "selfish" release (the Lotus Sūtra likens the arhat vehicle to a burning house escaped too soon), yet kept the title for the Buddha himself and for Śāriputra, whose "future Buddhahood" the Lotus explicitly prophesies. In China the arhat became the lohan — an immortal in Taoist dress — and in Tibet the great arhats of the canon were painted as the Buddha's original saṅgha, the lineage every ordination renews. Modern vipassanā movements restored the word to practice: the arhat is again a goal, not a museum piece.

entries.meaning: ‘sage of the Śākya clan’, epithet of the historical Buddha Siddhārtha Gautama, MW.

steps: Sanskrit Śākyamuni is written in Devanagari as शाक्यमुनि
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
