pronunciation.approximation: SHAHPSHOO — the first syllable is long, and the name ends in a bright, rounded 'oo' like 'shoe.'
pronunciation.note: Šāpšu is Tier-1: the caron on š and the macron on ā are distinctive features the ASCII form loses. The Ugaritic name is conventionally vocalized Šapšu or Šāpšu; the final u reflects the nominative case ending common in scholarly transliteration.

domains.title: Torch of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Sun, Justice, and the Messenger of El
domains.lead: Šāpšu is the sun goddess of Ugarit and Phoenicia, the brilliant torch that travels across the sky and descends into the underworld at evening. Unlike the male sun gods of Egypt and Mesopotamia, Šāpšu is female — one of the oldest female solar deities known — a radiant member of Ēl's court who sees everything and carries light to gods, mortals, and the dead.

cards.name: The Solar Torch
cards.desc: She is called 'Šāpšu the Torch' and 'the Luminary of the Gods' in Ugaritic hymns.

cards.name: All-Seeing Eye
cards.desc: Her light reveals hidden crimes and exposes those who break oaths before the gods.

cards.name: Guide of the Dead
cards.desc: She descends into the underworld and leads the shades of the dead to their rest.

cards.name: Messenger of El
cards.desc: She carries the decrees of the high god across heaven, earth, and the realm below.

symbols.name: Solar disk with rays
symbols.meaning: The sun's body; her light penetrates the hidden corners of earth and underworld alike

symbols.name: Torch or lamp
symbols.meaning: nrt ʾilm špš — 'the Lamp of the Gods' — her most frequent epithet (KTU 1.16 i)

symbols.name: Upraised hand or winged sun
symbols.meaning: The protective solar radiance of Phoenician and Aramaean royal iconography

symbols.name: Boat or chariot
symbols.meaning: Her vehicle across the day sky and through the night underworld

mythology.lead: Šāpšu's mythology is woven through the Baꜥal Cycle and Ugaritic ritual texts. She does not fight like ꜥAnat or Baꜥal; she illuminates, witnesses, and transmits divine will. Her descent into the underworld marks the boundary between day and night, life and death.

myths.title: The Lamp of the Gods
myths.text: No long narrative myth of Šāpšu survives; her personality must be gathered from epithets scattered across the tablets, and the most telling is nrt ʾilm špš — 'the Lamp of the Gods, Shapash' (KTU 1.16 i and parallels). The image is domestic and cosmic at once: the sun is the oil lamp of the divine household, lit each morning so that the gods can see their own world. Ugaritic hymns address her directly, and she is paired with the moon god Yarikh as the two great luminaries who measure out time, season, and oath. Where Baꜥal shouts, Šāpšu simply shines; her power is visibility itself. That the Levant imagined the sun as a woman — against the male suns of Egypt and Mesopotamia — is one of the quiet surprises of Bronze Age religion.

myths.title: Finding Baꜥal in the Dark
myths.text: When Baꜥal dies, the storm's sisters are helpless until the one goddess who can see in every direction is enlisted. In KTU 1.6 iv, ꜥAnat raises her voice to the sun goddess and begs Šāpšu to search for Baꜥal through the day and through the underworld itself. Šāpšu takes up the hunt — and it is she who finds the storm god dead, and she who tells ꜥAnat what must be done: bury Baꜥal on the heights of Zaphon and turn her rage on Mot. The scene assigns the goddess her exact cosmic office: illumination as the prerequisite of action. No one can fight for Baꜥal, mourn him, or bury him until someone has seen him. In a myth crowded with warriors, the decisive quest belongs to the light — and to the quiet goddess who carries it.

lore.culturalLegacy: The name Šāpšu survives less in popular culture than in scholarship, where she has become one of the most instructive figures of Ugaritic religion: proof that the Bronze Age Levant imagined the sun as a woman — a luminous, witnessing, underworld-traveling goddess rather than a warrior king in a solar boat. Phoenician inscriptions from across the Mediterranean still address her, and the winged sun spread over Near Eastern thrones is read by many scholars as her protective radiance. Modern feminist scholarship and Neopagan practice have reclaimed her as a symbol of clarity, justice, and the luminous feminine — a deity whose daily descent among the dead makes her a rare patron of honest sight: she sees the throne room and the grave with the same light.
lore.archaeology: Šāpshu is attested in the Ugaritic tablets from Ras Shamra (KTU corpus) and in Phoenician inscriptions across the Mediterranean. Her solar disk and winged sun imagery appear on Phoenician seals, ivories, and stelae. The Ugaritic texts preserve hymns and ritual references that show her importance in royal cult and daily religion, though no temple exclusively dedicated to her has been securely identified.
lore.syncretism: Šāpšu's nearest relative is the Mesopotamian sun god Shamash — another all-seeing luminary who patrols heaven and underworld and stands witness to oaths — though Šāpšu is a goddess where Shamash is a god, one of the few female solar deities of the ancient Near East. The winged sun disk that spreads over Phoenician, Aramaean, and Israelite royal iconography carries the protective radiance of the same solar court. In the Hebrew Bible the sun (šemeš) is never personified as a goddess, yet the Psalms still imagine it running its course like a bridegroom — an image that may dimly remember her. Later Greco-Roman tradition had no direct translation for a female sun, which is precisely why she matters: she shows how much was lost when the Levantine sky was redrawn by male suns.

pronunciation.note: Dāgan is a Tier-1 restoration because the long vowel ā is preserved. The name is common Semitic but its precise etymology is uncertain; it has been connected with 'grain' (Hebrew dāgān) and with 'fish' (Hebrew dāḡ), though the former is more widely accepted for the Northwest Semitic grain god.

domains.title: Lord of Grain
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Agriculture, and Divine Fatherhood
domains.lead: Dāgan is the grain god of the ancient Levant, the divine power who fills the storehouses and makes the fields fertile. In Ugaritic myth he is the father of Baal and the patron of the agricultural cycle; in Philistine religion he is the national god whose temple Samson pulls down. His domain is not the storm on the mountain but the quiet miracle by which seed becomes bread.

cards.name: God of Grain
cards.desc: His name and cult center on wheat, barley, and the harvest that sustains city and village alike.

cards.name: Father of Baal
cards.desc: In Ugaritic texts Dāgan is Baal's father, grounding the storm god's power in the agricultural cycle.

cards.name: Temple at Ugarit
cards.desc: A major temple area at Ugarit has long been attributed to Dāgan, receiving royal offerings.

cards.name: Philistine Dagon
cards.desc: Worshipped by the Philistines as a national god; his temples at Gaza and Ashdod are broken by Israel's heroes.

symbols.name: Plowed field

mythology.lead: Dāgan is a father figure rather than a warrior. In the Ugaritic texts he receives offerings and grants blessings; in the Hebrew Bible he is a foreign god whose temples symbolize Philistine power — and fall. His myths are few, but his importance is immense: he is the god of the staple crop on which every Near Eastern society depended.

myths.title: The Blessing of the Storehouse
myths.text: The Ugaritic tablets never tell a story about Dāgan; they do something more like accounting for him. Offering lists and ritual texts record his sacrifices at planting and harvest, and throughout the Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6) the storm god is styled bn dgn, 'son of Dāgan' — even when the plot sends messengers hurrying 'to the house of Dāgan' to announce Baal's victories (KTU 1.3 III). His temple stood among the great shrines of Ugarit, and his cult city Tuttul, on the middle Euphrates, gave him a second throne older than the city itself. The picture is of a god who sits at the center of the economy rather than at the center of the plot: the father of the storm because the storm is only the rain; the rain is only the grain; and the grain is his. Baal rides the clouds, but Dāgan owns the granary they fill — in a Bronze Age city, the more quietly tremendous office.

myths.title: The Feast That Buried Samson
myths.text: Judges 16:23–30 sets the scene in the temple of Dagon at Gaza, where the Philistine lords have gathered 'to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice,' saying 'our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand.' They call the blinded prisoner out to entertain them — 'about three thousand men and women' crowding the roof to watch. Samson prays for his strength back, embraces the two central pillars, and pulls the house down on the lords and all the people, dying with them. The narrative is the Bible's blackest comedy of divine irony: the victory feast becomes the funeral, the captive becomes the demolition, and the god's temple becomes his people's tomb. For the storytellers of Israel, Dagon's feast is what idolatry looks like from inside the rubble — power holding a banquet on a load-bearing floor.

lore.culturalLegacy: Dāgan survives in the Bible as the Philistine god toppled by Samson and humbled by the ark, and his name echoes in the Hebrew word for grain. In modern fantasy and role-playing games, 'Dagon' often appears as a tentacled or fish-like sea monster — a distortion of the ancient grain god produced by the medieval iconographic confusion. For scholars of religion he is a key case study in how an agricultural deity becomes a national patron and then a symbol of the enemy's false confidence. And the word itself never stopped feeding people: every speaker of Hebrew who says dāgān for grain is keeping the god's name in daily use, four thousand years after his first altar.
lore.archaeology: At Ugarit (Ras Shamra), a large temple area by the royal zone has long been attributed to Dāgan — the identification goes back to Schaeffer's excavations, though the tablets name several temples and the attributions are not all secure. On the middle Euphrates, German excavations at Tell Bi'a (ancient Tuttul) uncovered a major temple precinct with connections to Dāgan's cult. The Mari tablets supply the textual layer: dedications and oracles spanning the eighteenth century BCE. In Philistia, the biblical temples at Gaza and Ashdod have never been securely located — the story of Samson's demolition is beyond archaeological reach — but Philistine material culture at sites such as Tel Miqne (Ekron) frames the milieu. The famous 'fish-god' Dagon is a medieval iconographic development without ancient Near Eastern support.
lore.syncretism: Dāgan's cult spread from Mesopotamia to the Levantine coast and was adopted by the Philistines after their settlement in Canaan — a grain god inherited, or seized, as a national patron. The Hebrew noun dāgān, 'grain,' shares his root, though which came first — the god from the word or the word from the god — is undecidable. Some ancient interpreters, hearing the echo of dāḡ, 'fish,' invented a fish-god: the medieval and early modern image of a half-man, half-fish Dagon is that pun's long afterlife, with no support in the older Northwest Semitic evidence. In Ugarit the syncretism runs the other way: Dāgan is the father of Baal, marrying agricultural fertility to the storm in a single divine household — the Levant's quietest and most consequential theological merger.

domains.title: ARINNA — Queen of Heaven
domains.subtitle: Solar Sovereignty · State Cult · Divine Kingship
domains.lead: Arinna is the Sun Goddess of Arinna, supreme deity of the Hittite state pantheon. Her cult city made her the divine patron of Hittite kingship, and every monarch styled himself her beloved son. Her radiance guarantees fertility, justice, and cosmic order; prayers to her are among the most elaborate compositions in the Hittite language.

cards.name: Queen of Heaven
cards.desc: Supreme deity of the Hittite state pantheon, enthroned above gods and kings.

cards.name: Sun Disk
cards.desc: The radiant sun wheel whose light sustains grain, law, and life across Hatti.

cards.name: Divine Mother of Kings
cards.desc: Hittite kings are her beloved children; her blessing legitimates royal rule.

cards.name: Cult Center at Arinna
cards.desc: The city of Arinna housed her chief temple and seasonal state festivals.

symbols.name: Sun disk
symbols.meaning: The radiant wheel of the sun, source of life and royal authority.

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: Her animal companion and symbol of sovereign power.

symbols.name: Throne
symbols.meaning: The seat of supreme kingship in heaven and on earth.

symbols.name: Golden crown
symbols.meaning: The solar diadem that marks her as queen of the gods.

symbols.name: Winged sun
symbols.meaning: The sun in motion across the sky, seeing all that happens below.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Arinna is not a cycle of adventures but a theology of sovereignty. Her prayers present her as the all-seeing, all-ruling sun who knows the hearts of gods and mortals and who holds the king accountable for justice.

myths.title: One Goddess, Many Names
myths.text: The great prayer of King Muwatalli (CTH 376) opens by walking the goddess's names across the empire: my lady, queen of all the lands — in Hatti she is the Sun-goddess of Arinna; in Arzawa, the Sun-goddess of Arzawa; in the land of Lycia they call her Mother; and so on through the subject kingdoms, name after name, land after land, down toward the Syrian coast. The passage is the earliest surviving theology of a multi-ethnic state: one sovereign radiance, known in every subject people's tongue. Arinna is her headquarters — the city whose temple housed the state cult — but the prayer insists she is no local deity. What the Hittite empire held together by treaty and dynastic marriage, it worshipped as a single sun with many local spellings; and the king who prays does so as her servant, asking the queen of all lands to remember her servant in Hatti. The theology is deliberately imperial: as the sun sees every land, so the goddess rules them all, and so, by her delegation, does her beloved son.

myths.title: The Sun Who Crosses the Sky
myths.text: Each dawn the Sun-goddess rises in the east and rides her chariot across the heavens, and her light is the empire's clock: oaths were sworn to her as she cleared the horizon, festivals opened at her rising, and treaties took force under her witnessing disk. Sun-disc emblems cap Hittite stelae and gate monuments at Boğazköy, and winged suns fly over the empire's seals. At night she does not simply vanish: Hittite ritual knows a chthonic counterpart, the Sun-goddess of the Earth, who receives the dead and the setting light, so that solar sovereignty continues beneath the ground — a nocturnal voyage scholars have long compared, cautiously, to the Mesopotamian sun's nightly passage. Her heat is not the devouring fire of the desert but the ordered warmth that ripens the grain of Hatti; her regularity, not her brilliance, is her divinity. A goddess who never surprises her worshippers was the perfect patron of a bureaucratic state: in her courses, as in its archives, everything came round on time.

lore.culturalLegacy:
Arinna survives as a paradigm of sacred kingship and solar queenship.

Scholars of ancient Near Eastern religion study her cult to understand how a state creates a national deity, and feminist historians of religion note the unusual prominence of a supreme goddess in a major Bronze Age empire. Her name appears in studies of Hittite prayer, royal ideology, and comparative solar mythology. For PuniCodex, Arinna represents the restoration of a name that once stood at the center of an imperial state: the queen of heaven whose light was synonymous with legitimate rule.
lore.archaeology: The texts that name Arinna were excavated from the Hittite royal archives at Boğazköy-Hattusa and related sites in central Anatolia, including temple storerooms and administrative buildings within the citadel. The tablets belong to the corpus of Hittite cuneiform literature preserved in the imperial chancery, with duplicates and parallels in Hurrian, Hattic, Luwian, and other Anatolian traditions. Many were written or copied during the Empire period (c. 1400–1180 BCE), though some compositions may descend from older oral or written sources. The clay tablets were baked, either deliberately or by the fire that destroyed the city, which helped preserve them for modern excavation and study.
lore.syncretism:
Arinna absorbed and transformed older Hattic and Mesopotamian solar traditions.

The Hattian sun-god Estan was originally male; in the Hittite state pantheon the solar deity of Arinna became female and supreme, probably under Hurrian and Syrian influence. She has been compared to the Mesopotamian sun-god Shamash, who also oversees justice, and to the Egyptian sun-god Re as a royal patron. Yet her theology is distinct: she is not primarily a warrior but a mother-queen whose radiance is the condition for ordered life. The shift from a male to a female supreme solar deity is one of the most striking features of Hittite religious history.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Hittite cuneiform as 𒀭𒌓 𒌷𒀀𒊑𒅖𒈾 — the divine sun-god logogram combined with the city name Arinna. The scholarly transliteration is dUTU URUArinna. The Unicode restoration Arinna reproduces the capitalized citation form used in modern Hittitology; the ASCII form arinniti is a DNS compromise that does not correspond to the ancient spelling.

domains.title: Telipinu — The Vanishing God of the Hittite Plain
domains.subtitle: Agriculture, Anger, and Ritual Restoration
domains.lead:
Telipinu is the Hittite god who makes the grain grow — and the god who, when offended, takes his gift away. His myth is not a cosmic battle but a domestic crisis of divine temper: the deity storms out of the assembly, slams the door, and wanders off in a rage. Behind him the fields wither, cattle abandon their calves, mothers forget their children, and even the cooking fire goes out. The world does not end by flood or dragon; it ends because a god has left the room.

The Telipinu Myth (CTH 324) is one of the best-preserved Hittite religious narratives. It is also a ritual text: the story is performed in order to undo the very disaster it describes. Telipinu is therefore a god of restorable order — his absence is catastrophic, but his return, properly negotiated by magic and apology, brings everything back.

cards.name: The Vanishing God
cards.desc: When offended, Telipinu puts his right shoe on his left foot and his left shoe on his right foot, then storms into the wilderness — a formal gesture of inverted order.

cards.name: Famine & Forgetfulness
cards.desc: His absence dries up springs, kills the grain, and unbinds social bonds: sheep reject their lambs and mothers turn away from their children.

cards.name: The Bee Messenger
cards.desc: The gods send a bee to find Telipinu in the meadow; it stings him awake, inflaming his rage until the goddess Kamrušepa performs the calming ritual.

cards.name: Ritual Return
cards.desc: Kamrušepa, goddess of magic and healing, recites the ritual that turns Telipinu's anger aside and leads him home, restoring fertility and plenty.

symbols.name: Plough
symbols.meaning: The agricultural tool that defines Telipinu's blessing and the furrow he makes fertile

symbols.name: Bee
symbols.meaning: The divine messenger that finds Telipinu in hiding; also an emblem of Anatolian ritual language

symbols.name: Pine or staff
symbols.meaning: Telipinu is often depicted leaning on a staff; the pine is associated with his resting and return

symbols.name: Reversed shoes
symbols.meaning: The sign of a world turned upside-down when the god leaves in anger

symbols.name: Wagon or chariot
symbols.meaning: The vehicle in which Telipinu is ceremonially brought back to the city and the temple

mythology.lead: The mythology of Telipinu survives in Hittite tablets from Ḫattuša, above all in CTH 324. It is a myth about the fragility of fertility: the grain, the cattle, and the family all depend on a god who can choose to leave. The drama is not cosmic combat but divine temperament and its ritual repair.

myths.title: The God Who Stormed Out
myths.text: The myth opens in the divine assembly, where something unknown offends Telipinu. He rises, puts his shoes on the wrong feet, and leaves in a fury. As he goes, 'the mist seized the windows, smoke seized the house, in the fireplace the logs were stifled, at the altars the gods were stifled, in the fold the sheep were stifled, in the corral the cattle were stifled; the mother ignored her child, the ewe ignored her lamb.' The cosmos does not collapse; it simply forgets how to flourish.

myths.title: The Search in the Wilderness
myths.text: The great gods send out the Storm-God of Heaven, the Sun-Goddess of Arinna, and others to find Telipinu, but none can locate him. Finally the bee is dispatched: 'Go, search for Telipinu in the high country, in the meadow, in the swamp, and sting him!' The bee finds him asleep in a meadow or among the mountains, stings him, and wakes him — but this only enrages him further. He multiplies the disasters he has already caused.

lore.culturalLegacy: Telipinu is one of the most accessible Hittite deities for modern readers because his myth is so recognisably human: a family member storms out, the household falls apart, and a careful apology is required to restore harmony. In Assyriology and Hittitology, the Telipinu Myth is a standard text for teaching Hittite language and religion. Its legacy is the idea that fertility is a relationship, not a machine — maintained by ritual attention and capable of being ruptured by neglect or offense. For PuniCodex, Telipinu also illustrates the plain Tier-2 form: a name whose restoration preserves only its proper capitalization, inviting visitors to ask what the cuneiform recorded and what the voice once said.
lore.archaeology: The Telipinu myth is attested on cuneiform tablets excavated at Ḫattuša (modern Boğazkale), the Hittite capital, and in fragments from other Anatolian sites. The best-preserved manuscripts belong to the archives of the Great Temple and the House on the Slope. Telipinu also had a cult seat at the city of Tawiniya, and offerings to him appear in Hittite festival texts and royal oracle inquiries.
lore.syncretism: Telipinu belongs to a broader Anatolian type: the 'disappearing god' (der verschwundene Gott), a category first named by Hittitologists for deities whose absence causes agricultural and social collapse. Similar patterns appear for the weather-god of Nerik, the vegetation god Halki, and, in Greek Anatolia, figures such as Attis and Adonis whose death or departure marks the failing year. Unlike the Mesopotamian flood or the Egyptian solar eclipse, the Hittite crisis is not cosmic but relational: the god is offended, leaves, and must be coaxed back. This pattern influenced later Anatolian and Greek conceptions of dying-and-rising vegetation gods, though direct genealogical links remain debated.

domains.title: INARAS — Mistress of the Wild
domains.subtitle: Wild Animals · Hunt · Steppe
domains.lead: Inaras is the Hittite Mistress of Animals — goddess of the wild herds and open steppe — and the architect of the gods' most famous victory. When the storm-god lay defeated by the dragon Illuyanka, it was Inaras who set the trap, recruited a mortal ally, and fed the dragon to his own appetite: cunning, sovereignty over the wild, and an alliance across the divine-mortal boundary in a single story.

cards.name: Mistress of Animals
cards.desc: She rules the wild herds and the creatures of the steppe.

cards.name: The Trap
cards.desc: She devises the feast that lures the dragon Illuyanka to his doom.

cards.name: Steppe Wanderer
cards.desc: Her home is the open grassland, not the palace or the temple.

cards.name: Divine Huntress
cards.desc: She knows the ways of animals and the arts of the chase.

symbols.name: Gazelle
symbols.meaning: The swift animal of the steppe, emblem of her wild domain.

symbols.name: Bow and arrow
symbols.meaning: The tools of the hunt and the means by which she governs animals.

symbols.name: Feast

symbols.name: Steppe grass
symbols.meaning: The open land that is her kingdom.

symbols.name: Serpent/dragon

mythology.lead: Inaras is best known from a single, brilliant episode, but that episode reveals a goddess of cunning, sovereignty over animals, and alliance between divine and mortal — and the text that tells it belongs to one of the oldest dragon-fights in the Indo-European world. Her myths survive on a handful of clay tablets and in the spring festival that kept them alive.

myths.title: The Feast of the Dragon
myths.text: After the storm-god Tarḫunash is defeated by the dragon Illuyanka, it is Inaras who acts. She prepares an enormous feast — beer, wine, and every kind of food laid out by a spring — and goes to the mortal Ḫupašiya with a bargain: help me trap the dragon, and I will sleep with you. Ḫupašiya agrees. The dragon and his children come to the feast, eat and drink until they cannot fit back into their hole, and lie helpless; Ḫupašiya binds them, and Tarḫunash destroys them (CTH 321; Hoffner, Hittite Myths, 2nd ed.). The Hittite composition is linguistically old, and the scene has the feel of high archaic storytelling. Its surprise is the weapon: the dragon dies not of thunder but of appetite — the Mistress of Animals wins with hospitality sharpened into a trap, and the storm-god she saves never even appears at the feast.

myths.title: Inaras and Ḫupašiya
myths.text: The sequel is darker. Inaras warns Ḫupašiya not to look out the window while she is away on the gods' business; he looks, sees his wife and children, is overcome, and flees. The goddess hunts him down and kills him, and the story ends — as Hittite myths of this kind characteristically end — with the founding of a cult: offerings in memory of Ḫupašiya, so that the mortal helper who made the victory possible would not be forgotten (CTH 321). The text is bound to the Purulli, the spring festival of the storm-god, in whose ritual calendar the dragon's defeat was annually renewed. The mortal's fate is the myth's price-tag: divine bargains in Hatti are paid in full, and the helper who looks back loses everything — except a cult, which is immortality of a strictly Hittite kind.

lore.culturalLegacy:
Inaras survives in scholarly memory as the Hittite Mistress of Animals and the architect of the dragon's defeat.

She appears in studies of Indo-European dragon combat, comparative mythology, and the role of goddesses in ancient Near Eastern narrative. The Myth of Illuyanka is one of the most widely cited Hittite texts, and Inaras's role in it makes her a key figure for understanding how divine and mortal agency interact in Hittite thought. For PuniCodex, she represents the wild, cunning dimension of the pantheon: the goddess who knows the borderlands and how to turn an enemy's appetite into his destruction.
lore.archaeology: The texts that name Inaras were excavated from the Hittite royal archives at Boğazköy-Hattusa and related sites in central Anatolia, including temple storerooms and administrative buildings within the citadel. The tablets belong to the corpus of Hittite cuneiform literature preserved in the imperial chancery, with duplicates and parallels in Hurrian, Hattic, Luwian, and other Anatolian traditions. Many were written or copied during the Empire period (c. 1400–1180 BCE), though some compositions may descend from older oral or written sources. The clay tablets were baked, either deliberately or by the fire that destroyed the city, which helped preserve them for modern excavation and study.
lore.syncretism:
Inaras shares traits with several ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern figures.

Her role as mistress of animals recalls the Greek Potnia Theron, the Mistress of Animals who presides over wild creatures, and Artemis in her capacity as huntress. The dragon-slaying story has close Indo-European parallels, especially the dragon fight of the storm-god. Inaras's liaison with a mortal helper also resembles stories in which a goddess enlists a human hero. Yet her Hittite form is distinct: she is not a virgin huntress but a sovereign of the steppe who uses sex, food, and cunning as weapons.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Hittite cuneiform as 𒄿𒈾𒀸 (i-na-ra-aš). The Unicode restoration Inaras gives the scholarly citation form; the ASCII form inaras is a domain-name convenience.

domains.title: ALALU — The First Throne of Heaven
domains.subtitle: Primordial Kingship · Heavenly Sovereignty · Dynastic Succession
domains.lead:
Alalu is the first king of the gods in Hittite and Hurrian mythology, the original occupant of the celestial throne before Anu the sky-god and long before the storm-god Teššub. His reign is narrated in the 'Kingship in Heaven' myth, a Near Eastern succession story that parallels the Greek sequence of Ouranos, Kronos, and Zeus. For nine years Alalu rules in heaven; then his servant Anu rises against him, and Alalu flees to the dark earth below. The kingship he loses becomes the inheritance that shapes the entire Hittite pantheon.

This temple treats Alalu as the archetype of primordial sovereignty: the ruler whose authority is ancient, legitimate, and yet destined to be overthrown. He is not a storm-god or a creator; he is the first holder of the mandate of heaven, the figure against whom every later king defines himself.

cards.name: The Nine-Year Reign
cards.desc: Alalu sits on the throne of heaven for a fixed term of nine years before Anu succeeds him — a precise motif of cyclic kingship.

cards.name: The Servant Who Succeeded
cards.desc: Anu is Alalu's servant; his rise reverses the social order and begins the succession that leads to Kumarbi and Teššub.

cards.name: The Dark Earth Below
cards.desc: Defeated, Alalu descends to the dark earth — not a punishment but the place from which older powers watch newer gods reign.

cards.name: The Storm-God's Ancestry
cards.desc: Through Kumarbi, Alalu becomes the grandfather of Teššub, so the defeated first king fathers the line that rules the storm.

symbols.name: Throne
symbols.meaning: The first seat of divine kingship in heaven

symbols.name: Nine years

mythology.lead: Alalu's mythology is almost entirely contained in the 'Kingship in Heaven' narrative, but that single text is enough to make him one of the most important figures in Hittite and comparative mythology. He is the beginning of the dynasty of heaven.

myths.title: The First Reign
myths.text:
The Hittite 'Kingship in Heaven' myth (CTH 344) opens with Alalu seated on the throne in heaven. He is the first to hold kingship among the gods, and for nine years his word is law while mighty Anu, first among the gods, stands before him and passes him the cup — the ritual posture of a courtier before his king. The text, translated from a Hurrian original, presents kingship not as eternal but as a rotating office: even the highest god may be replaced when his term is fulfilled. Alalu's reign is therefore the prototype of legitimate rule, not its negation.

The fixed term is the text's most remarkable idea: kingship among the gods is an office with a lease. Where Greek theogony leaves succession to violence alone, the Hurrian scribes framed it as lawful rotation — Alalu's fall is the constitution working, not the constitution breaking.

myths.title: Anu Rises Against Alalu
myths.text:
After nine years, Alalu's servant Anu confronts him and defeats him. Alalu flees 'down to the dark earth' — a descent that removes him from active rule but does not annihilate him. Anu then takes the kingship and rules in turn for nine years, until the pattern repeats: his own servant Kumarbi rises, and Anu flees heaven with Kumarbi clinging to him, biting off his genitals and becoming thereby pregnant with the storm-god Teššub (Kingship in Heaven; Song of Kumarbi, CTH 345).

The myth thereby makes revolution structural rather than exceptional: every servant stands in the relation to his master that Anu stood in to Alalu, and the text presents that fact as an order of the cosmos, not a scandal. The dynasty of heaven is a relay of coups, each one legal the moment it succeeds.

lore.culturalLegacy:
Alalu survives chiefly as a comparative-mythological type: the first king of heaven.

Modern scholars cite the 'Kingship in Heaven' text as a key witness for the Near Eastern background of Greek theogony, and Alalu is regularly compared to Ouranos and Saturnus. He appears in encyclopedias of mythology and in studies of Hittite religion, but has little direct afterlife in popular culture — precisely because his myth is about abdication and memory rather than heroic action. For PuniCodex, Alalu is a restoration of the origin-point of kingship: the name that marks where the mandate of heaven begins. The name still means: the throne before the throne.
lore.archaeology: The 'Kingship in Heaven' myth is preserved in Hittite cuneiform tablets excavated at Boğazköy-Hattusa, the Hittite capital, notably KUB 33.120 with its duplicate and continuation. The tablets belong to the archives of the Hittite royal citadel and represent a Hittite translation or adaptation of a Hurrian original. No independent Hurrian manuscript has survived, so the Hittite copies are the sole direct witnesses to Alalu's myth.
lore.syncretism:
Alalu belongs to a widespread ancient Near Eastern and Mediterranean pattern of primordial king-gods who are overthrown by their successors.

The closest parallel is the Greek succession Ouranos → Kronos → Zeus: Ouranos, like Alalu, is the first celestial ruler who is deposed by a younger power and withdraws from the active cosmos. The Hittite-Hurrian version, however, makes the process explicit and contractual: each king rules for nine years before being replaced. Roman Saturnus preserves a memory of the golden-age king deposed by Jupiter. In Mesopotamian tradition, the succession of divine kingship from Anu to Enlil and later to Marduk follows a comparable logic, though Alalu himself is foreign to Sumerian and Akkadian sources. The name Alalu has no secure etymology; it may be Hurrian, Hattic, or a substrate survival from an earlier Anatolian layer.

pronunciation.note: Uppsala is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The holiest documented place in the Norse world carries a name of seven ordinary letters; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Temple, Freyr, Sacred Grove
domains.subtitle: The Upper Halls of the Swedish Kings
domains.lead: Uppsalir — 'the Upper Halls' — is the one sanctuary of the Norse world the medieval record describes beam by beam and tree by tree. Adam of Bremen, writing about 1075 from the reports of the Danish court, gives us the golden temple where [[thor|Þórr]] sat enthroned between Wodan and Fricco; the sacred grove beside it, every tree made divine by the offerings hung in its branches; and the nine-day festival, renewed every ninth year, at which nine males of every living kind were given to the gods. Snorri's Ynglingasaga makes the place the seat of [[freyr|Freyr]] himself — the god who built the temple, endowed it with the Uppsala wealth, and lies in a mound beside it. Below the ridge the three royal mounds of Gamla Uppsala still stand, the largest barrows in Sweden, the graves of kings the poems call the Scylfings.

cards.name: The Golden Temple
cards.desc: The temple at Uppsala that Adam of Bremen describes as entirely decked with gold, a golden chain hanging from its gable — the cult house of the Swedish commonwealth.

cards.name: The Sacred Grove
cards.desc: The grove adjoining the temple, every tree held sacred because of the death and decay of the victims — men, horses, and dogs hung among the branches.

cards.name: The Nine-Year Festival
cards.desc: Every ninth year, nine days of sacrifice at the turn of the cycle, one offering each day, nine of every male creature — a rite from which no Swede could absent himself without paying a price.

cards.name: The Royal Mounds
cards.desc: The three great barrows of Gamla Uppsala, cremation graves of sixth- and seventh-century kings; Ynglingasaga buries Freyr himself in such a mound on the same ground.

symbols.name: The gilded temple
symbols.meaning: The gold-decked hall where the triad sat enthroned — the sacral core of Swedish kingship, visible wealth offered to the gods

symbols.name: The enthroned triad
symbols.meaning: Þórr central with his sceptre, Wodan armed like Mars, Fricco shaped for peace and pleasure — sovereignty, war, and fertility enshrined in one room

symbols.name: The sacred grove
symbols.meaning: Trees made divine by sacrifice — the boundary where offering becomes landscape and the forest itself turns temple

symbols.name: The hanging offerings
symbols.meaning: Men, horses, and dogs suspended in the branches, nine of every kind — the commonwealth renewed at the price of nine-year blood

symbols.name: The royal mound
symbols.meaning: The barrow of kings and, by Snorri's account, of Freyr himself — dynasty made continuous with the god who endowed it

mythology.lead: Uppsala's dossier is not a god's biography but a sanctuary's record — and it is the fullest any Norse holy place receives. Adam of Bremen describes the temple and its rites from the testimony of the Danish court a generation before the old religion died in Sweden; Snorri gives the site its founding god and its dynasty; the saga of Hrólfr kraki sets a famous treasure-flight on the plain below it. Between the four witnesses, the Upper Halls emerge as the one place where the whole northern religion can be watched at prayer.

myths.title: The Golden Temple
myths.text:
Adam of Bremen, archbishop's scholar at Hamburg-Bremen, sets down about 1075 the most exact account of Norse cult that survives. Near Sigtuna, he writes, stands a famous temple called Ubsola, entirely decked with gold, and in it the people worship the statues of three gods: the most powerful, Thor, occupies the throne in the middle of the hall; on either side stand Wodan and Fricco. Thor, Adam explains, governs the air, thunder, lightning, winds, rains, fair weather and crops, and holds his sceptre like Jove; Wodan, 'that is, Frenzy', rules war and gives men strength against enemies, carved in the likeness of an armed man as Mars is shown; Fricco, bestower of peace and pleasure on mortals, is shaped with an immense phallus. Each god has his priests, and the people's vows follow need: in plague or famine they sacrifice to Thor, for war to Wodan, for weddings to Fricco. Adam worked from the reports of the Danish king Sven Estridsen, and the scholia fill in further colour — the temple ringed by a golden chain hanging from its gable, the feasting within.

What the account gives the record is irreplaceable: a working temple of the Æsir described in its last generation, by a churchman who wanted it abolished and could not help seeing it clearly.

myths.title: The Nine-Day Sacrifice
myths.text:
Adam's second chapter on the site records the great communal rite. Every nine years, he writes, all the provinces of Sweden hold a solemn assembly at Uppsala, from which no one may purchase exemption; every man sends offerings. The sacrifice is of this kind: of every living creature that is male, nine head are offered, by whose blood it is the custom to placate the gods. The bodies are hung in a grove adjoining the temple, a grove so sacred to the heathens that each tree is believed divine because of the death and putrefaction of the victims. Dogs and horses hang there with the men, and one of the Christians told Adam he had seen seventy-two bodies hanging together. The incantations sung at the rite, Adam adds, are so disgraceful that it is better to say nothing of them.

A scholion adds the spring beside the temple in which a living man was drowned; if he was not found again, the people's wish would be granted. Every element — the nine-year cycle, the nine of each kind, the grove, the hanging — belongs to the deep grammar of Germanic sacrifice: Thietmar of Merseburg records a parallel nine-year rite at Lejre in Denmark, and Tacitus had described the sacred groves of the continental Germans a thousand years before. Uppsala is where that grammar has its fullest surviving page.

lore.culturalLegacy: Uppsala never stopped being the stage on which Sweden remembers itself. The old cult centre became the church's: Gamla Uppsala was the seat of Sweden's first archbishopric from 1164 until the see moved to Östra Aros — the modern city of Uppsala — in 1273, and the medieval church still stands on the artificial plateau where Adam's temple is sought. Nineteenth-century romantic nationalism made the mounds the nation's Westminster; their excavation in 1846–47, ordered to still public argument about what they contained, yielded the cremated kings of the Vendel era and made Old Uppsala the birthplace of Swedish archaeology. The university at Uppsala, founded in 1477, gave the name a second, learned fame that now outruns the temple's. For modern scholarship the site remains the test case for the union of cult and kingship in the North — Olof Sundqvist's Freyr's Offspring is built on its ground — and for modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities the grove and the mounds are the north's most numinous standing landscape, the one address where the old religion can still be visited rather than merely read about.
lore.archaeology: Uppsala is the rare Norse holy place where the texts can be tested against the ground. The three royal mounds of Gamla Uppsala — the largest barrows in Sweden — were opened in 1846–47 under Bror Emil Hildebrand: beneath each lay a cremation of the sixth or seventh century, burned in its finery and sealed under birch bark, with weapons, game-boards, and sacrificed animals, the graves of the dynasty the poems call Ynglings or Scylfings. Beside them the medieval church — seat of Sweden's first archbishop from 1164 — stands on a great artificial plateau of levelled terraces, the one construction on the site that matches Adam's scale; Sune Lindqvist's excavation beneath the church floor in 1926 revealed the postholes of a very large wooden building, and the argument whether it was the pagan temple, a royal feasting hall, or both has run ever since — Olof Sundqvist's work on the Svea cult-and-kingship complex is the standard modern frame. The surrounding landscape is dense with the dynasty's furniture: boat-graves at Valsgärde a few miles north, the Vendel graves across the river, hundreds of smaller mounds on the Fyris plain. No runestone carves the place-name itself; the Younger Futhark rendering ᚢᛒᛒᛋᛅᛚᛅ (ubbsala) is a normalized reconstruction, though Uppland is the richest runestone province in Scandinavia.
lore.syncretism: Uppsala's closest kin are not gods but holy places. Thietmar of Merseburg, writing two generations before Adam, describes the nine-year sacrifice at Lejre in Denmark — ninety-nine men, horses, dogs and cocks offered to placate the gods — the Danish counterpart of the Uppsala rite and the proof that Adam's nine-year cycle was pan-Scandinavian grammar, not local invention. Behind both stands the deepest stratum: Tacitus' Germania records the sacred grove of the Semnones, entered bound and widened by human sacrifice, and the grove and wagon of Nerthus — the goddess whose name is the feminine counterpart of Njörðr, father of the Freyr whose seat was Uppsala. The enthroned triad itself has been read since Dumézil against the archaic Roman triad of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus — sovereignty, war, and the fertile commons — though Adam's own glosses (Thor as Jove, Wodan as Mars, Fricco as peace and pleasure) show the comparison began with the medieval churchman, not the modern comparatist. Modern handbooks urge the same caution they urge for Adam's secondhand testimony: Simek, Orchard, and Lindow treat the account as the fullest and most dangerous source for Norse cult — a Christian observer describing the rite he wanted abolished, through informants a kingdom away. What remains undisputed is the place: no other site in the North is so continuously written about, from the royal mounds' century to the last generation of the old religion.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Uppsalir — a nominative plural, genitive Uppsala, already plain ASCII with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚢᛒᛒᛋᛅᛚᛅ (ubbsala), a normalized phonetic reconstruction, since the sixteen-rune row distinguishes neither b from p nor long from short vowels. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: uppsala.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

domains.title: The Twilight River
domains.subtitle: Devotion, the Sangam, and Kṛṣṇa's Own Water
domains.lead: Yamunā is the second of India's great river-goddesses and the first of Kṛṣṇa's loves: daughter of the sun-god, sister of death, the dark-blue water on whose banks the cowherd god danced, battled the serpent, and made an entire land his memory.

cards.name: The Sangam
cards.desc: Her meeting with Gaṅgā at Prayāgrāj — the trivenī, the holiest confluence in India.

cards.name: Kāliya
cards.desc: The poison-serpent she hosted until the child-god danced on its heads — the river cleansed by dance.

cards.name: Daughter of Sūrya
cards.desc: The sun's daughter, Yama's twin — light and death sharing one water.

cards.name: Vṛndāvana
cards.desc: The pastoral heartland where Kṛṣṇa's līlā plays out on her banks.

symbols.name: The dark-blue water
symbols.meaning: Her twilight color — the river of the blue god

symbols.name: The tortoise
symbols.meaning: Her patient mount — the current that carries everything slowly

symbols.name: The confluence
symbols.meaning: Her union with Gaṅgā — twilight meeting clarity

symbols.name: The ghāṭs of Braj

symbols.name: The sangam kalaśa

mythology.lead: Yamunā's myths bind the solar and the pastoral: the sun's twin daughter flowing through the cowherd's land, purifying and purified by the god who plays in her. Her stories run from Purāṇic genealogy to the Bhāgavata's village epics to the sibling legend that still sets lamps on Indian doorsteps.

myths.title: The Sun's Twin Daughter
myths.text:
The Purāṇas give Yamunā a solar genealogy: she is the daughter of Sūrya, the sun, and of his wife Saṃjñā, and the twin sister of Yama, the lord of death — a pairing the tradition never explains and never abandons. Where her sister-river Gaṅgā descends from heaven through Śiva's matted hair, Yamunā rises from the sun itself, and the later texts give her a mountain birthplace as well: she is Kālindī, daughter of Mount Kalinda in the Garhwal Himalaya, which is why her best-loved name is Kālindī. The Purāṇas rank her among the holiest of rivers and the most intimate of goddesses: if Gaṅgā is the mother of India, Yamunā is its beloved.

The twinship does its quiet work beneath every later story: the river who gives life shares one womb with the god who ends it, and the tradition's most tender festival — Bhai Dooj — grew up around that single fact.

myths.title: The Dance on Kāliya
myths.text:
In the tenth book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the serpent Kāliya — driven from his former home by Garuḍa — poisoned a reach of Yamunā near Vṛndāvana, fouling the water so that cattle fell dead at the bank. The child Kṛṣṇa climbed a kadamba tree and dived into the black water; the cowherds watched for bubbles, then saw him floating on the serpent's expanding hoods. Kāliya wrapped him and struck; Kṛṣṇa rose and began to dance — each step a stamp upon the hundred heads — until the serpent's wives rose from the river with folded hands, offering jewels and prayer for their husband's life. Kṛṣṇa spared Kāliya on condition that he leave the river for the ocean's Ramaṇaka island, and the water ran sweet again; the herdsmen lifted the child from the river as from death itself.

The myth is the river's own purification narrative: her water was the serpent's crime scene, and the god who dances in her made her clean. Pilgrims at Kāliya-ghāṭa are shown the very reach of the healing.

lore.culturalLegacy: Delhi stands on her bank; the Taj Mahal reflects in her backwater; the Kumbh Mela is partly hers. Yamunā Jayanti (her descent-day) and Bhai Dooj (the sibling festival she shares with Yama) are national observances. Her pollution crisis — Delhi's stretch among the world's most contaminated urban rivers — makes her the central case of India's river-restoration debate: the goddess whose water pilgrims now filter before the ritual.
lore.archaeology: Yamunotri, her glacier source in the Garhwal Himalaya, keeps her temple (rebuilt after earthquakes, hot springs beside it). Mathurā and Vṛndāvana preserve the Kṛṣṇa-ghāts — Vishram Ghāt where the god rested after killing Kaṃsa — and Prayāgrāj's sangam fort and akshayavata tree mark the confluence. The medieval ghāt architecture of the Braj country documents five centuries of Krishna-pilgrimage on her banks.
lore.syncretism: Her cult runs parallel to Gaṅgā's but stays more intimate. The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition of Bengal holds her highest of all rivers because Kṛṣṇa played in her; the Harivaṃśa and later Kṛṣṇa literature make her a wife of Kṛṣṇa himself, as Kālindī, who waited by her father's river until the god came — a wedding the river-goddess stories share with Gaṅgā's descent through Śiva. In temple iconography the two stand flanking the doors of Viṣṇu and Śiva shrines across India, the dark and the fair, an inseparable pair that became the subcontinent's standard metaphor for complementary holiness. Krishnaism carried her along the trade routes into Javanese and Balinese temple cycles, and modern ISKCON temples enshrine her beside Gaṅgā wherever Kṛṣṇa is worshipped — the twin river still travelling.

domains.title: Sarnath
domains.subtitle: First Sermon
domains.lead: Sarnath is the deer park outside ancient Benares where, weeks after his awakening at Bodh Gayā, the Buddha delivered the first sermon and set the Wheel of Dhamma turning. Sacred to the Buddhist tradition, it marks the founding moment of the teaching and of the Sangha itself.

cards.name: The First Turning
cards.desc: Here the Buddha taught the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta — the middle way and the four noble truths — to the five ascetics, and the Sangha was born.

cards.name: The Deer Park
cards.desc: The grove called Ṛṣipatana, 'fall of the sages', and Mṛgadāva, 'deer park' — a landscape of gentleness, spared the hunt, chosen for the first teaching.

cards.name: Dharmachakra
cards.desc: The eight-spoked wheel 'first turned' at Sarnath; Buddhist art across Asia pairs it with two deer, the site's signature image.

cards.name: Lion Capital
cards.desc: Aśoka's polished pillar, crowned by four addorsed lions, stood here; its capital is now the state emblem of India.

symbols.name: Dharmachakra
symbols.meaning: The eight-spoked wheel of Dhamma 'first turned' at Sarnath; the earliest art shows it flanked by two deer.

symbols.name: Pair of deer
symbols.meaning: The gazelle pair flanking the wheel on Aśokan and later reliefs — the Deer Park's residents, traditionally spared the hunt by the Buddha's example.

symbols.name: Dhamek stupa
symbols.meaning: The great cylindrical brick-and-stone stupa raised over the sermon ground, its lower courses faced with Gupta floral carving.

symbols.name: Lion capital
symbols.meaning: Four addorsed Asiatic lions on Aśoka's pillar (c. 250 BCE) carrying a dharma wheel — adopted as the emblem of the Republic of India.

symbols.name: Cankamana
symbols.meaning: The raised promenade where the Buddha walked in meditation after the first sermon, marked by votive stupas.

mythology.lead: Sarnath is not a mythic battlefield but a sacred geography of events: here, tradition holds, the Buddha gave his first sermon, turned the Wheel of Dhamma, and founded the Sangha. Its lore weaves scripture, Jātaka story, and the long historical afterlife of Indian Buddhism into a single landscape.

myths.title: Setting the Wheel in Motion
myths.text: After the awakening beneath the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gayā, the tradition recorded in the Mahāvagga of the Vinaya says the Buddha hesitated to teach: the Dhamma he had seen was subtle, peaceable, beyond the net of opinion, and beings were pleasure-bent. The god Brahmā Sahampati descended from his heaven to beg him to open the doors of the Deathless, and the Buddha surveyed the world with the awakened eye and saw beings 'with little dust in their eyes' — enough to warrant the effort. He walked from Gayā to the deer park of Ṛṣipatana outside Benares, where the five ascetics who had attended him — Koṇḍañña, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, and Assaji — had sworn to shun him for abandoning severe austerity, yet rose to receive him. To them he preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (SN 56.11): the two extremes to avoid, the middle way, the four noble truths, and the three turnings of the wheel in their twelve modes. Koṇḍañña's mind opened with the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma — 'whatever is subject to arising is subject to cessation' — and the gods of ten thousand world-systems cried that the unsurpassed wheel had been set rolling. In a single sermon in a deer park, a private awakening became a public teaching and a solitary sage became the head of a community: that is Sarnath's primacy.

myths.title: Where the Sages Fell
myths.text: The commentarial tradition explains the ancient name Ṛṣipatana — Pali Isipatana, 'the place where the sages fell (rained down)' — with a legend: five hundred paccekabuddhas, solitary enlightened beings, foresaw that a fully awakened Buddha would arise and preach upon that very ground. At the appointed hour they rose into the air, flew through the sky, and descended in the deer park; having paid homage to the ground and circled it, they passed into final nirvāṇa together. Hence the ground where they 'fell' was called Ṛṣipatana. Whether read as legend or as etiological tale, the story fixes Sarnath's identity in Buddhist memory: not merely a pleasant grove outside Benares but a pre-appointed stage, reserved across cosmic time for the one sermon that would matter most. Modern philology reads the name more soberly — the 'fall' may mark where sages descended to attain the ground, or simply where a hermitage stood — but the tradition itself tells the grander version, and it is the tradition that drew pilgrims for two thousand years.

lore.culturalLegacy: For the Buddhist world Sarnath is a first-rank pilgrimage site, paired with Bodh Gayā, Kusinārā, and Lumbinī in the circuit of the four principal sacred places. Aśvaghoṣa already celebrated the first sermon in the Buddhacarita, and the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang recorded the monuments when the monasteries still functioned. After twelve centuries of silence, excavation returned the site to memory: the lion capital of Aśoka's pillar now serves as the Republic of India's state emblem, an extraordinary afterlife for a Buddhist monument in a modern secular state. The site's sculpture is divided between the Sarnath Museum and Kolkata; the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is still recited at the Dhamek stupa on full-moon days, two and a half millennia after the wheel was first turned. Few places on Earth can claim so long a continuous memory of a single afternoon.
lore.archaeology: Sarnath preserves one of India's great excavation landscapes. The Dhamek stupa, a massive cylindrical brick monument with a Mauryan core, was enlarged through the Gupta period, when its lower courses were faced with carved stone panels of flowers, swastikas, and honeysuckle. Beside it stand the foundations of the Dharmarajika stupa — Aśoka's original relic monument — and the Mulagandhakuti, the main shrine where the Buddha was believed to have spent his first rainy season. Aśoka's polished sandstone pillar, erected c. 250 BCE, bore his edicts and was crowned by four addorsed lions carrying a dharma wheel; the capital is now displayed in the Sarnath Museum. Systematic excavation began with Alexander Cunningham's surveys of the 1830s–60s and culminated under Sir John Marshall's campaign of 1904–05, which cleared the great monastery and mapped the Ashokan remains.
lore.syncretism: Sarnath is a site of pan-Buddhist, not merely Indian, devotion. The wheel flanked by two deer — carved on early Indian reliefs such as those at Bharhut and Sāñcī — became the international emblem of Buddhism, carried with the tradition to Sri Lanka, Central and Southeast Asia, China, Korea, and Japan, so that Sarnath's founding image adorns temples from Anuradhapura to Nara. The modern revival owes much to Anagārika Dharmapāla, whose Mahā Bodhi Society raised the Mulagandhakuti shrine in 1931 beside the excavated foundations. Diplomatic Buddhism now meets at Sarnath: Japanese, Thai, and Sri Lankan temples share the grounds with the Indian stupas, making the deer park a quiet concord of the tradition's nations — a concord entirely in the spirit of the first sermon, which was addressed to five skeptics and opened its doors to everyone.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ZDEH-phee-ros' — stress the first syllable; begin with the 'zd' of 'wisdom', and let the phi puff air like an English 'up-hill', not an 'f'
pronunciation.note: Tier-2 — Accent-Preserving. The restoration Zéphyros preserves the acute stress of Ζέφυρος on the first syllable, a feature plain ASCII loses; it carries no long-vowel mark, so a single preserved feature places the name in Tier 2.

domains.title: The Breath of Spring
domains.subtitle: The West Wind, Gentlest of the Anemoi
domains.lead: Zéphyros is the west wind of the Greeks — the mildest of the four Anemoi, the breeze that loosens winter and calls up the flowers. Where Bóreas rages and Nótos drowns ships in rain, Zéphyros is the wind the poets loved: the steady, fruit-bearing breath that fans the orchards of the blessed and carries spring north into the human world.

cards.name: Herald of Spring
cards.desc: Gentlest of the Anemoi, his west wind loosens winter’s grip and brings the swallow season home.

cards.name: Father of Swift Horses
cards.desc: With the harpy Podarge he sires Xánthos and Bálios, the immortal, wind-swift horses of Achilles (Iliad 16.148–151).

cards.name: Bridegroom of Flora
cards.desc: Roman poets wed him to Flora; Ovid lets her recall she was the nymph Chloris until Zéphyros took her as his bride (Fasti 5.195–212).

cards.name: The Bag of Aiolos
cards.desc: The keeper of winds gives Odysseus all the winds tied in an oxhide bag — Zéphyros first, the fair wind home (Odyssey 10.1–79).

symbols.name: Garland of Flowers
symbols.meaning: On the Tower of the Winds in Athens, Zéphyros is carved as a youth whose folded cloak spills blossoms — his spring-bearing nature made visible in stone.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: Like all the Anemoi, he is winged in Greek and Roman art; the winds fly, and their wings mark them as powers of the air rather than ordinary gods.

symbols.name: Swift Horses
symbols.meaning: By Pódargē the harpy he fathered Xánthos and Bálios, the immortal horses of Achilles — the wind's own speed given equine form.

symbols.name: The Swallow
symbols.meaning: The swallow's return was proverbially bound to the west wind's season; both were the first messengers that winter had broken.

symbols.name: Billowing Sail
symbols.meaning: A kind wind for sailors: steady, mild, and western — the breeze that fills canvas without violence and carries ships home.

symbols.name: Youthful Bloom
symbols.meaning: In art he appears as a beautiful, unbearded youth, a wind conceived not as a destroyer but as a lover — fitting the bridegroom of Chlōris.

mythology.lead: Zéphyros is a minor god with an outsized poetic life: born of Dawn, lover of flowers, father of the fastest horses ever to run. His myths are few but luminous — each one binds the west wind to speed, desire, and the returning spring.

myths.title: Son of Dawn and the Starry Sky
myths.text: In Theogony 378–380, Hesiod records that Eōs (Dawn) bore to Astraios, the starry dusk, the mighty winds: Zéphyros, Bóreas, and Nótos — 'a goddess lying in love with a god'. The genealogy is exact for Hesiod's purpose: the clearing west wind is the child of first light and the star-field, born at the seam where night opens into day. A breeze, the passage implies, is a child of the light's borderlands — and its gentleness is inherited, for what is born at the edge of dawn has no quarrel with the world. It is the one wind Homer and Hesiod can both praise without irony, because its parentage is the softest in the whole divine family tree.

myths.title: Father of Achilles's Horses
myths.text: In Iliad 16 (149–151), Patroklos harnesses Achilles's immortal pair, Xánthos and Bálios, 'whom Pódargē, the harpy swift of foot, bore to Zéphyros the west wind as she grazed in a meadow beside the stream of Ōkeanos'. A wind coupling with a storm-snatcher in a meadow: Homer makes the horses' supernatural speed a literal inheritance. It is Xánthos, this same wind-begotten colt, who later speaks with a human voice to foretell Achilles's death (Iliad 19, 404–417). The Iliad thus makes wind-begotten speed carry the hero to Troy, and the same wind-lineage makes the horse who warns him of the end: inherited speed, inherited doom — the wind's gift and the wind's price in one stable.

lore.culturalLegacy: English zephyr — 'a soft, gentle breeze' — descends directly from his name through Latin zephyrus, and has been a staple of English verse since Chaucer opened the Canterbury Tales with 'Zephirus… with his sweete breeth' quickening the spring crops. The word also gave its name to a fine, light yarn and to anything featherweight. Few Greek wind-gods survive so completely: not as a character, but as the very word English reaches for when the air turns kind.
lore.archaeology: Zéphyros's most famous monument is the Tower of the Winds (Horologion of Andronikos Kyrrhestēs, 1st c. BCE) in the Roman Agora of Athens, whose octagonal frieze personifies the eight winds — Zéphyros on the west face as a youth scattering flowers from his folded cloak. Pausanias (2.12.1) records a sanctuary with an altar of the Winds at Titanē in Sikyonia, where a priest sacrificed to them annually — one of the few attested cult sites for the Anemoi as a group. In Rome, his cult life ran through his bride: the temple of Flora near the Circus Maximus and the games of the Floralia.
lore.syncretism: The Romans called him Favōnius, from favēre, 'to favor' — the propitious wind — and married him to their own flower-goddess Flōra, whose festival, the Floralia, kept the Greek Chlōris-marriage alive in cult. Horace (Odes 1.4) sings winter loosening 'under the welcome west wind', and Virgil lets Favonius breathe through the Georgics as the air that unbinds the fields. Through Latin poetry the name passed intact into every European vernacular: the gentle west wind of Greece became the zephyr of the modern world.

entries.meaning: A fierce form of Durgā, so named because she slew the demons Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.

entries.meaning: The ruler of Laṅkā and chief of the Rākṣasas, whose destruction by Rāmacandra forms the subject of the Rāmāyaṇa

etymology.derivation: Sanskrit Rāvaṇa, from the causative of rū 'to roar, to cry'; the ten-headed king of Lanka.

pronunciation.approximation: 'RAA-vuh-nuh' — long open first syllable, a soft w-like v, and a tongue-curled n for the ṇ.
pronunciation.note: Rāvaṇa is Tier 1 because the Sanskrit form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: long ā and retroflex ṇ, both gone from plain ravana.

domains.title: Ten-Headed King
domains.subtitle: Ten-Headed King, Lanka
domains.lead: Rāvaṇa is the ten-headed king of Laṅkā in the Sanskrit Rāmāyaṇa — grandson of a mind-born sage, son of a demon princess, devotee of Śiva, master of the Vedas, and the abductor whose war against Rāma costs him his kingdom, his sons, and his life. The epic builds him as its most learned villain: every virtue but one.

cards.name: Ten-Headed King
cards.desc: Daśagrīva — ten heads, twenty arms; later readers counted the four Vedas and six śāstras among the ten.

cards.name: King of Laṅkā
cards.desc: Son of the sage Viśravas and the daitya princess Kaikasi; sovereign of the golden island fortress and its rākṣasa hosts (Rāmāyaṇa, Uttarakāṇḍa 9).

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Rāvaṇa recovers the long ā and retroflex ṇ that plain ASCII ravana flattens.

cards.name: Epic Attestation
cards.desc: Chief antagonist of Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa — and, in the Jain Paümacariya, the noblest king of the story.

symbols.name: Ten heads (daśānana)
symbols.meaning: The multiplied mind; later tradition glosses the ten as the four Vedas and six śāstras — mastery worn as anatomy.

symbols.name: The Pushpaka vimāna
symbols.meaning: His sky-going chariot, won from his brother Kubera — the vehicle of the abduction and, at the epic's end, of Rāma's triumphal return.

symbols.name: The Śivatāṇḍava stotra
symbols.meaning: The hymn he sang with crushed arms beneath Kailāsa — the one language, devotion, that he never lost.

symbols.name: Brahmā's boon
symbols.meaning: Near-invulnerability to gods, gandharvas, and demons — and the fatal contempt that left men out of the list.

symbols.name: The golden city of Laṅkā
symbols.meaning: The island fortress his brother Kubera ruled before him, built of gold by the divine architect Viśvakarman.

mythology.lead: The Rāmāyaṇa builds Rāvaṇa as a complete king — scholar, musician, ascetic, conqueror of the three worlds — whose single failure of self-command draws Rāma across the ocean. His story spans the epic's frame: born in its seventh book, he dies in its sixth.

myths.title: Born of Sage and Demoness
myths.text: In the Rāmāyaṇa's seventh book the villain's pedigree is nobler than his deeds: his father is Viśravas, a sage of flawless conduct, son of Pulastya, whom Brahmā generated from his own mind; his mother is Kaikasi, daughter of the daitya king Sumāli. From their union came four children — Rāvaṇa, the massive Kumbhakarṇa, the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, and the fierce Śūrpaṇakhā (Vālmīki, Uttarakāṇḍa 9–11). The young Daśagrīva performed a tapas of terrifying austerity — standing amid five fires, his arms raised, for a thousand years — until Brahmā, unable to refuse him, granted near-invulnerability: no god, gandharva, yakṣa, or demon might kill him. Men he omitted from the request, in contempt for their weakness (Uttarakāṇḍa 10). Later tellings deepen the bargain — nine times he offered his own head into the fire, and nine times it grew back, until ten heads stood where one had been. The epic's point is exact: its monster is born of a sage's house, and his doom is written into his own wish.

myths.title: The Shaking of Kailāsa
myths.text: Striding forth to conquer the quarters, Rāvaṇa found the way to Śiva barred by the bull-bannered gatekeeper Nandin; mocked for his boast, he took hold of the mountain itself and began to wrench it from its roots, so that the peaks, forests, and every creature upon them cried out (Vālmīki, Uttarakāṇḍa 16). Śiva pressed the peak down with the toe of his foot and pinned the upstart's arms beneath it; the agony tore a roar from him so tremendous that the three worlds shook, and the pleased god named him on the spot: Rāvaṇa, 'he who roars' — for older tradition the roar was the cry of the crushed, and Kālidāsa would later retell the whole confrontation in the Kumārasambhava (canto 7). Crushed but unrepentant, Rāvaṇa sang — the Śivatāṇḍava stotra, the hymn still recited in Śaiva mornings — until the mountain lifted and Śiva, mollified, gave him the sword Candrahāsa. The myth defines him in a single tableau: strength enough to move a mountain, devotion enough to sing to the god who crushes him, and a roar that becomes his name.

lore.culturalLegacy: Every autumn at Dussehra, across India and the diaspora, towering effigies of Rāvaṇa — ten-headed, twenty-armed, stuffed with firecrackers — are burned to cheers, reenacting the epic's climax on the festival that celebrates Rāma's victory. The ritual has its dissenters: in Bisrakh, the village near Delhi that claims his birthplace, some families keep mourning on the burning-day, and in Bastar, Gond tradition counts him an ancestor to be honored. His name lives in music through the rāvaṇahatthā, the spike-fiddle of Rajasthani folk players long described as his invention and famous in the West since the 1960s as the ravanastron, a claimed ancestor of the violin family. Modern retellings — from Bhavabhūti's sympathetic eighth-century Uttararāmacarita to television's 1987 Rāmāyaṇ and twenty-first-century novels narrated from Laṅkā's side — keep returning to him: the villain whose learning, grief, and grandeur make the hero's victory cost something.
lore.archaeology: There is no material record of Rāvaṇa — no inscription, coin, or image survives from any period that names him, and the giant belongs entirely to the textual tradition, whose oldest witnesses are the medieval manuscripts of the Rāmāyaṇa itself. The landscape, however, has been thoroughly claimed by the epic. In Sri Lanka — Laṅkā of the tradition — the rock fortress of Sigīrya is popularly his palace (in fact the work of King Kāśyapa I, fifth century CE), and the cave above the falls at Ella is toured as Rāvaṇa's own. Between India and the island runs Ādām's Bridge, the chain of shoals the epic calls Nala's bridge (Yuddhakāṇḍa 22), and at Rāmeśvaram in Tamil Nadu the Rāmanāthaswāmy temple stands at the epic's launching point, its corridors among the longest in India. The archaeology of Rāvaṇa is thus the archaeology of reception — geology, temples, and place-names retelling the story in stone.
lore.syncretism: The Jains refused the epic's verdict. In Vimalasūri's Prakrit Paümacariya (c. 3rd–5th century CE), the villain of Vālmīki becomes the noble King Rayaṇa of Laṅgka, a Jain layman of scrupulous conduct — it is Lakṣmaṇa who is the ruthless one, and the virtuous Rayaṇa who attains heaven. Southeast Asia recast him again: in the Thai Ramakien he is Thotsakan, the ten-faced titan of Ayutthaya drama, still the arch-villain but magnificent; in Cambodia's Reamker he is Krong Reap, the giant king of Laṅkā. In parts of South Asia the demon became a deity: villages in Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh keep Rāvaṇa shrines, and the Gonds of Bastar claim descent from a 'Rāvaṇa king' of old. His Śaiva devotion also survived independently of his epic crimes — the Śivatāṇḍava is still recited at Śiva's morning worship, and Ayurvedic tradition names him among its legendary physician-authors. The traditions disagree on whether he is to be burned or bowed to; both have been done, in different places, for two thousand years.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SEE-ghyn' — two syllables with the weight on the first, the g a soft gargled gh, the y rounded like German ü and kept short; never 'SIGH-in' and never 'sig-WIN'.
pronunciation.note: Sigyn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The y is a rounded vowel in sound, not in spelling; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Loyalty, Wife of Loki
domains.subtitle: The Wife Who Holds the Bowl
domains.lead: Sigyn is the wife of [[loki|Loki]] and the mother of his human sons — and the most patient figure in the whole Norse corpus. When the Æsir bound Loki beneath the earth for the death of Baldr, and [[skadi|Skaði]] fastened a venom-snake above his face, Sigyn took her place beside him with a basin, catching the poison drop by drop. Only when the basin fills and she turns away to empty it does the venom fall on Loki's face — and then he writhes so hard that the whole earth shakes, and men call it an earthquake.

cards.name: The Venom Basin
cards.desc: The bowl Sigyn holds above Loki's face, catching the snake's drip — the one mercy in the whole binding scene, and it is hers alone.

cards.name: The Falling Drop
cards.desc: When the basin is full she must turn away to empty it; for those moments the venom falls unchecked — the gap in mercy, measured in drops.

cards.name: The Three Stones
cards.desc: The three slabs — under shoulders, loins, and knees — to which Loki was bound with his own son's entrails turned to iron: the fixed point of her vigil.

cards.name: The Earthquake
cards.desc: Loki's writhing when the venom strikes: 'then he writhes so hard that all the earth shakes — those are now called earthquakes.'

symbols.name: The venom basin
symbols.meaning: Loyalty made object — the mercy she holds over him, measured drop by drop

symbols.name: The venom-snake
symbols.meaning: Skaði's sentence, fastened above Loki's face — the fixed threat Sigyn stands between

symbols.name: The iron bonds
symbols.meaning: Nari's entrails turned to iron — the binding her vigil softens but cannot loose

symbols.name: The three stones
symbols.meaning: Loki's anchor in the gorge — shoulders, loins, and knees pinned beneath the earth

symbols.name: The earthquake
symbols.meaning: The world shaking when the bowl is lifted — her brief absence, written in tremors

mythology.lead: Sigyn's dossier is small and strangely old: a naming in Snorri's catalogue of the gods, a kenning from a skald of Harald Fairhair's age, one stanza in the oldest poem of the Edda, and then the scene that made her immortal — the binding of Loki, where she does the only thing left to do and does it forever. The tradition never gives her a word to say. It gives her a bowl.

myths.title: The Wife of Loki
myths.text:
Snorri names her in the survey of the Æsir with his usual economy: Loki's wife is named Sigyn, and their son is Nari or Narfi. That is the whole introduction — no father, no hall, no office. The same catalogue gives Loki his other family: the giantess [[angrboda|Angrboða]], who bore him the wolf [[fenrir|Fenrir]], the World Serpent, and [[hel|Hel]]. Between the monster-brood and the human sons stands Sigyn, the wife within the walls of Ásgarðr.

That she was already Loki's established wife long before the Eddas were written is proven by the skalds: Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, composing Haustlöng around the year 900, calls Loki 'farmr Sigynjar arma' — the burden of Sigyn's arms — a kenning that works only if every listener already knew whose arms held him. The ásynja þulur preserved with Skáldskaparmál keep her in the catalogue of the goddesses by name.

myths.title: The Captive in the Grove of Kettles
myths.text:
The seeress of Völuspá, the oldest and greatest poem of the Codex Regius, sees the punishment before it happens: a captive lying under the grove of kettles, something evil-minded in form like Loki — 'and there sits Sigyn, by no means happy about her husband. Do you understand yet, or what more?'

The stanza is the whole of her eddic portrait, and it is enough: seated, sorrowing, and staying. A generation of readers has noted what the seeress does not say — that Sigyn is anywhere else. In the oldest witness the tradition has, she is already at her post.

lore.culturalLegacy: Sigyn's afterlife is the afterlife of one image. The medieval earthquake-theory — the earth shakes when she lifts the bowl — survived for centuries as the North's household explanation of tremors, and every retelling of Loki's punishment, from the Kearys' Victorian 'Heroes of Asgard' onward, keeps the wife and the basin at the centre of the scene: it is the one moment of grace in the flyting's long aftermath, and illustrators have never been able to leave it out. Nineteenth-century romanticism made her the Edda's type of wifely fidelity; twentieth-century scholarship made her the test case for how much a single stanza and a prose coda can hold. The name itself went quietly back into use — Sigyn is a rare but living given name in Sweden — and modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities honour her as the goddess of loyalty, fidelity, and endurance under an unjust sentence: the one who stays.
lore.archaeology: Sigyn has one candidate image and it is famous: the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria, carved in the first half of the tenth century, whose programme of Ragnarök scenes includes a bound male figure with a smaller figure kneeling beside him holding a bowl — standardly interpreted as Loki bound and Sigyn with the basin (Bailey; Lindow), the one Viking-Age monument that may show her at her post. Otherwise she is a wholly textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no other image can be securely identified. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the Loki cycle — the Codex Regius for Völuspá 35 and the Lokasenna prose epilogue, and the Codex Regius, Codex Wormianus, and Uppsala codices of Snorri's Edda for Gylfaginning 34 and 50 — with Þjóðólfr's Haustlöng (c. 900), quoted in Skáldskaparmál, proving the kenning 'the burden of Sigyn's arms' was already current a century before Iceland's conversion.
lore.syncretism: Sigyn's truest kin are inside the corpus itself. She is the mirror of [[nanna|Nanna]] — the two wives of the Baldr catastrophe, one following her dead husband into the fire, the other staying beside her living one in the pit; devotion answered by death in the one, by endurance without end in the other. Scholarship has been cool toward grander comparisons. Simek and Orchard treat Sigyn strictly within the Loki complex: her attestation is thin, her etymology only probable, and no cult can be reconstructed from a bowl held over a bound god. Lindow reads the scene as the tradition's darkest domestic image — the flyting's bill coming due at the household, not on the battlefield — and notes that the earthquake aetiology made Sigyn's vigil the medieval North's explanation for the trembling earth. What can be said cleanly is that no other figure in the Edda is defined so entirely by a single act of staying.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as Sigyn — Old Norse, attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius and related codices. In the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛋᛁᚴᚢᚾ (sikun), a normalized phonetic reconstruction: the sixteen-rune row distinguishes neither k from g nor short from long vowels, so the runic form underspecifies exactly the features the manuscript spelling records. No runic attestation of the theonym survives. The normalized form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — which fixes the name in Tier 2. Because it is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: sigyn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

etymology.derivation: Old Norse Angrboða, from angr 'sorrow, grief' + boða 'to offer, to announce'; mother of Fenrir, Jörmungandr, and Hel by Loki.
