Papa means 'earth, rock, foundation' and is found across Polynesia; tū means 'to stand'; ā is an emphatic particle; nuku means 'extended, far-reaching.' The macrons on ū and ā mark long vowels, distinctive features the ASCII form loses, and they place the name in Tier 1. Some dialects and orthographies write the short form Papa.

domains.title: Earth Mother
domains.subtitle: Creation, Fertility, and the Land
domains.lead: Papatūānuku is the broad earth lying beneath the sky, the mother from whose body all living things spring. In Māori cosmology she and Ranginui, the Sky Father, were once locked in an embrace so tight that their children lived in darkness between them. Their separation by Tāne brought light and space into the world — and a wound of separation that still marks every creature's relation to earth and sky.

cards.name: Mother of Life
cards.desc: All plants, animals, and humans arise from her body; she is the source of nourishment and growth.

cards.name: Partner of Ranginui
cards.desc: The Sky Father lies upon her; their separation is the primal act of creation.

cards.name: Whenua and Identity
cards.desc: The land (whenua) is her body; Māori identity is inseparable from the earth that names and sustains the people.

cards.name: Return and Renewal
cards.desc: The dead return to her; she receives all things and makes them grow again.

symbols.name: Flat, dark earth
symbols.meaning: Her body is the soil itself, often figured as lying prone beneath the sky

symbols.name: Mountains and valleys
symbols.meaning: The folds and ridges of her body, the places where her children still touch her

symbols.name: Caves
symbols.meaning: Openings into her body, places of birth, burial, and communication with the dead

symbols.name: The kūmara and food plants
symbols.meaning: Crops grown from her body, especially the sweet potato brought from Hawaiki

mythology.lead: Papatūānuku's central myth — the separation of the Sky Father and Earth Mother — is the best-known creation narrative of Polynesia, recorded in many regional variants. The Māori versions written down in the nineteenth century by George Grey, Elsdon Best, and others differ in detail and genealogy, and all of them are transcripts of a living oral tradition rather than a fixed scripture. What the versions share is the argument: the world we inhabit is the aftermath of a family crisis, and its beauty and its grief are the same event seen from two sides.

myths.title: The Separation of Rangi and Papa
myths.text: In the beginning there was no sky above and no earth below in our sense — only Ranginui, the Sky, and Papatūānuku, the Earth, locked in an embrace so close that no light could enter. Their children were born into the narrow darkness between their parents' bodies: Tāne, Tāwhirimātea, Tangaroa, Tūmatauenga, Rongo, and Haumia-tiketike, with the unborn Rūaumoko stirring in the womb. Cramped and blind, the children debated their escape. Rongo-mā-Tāne and Tangaroa proposed killing the parents; Tāne counselled separation instead. Attempt after attempt failed — pushing from within, shoving from without — until Tāne lay on his back against his mother, braced his legs against his father, and thrust upward with the full strength of his body. Ranginui rose into the air with a great cry, light flooded the world, and the children stood for the first time in open space. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology; Best, Māori Religion and Mythology.) The myth insists that creation is not making something from nothing but the painful rearrangement of an original unity — space, light, and life all purchased at the price of the parents' grief.

myths.title: The Rain and the Mist
myths.text: Ranginui did not leave without mourning. From his eyes fell the rain, and Papatūānuku's longing rises from her body as the morning mist, so that the two remain in perpetual touch — his tears falling on her, her sighing rising to him. The versions differ on what happened next among the children: in Grey's telling, Tūmatauenga cursed his parents for what had been done and turned his anger on his brothers, while Tāwhirimātea fled to his father and never forgave the separation; only those who accepted their mother's gifts — the forests and birds to Tāne, the sea to Tangaroa, the kūmara to Rongo, the wild fernroot to Haumia — stayed close to her. The myth reads the weather as family feeling: every rainstorm is an embrace interrupted, and the mist at dawn is the earth answering the sky.

lore.culturalLegacy: Papatūānuku has become a central figure in modern Māori cultural identity and in Aotearoa New Zealand's environmental and educational vocabulary. Schools, health services, and land-restoration projects invoke her name; environmental legislation and treaty settlements speak of the land in her terms. The phrase 'kaitiaki of Papatūānuku' expresses an ethic of guardianship that has entered national policy discourse. Internationally, she is one of the most widely recognized Polynesian deities, a symbol of indigenous earth-relationship in an era of climate crisis — proof that a nineteenth-century transcript of an older song can still govern how a nation thinks about its ground.
lore.archaeology: There are no monumental temple sculptures of Papatūānuku comparable to those of Aztec or Greek deities; Māori sacred expression was primarily oral, architectural, and environmental. Marae and carved meeting houses (wharenui) encode genealogical narratives linking the living community to Papatūānuku and Ranginui — the meeting house itself is often read as the body of an ancestor, ridgepole as backbone, rafters as ribs. Rock art, greenstone ornaments, and burial practices reflect the cosmology of return to the earth. Nineteenth-century written records by Grey, Best, and Smith preserve the oral mythology in detail; the tradition they transcribed is itself the primary artifact.
lore.syncretism: Papatūānuku is cognate with the Hawaiian earth mother Papa and with earth-deity figures across eastern Polynesia; her partner Ranginui answers to the Rangi-sky figures of the whole triangle. In Māoridom today she is paired with Ranginui in prayers, environmental discourse, and artistic representations of the creation story. Some Christian Māori theologians have drawn parallels between Papatūānuku and the created earth praised in the biblical psalms, without identifying the two. Contemporary environmental movements invoke her as the personification of ecological responsibility: 'kaitiaki of Papatūānuku' — guardians of the earth — has become a standard formula of Māori land-rights and conservation rhetoric, giving an ancestral name to what the West calls sustainability.

entries.meaning: Heaven and Earth; the natural order of the cosmos

etymology.derivation: Tiān 天 (heaven/sky) + dì 地 (earth/ground). The compound expresses the dyad that frames Chinese cosmology.

pronunciation.approximation: TYEHN-DEE — 'tian' high and level, like a held note; 'di' sharp and falling, like a command.
pronunciation.note: Tiāndì literally means 'Heaven and Earth.' It is not a personal god but the cosmological pair that grounds Chinese natural philosophy, state ritual, and ethics. The Pinyin restoration preserves the citation tones: first tone on tiān, fourth tone on dì.

domains.title: Heaven and Earth
domains.subtitle: Cosmology, Natural Order, and Imperial Ritual
domains.lead: Tiāndì is the Chinese cosmos in two characters. Tiān is Heaven: not a place above the clouds but the supreme moral and natural order, the source of seasons, rain, and legitimacy. Dì is Earth: the receptive ground that bears all things. Together they name the whole within which human life finds its proper place — and whose rupture, the myths insist, can be mended.

cards.name: Cosmic Dyad
cards.desc: Heaven is active and round; Earth is receptive and square. Together they generate the ten thousand things.

cards.name: Imperial Legitimacy
cards.desc: The emperor ruled by the Mandate of Heaven, sacrificing at the winter solstice on the Circular Mound of Heaven.

cards.name: Agricultural Order
cards.desc: The calendar, the seasons, and the harvest depend on the harmony of heaven above and earth below.

cards.name: Moral Cosmos
cards.desc: Right action aligns with the way of heaven; disaster signals its disruption — and repair is possible.

symbols.name: Round heaven and square earth
symbols.meaning: The circular altar and square terrace of Beijing's Temple of Heaven encode the cosmic dyad in architecture

symbols.name: Jade disc (bì)
symbols.meaning: The ritual jade offered to heaven, round like the sky and green like life

symbols.name: Yellow earth
symbols.meaning: The soil of the central plain, offered at the Altar of Earth — the nation's foundation

symbols.name: North Star
symbols.meaning: The pivot of heaven around which all stars turn; the emperor's celestial model

symbols.name: The five-colored stones
symbols.meaning: The minerals Nǚwā smelted to patch the broken sky — heaven's wounds are mended, not replaced

mythology.lead: Tiāndì is not a mythic protagonist but the setting within which Chinese myths unfold. Its stories are cosmogonic, ritual, and reparative: how the pair was separated, how the emperor keeps it speaking to the state, and how it was once broken — and mended.

myths.title: Pangu Separates Heaven and Earth
myths.text: The earliest full telling of Pangu's story survives in fragments of Xu Zheng's Sanwu liji (三五曆記, Records of the Three and Five, Three Kingdoms period, 3rd century CE), quoted in later encyclopedias, with a parallel in his Wuyun linian ji. In the beginning, heaven and earth were one chaos, like an egg, and inside it Pangu slept and grew for eighteen thousand years. When he woke, he took up a broadaxe, pushed the light heaven upward and pressed the heavy earth downward — and each day the sky rose ten feet, the earth thickened ten feet, and Pangu grew ten feet taller between them. When at last he died, his body became the landscape: his breath the wind and clouds, his voice the thunder, his left eye the sun and his right eye the moon, his limbs the five sacred mountains, his blood the rivers, his flesh the soil, his hair the stars and the plants, his teeth and marrow the metals and jade, his sweat the rain. The cosmos of Tiāndì is not a creator's throne but a giant's body — the world continuous with flesh, heaven and earth the two halves of a single sacrifice.

myths.title: The Son of Heaven at the Altars
myths.text: Shang dynasty oracle bones already record sacrifice to Dì, the high lord who governed harvest and victory; the Zhou recast him as Tiān, Heaven, whose Mandate (Tiānmìng) passed to rulers who governed rightly and withdrew from those who did not — the doctrine thundered in the Great Declaration chapters of the Shujing. The Liji and later ritual codices organized the response: the emperor, Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ), sacrificed to Heaven at the winter solstice and to Earth at the summer solstice, in round and square enclosures at the southern and northern suburbs. The Ming Yongle emperor rebuilt this liturgy in stone between 1406 and 1420: the Temple of Heaven's Circular Mound, where the sovereign stood at the center of an open sky speaking upward, remains the most eloquent ritual building on earth. The rite is the technology of legitimacy — heaven does not vote, but it is heard annually, and a dynasty that skipped the sacrifice had already begun to fall.

lore.culturalLegacy: Tiāndì remains the backbone of Chinese cosmological language. The phrase tiān xià — 'all under heaven' — still names the world in diplomacy and idiom. The Temple of Heaven in Beijing is a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most visited monuments in China; its round-and-square geometry is taught to every schoolchild as the shape of the cosmos. The Mandate of Heaven survives in political rhetoric as the ancient warrant for judging rulers by their results, and the ideal of harmony among heaven, earth, and humanity shapes everything from traditional medicine to urban feng shui. Even in secular China, 'heaven' and 'earth' are not physical terms; they carry the weight of moral and cultural order. The two characters are among the most compound-words in the language — tiāndì appears in hundreds of set phrases, the lexicon's proof that a cosmology can become grammar.
lore.archaeology: The cult of Heaven and Earth is materialized in China's imperial ritual landscape, above all the Temple of Heaven (Tiāntán) and the Altar of Earth (Dìtán) in Beijing, rebuilt under Yongle (1406–1420) on Ming cosmological principles — round for heaven, square for earth, blue glaze for the sky, yellow for the soil. Oracle-bone inscriptions from the Shang dynasty record sacrifices to Dì, the high lord of harvest and victory, and Zhou bronze inscriptions consolidate the dyad of Tiāndì as the foundation of political legitimacy. Han stone reliefs and Mawangdui silk paintings map the cosmography the rites addressed — heaven round above, earth square below, the human world set precisely between.
lore.syncretism: Tiāndì absorbed and was absorbed by every Chinese religious current. Confucian state ritual made the worship of Heaven the monopoly of the emperor and Earth the charge of the court. Popular religion localized the pair as the Jade Emperor above and Tǔdìgōng, the earth god of each village, below. Daoism reinterpreted Tiān as the celestial Dao and dì as the material field it orders, while Buddhism, entering China, had to map its Indic heavens and hells onto a Tiāndì-shaped cosmology — the Buddha himself was politely seated beneath heaven in temple iconography. Modern nationalism claimed Tiān as a proto-monotheistic deity for China's antiquity, and contemporary environmental thought reads Tiāndì as an early ecological holism: heaven, earth, and humanity as one body (tiān rén hé yī). The two characters have carried every Chinese worldview without once changing their shape.

entries.meaning: Sea; the deified primordial ocean in Ugaritic and Canaanite myth

variants.note: Nominative case form in Ugaritic scholarly transliteration

etymology.derivation: From Proto-Semitic *yamm- "sea"; cognate with Hebrew yām יָם. In Ugaritic myth Yām is a chaotic sea deity defeated by Baal.

steps: Yammu is written ym 𐎊𐎎 throughout the Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6)
An earlier name-form yw 𐎊𐎆 appears at KTU 1.1 IV before his renaming to Yammu
Syllabic cuneiform renders the name ᵈYa-a-mi (Emar); the logogram ᵈA.AB.BA (sea) also writes him at Ugarit

pronunciation.approximation: YAHM — a long, open 'ah' like 'father,' preceded by a smooth y-glide and closed by a humming m.
pronunciation.note: Yām is Tier-1: the macron on the long ā is a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The name is common Semitic for 'sea,' personified in Ugaritic myth as a chaotic divine antagonist.

domains.title: Prince Sea
domains.subtitle: Primordial Ocean, Chaos, and the Rival of Baal
domains.lead: Yām is the deified sea of the Ugaritic Baal Cycle, the vast primordial water that claims kingship over the gods before Baal defeats him. He is not simply the Mediterranean; he is the dangerous, chaotic deep that threatens to overwhelm the ordered world of dry land and storm-fed fields. In Canaanite myth, the storm god's victory over Yām is the founding act that makes civilization possible.

cards.name: The Primordial Deep
cards.desc: Yām represents the pre-creation waters that must be pushed back for land and life to appear.

cards.name: Rival of Baal
cards.desc: He demands that El hand over the divine kingship, setting up the central combat of the Baal Cycle.

cards.name: Seven-Headed Dragon
cards.desc: In battle Yām is a seven-headed sea monster, kin to the biblical Leviathan and Rahab.

cards.name: Judge of the Waters
cards.desc: His domain is the boundary between chaos and order, the sea that feeds and destroys.

symbols.name: Cresting wave
symbols.meaning: The uncontrollable deep he personifies — beautiful, wealthy, and fatal to those who mistake it for a road

symbols.name: Seven-headed serpent or dragon
symbols.meaning: btn ʿqltn, 'the twisting serpent with seven heads' (KTU 1.5 i), his combat form and Leviathan's twin

symbols.name: Net or muzzle
symbols.meaning: The binding weapons of the storm god's arsenal, named to leash the Sea he once ruled

symbols.name: Lotus or conch
symbols.meaning: Maritime wealth and fertility that follow once the sea accepts its bounds

mythology.lead: Yām's story is told in the Ugaritic Baal Cycle, where he plays the role of the chaos monster that the young storm god must defeat to establish his kingship. The myth is one of the oldest and most influential combat narratives in the ancient Near East, echoed in the Bible's Leviathan, Babylonian Tiamat, and Greek Typhon.

myths.title: Yamm Demands the Kingship
myths.text: Before Baꜥal can be king, the Sea claims the crown. In KTU 1.2 i, the deified ocean — Yamm, 'Prince Sea, Judge River' — sends two terrible emissaries into the divine assembly with a demand for Ēl, the father of gods: hand over the storm god Baꜥal for his watery house. Yamm wants Baꜥal as a slave, and Ēl, reluctant, is constrained to agree. The scene establishes the myth's central tension: the primordial deep does not attack the order of the gods from outside; it claims to be the order, the senior claimant to cosmic rule, and it speaks the language of law and tribute. Chaos, in this telling, arrives as a creditor with impeccable credentials. That is what makes Baꜥal's eventual resistance theologically daring — and why the whole assembly holds its breath when the storm god finally refuses to surrender.

myths.title: The Maces of Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs
myths.text: The decisive battle occupies a single magnificent tablet (KTU 1.2 iv). Baꜥal, armed by the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs with two named maces — Yagrush, 'Chaser,' and Ayamur, 'Driver' — advances on Yamm and strikes the Sea between the eyes. Yamm collapses, and Baꜥal scatters him. Then, in a famous crux, the text seems to show the victor pausing — is he finishing Yamm off, or is he being told to stay his hand? The surviving copies do not agree, and translators have argued over the lines for a century. What is beyond dispute is the outcome: the Sea is subdued, and the assembly acclaims Baꜥal king on the cosmic mountain Ṣaphon. The combat re-enacts the primal separation of sea and land: dry ground, cities, harbors, and fields exist only because a storm god once beat the ocean into bounds.

lore.culturalLegacy: The myth of Yām survives most powerfully in the biblical Leviathan and in the combat hymns of the Psalms, which shaped Jewish, Christian, and Islamic imagery of cosmic evil defeated by divine power. The seven-headed sea dragon remains a staple of modern fantasy and role-playing games, usually without any memory of its Ugaritic ancestor. For scholars of mythology, Yām is a textbook example of the chaoskampf pattern — the victory of order over primordial water that underlies civilizations from Mesopotamia to the Hebrew Bible. And for the coastal cities of the Levant, his cult was once practical theology: the harbor, the fleet, and the storm warning were all arguments in his favor. Every age that lives by the sea rewrites his myth; none has yet retired it.
lore.archaeology: Yām's mythology is preserved in the Ugaritic tablets from Ras Shamra (KTU 1.2), written in alphabetic cuneiform in the Late Bronze Age. The coastal setting of Ugarit itself — a trading city dependent on the Mediterranean — explains the cultural importance of a sea-god who must be both propitiated and subdued. Iconographic parallels include Levantine seals and ivory plaques showing a storm god battling a serpentine or aquatic foe.
lore.syncretism: Yām is closely related to the Babylonian Tiamat and to the biblical Leviathan and Rahab: all three embody primordial watery chaos subdued by a younger storm or creator god, and all three belong to the combat pattern scholars call the chaoskampf. In Greek myth, Zeus's battle against Typhon carries a related structure, though the genealogies differ; in Egypt, the nightly defeat of the serpent Apophis answers the same anxiety. Yām also overlaps with the Hurrian-Hittite sea and river gods known from treaty lists, and the Ugaritic tablets themselves show him as part of a wider Bronze Age diplomatic world in which the Sea was a boundary to be governed, not merely feared. The sea remained a boundary zone in Canaanite religion: source of wealth, highway of trade, and home of the monster who would reclaim the land if the storm god ever slept.

entries.meaning: Unbreakable; the adamant; the hardest substance; origin of "diamond"

variants.note: Plain ASCII form used in English etymological discussion

etymology.derivation: Privative ἀ- "not" + δάμ- (root of δαμάζω "to tame, subdue"). The word denotes anything unbreakable, especially hardened steel or diamond.

cognates.note: To tame, from the same PIE root *demh₂-
Via Old French diamant and Vulgar Latin *diamantem
Direct borrowing of Greek adámas via Latin

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-DAH-mahs' — stress falls on the middle syllable, with a crisp final -s.
pronunciation.note: Adámas is Tier 2 because the Greek ἀδάμας preserves the acute stress on the second syllable but lacks a long vowel. The word is not a deity but a material concept that became a philosophical emblem of invincibility.

domains.title: The Unbreakable
domains.subtitle: Invincible Substance, Obdurate Will, Philosophical Symbol
domains.lead: Adámas is the Greek word for the hardest, most untamable substance — the adamant. In Homer it is the metal of chains that bind even gods; in later philosophy it becomes a metaphor for an unyielding soul. The word carries no cult of its own, yet it cuts across Greek literature as the image of absolute resistance.

cards.name: Adamantine Substance
cards.desc: The hardest material known to Greek poets; used for chains, weapons, and the unbreakable core of things.

cards.name: Bonds of the Gods
cards.desc: In Homer and tragedy, adamantine fetters hold Prometheus, Ares, and other immortals fast.

cards.name: Invincible Resolve
cards.desc: Philosophers from Plato to the Stoics use adámas as an image of an unconquerable mind.

cards.name: Diamond Legacy
cards.desc: The medieval and modern word 'diamond' descends from this Greek root, preserving its brilliance and hardness.

symbols.name: Adamantine sickle
symbols.meaning: The weapon used by Kronos to castrate Ouranos, and by Zeus in some traditions

symbols.name: Chains of Prometheus
symbols.meaning: The unbreakable bonds that fix the Titan to the Caucasus in Aeschylus

symbols.name: Diamond
symbols.meaning: The later gemstone identified with adámas because of its incomparable hardness

symbols.name: Anvil and forge
symbols.meaning: The context in which adamantine metal is worked, if at all, by divine smiths

mythology.lead: Adámas appears in Greek myth not as a character but as a substance that binds, wounds, or pivots the cosmos itself. Its hardness creates the drama: what can hold an immortal must be stronger than the divine. From the sickle that cuts the sky to the spindle that turns the heavens, the unbreakable metal marks the exact points where Greek imagination needed something stronger than god.

myths.title: The Sickle That Wounded the Sky
myths.text: Gaia, weary of Ouranos pressing down upon her and hiding their children inside her depths, fashioned a plan and set her youngest, Kronos, to ambush his father. She made a great long sickle with jagged teeth — of adamant, ἅρπη ἀδάμαντος (Hesiod, Theogony 161) — and bade Kronos wait in a hidden place. When Ouranos came at night, 'stretched all over Gaia, desiring love,' Kronos reached out with his left hand and swung with his right, severing his father's genitals and hurling them behind him. From the blood that fell on the earth were born the Erinyes, the great Giants, and the Meliai; from the sea-foam where they landed, Aphrodite (Theogony 173–192). Adamant matters here because the myth needs a material harder than the sky: only the unbreakable can break the original order. The word appears at the exact hinge where cosmic succession — and all Greek generation — begins.

myths.title: Chains That Hold a Titan
myths.text: Aeschylus opens Prometheus Bound at the edge of the world, where Hephaistos, ordered by Strength and Force, must rivet the rebel Titan to the crags of the Caucasus. His bonds are adamantine — the material whose name means 'unconquerable' — and Hephaistos grieves as he works: his own craft, the fire he gave the world, is being turned to chain the god who gave it to men. The cosmology behind the image is already in Hesiod (Theogony 521–616): Zeus bound Prometheus in indissoluble fetters and set an eagle to tear his liver, because the Titan had tricked him over the sacrifice and stolen the fire. But Aeschylus sharpens the metal's meaning: adamant is not merely strong — it is the substance of the new regime, the hardness of power that will not negotiate, set against a mind that will not yield. The chains hold. The argument, Prometheus insists, will outlast them.

lore.culturalLegacy: Every diamond engagement ring carries a fragment of adámas. The word's legacy is the cultural equation of hardness with value, permanence, and indestructibility. In literature, 'adamantine' still describes an unyielding will or an irrefutable argument. The Greek concept thus survives not in cult but in language — as the ultimate measure of resistance.
lore.archaeology: No material object can be securely identified as 'adamant' in the archaeological record; the term is literary and lapidary. Greek and Roman texts describe it as a dark, extremely hard mineral or metal, perhaps magnetite, emery, or corundum before diamond was recognized. The word's archaeological trace is therefore lexical and iconographic — sickles, chains, and forge scenes in vase painting and relief.
lore.syncretism: The Greek adámas traveled into Latin as a precious stone and, through medieval lapidaries, became the 'diamond.' Christian writers borrowed its hardness as a symbol of unwavering faith and the invincible word of God. In alchemy and Renaissance emblem books, the diamond stood for constancy and the philosopher's indestructible stone. Modern materials science has returned the metaphor to its Greek root: diamond remains the hardest known natural material.

etymology.derivation: Probably from a Pre-Greek or Mediterranean substrate; the root is associated with numbness and sleep-inducing substances.
From a root meaning "to fit, join"; peace as the state of things properly joined together.

entries.meaning: Daughter of Atlas; the legendary lost island civilization

etymology.derivation: From Atlas (Ἄτλας), the Titan who holds up the heavens; Atlantis is "the island of Atlas."

cognates.note: The Titan after whom the island is named

pronunciation.approximation: 'at-lahn-TEES' — the final syllable carries the acute, marking the stress.
pronunciation.note: Atlantís is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἀτλαντίς preserves the acute stress on the final syllable but has no long vowel in the standard domain restoration. The name is a patronymic adjective, 'of Atlas,' turned into a place name.

domains.title: The Lost Island
domains.subtitle: Legendary Civilization, Hubris, Cataclysm
domains.lead: Atlantís is the legendary island civilization described by Plato, a powerful naval empire that angered the gods and sank beneath the waves in a single day and night. It is the archetype of the golden age destroyed by its own ambition.

cards.name: Island Empire
cards.desc: A ringed island beyond the Pillars of Herakles, rich in metals, timber, and fertile soil.

cards.name: Naval Power
cards.desc: Its fleet dominated the Mediterranean until Athens led a resistance of free Greeks.

cards.name: Hubris and Fall
cards.desc: Its kings grew greedy and impious; Zeus punished them with earthquakes and floods.

cards.name: Underwater Ruin
cards.desc: Sank beneath the Atlantic, becoming the template for every lost-civilization legend.

symbols.name: Concentric rings of land and water
symbols.meaning: The engineered geography of the Atlantean capital

symbols.name: Poseidon's trident
symbols.meaning: The island's divine patron and the instrument of its destruction

symbols.name: Orichalcum
symbols.meaning: The legendary precious metal of Atlantis, second in value only to gold (Plato, Critias 114e)

symbols.name: Sinking temple
symbols.meaning: The image of a civilization's architecture overwhelmed by the sea

mythology.lead: Atlantís is Plato's story, whether invented or adapted from older traditions. It serves as a philosophical allegory about the corruption of power and the fragility of civilization.

myths.title: The Egyptian Priest's Tale
myths.text:
The story reaches us nested three layers deep. Solon, the Athenian lawmaker, visits Saïs in Egypt, and the priests there show him how young Greece's memory is: floods repeatedly wipe out the Greeks' records, while the Nile preserves Egypt's. One priest then produces a marvel: nine thousand years before Solon — a deliberate impossibility, before Athens itself existed — the city of Athens led the resistance against a great Atlantic power that had enslaved the Mediterranean as far as Egypt and Tyrrhenia, and drove it back in a single victorious stroke (Plato, Timaeus 25b–c). Atlantis, the priest says, lay beyond the Pillars of Herakles, 'larger than Libya and Asia together'. Kritias heard the tale from his grandfather, who heard it from Solon himself; Socrates, hearing it retold, is asked to imagine Athens' ancient constitution in action against the island's might.

The frame is the point: Plato hides an invented world inside a claimed memory, and dares his readers to ask which of their own certainties are merely the oldest surviving copy.

myths.title: The Island and Its Kings
myths.text:
The Critias supplies what the Timaeus only sketches. Poseidon receives the island, falls in love with the mortal Kleitō, and carves the hill around her dwelling into concentric rings of land and sea — two of earth and three of water — spanned by bridges and girdled with a wall of orichalcum. Their five pairs of twin sons rule the ten kingdoms, the eldest named Atlas, who gives the island and the ocean their names. Behind the capital stretches a plain divided by a grid of canals; on the hilltop stands the temple of Poseidon and Kleitō, walled in orichalcum, roofed in ivory, and filled with gold — and inside, a gold statue of the god in a chariot drawn by six winged horses stands so tall 'his head touched the roof' (Critias 116e–117a).

For generations the kings keep the divine portion of their law inscribed on the temple's orichalcum pillars; then the admixture of mortality thickens, and the very wealth Plato has just finished cataloguing begins to rot the virtue that built it.

lore.culturalLegacy: Atlantis is the most influential fictional civilization in Western history. It appears in novels, films, comics, and New Age belief as a symbol of lost wisdom, advanced technology, and catastrophic hubris. The story warns every empire: greatness does not exempt a civilization from destruction. It also fuels endless real-world searches, proving that a well-told lie can outlive many truths.
lore.archaeology: No archaeological site has been convincingly identified with Plato's Atlantis. The story has inspired searches at Santorini (Thera), the Spartel Bank, Andalusia, and elsewhere, but these remain speculative. The material legacy of Atlantis is therefore literary and cultural: Plato's dialogues, later ancient geographies, and two millennia of subsequent interpretation, art, and pseudo-archaeology.
lore.syncretism: Plato's Atlantis may draw on memories of the Minoan eruption on Thera, the Bronze Age collapse, or Egyptian traditions of the distant west. It has been identified with Tartessos, Santorini, Malta, and countless other places. In Renaissance and modern times it became a blank screen for utopian, occult, and pseudo-historical speculation. The name 'Atlantic Ocean' comes from the same Atlas root.

entries.meaning: Elysian plain; abode of the blessed dead

etymology.derivation: Possibly from a root meaning "concealed" or "deep"; Elysion was imagined as a hidden paradise at the ends of the earth.

entries.meaning: Beyond the north wind; a legendary northern paradise

etymology.derivation: From ὑπέρ "over, beyond" + Βορέας "the North Wind." Hyperborea is the land beyond the north wind.

cognates.note: Of or relating to the far north

etymology.derivation: From φαέθω "to shine"; an epithet of Helios and the name of his ill-fated son.

cognates.note: Used poetically for the sun and for the mythological figure

etymology.derivation: Probably a Semitic loanword into Greek; related to Akkadian barraqtu and Hebrew bareqet. The word passed into Latin as smaragdus and into Romance languages.

cognates.note: Via Old French esmeraude and Latin smaragdus

entries.meaning: Hyacinth; blue gem or flower; youth loved by Apollo

etymology.derivation: Possibly from a Mediterranean or Pre-Greek word for a blue/violet flower; later applied to the blue sapphire-like gem.
From ἀ- "not" + μέθυ "wine." The Greeks believed amethyst prevented intoxication.

cognates.note: Honey wine from the same PIE root *médu-

etymology.derivation: Probably a Pre-Greek Mediterranean loanword; the origin is disputed. Thálassa is the ordinary word for the sea in Greek.

entries.meaning: Feminine nominative singular article in Ancient Greek; in Orphic and Neoplatonic thought, the receptacle of divine overflow and counterpart to τὸ ἕν (Hén).
entries.domain: The Divine Feminine Principle, She Who Is

variants.note: Lowercase owned domain form
Plain ASCII form

etymology.derivation: Ancient Greek definite article ἡ, feminine nominative singular of ὁ. Philosophically reinterpreted in later Platonism as the feminine principle of manifestation.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAY' — one long syllable, beginning with a soft 'h' and drawn out like a breath.
pronunciation.note: Hē is Tier 2 because the Greek ἡ preserves the long vowel (eta) but is a grammatical particle, not a stressed lexical word in ordinary syntax. Its theological reinterpretation comes from later Platonism, which treated the article as a metaphysical principle.

domains.title: The Feminine Principle
domains.subtitle: Receptivity, Manifestation, She Who Is
domains.lead: Hē is the Ancient Greek feminine article, later reinterpreted by philosophers as a name for the feminine principle of being. It is the grammatical 'she' that becomes, in Neoplatonic and esoteric thought, the counterpart to the One.

cards.name: Grammatical Goddess
cards.desc: The definite article 'she,' personified by later mystical thought as feminine being.

cards.name: Receptacle of Form
cards.desc: In Platonic interpretation, Hē is the hupodochē, the receiving matter in which forms appear.

cards.name: Counterpart to Hén
cards.desc: If τὸ ἕν (Hén) is the One, ἡ (Hē) is the manifested other, the dyad that follows unity.

cards.name: Linguistic Mysticism
cards.desc: A case where grammar becomes theology: the smallest word elevated to cosmic status.

symbols.name: The letter eta (Η)
symbols.meaning: The long vowel that carries the feminine article and the name

symbols.name: Vessel or cup
symbols.meaning: The receptacle that receives and holds form

symbols.name: Mirror
symbols.meaning: The reflecting surface in which the One becomes visible as many

symbols.name: Open door
symbols.meaning: Manifestation as the threshold through which being enters appearance

mythology.lead: Hē has no myth in the traditional sense. Its 'mythology' is the history of interpretation: how a tiny grammatical word became, for some philosophers, a divine name.

myths.title: The Receptacle
myths.text: Plato calls the principle of becoming the hupodochē, the 'receptacle' (Timaeus 49a–51b): that in which things come to be and perish while it itself never alters — 'like a mother receiving seed.' The dialogue famously refuses to give it a stable name; it partakes of the intelligible 'in a most puzzling and difficult way,' being neither this nor that, yet all thises and thats appear in it. Aristotle reports the same pairing as Plato's own 'unwritten doctrines': the One and the Unlimited, the active and passive principles of all things (Metaphysics A 6, 987b). Later readers — Neoplatonists above all — identified this receptive principle with the feminine and, through the grammar of manifestation, with the word ἡ itself. The myth means that matter, whatever receives form, was philosophically gendered female from the very beginning of Western metaphysics — and the smallest word in Greek became its name.

myths.title: Hē and Hén
myths.text: In Neoplatonic and theurgical texts the masculine tò hén (Hén, the One) is paired with hē, the feminine principle of procession and manifestation — the dyad that follows unity and generates the multiplicity of the cosmos. The tradition read the pair out of Plato's own Parmenides, whose second hypothesis explores 'if the one is': the One-that-becomes-many. Iamblichus made the One and the dyad the first principles of number, and Proclus calls the dyad 'the cause of difference and the first multiplicity'; Damascius, last head of the Athenian school, named the dyad 'the Unlimited' itself, the first otherness from which all number and all form flow. The myth means the cosmos is born grammatically: unity speaks as masculine, manifestation as feminine — and the article 'she' becomes the name of everything the One is not.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hē is the smallest flagship in the PUNICODEX pantheon: two letters, one syllable, infinite interpretive weight. It reminds us that language itself can become sacred, and that grammar carries gendered philosophy. In modern gender discourse, the feminine article's elevation to a divine name can be read as an affirmation of feminine principle — or as a caution that abstraction is not the same as personhood.
lore.archaeology: There is no archaeological evidence for a cult of 'Hē' as a personified goddess; the entry is a philosophical and linguistic construction. The material context is textual: manuscripts of Plato, Plotinus, and Proclus, where the article ἡ is interpreted metaphysically. The PUNICODEX temple thus preserves an idea rather than a site.
lore.syncretism: Hē as a theological principle resonates with many traditions: the Chinese yin, the Indian prakṛti, the Gnostic Sophia, and the Jewish Shekhinah all name a feminine receptive power. Within Greek thought it overlaps with Gē/Gaia as earth-mother and with the Platonic hupodochē. The PUNICODEX entry treats ἡ as a philosophical personification rather than a traditional deity, making it unique among the flagship entries.

entries.meaning: Lithuanian/Baltic thunder deity, cognate with Slavic Perun and Indo-Iranian Parjanya.
entries.domain: God of Thunder, Lightning and Storms

variants.note: Owned domain form
Plain ASCII form

etymology.derivation: From Proto-Baltic *Perkūnas, from PIE *perkʷu- "oak; thunderer", also reflected in Slavic Perun and Vedic Parjanya.

pronunciation.approximation: pyair-KOO-nuss — roll the 'r,' make the 'oo' long, and give the final syllable a light hiss.
pronunciation.note: Perkūnas is Tier-1: the macron on the long ū is a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The name descends from Proto-Baltic *Perkūnas and is cognate with Slavic Perun, reflecting a common Indo-European thunder deity.

domains.title: Thunder on the Oak
domains.subtitle: Storms, Justice, and the Baltic Sky-Father
domains.lead: Perkūnas is the Lithuanian thunder god, the voice of the oak and the bolt that strikes the unjust. In Baltic folklore he rides across the sky in a flaming chariot, hurling stone axes and lightning arrows at demons, liars, and those who break their oaths. He is not merely weather; he is the moral sky, the enforcer of cosmic law in a world of dark forests and hidden spirits.

cards.name: Thunder and Lightning
cards.desc: His voice is thunder and his weapon is the lightning bolt that splits the sky.

cards.name: The Sacred Oak
cards.desc: The oak is his tree; sacrifices were made at oak groves and stones struck by lightning.

cards.name: Divine Justice
cards.desc: He punishes oath-breakers, murderers, and those who wrong the innocent.

cards.name: Foe of the Underworld
cards.desc: He battles Velnias, the devil or forest spirit, and other chthonic forces.

symbols.name: Stone axe or hammer
symbols.meaning: The thunderbolt weapon that Perkūnas hurls and that Neolithic axes symbolized as fallen from the sky

symbols.name: Oak tree
symbols.meaning: His sacred tree, struck by lightning and used for offerings

symbols.name: Flaming chariot or cart
symbols.meaning: His vehicle as he rumbles across the sky in Lithuanian songs

symbols.name: Fire and spark
symbols.meaning: The sacred fire struck from the sky and preserved in Baltic ritual

mythology.lead: Perkūnas's mythology is preserved largely in Lithuanian and Latvian folklore recorded in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, after the medieval church had suppressed his cult. The peasants remembered him as the thunderer who defended the moral order against devils, witches, and the chaos of the wilderness — and the recorders wrote it down just in time.

myths.title: Perkūnas and the Oak
myths.text: In Lithuanian folklore Perkūnas's tree is the oak, and the lightning-struck oak is his signature. Jonas Basanavičius and the nineteenth-century collectors recorded what the peasantry still practiced: when his bolt split a tree, the fire that remained was gathered as sacred and carried home without letting it die, to kindle the hearth anew; splinters of the struck wood were kept against lightning and illness, and offerings were left at the lightning-stones at the roots. The oak grove itself was his temple — an open-air sanctuary needing no roof, since its congregation met under thunderheads. Folklore adds the companion image of his forge: in the deep of the storm the god hammers his bolts on the anvil of the sky, and the long rolling after-clap is the echo of his work. The theology is exact: the tree that stands highest takes the blow, and the fire that kills the tree feeds the house. What strikes the sacred thing becomes the sacred thing.

myths.title: Pērkons Judges the Liar
myths.text: The Latvian dainas — the hundreds of thousands of short folk songs gathered by Krišjānis Barons in the nineteenth century — give Pērkons his juridical office. Thunder, the dainas say, does not strike at random: it searches out the perjurer, the thief whose theft was never confessed, the master who cheated his laborers, the miser who turned the beggar from his door. One strain has Pērkons striking the oath-breaker's barns; another has the thunder god walking the roads in human disguise, asking shelter and rewarding or punishing what he finds. A clap of thunder during a quarrel or a lawsuit was heard as his verdict entering the record. The tradition is not naive about this: some dainas admit the bolt sometimes falls on the innocent cottage, and the people's answer is that hidden guilt must have been there. In a land without effective courts for the poor, the thunderer's roll was the appeal that always found a judge — the sky, unlike the manor, could not be bribed.

lore.culturalLegacy: Perkūnas remains a living symbol of Lithuanian and Latvian national identity. His name appears in place names, folk songs, and contemporary pagan (Romuva) revival rituals. Oak groves are still protected in the Baltic states as natural and cultural heritage, and the thunder god features in metal music, fantasy literature, and neo-pagan art. The Romuva movement — the name itself is the old word for a Baltic sanctuary — has restored public fire-rituals to his groves, and Lithuania's independence movement of the late twentieth century reached readily for his imagery as a badge of pre-Soviet, pre-Christian identity. For linguists, Perkūnas is a key witness to the survival of Indo-European theonyms in a region that preserved archaic traditions longer than most of Europe — a god whose cult the church suppressed for six centuries without ever quite managing to replace him.
lore.archaeology: Direct evidence for Perkūnas's cult is scarce precisely because the cult was suppressed and practiced in groves, not masonry. What the ground keeps is indirect: Baltic hillfort complexes such as Kernavė in Lithuania — a medieval capital whose five hillforts and unexcavated cult layers long identified with the open-air sanctuary tradition — and, across the region, thousands of Neolithic and Bronze Age stone axes kept in farmhouses as Perkūno kirviai, 'Perkūnas's axes', believed to be the thunderer's own bolts fallen from the sky and prized as lightning-charms. The textual witnesses predate the folklore collections: the sixteenth-century Old Prussian catechisms record the name Percunis on a converted heathen's lips, and Grunau's chronicle describes the idol in its grove. Christian crosses and chapel sites across the Baltic often stand where the lightning-oaks stood — the map of the new religion drawn directly over the old one.
lore.syncretism: Perkūnas is cognate with Slavic Perun and Indo-Iranian Parjanya, all descendants of a Proto-Indo-European thunder deity. Slavic Perun, worshipped at Kiev and other centers, is the closest historical parallel. In Christianized folklore, Perkūnas was partially displaced by Saint Michael, Elijah, or God the Father, but his oak cult, thunder lore, and moral role survived under Christian names. The Old Prussian evidence shows how the church read him: the sixteenth-century catechisms record converts still swearing by Percunis, and Simon Grunau's Preussische Chronik describes his idol in its grove beside the harvest god Potrimpo and the death-god Peckols. Scholars have compared him to Germanic Thor, Greek Zeus, and Vedic Indra, though each culture shaped the thunder god according to its own landscape — and in the Baltic, uniquely, the thunderer stayed a working judge of the peasantry's daily affairs.

entries.meaning: In the Prose Edda, Búri is the primeval ancestor born from the salty rime, father of Borr and grandfather of Óðinn.
entries.domain: First God of the Norse Pantheon, Progenitor of the Æsir

variants.note: Owned domain form
Plain ASCII form

etymology.derivation: Old Norse Búri, possibly from a root meaning "producer, begetter" (compare Old Norse búa "to dwell, to be").

steps: ᛒ (bjarkan) writes /b/.
ᚢ (úr) writes /u/ and /ú/.
ᚱ (reið) writes /r/.
ᛁ (ís) writes /i/.
The runic spelling reflects normalized Old Norse Búri; Younger Futhark does not distinguish short and long vowels.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BOO-ree' — hold the 'oo' long and stress it, then finish with a quick trilled r and short 'ee'.
pronunciation.note: Búri is Tier 1: the acute on ú is a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The etymology is uncertain; the lexicon records a speculative connection to a root meaning 'to be, become' and the Old Norse verb búa. We describe attested cosmogony rather than claiming a settled word-origin.

domains.title: First God of the Norse Pantheon
domains.subtitle: The Primeval Ancestor of the Æsir
domains.lead: Búri is the first god in Norse mythology, the ancestor from whom all the Æsir descend. He was not born but revealed: the primeval cow Auðumla licked the salty rime of Niflheimr until a human shape emerged. From Búri came Burr, from Burr came Óðinn, Vili, and Vé, and from them came the world as we know it.

cards.name: Born from the Rime
cards.desc: Licked free from the ice of Niflheimr by the primeval cow Auðumla.

cards.name: Father of Burr
cards.desc: His son Borr/Burr fathers Óðinn, Vili, and Vé.

cards.name: Progenitor of the Æsir
cards.desc: Every major god of the Norse pantheon traces descent from him.

cards.name: Primeval Form
cards.desc: A human-shaped god emerging from the inanimate ice, the first animate divine being.

symbols.name: Salt rime
symbols.meaning: The icy substance from which Búri was licked into shape — creation as uncovering, not making

symbols.name: Primeval cow Auðumla
symbols.meaning: The nourisher whose licking revealed the first god while her milk fed his future enemy

symbols.name: Genealogical tree
symbols.meaning: The root of the Æsir family, from which all later gods branch

symbols.name: Ice and thaw
symbols.meaning: The cosmogonic transition from frozen chaos to living divinity

mythology.lead: Búri has no adventures, no conflicts, no cult. His entire myth is cosmogonic: he is the first divine being, the point at which the inanimate cosmos becomes personal. Everything that follows in Norse mythology follows from his emergence.

myths.title: The Licking of the Rime
myths.text: In Gylfaginning 6 Snorri gives Búri his entire recorded life in one scene. The primeval cow Auðumla, who fed herself by licking the salty rime that covered the stones of Niflheimr, licked and licked until a shape appeared in the ice: on the first day, hair; on the second, a head; on the third, a whole man. This was Búri — beautiful to look at, great in size and strength — and he begot a son, Burr, who married Bestla, daughter of the giant Bölþorn. Her sons were Óðinn, Vili, and Vé, who would one day kill the giant Ymir and make the world of his body. A god is not born here but uncovered, licked into personhood by patient animal care: the first theology of the North is a cow grooming the ice until it wakes. Creation as tending, not commanding, is the note the whole cosmogony sounds.

myths.title: The Ice and the Rivers
myths.text: Búri's emergence only makes sense against the world that produced him. Snorri describes Ginnungagap, the yawning void, lying between the blazing Múspellsheimr to the south and the frozen Niflheimr to the north, from whose rivers, the Élivágar, flowed a venom that hardened into the rime. Where the hot air from the south met the rime, the ice thawed and quickened, and from the drops of poisoned meltwater grew the hermaphroditic giant Ymir, ancestor of every frost giant. The same thaw that quickened Ymir nourished the rime that Auðumla licked: giant and god are siblings of a single thaw, one formed from venom-melt, the other revealed by a cow's tongue. The Norse cosmos begins with a paradox it never resolves — life and the forces of chaos are made of the same water, at the same temperature, at the same moment. The war of gods and giants is, cosmically speaking, a family quarrel between two kinds of meltwater.

lore.culturalLegacy: Búri is rarely a major figure in popular retellings, but he is essential to the Norse cosmic map. Whenever the genealogy of the gods is traced, he stands at the root. In modern Heathenry he is sometimes honored as the divine ancestor, the first spark of consciousness in the frozen cosmos. For artists and writers, the image of a human shape emerging from ice through the patient licking of a cow is one of the most striking origin images in world mythology.
lore.archaeology: No archaeological find names Búri. His attestation is entirely literary, dependent on the Prose Edda of Snorri Sturluson and its manuscript tradition, with the shadowy confirmation of Völuspá's 'Búrs synir.' The cosmogonic scene he anchors — the primeval cow, the rime, the emergence of the first being — belongs to the mythic imagination rather than to material cult. Scandinavian rock art and Bronze-Age imagery do include cattle and solar motifs, but none can be securely linked to Búri.
lore.syncretism: Búri has no direct counterpart in other Germanic or Indo-European traditions, but his emergence from ice through the action of a primeval cow resembles other cosmogonic motifs in which the first being is shaped from inanimate matter or nourished by a bovine creature. Comparisons have been made to the Vedic primeval bull, the Iranian Gavaevodata, and various Indo-European cow/cosmogony figures. Auðumla's licking of Búri from the rime has also invited comparison with creation-through-licking in Finno-Ugric and other northern Eurasian traditions. Medieval Christian readers, including Snorri, often framed such stories as euhemerized or rationalized accounts of pre-Christian cosmology.

entries.meaning: The supreme celestial force and moral order of the cosmos

variants.note: Plain ASCII form

pronunciation.ipaLabel: Modern Standard Chinese / Old Chinese Reconstruction
pronunciation.approximation: 'tyehn' — say 't-yeh-n' in one crisp syllable, on a high, level pitch like a sustained musical note.
pronunciation.note: Tiān is Tier 1: the macron preserves Mandarin first tone, a distinctive diacritic the ASCII form loses. The registrable form uses the standard Pinyin macron.

domains.title: Heaven and the Mandate
domains.subtitle: Cosmic Sovereignty and Moral Order
domains.lead: Tiān 天 is not a creator god in the Western sense. It is Heaven as supreme moral authority: the sky that watches, judges, and withdraws its favour from unworthy kings. From the Shang oracle bones to the Temple of Heaven, Tiān binds political legitimacy to cosmic virtue.

cards.name: Pole Star
cards.desc: The unmoving axis around which the heavens revolve; Tiān dwells at the northern celestial pivot.

cards.name: Mandate of Heaven
cards.desc: Political legitimacy granted only to virtuous rulers; famine, flood, or defeat signal its loss.

cards.name: High Di
cards.desc: Successor to the Shang supreme deity Shàngdì 上帝, the celestial ancestor who receives royal sacrifice.

cards.name: Ritual Centre
cards.desc: The Temple of Heaven in Beijing, where the emperor prayed as the Son of Heaven for cosmic harmony.

symbols.name: Azure Dragon
symbols.meaning: The eastern quadrant of the sky, guardian of spring and imperial auspice.

symbols.name: Jade disk (bi 璧)
symbols.meaning: Ritual object offered to Heaven, the circular sky matching the square earth.

symbols.name: North celestial pole
symbols.meaning: The still centre of the turning sky, the astral throne of Tiān.

symbols.name: Sacrificial bull
symbols.meaning: The highest offering, presented at the border sacrifice to honour Heaven.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Tiān is inseparable from the history of Chinese kingship: less a corpus of tales than a cosmology in which Heaven speaks through weather, eclipse, dynasty, and the virtue of the ruler. Its central text is political — the Mandate of Heaven (tiānmìng 天命), which made every reign a moral verdict.

myths.title: From Shàngdì to Tiān
myths.text:
In Shang times the supreme power was Shàngdì 上帝, the High Lord or high ancestor-deity above, who commanded wind and rain and received the Shang king's sacrifices in person. The oracle bones of Anyang are his archive: diviners cracked turtle shell and ox bone to learn his will on harvest, war, and the royal health. When the Zhou — a western people — overthrew the Shang at Mùyě c. 1046 BCE, they faced a theological problem: how could a lesser house displace the anointed? Their answer, canonized in the Shàngshū 尚書 (Book of Documents) and the Dà Yǎ odes of the Shījīng 詩經, reframed supreme authority as Tiān 天, 'Heaven' — a moral order rather than a clan ancestor. The Zhou king ruled as tiānzǐ 天子, Son of Heaven, because Heaven's Mandate (tiānmìng 天命) had passed from the dissolute Shang.

Victory was thereby rewritten as verdict: Heaven does not favour blood, it favours virtue. The conquest myth of China is a change of pronouns — from 'my ancestor' to 'the sky' — and three millennia of Chinese politics lived inside that change.

myths.title: The Duke of Zhou and the Mandate
myths.text:
The Duke of Zhou, brother of the conquering King Wu and regent for the boy King Cheng, is credited with formulating the Mandate as a check on arbitrary power — the tradition makes the statesman a theologian. When rebellion shook the young dynasty, the Duke's response in the documents preserved in the Shàngshū (the 'Great Announcement' 大誥 and 'Establishment of Government' 立政) is consistent: Heaven's charge is hard to keep, won by the virtue of former kings and lost through drunkenness and cruelty. The Shǐjì 史記 of Sima Qian adds the human drama: the Duke is slandered into exile, and returns only when a great storm uproots the royal grain and the frightened king opens the sealed archive that proves his loyalty beyond doubt.

The story fixed the Mandate's logic for three millennia: Heaven speaks through portent — storm, eclipse, flood, defeat — and portent demands moral repair, not merely ritual repair. No figure in Chinese tradition did more to make the sky a constitutional court.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Mandate of Heaven remains one of the most consequential ideas in Chinese political thought, invoked by rebels and regimes alike. The Temple of Heaven in Beijing, a UNESCO World Heritage site, still stands as its architectural signature. Modern Chinese uses Tiān in dozens of compounds—tiānkōng 天空 (sky), tiānqì 天气 (weather), tiānxià 天下 (all under Heaven)—so thoroughly that the word is almost invisible, yet everywhere present.
lore.syncretism: Tiān absorbed and was absorbed by later traditions. Confucians spoke of Tiān as moral destiny; Daoists located it within a larger cosmos of qi and the Dao; Chinese Buddhists translated the Sanskrit deva with Tiān. Jesuit missionaries of the late Ming identified the Christian God with Tiānzhǔ 天主, 'Lord of Heaven', sparking centuries of debate about whether Heaven was a personal deity or an impersonal order.
lore.originalScriptNote: The character 天 combines the graph for 'one' 一 with 'great' 大; traditional etymology sees it as the greatest One above. Oracle-bone forms sometimes show a rounded head or a dome, suggesting a human-shaped sky ancestor. The word was written before the Qin standardisation in a variety of Zhou forms; the modern character is the Clerical and Regular script descendant. PUNICODEX uses the Pinyin form Tiān with a macron to mark the first tone, since 天 itself cannot be directly registered as a domain string.

entries.meaning: Lord of the Land of the Dead

variants.note: Plain ASCII form

pronunciation.approximation: 'meek-TLAHN-tay-KOOT-lee' — keep the first 'a' and 'e' long, and release the final -tl as one tongue-flip.
pronunciation.note: The macrons on ā and ē mark reconstructed Classical Nahuatl vowel length, the feature that makes the restoration Tier 1. Final -tl is never pronounced as separate English 't' and 'l'.

domains.title: Lord of Mictlān
domains.subtitle: Death, the Underworld, and the Nine Descents
domains.lead: Mictlāntēcutli is the terrible king of Mictlān, the deepest underworld beneath the earth. He does not judge souls; he receives them. After a long descent through nine perilous levels, the dead arrive at his ash-coloured realm, where life is finally, utterly extinguished.

cards.name: Nine Levels
cards.desc: The soul descends four years through wind, mountains, jaguars, and knives before reaching rest.

cards.name: Lord of Bone
cards.desc: He appears as a flayed or skeletal figure with staring eyes and a jawless skull, adorned with paper banners.

cards.name: Death as Cycle
cards.desc: Mictlān is not hellish punishment but the necessary destination of most mortals; new life rises from decay.

cards.name: Impersonator
cards.desc: A living ixiptla wore the god's regalia and was sacrificed at the feast of Tititl.

symbols.name: Skull
symbols.meaning: The face of the underworld lord and the memento mori carried by priests.

symbols.name: Owl
symbols.meaning: Night bird and messenger between the living and the dead.

symbols.name: Obsidian blade
symbols.meaning: The sacrificial knife (tecpatl) that opens the doorway to Mictlān.

symbols.name: Paper banner (amate)
symbols.meaning: Ritual paper streamers marking the wind that blows through the land of the dead.

mythology.lead: Mictlāntēcutli’s myths are few but pivotal: he is the custodian of the bones of an extinguished humanity, the landlord of the stars, and the end of every road that does not end in battle. The future of the Fifth Sun depends on outwitting him, and every ordinary death in the Aztec world spends four years travelling down to his door.

myths.title: The Bones of the Old Age
myths.text: After the Fourth Sun perished in flood, the gods gathered at Teotihuacan to make a new race, and they needed raw material: the bones of the people of the previous ages, kept in the deepest house of Mictlān. Quetzalcōātl volunteered for the theft. The lord of the dead received him politely and set a condition — that he walk four times around Mictlān blowing a conch shell that had no holes. Quetzalcōātl called worms to bore the shell and bees to hum inside it, and the trumpet sounded. He seized the bones and ran; Mictlāntēcutli sent a quail to startle him at the boundary, and the bones fell into a pit and shattered. The story, told in the Leyenda de los Soles and remembered by Sahagún, ends with the gods grinding the fragments in a bowl: from the broken bones of the dead they fashion human beings of every stature. The meaning is the myth’s quiet engine — the new humanity is built literally from death’s losses, and human difference itself is the scar tissue of mortality.

myths.title: Lord of the Starry Host
myths.text: Aztec cosmology handed the night sky to the dead. The stars that wheel overhead were read as the host of Mictlāntēcutli — in the great screenfold of the Codex Borgia he presides over the nocturnal hours flanked by skeletal powers — and the most dangerous of them, the tzitzimime, were star-demons who could leave heaven and fall upon the earth. Sahagún records the terror of the eclipse: when the tzitzimime descended to attack the sun, the whole city raised a din of shouts and slaps to drive them back, for if the sun were devoured the Fifth Sun would end and the demons would feast on humankind. The calendar’s five unlucky days, the nemontemi, were likewise watched in fear as days when the star-demons pressed closest. The lord of bones thus ruled not only beneath the earth but across the dome of night: every darkness, subterranean or celestial, answered to the same throne.

lore.culturalLegacy: Mictlāntēcutli presides over one of the world’s most visually powerful death traditions, and his modern presence is out of proportion to his few surviving myths. The great monolith in the Museo Nacional de Antropología — its goggle eyes, fanged jaw, and paper banners frozen mid-snarl — has become an emblem of Mexica antiquity as recognizable as any object in the Americas. Around him gathers the living festival: the Day of the Dead, inscribed by UNESCO in 2008 on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, whose ofrendas, sugar skulls, and La Catrina processions keep the old underworld commerce with the dead in full public view. Contemporary artists, muralists, metal bands, and graphic novelists return to him not as a monster but as the dignified keeper of an unavoidable truth. In a global culture that hides death behind curtains, Mictlāntēcutli remains the great counter-example: death as destiny, shared equally, and faced with offerings, flowers, and even jokes.
lore.archaeology: The most arresting artifact is the monumental stone figure of Mictlāntēcutli excavated in Mexico City in the 1930s and now the centerpiece of the Mexica hall of the Museo Nacional de Antropología — nearly two metres of basalt, arms raised, eye-sockets once inlaid, its torso stripped of flesh in the god’s flayed aspect. The great double pyramid of the Templo Mayor was dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlāloc, but the precinct beneath it is layered with the lord of bones’ own archaeology: caches of skulls, sacrificial victims interred with death-god regalia, and — excavated beside the temple in 2015 — a massive tzompantli, a skull rack that once displayed the heads of the sacrificed above the sacred precinct. The painted record survives equally well: the Codex Borgia, a screenfold produced around 1500 in the Puebla–Cholula region and now in the Vatican Library, devotes whole registers to the skeletal lords of the underworld enthroned among the night hours.
lore.syncretism: Spanish friars identified Mictlāntēcutli with the Christian Devil almost at once, and colonial painting gave him European horns, bat wings, and infernal gloom. The identification flattened him: the pre-contact lord was no tempter and no torturer, merely the necessary terminus of every ordinary life. His consort Mictecacihuatl survived the conquest far more visibly. In the nineteenth century the printmaker José Guadalupe Posada turned the elegant death’s-head Calavera into Mexico’s national memento mori; Diego Rivera enthroned her as La Catrina, and she now presides over the Día de los Muertos, whose whole grammar — food for the dead, skulls that grin — descends from the Mictlān complex. Modern Mexico has reclaimed the lord himself as heritage rather than horror: his monolith anchors the national museum, and his name, no longer diabolized, titles artworks, scholarly institutes, and works of fantasy across the Americas.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is Nahuatl: mictlan ('place of the dead') + tēcutli ('lord'). Classical Nahuatl was written in a logophonetic tradition of pictographic glyphs, many of which were burned or lost after the conquest; the name now reaches us through alphabetic transcription in colonial sources such as the Florentine Codex. The macrons mark long vowels reconstructed by linguists; Spanish colonial spellings such as Mictlantecuhtli sometimes omit them.

pronunciation.approximation: 'see-wah-KOH-ahtl' — the first vowel is short, the 'c' is a hard 'k,' and the final -tl is one crisp tongue-stop.
pronunciation.note: The name is a transparent compound of cihuātl ('woman') and cōātl ('snake'). The first vowel (i) is short; the long vowel the written compound leaves unmarked is the ā of cihuātl, shortened in the compound (compound-shortening). The same word was used as a political title, the Cihuacōātl or 'Woman-Snake,' a high official of the Mexica state. In religion, Cihuacōātl is a powerful goddess of childbirth, maternity, and the dangers that attend both. Tier 1: the macrons preserve vowel length, a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: The Snake Woman
domains.subtitle: Childbirth, Midwifery, and the Fate of Mothers
domains.lead: Cihuacōātl is the divine midwife and the spectral woman who haunts the crossroads. In one aspect she protects women in labor; in another she wanders at night weeping for children who died unbaptized into life. She embodies the dangerous threshold between pregnancy and birth, life and death, the domestic hearth and the wild road.

cards.name: Goddess of Childbirth
cards.desc: She aids women in labor and receives the afterbirth; midwives call upon her and make offerings.

cards.name: Protector of Midwives
cards.desc: The tēntitl 'midwife' served as her human representative; birthing rituals invoked her power.

cards.name: The Weeping Woman
cards.desc: La Llorona, the wailing specter of crossroads and waterways, descends partly from Cihuacōātl lore.

cards.name: Fate and Threshold
cards.desc: She governs the dangerous moment when a new life crosses from the spirit world into the body.

symbols.name: Serpent
symbols.meaning: The snake element shared with Cōātlīcue, linking her to earth powers and regeneration

symbols.name: Child swaddling-clothes
symbols.meaning: Midwives' equipment associated with her protection of births

symbols.name: Crossroads at night
symbols.meaning: The liminal space where she appears as a weeping woman carrying a dead child

symbols.name: Cihuapipiltin spirits
symbols.meaning: The 'noble women' who died in childbirth and became fierce omens and warriors of the sun

mythology.lead: Cihuacōātl's mythology is preserved in the birth rituals recorded by Sahagún and in the widespread Mexican legend of the weeping woman. She is both a beneficent guardian and a terrifying ghost, a duality that reflects the high mortality of childbirth in the pre-modern world.

myths.title: The Midwives’ Prayer
myths.text: Sahagún’s informants describe how the midwife received the newborn as a captive taken in sacred battle: the child, they said, had been chosen in the land of the dead by the gods and delivered into the midwife’s hands. She addressed the infant as a warrior arriving from the sky, invoked the divine protectresses of the birthing chamber — among them Cihuacōātl — cut the umbilicus over an open vessel, and buried the afterbirth in the corner of the house as an offering. The child was bathed, named, and ritually presented to the gods; the cord of a girl child was buried by the hearth, that of a boy by the fields, fixing each life to its future work. Cihuacōātl’s presence ensured the dangerous passage from womb to world ended in life rather than death (Florentine Codex, Book VI). The ritual means birth was classified as war: the mother a battlefield, the midwife a commander, and the goddess the power holding the door.

myths.title: The Cihuapipiltin and the Crossroads
myths.text: Women who died in childbirth — above all in a first labor — were believed to become cihuāpīpiltin, “noble women,” spirits of enormous and ambivalent power. They wandered at night dressed in white, faces chalked, hair loose, weeping at crossroads and waterways for the children they had lost; they could seize or strike men who mocked them, appear as omens of war, and visit fathers in dreams. Yet the same powers defended their communities: the spirits of women dead in childbirth were counted among the fierce dead who carried the sun from noon to setting, soldiers in the sky’s war. Over centuries this figure merged with Spanish colonial ghost-lore to produce La Llorona, the weeping woman of Mexican folklore. The transformation means a goddess of childbirth survived conquest by becoming a ghost — the cult suppressed, the grief irrepressible.

lore.culturalLegacy: Cihuacōātl survives most visibly in La Llorona, a figure known throughout Mexico and the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. The weeping woman at the water's edge, mourning children lost to drowning, violence, or history, carries the ancient goddess into contemporary song, film, and political allegory. Feminist and Chicana writers have reclaimed both Cihuacōātl and La Llorona as symbols of maternal grief, female autonomy, and the suppressed voices of indigenous women.
lore.archaeology: Cihuacōātl is not represented by a single monumental sculpture comparable to Cōātlīcue, but her presence is documented in the birth rituals recorded by Sahagún, in ceramic figurines of women in childbirth, and in the large corpus of Nahuatl ritual speech preserved in colonial manuscripts. Cross-cultural parallels with Maya childbirth deities and with colonial-period ex-votos suggest a long history of female-divine assistance at birth in Mesoamerica.
lore.syncretism: Cihuacōātl merges in popular memory with La Llorona, the weeping woman of crossroads and rivers, and with the Virgin Mary in her sorrowful or protective aspects. The cihuapipiltin spirits share traits with the Celtic-Spanish banshee and with other worldwide figures of the woman who died in childbirth. In Nahuatl religion she is closely related to Cōātlīcue and Tlāltēcuhtli, forming a cluster of serpent-and-earth maternal powers.

entries.meaning: Possibly 'grief of the people' (from ἄχος + λαός), or a pre-Greek name

variants.note: Latinized form (English Achilles); the temple uses the Greek Achilleús.

pronunciation.approximation: ah-khil-LEWS, stress on the final syllable.
pronunciation.note: Homeric Greek Ἀχιλλεύς scans with a short i and a stressed final syllable; the geminate λλ is attested in the best manuscripts beside the single-λ variant Ἀχιλεύς. The restoration Achilleús keeps the acute on the final syllable exactly where the Greek puts it. In the epic hexameter the name scans ⏑ – —: a short first alpha followed by two long syllables, and that short first syllable is precisely why the single-λ variant Ἀχιλεύς exists.

domains.title: The Best of the Achaeans
domains.subtitle: War, Glory, Rage, and the Short Bright Life
domains.lead: Achilleús is the hero the Iliad is named around: the man who chose a short life with imperishable fame (kleos aphthiton) over a long life in obscurity. His wrath is the poem's first word — mēnin — and his heel is the world's oldest named weakness.

cards.name: The Wrath
cards.desc: The Iliad opens on his mēnis — a rage that costs the Achaeans thousands of lives and remakes epic poetry.

cards.name: The Heel
cards.desc: The single unarmoured point of an otherwise deathless fighter; the West's shorthand for a fatal flaw.

cards.name: Kleos Aphthiton
cards.desc: Imperishable fame — the bargain every brand strikes: burn briefly and be remembered forever.

cards.name: Leuke the White Isle
cards.desc: His afterlife island in the Black Sea, where sailors left offerings to the hero for a thousand years.

symbols.name: The ash spear
symbols.meaning: The Pelian spear only he could wield — strength that cannot be inherited

symbols.name: The heel
symbols.meaning: The mortal point in the immortal frame; vulnerability as destiny

symbols.name: The lyre
symbols.meaning: He sang of heroes' fame in his tent — the warrior who is also a poet

symbols.name: The Scamander
symbols.meaning: The river that rose against him when his killing choked its waters

mythology.lead: Son of the mortal Pēleús and the sea-goddess Thetis, Achilleús stands exactly between god and man: the strongest argument the Greeks ever made that excellence cannot cancel mortality.

myths.title: Two Fates, Weighed Aloud
myths.text: Book 9 of the Iliad stages the first great decision scene of Western literature. Agamemnon's embassy — Odysseus, Aias, and old Phoinix, bearing the offer of treasure, one of Agamemnon's daughters, and restored honor — finds Achilleús in his tent, singing “the famous deeds of men” to his lyre (9.186–189). His answer is the speech every later hero rehearses: his mother has told him he carries two fates — “if I stay here and fight around the city of the Trojans, my return home is lost, but my fame will be imperishable; if I sail back to my dear fatherland, my noble fame is lost, but my life will be long” (9.412–416). He refuses the gifts, unconverted even by Phoinix's tale of Meleager, and chooses, in effect, to wait for Patroklos. The scene matters because the choice is made aloud, with the cost stated first: Achilleús never trades his life by accident — he prices it, in public, every time.

myths.title: The Death of Patroklos
myths.text: When Patroklos begged to enter the fighting in Achilleús' armor, the hero warned him: drive the Trojans from the ships and come back — do not press on to Troy (16.87–96). Patroklos drove them, pressed on, and Hektōr killed him in the borrowed armor, prophesying with his dying breath that Achilleús would soon die beneath the same wall (16.816–854). Achilleús' grief was absolute: Thetis found him face-down in the dust, groaning, holding his head while he chose revenge and death together (18.23–126). Hephaistos forged him new armor — the shield whose rim is Ocean, the most famous description in Greek verse (18.468–613) — and he returned a changed thing, “raging, grim,” his own horses weeping for Patroklos (19.392–424). He killed Hektōr, tied the corpse to his chariot, and dragged it round his friend's tomb (22.395–404; 24.14–18) — until Priam came alone to the tent at night, kissed the hands that had killed his sons, and the two enemies wept together, one for Pēleús and Patroklos, one for Hektōr (24.468–676). The Iliad's argument completes itself here: wrath becomes grief, grief becomes pity, and the hardest man in the poem learns the one thing strength cannot seize.

lore.culturalLegacy:
His name seeded two everyday terms: the Achilles heel (a single fatal weakness) and the Achilles tendon, named by the anatomist Verheyen in 1693 for the tendon nearest the mythic wound. "The wrath of Achilles" remains the standard translation exercise for every student of Greek, the μῆνιν ἄειδε θεά that begins Western literature.

Every sport that sells invincibility borrows his silhouette — until the heel reminds the audience how the story ends.
lore.archaeology: A hero-cult of Achilleús is documented at his tomb in the Troad (the tumulus at Sivri Tepe) and, most vividly, on the island of Leuke off the Danube delta, where Arrian reports a temple, votive offerings, and the hero appearing to sailors. Vase painting made him one of the most depicted figures in Greek art: the François Vase shows his pursuit of Troilos, and the Achilles-and-Ajax dice game survives in dozens of black-figure cups, including Exekias' masterpiece. Roman-era stamps and lamps from Olbia confirm the Black Sea cult lasted centuries.
lore.syncretism:
Rome read him through the Aeneid's mirror: Achilles is what Aeneas must not be — brilliant, doomed, and defiant of fate. Alexander the Great slept with the Iliad under his pillow and ran a victory lap around Achilleús' supposed tomb at Troy, consciously modelling his own short bright career on the hero's choice; his successors commissioned the Alexandrian portraiture of Achilles as the template of royal arete.

In late antiquity and Byzantium he survived as a romance figure — the Achilleid tradition and the Byzantine Achilleis kept him wandering long after Homer had closed his account — and in the Renaissance he returned as the measure of martial virtue. Modern Greece claims him as a national ancestor whose very untranslatability — rage, grief, honour — defines the epic imagination.

entries.meaning: Uncertain; possibly related to ἀσκαλαβώτης (lizard) or a pre-Greek healing root

variants.note: LSJ convention: length only, no stress mark

pronunciation.approximation: ah-SKLAY-pee-OSS, with the stress on the ultima and a long ē.
pronunciation.note: Attic Ἀσκληπιός places the acute on the final syllable; the η is unambiguously long, so the stacked macron-acute of the ideal form ḗ is philologically defensible. The owned form Asklēpiós follows the house rule against stacked marks while preserving both features across two characters.

domains.title: The Physician of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Medicine, Healing, Incubation, and the Boundary of Death
domains.lead: Asklēpiós is the only hero whose skill frightened the gods: the surgeon-son of Apóllōn who healed so well that Zeús destroyed him for emptying the underworld. His sanctuaries were the hospitals of the ancient world, and his snake-entwined staff still hangs over every pharmacy on earth.

cards.name: The Rod
cards.desc: A single serpent on a staff — the true emblem of medicine, distinct from Hermês' two-snaked caduceus.

cards.name: Epidaurus
cards.desc: The greatest healing sanctuary of antiquity, where patients slept among sacred snakes and dogs.

cards.name: Incubation
cards.desc: Temple sleep: the god visited dreams and prescribed the cure, recorded on the iamata tablets.

cards.name: The Thunderbolt
cards.desc: Zeús' answer to resurrection — the line past which even healing becomes transgression.

symbols.name: The serpent
symbols.meaning: Renewal through the shed skin; the chthonic knowledge of roots and venoms

symbols.name: The staff
symbols.meaning: The physician's walking stick; authority without weaponry

symbols.name: The dog
symbols.meaning: The wound-licking guardian of the sanctuary floor

symbols.name: The cock
symbols.meaning: The vigil-bird sacrificed to him — Sócrates' famous last debt
