The hymn distributes the offering — 'this share to Agni, this to Soma' — and the Brāhmaṇas legislate that the gods' shares were fixed at the beginning of things: the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.7.3–4) tells how the gods and the anti-gods contended for the sacrifice, how the gods took it for their own and assigned its parts — the ghee, the grains, the portions of the carcass — so that every deity receives the measure that is his. Aṃśa is the personification of that fixing: without the allotted share, no ritual holds, no inheritance stands, no year completes. The deepest grammar of the idea is already in the Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90.11–14), where the gods divide the primal being himself — from whose mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the orders of society arise. Creation, in this vision, is a division; and the share-god is creation's own arithmetic made divine.

lore.culturalLegacy: His word outlived his cult: aṃśa remains the everyday Sanskrit and Hindi word for "part," and technical vocabularies are built on it — navāṃśa (the ninth harmonic chart in Jyotisha astrology), kalāṃśa in music, daśāṃśa in taxation records. Wherever Indian thought divides a whole into rightful portions — astrology, inheritance law, music theory — the god's name is the operative term. The languages kept what the rituals let go: ask any Hindi speaker how many aṃśa are in a thing, and the share-god answers, unnamed, on every tongue.
lore.archaeology: Early Vedic religion was aniconic: no image of Aṃśa was ever made, and none was wanted — the fire altar was his only temple. The archaeology of the Ādityas is textual and structural: the śrauta fire-altars of the Śulba tradition, laid out with the geometry of portions (the altar's bricks counted and placed by rule), are the material form of his theology. Later Surya temples — Konarak, Modhera — give the solar Ādityas a collective home in stone.
lore.syncretism: He overlaps with Bhaga, the older "dispenser" of shares — the two are so close that Vedic lists sometimes trade their places — and with Mitra and Varuṇa, whose covenant-keeping the Ādityas collectively perform. The comparison that travels farthest is linguistic: Avestan aṃša-, the exact cognate of aṃśa, survives inside the very name Aməša Spənta, the 'Bounteous Immortals' of Zoroastrian theology — the portion raised from common noun to archangel. What in India stayed a quiet solar function became in Iran a rank of cosmic beings; the word crossed the religions intact while the god it named dissolved into his own meaning. Within Hinduism he was never independently worshipped, and needed no adoption: the share-god was already present at every sacrifice, in every portion of ghee measured out by the ladle.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written अंश in Devanagari: the short a, the anusvāra dot above it, then śa. The same spelling covers the god and the common noun "share," which is precisely the theology — the Āditya is the portion, personified.

entries.meaning: 'The skilled, the able' (from dakṣa), a Prajāpati

steps: द = da
क = ka
ष = ṣa (retroflex)
dakṣa is the Prajāpati of ritual order and father of many gods

pronunciation.approximation: DUCK-shah; the ṣ is the retroflex sh.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit dakṣa — 'able, skilled, dexterous' — carries the kṣa cluster written with the conjunct क्ष, a single glyph for k plus ṣ. Indo-Europeanists connect the word to the root *deks-, 'right hand, skill': Latin dexter is its cousin, and 'dexterity' its English echo. The kṣa conjunct is a single articulation — k releasing directly into the retroflex ṣ — which romanization splits in two.

domains.title: The Skilled Father
domains.subtitle: Progeny, Sacrifice, and the Goat's Head
domains.lead: Dakṣa is the Prajāpati of competence: the 'skilled one' whose sixty daughters married the Moon, Dharma, and the sage Kaśyapa to people the world — and whose flawless sacrifice, performed without Śiva, became the great cautionary tale of Indian religion.

cards.name: The Sixty Daughters
cards.desc: Father of the Nakṣatras — the 27 lunar mansions are his girls, wed to the Moon.

cards.name: The Great Sacrifice
cards.desc: The yajña to which Śiva was not invited — the snub that shattered heaven and earth.

cards.name: The Goat's Head
cards.desc: His punishment and restoration: beheaded in the ruined rite, revived with the head of a goat.

cards.name: Prajāpati
cards.desc: 'Lord of progeny' — the office of populating the cosmos, held by a committee of the skilled.

symbols.name: The sacrificial post
symbols.meaning: The yūpa of his cosmic rite — order raised, then ruined by pride

symbols.name: The goat
symbols.meaning: His second head — humility grafted onto skill

symbols.name: The rosary
symbols.meaning: The Prajāpati's counting of creatures and years

mythology.lead: Dakṣa's cycle is the Indian study of procedure versus devotion: the man who performs the rite perfectly and loses everything because of who was left off the list — and the moon he cursed, still waning monthly in witness against favoritism.

myths.title: Satī and the Ascetic
myths.text: His daughter Satī loved Śiva — the ash-smeared, skull-garlanded wanderer whom Dakṣa regarded as no fit match for a Prajāpati's house. The Purāṇas make the marriage the scandal of the age: Dakṣa's open scorn, Satī's immovable devotion, Śiva serenely indifferent to court opinion (Śiva Purāṇa, Rudrasaṃhitā, Satīkhaṇḍa). She married him anyway, against her father's will, and went to live on Kailāsa, in the realm of the gods of the uncivilized places. When Dakṣa later held the great sacrifice at Kankhal — the rite of the age, to which every god, every seer, and every daughter was summoned — two names were missing from the guest list: Śiva and Satī. The omission was deliberate, public, and meant. In the theology of the story the list is the sacrifice's whole substance: what is deliberately left out is what brings it all down.

myths.title: Satī's Self-Immolation
myths.text: Satī came uninvited to her father's rite and endured his contempt until she could endure no more: declaring that she would no longer wear a body born of one who insulted her lord, she entered the sacrificial fire and burned (Śiva Purāṇa, Satīkhaṇḍa; the Devībhāgavata gives the Goddess's own version). Her body, scattered in Śiva's grief-stricken dance across the land, seeded the fifty-one Śakti Pīṭhas — the holiest map of Śakta India, from Kamakhya in Assam to Hinglaj beyond the Indus. The tradition is exact about the meaning: the daughter's death is not defeat but sovereignty, the first self-offering by which the Goddess teaches that the body insulted is the body withdrawn. Every pīṭha is a place where the story says a piece of her fell — and where her power, not her father's, is worshipped.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Dakṣa-yajña cycle is among the most retold stories in India — sculpture, dance-drama, and television epics return to it constantly — and the Śakti Pīṭha pilgrimage map it generates still organizes Śakta devotion. His name lives in the language: dakṣa/daksh remains the word for the capable professional, and the dakṣiṇā, the ritual fee 'of the skilled hand,' is paid at every Hindu rite today.
lore.archaeology: The Kankhal complex at Haridwar — the Daksha Mahadev temple and the Śrī Daksheśvara site on the Ganga — marks the traditional ground of the great sacrifice, continuously rebuilt from early times and renovated in 1810 and 1962. Satī's pīṭhas, from Kamakhya to Hinglaj, give the myth the largest sacred geography of any Indian story. Iconography shows him goat-headed in the act of worship — the humbled adept — in Purāṇic panels across the Deccan and the South.
lore.syncretism: As Prajāpati he absorbed and was absorbed by Brahmā: the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas shift 'lord of progeny' between them until the offices blur. His daughter-lineages map the whole Purāṇic cosmos — through Kaśyapa's wives descend gods, demons, birds, and serpents; through Dharma's, the virtues. The Śakta tradition reframed his sacrifice entirely: not a tale of Śiva's wrath but of the Goddess's sovereignty, with Satī as the first self-offering. And because his name is simply the common word for 'the able one', the god of skill survives anonymously in every modern Indian compliment — the daksh professional — and in the dakṣiṇā, the ritual fee of the skilled hand, paid at every Hindu rite today.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written दक्ष in Devanagari: da plus the conjunct kṣa. The same spelling names the Prajāpati and the everyday adjective 'skilled' — the god is competence enthroned among the creators.

entries.meaning: 'The Ordainer, the Establisher' (from dhā, to place), an Āditya

steps: ध = dha
आ = ā (long)
तृ = tṛ (vocalic ṛ)
dhātṛ is the Āditya of creation and ordinance, "the Establisher"

pronunciation.approximation: dhah-TRUH; the ṛ is a rolled vocalic r.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit dhātṛ is an agent noun from the root dhā, "to set, place, establish," with the syllabic ṛ of the nominative — the vowel that is also a consonant, written ऋ. The restoration Dhātṛ keeps both the long ā and the vocalic ṛ that dictionaries print. The syllabic ṛ is a vowel made of the consonant itself: dhātṛ, two syllables, the final one vocalized r.

domains.title: The Establisher
domains.subtitle: Ordinance, Creation, and the Set-Down World
domains.lead: Dhātṛ is the Vedic verb of creation made personal: "the Establisher," the one who sets the sun in the sky and the child in the womb. Where Brahmā would later be a personality, Dhātṛ is still a function radiant with worship — creation as the act of setting-down.

cards.name: The Setter of Suns
cards.desc: Ṛgveda 10.190: he established heaven and earth, the waters and the light.

cards.name: With Vidhātṛ
cards.desc: Paired with the "Disposer" — the Establisher founds, the Disposer assigns each thing its law.

cards.name: Dhātu
cards.desc: His root-word: the elements of grammar and of medicine — the set-down units of reality.

cards.name: The Womb
cards.desc: He "establishes the embryo" — creation biological as well as cosmic.

symbols.name: The measuring line
symbols.meaning: The demarcation by which the formless receives form

symbols.name: The lotus seat
symbols.meaning: Later iconography's gift to the establishing powers

symbols.name: The syllable dhā
symbols.meaning: The root as emblem — setting, placing, founding

mythology.lead: Dhātṛ's mythology is the Ṛgveda's creation poetry itself: he appears wherever the text needs not a story but the act — the setting of each thing in its station.

myths.title: Ṛgveda 10.190
myths.text: The hymn of the ordering is Ṛgveda 10.190, among the oldest creation texts on earth. From tapas — ardor, heat — was born order (ṛta) and truth (satya); from them, night; from night, the ocean; from the ocean, the year, apportioning its days and nights. And then the poem names its maker: 'Dhātṛ, as he had made the sun and moon, established heaven and earth, the mid-air and the light' (RV 10.190.1–3). There is no battle here, no dismembered giant, no world-egg — only a sequence of set-downs, each thing placed where it belongs, the world's making told in the grammar of a verb: dhā, to set. Creation in the Ṛgveda's most abstract hymn is not an event but a placement. The wonder the hymn asks for is quiet and enormous: that anything is where it is — the moon in its month, the air between the worlds — is an act, and the act has a name.

myths.title: Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ
myths.text: The Vedic ritualists soon found that establishing needs disposing. In the Atharvaveda's domestic hymns and throughout the Brāhmaṇas, Dhātṛ appears with his twin Vidhātṛ — the Establisher and the Disposer: one fixes a thing's place, the other fixes its lot. Together they are invoked at the thresholds of a life, in the marriage rite where a new household is set down and the birth rites where the child's fortune must be founded. Later tradition, keeping the pair, made them the joint signatories of destiny: Dhātṛ-Vidhātṛ become the formula in the epics and Purāṇas for 'as the powers ordained.' The pairing is subtle and complete — a thing is not only where it is but what it is for — and it survives in vernacular birth invocations still spoken today, where parents ask that the child be well-established. The two gods are one insight wearing two faces: no foundation without an allotment, no world without its law.

lore.culturalLegacy: His root-word dhātu became a foundational term of two civilizations of learning: Pāṇini's grammar organizes Sanskrit as a list of dhātus (verbal roots), and Āyurveda organizes the body as seven dhātus (tissue-elements). "Dhātṛ" survives as a name for fate in the vernaculars; the formula "dhātā-vidhātā" still opens Hindu birth-rite invocations. The idea that grammar and medicine share one word for "the set-down units" is his unnoticed monument.
lore.archaeology: An aniconic god leaves no temples: Dhātṛ's material trace is the textual tradition — the Ṛgveda manuscripts (among the world's oldest continuously transmitted texts, UNESCO Memory of the World) and the ritual manuals that prescribe his invocation. The birth-rites (garbhādhāna and jātakarman) where he and Vidhātṛ are called to establish the child's fortune are performed, archaeologically invisible but ethnographically continuous, to this day.
lore.syncretism: Comparative philology hears his cognates across the Indo-European family: the root *dheh₁- gives Greek títhēmi ("I set") and English "do" — the Establisher's verb is one of the family's deepest. Within India he merges with Brahmā and, in the Smarta synthesis, with the abstract Brahman: the person dissolves into the principle. The Avestan dātā ("the Law-giver") is his Iranian counterpart in office if not in name.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written धातृ in Devanagari: dhā with its long vowel mark, then tṛ with the vocalic ṛ sign below. The root dhā underlies a family of cosmic-order words — dhāman (ordinance), dhārman (law), dhātu (element) — and the god is their shared agent.

entries.meaning: 'The Nourisher' (from puṣ, to thrive), Vedic solar guide of roads

steps: प = pa
ू = ū (long)
ष = ṣa
न् = na
pūṣan is the Vedic solar god who protects travelers and herds

pronunciation.approximation: POO-shan, long ū on the first syllable.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit pūṣan carries the long ū of the root puṣ, "to thrive, nourish," with the retroflex ṣ that English tongues must learn — written पूषन् with the dot beneath the sibilant. The restoration Pūṣan marks both: the length on the root, the retroflex on the close. The retroflex ṣ curls the tongue back — the sound romanization renders sh, though no English sh truly matches it.

domains.title: The Guide of Roads
domains.subtitle: Herds, Journeys, the Dead, and the Lost Tooth
domains.lead: Pūṣan is the Vedic herdsman-sun: guardian of cattle and roads, escort of brides to their weddings and souls to the fathers, the god who finds what is lost on the way. He carries a goad, rides a goat-drawn chariot, and eats gruel — because, the myth insists, he once lost his teeth.

cards.name: The Goad
cards.desc: His attribute: the herdsman's prod that keeps the herd — and the journey — moving.

cards.name: The Road
cards.desc: Paths of earth and paths of heaven: he knows "all the roads," the hymns repeat.

cards.name: The Psychopomp
cards.desc: Ṛgveda 10.17 entrusts the dead to him: he conducts souls to the fathers.

cards.name: The Lost Teeth
cards.desc: At Dakṣa's sacrifice his teeth were struck out — the gruel-eating god of the ruined rite.

symbols.name: The goad
symbols.meaning: Guidance by encouragement — the herdsman's gentle compulsion

symbols.name: The goat chariot
symbols.meaning: His humble vehicle among the horse-gods — the commoner's deity

symbols.name: The gruel
symbols.meaning: His toothless fare — karambha, the offering only he receives

symbols.name: The mended wheel
symbols.meaning: His chariot-wheel, broken on the road and remade by the Aśvins (RV 1.119) — even the guide of all journeys must sometimes be guided

symbols.name: The path
symbols.meaning: Roads earthly and celestial are his jurisdiction; the hymns call him the knower of all paths (RV 6.53), and his blessing opens every journey

mythology.lead: Pūṣan is the most companionable of Vedic gods: where others blaze, he accompanies. His myths are all journeys — of cattle, of brides, of the dead — and one memorable injury.

myths.title: Guide of Souls
myths.text: The Ṛgveda’s funeral hymn entrusts the dead to him with startling tenderness: ‘May Pūṣan take your hand and lead you onward; may the two Aśvins, mounted on their chariot, carry you; go to the well-prepared place, go where the fathers have gone before’ (RV 10.17). He is chosen because he knows every road: the hymns repeat that he travels the paths between heaven and earth daily at the sun’s flank, and that no path of his is ever blocked. Where Yama rules the dead and Agni carries the offering, Pūṣan is the escort — the god whose whole office is accompaniment. The Vedic poets seem to have understood something modern grief still discovers: what the dying most need is not a judge but a guide who knows the way by heart, having walked it every day of the world’s turning. The herdsman who loses no animal from the herd is exactly the god to trust with a soul.

myths.title: The Giving of Sūryā
myths.text: At the wedding of the Sun-maiden Sūryā — the Ṛgveda’s great marriage hymn, RV 10.85 — the gods themselves form the procession: Mitra, Varuna, and Aryaman escort her, the Aśvins are her eager suitors, and Soma wins her, ‘for Soma her father gave the maiden’. Pūṣan has the office that outlasts them all: as her kinsman he takes the bride’s hand to give her away — the kanyādāna performed by a god. The hymn’s formulas did not stay in the book. They passed into the living Hindu wedding, where verses of the Sūryā-sūkta are still recited as the father places his daughter’s hand in the groom’s — which means that at millions of weddings every year, Pūṣan is still, liturgically, the one conducting the bride down the aisle. The Veda here is not an artifact but a living officiant: the guide of the road presides over the shortest and most auspicious journey a person makes.

lore.culturalLegacy: His liturgy survives wherever the Ṛgveda’s wedding hymn is sung — at millions of Hindu weddings every year — and journeyers still open travel with his sūkta, a recitation older than any living temple. The asterism Puṣya, ‘the Nourisher’, keeps his root puṣ in the Hindu lunar calendar, naming one of the twenty-seven nakṣatras under which children are still named and rites still timed. In the history of religions he is the type-case of the pastoral solar guide: the comparison with Pan stands in every textbook, making his name one of the bridges on which comparative mythology was first built. And in ordinary Indian English his memory persists unremarked in the countless shops, schools, and sons named Pushan after the finder of lost things — a god of the second rank whose one surviving office, giving the bride away, outranks most first-rank gods entirely.
lore.archaeology: An aniconic Vedic god has no statues, but his world has strata: the pastoral economy of the Ṛgvedic Punjab — cattle-counts, drove-roads, the archaeology of the Painted Grey Ware and earlier Harappan cattle iconography — is the social ground of his cult. The goat-drawn chariot of his hymns is remembered in later folk vehicles of Rajasthani pastoral gods like Pabuji, whose own oral epic of rustled and recovered cattle keeps Pūṣan's oldest story-pattern alive.
lore.syncretism: Comparativists have long paired him with Greek Pan — the pastoral guardian whose Arcadian by-form Páōn sits temptingly close to Pūṣáṇ, and whose name the ancients themselves derived from a root of ‘watching over’ — and with Hermês in function: herds, roads, theft-recovery, and the escort of souls are Hermês’ offices too. The equations are old and famous, but they are scholarship, not scripture: Mayrhofer registers the comparison and judges it uncertain, and Beekes urges outright caution on the Greek side. Within the Veda he works in harness with Soma, Bhaga, and the Aśvins, the diplomat of the pantheon’s second rank; and as the Vedic age closed, his independent cult quietly merged into Sūrya’s, the guide absorbed into the light he guided. What survived the absorption was his liturgy — which, unlike his cult, never had to be revived, because it never stopped being performed.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written पूषन् in Devanagari: pū with its long stroke, then ṣa with the retroflex dot, and the final n. The same root gives poṣa, "nourishment," and puṣṭi, "prosperity" — the god is thriving itself, shepherded into personhood.

entries.meaning: 'The Fashioner, the Maker' (from tvaṣ, to form), the divine craftsman

steps: त्व = tva
ष = ṣa
टृ = ṭṛ (vocalic ṛ)
tvaṣṭṛ is the divine craftsman who shapes the forms of the gods

pronunciation.approximation: TVASH-tuh; the ṭṛ is a rolled vocalic retroflex r.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit tvaṣṭṛ carries two retroflexes — the ṣ and the final syllabic ṛ — written त्वष्टृ in Devanagari. The name derives from the root tvakṣ, "to fashion, form," making him literally "the Fashioner": the oldest artisan theonym in the Indo-European record. Both sibilants are retroflex: tvaṣṭṛ, with the tongue curled on ṣ and the vocalic ṛ closing the name.

domains.title: The Fashioner
domains.subtitle: The Forge of the Gods, the Vajra, and the Avenging of a Son
domains.lead: Tvaṣṭṛ is the divine smith of the Ṛgveda: maker of Indra's thunderbolt, shaper of the soma cup, fashioner of wombs and forms — and the father whose grief over his slain son produced the greatest monster of Vedic myth.

cards.name: The Vajra
cards.desc: He forged Indra's thunderbolt — the weapon that split the dragon's fortress.

cards.name: Vṛtra's Father
cards.desc: In grief he shaped the avenger: Vṛtra, born to kill Indra, by the rite gone wrong.

cards.name: Viśvarūpa
cards.desc: His three-headed son, the gods' priest, slain by Indra — the wound that drove the forge.

cards.name: The Soma Cup
cards.desc: He fashioned the very cup from which the gods drink immortality.

symbols.name: The axe and chisel
symbols.meaning: The fashioner’s tools — form struck from the formless

symbols.name: The cup
symbols.meaning: The soma vessel — liturgy’s finest object, from his bench

symbols.name: The thunderbolt
symbols.meaning: His masterpiece: vajra, both weapon and symbol of the awakened mind

symbols.name: The forge of the gods
symbols.meaning: His hidden workshop where forms are struck — the oldest artisan’s theonym in the Indo-European record, from the root tvakṣ, “to fashion”

symbols.name: The slipped accent
symbols.meaning: The mispronounced mantra that doomed Vṛtra (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.12) — the syllable that turned “slayer of Indra” into “slain by Indra”: in Vedic thought, pronunciation is destiny

mythology.lead: Tvaṣṭṛ's cycle is the Vedic meditation on craft and consequence: the hands that make the weapons, the cups, and the children are the same — and what is made can turn on its maker's world.

myths.title: Forging the Vajra
myths.text: When the dragon Vṛtra held the waters captive, Indra needed a weapon worthy of the deed: Tvaṣṭṛ forged the vajra, the bolt that smashed the ninety-nine fortresses and split the dragon's jaw. The Ṛgveda repeats the attribution like a signature — "the bolt that Tvaṣṭṛ made for thee" — the smith's name stamped on the pantheon's supreme weapon.

myths.title: Viśvarūpa's Three Heads
myths.text: Tvaṣṭṛ's son Viśvarūpa — three-headed, six-eyed — served as priest of the gods while secretly feeding the anti-gods' share of the offerings. Indra struck off the heads; from them sprang the partridge, the sparrow, and the quail. The smith's grief at his son's death is the hinge of the whole cycle: the forge turns from weapons for the gods to a weapon against them.

lore.culturalLegacy: Viśvakarman Pūjā — the festival when artisans, engineers, and factory workers worship their tools — is his living descendant, kept across industrial India every September. His name survives in linguistic memory: takṣan (carpenter), and the Takṣaka serpent-lineages of epic, carry the root. The Vṛtra story's famous "accent that doomed a monster" is the standard classroom example of why the Veda guards its phonetics: in the oldest liturgy, pronunciation is destiny.
lore.archaeology: An aniconic Ṛgvedic god has no image-strata, but his craft does: the copper-bronze technology of the Harappan world — the lost-wax dancing girl, the forged tools of Chanhu-daro — is the material background of the Age in which a smith could be a god. The Viśvakarman iconography of later temple sculpture (the white-bearded architect with his tools, at Vijayanagara and across the Deccan) gives the ancient fashioner his visible afterlife.
lore.syncretism: He is India's Hephaestus in function — the lame-footed Greek smith and the Vedic fashioner are the classic comparative pair, and scholars note the shared motif of the artisan who arms both gods and their enemies. Later Hinduism merged him into Viśvakarman, "All-Maker," the architect of the universe: the Ṛgvedic name faded as the office expanded, until the carpenter's caste-god absorbed the ancient smith entirely.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written त्वष्टृ in Devanagari: tva with its conjunct, ṣa with the retroflex dot, and tṛ with the vocalic ṛ sign. The same root family gives takṣan, the carpenter — the god's name and the village craft are one word apart.

entries.meaning: 'Old Lady Meng' (孟婆), the goddess who brews the tea of forgetfulness

pronunciation.approximation: mung-pwoh, falling tone on Meng, rising on Po.
pronunciation.note: Mèngpó 孟婆 means "Old Lady Meng": mèng in the falling tone, a surname suggesting seniority; pó, "grandmother, old woman," in the rising tone. The name belongs to folk religion rather than scripture — which is why its spelling never needed the scholar's precision the goddess herself so carefully erases.

domains.title: The Tea of Oblivion
domains.subtitle: The Bridge, the Brew, and the Mercy of Forgetting
domains.lead: Mèngpó keeps the last station of the Chinese underworld: at the Nàihé Bridge, where souls cross to rebirth, she serves her five-flavored tea — and every soul that drinks forgets its life, its loves, and its griefs, clean for the next beginning.

cards.name: The Five Flavors
cards.desc: Sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty — the whole of a life, steeped into one last cup.

cards.name: Nàihé Bridge
cards.desc: The "Bridge of No Alternative": every soul crosses, and none crosses back remembering.

cards.name: The Records
cards.desc: Yánluó's courts judge the life; her tea releases it — bureaucracy's final kindness.

cards.name: The River of Forgetfulness
cards.desc: China's own Lethe — the waters beneath the bridge that wash the old self away.

symbols.name: The teapot
symbols.meaning: Her instrument: oblivion brewed with care, not inflicted

symbols.name: The bowl
symbols.meaning: The single serving every soul receives — neither more nor less

symbols.name: The bridge
symbols.meaning: The crossing between judgment and rebirth, where memory ends

mythology.lead: Mèngpó's myth is a single scene, retold for centuries: the old woman, the bridge, the bowl — the gentlest moment in the whole machinery of the afterlife.

myths.title: The Last Station
myths.text: Chinese folk cosmology orders the underworld like an administration: Yánluó's ten courts judge the deeds of the life, assign the punishments and the repayments — and then send the soul to Mèngpó. At the Nàihé Bridge she ladles her tea of five flavors; the soul drinks, and the record of the life — the loves, the hatreds, the unfinished business — dissolves. Only then is it fit to be reborn.

myths.title: Why She Serves
myths.text: Folk tellings give her a biography: she was, some say, a woman of the mortal world who grieved her dead so deeply that heaven gave her this office — that no other soul need carry grief across the boundary. Others make her a wind-spirit of antiquity, or a servant of the underworld's lord promoted for her gentle hand. The variants agree on the point: the one who erases memory does it out of mercy, having known what memory costs.

lore.culturalLegacy: "Mèngpó's soup" (孟婆湯) is a living idiom for oblivion — offered ruefully at partings and breakups across the Chinese internet. Her imagery saturates East Asian popular culture: the Nàihé Bridge scene is a fixture of afterlife drama from opera to anime-adjacent fantasy. The deeper legacy is conceptual: she embodies a mercy the modern world debates — whether healing requires forgetting — and gives the debate a face, a bridge, and a bowl.
lore.archaeology: A folk goddess has no canonical temple archive, but her cosmology has monuments: the Fengdu ghost city on the Yangtze — China's "capital of the underworld" — preserves the Nàihé Bridge in stone, crossed by pilgrims and tourists for centuries, with its three arches for the virtuous, the ordinary, and the damned. Ming-Qing underworld scroll-paintings and the woodblock illustrations of the Jade Record (Yùlì) show her at her station, ladle in hand, among the ten courts' bureaucrats.
lore.syncretism: She is the folk fusion at its most organic: Buddhist rebirth doctrine, Daoist underworld bureaucracy, and village storytelling meet in her bowl. Comparative scholars line her up beside Lethe — the Greek river of forgetfulness the dead must drink — noting that two civilizations independently decided memory cannot survive rebirth. In modern Chinese media she has become a star: films, songs, and web novels cast her as the melancholy romantic of the underworld, the goddess who remembers everything precisely so that others may forget.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 孟婆: Mèng (eldest; a surname) above pó (old woman, with the woman radical). Her name appears in Ming and Qing fiction and in the vivid bureaucratic cosmologies of Chinese folk religion — a goddess documented by storytellers rather than canonized by councils.

entries.meaning: 'Coiled antiquity' (盤古), the giant who split heaven from earth

pronunciation.approximation: pahng-goo, rising tone on Pang, low-dipping on Gu.
pronunciation.note: Pángǔ 盘古 carries the rising tone on páng and the dipping third tone on gǔ ("antiquity"); the name pairs "coiling" with "ancient" — the coiled one of the primordial egg. Written 盤古 in traditional characters, it is Chinese myth's youngest great name: the giant is attested only from the 3rd century CE.

domains.title: The First Giant
domains.subtitle: The Egg, the Eighteen Thousand Years, and the Body of the World
domains.lead: Pángǔ is China's creation made flesh: the giant who grew for eighteen thousand years inside the cosmic egg, pushed heaven and earth apart with his own body, and — dying at last — became the world itself: his eyes the sun and moon, his breath the wind, his voice the thunder.

cards.name: The Cosmic Egg
cards.desc: Chaos like a hen's egg — and Pángǔ born within it, the first form in the formless.

cards.name: The Separation
cards.desc: Heaven rose ten feet daily, earth thickened ten feet, and he grew between them — 18,000 years of pushing.

cards.name: The Transformation
cards.desc: His body becomes the world: eyes to sun and moon, limbs to mountains, blood to rivers.

cards.name: The Chisel and Axe
cards.desc: Folk art arms him with the tools of separation — the first worker, carving sky from stone.

symbols.name: The egg
symbols.meaning: Chaos as potential — the undivided whole that must crack to become a world

symbols.name: The horns
symbols.meaning: His folk-iconography — the shaggy, horned giant of the first morning

symbols.name: The pillars of his limbs
symbols.meaning: The four limbs as the four sacred mountains — the body as geography

mythology.lead: Pángǔ's myth exists in two sentences of immense consequence, recorded by Xú Zhěng in the 3rd century CE — and expanded by a civilization into its canonical account of how the world began.

myths.title: Three-Five Calendar Record
myths.text: Xú Zhěng's Sānwǔ lìjì (3rd century CE, preserved in later encyclopedias) gives the founding text: 'Heaven and earth were chaos like a hen's egg, and Pángǔ was born within it. After eighteen thousand years, heaven and earth opened: the bright, light qì rose to become heaven; the dark, heavy qì sank to become earth. Pángǔ stood between them, changing nine times daily — heaven rising ten feet a day, earth thickening ten feet, and Pángǔ growing ten feet — for eighteen thousand years more, until heaven stood ninety thousand li above the earth.' The arithmetic is the myth's own poetry: the world is not spoken into being but pushed apart by increments, against a measurable resistance — creation as the first and longest labor, and the giant as the one who never stops growing because his work is never done.

myths.title: The Body Becomes the World
myths.text: When the separation was fixed, Pángǔ died — and the transformation began, in the same text's most famous lines: his breath became wind and cloud, his voice thunder, his left eye the sun and his right the moon, his four limbs the four sacred mountains, his blood the rivers, his veins the roads, his flesh the soil, his hair the stars, his skin and body-hair grass and trees, his sweat the rain — and, in the most anthropologically piquant line, the fleas and lice of his body, quickened by the wind, became the black-haired people. Nothing in the list is wasted and nothing is decorative: the myth insists that geography is biography — that every mountain is a limb and every river a vein — so that to wound the landscape is to wound the body one lives inside. It is the world's most complete statement of the sacredness of place.

lore.culturalLegacy: "Since Pángǔ separated heaven and earth" is the standard Chinese formula for "since the beginning of time," and his myth opens every children's account of Chinese prehistory. The transformation — body to landscape — gave Chinese poetry one of its deepest image-families, the mountain-as-body. UNESCO-listed school textbooks, animated films, and the giant's statues across southern China (Henan's Tongbai county claims his birthplace) keep the youngest creator as the most familiar.
lore.archaeology: No cult-temple of Pángǔ predates the myth's literary arrival, but his material afterlife is real: the Pángǔ temples of Tóngbái (Henan) and the southern shrines of Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī mark the festival of his 'birth' in the tenth lunar month, and the Shùyì jì's report of a Pángǔ country in the southern sea whose people carried his name as a surname shows the cult travelling on genealogies as much as on festivals. The textual archaeology is exact — Xú Zhěng's Sānwǔ lìjì and the Wǔyùn lìnián jì (both 3rd century, preserved in encyclopedias) are the two struts of the whole tradition, and the history of their quotation is the history of the myth itself.
lore.syncretism: The Pángǔ–Pán Hù debate is one of Chinese mythology's famous problems: the southern dog-ancestor of the Yao and She peoples and the cosmic giant share a syllable and a region, and scholars from the Republican era onward have argued transmission in both directions. Comparative mythology places him with the dismembered primordial beings — Vedic Púruṣa, Norse Ymir — whose bodies become worlds: China's version is distinctive for making the giant's death not a murder but a completion.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 盘古 (盤古 traditional): pán (coil, tray, the great basin) plus gǔ (ancient). The graphs describe him exactly — the coiled giant of antiquity, curled inside the cosmic egg before there was a world to be ancient in.

entries.meaning: 'King Yan' (閻羅, from Yama), the judge of the dead

pronunciation.approximation: yen-lwoh, rising tone on both syllables.
pronunciation.note: Yánluó 阎罗 abbreviates Yánluówáng 阎罗王, "King Yama" — the Sanskrit Yamarāja worn down by two millennia of Chinese speech. The second tone on yán and the rising luó are fixed by tradition; the full Sanskrit form survives in Buddhist ritual language beside the everyday king.

domains.title: The Judge of the Dead
domains.subtitle: The Ten Courts, the Record Books, and the Mirror of Deeds
domains.lead: Yánluó is the magistrate at the centre of the Chinese afterlife: the Indian god Yama enthroned in a Chinese courtroom, judging the dead from their own record books. Before him, the myth insists, wealth and rank are nothing — the only evidence is what you did.

cards.name: The Record Books
cards.desc: The registers of life and death: every deed entered, nothing argued away.

cards.name: The Mirror
cards.desc: The karma-mirror that shows each soul its own actions — the courtroom's only witness.

cards.name: The Ten Courts
cards.desc: Dìyù's bureaucracy: ten tribunals, his the fifth and most feared.

cards.name: The Ledger of Lifespan
cards.desc: He holds the book of allotted years — the deadline no bribe extends.

symbols.name: The judge's cap
symbols.meaning: The Chinese magistrate's hat on an Indian god — the Silk Road in one image

symbols.name: The brush
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the verdict — deaths recorded, sentences written

symbols.name: The ox-head and horse-face
symbols.meaning: His bailiffs: the two wardens who fetch the souls of the dead

symbols.name: The golden bridge and silver path
symbols.meaning: The crossings of the third court: the good walk a golden bridge, the middling a silver path, the wicked fall to the blood-pool below — the geography of the verdict.

symbols.name: Mèngpō's tea
symbols.meaning: The old woman's soup of oblivion at the Bridge of Sighs: rebirth requires forgetfulness — the court's last, merciful erasure of every file.

mythology.lead: Yánluó's mythology is procedural: not adventures but cases. His stories are judgments — and the judgments are always, the texts insist, simply the soul's own deeds read back to it.

myths.title: Yama, the First Mortal
myths.text: Before he was a king of hell, Yama was the first human to die. The Ṛgveda (10.14) calls him the one who found the road away from the world of the fathers; he became the gatherer of the dead, honoured with offerings as the king who presides over the ancestors. Buddhism inherited him and sharpened him: in the Devadūta Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 130) the newly dead stand before King Yama, who asks why they ignored the three divine messengers — an old person, a sick person, a corpse — sent to every house as warnings. Yánluó's court thus rests on an Indian foundation two millennia deep: judgment begins with mortality itself, and the first judge is the first man who had to die.

myths.title: The Fifth Tribunal
myths.text: The Chinese Ten Kings system, documented from the Tang dynasty onward, receives the dead at set intervals — the seventh day after death, the hundredth day, the first and third anniversaries — distributing them among ten courts (The Scripture of the Ten Kings; trans. Teiser, 1994; the sūtra's Dunhuang manuscripts). Yánluó presides over the fifth, the great reckoning after the first four screenings. There the record books of each life are opened and the karma-mirror raised — it shows every deed as it was done, neither argued nor appealed — and the sentence is assigned: paradise, rebirth, or the numbered hells. One legend demoted him from the first court for undue leniency: even the king of the dead is audited, and mercy itself must answer to the ledger.

lore.culturalLegacy: "Meeting Yánluó" (见阎罗) remains the everyday Chinese idiom for dying; "Yánwáng ye" names any pitiless authority. Japanese Enma anchors a thousand festivals and anime (Jigoku Shōjo's Enma Ai made him a household name to a new century). The judgment imagery — mirror, ledger, no bribes — shaped East Asian ethics as deeply as any scripture: a whole civilization's conscience, staffed by one borrowed god.
lore.archaeology: The Ten Kings paintings — sets of hanging scrolls showing each court — survive from the Ningbo workshops of the 12th–13th centuries (the finest sets in Nara and the Metropolitan Museum), with Yánluó's tribunal at their dramatic centre. Fengdu ghost city's temples stage the full bureaucratic underworld in statuary. Dunhuang documents preserve the Sūtra of the Ten Kings, the charter-text of the whole system, copied in tens of thousands for the dead's benefit.
lore.syncretism: He is the supreme case of Buddhist localization: Yama became Yánluó in China, Enma in Japan (with his own mirror and the red-faced scowl of a thousand temple gates), Yeomna in Korea, and the judges of Vietnamese and Central Asian afterlives. Daoism staffed his courts with its own celestial bureaucrats; folk religion added Mèngpó's tea and the City God as his local deputies. The whole edifice — Indian god, Chinese paperwork, village morality — is East Asia's most successful religious import.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 阎罗 (simplified) / 閻羅 (traditional): the gate-radical graphs chosen purely for sound, transcribing Yama-. The Chinese name is thus a phonetic fossil of the Silk Road — Sanskrit carried into characters, then naturalized so completely that most speakers never know it was a loanword.

pronunciation.approximation: HON-shoo, with a long final ū.
pronunciation.note: Honshū 本州 — "Main Province" — closes with the long ū of shū, preserved in the macron. The name is descriptive geography elevated to a proper name: the largest of Japan's islands, holding Tokyo, Kyōto, Ōsaka, and some three-quarters of the nation. Both syllables carry long vowels in kana (ほんしゅう); the macron on the final ū marks the doubled u.

domains.title: The Main Island
domains.subtitle: The Heartland, the Capitals, and the Spine of Japan
domains.lead: Honshū is the island that became a civilization: largest of the Japanese archipelago, home of every historic capital from Nara to Kyōto to Edo-Tōkyō, and the ground on which the Jōmon, the Yayoi, and the Yamato state built the longest continuous imperial tradition on earth.

cards.name: Fuji
cards.desc: The sacred cone at the island's heart — climbed, painted, and worshipped for a thousand years.

cards.name: The Capitals
cards.desc: Nara, Kyōto, Kamakura, Edo: every seat of Japanese power stands on this one island.

cards.name: The Inland Sea
cards.desc: The Seto Naikai — the sheltered water-road that bound the heartland together.

cards.name: The Kinai
cards.desc: The "home provinces" around the Nara basin: the kernel from which the state grew.

symbols.name: The three regalia
symbols.meaning: Mirror, sword, and jewel — enshrined on Honshū at Ise, Atsuta, and the palace

symbols.name: The rice paddy
symbols.meaning: The Yayoi inheritance: wet-rice civilization as the island's second foundation

symbols.name: The cedar avenue
symbols.meaning: The planted forests of the pilgrim roads and shrine precincts

mythology.lead: Honshū's mythology is the national charter itself: the Kojiki's island-birth, the sun goddess's gift of the land, and the descent of her grandson to rule it.

myths.title: The Islands from the Spear
myths.text: The Kojiki opens on the heavenly bridge: Izanagi and Izanami stir the ocean with the jewelled spear, and from the brine dripping from its point the first island coagulates. Descending, they wed and give birth to the islands of Japan — the "great eight islands" culminating in Ōyashima — and then to the kami of wind, sea, mountain, and tree. The archipelago is not created but born: the land is kin.

myths.title: Amaterasu's Realm
myths.text: When the sun goddess Amaterasu withdrew into the Heavenly Rock-Cave — outraged by her brother Susanoo's rampage — the world went dark until the gods' comic dance lured her out. Her mirror, hung outside the cave, caught her own light back to her; that mirror rests at Ise on Honshū's Kii coast, and her shrine there has been ritually rebuilt every twenty years for thirteen centuries: the island's heartwood, renewed.

lore.culturalLegacy: Honshū carries roughly 104 million people — the largest island population on earth — and its corridor from Tōkyō to Ōsaka is the most studied urban megalopolis in geography. Its cultural exports need no list: the world's first novel (The Tale of Genji) was written here, Zen gardens and ukiyo-e and kabuki were born here, and the shinkansen that shrank the island in 1964 taught the world high-speed rail.
lore.archaeology: Sannai-Maruyama near Aomori preserves a Jōmon city of 5,500 years ago — great cedar pillars, longhouses, and chestnut stores that rewrote the era's reputation from "primitive" to prosperous. The Yayoi's moated villages and the keyhole-shaped kofun tombs (Daisenryō in Ōsaka is among the largest tombs on earth by area) trace the state's rise. Nara's Tōdai-ji holds the world's largest bronze Buddha in the world's largest wooden building; Ise's shikinen sengū — the twenty-year rebuilding — is living archaeology, a Bronze Age rite performed on schedule into the present.
lore.syncretism: The island is the great syncretist of Asia: Buddhism arriving from Korea in the 6th century was fused with kami-worship into shinbutsu-shūgō — the dual-identity system that ran Japanese religion for a millennium; Zen and the tea culture of Kyōto fused with warrior aesthetics; and the Meiji restoration engineered State Shinto on top of it all. Honshū's mountains hold the shugendō tradition — Yamabushi ascetics practicing the oldest fusion of all: kami, buddha, and mountain as one path.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 本州: hon (root, main, origin) plus shū (province). The Kojiki's mythic name for the island is Ōyashima, "the great eight islands" — the archipelago's whole body, of which Honshū is the spine.

pronunciation.approximation: KYOO-shoo, with the compressed ky- onset and long vowels.
pronunciation.note: Kyūshū 九州 — "Nine Provinces" — carries the long ū in both syllables, both preserved in the restoration. The name remembers the island's ancient division into nine provinces; its older name, Tsukushi, appears in the earliest chronicles as the gateway of the gods' descent. Both syllables are long in kana (きゅうしゅう); the two macrons of the restoration are the two doubled vowels.

domains.title: The Nine Provinces
domains.subtitle: The Gateway, the Kamikaze, and the Christian Century
domains.lead: Kyūshū is Japan's front door: the island facing Korea and China across the narrowest straits, where the continent's rice, Buddhism, and iron first arrived — and where the Mongol fleets, the Portuguese traders, and the Jesuit fathers all made their landfall. The gateway of Japan has always stood open on this shore, even when the country tried to shut it.

cards.name: The Straits
cards.desc: Tsushima and Korea are a day's sail — Asia has always been closer here than Tōkyō.

cards.name: The Kamikaze
cards.desc: The "divine wind" typhoons of 1274 and 1281 that shattered two Mongol invasion fleets off this coast.

cards.name: Nagasaki
cards.desc: The one window kept open in the closed country: two centuries of Dutch and Chinese trade through a single fan-shaped island.

cards.name: The Christian Century
cards.desc: Xavier's 1549 landing, a quarter-million converts, the Shimabara rising, and the hidden Christians' 250-year secret.

symbols.name: The kamikaze banner
symbols.meaning: The storm as protector — weather enlisted in the national myth

symbols.name: The Aso caldera
symbols.meaning: One of the world's great volcanic craters — the island's fiery heart

symbols.name: The Dejima fan
symbols.meaning: The tiny artificial island that carried Europe into Japan for 200 years

mythology.lead: Kyūshū claims the mythology of beginnings: the chronicles land the sun goddess's grandson on its peaks, send the first emperor out from its shores, and let its storms write themselves into the national soul.

myths.title: Ninigi on Takachiho
myths.text: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki bring the heavenly grandson Ninigi down to earth on the peak of Takachiho — placed by tradition in Kyūshū's mountains — where he marries the blossom-princess Konohanasakuya-hime. She proves her divine conception by setting fire to the birthing hut and delivering three sons amid the flames; their line leads to Jimmu, the first emperor. The imperial charter myth is, geographically, a Kyūshū story. The shrine at Takachiho still marks the descent-spot, and the Ama-no-iwato cave in the gorge beside it — where the sun goddess Amaterasu once hid — anchors the whole island as the stage of the Age of the Gods. The myth means Japan's sacred geography begins not at the capital but at the gateway: the gods landed where the continent first appears.

myths.title: Jimmu's Departure
myths.text: The chronicles begin Japan's history on this island. Jimmu, the great-grandson of Ninigi, tired of ruling only the Hyūga coast and resolved on the eastern expedition to Yamato: 'the land to the east is fair... let us go to the land of the rising sun.' His first fleet was wrecked, his brother Itsuse died of a wound, and the way was cleared only after the vanishing sacrifice of the empress — but the divine crow Yatagarasu, three-legged, was sent to guide him, and after the mountain campaign against Nagasunehiko he founded the dynasty at Kashihara, in 660 BCE by the chronicles' reckoning. Myth means history here in the full sense: Japan's imperial charter is a Kyūshū story of leaving Kyūshū. The gateway completes its service by producing the one who crosses it.

lore.culturalLegacy: The kamikaze of 1281 gave the 20th century its most terrible word; Nagasaki's 1945 atomic bombing made the island a symbol of the nuclear age's cost, and its peace park one of the world's pilgrimage sites of memory. Arita and Imari porcelain conquered European markets and imitators for three centuries. Today the island's universities and semiconductor fabs continue the oldest pattern: the gateway as Japan's technology shore.
lore.archaeology: Yoshinogari, in Saga, is East Asia's great Yayoi site: a moated, towered settlement of two thousand years ago, with mass jar-burials and bronze-weapon caches — the archaeological face of the Wa people whom Chinese chronicles describe. The underwater archaeology of Takashima's Mongol wrecks — anchor stones, bombs, and hulls preserved in Imari Bay — has recovered the kamikaze fleets themselves. The hidden Christian sites of the Amakusa islands and Nagasaki's Ōura Cathedral (1864, built for the returned faith) are UNESCO-listed as the "Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region."
lore.syncretism: Kyūshū is Japan's syncretic laboratory: Korean potters founding Arita porcelain, Chinese merchant quarters at Nagasaki, Portuguese words entering the language (pan, tempura, kappa), Dutch learning (Rangaku) flowing through Dejima into Japanese science — anatomy, astronomy, and artillery smuggled in translation. The island's cuisine, dialects, and crafts all carry the gateway's mark: everything Japanese that came from outside came here first.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 九州: kyū (nine) plus shū (province). The island's ancient name 筑紫 (Tsukushi) is preserved in the Kojiki's island-birth account — "Kyūshū" is the administrative name that replaced the mythic one and quietly kept the older island's memory of division.

entries.meaning: 'The man of furious face' (tū + mata + ēngā), god of war and of humankind

pronunciation.approximation: TOO-mah-tow-ENG-ah, long ū on the first syllable.
pronunciation.note: Tūmatauenga is pronounced with the long ū of the first syllable — the macron the restoration keeps — and the name means 'Tū of the furious face': tū (to stand — also the god's own name) plus mata (face) plus ēngā/anga (fury, the making of an appearance). He is the Māori war-god and the father of humankind, and his name is a face set for war.

domains.title: The Standing One
domains.subtitle: War, the Angry Face, and the Taming of the Brothers
domains.lead: Tūmatauenga is the Māori god of war and of humanity's fierce inheritance: the one son of the Sky Father who stood firm when the storm-god attacked, and who then subdued his own brothers — taking their fishes, their birds, and their crops — to feed the people he had made. War, in his story, is the price of standing.

cards.name: The Mere
cards.desc: The flat greenstone club of the chief — the weapon that is also a badge of rank and a gift of state.

cards.name: The Angry Face
cards.desc: His name: the war-face (pūkana) that the haka still performs with widened eyes and out-thrust tongue.

cards.name: The Nets and Hooks
cards.desc: He snared his brother Tangaroa's fish: the arts of fishing, won by war and given to man.

cards.name: The Pa
cards.desc: The fortified hill-settlement — his architecture, crowning New Zealand's ridgelines by the thousand.

symbols.name: The taiaha
symbols.meaning: The long staff-weapon of chiefly combat — spear and club in one lineage

symbols.name: The haka
symbols.meaning: The war-dance: the body made into the angry face of the god, rehearsed before every contest of the tribe

symbols.name: The pūkana
symbols.meaning: The widened eyes and out-thrust tongue of the war-face — the literal mata of his name, worn by every performer

symbols.name: The feather cloak
symbols.meaning: The kahu huruhuru of the war-chief — honour worn on the shoulders, ransom and glory in one garment

mythology.lead: Tūmatauenga's cycle is the Polynesian account of how humanity got its arts: not by gift but by conquest — the war-god subduing his elemental brothers and distributing the spoils to his mortal children.

myths.title: The Sons of Ranginui and Papatūānuku
myths.text: In the beginning the Sky Father Ranginui and the Earth Mother Papatūānuku lay locked together in an embrace, and their children lived crushed in darkness between them. Among the sons was Tūmatauenga, fiercest of them all. When the brothers debated what to do, it was Tū who urged the final solution — kill the parents and have done. The others recoiled at the thought of slaying their own father and mother, and the gentler counsel of Tāne prevailed: the parents would be forced apart, not slain (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, the legend of the children of Rangi and Papa). Rongo, Tangaroa, Haumia, and Tū himself tried to push the parents and failed; then Tāne set his head on the earth, his feet against the sky, and tore the parents open. Light came into the world — and Tāwhirimātea, who had loved the darkness, went to war over it. The myth is exact about its genealogy of war: strife is not an intruder into creation but a sibling of the light itself, born the moment separation was chosen.

myths.title: The One Who Stood
myths.text: Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, had opposed the separation of his parents, and now he took war to his brothers in revenge, riding the weapon-winds of his storm-army. Tangaroa fled to the sea; Tāne withdrew into the forests; Rongo and Haumia thrust themselves into the earth — but Tūmatauenga alone stood fast on the open plain, unbowed under the tempest (Grey, Polynesian Mythology). When the storm at last spent itself, the standing one turned on his fleeing brothers and made their domains his own: he wove nets and took Tangaroa's fish, set snares for Tāne's birds, and dug into the earth for Rongo's kūmara and Haumia's fern-root. His name is the doctrine: tū means 'to stand'. War, in the Māori telling, is first of all a posture — the refusal to move when everything else runs — and only secondly a weapon; the whole later tradition of the haka, the pūkana, and the pa is that posture made communal.

lore.culturalLegacy: The haka — performed by the All Blacks before every match and by the army at every farewell — is his face in modern life: the widened eyes and out-thrust tongue are the literal mata of his name. Ngāti Tūmatauenga, the army's Māori designation, makes him the only ancient god officially patron of a modern state's armed forces. His cycle — the standing against the storm, the conquest that feeds the people — remains the charter myth of Māori resilience, quoted in land-march speeches and waiata alike.
lore.archaeology: New Zealand's ridgelines keep his monuments: thousands of pa — terraced, ditched, and palisaded hill-forts — from the classic period, with sites like Maungakiekie (One Tree Hill) among the largest earthworks of the Pacific. The greenstone mere and the carved taiaha of the museum collections (Te Papa's among them) are his regalia; the Auckland War Memorial Museum — itself a cenotaph to the fallen — houses the war-canoes and the martial taonga of his people. The kūmara storage-pits beside every pa tie his war-and-garden cycle into the ground itself.
lore.syncretism: He is one face of a Polynesian-wide god: Hawaiian Kū — the great war-god of the heiau temples — Tahitian Tū, first ancestor as well as war-god, and the Cook Islands' war deities share his name and his office, the deepest layer of pan-Polynesian religion. In New Zealand his worship ran through the war-parties and their tohunga; the nineteenth-century Māori military genius — the gunfighter pa of the New Zealand Wars — applied his standing to musket and trench, and the New Zealand Army today bears his name as its own: Ngāti Tūmatauenga, 'the tribe of the war-god.' The identification is unique in the modern world: no other ancient deity is the officially patron ancestor of a modern state's armed forces.
lore.originalScriptNote: Te reo Māori writes him with the macron as the vowel-length it is: Tūmatauenga. The oral text is the truer scripture — the whakataukī 'Ka mate kāinga tahi, ka ora kāinga rua' and the karakia of war and planting carry his name in the living language, and the New Zealand Army's Māori name, Ngāti Tūmatauenga, writes it into the state itself.

entries.meaning: "Emperor Guan" — the deified general Guān Yǔ, god of war, loyalty, and righteousness

pronunciation.approximation: gwahn-DEE — level tone, then a firm falling tone.
pronunciation.note: Guāndì 關帝 — "Emperor Guan" — carries the first tone on guān and the falling fourth on dì. The name is a title, not a personal name: the deified Guān Yǔ of the Three Kingdoms, raised by eight centuries of imperial investitures to the rank of Emperor. The restoration keeps the macron that marks his tone.

domains.title: The General Who Became a God
domains.subtitle: War, Loyalty, Righteousness, and the Brotherhood of the Peach Garden
domains.lead: Guāndì is China's god of the kept oath: the historical general Guān Yǔ (d. 220 CE) whose loyalty outlasted his dynasty, deified by emperors, merchants, and underworld alike until his red-faced statue stood in more temples than any other figure in the Chinese world — the one witness before whom both police and triads refuse to lie.

cards.name: The Crescent Blade
cards.desc: Qīnglóng Yǎnyuèdāo — the Green Dragon Crescent Blade, his legendary weapon and temple attribute.

cards.name: The Peach Garden Oath
cards.desc: The brotherhood sworn with Liú Bèi and Zhāng Fēi — China's founding myth of loyalty.

cards.name: The Red Face
cards.desc: His temple image: crimson countenance of righteous wrath, green robe, long beard.

cards.name: The God of Commerce
cards.desc: Merchants worship him as the enforcer of contracts — loyalty monetized into trust.

symbols.name: The crescent halberd
symbols.meaning: Martial honor wielded with precision — war in service of the oath

symbols.name: The red face
symbols.meaning: Righteousness made visible; loyalty that cannot hide

symbols.name: The green robe
symbols.meaning: The gift he refused to surrender to Cao Cao — fidelity to the old lord

symbols.name: The long beard
symbols.meaning: The beautiful beard he protected with a silk bag — dignity kept

symbols.name: The Red Hare horse
symbols.meaning: The empire's finest horse, the one gift he prized — speed pledged entirely to the search for a brother

symbols.name: The seal hung on the gate
symbols.meaning: The badge of office returned with a letter of thanks — authority handed back intact, the accounting of honor complete

mythology.lead: Guāndì's myth is history sanctified: the Records of the Three Kingdoms gave him a life, the Romance gave him a legend, and eight dynasties gave him a godhood — loyalty tested by gold, exile, and death, then canonized rank by rank until the executed general stood beside Confucius. What is worshipped is the word that outlasts its usefulness.

myths.title: The Peach Garden
myths.text: The Romance of the Three Kingdoms (ch. 1) opens not with a battle but with an oath: in the blossom of Zhang Fei's peach garden, the three — Liu Bei the petitioner, Guan Yu the bearded giant, Zhang Fei the hot-tempered butcher — kneel before heaven and earth: "We ask not to be born on the same day, but we beg to die on the same day." The history behind the novel, the Sanguozhi (ch. 36), knows no oath; it records only that the three were close as brothers and shared everything. The oath is the Romance's invention, and it is one of the most consequential inventions in Chinese literature: for six centuries sworn brotherhood (結義) has been the template for loyalty between men who are not kin, quoted at initiations, in opera, film, and lodge ceremonies alike. The myth teaches that the deepest bonds are chosen, witnessed, and paid for in the same coin — a day of death, whenever it comes.

myths.title: Three Conditions, One Horse
myths.text: Captured with Liu Bei's household when Xiapi fell, Guan Yu dictated his own terms of surrender (Romance, ch. 25): he would yield only to the Han emperor, not to Cao Cao; the two sisters-in-law must be guarded with full propriety; and the moment his brother was found he would leave. Cao Cao tested the terms with gifts — gold, silks, ten beauties, and finally the Red Hare, the empire's finest horse. Guan Yu bowed twice for the horse alone: "once I hear where my brother is, I can reach him in a day." He repaid the courtesies in full — riding alone into a hundred thousand men to take the enemy general Yan Liang's head at Baima (ch. 26) — then hung his seal, left letters of thanks, and rode a thousand li through five passes and six of Cao's garrisons to rejoin a lord far poorer than his captor (ch. 27). Honor, the novel says, answers courtesy with interest — and keeps accounts with everyone.

lore.culturalLegacy: His temples outnumber Confucius' in the Chinese world; his birthday (24th day of the 6th lunar month) is a national observance from Shanxi to Singapore. The "Guān Gōng" of business is the unwritten clause of every contract; his image guards mahjong parlors, restaurants, and police stations alike. The Romance's peach-garden oath remains East Asia's template for sworn brotherhood, quoted in films, games (Dynasty Warriors made him a global icon), and every oath of office sworn with a hand on his name.
lore.archaeology: The Guān Lín tomb-temple at Luoyang (where Cáo Cāo buried his head with honors) and the Guān Dì Miào at his birthplace in Yuncheng, Shanxi — the largest Guandi complex, repeatedly rebuilt since the Sui — anchor his cult geography. Ming-Qing Guandi temples survive in every southern port city; Yokohama's Kanteibyō (1862) preserves the diaspora form. His statues' iconography — red face, green robe, crescent blade, the beard-bag — is among the most standardized in world religion.
lore.syncretism: He is the one deity all three teachings claim: Taoism's Guān Shèng Dì Jūn (Holy Emperor), Buddhism's Sānghārāma, Confucianism's co-Sage. The diaspora carried him everywhere — his altar stands in Yokohama's Kanteibyō, in San Francisco's oldest Chinatown temples, and in every Hong Kong police station, where officers and triads bow to the same red face: the god both sides trust because both sides fear to lie before him.

entries.meaning: "The Golden One" — the radiant form of the Great Goddess, mother of the universe

steps: Sanskrit Gaurī is written in Devanagari as गौरी
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: GOW-ree — the diphthong of "cow," then a long ee.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit gaurī — "the golden, the radiant" — carries the long ī of the feminine epithet, which the restoration keeps. The same word is the adjective "golden-complexioned": her name is her skin, the color of turmeric, ripe wheat, and morning light. The diphthong au is inherent and unmarked in IAST, like e and o — her name needs no further marks to be read exactly.

domains.title: The Golden Mother
domains.subtitle: Beauty, Austerity, Marriage, and the Gentle Śakti
domains.lead: Gaurī is the Great Goddess at her most benevolent: the golden-skinned Mother whose austerity won Śiva himself, whose festivals celebrate marriage and motherhood. Her name — "the radiant one" — in the Ṛgveda simply means a female gaura, the golden one of the herds; the goddess's first secure appearance comes later, as the Kena Upaniṣad's Umā.

cards.name: The Golden Skin
cards.desc: Her color: turmeric and dawn — the glow that names her.

cards.name: The Austerity
cards.desc: The tapas by which she won Śiva — devotion as fierce as any warrior's.

cards.name: The Festivals
cards.desc: Gaurī Pūjā and the Tṛtīyā fasts — the mother's days kept by millions of women.

cards.name: Mother of Heroes
cards.desc: Mother of Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya — the goddess behind the gods.

symbols.name: The golden complexion
symbols.meaning: Radiance as nature — beauty without artifice

symbols.name: The lotus
symbols.meaning: Her seat and offering — purity of the household goddess

symbols.name: The bilva leaf
symbols.meaning: Her austerity — the tree of Śiva she tended in penance

mythology.lead: Gaurī's myths are the Great Goddess's domestic epic: the mountain-daughter who becomes the universe's mother through patience — Satī reborn, Śiva out-waited, two sons made, and a calendar of festivals that still re-enacts her story in millions of homes.

myths.title: Daughter of the Mountain
myths.text: The Purāṇas remember her previous body: Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, who burned herself in the sacrificial fire when her father insulted her husband Śiva — and whose scattered limbs became the Śakti-pīṭhas, the goddess's seats of power spread across the subcontinent. Reborn as Pārvatī, daughter of Himavat the mountain-king, she was Gaurī from the first: the golden girl of the peaks, destined from birth for the ash-covered wanderer who had forgotten how to love. Her name is older than her story — in the Ṛgveda gaurī is simply the feminine of gaura, the golden one of the herds — and the Purāṇas' point is that the name waited: the cow-gold of the dawn hymns becomes, in time, the skin of the Mother. The myth means the goddess keeps her bodies the way a lineage keeps its house: burned down and rebuilt, but never homeless.

myths.title: Winning the Unwinnable
myths.text: When beauty and Kāma's flower-arrows failed to move Śiva in his grief for Satī, she chose tapas: years of austerity in the forest — leaves for food, rain for bath, standing on one leg through the seasons. The Śiva Purāṇa tells the test: Śiva came disguised as a stammering young brahmin and mocked her wasted devotion and her emaciated god; offered instead his own beautiful form; everything but her vow was negotiable, and she would not be dissuaded. Conquered by patience, the ascetic asked for her hand, and the gods gathered at Kailāsa for the wedding the Purāṇas tell as the universe's own — Himavat giving the bride, the Ganges and the moon attending, the mountains dancing. The myth means that in the Śākta world the courtship is reversed: it is the goddess who woos, the god who is won, and the victory belongs to work rather than grace.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Gaurī festivals — Gaṇeśa's mother welcomed for three days before her son's own ten — anchor the Maharashtrian religious year; the phrase "gaurī kā vivāha" (the ideal marriage) is everyday Hindi. Turmeric, her color, remains the ritual substance of Indian womanhood. She is the Śākta answer to the question of what a goddess of the home looks like when she also happens to be the energy of the universe.
lore.archaeology: Her temples stand with Pārvatī's: the great Śiva-Pārvatī shrines from Elephanta's marriage-panel to the Kailāsa of Ellora — where the wedding of Gaurī and Śiva fills the whole south wall — document her in stone. The Gaurī Shankar temples of the Kathmandu valley and the festival-images of Maharashtra (made annually in the potters' quarters) carry her golden form into the present.
lore.syncretism: She is the gentle face of the same goddess who is Durgā in battle and Kālī in wrath — the Śākta tradition's proof that power has a domestic form. Her golden form travels: as the benevolent mother of Balinese Hinduism (Mā Gaurī), and into the syncretic Devi temples of the diaspora from Fiji to Trinidad, where her immersion-festivals kept the homeland's calendar across two oceans.

entries.meaning: "The Slow One" — Saturn as the lord of karma, justice, discipline, and time

steps: Sanskrit Śani is written in Devanagari as शनि
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: SHUH-nee — soft palatal sh, short and even.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit śani — "the slow one" — begins with the palatal ś (IAST's acute-accented s) and the short a and i. The restoration keeps the ś that English writes "sh": Śani, the slow planet, whose very name is a warning about haste. The ś is the palatal sibilant, made at the roof of the mouth farther forward than sh — the sound English approximates but never quite keeps.

domains.title: The Slow Reckoning
domains.subtitle: Saturn, Karma, Justice, and the Seven-and-a-Half Years
domains.lead: Śani is the most feared of the nine planets: Saturn as the auditor of karma, whose slow passage through the zodiac delivers every deed's return — never early, never late, and never, ever argued with. India loves him exactly as much as it fears him, which is to say, enormously.

cards.name: Sade Sati
cards.desc: The seven-and-a-half years of his transit over your moon — India's most-dreaded astrological season.

cards.name: The Auditor
cards.desc: Karma's bookkeeper: no bribe, no appeal, no clerical error — only the account.

cards.name: Son of the Sun
cards.desc: Sūrya's estranged son — the shadow the light itself begot.

cards.name: The Crow
cards.desc: His vāhana: the dark bird that sees what others will not look at.

symbols.name: The crow
symbols.meaning: The dark mount — witness of the unavoidable

symbols.name: The iron
symbols.meaning: His metal — hard, cold, unglamorous, indispensable

symbols.name: The slow orbit
symbols.meaning: Twenty-nine-and-a-half years — time as the measure of justice

mythology.lead: Śani's myths are about the impossibility of escaping consequence — even for gods, and especially for kings.

myths.title: The Shadow of the Sun
myths.text: The Purāṇas make him the child of a substitution. Sūrya's wife Saṃjñā, unable to bear the sun's fierce radiance, left her shadow-double Chhāyā ('Shade') in her place and returned to her father's house; of Chhāyā were born Śani and his siblings. When the truth came out, the sun's household split forever: Śani, the shadow's son, cast so baleful a gaze that his own father's countenance darkened at their meeting — the Purāṇas explain the sun's dimming and the rift between father and son with the same myth. The estrangement is permanent and instructive: the planet of justice is the sun's shadow-child, and no brilliance in the family exempts it from audit. Every solar dynasty — every royal line claiming descent from Sūrya — carries a slow auditor in its own blood.

myths.title: Even the Gods Are Judged
myths.text: His stories form a single syllabus of the gaze. When Śani's eye fell on gods and heroes, even the great bowed: the Purāṇic and epic cycles send the afflicted into wandering, beggary, and exile, until the debt is paid in full. The Hanumān legend gives the tradition its one counter-story and its favorite: when the slow planet pressed his power on Hanumān, the mighty one simply pinned him — under foot, in some tellings under his tail — and Śani, begging release, swore never to afflict Hanumān's devotees. The tale sets the exact boundary of his empire: devotion freely given (bhakti) is the one force he will not audit. He is the one god who bows to love — and the tradition treasures the exception precisely because everything else about him is exceptionless.

lore.culturalLegacy: "Śani chal raha hai" (Saturn is upon us) is the everyday explanation for every run of bad luck from Mumbai to Trinidad. His Saturday fast, his black-and-blue colors, his iron-and-sesame remedies constitute the largest planetary cult in the world. The fear is genuinely democratic: billionaires and bus-drivers check the same ephemeris, and Shingnapur's donations fund entire towns. Jyotiṣa, India's living astrology, centers on his slow clock.
lore.archaeology: Shani Shingnapur's open-air black boulder — the village with famously doorless houses, trusting his protection — is his great shrine; the queue on Saturdays runs for kilometers. Navagraha temples across the South (the Kumbakonam circuit) install him among the nine planets in fixed order, and his bronze from the Chola period shows the stiff, dark, crow-mounted figure unchanged.
lore.syncretism: Saturn's malefic reputation is Indo-European common ground — the Greek Kronos' devouring shadow and Rome's cold planet carry the same dread — but India alone made the planet a judge to be appeased weekly. His temple at Shingnapur (Maharashtra), where the god is an unwalled black stone under open sky, is the anti-temple: no roof over the planet, as if architecture itself feared to constrain him.

entries.meaning: "Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world

pronunciation.approximation: aw-ROON — open o (dot-below), low-high melody.
pronunciation.note: Ọrun is Yoruba for 'heaven': the precomposed dot-below Ọ is the domain-maximal form — the full tone marks (Ọ̀run, low-high) cannot be registered as a domain, so the temple preserves the tone in text while the address bar carries what the DNS allows. The dot-below is the open-mid vowel — the open aw of law — distinct from the close o; the tone is low-high, rising from the grave to the acute.

domains.title: The Heaven Above the Heavens
domains.subtitle: Sky, Destiny, and the Realm of Olódùmarè
domains.lead: Ọrun is the Yoruba name of heaven itself: the sky-realm where Olódùmarè and the orisha dwell, from which every soul descends to earth (ayé) — and to which every destiny (orí) is assigned before birth. It is not a god but the address of the gods.

cards.name: Ọrun and Ayé
cards.desc: Heaven and earth: the two halves of reality, with the soul commuting between them.

cards.name: Orí
cards.desc: The inner head — the personal destiny each soul chooses (or receives) in Ọrun before birth.

cards.name: Olódùmarè
cards.desc: The Owner of Heaven — the supreme being whose realm Ọrun is.

cards.name: The Descent
cards.desc: Every birth is an emigration from heaven; every death, the return journey.

symbols.name: The white cloth
symbols.meaning: Heaven's color — purity and the unblemished sky

symbols.name: The palm nuts
symbols.meaning: Ifá's instruments — heaven's messages read on earth

symbols.name: The head
symbols.meaning: Orí, the chosen destiny — heaven carried inside the skull

symbols.name: The golden chain
symbols.meaning: The road from Ọrun down which the first orisha descended to found Ilé-Ifẹ̀ — and by which every soul since has commuted between heaven and earth

mythology.lead: Ọrun's myths are the architecture of Yoruba cosmology: how heaven was connected to earth, how every soul is commissioned before birth, and how the traffic between the two realms has never once stopped.

myths.title: The Chain to Earth
myths.text: In the beginning there was only sky. Below Ọrun lay the primeval waters, and on the water floated nothing but the command of Olódùmarè. The creation account recorded across Yorubaland — set down by the Rev. Samuel Johnson in the early twentieth century and analyzed by Bolaji Idowu — tells how Olódùmarè sent the orisha down a golden chain from heaven with a hen, a chameleon, and a handful of sand. Where the sand fell and the hen scratched, a mound rose from the flood: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, 'the house that spreads', the navel of the earth. The chain did not come back up; it anchored heaven to the new ground, and orisha, ancestors, and newborn souls have traveled it in both directions ever since. The myth means that Yoruba cosmology is a story of migration. Every birth repeats the first descent, and the road between Ọrun and ayé has never once been closed.

myths.title: The Choosing of Orí
myths.text: Before a child is born, the Ifá corpus teaches, its soul kneels in Ọrun at the workshop of Ajala, the celestial potter, to choose its orí — the inner head that is its personal destiny. The odu narratives (see Abimbola, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus, and Bascom, Ifá Divination) tell of souls who chose carelessly, who bargained, or who arrived too late and had to take whatever heads remained. The choice is then sealed and the memory wiped: the child is born carrying an unread contract, and life is the slow reading of it. This is why Yoruba religion lavishes its attention on the head itself — offerings are made to the orí, the physical crown of the body, the one shrine every person carries everywhere. The myth means that destiny is chosen, not imposed — but chosen by a self you no longer remember being.

lore.culturalLegacy: The word lives in a thousand names: Ọrunmila (heaven-knows-salvation), Ọlọrun (owner-of-heaven), Ọrúnmìlà, Ọba-Ọrun. Ifá divination — UNESCO-listed — is its daily news service, and the Egúngún festivals keep the ancestors' visits on the calendar. Every Yoruba funeral says the same thing in ten thousand voices: 'the journey to Ọrun is well-traveled' — heaven as home, not as hope.
lore.archaeology: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the city founded on the scattered earth, keeps the creation-site shrines: the Oke Itase hill and the palace of the Ọọni, whose crown descends from heaven's own. The bronze and terracotta heads of Ifẹ̀ (12th–15th c.), among Africa's supreme artworks, are the faces of heaven's first citizens. The Ifá corpus — the great oral archive — is preserved by the babaláwo lineages of Yorubaland and the diaspora.
lore.syncretism: The Ọrun-ayé structure traveled with the diaspora: Candomblé's Oxalá-realm, Santería's heaven of Olófin, and Haiti's lwa-cosmology all keep the two-world map. Christian heaven merged with Ọrun in the New World without ever absorbing it: the Yoruba sky remains a realm of traffic and traffic-officers (the orisha), not of distant thrones — heaven as the next city over, not the next world.

entries.meaning: "Fire Lord" — the Aztec fire god, lord of the hearth and of the year

pronunciation.approximation: shee-oo-TEH-kwtlee — the kʷtɬ cluster released as one, no extra vowel; the final -tl sideways.
pronunciation.note: Xiuhtēcuhtli — "Fire Lord" — takes the long ē of tēcuhtli (lord) in Nahuatl; the domain keeps the plain ASCII form xiuhtecuhtli.com, which the temple explains: the canonical form bears the macron, the address bar carries what the registrar allows.

domains.title: The First Fire
domains.subtitle: Hearth, Year, and the New Fire Ceremony
