domains.lead: Xiuhtēcuhtli is the Aztec fire itself: first and last of the gods, the hearth at the center of every home and of the universe, and the god whose great ceremony — the drilling of the New Fire — restarted time itself every fifty-two years.

cards.name: The Hearth
cards.desc: The three stones of every Aztec kitchen — his throne in every house.

cards.name: The New Fire
cards.desc: Every 52 years, all fires died and one was drilled anew — the cosmos restarted.

cards.name: Huehueteotl
cards.desc: "The Old God" — his other name: the ancient of days, wrinkled with a brazier on his back.

cards.name: The Center
cards.desc: The axis mundi: fire as the pillar between the levels of the world.

symbols.name: The fire drill
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the New Fire — time kindled by friction

symbols.name: The brazier
symbols.meaning: His back-mounted bowl — the old god carrying the hearth

symbols.name: The three hearthstones (tenamaxtli)
symbols.meaning: The tripod of stones in every kitchen — the smallest shrine in the empire, rebuilt nightly

symbols.name: Turquoise (xiuhuitl)
symbols.meaning: His name shares xiuh- with 'turquoise' and 'year' — fire, time, and the blue-green stone are one phoneme

symbols.name: The butterfly
symbols.meaning: The fire-moth drawn to his flame — the soul seeking the light

mythology.lead: Xiuhtēcuhtli's myths are the calendar's: the fire that must be renewed, and the darkness that waits if it is not.

myths.title: The Drilling of the New Fire
myths.text: At the close of each 52-year cycle (the xiuhmolpilli, the 'tying of the years'), the Aztec world extinguished every flame: households went dark, pots were smashed, debts were settled, and the people waited on their rooftops, fasting, watching the sky. Sahagún's informants told him the terror plainly — if the Pleiades (tianquiztli) had not yet crossed the zenith by midnight, some said, the sun would not rise and the demons of darkness would come down to eat the last men (Florentine Codex, Book 7). When the star-merchants passed, the fire-priests climbed Huixachtlan, the Hill of the Star, and drilled the new flame on a captive's chest with the fire-sticks. The fire caught; a runner carried it down to the Templo Mayor; relays carried it to every city, and every hearth in the empire was relit from the one flame. Time is a fire that must be relit by hands — a civilization whose calendar had an ignition switch, and one night in fifty-two years when everyone held their breath.

myths.title: Huehueteotl, the Old One
myths.text: Under his other name he is the oldest thing in the cosmos: Huehueteotl, 'the Old, Old God,' the wrinkled figure who carries the fire-bowl on his bent back, present before the suns were set in motion. Sahagún lists him among the primordial gods (Florentine Codex, Book 1), and the tonalamatl — the book of days — set him at the head of the first trecena, 1-Cipactli: the count of time begins under his sign. The Aztecs put him at the center of the world's four directions, the fire-pillar between the levels, and every domestic hearth was his shrine: the three stones of the kitchen, the offering of copal before the pot went on. It is the smallest and the greatest cult at once — the god of the kitchen who is also the god of the calendar, worshipped in the millions of hearths no army could ever close. The Old God never needed a temple because he had already been given one: the floor of every house.

lore.culturalLegacy: The 52-year cycle's shadow falls on Mexico's calendar still; Huixachtlan's hill is in today's Mexico City sprawl, and the last New Fire was drilled in 1507 — the empire fell before the next. His wrinkled, brazier-backed figure is one of the most-recognized images of Aztec art (the great stone Huehueteotl of the Museo Nacional), and the fire-drill remains the emblem of renewal ceremonies across Mexican civic culture.
lore.archaeology: The Templo Mayor's excavations found his shrine among the precinct's gods; the great Huehueteotl brazier-figures — stone elders carrying the fire-bowl — survive from Teotihuacan to Tenochtitlan, making him the longest-documented god-image in Mesoamerica (a thousand years of the same bent back). Huixachtlan's summit is preserved within Mexico City, and the Florentine Codex's New Fire account is the fullest ritual description from the pre-Columbian world.
lore.syncretism: The friars saw him as the devil's furnace — and the people quietly kept lighting the hearth: the vigil-candle of Mexican folk Catholicism and the copal-smoke of Day of the Dead altars are his continuing liturgy. The Maya fire-lords and the Zapotec coquihani are his southern cousins; the New Fire concept — the cosmos rekindled by human hands — has no closer parallel than the Vedic agni-liturgies on the other side of the world.

entries.meaning: "The Rich One" — Roman lord of the underworld and of buried wealth

steps: Epigraphic Latin wrote V for u: Pluto appears as PLVTO

pronunciation.approximation: PLOO-toh — both vowels long.
pronunciation.note: Latin Plūtō carries two long vowels, both marked by the restoration. His name is Rome's calque of the Greek Πλούτων — "the Rich One" — the underworld god whose buried wealth made death and riches share a single name. Both vowels are long in the classical scansion; Lewis & Short print the macrons that the restoration keeps.

domains.title: The Rich One Below
domains.subtitle: Underworld, Wealth, and the Doors of the Deep
domains.lead: Plūtō is Rome's underworld god in his own right — not merely Hádēs renamed, but the Latin "Rich One" who rules the dead and the buried treasure together: the god in whose name the ground gives up both its wealth and its silence.

cards.name: The Doors
cards.desc: The Plutonia — the underworld gates; Rome's own door to his realm stood at the Tarentum in the Campus Martius, opened three days a year.

cards.name: Plūtus
cards.desc: His twin-name: the wealth-god Plutus — cornucopia from below, Demeter's son in the Greek telling.

cards.name: Cerberus
cards.desc: The three-headed hound of the threshold — the deep's own border guard, charmed once by Orpheus' song.

cards.name: Proserpina
cards.desc: The queen he took by force and kept by season — Rome's Persephonē, arbiter of the returning year.

symbols.name: The bident
symbols.meaning: His two-pronged staff — the scepter of the depths

symbols.name: The cornucopia
symbols.meaning: Wealth rising from the earth — his benign face as Plūtus

symbols.name: The cypress
symbols.meaning: The underworld's tree — the dark column of the graveyard

symbols.name: Cerberus
symbols.meaning: The three-headed threshold-guard who admits the dead and refuses the living

symbols.name: The narcissus
symbols.meaning: The flower that sprang as a trap in the meadow and lured Proserpina within reach of the deep (Ovid, Met. 5.392–401)

symbols.name: The pomegranate
symbols.meaning: The seed that binds the queen to her season — six seeds, six months below

mythology.lead: Plūtō's Roman myths retell the Greek cycle with a merchant's accent: the underworld as treasury as much as tribunal. Ovid gives the rape of Proserpina, Virgil and Ovid the one descent that moved him, Apollodorus the thieves who failed, Hesiod the older wealth-god beneath the name, and Rome's own calendars the gate that opened three days a year.

myths.title: Proserpina in the Meadow
myths.text: Ovid tells the Roman rape with a landscape's grief (Metamorphoses 5.385–571). In the meadow below Henna, Proserpina gathers flowers — violets, lilies, crocuses — and laughs when the narcissus springs up, a trap set by Venus for the sake of her son Cupid's empire. The ground opens; Plūtō, 'the lord of the dark', carries her down through the pool of Cyane, whose waters, forbidden to speak, dissolve the nymph herself into a spring. Cerēs searches with torches lit at Etna's flame; she turns the mocking boy Ascalabus into a spotted gecko, and opens the cattle of the old man who sheltered her until he curses his own gift. Jupiter arbitrates: the girl who has eaten is bound to the deep. Six pomegranate seeds — or one, in the older Greek telling — divide the year between mother and husband, spring and summer above, autumn and winter below. The myth is Rome's charter for the agricultural year: what is buried is not lost, and what returns must first have descended.

myths.title: Orpheus Charms the Deep
myths.text: When Orpheus lost Eurydice to a snake, he did what no mortal does: he went down singing. Virgil's account (Georgics 4.453–527) makes the underworld itself soften — the Danaids' urn rests, Ixion's wheel stands still, Tityos' vultures pause — and Ovid adds (Metamorphoses 10.1–85) that even the king and queen of the deep wept, a first for both. The condition was set: lead her up, and do not look back until you stand in daylight. At the very border, love or doubt turned his head, and she was reclaimed — a second death, and this one his own doing. The Romans read the myth as Plūtō's one audited exception: the deep can be moved, exactly once, and only by the thing it does not possess — a mortal voice persuasive enough to make law pause. Every later descent of European poetry, Dante's, Monteverdi's, Gluck's, walks the same road under the same rule.

lore.culturalLegacy: The dwarf planet, discovered in 1930 and named at the suggestion of the eleven-year-old Venetia Burney, carries his name — and the irony is his: the richest name in the sky given to the smallest body, demoted in 2006 and beloved still. Walt Disney's Pluto debuted the same year, a dog answering to the god of the underworld; Glenn T. Seaborg's plutonium (1941) took the name secondhand from the planet. 'Plutocracy' is his grammar of wealth, 'plutonic' his geology of deep-formed stone; financiers still speak of markets' 'underworld' without knowing they are citing him. In the Renaissance his image became Fortune's dark twin — cornucopia in one hand, bident in the other — and every treasury and cemetery remains his bookkeeping. He asked only one question of the living: what will you trust to the deep, and what will it give back in your season?
lore.archaeology: His monuments are pits and absences. In 1888 workmen on the Quirinal uncovered a subterranean altar-chamber identified with the Tarentum, the roofed pit where Rome sacrificed to Dis Pater and Proserpina — the closest archaeology comes to his door. The Severan copy of the Augustan acta (CIL VI 32323) preserves the 17 BCE liturgy in stone, including the nocturnal offerings to the 'inferis' on three successive nights. Before Rome, Etruria painted his face: the tombs of Tarquinia — the Tomb of the Augurs, the Tomb of the Leopards — banquet amid underworld watch-dogs and demons two centuries before the Secular Games, and funerary urns from Chiusi show Aita wrenching Phersipnai into his chariot. Rome's own grand Plūtō-temple is a negative space the texts acknowledge: the city preferred to worship the giver with Cerēs and to wall the taker into three dark days.
lore.syncretism: His equation with the Greek Hádēs was total and early, but Rome kept the distinction of names: Hádēs the Unseen, Plūtō the Rich — the wealth-emphasis distinctly Roman. Etruria's Aita presides over his infernal quarter of the Piacenza bronze liver, beside Phersipnai; Gaul's Dis Pater, whom Caesar (Bellum Gallicum 6.18) reports as the ancestor the Gauls claimed, absorbed the cult northward. The mystery religions deepened the syncretism: in the Orphic-Platonic tradition Plouton rules the generative womb of the earth, whence seeds rise, and the Orphic Hymn to Plouton invokes him as 'wealth-giver' and earth-shaker. Late antique Hermetists and the medieval alchemists kept 'plutonic' for all deep-earth fire — the lineage that ends in the element plutonium, named in 1941 for the planet that had taken the god's name. The Romans worshipped the giver and walled out the taker, and quietly knew them for one door.

entries.meaning: Goddess of grain and growth — the source of the word "cereal"

steps: Roman inscriptions wrote in monumental capitals; CERES needs no V-for-U substitution

pronunciation.approximation: KEH-rehs — hard c, long second vowel.
pronunciation.note: Latin Cerēs carries the long ē of the second syllable — Cĕ-rēs — traditionally derived from the root of crescere, ‘to grow’, so the goddess is named for growth itself. Her name is the ancestor of the word ‘cereal’, which is why her temple’s bread is etymological. The hard c of the classical period later softened in Italian mouths; the temple keeps the older, harder reading.

domains.title: The Grain Mother
domains.subtitle: Agriculture, Bread, Law, and the People's Goddess
domains.lead: Cerēs is Rome's oldest working goddess: the power of grain and growth, patron of the plebeians who eat it, and the deity whose Greek sister's myth (Dēmētēr and Persephonē) she borrowed so completely that Rome's religion of the field became one with the mystery of the seasons.

cards.name: The Sheaf
cards.desc: The wheat-sheaf she carries — the staff of civilization.

cards.name: The Torches
cards.desc: Her search for Proserpina by torchlight — the mother who would not stop.

cards.name: The Plebeian Triad
cards.desc: Cerēs, Liber, Libera — the Aventine trinity of the common people.

cards.name: The Grain Fleet
cards.desc: Rome's annona: the wheat-ships of Sicily and Egypt under her protection.

symbols.name: The wheat-sheaf
symbols.meaning: The gift that made agriculture — and law — possible

symbols.name: The torch
symbols.meaning: The search that never ends — maternal persistence as cosmic order

symbols.name: The poppy
symbols.meaning: Sleep and renewal — the flower of the fallow field

symbols.name: The sow
symbols.meaning: Her sacrificial animal — the pig offered to Cerēs at funerals (the porca praesentanea), guardian of the boundary between grain and the dead

mythology.lead: Cerēs' myths are Rome's double helix: the Greek mother-goddess woven into the Italian grain-god, until the field and the mystery were one.

myths.title: The Teaching of the Furrow
myths.text: Before Cerēs, Ovid says, the acorn was the meal and the woodland the pantry. The goddess changed the menu and the world with it: she first broke the soil with the curved plough, yoked the ox, gave mortals the grains, and taught them to bind harvest to seed (Fasti 4.401–416; Hyginus, Fabulae 277). Rome drew the conclusion itself: where grain is stored, surplus exists, and where surplus exists, property, boundaries, and law must follow — the flamen Cerealis and the Vestals’ salted meal kept her ritual at the very center of the civic year, and Cicero could treat her mysteries as a moral foundation of the state. Varro explains her name as taken a creando, ‘from creating’ (De lingua Latina 5.64). The myth is an etymology acted out: the goddess named for growth grows law itself, and the furrow becomes the first line of Rome’s constitution.

myths.title: The Torches of Cerēs
myths.text: While the nymph Cyane reached out to stop him, Pluto split the earth and carried off Proserpina from her Sicilian meadow by the lake of Pergusa — and Cerēs, lighting torches at Aetna’s fires, searched the world nine days without tasting food (Metamorphoses 5.341–508; Fasti 4.417–620). At Eleusis an old woman offered her barley-water; mocked by a boy as she drank, the goddess sprinkled him with meal and turned him into a star-backed lizard. Joy returned only when Jupiter ruled that Proserpina, having eaten of the pomegranate, should spend that portion of the year below — and the myth explains the seasons in the grammar of a mother’s grief. But the Roman telling adds its own office: the search founded the rites at the grain’s return, and Ovid closes the sequence with Cerēs sending Triptolemus across the world in a dragon chariot to teach the plough. Grief here is not the opposite of agriculture; it is agriculture — the year measured by a loss that repeats and a return that rescues.

lore.culturalLegacy: ‘Cereal’ is her everyday immortality: every breakfast bowl in the West carries her name, from the Latin Cerialia, her festival’s gifts. The dwarf planet Ceres — first asteroid discovered, by Piazzi in 1801, and explored by NASA’s Dawn probe in 2015 — keeps her aloft in the heavens, and her surface features are named for agricultural spirits of every nation. In America she is a civic deity: her statue crowns the Chicago Board of Trade, the world’s great grain market, and her face appears on the state seals of New Jersey and North Carolina, holding the cornucopia of plenty. Currency, too, once carried her — revolutionary France printed her on its assignats as the guarantor of subsistence. Of all the Roman gods, she is the one whose name a modern speaker is most likely to speak daily, three times a day, without knowing it: the goddess of breakfast.
lore.archaeology: The Aventine temple’s podium still stands beside the Circus Maximus, its massive concrete-and-travertine platform the surviving footprint of the plebeian triad’s house. In Sicily, her true archaeological homeland, the sanctuary treasures were so famous that Cicero built a prosecution around them: the Verrines catalogue the gold, ivory, and bronze of the temple at Enna, whose priesthood Verres’ theft violated. At Morgantina in central Sicily, excavation of the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore yielded a cache of silver vessels looted in the twentieth century and repatriated from the Metropolitan Museum and the Getty in 2010–2011 — the most celebrated restitution in classical archaeology, and a direct material thread from the grain goddess’s cult to the modern museum. The Cerealia’s games are fixed in the fasti, and votive terracottas from the grain districts of Latium and Sicily fill the cases of the Roman and Agrigento museums with her ears of wheat.
lore.syncretism: Her equation with Dēmētēr was near-total and early: Greek foundations in southern Italy had long paired the grain goddesses, and when famine struck in 496 BCE the Sibylline Books prescribed the importation of rites ‘in the Greek manner’ — the process that Dionysius of Halicarnassus (6.17) records as the making of the Aventine cult. Rome nonetheless bent the figure to its own stresses: the plebeian politics of the triad, the annōna that made her the patron of the grain fleet, and the Cerealia’s games. Sicily — her mythic homeland, with the meadow at Enna — became Rome’s first granary and her most pious province; Cicero’s Verrines preserve the inventory of her temple’s treasures. Late antiquity folded her further: her iconography passed into Isis’, and Augustine (City of God 18.13) sneered at the Roman mysteries as Greek rites wearing Latin names. The syncretism was so complete that the goddess’s Roman core — bread, law, the plebs — is visible only against the Greek outline she borrowed.

entries.meaning: "Cloud Serpent" — god of the hunt, of clouds, and of the starry road

pronunciation.approximation: meesh-KOH-ahtl — long o, lateral finish.
pronunciation.note: Mixcōātl is Nahuatl for "cloud serpent" (mixtli + cōātl); the macron on the ō marks the long vowel of the serpent-word, the same one in Quetzalcōātl and Xōlōtl. The restoration keeps it — the serpent is always long. The x of Nahuatl is the sh-sound, not ks: meesh, not mix — the single most misread letter in the language.

domains.title: The Serpent in the Clouds
domains.subtitle: Hunting, Stars, and the Milky Way
domains.lead: Mixcōātl is the Aztec god of the hunt and the starry road: the cloud-serpent who slides along the Milky Way, patron of the nomadic hunters who became the Aztecs' ancestors — the oldest god of the road that leads to the empire.

cards.name: The Milky Way
cards.desc: His body in the sky: the star-serpent, the road of the night that the migrating tribes read as their path south.

cards.name: The Hunt
cards.desc: Patron of hunters — his bow, his net and his fire-drill, the Chichimec tool-kit of a people who lived by the road.

cards.name: The Cloud
cards.desc: The weather-serpent: rain and sky in motion — mixtli, the cloud that names him.

cards.name: Camaxtle
cards.desc: His other name — the ancient hunting god of the Chichimecs, remembered in the high god's genealogy.

symbols.name: The bow and arrows
symbols.meaning: The hunt — his gift to the wandering tribes

symbols.name: The star-serpent
symbols.meaning: The Milky Way as a living road, his body across the night

symbols.name: The white stripes
symbols.meaning: His hunting-paint, cloud on dark sky, worn by his dancers at Quecholli

symbols.name: The fire-drill
symbols.meaning: Kindled beside the bow — the two technologies that made the wandering life possible

symbols.name: The hunting net
symbols.meaning: His snare and the badge of his hunters; a net full of stars is his sky

mythology.lead: Mixcōātl's myths are the Aztec origin-story in one figure: the wilderness god who taught the city-builders how to hunt, whose star-road they followed south, and whose household quarrel is written nightly across his own body. The sources are colonial but faithful — Sahagún's informants, the indigenous annals, the picture-histories — and where they disagree, the disagreement is itself instructive.

myths.title: The Serpent of Stars
myths.text:
The Chichimec tribes who became the Aztec nobility followed his road: the Milky Way, which the Nahuatl called Mixcōātl, the Cloud Serpent, slithering nightly across the sky. The migrating peoples read their path in his body — the desert crossed by the serpent's light — and when they founded Tenochtitlan they enthroned the wilderness-guide among the city's great gods, the god of where they had come from. The migration theology is the point: an empire founded by wanderers reads its own founding as a following, and the chronicle tradition keeps the memory of tribes who lived by the hunt before they had fields.

Mixcōātl's body across the sky is the oldest road-map of Mexican legitimacy — the empire's charter written in stars, followed long before it was written.

myths.title: The Bow of the Chichimecs
myths.text:
As Camaxtle, he gave the wandering tribes the bow and the fire-drill — the two tools of a life in motion. The city never forgot the debt: in the fourteenth month, Quecholli, 'the precious feather', the hunters' own liturgy filled the temple precinct — arrows, nets and deer brought to the god's altar, the rite of the hunt performed at the heart of the greatest city of the valley (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 2). The coronation tradition dressed the new ruler in the insignia of war and the hunt, and the tlatoani's wars opened under the god's banners.

The weapons on the altar are the archaeology of gratitude: once a year the city laid down the tools that fed it before it had fields — an empire paying honest tribute to its own wilderness.

lore.culturalLegacy: His name survives in the Milky Way's Nahuatl name itself; the Quecholli weapons-festival is documented in the Florentine Codex's fullest ritual detail; and the Chichimec hunting mythology is the standard account of the Aztecs' own self-image: the empire that began as wanderers following a serpent of stars. The Mexican National Museum of Anthropology's Mixcōātl figures — striped, netted, bowed — are his standing portraits.
lore.archaeology: Teotihuacan's hunting-god precedes him; the Toltec-Aztec Camaxtle cult at Tula and the Templo Mayor's offerings (his arrows among the buried gifts) anchor his archaeology. The Florentine Codex's Quecholli chapter — weapons, dance, and the hunt's liturgy — is the fullest record, and the rock-art of the northern deserts (the bowmen of the Sierra Madre) keeps his people's original ground.
lore.syncretism: The hunt-gods of North America stand in his lineage: the Huichol's Kauyumari (the blue deer-guide) and the Maya hunting-lords share his road-and-prey theology. Colonial chroniclers merged him with Santiago and with Nimrod (the hunter-king of the missionaries' Genesis); the people kept the star-serpent — and hunters in rural Mexico still note the sky's deer-road on the way to the field.

entries.meaning: The river orisha Ọba — co-wife of the thunder god, lady of the sacred waters

variants.note: Previous owned form; the current primary adds the final low tone (Ọbà)

steps: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality.
The underdot marks the open vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ and the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/; these are the obligatory phonemic marks.
Tone marks (grave low, acute high) are fully written in dictionaries but routinely omitted in everyday Yoruba writing.
The owned Unicode form preserves the underdots and the tone marks the domain could carry; the fully tone-marked dictionary form is documented in the variants and here.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-bah — open o, low-low melody.
pronunciation.note: Ọba names the river orisha of the Ọba River; the precomposed dot-below Ọ is the domain-maximal form (tone marks cannot be registered), and the fuller tone-marked Ọ̀bà is preserved in the temple's display text. The dot-below marks the open-mid vowel.

domains.title: The River that Endures
domains.subtitle: Devotion, Jealousy, and the Lake of the Co-Wife
domains.lead: Ọba is the river orisha who loved and lost: the senior wife of Ṣàngó, whose jealousy cost her an ear and whose grief became a lake. She is the Yoruba study of endurance — the quiet river that outlasts the storm-god's louder wives, and whose crown was redesigned to hide, and honor, the wound at once.

cards.name: The Ọba River
cards.desc: Her water in Yorubaland — the stream that bears her name and her temperament, quiet where the storm-wives are loud.

cards.name: The Hidden Ear
cards.desc: The ear she lost to the co-wives' trick — hidden under her crown and her hair, which is why her images never show the ears.

cards.name: The Senior Wife
cards.desc: The first wife of the thunder-king — and the last to be believed when the household turned cruel.

cards.name: The Lake
cards.desc: Her grief made geography: the lake where the faithful still mourn with her, season after season.

symbols.name: The covered ear
symbols.meaning: Wounds hidden and endured — dignity after injury; her images never show the ears

symbols.name: The crown of the hidden ear
symbols.meaning: Regalia redesigned around the wound — the only crown in the corpus that exists to hide and honor at once

symbols.name: The brass bracelet
symbols.meaning: Her marriage-token from the thunder-king, kept after the palace cast her out

symbols.name: The red parrot feather
symbols.meaning: Her sign beside the other wives' red — the household's colors she was never allowed to outshine

symbols.name: The river Ọba
symbols.meaning: Her name made water — the stream in Yorubaland that keeps her longer than any palace could

mythology.lead: Ọba's myths are domestic tragedy told as hydrology: the co-wife's war that became a river and a lake. The cycle survives in Yoruba oral tradition — oríkì praise-poetry and the folktale corpus recorded by Bascom and others — and crossed the Atlantic to become the diaspora's parable of the polygamous household.

myths.title: Three Wives, One Storm
myths.text: Ṣàngó, the thunder-king, took three river-wives: Ọba the senior, Ọṣun the beloved, and Ọya the storm-sharer. The cycle survives in the oríkì praise-poetry and the folktale corpus recorded by Yoruba specialists from the mid-twentieth century — Wande Abimbola's editions of Ifá verse, William Bascom's collections of tales — and in the diaspora the three wives became the standard cast of every household drama. The tellings agree on the shape: Ọba, the first wife, watched her husband's love flow downhill to Ọṣun, and love that is watched curdles into jealousy. In the fullest tellings Ọba schemed against Ọṣun — and Ọṣun, the shrewdest of the household, let the scheme come to her first and answered it with one that would end the rivalry. The seniority that should have protected Ọba is exactly what the story burns: in the thunder-king's house, the first wife is the last to be believed, and the household's peace is purchased with her humiliation.

myths.title: The Ear in the Soup
myths.text: The trap is the cycle's most famous scene, preserved in the folktale collections (Bascom, African Folktales) and endlessly retold in the diaspora. Ọṣun — in some tellings Ọya — let fall that the king loved, above all things, the taste of his beloved's ear in his soup. Ọba, desperate to be loved again, cut off her own ear and cooked it for him. When the bowl came before Ṣàngó and the trick stood revealed, his disgust and rage drove her from the palace; the co-wives laughed, and Ọba fled north weeping, her maimed head hidden under her crown and her hair. The sources disagree on which co-wife set the trap and on how much of the truth Ṣàngó ever learned — the oral tradition keeps the variants alive rather than settling them. What every telling keeps is the ear: the organ of obedience, cut off to buy a love that was never for sale. The myth is the Yoruba anatomy of jealousy — not the villain's punishment, but the victim's self-mutilation, and the crown she designed afterward to live with it.

lore.culturalLegacy: Her image — the crowned figure hiding her ears — is one of Yoruba art's most intimate: the wound as regalia. The co-wives' cycle structures the orisha households of two continents; her river in Yorubaland keeps her shrines active; and the 'Obá' of Cuban Santería is beloved as the most patient of the female orisha — the one who teaches that endurance is also a form of power. The brass bracelet of her marriage and the red parrot feather of her household appear in shrine and carnival alike, and the forward-combed hair of her initiates remains, in Thompson's phrase, a liturgy anyone can read: everyone who has dressed carefully on a difficult morning knows her rite. The quiet one, her cult insists, was the permanent one all along.
lore.archaeology: Her river rises in the hills of the Ọyọ country, and her cult-centers at Ọṣogbo and the Ọba lake preserve her shrines and her priests; the brass and terracotta figures of the covered-ear goddess are documented in museum collections from Ifẹ̀ to Havana. The oríkì of the three wives, recorded by Bascom and others, is among the finest domestic myth-cycles in the Yoruba corpus — an archive kept not in stone but in living recitation, which is precisely the kind of evidence this tradition chose to leave.
lore.syncretism: In Cuba's Santería she is Obá, syncretized with Santa Catalina de Alejandría (Saint Catherine, whose wheel she shares) — her cult strong in Matanzas; in Brazil's Candomblé, Obá keeps her river and her covered ear, the devotee-dancers' hair arranged to hide what the king did. The three-wife cycle (Ọba-Ọṣun-Ọya) is the diaspora's standard parable of the polygamous household, told wherever the orisha went — and the co-wives' ritual incompatibility, the rule that Ọba and Ọya never share a shrine, was carried across the Atlantic as faithfully as any scripture. Thompson's Flash of the Spirit traces her iconography through Lucumí altars from Havana to Miami: the covered ear is one of the most durable images in the African-Atlantic world, a wound turned into regalia by four centuries of women's hands.

entries.meaning: "Best Truth" — the Amesha Spenta of cosmic order (Aša), guardian of the sacred fire and the moral law

variants.note: Alternate Avestan orthography with explicit h before šta; canonical PuniCodex form is Ašavahišta

steps: Written aṣ̌a vahišta in the Avesta; the Aṣ̌əm Vohū prayer gives the oblique forms aṣ̌əm… vahištəm
ṣ̌ is written 𐬴 (SSHE) and š 𐬱 (SHE)

pronunciation.approximation: ah-shah-vah-HISH-tah — two sharp š sibilants, even vowels.
pronunciation.note: Avestan aša vahišta — "Best Truth/Righteousness" — is written in the scholarly transliteration with the palatal š of the Avestan alphabet, twice: Ašavahišta. The restoration keeps both sibilants exactly where the Gathas put them; English "Asha Vahishta" softens what the Avesta writes sharp.

domains.title: The Best Truth
domains.subtitle: Righteousness, the Sacred Fire, and the Moral Order
domains.lead: Ašavahišta is the Amesha Spenta of Aša — "Best Righteousness": the Bounteous Immortal who is cosmic order itself, the truth the universe is built to run on, and the sacred fire that tests every soul and every word against it.

cards.name: The Sacred Fire
cards.desc: His element: the altar-flame of the Avesta, purifier and witness.

cards.name: Aša
cards.desc: Cosmic order as a person — the truth against which all thought, word, and deed is measured.

cards.name: The Six
cards.desc: One of the Amesha Spentas — the Bounteous Immortals who form Ahura Mazda's council.

cards.name: The Ordeal
cards.desc: Fire as the test: the Avestan ordeal that proves the truthful from the deceitful.

symbols.name: The altar flame
symbols.meaning: The fire of the Avesta — his presence in every Zoroastrian temple

symbols.name: The ašem-vohū verse
symbols.meaning: The most-recited prayer of the faith: “Aša is the best, it is happiness” (Yasna 27.14)

symbols.name: The winged sun
symbols.meaning: The fravašis’ symbol he shares with the whole order

symbols.name: The molten metal
symbols.meaning: The river of ordeal-fire at the world’s end — warm milk to the truthful, burning to the deceitful

mythology.lead: Ašavahišta’s mythology is the Gathas’ own theology made personal: truth not as an idea but as an immortal who must be fed, fought for, and kept alight. Every fire-temple flame is his dwelling, every honest word his territory, and the final fire of the world’s end his last and clearest sermon.

myths.title: The Bounteous Immortals
myths.text: The Avesta’s great hymn-names them: Vohu Manah (Good Mind), Aša Vahišta (Best Truth), Xšaθra Vairya (Chosen Power), Spenta Ārmaiti (Holy Devotion), Haurvatāt (Wholeness), Amərətāt (Immortality) — the Amesha Spentas, the Bounteous Immortals who are at once Ahura Mazda’s powers and persons, his council and his limbs. Ašavahišta is the second, named beside Good Mind in the Gathas’ own theology: he is the Truth the Good Mind thinks, the order every right word and deed must match. In the earliest stratum he is not one power among others but the standard they all serve — the thing the two spirits contested at creation (Yasna 30.3–5), and the stake of the entire cosmic war between Aša and Druj, Truth and the Lie. Later tradition systematised the six into a household of creation, giving each an element, a metal, a month, a day; but the Gathas already meet him as a presence, not a principle — an immortal who must be fed with rightness and fought for, or lost.

myths.title: The Fire of Aša
myths.text: His element is fire — not the destroyer but the tester. The Avesta gives fire to Aša Vahišta as his very domain: the altar-flame through which prayers rise — the Yasna calls it the most swift and powerful force of Ahura Mazda (Yasna 34.4) — and the ordeal-fire through which innocence is proven. In the Gathas, fire is the wisdom that discerns the true from the false in thought, word, and deed: swift to reward, swift to punish. Every Zoroastrian fire-temple keeps his presence: the flame tended in an urn for centuries without interruption is, in the faith, Ašavahišta made visible — the light that does not lie. Priests feed it five times a day with sandalwood and recite his verse over it; the laity honour it by refusing to defile it with breath, smoke, or the touch of the impure. A god of truth needs no statue: his icon is the one thing every honest eye can audit — a flame.

lore.culturalLegacy: He is the reason "truth" has a temple: the Zoroastrian moral tradition — good thought, good word, good deed — is his liturgy, and the fire-temples of Yazd and the diaspora are his addresses. The word "Asha" lives in modern Persian and as a common name across South Asia. Scholars read him as the hinge on which the Abrahamic heaven-and-judgment traditions later turned: the first theology of a universe audited for truth.
lore.archaeology: The fire-temples are his monuments: Adur Gušnasp at Takht-e Soleyman (Sasanian, UNESCO) — the shrine of kings; Adur Farnbag in Fars; and the working Atash Behram of Yazd, whose flame has burned since 470 CE. The Achaemenid reliefs of Persepolis show the fire-altar in royal worship, and the Gathas themselves — the oldest hymns of any living scripture — are his charter, preserved in the oldest Avestan manuscripts (K7, 14th c. copies of much older work).
lore.syncretism: His cognate is the Vedic ṛta and its guardian: scholars pair Aša with the Vedic order-principle and note the shared Indo-Iranian root (*rtá/aša). In the Sasanian era his fire became state cult — the great fire-temples of Adur Gušnasp and Adur Farnbag bore his element as national shrines; and the Yasna's ašem-vohū verse ("aša is the best, it is happiness") remains the most-recited line of the living faith. He survives wherever the fire is kept: Yazd's perpetual flame is, by every account, still his.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-doh-nis' — pitch falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowel is long.
pronunciation.note: The Greek form Ἄδωνις reproduces the Semitic title ʾādōn ('lord') with Greek inflection. The restoration Ádōnis preserves both the acute stress and the long omega.

domains.title: Lord of Beauty and Brief Return
domains.subtitle: Desire, Vegetation, and the Cycle of Death and Renewal
domains.lead: Ádōnis is the beautiful youth whom love and death divide. Born from the grief of Myrrha and the myrrh tree, desired by Aphrodítē and Persephonē alike, he embodies the fragile glory of spring: flowers that bloom brilliantly and die young. His cult spread across the Greek East as a women's rite of lament and rebirth.

cards.name: Beauty and Desire
cards.desc: A youth of such beauty that the goddess of love herself cannot leave him.

cards.name: Vegetation and Renewal
cards.desc: The anemone and the myrrh tree mark his blood and birth; his death is the death of the green year.

cards.name: Women's Lament
cards.desc: The Adṓnia was a rite of mourning women, planting gardens that withered to enact grief.

cards.name: Hunter Hunted
cards.desc: A boar, the animal of Aphrodítē's anger or of his own hubris, tears him open.

symbols.name: Anemone
symbols.meaning: The flower that sprang from Ádōnis's blood, red and short-lived

symbols.name: Myrrh tree
symbols.meaning: His mother Myrrha's metamorphosis; the tree from whose bark he was born

symbols.name: Boar
symbols.meaning: The animal that killed him in the hunt

symbols.name: Hunter's gear
symbols.meaning: Spear and nets; the masculine pursuit that leads to his death

mythology.lead: Ádōnis's myth turns on beauty that cannot be kept. He is desired, born, killed, and divided — a story the Greeks borrowed from the dying-god cults of the Near East and made their own, and a women's rite of lament that gives rare direct voice to female grief in the classical city.

myths.title: The Myrrh Tree Splits
myths.text: Myrrha, daughter of King Kinyras of Cyprus — or of Assyria, in the older eastern versions — conceived a hopeless passion for her own father. Her nurse smuggled her into the royal bed on a night when the king's wife was away at a festival of Demeter; when Kinyras discovered the truth by lamplight he reached for his sword, and the gods transformed the fleeing girl into a myrrh tree (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.4; Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.298–502). Ten months later the bark split and the infant Adonis was born — Ovid's loveliest detail has the tree tear 'like a girl's body opening in childbirth'. The tale makes his beauty the fruit of transgression: he is born where the boundary of the family was crossed, and his whole career will be spent on boundaries — between women and men, love and death, the earth and the underworld.

myths.title: Divided Between Two Queens
myths.text: Aphrodite hid the infant in a chest and entrusted him to Persephone, queen of the dead — but Persephone opened the chest, looked, and refused to give him back. Zeus judged between the goddesses: Adonis would spend a third of the year with Persephone below, a third with Aphrodite above, and a third as he chose — and he chose Aphrodite, for love of her beauty and the living world (Apollodorus 3.14.4). Sappho preserves the women's lament for the dying season — 'tender Adonis is dying, Cyprian; what shall we do?' (fr. 140a) — and a variant has the division decided by lots weighed on a scale, Aphrodite cheating with her girdle to tip the outcome. The myth is transparent seasonal allegory: the year itself divided between the queen of life and the queen of death. Its honesty is the point — desire and mortality get exactly equal terms.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ádōnis survives in the anemone, in the word 'Adonis' applied to handsome young men, and in the long Western tradition of Venus and Adonis from Ovid to Shakespeare to Titian. His cult is one of the clearest cases of religious borrowing across the Aegean and Levant, and the Adṓnia gives rare evidence for women's religious practice in classical Greece. In modern wellness and beauty branding, his name still signals youth, desire, and the fleeting bloom of physical perfection.
lore.archaeology: Adonis has left no excavated sanctuary in the Greek world — the Adonia were rooftop and garden rites that leave no foundations — but his cult has a concrete Levantine landscape. At Afqa in the mountains above Byblos, a great grotto and spring burst from the cliff: the source of the river the Greeks called Adonis, the modern Nahr Ibrahim, whose floodwaters stained red with mountain clay were read as the god's annual blood (Lucian, On the Syrian Goddess 6). Roman remains at the site include temple platforms and aqueduct lines of the sanctuary of Venus and Adonis. Below, the harbours of Byblos — whose royal house claimed kinship with Adonis's father Kinyras — anchor the myth to one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth.
lore.syncretism: Ádōnis is transparently the Greek adaptation of the Semitic Tammuz (Sumerian Dumuzi), the dying-and-rising vegetation god mourned by women in Mesopotamia and the Levant. The name itself comes from the Canaanite/Phoenician ʾādōn, 'lord'. In Roman poetry he becomes a byword for youthful male beauty — Venus and Adonis is a staple of Ovid and later painters, and Shakespeare's poem and Titian's canvases carry the pair into the modern canon. The figure also overlaps with Near Eastern dying-god typologies studied by Frazer, though modern scholars resist collapsing every vegetation deity into a single pattern.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Greek as Ἄδωνις. The initial alpha carries an acute, and the omega is long. PUNICODEX restores these features as Ádōnis; the Semitic original ʾādōn is not registrable in the .com IDN table and is preserved here as scholarly annotation.

entries.meaning: Sea (the sea giant who brews ale for the gods)
Lord who looks down in compassion

etymology.derivation: Sanskrit Avalokiteśvara, from avalokita 'beheld, looked down upon' + īśvara 'lord'; the bodhisattva of compassion, source-form of Guānyīn and Kannon.

steps: Sanskrit Avalokiteśvara is written in Devanagari as अवलोकितेश्वर
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: 'uh-vuh-LOH-kee-TAY-shvuh-ruh' — the ś is the soft 'sh' of 'ship'; hold both long vowels; the name ends lightly.
pronunciation.note: Avalokiteśvara is Tier 1 by rule: the restoration preserves three features ASCII loses — the long ō of lōkita, the long ē of tēśvara, and the palatal ś. The Chinese translated rather than transliterated (Guanshiyin, 'Perceiver of the World's Sounds'), which is why East Asia knows him by the listening, not the Sanskrit.

domains.title: Compassion
domains.subtitle: The Lord Who Looks Down in Compassion — Bodhisattva of Mercy, Lord of the World's Cries
domains.lead: Avalokiteśvara is compassion made a person: the bodhisattva who looks down upon every cry of suffering and answers it, postponing his own Buddhahood until no being is left unsaved. From the Lotus Sūtra's Universal Gateway to Tibet's patron deity and China's beloved Guanyin, he is the most widely venerated bodhisattva in the world.

cards.name: The Universal Gateway
cards.desc: Lotus Sūtra ch. 25: whoever calls his name in fire, flood, chains, or the jaws of demons is delivered at once.

cards.name: Thousand Arms, Thousand Eyes
cards.desc: His Great Compassion form: an arm for every cry, an eye in every palm so that seeing and saving happen together.

cards.name: Perceiver of Sounds
cards.desc: ava-lokita, 'perceived, looked down upon': his very name is an act of attention that never lifts.

cards.name: Om Mani Padme Hum
cards.desc: His mantra on the lips of half the Himalaya — the jewel in the lotus — recited for every suffering being.

symbols.name: The lotus
symbols.meaning: Purity rising unstained from the mud of samsara — the flower on which he stands above the world he refuses to leave

symbols.name: The vase of amrita
symbols.meaning: The nectar of compassion in his left hand, poured out drop by drop on the burning places of beings

symbols.name: Thousand arms with an eye in each palm
symbols.meaning: His vow rendered anatomically: a hand for every cry, an eye in every palm so that seeing and saving are one motion

symbols.name: Om Mani Padme Hum
symbols.meaning: The six-syllable mantra — 'the jewel in the lotus' — recited across Tibet, Mongolia, and the Himalaya for a thousand years

symbols.name: The blue throat of Nīlakaṇṭha
symbols.meaning: The wrathful form's throat stained blue from drinking the world's poison — compassion willing to take on even Śiva's darkest work

mythology.lead: Avalokiteśvara's mythology is a geography of mercy: the Indian lord who hears cries, the Chinese princess who gave her eyes and arms, the Tibetan ancestor of a nation, the Japanese savior of the drowning. His stories share one grammar — someone suffers, and compassion arrives already looking.

myths.title: The Lord Who Looks Down
myths.text: The name is an act of attention: ava-lokita, 'perceived, looked down upon,' joined to īśvara, 'lord' — the Lord Who Looks Down, as Monier-Williams parses the Sanskrit. The Lotus Sūtra's twenty-fifth chapter, the Universal Gateway, turns the etymology into a program: the Buddha declares that whoever calls Avalokiteśvara's name in the moment of terror — surrounded by fire, swept by flood, bound in chains, cornered by demons — will be saved, because this bodhisattva scans the world the way a parent scans a crowd for a child. Kumārajīva translated the name into Chinese as Guanshiyin, 'Perceiver of the World's Sounds,' and the translation stuck: East Asia knows him by the listening. The name is the whole doctrine — compassion is not a mood but a gaze that never lifts.

myths.title: Thirty-Three Forms for Every Kind of Suffering
myths.text: The Lotus Sūtra (ch. 25) closes its gateway chapter with a list that reads like a census of the human condition: to beings who can be saved through a Buddha's body, Avalokiteśvara appears as a Buddha; likewise as a pratyekabuddha, a śrāvaka, a king, a householder, a government official, a monk, a nun, a layman, a laywoman, a boy, a girl, a god, a nāga, a yaksha, a gandharva, an asura, a garuḍa, a kinnara, a mahoraga — the sūtra counts thirty-three bodies in all. Śāriputra asks why he is called Perceiver of Sounds, and the answer is simplicity itself: he perceives the world's sounds and responds to each. The list is the myth's meaning: suffering has no shape the bodhisattva will not borrow to reach the sufferer, and mercy wears every uniform the world issues.

lore.culturalLegacy: Avalokiteśvara is, by nearly any measure, the most venerated bodhisattva on earth. His chapter of the Lotus Sūtra is chanted as a protective rite across East Asia; his mantra turns the prayer wheels of the entire Himalaya; and the Guanyin temples of the Chinese diaspora — from Putuo Island to San Francisco — count their visitors in the tens of millions. Japan's thirty-three Kannon pilgrimage circuits are walked today as they were in the Heian period. Modern culture keeps finding him: the Dalai Lama's name is Chenrezig's in translation, and the phrase 'compassion' in contemporary mindfulness and hospice movements is, knowingly or not, Avalokiteśvara's old gaze still lowered on the suffering.
lore.archaeology: Avalokiteśvara enters art early and never leaves: the fifth- and sixth-century cave paintings at Ajanta give him some of his oldest monumental images, compassionate bodhisattvas looming over the chaitya halls. The Library Cave at Dunhuang (sealed c. 1000, opened 1900) yielded painted banners of Guanyin among the most exquisite Buddhist paintings surviving — several now in the British Museum and Musée Guimet. At Borobudur in Java the Śailendra dynasty carved Lokeśvara into the monument's galleries in the eighth and ninth centuries, and the Kathmandu valley's Licchavi-period inscriptions invoke him by name. From Gandhāra's earliest standing bodhisattvas to the colossal Song dynasty Guanyin at Dazu, his is the longest continuous iconographic career of any Buddhist figure.
lore.syncretism: In China the lord became a lady: by the Song dynasty Guanyin was predominantly female, and her cult absorbed the island goddess Mazu and the water-and-child-bestowing Songzi Guanyin, so that the Indian bodhisattva now answers a grandmother's prayer in a Fujian dialect. Japan received Kannon, patron of the great thirty-three-temple pilgrimage circuits (Saigoku, Bandō, Chichibu) and of sacred sites like Kiyomizu, 'pure water,' where her spring still runs. Tibet made Chenrezig the patron deity of the land and the source of the Dalai Lama lineage, each holder revered as his emanation. And in seventh-century Java the Śailendra kings named themselves servants of Lokeśvara — Avalokiteśvara by his older title — carving him at Borobudur before the Sanskrit name had finished traveling. One bodhisattva, five civilizations, each certain he had been theirs all along.

entries.meaning: Fomorian king whose destructive eye blasts armies when its lid is raised, slain by his grandson Lúg with a sling-stone at Cath Maige Tuired.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-lor' — stress the first syllable hard, keep the l dark and broad, and let the final r stay tapped. Modern Irish 'Balor' keeps essentially the same shape.
pronunciation.note: Balor is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Irish form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the Fomorian king's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: The King of the Evil Eye
domains.subtitle: The Venomed Gaze, the Fomorian Tribute, the Fortress of Tory, the Grandson's Stone
domains.lead: Balor — Balor Béimnech, 'Balor of the Mighty Blows' — is king of the Fomorians, the sea-borne oppressors of medieval Irish tradition, and owner of the most feared weapon in the whole corpus: a single eye so venomed by the fumes of a druids' brew that no army could stand before its gaze. Grandfather of Lugh and doomed by that very grandson's sling-stone at Mag Tuired, he is the Irish tradition's great figure of destructive sovereignty — power that poisons its possessor and is answered, in the end, by his own blood.

cards.name: The Venomed Eye
cards.desc: One eye, poisoned in boyhood by the fumes of a druids' charm-brew; any army it looked upon was worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

cards.name: The Fomorian Tribute
cards.desc: Under Balor and Indech the Fomorians taxed Ireland from the sea, and set the very gods to serf-work until Mag Tuired broke the yoke.

cards.name: The Tower of Tory
cards.desc: In the Donegal oral tradition, the sea-girt tower where Balor prisoned his daughter Eithne against the prophecy of a grandson's hand.

cards.name: The Grandson's Stone
cards.desc: Lugh's sling-stone at Mag Tuired drove the eye backward through Balor's head, so that its own gaze blasted the Fomorian host.

symbols.name: The venomed eye
symbols.meaning: A weapon the owner cannot aim without an army to raise the lid — power that outgrew its possessor.

symbols.name: The polished lid-lifter
symbols.meaning: Four men with a handle passed through the eyelid — kingship reduced to machinery, a gaze other men must operate.

symbols.name: The tower of Tory
symbols.meaning: The sea-girt prison built against a prophecy — the fortress that made the doom it feared.

symbols.name: The Glas Gaibhnenn
symbols.meaning: The grey-green cow Balor stole from Cian in the oral tradition — the theft that set the grandson's birth in motion.

symbols.name: The sling-stone
symbols.meaning: The small, aimed answer to the vast, unaimed gaze — the grandson's hand the druids foretold.

mythology.lead: Balor's dossier is short and total: he exists in the tradition to be the thing that must be brought down. Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's most famous single stroke, the Lebor Gabála fixes his lineage and his wife's vengeance, and the Donegal oral tradition supplies the prophecy, the tower, and the stolen cow that the medieval manuscripts only glance at. The sources disagree on the details and never on the architecture: a gaze that can only destroy, contained at terrible cost, and turned home at last by his own blood.

myths.title: Balor Son of Dot, Grandson of Nét
myths.text: The book of invasions fixes Balor's place before it tells his deeds: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét', king of the Fomorians — the sea-going race who had pressed on Ireland since the age of the Nemedians, exacting tribute from the outer islands. His wife was Cethlenn of the crooked teeth, whose spear struck the Dagda at Mag Tuired; the Lebor Gabála records that the All-Father afterwards died of Cethlenn's wound — the settled price of Balor's war, long counted in the tally of the battle. His daughter was Ethniu, and by Cian — in the Lebor Gabála's genealogy the son of the healer Dian Cécht — she bore Lugh, the Samildánach, equally skilled in all the arts. Thus the Fomorian king was the grandfather of the Túatha Dé Danann's deliverer: the genealogy on which the whole tragedy of Mag Tuired turns, and the reason no tower, sea, or tax could keep the grandson away.

myths.title: How the Eye Was Poisoned
myths.text:
Cath Maige Tuired explains the weapon before it uses it. Balor had a destructive eye, never opened except on a battlefield, and four men were needed to raise its lid with a polished handle that passed through it; any army that eye looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

The poison had a childhood. When Balor was a boy, his father's druids were brewing a charm, and the boy looked in on the work; the fumes of the brew rose and struck the eye, and from that day its gaze was venom. The detail is the tradition's whole theory of the figure in one image: power taken in unguarded, as a child takes in smoke, and carried incurably for a lifetime. What entered by accident becomes the foundation of a tyranny — and a tyranny that must hire four men to open its own weapon has already told you how it will end.

lore.culturalLegacy: Balor entered the modern world through two doors. The first was scholarship: Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried the sling-stone and the tower into English reading, and O'Rahilly's Early Irish History and Mythology (1946) made him the type-case of the Irish death-king — a scholarly afterlife as large as his medieval dossier is short. The second was the folklore itself: the Donegal oral versions — the tower, the stolen cow, the child cast into the sea — were collected in the nineteenth century and never stopped being retold, and 'Balor of the Evil Eye' remains the standing name of the figure in Irish and in English. In the modern imagination he has become the Celtic dark lord par excellence: the remote tyrant in his island fortress whose one weapon poisons everything it touches, answered not by a greater weapon but by the prophesied grandchild the fortress was built to prevent. Tory Island keeps his address; the Irish language never lost his name.
lore.archaeology: Balor is a textual and oral figure: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. His manuscript witnesses are exact — Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition, while Lebor Gabála Érenn is preserved in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster and its sister codices. His geographical anchor is one of the most dramatic pieces of coastline in Europe: Tory Island (Toraigh), nine miles off the Bloody Foreland of Donegal, whose cliffs and sea-stacks — above all the great rock called Tór Mór — the oral tradition names as Balor's fortress and the site of Eithne's tower. The nineteenth-century collectors who wrote the tower story down were recording a living Donegal tradition anchored to those rocks, and the island's medieval monastic remains and round tower have kept the name in continuous local memory.
lore.syncretism: Balor's clearest cross-border witnesses are comparative, not cognate. The Welsh corpus preserves no figure derived from the same name — the Brythonic silence is total, as it is for so many of the Fomorian cycle. The parallels the scholarship actually leans on are typological. First, the Greek Acrisius: the king who prisoned his daughter Danaë because a prophecy named her son his slayer, and died by that grandson Perseus all the same — the Eithne tower is the same tale-shape, and comparatists have set the two side by side since the nineteenth century. Second, the one-eyed monster answered by aimed cunning — the Polyphemus pattern — where the single enormous eye is both the ogre's strength and the one place he can be struck. Third, and nearest home, the Irish and Mediterranean complex of the evil eye itself: the belief that a look can wither cattle, milk, and men, which Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both treat as the living folk-ground of Balor's venomed gaze. O'Rahilly read him further, as a figure of death and the western sea; the handbooks register the reading without making it doctrine.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Balor — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: balor.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

etymology.derivation: Sanskrit Bhaiṣajyaguru, from bhaiṣajya 'healing, remedy' + guru 'teacher'; the Medicine Buddha of lapis-lazuli radiance.

steps: Sanskrit Bhaiṣajyaguru is written in Devanagari as भैषज्यगुरु
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: 'BY-shaj-yah-GOO-roo' — the 'sh' is retroflex, tongue curled back; the first syllable is aspirated and the last is lengthened.
pronunciation.note: Bhaiṣajyaguru is Tier 1 by the mechanical rule: the retroflex ṣ and the conjunct -jy- carry diacritics and script features the ASCII 'bhaisajyaguru' flattens beyond recognition. The full Sanskrit title is Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhārāja, 'Medicine Master, King of Lapis-Lazuli Radiance' (IAST).

domains.title: Healing
domains.subtitle: Healing, Medicine, Lapis-Lazuli Light
domains.lead: Bhaiṣajyaguru is the Buddha of medicine — the Medicine Master whose eastern paradise glows with lapis-lazuli light and whose twelve great vows promise healing not only for the sick but for the poor, the imprisoned, and the misled. In a Buddhist cosmos crowded with transcendent realms, his is the one built like a hospital.

cards.name: Healing
cards.desc: The central domain: his twelve vows promise to cure disease and deformity — and the poverty that makes sickness fatal.

cards.name: Medicine master
cards.desc: The name means "Medicine Master" — guru of bhaiṣajya, the healer's art, from bhiṣaj "healer."

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Bhaiṣajyaguru recovers what plain ASCII bhaisajyaguru flattens.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Attested in Sanskrit manuscripts in Devanāgarī as भैषज्यगुरु; carried to China as Yàoshī, to Japan as Yakushi.

symbols.name: Lapis-lazuli light
symbols.meaning: The radiance of his eastern paradise — in his second vow, his very body is to shine like vaidūrya, the blue stone that gives him his title.

symbols.name: The medicine bowl
symbols.meaning: Held in his left hand, it carries the myrobalan (harītakī) — the one attribute no other major buddha needs.

symbols.name: The myrobalan fruit
symbols.meaning: The healing berry he offers, called in Ayurveda 'the remover of disease' — medicine as a concrete object, not a metaphor.

symbols.name: The eastern direction
symbols.meaning: His pure land lies in the east, balancing Amitābha's western paradise — dawn against sunset.

symbols.name: Sun and moon radiance
symbols.meaning: The bodhisattvas Sūryaprabha and Candraprabha attend him — light and its reflection as healing's witnesses.

mythology.lead: The stories of Bhaiṣajyaguru are sutras, not epics: scripture built from his twelve vows, his lapis-lit eastern paradise, and the liturgy of healing his name still powers across Asia.

myths.title: What He Promised Before He Was Buddha
myths.text:
The Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhārājasūtra — in Xuanzang's Chinese translation of 650 CE (T. 450), the standard form in East Asia — first tells what the future Medicine Buddha swore as a bodhisattva: twelve vows. He would make his body shine like lapis lazuli to dispel the darkness of ignorance; he would give beings 'inexhaustible' wealth of goods; he would set those on false paths on the bodhisattva road; he would restore broken precepts and heal 'bodies incomplete' — the blind, the lame, the deaf; he would cure the destitute sick and free the imprisoned from their chains; he would feed the hungry and clothe the naked. One vow — that women who wish it be reborn as men — belongs to its century, and modern translators note it without flinching.

The list is the myth: a buddha defined entirely by his promises, and a definition of healing broad enough to include poverty, fear, and error along with disease.

myths.title: The World of Lapis Light
myths.text:
Having fulfilled the vows, Bhaiṣajyaguru presides over the eastern pure land the sutras call Vaidūryanirbhāsa — 'Pure Lapis-Lazuli Radiance'. Its ground is vaidūrya itself, transparent as glass; its avenues are bounded by cords of jewels; streams run through it sounding the teaching, and music plays without any musician touching an instrument — Yijing's longer translation of 707 (T. 451) spells the geography out in loving detail. There is no trace of the lower destinies — no hells, no hungry ghosts, no animal births — and beings in difficulty who hear his name and remember it are, the sutra promises, rescued at the moment of death. Devotees who wish it may also choose rebirth in Amitābha's western paradise; the two buddhas are colleagues, not rivals.

If Amitābha's west is the sunset of this life's grief, Bhaiṣajyaguru's east is its remedy: a paradise designed like a hospital, staffed like a pharmacy.

lore.culturalLegacy: Yakushi-ji in Nara — UNESCO-listed, its East Pagoda a surviving seventh-century original — is his most famous monument, and the temple's Hossō-school triad became the template for a thousand Japanese healers' images; Shin Yakushi-ji, also in Nara, preserves the finest set of the twelve generals in clay, a designated National Treasure. In the modern West, 'the Medicine Buddha' has become a familiar presence: Birnbaum's The Healing Buddha (1979) introduced his cult to English readers, his image hangs in hospitals and hospices, and the dhāraṇī is chanted in meditation centers from Kyoto to California. The myrobalan in his bowl — harītakī, the 'remover of disease' — is still stocked in Ayurvedic pharmacies. His oldest promise, that no one should die for want of medicine, reads now like a plank of public health policy.
lore.archaeology: The iconographic record is rich and datable. Dunhuang's Mogao caves preserve Tang-dynasty wall paintings of the Bhaiṣajyaguru paradise — lapis ground, jewel cords, celestial musicians — among the most complete sutra illustrations surviving. In bronze, gilt-copper Yakushi triads of the Asuka and Hakuho periods mark the cult's arrival in Japan; the Yakushi-ji founding of 680 under Emperor Tenmu is documented in the Nihon Shoki, and the temple's excavated foundations and surviving East Pagoda anchor the tradition in seventh-century fact. Shin Yakushi-ji in Nara preserves its eighth-century Twelve Generals in near-original clay — the single most important sculptural set of the cult. Dedicatory inscriptions across northern China and the Korean peninsula record the sutra's recitation for named donors, giving the healing cult thousands of individual faces.
lore.syncretism: Every Buddhist culture adopted the Medicine Master and filed him differently. In China he heads the 'Three Saints of the East' with Sūryaprabha and Candraprabha, and his sutra joined the scriptures chanted for the dead and the dying in the standard funerary liturgy alongside the Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara texts. Japan made him one of the most-culted buddhas of all: Emperor Tenmu vowed a temple to Yakushi for his ailing empress in 680 — the temple is Nara's Yakushi-ji — and esoteric Buddhism paired him with Amida as healer of body and soul. Tibet received him as one of the Eight Medicine Buddhas, invoked against illness through the dhāraṇī Yijing translated. Korean Buddhism chants his name in the Yaksa-je rite still held for the sick. Across all of it, the constant is concrete: medicine for the body first, metaphysics second.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written in Devanāgarī as भैषज्यगुरु: bhaiṣajyaguru joins bhaiṣajya, 'medicine, healing' (from bhiṣaj, 'healer'), to guru, 'master, venerable teacher.' The retroflex ṣ — tongue-tip curled back — is a phoneme English lacks entirely, and the conjunct -jya- packs three letters into one syllable. Xuanzang rendered the full title 藥師琉璃光如來, 'Medicine Master, Lapis-Lazuli Light, Thus-Come-One'; Japanese monks compressed it to the two syllables Yakushi.

entries.meaning: Trembling pathway (from bifa, to shake, + rǫst, league)

steps: The name Bifrǫst is recorded in the Poetic and Prose Eddas in medieval Icelandic manuscripts.
Younger Futhark inscriptions do not preserve the name directly; the runic spelling is a scholarly reconstruction.
ᛒ = b, ᛁ = i, ᚠ = f, ᚱ = r, ᚬ = ǫ (rounded back vowel), ᛋ = s, ᛏ = t.
The Unicode restoration Bifrǫst preserves the normalized Norse spelling; the runic form is displayed as the original script.
provenanceSources: Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic

pronunciation.approximation: 'BIV-rost' — stress the first syllable; let the f pass as a soft breath between the lips, almost a 'v'; say the ǫ as a short, open 'aw' cut in half, not the long 'oh' of the English Bifrost.
pronunciation.note: Cleasby–Vigfusson (s.v. bifrǫst) glosses the name 'the trembling way,' from bifa 'to shake, tremble' and rǫst 'a league, a distance to be traversed'; Zoëga (s.v.) gives the same etymology and records the alternate name Ásbrú 'the Æsir-bridge.' The Eddic codex reads Bilrǫst, with bil 'moment, lapse of time,' and editors still debate which compound is original; Snorri's Bifrǫst is the form that prevailed. The o-ogonek ǫ is a distinctive atomic letter that the ASCII form loses, so the restoration is Tier 1 under the mechanical rule.

domains.title: Rainbow, Fire, Threshold
domains.subtitle: The domain of Bifrǫst
domains.lead:
In the norse tradition, Bifrǫst is the burning rainbow that joins Miðgarðr to Ásgarðr — the trembling path, from bifa 'to shake' and rǫst 'a league, a distance to be traversed.' The gods themselves call it Ásbrú, the Æsir-bridge, and ride it daily to hold court beneath Yggdrasill.

The name encodes a structure built to fail: strong beyond any other work, as Snorri insists, yet fated to shake, to burn, and at last to break beneath the sons of Muspell. Between its watchman's horn and its final shattering, the bridge is the measure of the distance between gods and everything else.

cards.name: The Trembling Way
cards.desc: From bifa 'to shake' and rǫst 'league, path': the bridge is a trembling span of three colors, made with more skill and cunning than any other structure.

cards.name: The Red Band of Fire
cards.desc: Snorri explains the red stripe as burning fire: the bridge is warded in flame so that frost-giants and mountain-giants cannot climb it into heaven.

cards.name: Heimdallr's Watch
cards.desc: At Himinbjǫrg, where the bridge reaches heaven's edge, Heimdallr keeps guard — hearing the grass grow, seeing a hundred leagues by night, holding the Gjallarhorn.

cards.name: The Breaking at Ragnarǫk
cards.desc: When the sons of Muspell ride over it toward the field of Vígríðr, the bridge shatters beneath them; the horses of the gods must swim the flood.

symbols.name: The red band
symbols.meaning: The stripe of burning fire within the rainbow that bars the giants from heaven

symbols.name: Gjallarhorn
symbols.meaning: Heimdallr's horn, kept at the bridge and winded to wake the gods at Ragnarǫk

symbols.name: Himinbjǫrg
symbols.meaning: 'Heaven's castle,' Heimdallr's hall at the bridge's head where it touches the sky

symbols.name: Urðr's well
symbols.meaning: The spring beneath Yggdrasil where the gods ride each day to sit in judgment

symbols.name: The horses of the Æsir
symbols.meaning: The steeds named in Grímnismál — Glad, Gyllir, Glær, Skeiðbrimir and the rest — that bear the gods over the burning span

mythology.lead: Bifrǫst is the one road between the worlds of gods and men, and every story told of it is a story about passage: who may cross, what the crossing costs, and what happens when the road itself gives way. Snorri describes it as the strongest of all constructions and yet builds its destruction into the end of the world. The poems of the Codex Regius, which read the name as Bilrǫst, already know that the bridge will break. Around it gather Heimdallr the watchman, the daily assize at Urðr's well, and the solitary figure of Þórr, who is forbidden the span and wades the rivers instead.

myths.title: The Bridge of Three Colors
myths.text:
Gangleri asks how the gods pass from heaven to earth, and Hárr answers that they built Bifrǫst from earth to heaven: a bridge of three colors, very strong, and made with more skill and cunning than any other work. The red in the rainbow, Hárr explains, is burning fire, so that the frost-giants and mountain-giants cannot mount into heaven over the bridge.

At the bridge's head, where it reaches the edge of heaven, stands Himinbjǫrg, the hall of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods. He needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues by night as by day, and hears the grass growing on the earth and the wool on the sheep. Beside him waits the Gjallarhorn, whose blast is heard in all worlds. The bridge is the strongest thing in the world, and it is guarded by the one god who never sleeps — the Edda's way of saying that the way between worlds is always open, and never safe.

myths.title: The Daily Ride to Judgment
myths.text:
Every day the Æsir ride up over Ásbrú — the Æsir-bridge — on their named horses, to sit in judgment at the ash Yggdrasill. But Þórr does not ride. Grímnismál says that he must wade the rivers Kǫrmt and Ǫrmt and the two Kerlaugar each day on his way to the doomstead, for the Æsir-bridge stands all aflame and the holy waters seethe.

Snorri gives the same exception a physical cause: the thunder-god's passage, with the heat and weight of his thunder, would break the span. The strongest of the gods is thus the one who walks — the bridge that carries everyone else cannot carry him. The daily wading is Þórr's liturgy: the god of the common people keeps both feet on the ground, even on his way to judgment.

lore.culturalLegacy: Wagner fixed the bridge in the modern imagination at the close of Das Rheingold: Donner's hammer summons the storm that clears the air, the rainbow appears, Froh names it as the way to the gods' new castle, and the gods process over it into Valhalla while Loge mutters that they are hastening toward their end — a reading of Bifrǫst's built-in doom that Snorri would have recognized. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century book illustration kept the burning arc as the standard emblem of the passage to Ásgarðr. Marvel's comics and films made Bifrost a household word, reimagining it as a wormhole guarded by Heimdall and gate-keeping travel between realms; games from God of War Ragnarök to Assassin's Creed Valhalla render it as the shimmering road between worlds. Modern heathen practice uses the rainbow bridge as a symbol of the live connection between Miðgarðr and the gods, while the unrelated 'Rainbow Bridge' poem of pet bereavement shows how far the idiom of the shining span has travelled from its Old Norse root. Restoring Bifrǫst in Unicode keeps the trembling in the name — the ASCII Bifrost has forgotten that the bridge shakes.
lore.archaeology: Bifrǫst is a textual figure with no known pictorial or runic attestation: no picture stone, amulet, or runestone names or unambiguously depicts the rainbow bridge, and the riders carved on stones such as Ardre VIII cannot be securely tied to it. Its transmission is manuscriptal. The mythological poems that preserve it — Grímnismál, Fáfnismál, Grípisspá, Lokasenna, Vafþrúðnismál — survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), which reads the name as Bilrǫst. Snorri's extended account in Gylfaginning survives in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, early fourteenth century), the Codex Wormianus (AM 242 fol.), the Codex Upsaliensis (DG 11), and the Codex Trajectinus (Traj 1374), whose divergences editors weigh stanza by stanza.
lore.syncretism: The burning rainbow has no attested continental Germanic counterpart — no Old English or Old High German source names the bridge, so Bifrǫst belongs to the Old Norse material alone, and any deeper common-Germanic pedigree is conjecture. Comparanda crowd around it nonetheless. In Greek tradition Iris is the rainbow made person, the messenger who moves between heaven and earth along the arc; in the Rig Veda the rainbow is Indra's bow (Indradhanush), a weapon hung in the sky; and the rainbow covenant of Genesis 9 was familiar to the Christian Icelanders who copied the Eddas, a juxtaposition that colors, though it does not explain, Snorri's red band of fire. In Finnic and Baltic folklore the Milky Way is a road of birds or souls, another shining path overhead. Later European folk belief kept the rainbow as a bridge and a boundary — the treasure at its foot, the impossibility of reaching its end — and modern popular culture, most openly Marvel's Einstein–Rosen 'Bifrost,' has translated the trembling way into a wormhole, which is the same intuition in newer physics: a bridge that burns, shakes, and cannot be trusted to hold.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is Old Norse Bifrǫst, transmitted in Latin-script codices; no runic inscription preserves it. In a normalized Younger Futhark rendering it would be written ᛒᛁᚠᚱᛅᛋᛏ, with ᛅ for the ǫ. The ǫ is the o-ogonek, the u-umlaut of a — a short open-mid vowel, written ö in Modern Icelandic — and it is the one distinctive feature the ASCII form destroys. The restored registrable form is bifrǫst.com (punycode xn--bifrst-zcc.com); the ASCII fallback bifrost.com flattens the trembling vowel into a plain 'o'.

entries.meaning: 'Cloth sack' (bù 'cloth' + dài 'sack'), the laughing, sack-carrying monk of the Chinese Buddhist tradition, identified as an incarnation of Maitreya.

etymology.derivation: Cái (財) 'wealth, riches'; Shén (神) 'god, spirit' — the popular deity of prosperity worshipped at New Year.

pronunciation.approximation: 'CAISHEN' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.
pronunciation.note: Cáishén is Tier 1 because the name is natively written in Chinese characters (財神) — a script with no ASCII equivalent — and the tone-marked pinyin preserves the pronunciation that plain romanization flattens.

domains.title: Wealth
domains.subtitle: Wealth, Prosperity, New Year
domains.lead: Cáishén (財神, 'God of Wealth') is less a single god than an office, filled across the centuries by a canonized marshal, a heartless minister, and an honest merchant. He presides over trade, treasure, and the New Year, when every household races to be the first to welcome him.

cards.name: Marshal Zhao
cards.desc: Zhao Gongming: black tiger, iron whip, gold ingot — the Martial God of Wealth canonized in the Fengshen Yanyi.

cards.name: The Civil God
cards.desc: Bi Gan, the Shang minister whose heart King Zhou cut out; without a heart, he cannot be greedy, so merchants trust him.

cards.name: Welcoming the God
cards.desc: On the fifth day of the New Year, businesses reopen with firecrackers to be first to receive him.

cards.name: The Five Paths
cards.desc: Worshipped in sets of five — the Five Gods of Wealth, bringing fortune from every direction of the compass.

symbols.name: The gold ingot (yuanbao)
symbols.meaning: The boat-shaped silver-gold ingot held by every avatar of Cáishén — wealth made visible and graspable.

symbols.name: The black tiger
symbols.meaning: Marshal Zhao's mount; the tiger that can carry wealth away as easily as it brings it.

symbols.name: The iron whip
symbols.meaning: Zhao Gongming's weapon, disciplining the pursuit of riches — wealth taken unjustly is wealth reclaimed.

symbols.name: The ruyi scepter
symbols.meaning: 'As you wish' — the wish-granting wand of the Civil God of Wealth.

symbols.name: The account book
symbols.meaning: The ledger in which the god's office records each household's fortune for the coming year.

symbols.name: The Five Paths
symbols.meaning: Five directional gods of wealth — east, south, west, north, and center — for fortune has a road from every quarter.

mythology.lead: Cáishén's mythology is young and openly composite. The cult is a Song-dynasty growth over older roots, and every avatar brings his own story: a Ming novel supplies the marshal, a Han historian the heartless minister, merchants the retired sage. The tradition never pretends otherwise — and its honesty is part of its power.

myths.title: One Office, Many Gods
myths.text: The two characters 財神 simply mean 'god of wealth' — a title, not a personal name, and the tradition treats it that way. There is no canonical birth-story of Cáishén; instead, the office has been filled, again and again, by figures the culture wished to honor: a loyal minister, a canonized marshal, an honest merchant, even the red-faced war-god Guan Yu in some regions.
