The clearest early attestations belong to the Song dynasty (960–1279), when China's commercial revolution made wealth a god worth petitioning; the Ming-era compendium Santjiao soushen daquan and the novel Fengshen Yanyi then fixed the cast of avatars. The sources disagree openly about who 'really' holds the office — which is the honest thing for a god of fortune, since every trade, region, and dynasty wants to claim him. A god with many faces is a god owned by many classes; Cáishén's multiplicity is the theology of a civilization that decided prosperity itself was divine.

myths.title: Zhao Gongming on the Black Tiger
myths.text: The fullest avatar-story comes from the Ming novel Fengshen Yanyi (Investiture of the Gods). During the fall of the Shang dynasty, Zhao Gongming, a hermit of Mount Emei, comes down to aid the doomed house with his black tiger, his iron whip, and his magic pearls; battle after battle turns on his power, until Jiang Ziya's side breaks him with Lu Ya's sorcery — an effigy of straw pierced by arrows. When the war ends and the fallen are canonized, Jiang Ziya invests the dead marshal as the God of Wealth, true lord of the dragon-tiger altar, mounted on his tiger, whip in hand, gold ingot ready — with four assistant deities who manage the welcoming of treasure, the gathering of valuables, the inviting of wealth, and the profiting of markets. The novel turns fortune into a bureaucracy: wealth flows not from luck but from an office, staffed, audited, and answerable — a very Chinese answer to the oldest of prayers.

lore.culturalLegacy: At Lunar New Year, Cáishén is the busiest god alive. The fifth-day welcome, the firecrackers, the reopened shops, the paper icons, and the greeting Gong Xi Fa Cai — 'wishing you prosperity' — all run on his calendar, from Harbin to Singapore to San Francisco. Hong Kong's markets watch the god's day; diaspora restaurants keep his altar by the register, oranges and gold ingots before the red-faced image. The digital age has not displaced him but multiplied his mediums: apps send red envelopes, and his portrait rides phone wallpapers through the New Year. A god minted by Song-dynasty commerce now banks the hopes of two billion people a year — the largest recurring act of popular worship on earth.
lore.archaeology: The material record of Cáishén is popular, mass-produced, and deliberately ephemeral — which is itself testimony. Late-imperial woodblock New Year prints (nianhua) from Yangliuqing (Tianjin), Taohuawu (Suzhou), and Mianzhu (Sichuan) turned out hundreds of thousands of red-and-gold god-images each winter, to be pasted above doorways and burned in the fourth-night send-off. The Yuan–Ming god-compendium Santjiao soushen daquan reached households in cheap woodblock editions that carried the mythology to the non-literate. Wealth-god shrines stand in guild halls and temples across the Sinosphere, usually flanked by his assistants with the tiger at his feet; paper and porcelain icons still sit on shop altars everywhere, replaced annually — wealth itself made a renewable rite.
lore.syncretism: Cáishén was assembled by borrowing. The novel's machinery of canonization is Daoist — Jiang Ziya's investiture lists are pure Daoist pantheon-building, and temple practice couches the god in Daoist liturgy. From Buddhism came wealth-deities the Tang already naturalized: Vaiśravaṇa (Bishamonten), the northern king and treasure-guardian, and Jambhala in the Tibetan and Mongolian lands. The closest foreign counterpart is Japan's Daikokuten — Mahākāla turned money-god, often fused with Ōkuninushi — one of the Seven Gods of Fortune. Vietnam keeps Thần Tài beside the earth-god Ông Địa on every family altar, and Hong Kong's banks host the lion dance at New Year. Across the Sinosphere, wealth was the one god every household kept — and each culture built its own face for him.

entries.meaning: The Roman god of desire, son of Venus; from cupīdō, 'desire, longing, passion' (epigraphic CVPIDO)
'Hard to Conquer in Battle' (dur- 'hard' + yodhana 'fighting') — the eldest Kaurava, rival of the Pāṇḍavas whose refusal to yield their share of the kingdom brings about the Kurukṣetra war

steps: Sanskrit Duryodhana is written in Devanagari as दुर्योधन
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

etymology.derivation: Possibly related to Greek ἑλένη 'torch'; the name of Helen of Troy, whose abduction launched the Trojan War.

pronunciation.approximation: 'heh-LEH-nay' — three syllables, the high note on the middle, and the final vowel long; nothing like the two-beat English 'HEH-len.'
pronunciation.note: Helénē is Tier 1: the Greek Ἑλένη carries both the acute accent on the penult and the long eta of the final syllable — two features the ASCII 'helene' flattens. She is among the most storied mortals in the catalog: daughter of Zeús, queen of Sparta, and the woman for whom Troy burned.

domains.title: Beauty
domains.subtitle: Beauty, Sparta, Troy
domains.lead: Helénē is the daughter of Zeús whose face became the standard of beauty and the cause of the Trojan War — queen of Sparta, woman of Troy, and the most discussed mortal in Greek literature. Around her the Greeks wound every question they had about beauty, desire, blame, and whether a woman can ever be only a prize.

cards.name: Beauty
cards.desc: Iliad 3.156-158: even the Trojan elders on the wall murmur that 'no wonder' men fight for her — beauty made measurable in armies.

cards.name: Daughter of Zeús
cards.desc: Born of Zeus in the shape of a swan and Leda of Sparta; sister of the Dioscuri and of Clytemnestra, twin in blood if not in fate.

cards.name: Queen of Sparta
cards.desc: Wife of Menelaus; her palace at Sparta, with its silver bathtub and chamber of perfumes, is described in Odyssey 4.

cards.name: Helen of Troy
cards.desc: Ten years inside Priam's walls, weaving the war into cloth — the face for which a thousand ships became proverb already to Marlowe.

symbols.name: The Swan
symbols.meaning: Zeus came to Leda in the shape of a swan; beauty enters the world disguised, and the disguise is never entirely lifted.

symbols.name: Leda's Egg
symbols.meaning: Helen was hatched, not born — found in an egg beside the Eurōtas, in the account of the Catalogue of Women; beauty as something that must be broken open.

symbols.name: The Golden Apple
symbols.meaning: 'For the fairest' — the apple that made beauty contestable and therefore catastrophic; her prize and her sentence.

symbols.name: The Loom
symbols.meaning: In Troy she weaves the battles of the war into a purple web (Iliad 3.125-128): the woman's work that archives what men die for.

symbols.name: The Phantom (Eidôlon)
symbols.meaning: Stesichorus' double: 'that story is not true — you never went in the benched ships'; doubt about her guilt made into a second Helen.

symbols.name: The Tree
symbols.meaning: Helen Dendritis, 'Helen of the Tree,' received a tree-cult at Rhodes (Pausanias 3.19.10) — the goddess glimmering through the woman.

mythology.lead: Helénē's story is told by Homer, Hesiod, Stesichorus, Euripides, and Herodotus — and the tradition argues with itself at every turn: abduction or seduction, guilt or phantom, goddess or woman. She is the most examined face in Greek myth.

myths.title: Leda and the Swan
myths.text: Zeus desired Leda, the wife of King Tyndareus of Sparta, and came to her in the shape of a swan — fleeing, in the usual telling, an eagle's pursuit, so that the queen received the god under her wing. From her egg, and from a second egg, came the mixed brood of the house of Tyndareus: Helénē and her sister Clytemnestra, and the twins Kastor and Polydeukes, the Dioscuri — only some of them children of Zeus, the tradition says, though which is disputed. The earliest witness is Hesiod's Catalogue of Women (fr. 23a M-W), and Euripides opens his Helen with Leda finding the egg and hatching the child within. Aeschylus' Agamemnon (1455ff.) remembers the swan as a bird that sang for its death. The myth gives Helen a double nature from the first breath: born of a god's disguise and a mortal's bed, sister of the saviors of sailors and of the woman who would murder a king. Beauty, the story says, is never simply born — it arrives already entangled with power.

myths.title: The Oath of Tyndareus
myths.text: So renowned was Helen's beauty that suitors came to Sparta from every Greek land — and so dangerous was their number that King Tyndareus feared bloodshed whoever won. Odysseus, himself a suitor in some tellings but wise beyond courtship, proposed the oath that bears the king's name: each suitor swore to defend the marriage-rights of the chosen man, with arms if necessary. Then Helen chose Menelaus, brother of Agamemnon, and the oath bound all of Greece to her marriage. The story is preserved in Hesiod's Catalogue (fr. 198 M-W) and in the Cypria tradition; Homer has Helen on the walls of Troy look down at the Achaean champions and ask, without irony, whom they have left at home for her sake (Iliad 3.205-224). The oath converts a wedding into a treaty — and a treaty, as the next generation would learn, is only a war waiting for its pretext.

lore.culturalLegacy: No woman of myth has been more named, blamed, or measured. 'Helen of Troy' entered every European language as shorthand for beauty that moves armies; Marlowe's 'thousand ships' made her face a unit of rhetorical currency, and to be 'a Helen' is still to be dangerously beautiful. Her name never left use — Helena, Elena, Helen remain among the most widespread given names in Christendom, from St. Helen, mother of Constantine, to innumerable Helens since. In Sparta the memory is local and warm: the Menelaion site at Therapne still carries her, and modern Greece sells 'Helen's Troy' from Mycenae to Hisarlik. Scholarship keeps re-telling her, from Homeric analysts to feminist readings that relocate the blame from Helen to the oath of the men who made her a casus belli. And the idiom endures in reverse, too — to call a conflict 'a Helen' is to admit it was fought over something not quite real.
lore.archaeology: The cult at Therapne is archaeologically secure: excavations at the Menelaion (first by the British School in 1900, decisively by H. W. Catling in the 1970s) uncovered a Mycenaean mansion beneath the Archaic-Classical shrine, with votive offerings — bronze and terracotta figurines, plaques, jewelry — addressed to Menelaus and Helen from the seventh century BCE onward, confirming the paired heroön Isocrates and Pausanias describe. The Rhodian cult of Helen Dendritis is attested textually rather than excavated. In art, Attic vase-painters of the late sixth and fifth centuries BCE made the recovery-scene a favorite: Menelaus dropping his sword at the sight of Helen among Troy's ruins (the circle of the so-called Menelaus Painter). Her 'Troy' itself — Hisarlik, excavated by Schliemann and Blegen — supplies the landscape of the legend, whatever one thinks of its historicity; the burned layers of Troy VIIa remain the war's only possible material witness.
lore.syncretism: Behind the heroine a goddess keeps glimmering. At Therapne above the Eurōtas, Helen was worshipped beside Menelaus in a heroön — the dead honored as divine — which Isocrates (10.63) cites and Pausanias (3.15.3, 19.9) describes; Alcman already sang her as a power of Laconia. At Rhodes she was Helen Dendritis, 'Helen of the Tree,' hung in effigy, in one grim version, by the Rhodian women whose husbands she had cost (Pausanias 3.19.10). On this evidence twentieth-century scholarship proposed that a vegetation or light divinity lay behind the Homeric woman, the torch etymology her surviving trace. The Rome-ward path was quieter: Ovid stages the lovers' correspondence in Heroides 16-17, and Helen survives euhemerized as every era's emblem of fatal beauty — in Marlowe's Faustus ('Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?'), in Goethe's Faust II, where the Helena-act descends into classical Walpurgisnight, and in Rossetti's 'Helen of Troy,' who holds the apple and knows exactly what it cost.

pronunciation.approximation: ee-fee-GEH-neh-ee-ah — five syllables, the classical p aspirated, the g hard as in 'go'; the Greek acute falls on GE.
pronunciation.note: Iphigéneia is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the acute accent preserves the inherited Greek stress, but every vowel in Ἰφιγένεια is short — the antepenult accent itself proves the ultima is light. Nothing further distinguishes the name from its ASCII form.

domains.title: Iphigeneia
domains.subtitle: Sacrifice
domains.lead: Iphigéneia is sacrifice, winds, aulis. The name means "Mighty-born" — ἶφι, "by might," joined to γένος, "birth, race" — and hers is the Greek tradition's most searching account of what the Trojan War cost before it ever reached Troy.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The restoration Iphigéneia returns the acute of Ἰφιγένεια and the name's full weight: "Mighty-born," the girl who carried her fate in her name.

cards.name: Sacrifice
cards.desc: Summoned to Aulis on the pretext of marriage to Achilles, she became the price of the wind that would carry a thousand ships to Troy (Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis).

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Priestess of Artemis among the Taurians, then guardian of girls' passage at Brauron, where Athens showed her tomb (Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris; Pausanias 1.33.1).

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

symbols.name: The saffron robe
symbols.meaning: The garment that poured to the ground at the altar (Aeschylus, Agamemnon 239) — maidenhood offered up in fabric.

symbols.name: The deer
symbols.meaning: The substitute Artemis set on the altar in the Cypria's version — the rescue the epic grants her, taken back as suddenly as given.

symbols.name: The letter
symbols.meaning: The written word that reunited her with Orestes in the Tauris — recognition carried by text, not tokens or scars.

symbols.name: The bear (arktos)
symbols.meaning: The little girls who served Artemis Brauronia before marriage — Iphigéneia's Athenian afterlife as guardian of the passage she never lived.

symbols.name: The becalmed sea
symbols.meaning: Aulis's windless harbor — the fleet's stillness ended only at her altar.

mythology.lead: Iphigéneia's story is the price of the Trojan War paid in advance: the maiden summoned to Aulis as a bride, lifted over her father's altar as the fleet's ransom, and — in the tellings that spare her — swept to the far shore of the Black Sea, where the gods set her a second altar and made her its keeper.

myths.title: The Fleet That Would Not Sail
myths.text:
The Cypria, the lost epic of the war's beginnings, told it first: the Greek fleet gathers at Aulis and the winds die. Agamemnon has angered Artemis — in the epic's account by killing a stag in the goddess's grove and boasting he could outshoot her. The seer Kalkhas announces the price: the fleet will sail only when the king gives his daughter Iphigéneia to the goddess. Aeschylus compresses the whole unbearable machinery into the parodos of the Agamemnon (104–257): the portent of two eagles tearing a hare — 'sacrifice a suffering thing' — and the elder king, 'clothed in ruinous frenzy', willing the act with 'a wretched holiness'.

What the tradition insists on is not the savagery but the logic: the war against Troy begins by consuming the Greeks' own, at home, before a single ship clears the harbor. Ten years of foreign slaughter are inaugurated by one deliberate domestic one.

myths.title: The Deer on the Altar
myths.text:
Aeschylus stages what the epic only reported, and makes it the most harrowing scene in surviving Greek poetry (Agamemnon 228–247): the girl, 'gagged like a goat', lifted over the altar by her father's men; 'her saffron robe pouring to the ground'; one glance, one cry for her brother — and her father, 'after that decision, willed it', 'and so the ships sailed'. The Cypria softened the blow for its audiences: Artemis snatched the maiden from the altar, set a deer in her place, and carried Iphigéneia to the land of the Taurians, where she made her immortal.

Euripides, in Iphigenia at Aulis, splits the difference and finds the truth inside the contradiction: his Iphigéneia arrives deceived — promised to Achilles — and then, at the last, chooses the sacrifice herself, declaring her death shall be Greece's freedom. The tradition never lets us settle whether she was murdered, rescued, or volunteered; the ambiguity is the point, because all three answers say the same thing about war's arithmetic.

lore.culturalLegacy: Iphigéneia's afterlife is a one-woman argument across Western art. Euripides left a matched pair — the Iphigenia at Aulis, where she consents to die, and the Iphigenia in Tauris, where she refuses to kill — and every age has staged the two against each other. Racine's Iphigénie (1674) made her the tragedy of state reason; Gluck's operas Iphigénie en Aulide (1774) and en Tauride (1779) gave her the century's most humane music; Goethe's Iphigenie auf Tauris (1787) rewrote the escape as the triumph of pure humanity over custom — 'when humans help themselves, the gods are well disposed.' Her name survives in scholarship as the archetype of the sacrificed child, invoked wherever a society's great project demands a small victim. The cult memory is real too: Brauron's sanctuary still stands, and the arkteia it served remains a cornerstone of what we know about Greek girls' lives.
lore.archaeology: The material record belongs to her cult, not her story. The sanctuary of Artemis at Brauron in eastern Attica, excavated by the Athens Archaeological Society from 1948 onward under Ioanna Papadimitriou, preserves the stoa and spring-house where the young arktoi served, along with vast deposits of votive offerings — miniature vessels, jewelry, and the garments dedicated by girls completing their service. Pausanias (1.33.1) saw Iphigéneia's tomb there and the clothes of women dead in childbirth dedicated at her shrine; Megara showed a rival tomb (1.43.1). At Aulis, excavation has identified the Classical temple terrace traditionally linked to the fleet's gathering, and at Chersonesos Taurica in Crimea the Greek city's remains long carried the later identification with her Taurian prison.
lore.syncretism: Greek tradition quietly merged two figures: the Iliad (9.145, 287) knows Agamemnon's daughter only as Iphianassa, and the cyclic tradition's Iphigéneia was long read as the same girl under an older name. Antoninus Liberalis (27), following Nikander, reports her final promotion: Artemis made her immortal as Hekátē — a striking equation, since both receive offerings at liminal places and both govern the marginal. Roman poets kept the Aulis scene central: Lucretius (De Rerum Natura 1.84–101) names her 'the maiden of Trivia' and sets the sacrificial fillet among religion's cruelties, while Ovid (Metamorphoses 12.24–38) repeats the stag substitution in his roll-call of the war's causes. Later antiquity fixed her geography, identifying the Taurian temple with the Chersonesos in Crimea — the identification still printed beside maps of the myth.

entries.meaning: Moon (the personified moon, brother of Sól)

steps: Máni is the personified moon in Norse mythology, brother of Sól.
The runic spelling ᛘᛅᚾᛁ is a normalized scholarly reconstruction; no direct runic inscription of the name is known.
ᛘ = m, ᛅ = á (long a), ᚾ = n, ᛁ = i.
provenanceSources: Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic

pronunciation.approximation: 'MAH-nee' — hold the first vowel long and open, as in 'father', with the weight squarely on the first syllable and a quick, light '-nee' to close.
pronunciation.note: Máni is Tier 1: the acute on á marks the long vowel [ɑː], a distinctive feature the ASCII form Mani loses; Old Norse initial stress is the default and needs no further mark. The name is simply the common noun máni, 'moon', raised to a person — the same word that gives mánaðr, 'month'. Attestation and reconstruction follow Cleasby & Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary (1874), s.v. máni; and Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (1910), s.v. máni.

domains.title: Moon, Night, Time
domains.subtitle: The domain of Máni
domains.lead: In the Norse tradition, Máni is the moon itself made personal — the shining body that crosses the night sky, imagined as a god who steers it. Where Sól, his sister, drives the sun, Máni governs the gentler light: Snorri says he 'steers the course of the moon and rules the new and the waning moons,' the phases by which men first learned to count their days. Every month that turns is his signature: mánaðr, 'month', is his own word, and Monday is his day.

cards.name: Mundilfari's Boast
cards.desc: A father's pride named his children Moon and Sun; the gods answered the boast by setting the pair to drive the lights of heaven.

cards.name: Hati's Pursuit
cards.desc: The wolf Hati Hróðvitnisson runs before the moon and will one day take it; at Ragnarǫk the Moon-Hound swallows the light and spatters the sky with blood.

cards.name: Bil and Hjúki
cards.desc: Two children with a pail on a pole, taken up from the well Byrgir; they follow Máni, Snorri says, 'as can be seen from earth' — the man in the moon.

cards.name: Measurer of Months
cards.desc: He rules the new and waning moons, the counting of time itself; mánaðr, 'month', is his word, and the calendar was his first temple.

symbols.name: Ný ok nið (new and waning moons)
symbols.meaning: The phases over which Máni rules, the divine charge by which the gods ordained the counting of years for men

symbols.name: Hati Hróðvitnisson
symbols.meaning: The wolf who runs before the moon and gives its crossing its haste, the promise that even the lights of heaven are hunted

symbols.name: Mánagarmr (Moon-Hound)
symbols.meaning: The mightiest of the Iron-Wood brood, who fattens on the lives of the dying and swallows the moon at the world's end

symbols.name: Sægr and Simul (pail and pole)
symbols.meaning: The burden Bil and Hjúki carried from the well Byrgir, still legible as the markings on the moon's face

symbols.name: The month-mark
symbols.meaning: Mánaðr, the month — the unit of time that bears his name in every Germanic calendar

mythology.lead: Máni's mythology is brief but exact: he has no hammer-duels and no disguises, only a course to keep and a hunter behind him. The Eddas give him four scenes — a father's fatal boast, the breeding of the wolf that hunts him, two children lifted from a well, and the swallowing that ends the sky — and together they explain both why the moon moves and why it keeps its human face.

myths.title: Mundilfari's Boast
myths.text:
In the Vafþrúðnismál, the giant Vafþrúðnir tells Óðinn that Mundilfari is the father of Máni and of Sól alike. Snorri, in Gylfaginning (ch. 11), gives the story its edge: Mundilfari's two children were so fair that he named his son Máni, 'Moon', and his daughter Sól, 'Sun', and married Sól to a man named Glenr. The gods were angered by this ofdramb — this overweening pride — and took the siblings and set them in the heavens.

The punishment is an appointment. Sól is made to drive the horses of the sun, Árvakr and Alsviðr, while Máni is charged with steering the course of the moon and ruling its waxing and waning. What a father claimed in arrogance, the gods confirmed in office: the names became the duties, and the children became the sky. The myth is the Eddas' quiet essay on vanity — the one boast the gods could not leave unpunished was a claim of ownership over light.

myths.title: The Iron-Wood Brood
myths.text: Why does the moon flee? Because something was bred to chase it. Snorri preserves the genealogy (Gylfaginning, ch. 12): east of Midgard, in the forest called Járnviðr — Iron Wood — a giantess in troll-woman's shape bore a brood of giant sons in wolf forms, and from that pack come the wolves that hunt the lights. Two of them the Æsir caught and set to their courses: Skǫll runs after the sun, and Hati Hróðvitnisson runs before the moon, and he will catch it — so it must be. The Grímnismál names them in verse: Skǫll follows the shining god, while Hati, Hróðvitnir's son, runs before the bright bride of heaven (st. 39). And the brood is not finished: from the same Iron Wood, Snorri says, will come the mightiest of all, Mánagarmr, the Moon-Hound, who feeds on the lives of the dead; the Vǫluspá laments the coming tormentor in a troll's shape (st. 40). The myth makes the night sky a battlefield of kinship: the lights of heaven are pursued by the children of the giantess, and Máni's speed is the speed of survival.

lore.culturalLegacy: Máni's deepest legacy is calendrical: every month and every Monday in the Germanic-speaking world is his, for Mōnandæg and its Norse kin are simply the moon's day, and the words descend from his name. In literature his clearest heir is Tolkien's Tilion, the Maia who steers the vessel of the moon across the sky — the personified moon-driver of the Eddas translated into a new mythology. Notably, Wagner left him out: the Ring runs on gold, fire, and Wotan's will, and the moon-driver never steps onto that stage, a measure of how thin Máni's high-cultural afterlife is beside Þórr's or Óðinn's. The chase around him fares better: the pursuing wolves Skǫll and Hati stalk recent retellings, including God of War Ragnarök (2022), where the stolen moon and its hunters drive a whole arc of the story. And the oldest survival is still the most democratic — the face and figures people point out to children in the full moon, which Snorri already explained by Bil and Hjúki eight centuries ago. In modern heathenry Máni is honored quietly, at the turning of the months he still measures.
lore.archaeology: Máni has no secure iconography: no picture stone, runestone, or amulet has been convincingly identified as his image, and his attestation is essentially textual. The Poetic Edda poems that name him — Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál, and Vǫluspá — survive chiefly in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), with Vǫluspá also in the Hauksbók; Snorri's account in Gylfaginning is transmitted by the main Snorra Edda manuscripts. The older strata of Scandinavian sky-religion are, however, material: the Bronze Age Trundholm sun chariot (c. 1400 BC) proves a native tradition of a heavenly body drawn by horse across the sky, and wheel- and disc-marked Gotland picture stones show the sun and moon as enduring cultic signs. The runic record knows the common noun máni and the month-names descended from it, but no runic inscription names the god directly.
lore.syncretism: Máni belongs to the common Germanic inheritance in which the moon is grammatically and mythologically masculine — Old English Mōna, Old High German Māno, Gothic mēna — a striking counterweight to the feminine moons of the classical world, Greek Selēnē and Latin Luna. The word itself runs deeper: Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁nōt- / *mḗh₁n̥s meant both 'moon' and 'month', the double sense Máni still carries in mánaðr, so that his personification is the personification of time-reckoning itself. The pairing of a moon-god with a sun-goddess, brother and sister, is the Germanic reversal of the Greek Selene and Helios pattern, though the daily celestial chase — light pursued by devourer — has echoes from the wolves of Ragnarǫk back to the eclipse-monsters of other traditions. The liveliest survival is folkloric: the Norse reading of the moon's markings as two children with a pail stands at the head of the whole northern 'man in the moon' tradition that later fills English ballads and nursery rhymes, and the tempting equation of Hjúki and Bil with Jack and Jill has been argued since the nineteenth century — as speculation, never as proof.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Old Norse form is máni, the ordinary common noun 'moon' borne as a theonym, attested throughout the manuscript tradition of both Eddas. In the earlier epigraphic medium, the Younger Futhark, the name would be rendered approximately ᛘᛅᚾᛁ — the long á written with the ᛅ (óss) rune, the Younger Futhark's sign for the a-family vowels, nasalized and long alike; no runic inscription preserves the theonym itself. In the normalized Old Norse spelling the acute on á marks vowel length, [ɑː], the same long vowel heard in 'father'. The PUNICODEX registrable form Máni preserves that acute as a Tier-1 restoration — the single distinctive feature the ASCII form Mani loses — carrying the long vowel that links the god directly to mánaðr, the month he measures.

entries.meaning: The Roman god of war and guardian of agriculture, father of Rōmulus and Rēmus; namesake of the planet Mars and the month of March (epigraphic MARS)
'The intoxicating one' (Old Irish medb, cognate with 'mead'), Queen of Connacht who drives the cattle raid of the Táin Bó Cúailnge.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MYETHV' — one short syllable: slender m, brief e, the d melted into the soft 'th' of 'this', finishing on 'v'. The modern Irish Meadhbh, anglicized Maeve, has collapsed the middle consonant and sounds simply 'mayv'.
pronunciation.note: Medb is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: normalized Old Irish writes the name in plain Latin letters — no diacritic and no distinctive letter for ASCII to lose. The temple form differs from the lowercase entry only by the capital; the queen's standing in the tradition is beside the point. The etymology, by contrast, is one of the most secure in the Celtic corpus: Old Irish medb, 'intoxicating, she who intoxicates', cognate with the noun medb, 'mead', continuing Proto-Indo-European *médhu, 'sweet drink'. The name is the sovereignty drink made personal.

domains.title: The Queen Who Chooses
domains.subtitle: The Pillow-Talk, the Bride-Gift Speech, and the Cattle Raid of Cooley
domains.lead: Medb of Crúachan is the ruling queen of Connacht and the driving will of the Táin Bó Cúailnge: the woman who audited fortunes with her husband in the night and invaded Ulster in the morning, who set the terms of her own marriages — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear — and whom scholarship reads as Ireland's clearest survival of the sovereignty goddess, the land's own power to make and unmake kings.

cards.name: The Pillow-Talk
cards.desc: The night audit at Crúachan: Medb and Ailill count their wealth and find themselves equal in everything — save one bull.

cards.name: The Two Bulls
cards.desc: Finnbennach the White-Horned, who scorned a woman's keeping, and the Donn of Cúailnge — the balance of power on four legs.

cards.name: The Bride-Gift Terms
cards.desc: A husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear — the bride-gift no woman before her had asked of a man of Ireland.

cards.name: Crúachan and Oweynagat
cards.desc: Her royal rath at Rathcroghan, and beneath it the Cave of the Cats — the gate of the Otherworld in the medieval tales.

symbols.name: The marriage-bed of Crúachan
symbols.meaning: The pillow-talk itself: sovereignty as an audit — equality counted coin for coin in the dark

symbols.name: The two bulls
symbols.meaning: Finnbennach and the Donn of Cúailnge: wealth, prestige, and the one point on which two rulers cannot be equal

symbols.name: The bride-gift terms
symbols.meaning: No meanness, no jealousy, no fear: the queen's own charter, demanded where a dowry was expected

symbols.name: The march of the four provinces
symbols.meaning: The raid she willed into being: armies moved by a single insistence that the account be balanced

symbols.name: Oweynagat, the Cave of the Cats
symbols.meaning: The Otherworld gate beneath her rath — the source in the tales of the things that come up on Samain night

mythology.lead: Medb's dossier is the Táin Bó Cúailnge, the longest and greatest tale of the Ulster Cycle — and unlike every other great name in Irish myth, she is not a goddess remembered as a woman but a queen the tradition may once have worshipped as a goddess. The tale itself never says which.

myths.title: The Pillow-Talk
myths.text:
One night at Crúachan, when the royal bed had been made for Medb and Ailill, they fell into a 'bolster-conversation' — comrac chind cherchailli — and Ailill boasted that the woman married to a wealthy man is well off. Medb answered that she was well off before him: daughter of Eochu Feidlech, high king of Ireland, and the wealthier of the two. To settle it they had every treasure counted — cups, rings, cattle, sheep, horses — and the tally came out exactly even, save one item: the great bull Finnbennach, born in Medb's herd, had scorned to be counted a woman's chattel and walked over into Ailill's, where he stood as the White-Horned of Connacht.

That one beast broke the equality Medb would not live without. Her steward Mac Roth found the match: the Donn of Cúailnge, the Brown Bull of Cooley, kept by Dáire mac Fiachna in Ulster. Medb sent for a year's loan of him at princely terms — fifty heifers a year, a stretch of the plain of Aí, her own chariot, and the friendship of her thighs — and Dáire agreed. But the messengers drank and boasted that had the loan been refused they would have taken the bull by force, and Dáire swore that only by force would he ever be taken. The embassy came home empty, and Medb resolved on war.

myths.title: The Bride-Gift Speech
myths.text:
The Táin lets Medb state her own terms, and the speech is the charter of her queenship. Daughter of the high king, wooed by the kings of Ireland, she refused them all, she says, 'for I asked a strange bride-gift such as no woman before me had asked of a man of the men of Ireland — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear.' If he were mean, their wealth could not sit together, for she is generous in gifts; if jealous, she could not live beside him, 'for I was never without one man in the shadow of another'; if fearful, he would shame her in the front of every fight.

Such a man she found in Ailill mac Máta: no meanness, no jealousy, no fear. She brought him the bride-gift — the clothing of twelve men, a chariot worth thrice seven cumals, the width of his face in red gold, the weight of his left forearm in bronze — and it is into her province, not his, that he came. The Táin is blunt about the arithmetic: he is king of Connacht because he is married to Medb of Crúachan.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Táin's modern reception made Medb the most argued-over woman in Irish literature. Lady Gregory's Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) carried the epic into English; Thomas Kinsella's translation (1969), with Louis le Brocquy's ink drawings, fixed the Táin as the Irish national epic for the modern reader — and Medb at its centre as its engine, not its ornament. Scholarship split over her nature: Mac Cana read her as the sovereignty goddess of Connacht demoted to a queen, the standing type-case of the king-and-goddess theme; more skeptical voices, notably J. P. Mallory's, have tested the Táin against the Iron Age record and found a tale shaped by its medieval tellers rather than a window on the pagan past. Popular culture settled the argument in its own way: the Anglicized Maeve has become one of the most fashionable Irish girls' names in the English-speaking world, and 'Queen Maeve' — the woman who wrote her own terms, chose her own husbands, and out-argued every man in the tale — stands as a feminist icon far beyond the universities. The cairn on Knocknarea that folklore calls her grave draws climbers every summer; the visitor centre at Rathcroghan interprets her rath; and in Irish itself Meadhbh never left: the living name has meant the same ungovernable queen for twelve hundred years of the written language.
lore.archaeology: Medb's mythic address is the best-documented royal landscape in Ireland: Crúachan Aí, the Rathcroghan complex in County Roscommon, a five-kilometre spread of more than two hundred and forty recorded monuments — ring-barrows, mounds, and enclosures — dominated by the great flat-topped Rathcroghan Mound itself. Beneath the complex opens Oweynagat, the Cave of the Cats, the souterrain-fed natural cave the medieval tales call a gate of the Otherworld; within it stand two ogham stones, one reading VRAICCI MAQI MEDVVI, '(the stone of) Fráech, son of Medb' — the name-type's only epigraphic attestation, at the site the tradition assigns to the queen herself. Her death-place, Inis Cloithrinn (Inchcleraun), survives as the largest island of Lough Ree on the Shannon, crowned by the early monastic ruins of Templemurray; her reputed grave is the great unexcavated Neolithic cairn (c. 3200 BCE) on the summit of Knocknarea above Sligo — Miosgán Meadhbha, 'Medb's heap', which local tradition insists she fills standing upright, spear in hand, facing Ulster. The textual witnesses are exact: the oldest substantially complete Táin (Recension I) is in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow, written at Clonmacnoise around 1106, and the fullest recension in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster; O'Rahilly's editions are the modern bases. J. P. Mallory's In Search of the Irish Dreamtime (2016) is the standard archaeological cross-examination of the whole epic.
lore.syncretism: The Welsh corpus preserves no Medb — but it preserves her word: Welsh meddw, 'drunk', is the same adjective, and the Mabinogi gives the Brythonic side of the theme she embodies: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] arriving as a mounted marvel no rider can catch, and the footholder Goewin whose office is bound to Math's life, are the Welsh faces of the kingship-and-goddess complex that Mac Cana traced through Irish literature. Medb's deepest kin are lexical and ritual at once. Her name is the same word as the drink by which kings were made: the Irish inauguration knew the banais ríghe, the 'wedding-feast of kingship', in which the goddess of the territory offered the king the cup — or the bed — and scholars since Mac Cana's foundational study of king and goddess have read Medb of Crúachan as that figure euhemerized into a queen. The tradition kept a second Medb to prove the point: Medb Lethderg of Tara, of whom the Book of Leinster records that she slept with nine kings of Ireland and that no king ruled at Tara who had not slept with her. Her closest kin inside the lexicon are the pantheon's other keepers of the land's consent: [[macha|Macha]], whose curse opened Ulster to her army, and [[morrigan|the Mórrígan]], who rides the same war-paths from the Otherworld side.
lore.originalScriptNote: Old Irish writes the name Medb (genitive Medba) in the Insular Latin script of the great codices — Lebor na hUidre and the Book of Leinster preserve the Táin; normalized Old Irish spells it with plain Latin letters and no diacritic. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, carries the name-type exactly once, and in the most suggestive place in Ireland: on a stone in the Oweynagat cave at Rathcroghan, Medb's own royal complex, reading VRAICCI MAQI MEDVVI — '(the stone of) Fráech, son of Medb'. Because the normalized form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: medb.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'PUD-muh-sum-BHUH-vuh' — even syllables, the stress spread; the bh is a voiced breath, not an English 'v'.
pronunciation.note: Tier 2: 'Padmasambhava' is ASCII-canonical in spelling; the restoration's weight is etymological and hagiographic — padma + sambhava, 'Lotus-Born,' the name that is also his origin story.

domains.title: Padmasambhava
domains.subtitle: The Lotus-Born — Guru Rinpoche, the Second Buddha of Tibet
domains.lead: Padmasambhava — the Lotus-Born, revered across the Tibetan world as Guru Rinpoche, 'Precious Teacher' — is the tantric master credited with planting Buddhism in Tibet: taming its spirits, raising its first monastery, and hiding its deepest teachings as treasures for future ages.

cards.name: The Lotus Birth
cards.desc: Found as a child on a lotus in Lake Dhanakośa and adopted by King Indrabhūti of Uḍḍiyāna — a nativity with no mother, made for a teacher with no homeland.

cards.name: The Taming of Tibet
cards.desc: Binding the nāgas and demonesses of the Tibetan landscape by oath into dharmapālas — protectors — until the walls of Samye could stand.

cards.name: Samye and the Debate
cards.desc: Tibet's first monastery (consecrated c. 779) and the council where Indian gradualism defeated Chinese Chan — shaping Tibetan Buddhism for twelve centuries.

cards.name: The Hidden Treasures
cards.desc: Terma — texts, statues, and rituals sealed in rock and lake to be rediscovered when the age can bear them; the Padma bKa' thang is itself one.

symbols.name: The lotus of his birth
symbols.meaning: The eight-petaled bloom on Lake Dhanakośa that bore him — purity without parentage; the name and the origin are the same word

symbols.name: The vajra
symbols.meaning: The thunderbolt-scepter of tantric power — with which he struck the spirits of Tibet into oath-bound protectors, converting the landscape itself

symbols.name: The khaṭvāṅga staff
symbols.meaning: The trident-staff crowned with skulls and ribbons — tantric mastery over death, carried by the Guru in his wandering iconography

symbols.name: The pregnant tigress
symbols.meaning: His steed out of Tibet — flying from the Gungthang pass to the Copper-Colored Mountain, wrath and compassion yoked together

symbols.name: Zangdok Palri
symbols.meaning: The Copper-Colored Mountain of Glory, his paradise in the southwest — every Nyingma altar's painted destination

symbols.name: The treasure vase
symbols.meaning: Terma sealed and waiting — the teaching buried as a promise that the future will deserve it

mythology.lead: Padmasambhava's mythology is a hagiography written centuries after its hero — the principal source, the Padma bKa' thang, is a 14th-century treasure-text about an 8th-century man. That distance is not a defect to apologize for; it is the figure's native element, a teacher whose whole meaning is that the teaching keeps being found.

myths.title: Found on a Lotus in the Lake
myths.text: No ordinary birth attaches to him. The Padma bKa' thang — the "Chronicle of Padma," a terma (treasure-text) revealed by Orgyen Lingpa in the 14th century, our principal source, composed five centuries after its hero — tells how he appeared as an eight-year-old child seated on a blooming lotus in the middle of Lake Dhanakośa, in the land of Uḍḍiyāna, the Swat valley. King Indrabhūti, warned by prophecy and mourning a son lost to the lake, adopted the lotus-child and named him Padmasambhava — Lotus-Born. A being without parents comes from nowhere in particular, so his teaching belongs everywhere; the story inverts the Buddha's nativity deliberately — not a queen's grove but an empty lake, not a clan but no lineage at all. Later scholars note what the myth performs: the historical 8th-century teacher is all but unrecoverable, and the tradition seems not to mind — a founder born of a flower needs no biography, only a legend.

myths.title: The Guru Who Tamed the Land
myths.text: In the 8th century, tradition says, King Trisong Detsen (r. 755–797) invited first the abbot Śāntarakṣita to build a monastery — and watched the local spirits demolish every wall the workers raised by day. The abbot's counsel: send for the master of the vajra. Padmasambhava traveled from Nepal through the passes, and Tibet's own account of his progress — the Padma bKa' thang again — reads like a conquest itinerary: at each valley he bound the nyen, the nāgas, and the demoness of the land by oath, converting them into dharmapālas, sworn protectors of the teaching. Only then could Bsam yas (Samye) rise (consecrated c. 779) — monastery, academy, and debating courtyard in one, modeled on the cosmic mountain. The myth's geography is exact: Buddhism in Tibet is pictured as a conquest not of men but of landscape, every river and pass given its oath-bound guardian. The teacher who entered Tibet as an exorcist left as its father.

lore.culturalLegacy: Every Nyingma monastery is his house twice over: Samye, Tibet's first, was raised on his taming; and in Bhutan, the cliff-hanging Tiger's Nest (Taktsang) marks the cave where he is said to have meditated on the tigress's back — the kingdom's defining image. The annual 10th-day rituals across the Tibetan world re-enact his arrival; the Seven Line Prayer — "I pray to the Lotus-Born of Uḍḍiyāna..." — is the most recited invocation in Tibetan Buddhism. In the 20th century his treasure-doctrine proved its worth: as Tibet's texts scattered, the terma logic rediscovered them — libraries sealed by exile, waiting in Dharamsala and Kathmandu to be read again. The Lotus-Born, who hid the teaching against the dark age, became the patron saint of a tradition that had to bury itself to survive — and then, as promised, was found.
lore.archaeology: The historical Padmasambhava leaves no contemporary trace — the earliest sources are three to five centuries later — and the archaeology of his legend is the archaeology of Samye itself: excavations at Dranang have confirmed an 8th-century mandala-planned monastery with central Wutse and four temples matching the chronicles, and Dunhuang manuscripts (closed c. 1000) already circulate his name. His landscape, though, is thoroughly mapped: the Tiger's Nest (Taktsang) above the Paro valley, the cave-temples of Nepal's upper valleys where he meditated en route, the statue at Tso Pema (Rewalsar) where he hid from the king of Zahor — every site an enacted chapter. Uḍḍiyāna, his birthplace, is fixed by the Swat valley's ruins and inscriptions. The figure is a study in how a people builds monuments to a man the record cannot see — and calls the monuments evidence.
lore.syncretism: Padmasambhava is syncretism's master key. In Tibet he absorbed the thunderbolt of the vajra and the oath-bound demons of the old religion, so that every mountain god of the plateau became a dharmapāla with a Buddhist name. Bon, Tibet's indigenous tradition, answered in kind: its later texts speak of the Guru as bound and outwitted, a rival's way of admitting his power. In the Himalayas his cult merged with local spirit-lords — he is the guru of Nepal's caves as much as Tibet's — and in Sikkim and Bhutan he is a national ancestor, his flight-route on the tigress mapped as pilgrimage. The 19th-century nonsectarian Rimé movement made him the shared treasure of all schools, and the modern global spread of Dzogchen and Vajrayāna rides on his name: where Tibetan Buddhism goes, Guru Rinpoche has already flown.

entries.meaning: 'Rāma with the Axe' (paraśu 'axe') — the sixth avatāra of Viṣṇu, the Brahmin warrior who exterminates the kṣatriyas, counted among the immortal Cirañjīvī

'Great heaven' (Māori rangi 'sky, heavens' + nui 'great'), the sky father prised apart from the earth mother Papatūānuku by their children.

pronunciation.approximation: 'RAH-ngi-NOO-ee' — tap the 'r' as in Spanish 'pero'; 'ng' is the sound in 'singer'; the four light syllables run together.
pronunciation.note: The form Ranginui is plain ASCII — Māori writes this name with no diacritics — so the restoration recovers nothing but the capital that marks a proper name, and the name stands at Tier 2 by the mechanical rule. Its authenticity needs no orthographic argument: the name has been transmitted without break in Māori oral and ceremonial tradition.

domains.title: Ranginui
domains.subtitle: Sky
domains.lead: Ranginui is the sky father of Māori cosmogony — rangi, 'sky', with nui, 'great'. He and the earth mother Papatūānuku lay locked in an embrace that left the world in darkness, until their children forced them apart so that light, and humanity, could live between them. He is separation and longing: the rain is his tears, the mist her sighs, and the space between sky and earth the world we inhabit.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: Rangi 'sky' + nui 'great': Great Heaven, the primordial sky father of Māori cosmogony (Williams, Dictionary of the Māori Language).

cards.name: Sky
cards.desc: The primordial sky locked in darkness with the earth mother Papatūānuku until their children prised them apart.

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: The separation of Rangi and Papa is the founding story of the Māori world, still told on every marae and carved into every wharenui.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Honored as a flagship temple; the Māori form needs no diacritics, so the restoration is the scholarly citation form, capitalization and all.

symbols.name: Rain
symbols.meaning: The tears of Rangi falling on Papatūānuku — the sky father's enduring grief at the separation (Grey, Polynesian Mythology).

symbols.name: Mist
symbols.meaning: The sighs of Papatūānuku rising to meet him — the parents' continuing dialogue written on the morning air (Orbell, Māori Myth and Legend).

symbols.name: The ridge-pole (tahuhu)
symbols.meaning: In the wharenui the ridge-beam is Rangi held above the earth floor, Papa: every meeting house re-enacts the separation.

symbols.name: The stars
symbols.meaning: The children hung in the sky by Tāne to give their father light and to adorn his darkness (White, Ancient History of the Māori).

mythology.lead: Ranginui's mythology is Māori cosmogony itself, as recorded by Sir George Grey and John White from oral tradition in the nineteenth century: the primordial embrace, the separation, and the war among the children that followed. It is a living narrative — still told on marae, still carved into meeting houses — and it explains the visible world: rain, mist, storm, and the light between sky and earth.

myths.title: The Embrace of Rangi and Papa
myths.text: In the beginning the sky father Ranginui and the earth mother Papatūānuku clung together in an embrace that knew no end, and in the darkness between their bodies their children were born — seventy sons in the telling recorded by Grey in Polynesian Mythology (1854). There was no light: the world was the cramped hollow of the parents' clasp, and the children grew hemmed in on every side, some of them longing for room and for brightness, others content in the warm dark. The myth opens not with a bang but with an embrace, and its first claim is psychological before it is cosmological — love so complete that it suffocates: the parents' happiness is the children's captivity, and creation cannot begin until something beloved breaks.

myths.title: Tāne Pushes the Sky Away
myths.text: The children argued over how to win light. Tūmatauenga, the fierce one, proposed killing the parents — a plan the others rejected with horror. Then Tāne, the resourceful one, lay on his back between them and, bracing his head against the earth and his feet against the sky, pushed (Grey; White, Ancient History of the Māori). Ranginui cried out in agony as he was lifted, and Papatūānuku groaned beneath him, still clinging, her torn body leaving the marks of her grief in the hills and valleys of the earth. Alone among the brothers, Tāwhirimāteā, lord of winds, sided with his father and withdrew in rage to the sky. The separation is the Māori account of why there is a world at all: light, space, and death itself enter existence in the moment the divided parents grieve — the world begins as an act of necessary violence against love.

lore.culturalLegacy: The separation of Ranginui and Papatūānuku remains the founding narrative of Māori identity — taught in schools, sung in waiata, and carved into the wharenui of every marae, where the building itself is the myth: ridge-pole as sky, floor as earth, ancestors as the space between. The national museum of New Zealand takes its name, Te Papa Tongarewa, from the earth mother of his embrace. Rangi is a living given name, and the pair have travelled far beyond Aotearoa: the story appears in environmental theology, indigenous-rights discourse, and the global revival of creation narratives as title-deeds of belonging. And the rain-as-tears reading gives Māori weather its poetry and its pedagogy — the landscape is a family, and the family is still speaking.
lore.archaeology: Māori tradition built no temples, so Ranginui's archaeology is the archaeology of the meeting house: the great carved wharenui of the nineteenth century are material cosmogonies. Te Hau-ki-Tūranga (carved c. 1842, now at Te Papa Tongarewa) shows the convention fully formed — the tahuhu ridge-pole as the sky father, the earth floor as Papatūānuku, and the carved ancestors standing between them. The textual witnesses are themselves artifacts: Grey recorded the separation cycle from Māori informants in Nga Mahi a nga Tupuna (1854), and White's Ancient History of the Māori (1887–90) preserved variants from the Tainui and Te Arawa traditions. Earlier than both stands the transmission they committed to paper — an unbroken oral and ceremonial custody, measured in centuries, that no excavation is needed to prove.
lore.syncretism: Ranginui is the Māori face of the Polynesian sky father, whose other avatars include the Hawaiian Wākea — the sky paired with Papahānaumoku, whose very name repeats the Papa of Māori tradition (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology) — and the Tahitian and Rarotongan ra'i and rangi of cognate cosmogonies; the separation of a primordial parental pair recurs across the Pacific. Nineteenth-century European recorders, Grey among them, were quick to hear biblical echoes — a sky father, an earth mother, children thrust out of a dark paradise — and Māori Christianity in turn folded Rangi and Papa into a theology of creation that could be preached from the pulpit. The carved meeting house became the permanent site of the synthesis: its ridge-pole is Rangi, its floor Papa, its ancestors the children between them. Later Māori thought, including the contested twentieth-century traditions gathered around the god Io, debated whether the sky father pointed toward a single supreme being; the scholarly consensus treats the separation myth as the genuine core and the monotheistic framing as accretion (Orbell).

steps: Sigurðr is the great dragon-slaying hero of the Volsunga saga and Poetic Edda.
The runic spelling is a normalized reconstruction; ᚦ writes /ð/ and final ᛦ represents the nominative -r ending.
ᛋ = s, ᛁ = i, ᚴ = k/g, ᚢ = u, ᚱ = r, ᚦ = ð, ᛦ = r (nom. ending).

pronunciation.approximation: 'SIG-urthr' — stress the first syllable, soften the middle g almost to a glide, sound the ð as the soft 'th' of 'father', and let the final -r hang as a light voiced syllable; it is the Old Norse nominative ending, not a separate vowel.
pronunciation.note: Sigurðr is Tier 1: the eth ð is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses, and the final -r preserves the Old Norse nominative ending that English drops entirely. Cleasby-Vigfusson (s.v. Sigurðr) and Zoëga (s.v. Sigurðr) record the form as the name of the Vǫlsung hero; the name compounds sigr, 'victory', with -vǫrðr, 'guardian', yielding 'victory-guardian', and answers to the continental German Siegfried.

domains.title: Victory, Dragon-Slaying, Heroism
domains.subtitle: The domain of Sigurðr
domains.lead:
In the norse tradition, Sigurðr governed victory, dragon-slaying, heroism. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

His is the northern form of the greatest heroic story the Germanic world ever told: the foster-son of a smith who reforged his father's shattered sword, the slayer of the dragon Fáfnir, the wooer of the valkyrie behind the flame, and the oath-brother destroyed by the very loyalty that made him great. What the Iliad is to Greece, the Vǫlsunga cycle is to the North.

cards.name: Gramr
cards.desc: The sword Óðinn thrust into the tree Barnstokkr and only Sigmundr could draw; shattered in his last battle, reforged by Reginn for the son who would avenge him.

cards.name: Fáfnir at Gnitaheiðr
cards.desc: The brother turned dragon by greed, slain by a hero lying in a trench; from his heart-blood Sigurðr learned the speech of birds.

cards.name: The Flame-Wall
cards.desc: Through the vafrlogi on Hindarfjall rode Grani's rider to wake Brynhildr, the valkyrie Óðinn had sunk in sleep — the oath sworn there could not survive the world of men.

cards.name: The Cursed Hoard
cards.desc: Andvari's gold, paid as weregild for Ótr and cursed at its surrender; every hand it passed through — Hreiðmarr, Fáfnir, Sigurðr, the Gjúkings — it brought to ruin.

symbols.name: Gramr
symbols.meaning: The reforged sword of Sigmundr, drawn from Barnstokkr and mended by Reginn; with it Sigurðr slew Fáfnir

symbols.name: Grani
symbols.meaning: The grey horse of Sleipnir's line who bore Sigurðr through the flame-wall and carried the dragon's gold from Gnitaheiðr

symbols.name: Andvaranautr and the hoard
symbols.meaning: The dwarf Andvari's ring and gold, taken as ransom and cursed at the taking — the engine of every death in the cycle

symbols.name: The dragon's heart-blood
symbols.meaning: Roasting Fáfnir's heart, Sigurðr tasted the blood and understood the birds — knowledge bought from the monster he killed

symbols.name: The vafrlogi flame-wall
symbols.meaning: The ring of fire around the sleeping Brynhildr, crossable only by the destined rider; crossed twice, once for love and once in betrayal

mythology.lead: Sigurðr is the dragonslayer of the Vǫlsunga cycle, the Norse original of the German Siegfried and the last great hero of the legendary North. Son of Sigmundr and Hjǫrdís, fostered by the smith Reginn, he reforged his father's sword, killed the dragon Fáfnir, and woke the valkyrie Brynhildr from her enchanted sleep — then lost her, and his life, to a draught of forgetfulness and the plotting of his sworn brothers. His story survives in the Poetic Edda, the Prose Edda, and Vǫlsunga saga, and through the Middle High German Nibelungenlied it became the backbone of Wagner's Ring. Where the gods of the Edda face a doom they know is coming, Sigurðr faces one he has forgotten — and that is the more human tragedy.

myths.title: The Reforging of Gramr
myths.text:
At the wedding feast of his sister Signý, a one-eyed stranger — Óðinn — thrust a sword to the hilt into the tree Barnstokkr that grew through the hall of Vǫlsungr, and only Sigmundr of all the company could draw it. Years later Sigmundr fell in battle, the sword shattering beneath him against the same god's spear, and his widow Hjǫrdís carried the shards away for her unborn son. That son, Sigurðr, was fostered by Reginn, a smith of the dwarf-kin, who urged him against the dragon Fáfnir and forged blade after blade that broke under the boy's testing — until Sigurðr demanded the shards of his father's sword be worked into the new steel. Reginn reforged them into Gramr, and the boy clove the smith's anvil to the stock and sheared a tuft of wool drifting on the current as though it were standing stone (Vǫlsunga saga 13–15; Reginsmál).

The blade binds the hero to Óðinn from birth: the god who gave the sword also broke it, and the steel that passes from father to son is the visible thread of a destiny the boy never chose. In the North, inheritance is not property but appointment.

myths.title: The Slaying of Fáfnir
myths.text:
Fáfnir was Reginn's brother, who had killed their father Hreiðmarr for the hoard paid as weregild for the slain Ótr, and crawled away to Gnitaheiðr, where greed long brooding over gold twisted him into a dragon. Guided by a one-eyed old man who would not give his name, Sigurðr dug a trench across the worm's path to the water and lay in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead he thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The dying dragon warned him that the gold would be his death, and the hero answered with the northern creed: every man must die, and wealth must serve until that day (Fáfnismál; Vǫlsunga saga 18–20). Roasting the heart for Reginn, Sigurðr burned his finger, set it in his mouth, and the heart-blood opened the speech of birds to him: the nuthatches in the branches warned that the smith meant to kill him. He took Reginn's head, loaded the cursed gold onto Grani, and rode away the richest and most doomed man in the North.

The birds that save him here will not be there at the end. The episode's point is exact: the monster's death transfers the monster's curse, and every new owner of the gold only inherits it.

lore.culturalLegacy: No Norse figure has had a longer second life. William Morris retold the cycle in his epic The Story of Sigurd the Volsung and the Fall of the Niblungs (1876), which he called the great story of the North that should be to all his race what the tale of Troy was to the Greeks. Richard Wagner made it the armature of Der Ring des Nibelungen — Siegfried and Götterdämmerung follow the Norse sources where the Nibelungenlied had softened them, restoring the valkyrie Brünnhilde to the centre. Arthur Rackham's illustrations fixed the cycle's visual grammar for a century, and J. R. R. Tolkien, who read the Eddas closely, composed his own The Legend of Sigurd and Gudrún in Eddic metre. The dragonslayer persists in opera houses, novels, games, and film wherever a hero wins gold and is destroyed by it. In modern heathenry Sigurðr is honoured less as an object of cult than as the model of the heroic ethic — courage held fast inside a fate already written — and the runestones that depict him are among the tradition's most cited monuments. Restoring Sigurðr in Unicode keeps the eth and the nominative -r that the German Siegfried and the anglicized Sigurd alike have lost.
lore.archaeology: The Sigurðr cycle is the most widely depicted heroic legend of the Viking Age. The Ramsund carving (Sö 101) in Södermanland, Sweden, shows the whole Gnitaheiðr episode in one frame — Sigurðr piercing the serpent from below, the heart roasting over the fire, the thumb in his mouth, the listening birds, the headless Reginn, and Grani laden with the gold — and the nearby Gök stone (Sö 327) quotes the same scene within a runic serpent band. The Drävle runestone (U 1163) in Uppland adds a further Swedish depiction, while across the North Sea the Manx cross-slabs, above all the Kirk Andreas cross, show Sigurðr roasting Fáfnir's heart, proof the legend travelled with Norse settlers. In Norway the carved portal of Hylestad stave church (c. 1200) narrates the cycle panel by panel, from the forging of Gramr to Reginn's death. The textual tradition is Icelandic and later: the heroic lays of the Poetic Edda survive chiefly in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), whose famous eight-leaf lacuna has cost us the fullest form of the Sigurðr lays — Brot af Sigurðarkviðu preserves only a fragment — while Vǫlsunga saga itself (c. 1270) survives in paper copies of the lost vellum NKS 1824 b 4to.
lore.syncretism: Sigurðr is the northern twin of a pan-Germanic hero. The continental tradition — preserved in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied (c. 1200), the Lied vom Hürnen Seyfrid, and the Old Norse Þiðreks saga, which repatriates German material — tells of the same dragon-fight, hoard, and betrayal under the name Siegfried, with the details reworked: the valkyrie becomes a Burgundian queen, the flame-wall drops away, and the murder moves to a forest spring. Scholars have long read the cycle's skeleton against history, seeing in Gunnarr and the fall of the Gjúkings the shadow of the Burgundian kingdom destroyed by the Huns in 437 — legend crystallized around remembered catastrophe. The dragon-slaying itself belongs to a still older inheritance: the Indo-European formula of the hero who kills the serpent, traced by Calvert Watkins through Indra and Vṛtra, Herakles and the Lernaean hydra, and Beowulf's fatal last fight. In later folklore the story lived on in the Faroese Sjúrðar kvæði ballads, still sung and danced in the islands centuries after the saga manuscripts were copied.
lore.originalScriptNote: The medieval Norse wrote Sigurðr in the Latin alphabet the Icelanders adapted for their vernacular, and it is in that script — Codex Regius, the Vǫlsunga saga manuscripts — that the name is preserved. The hero's own age wrote in the Younger Futhark, the sixteen-rune alphabet carved on the memorial stones that depict his deeds; reduced to sixteen signs, it did not even distinguish ð from þ or d from t, so the full sound of the name was never recoverable from runes alone. The restored form Sigurðr keeps both features the Latin-script manuscripts attest: the eth ð, the voiced dental fricative, and the nominative ending -r. As a registrable domain the Unicode form carries the eth that the ASCII sigurd flattens to d — the punycode encodes exactly what the saga scribes wrote.

entries.domain: Eight-Legged Steed, Journey, Offspring of Loki

steps: Sleipnir is Óðinn’s eight-legged steed, born of Loki and the giant Svaðilfari.
The runic spelling is a scholarly reconstruction; the name is not attested in runic inscriptions.
ᛋ = s, ᛚ = l, ᛅ = æ (or e/æ), ᛁ = i, ᛒ = b, ᚾ = n, ᛁ = i, ᛦ = r (nom. ending).
provenanceSources: Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic

pronunciation.approximation: 'SLAYP-nir' — stress on the first syllable as in every Old Norse word, the ei a true two-part glide, the final r rolled and audible.
pronunciation.note: Sleipnir is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input; the name's fame does nothing to change its orthography.

domains.title: Eight-Legged Steed, Journey, Offspring of Loki
domains.subtitle: The Gliding One Who Rides All Roads
domains.lead: Sleipnir, the grey eight-legged horse of Óðinn, is the best of horses among gods and men — and the strangest birth in the Edda. When the gods broke their bargain with the master builder of Ásgarðr's wall, it was Loki, in mare's shape, who lured away the giant's stallion Svaðilfari; and it was Loki who later bore the foal, grey, with eight legs. On Sleipnir's back Hermóðr rides nine nights down the Hel-road to ransom Baldr, and the horse leaps the gate of the dead with room to spare. His name means the gliding one — the creature for whom every boundary becomes a road.

cards.name: The Eight Legs
cards.desc: The mark no retelling can omit: eight legs where every honest horse has four — the body that outruns every other mount in the nine worlds, carved already on the Gotland picture stones.

cards.name: The Grey Foal
cards.desc: Born of Loki in mare's form and the giant's stallion Svaðilfari, after the night that broke the wall-builder's bargain — the only one of Loki's monstrous children who serves the gods instead of threatening them.

cards.name: The Hel-Road
cards.desc: The nine-night ride: Hermóðr borrows Sleipnir to ransom Baldr, crosses the gold-roofed Gjallarbrú, and the horse leaps Hel's gate 'with so much to spare' — the road down taken at full gallop.

cards.name: The Rune-Carved Teeth
cards.desc: Sigrdrífumál remembers runes cut 'on Sleipnir's teeth' among the places where victory-runes and mind-runes were lodged — even the horse's mouth was writing's place.

symbols.name: The eight legs
symbols.meaning: Speed beyond nature's allowance — the mount that outruns every horse in the nine worlds

symbols.name: The grey coat
symbols.meaning: The foal's colour at birth, noted by Snorri — grey, the working colour of northern horses

symbols.name: Svaðilfari
symbols.meaning: The giant builder's stallion, the sire — the bargain's price become a gift

symbols.name: The leap over Helgrindr
symbols.meaning: The gate of the dead cleared with room to spare — no boundary holds the gliding one

symbols.name: The rune-carved teeth
symbols.meaning: Sigrdrífumál's image of runes lodged in the horse's mouth — the steed as a carrier of signs as well as riders

mythology.lead: Sleipnir's dossier is three scenes and a pedigree: his begetting at the wall of Ásgarðr, his ride down the Hel-road for Baldr's sake, and the verse that crowns him best of horses. Around them the corpus keeps him the way the þulur keep him — catalogued, superlative, and never once ridden in vain.

myths.title: The Master Builder's Wage
myths.text:
A smith came to Ásgarðr offering to build the gods a wall in three seasons, high and strong against the mountain-giants — and named his wage: Freyja, and the sun and the moon. The Æsir bargained him down to one winter, alone; at Loki's urging they granted him the use of his stallion, Svaðilfari. The horse hauled boulders by night that the builder set by day, and with three days left before summer the gate-pillars stood nearly finished. The gods blamed Loki, who had advised the bargain, and swore he would die an evil death unless he made the builder lose. That night, when Svaðilfari was led out to the stones, a mare ran from the wood and whinnied; the stallion broke his traces and ran after her, and the work stood still. The builder flew into a giant's rage — and the gods called on Þórr, who smashed the smith's skull with Mjölnir and sent him down to Niflhel (Snorri, Gylfaginning 42).

Snorri closes the episode with the strangest sentence in his Edda: Loki had had such dealings with Svaðilfari that somewhat later he bore a foal. It was grey and had eight legs, and this is the best horse among gods and men. The gods' broken bargain, Loki's shame, the giant's death — and out of all of it, the greatest gift Óðinn ever received.

myths.title: The Ride Down the Hel-Road
myths.text:
When Baldr lay dead and Frigg asked who would win her love by riding to Hel to ransom him, Hermóðr the Bold, Óðinn's son, stood up. Sleipnir was led out, and Hermóðr mounted and galloped away. He rode nine nights through dark and deep valleys, seeing nothing, until he came to the river Gjöll and rode onto the Gjallarbrú, the bridge roofed with shining gold, where the maiden Móðguðr guards the crossing. She told him the dead had passed that way the day before — five companies of them — and that the road to Hel lay downward and northward. He rode on to the gates of Hel, and there Sleipnir showed what eight legs are for: Hermóðr spurred him, and the horse leapt the gate with so much to spare that the leap itself became proverb (Gylfaginning 49).

Inside, Hermóðr found Baldr in the high seat and Nanna beside him, and delivered the Æsir's plea. Hel set her famous condition — all things in the world, living and lifeless, must weep Baldr out — and the errand failed at the giantess Þökk's dry tears. But the ride succeeded: the only journey in the corpus that goes down the Hel-road and comes back, made on the back of Loki's foal.

lore.culturalLegacy: Sleipnir's afterlife is the afterlife of the image: the eight-legged rider of the Gotland stones has become one of the most reproduced figures of Norse art, carried from nineteenth-century antiquarian plates into every modern handbook of the mythology. In the North itself the name never quite left the stables — Swedish and Norwegian kept Sleipner for engines and hulls, from locomotives to naval vessels, and Norway gave the name to the Sleipner gas field in the North Sea, the undersea treasure-house named for the underworld runner. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities remember Sleipnir in Óðinn rites as the mount of the road between worlds, and retellings of the Baldr cycle keep his two great moments: the leap over Hel's gate, and the grey foal standing in the wreckage of the gods' broken bargain.
lore.archaeology: Sleipnir has the strongest material attestation of any horse in the corpus: the Gotland picture stones. The Tjängvide stone (Alskog parish) and Ardre VIII, carved in the eighth and ninth centuries, show an eight-legged horse bearing a rider toward a welcoming figure — an image the standard scholarship (Lindqvist; Simek s.v. Sleipnir) identifies as Óðinn carried by Sleipnir, centuries older than any written telling. No runic inscription names the horse, and no votive deposit can be tied to him — his cult, if any, was his master's. The textual witnesses are the Codex Regius and related codices of the Prose Edda for Gylfaginning 42 and 49, and the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Grímnismál and Sigrdrífumál.
lore.syncretism: Sleipnir's closest kin is inside the corpus: Grani, Sigurðr's grey, whom Reginsmál's prose calls 'of Sleipnir's lineage' — the mythic superlative breeding the heroic one, as if the gods' stable stocked the sagas. Beyond the North, scholars have ranged widely and cautiously. The eight-legged world-crosser has been read as the ritual mount of shamanic journey — the animal that carries its rider through the levels of the cosmos — an interpretation Simek registers as one modern reading among others, not an attestation. The old folkloric fancy that eight legs picture four pallbearers carrying a corpse has no medieval warrant at all and the handbooks give it no house-room. What the sources support is narrower and stronger: a horse that belongs to no stable but Óðinn's, born of the one god who crosses every boundary himself, and used for the one ride — down to Hel and back — that no other mount could survive. Within the corpus his story binds Loki, Óðinn, Hermóðr, and the house of Baldr; he is the only one of Loki's children — beside the wolf, the serpent, and Hel — whose existence is a gift and not a threat.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Sleipnir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛋᛚᛁᛒᚾᛁᛦ (s-l-i-p-n-i-R), the short-twig row merging e with i under ᛁ and p with b under ᛒ. No runic carving of the name is known; the manuscript spelling is the primary witness. Because the name is pure ASCII, no form of it is currently owned by the project: the plain-ASCII sleipnir.com is watched for release, and this temple claims nothing it does not hold.

entries.meaning: Sun (the personified sun, sister of Máni)
The Boar — third avatāra of Viṣṇu, who dives into the cosmic waters and raises the sunken Earth (Bhūdevī) on his tusks

'Steadfast in Battle' (yudhi 'in battle' + sthira 'firm') — the eldest Pāṇḍava, son of the god Dharma, famed for truthfulness and crowned king at Hāstinapura after the Kurukṣetra war

The dental fricative θ (𐬚) and the postalveolar š (𐬱) have distinct Avestan letters.

The Unicode restoration Zaraθuštra is registrable in .com; the Avestan script is not in the .com IDN table.

entries.meaning: Navel (of the earth); the stone at Delphi regarded as the centre of the world

etymology.derivation: Greek ὀμφαλός 'navel, boss, centre'; the Delphic omphalos marked the world's centre in archaic Greek geography.

pronunciation.approximation: 'om-fah-LOSS' — the accent falls on the last syllable; classical phi is an aspirated p, not the modern f.
pronunciation.note: Omphalós is Tier 2: the restoration preserves exactly one feature ASCII loses — the final acute accent marking stress. There is no long vowel (η/ω) and no circumflex, so the name stands at Tier 2.

domains.title: Navel
domains.subtitle: Navel, Center, Delphi
domains.lead: The omphalós was the stone at Delphi regarded as the navel — the exact center — of the world. Set in the innermost sanctuary, wrapped in a woolen net and flanked by golden eagles, it was not an image of a god but a marker of where the world's middle lay, and the Pythia prophesied beside it.

cards.name: The Stone at Delphi
cards.desc: A rounded Hymettian-marble boss, carved with a net pattern, that stood in the adyton where the Pythia gave her oracles (Pausanias 10.16.3).

cards.name: The Navel of the Earth
cards.desc: Zeus released two eagles from the ends of the world; where they met, at Delphi, the stone marked the center of all lands (Strabo 9.3.6).

cards.name: The Swaddled Stone
cards.desc: The stone Kronos swallowed in place of the infant Zeus was, in the later tradition, set up at Delphi as a wonder and a sign (Hesiod, Theogony 485–497; Pausanias 10.24.6).

cards.name: The Seat of Prophecy
cards.desc: Apollo's oracle spoke beside the stone, in the sanctuary where the god had struck down the serpent Python (Homeric Hymn to Apollo 300ff.).

symbols.name: The net-covered stone
symbols.meaning: The omphalos itself, wrapped in the woolen agrenon net that veiled the world's center (Pausanias 10.16.3)

symbols.name: The two golden eagles
symbols.meaning: Zeus's birds, set one on either side of the stone as witnesses to the center-finding

symbols.name: The navel of a newborn
symbols.meaning: The body's own center — ὀμφαλός is the infant's navel, the mark where nourishment once entered

symbols.name: The cleft of Delphi
symbols.meaning: The rock fissure beneath the temple where Apollo's arrows struck Python and the prophetic power rose

mythology.lead: The omphalós has no biography because it is a place made stone: the story of Delphi's navel is the story of how the Greeks decided where the middle of the world was — by eagle, by oracle, and by the stone that stood for the infant god.

myths.title: The Eagles of Zeus
myths.text: In the story told at Delphi, Zeus wished to know where the exact center of the earth lay. He released two eagles — some say from the eastern and western edges of the world — and bade them fly toward each other; they met above Delphi, and where they met the god fixed the omphalós, the navel-stone. The tale is preserved in the geographical tradition that culminates in Strabo (9.3.6), who repeats it as the sanctuary's own account of itself. The myth is a cartography in miniature: instead of measuring the world, the Greeks let two birds draw its diagonals and set a stone where the lines crossed. Delphi did not claim to be everywhere; it claimed to be the middle — the one point from which the whole could be surveyed, and the one point, therefore, where a god might conveniently speak to all mortals at once. Every subsequent oracle of the sanctuary traded on this founding geometry.

myths.title: The Stone in the Innermost Room
myths.text: Pausanias (10.16.3) describes what the visitor could actually see: in the innermost sanctuary of Apollo's temple, the adyton, lay the omphalos, covered — the Delphians said — with the net thrown over it, with two golden eagles standing upon it. Beside it, in the same most-holy space, stood the tripod on which the Pythia mounted to give her responses, and the ever-burning hearth of the sanctuary. The stone was thus not a cult statue but a boundary-marker of the cosmos, kept in the room where heaven and earth touched. Its material facts are modest — a carved marble boss a little over a meter high — but its placement was the whole argument: the center of the world was a place you could stand next to, touch, and consult. Pausanias's description is the one fixed point on which the identification of the surviving stone rests.

lore.culturalLegacy: Delphi's omphalos made 'center' a claim any city could dream of. Roman emperors consulted the oracle and copied the stone; medieval mapmakers drew Jerusalem at the world's middle; and the modern phrase 'navel-gazing' preserves the Greek word in everyday speech. The archaeological site of Delphi, a UNESCO World Heritage site, still draws travelers to the temple foundations where the adyton — and the stone — once stood. In psychology, the Delphic 'know thyself' has been read together with the omphalos as an emblem of the inward journey to the center of the self, a reading popularized by Jung's school. The word also lives quietly in anatomy, where the umbilicus keeps the Greek root in every newborn's first scar.
