Few small stones have spread so far: a marble boss from a mountain sanctuary became the template for every claim, sacred or secular, to be the middle of things.
lore.archaeology: The omphalos survives in the Delphi Archaeological Museum: a Hymettian-marble boss carved with a net pattern, a little over a meter high, found in the temple precinct and conventionally identified with the stone Pausanias saw in the adyton. The temple of Apollo — its fourth, stone, phase — still shows the foundations of the inner sanctuary where the stone and the Pythia's tripod stood. The form appears on imperial-period coins of Delphi, always with the net pattern and flanking eagles, and Roman copies of the omphalos type are known from the city of Rome itself. No inscription names the stone; its identification rests on the match between Pausanias's description and the carved marble found on site.
lore.syncretism: Rome built its own navel: the Umbilicus Urbis Romae, a travertine marker in the Roman Forum, where the symbolic center of the empire was ritually defined, its rounded form echoing the Delphic original. In late antiquity and the Middle Ages the idea of a world-navel multiplied — Jerusalem, Constantinople, even Glastonbury in English legend each claimed a central, omphalic status — proof that the Greek idea had become a portable form of pride. The English language keeps the word as a learned synonym for the center of anything, and the modern mockery of self-absorption as 'navel-gazing' (omphaloskepsis) returns the word to its first, bodily meaning. The stone at Delphi thus survived its own religion: a pagan center-marker became the West's standing metaphor for wherever people believe the world's meaning is concentrated.

etymology.derivation: Greek κεραυνός 'thunderbolt'; from κεραυνός, the smiting weapon of Zeus.

pronunciation.approximation: 'keh-raow-NOSS' — the pitch rises on the final syllable, which stays short and sharp.
pronunciation.note: Keraunós is Tier 2: the acute on the final syllable preserves Greek pitch accent, but no long vowel (η/ω) survives — the final omicron is short — so only one of the two Tier-1 features is present. The diphthong αυ is long for accent, but it is not a long vowel in the tier rule's sense.

domains.title: Thunderbolt
domains.subtitle: Thunderbolt
domains.lead: Keraunós is the thunderbolt of Zeus — the weapon forged by the Cyclopes and never once missing its mark. It is at once an instrument of war, the badge of sovereignty, and an omen read in the sky; Homer makes all of heaven tremble when Zeus rises with it.

cards.name: The Bolt
cards.desc: Forged by the Cyclopes with thunder and lightning as Zeus's arms (Hesiod, Theogony 501–506).

cards.name: The War of the Gods
cards.desc: With it Zeus broke the Titans and blasted Typhon — cosmic order enforced by a single weapon (Theogony 687–721, 853–868).

cards.name: The Boundary of Mortals
cards.desc: It killed Semele, beloved of Zeus, and the blasphemer Salmoneus — love and hubris struck by the same fire (Apollodorus 3.4.3, 1.9.7).

cards.name: The Sign in the Sky
cards.desc: Lightning read as Zeus's omen before assembly and battle — a flash on the right meant assent (Iliad 2.353–354).

symbols.name: The twin-tined bolt
symbols.meaning: The stylized lightning of Greek art — a ribbed, double-pointed shaft, always shown in Zeus's raised hand.

symbols.name: Eagle
symbols.meaning: The thunder-bird that carries the bolt in myth and holds it on coinage.

symbols.name: Lightning as omen
symbols.meaning: A flash on the right read as Zeus's assent; armies waited for it before advancing (Iliad 2.353–354).

symbols.name: The oak of Dodona
symbols.meaning: Zeus's prophetic tree, where the storm-god spoke through rustling leaves (Iliad 16.233–235).

mythology.lead: The keraunós is not merely a weapon but the emblem of Zeus's rule — forged at the beginning of his reign, decisive in his two great wars, and terrible against mortals who reach too high or are loved too much.

myths.title: The Cyclopes Arm Zeus
myths.text: When Zeus came of age to challenge Kronos, Gaiä named his allies: the Cyclopes, one-eyed smiths imprisoned in the depths. Zeus freed them, and they repaid him with the three weapons of heaven — thunder, lightning, and 'the glowing thunderbolt' (Hesiod, Theogony 501–506); the same passage remembers their earlier craft, arms for the gods at the beginning (Theogony 139–141). The bolt is thus born at the exact moment Zeus's power needs a form: before it he is a younger god with grievances, after it he is the storm. Homer never forgets the connection, and calls the bolt simply the weapon when Zeus arms himself at the brink of the Trojan War (Iliad 8.75). The myth explains why no one else may hold it: the keraunós is the signature of sovereignty, forged once and never re-made.

myths.title: Breaking the Old Order
myths.text: The war between the Olympians and the Titans lasted ten years with no advantage on either side, until Zeus brought up the Cyclopes' gifts. Then heaven changed hands: 'from Olympus he hurled his bolts in succession, and the earth groaned, burning, and the great forests crackled on every side; the whole earth boiled, and the streams of Ocean, and the unharvested sea' (Hesiod, Theogony 687–713). The Titans were struck down, bound, and cast into misty Tartarus behind gates of bronze. The keraunós here is not one throw but a barrage — the first use of concentrated, overwhelming force in Greek myth, and the poem's theological argument that raw elder power yields to armed, organized thunder. Every later bolt-throw reenacts this one: order established by a weapon that cannot be answered, and therefore never has to be.

lore.culturalLegacy: The keraunós became the default metaphor for suddenness itself; Greek and Latin writers reach for it whenever fate moves faster than thought. In the modern world the bolt's silhouette — a jagged zigzag — became the universal icon of electricity, the god's weapon re-signed as physics: every switch-plate and warning label still carries a little Olympus. The word echoed back into theology as well — thunderbolt imagery anchors theophany from Sinai to Delphi — and forward into fantasy, where the lightning bolt remains the grammar of divine anger in every mythology that never knew Hesiod. Restoring the acute accent of Keraunós returns the pitch to the word the sky was supposed to speak with.
lore.archaeology: The bolt's material life was votive: Greeks and Romans dedicated cast bronze and terracotta thunderbolts by the hundreds at Olympia, Dodona, and on the Capitoline — small zigzag ingots left where lightning had been read as a sign. The masterpiece was cult-size: Phidias's chryselephantine Zeus at Olympia held a thunderbolt tipped with gold in his right hand and an eagle on his sceptre, and was counted among the wonders of the world (Pausanias 5.11). Coins of Elis and of countless Greek cities mint the bolt beside the eagle until it becomes the god's signature. Rome carried it too: the fulmen decorates legionary standards and the cuirasses of emperors claiming Jove's protection, an emblem that marched.
lore.syncretism: Rome received the bolt as the fulmen of Jupiter, and made of it a monument: the temple of Jupiter Tonans on the Capitoline was vowed by Augustus after a lightning strike narrowly spared his life (Suetonius, Augustus 29.3), turning the weapon into a memorial of divine warning rather than mere force. Imperial coinage pairs eagle and bolt until the emblem outgrows any single god — by late antiquity the thunderbolt is simply the sign of heaven's displeasure, and Christian art keeps it flickering in the margins of judgment scenes. The word itself survives in Modern Greek κεραυνός, 'lightning', and in the learned coinage 'keraunograph', the lightning recorder: a weapon of the gods still employed, as technology, to listen to storms.

entries.meaning: Swift impetuous male deity; the Shinto storm god

variants.note: Common Hepburn romanization

etymology.derivation: From Old Japanese susanowo, 'swift impetuous male'; brother of Amaterasu, expelled from the high plain of heaven for his violence.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SOO-sah-noh' — pure Japanese vowels, the final 'oh' held long; the macron over the ō is the mark plain ASCII removes.
pronunciation.note: Susanō is Tier 1: the macron on ō marks the long final vowel that the ASCII 'susanoo' flattens into two silent letters. The length is not decorative — it is the difference between the storm god's name and a typo.

domains.title: Storms
domains.subtitle: Storms, Sea, Chaos
domains.lead: Susanoo is the storm god of Japanese myth — impetuous weeper, vandal of heaven, and slayer of the eight-headed serpent. Brother of the sun and the moon, he embodies the chaos that must be expelled for order to shine, yet also the heroic force that rescues the land's last daughter. His biography moves from expulsion to settlement: the destroyer of heaven becomes the founder of Izumo.

cards.name: Storms
cards.desc: Thunder, wind, and raging sea made flesh; his weeping shakes mountains and dries rivers.

cards.name: The Impetuous One
cards.desc: His name is glossed 'swift, impetuous male deity'; the impetuosity is at once his crime and his heroic energy.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The macron over Susanō recovers the long final vowel that plain ASCII susanoo flattens.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Written 須佐之男命 in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki — 'His Augustness Swift-Impetuous-Male.'

symbols.name: Kusanagi sword
symbols.meaning: The blade drawn from the tail of Yamata no Orochi and given to Amaterasu; as one of the Three Imperial Regalia it binds the storm to sovereignty

symbols.name: Yamata no Orochi
symbols.meaning: The eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent whose yearly tribute of daughters ended at Kushinadahime — chaos given dragon-form

symbols.name: Eight sake vats
symbols.meaning: The eightfold-refined sake with which he plied the serpent — drunkenness itself turned into a weapon

symbols.name: Suga, the clearing palace
symbols.meaning: The palace he built where his spirit cleared after the serpent-slaying, giving Izumo its sacred center

symbols.name: The piebald horse
symbols.meaning: Ame-no-Fuchikoma, the heavenly piebald he flayed and hurled into the weaving hall — the outrage that cost heaven its light

mythology.lead: Susanoo's cycle in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki runs from cosmic vandal to culture hero: expelled from heaven, he conquers the dragon of chaos and founds a kingdom in song — the most humanly told arc of any Japanese deity.

myths.title: From the Nose of Izanagi
myths.text: When Izanagi purified himself after his flight from Yomi, Amaterasu was born from his left eye and Tsukuyomi from his right; from his nose came Susanoo, whose name the Kojiki writes 須佐之男 and glosses as the swift, impetuous male deity. Izanagi charged him with rule of the sea. But Susanoo never ceased weeping for his dead mother, crying so hard that the mountains withered and the rivers dried. Exasperated, Izanagi expelled him: 'If that is your wish, go to the land of your mother, then' (Kojiki 1). The storm god is thus the grieving child of creation, defined from birth by a longing for what cannot be retrieved — the sea he was given to rule is, after all, the element his father had fled into to escape death.

myths.title: The Test and the Trampling
myths.text: Climbing to heaven to bid his sister farewell, Susanoo alarmed Amaterasu, who went out armed; he protested his innocence and proposed an ukei, a covenant of sincerity, exchanging ornaments so that she bore three goddesses from his sword and he five gods from her necklace (Kojiki 1). The test cleared him — and he repaid it by trampling down the ridges of her rice-fields, filling the ditches, and flaying the heavenly piebald horse, whose carcass he hurled through the roof of her weaving hall, killing the maiden within. Amaterasu fled into the rock cave and sealed the door. Every one of his crimes strikes at cultivation — field, ditch, loom — the arts by which heaven imposes order on nature. Susanoo's rage is the sacred vandalism of the untamed.

lore.culturalLegacy: Izumo keeps his memory at Suga Jinja, and the sword he won from the serpent is counted among the imperial regalia — its physical keeper is Atsuta Jingū in Nagoya, which has revered Kusanagi since the Kofun period. The Gion Matsuri, among Japan's most famous festivals, descends from rites to his epidemic-fusing form, and serpent-quelling imagery guards thresholds in shrines across the country. His name rides typhoon warnings, sports teams, and the arsenal of fantasy fiction. Few gods better illustrate the double legacy of the storm: what a culture fears, it also celebrates.
lore.archaeology: Susanoo's cult centers mark the geography of his myth. Suga Jinja in Izumo City preserves the site of his post-serpent palace within the orbit of Izumo Ōyashiro, Japan's oldest shrine tradition. In Kyōto, Yasaka Shrine — the medieval home of his Gozu Tennō identity — is documented from the ninth century, and the Gion Matsuri's plague-warding origins are recorded in the late ninth-century court chronicles. Atsuta Jingū in Nagoya has revered the Kusanagi sword, said to rest there, since the Kofun period. Serpent-quelling imagery recurs in shrine carvings and festival regalia across Japan, where dragon-slaying scenes guard thresholds to this day.
lore.syncretism: In the medieval combinatory cult Susanoo was fused with Gozu Tennō, the ox-headed 'heavenly king' of epidemics, and enshrined as guardian of Kyōto's Gion quarter — the origin of Yasaka Shrine and its great Gion Matsuri, founded in 869 CE to ward off plague. The logic is the Kojiki's own: the god who brings destruction is the god who can forbid it. In Shugendō and in the Yoshida synthesis he absorbed further identities, while popular religion remembered him chiefly as the dragon-slayer of Izumo. Modern media have made him the most exported of the storm gods: the spectral warrior Susanoo of manga and games, and his namesake jutsu, carry the old name to audiences who never open the Kojiki.

variants.note: Standard Latin/English form

etymology.derivation: Greek Οἰδίπους 'swollen-foot', from οἰδάω 'to swell' and πούς 'foot'; the name encodes the injury inflicted on the infant exposed by his parents.

pronunciation.approximation: 'oy-DEE-poos' — stress the middle syllable; the diphthong is the 'oy' of 'boy', and the final syllable is long.
pronunciation.note: Oidípous is Tier 1 in the canonical classification: the restoration preserves the acute accent (ί) that plain ASCII flattens. The name is a speaking wound — ‘Swollen-foot’ — from the pins driven through the infant's ankles when he was exposed on Kithairon (οἰδάω + πούς).

domains.title: Fate
domains.subtitle: Fate, Riddles, Thebes
domains.lead: Oidípous is the Theban hero of fate, riddles and the terrible price of knowledge: the stranger who solved the Sphinx's riddle and could not read his own life. His story, told from Homer to Sophocles, made his name the Greek byword for what happens when human cleverness meets a destiny that has already been spoken.

cards.name: The Oracle of Delphi
cards.desc: Laios is told that his son will kill him — and every measure he takes to escape the prophecy drives it forward (Sophocles, Oidipous Tyrannos 711–725).

cards.name: Swollen-foot (from οἰδάω + πούς)
cards.desc: The name is the wound: the exposed infant's ankles were pierced and bound, and the pins gave him his name (Sophocles, OT 1034–1046).

cards.name: The Sphinx's Riddle
cards.desc: The creature with four feet, then two, then three held Thebes hostage; Oidípous answered where every citizen had failed (Sophocles, OT 391–402).

cards.name: The Crossroads
cards.desc: Where the roads from Delphi and Daulia meet, a chariot forced the stranger aside — and Laios died by his son's hand (Sophocles, OT 716–813).

symbols.name: The pierced ankles
symbols.meaning: The wound in the name: the pins that made the exposed child ‘Oidípous’

symbols.name: The Sphinx
symbols.meaning: The daughter of Typhon and Echidna who held Thebes hostage on her mountain (Hesiod, Theogony 326–329)

symbols.name: The golden brooches
symbols.meaning: Jocasta's dress-pins, with which Oidípous put out his own eyes at the hour of recognition (Sophocles, OT 1268–1279)

symbols.name: The crossroads
symbols.meaning: The place where three roads meet — the geometry of a prophecy fulfilling itself

symbols.name: The grove at Colonus
symbols.meaning: The Eumenides' ground outside Athens where the exile found his rest (Sophocles, Oidipous at Colonus 84–110)

mythology.lead: Oidípous is the subject of the most perfectly constructed tragedy in the Greek corpus. Homer, Hesiod and Pindar preserve fragments of his story; Sophocles gave it its final form in two plays set forty years apart — one the anatomy of self-discovery, the other the redemption of the polluted man. His fate is never a secret: the audience knows it from the first line, and that is the point.

myths.title: Pinned Ankles on Kithairon
myths.text:
Laios, king of Thebes, was warned by the Delphic oracle that the son born to him would kill his father. When the child came, he ordered it exposed on Mount Kithairon with a pin driven through its ankles to fix it to the ground; a shepherd took pity and passed the baby to a Corinthian, who carried it to the childless king Polybos. The wound named the child — Oidípous, ‘Swollen-foot’ — and the name told the story to every Greek who heard it. Homer already knows the tale in outline (Odyssey 11.271–280), Pindar tells how Laios, ‘who met the glorious oracle’, was destroyed by the son he feared (Olympian 2.35–42), and Sophocles keeps the pins (Oidipous Tyrannos 1034–1046).

The myth's engine is visible from the first scene: every act of prevention is a further link in the chain. The shepherd's pity — the one merciful gesture in the story — is exactly the mechanism by which the oracle is armed.

myths.title: The Singer at the Gates
myths.text:
On his road to Thebes Oidípous met the Sphinx — ‘who plagued the Cadmeans’, as Hesiod calls her, the daughter of Typhon and Echidna (Theogony 326–329) — and she put the riddle: what creature walks on four legs at dawn, two at noon and three in the evening. Citizens of Thebes had died for failing it; Oidípous answered man, who crawls, walks upright and leans on a staff in old age, and the Sphinx threw herself down from her rock. Grateful Thebes gave him the vacant throne and the widowed queen Jocasta. Sophocles has him tell it plainly: the man who saved the city by answering a question about the human condition could not ask the question that mattered about himself (OT 391–402).

The riddle is the tragedy in miniature. He solved the case of humanity in general and failed his own — and the two failures are one failure, of self-knowledge.

lore.culturalLegacy: The hero left two cults and a vocabulary. At Colonus the grove he sanctified remained sacred ground beside the Academy; at Thebes Pausanias (9.5) records the tomb of Oidipous and the tradition that his bones were brought back from Attica to protect the city that had exiled him — the polluted body as talisman. From the name come ‘oedipal’ and its compounds in every modern psychology; from the play come the critic's terms — peripeteia, anagnorisis, hamartia — that Aristotle coined while reading this one tragedy. Every retelling, from Seneca to the present, rehearses the same discovery: the story is not about incest and patricide, which Oidípous committed in ignorance, but about the moment a man learns what he is.
lore.archaeology: Oidipous is a Bronze Age memory wearing a Classical costume. Excavations on the Kadmeia at Thebes have uncovered a Mycenaean palace with its archive of Linear B tablets — a real Theban kingdom of the thirteenth century BC whose dynastic troubles could seed a legend of cursed kingship. The Sphinx he defeated still stands in stone: the Sphinx of the Naxians, dedicated at Delphi around 560 BC, is the very monster type, and Attic red-figure cups of the fifth century show Oidípous seated before her with the answer on his lips. No sanctuary of Oidipous has been excavated; his cult was a literary and civic one, kept at Colonus in the grove Sophocles describes and at Thebes in the tomb tradition Pausanias records.
lore.syncretism: The Romans received Oidipous chiefly as a name of terror and gave him a Latin tragedy of his own, Seneca's Oedipus, which rebuilt the story around oracular dread and kept the play alive through the Middle Ages into the Renaissance. Aristotle's Poetics, working from Oidipous Tyrannos, made its plot — peripeteia and anagnorisis combined in one stroke — the theory of tragedy for two millennia. In 1899 Freud named the ‘Oedipus complex’ after the hero, translating public fate into private childhood, and the twentieth century ran the change back through the arts: Cocteau's La Machine infernale, Gide's Oedipe, O'Neill's Mourning Becomes Electra, Pasolini's Edipo Re, Stravinsky's Oedipus Rex staged in Latin. The Greek original survives every translation because its subject — the unbearable speed of self-knowledge — is not antique.

variants.note: Standard Latin/English form

etymology.derivation: Kǒng (孔) the clan name; zǐ (子) 'master' — the honorific title of the philosopher Confucius (Kong Qiu).

pronunciation.approximation: “KOHNG-dzuh,” each syllable on a dipping-then-rising melody; said in one breath, the first tone lifts and the second dips.
pronunciation.note: Kǒngzǐ is Tier 1 because both syllables carry the third tone, marked by the carons ǒ and ǐ — tone is a lexical feature of Mandarin that the plain ASCII “kongzi” erases entirely. (The older entry described “stress and length”; the operative features are the two tone marks.)

domains.title: Confucius
domains.subtitle: Confucius, Moral Teaching, Ritual
domains.lead: Kǒngzǐ — Master Kong, Latinized by Jesuits as Confucius — is the teacher of China: the man who made learning, ritual propriety (lǐ 禮), and humaneness (rén 仁) the foundation of the good life and the good state. He claimed no revelation and no divinity — only transmission of the ancients — and became, for two and a half millennia, the archetype of the teacher.

cards.name: Rén — Humaneness
cards.desc: The core of his ethics: the fellow-feeling that makes one truly human; “loving others” is its shortest definition (Analects 12.22).

cards.name: Lǐ — Ritual Propriety
cards.desc: The rites that choreograph every relationship, from ancestral sacrifice to the cup offered a guest: reverence made visible.

cards.name: Tiān — Heaven
cards.desc: He spoke rarely of spirits but constantly of Heaven’s mandate (tiānmìng) as the moral horizon of conduct (Analects 3.13).

cards.name: The Analects
cards.desc: The Lúnyǔ 論語, “selected sayings,” compiled by disciples after his death — the core text of East Asian education for two thousand years.

symbols.name: Qilin of the birth-omen
symbols.meaning: The peace-beast said to have appeared before his birth, spitting a jade tablet announcing a child whose teaching would rule all under Heaven though he sat on no throne (later legend built on Shiji 47).

symbols.name: The Apricot Altar (Xíngtán 杏壇)
symbols.meaning: The teaching ground at Qufu where tradition seats the Master among his disciples; the phrase became a synonym for the school itself.

symbols.name: The Analects (Lúnyǔ 論語)
symbols.meaning: Twenty books of short exchanges — question, answer, sometimes only a sigh: the irreducible core of the tradition, memorized by every educated East Asian for two millennia.

symbols.name: The Stone Classics
symbols.meaning: The canon carved into stone at the imperial academy (the Xīpíng stones, 175–183 CE) so that no scribal error could corrupt the Master’s text.

symbols.name: The cypress of Qufu
symbols.meaning: The ancient cypresses at his tomb in the Kong Lin forest cemetery — living links in the longest documented family line on earth.

mythology.lead: Kǒngzǐ is a historical man — born 551 BCE in the state of Lǔ — but the tradition did with his biography what it does with all founders: it polished it into legend. The Shǐjì of Sīmǎ Qiān (ch. 47) supplies the framework, the Lúnyǔ the voice; between them stands the mythic Master, born under a portent, refused by every court, and vindicated only after death.

myths.title: The Qilin’s Jade Tablet (551 BCE)
myths.text: The legends of the Master’s birth are later embroidery on a plain record — Sīmǎ Qiān’s Shiji 47 says only that Kǒng Qiū was born in 551 BCE at Zōu in Lǔ, posthumous son of the aged soldier Kǒng Shūliáng Hé and the young Yán Zhēngzài. But tradition could not leave a founder without a portent: a qilin, the unicorn-beast that appears only when a sage is to come, was said to have entered the family courtyard and spat a jade tablet announcing a son whose doctrine would rule all under Heaven, though he would sit on no throne. The tablet bore the character for “hill” (qiū), and the child received it as his personal name — matching Mount Ni, beside which he was born — and the courtesy name Zhòngní, “second-born Ni.” Han thinkers gave the idea its name: the Master was the sùwáng, the “uncrowned king,” whose kingdom was the text. The legend means the tradition knew exactly what it had.

myths.title: The Master Asks Lǎozǐ About Rites
myths.text: In his thirties the young Kǒngzǐ travelled west to the royal capital of Zhōu to question the aged archivist Lǎozǐ about the rites of burial and mourning. Lǎozǐ, tradition says, received him coolly: “The men of whom you speak are bones now, and their words died with them… I have heard that a good merchant hides his store as though it were empty, and that a noble man in his bearing looks like a fool. Cast off your pride and your many desires — for neither profits you. That is all I have to say to you.” The Master returned and told his disciples: “I know how birds fly, how fish swim, how beasts run — but the dragon I cannot fathom, riding the wind and clouds up into Heaven. Today I have seen Lǎozǐ: he is such a dragon.” (Shiji 63.) The meeting is the tradition’s way of contrasting its two great teachers — the one who withdrew, and the one who knocked on every door.

lore.culturalLegacy: His living monument is Qufu: the Temple of Confucius — consecrated in 478 BCE, the year after his death, when Duke Āi of Lǔ turned his former residence into a shrine — the adjacent Kong Mansion, and the Kong Lin cemetery, together the largest classical building complex in China after the Forbidden City. His bloodline is on record longer than any other on earth: the Kong genealogy counts more than eighty documented generations. From 605 to 1905 the empire’s examinations were built on his classics, making him — by crib-book, temple sacrifice, and schoolhouse portrait — the single most studied author in human history. Taiwan still keeps Teachers’ Day on his traditional birthday, 28 September; and the everyday word rú 儒, “scholar,” is his school’s oldest name.
lore.archaeology: Qufu is the material anchor: the Temple of Confucius stands on the site of his residence, consecrated by Duke Āi of Lǔ in 478 BCE and rebuilt to its present Ming-era scale; beside it the Kong Mansion housed his descendants until 1949, and the Kong Lin cemetery holds over 100,000 lineage burials with thousands of stelae. Far older than any temple, the Guōdiàn bamboo slips — a Warring States library buried c. 300 BCE at Hubei and excavated in 1993 — preserve pre-imperial versions of texts in his tradition, proving the school was copying and teaching his books within three centuries of his death. And the Wǔ Liáng shrine stone reliefs (Shandong, 151 CE) already show the iconic scene of the young Kǒngzǐ asking Lǎozǐ about the rites: the myth cut in stone within three and a half centuries of the man.
lore.syncretism: The Master resisted deification in life — “while you do not yet know life, how can you know death?” (Analects 11.12) — but the Han state deified him anyway. Emperor Gāozǔ offered the first imperial sacrifice at his tomb in 195 BCE; by the Tang his posthumous titles swelled toward “King” and “Perfect Sage,” and Dǒng Zhòngshū gave his teaching cosmological armor. From Sòng times the neo-Confucians — above all Zhū Xī — rebuilt it into the metaphysics of East Asia, and for thirteen centuries the civil examinations made his classics the gateway to office in China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam. The West received him through the Jesuits: Ricci’s circle Latinized Kǒng Fūzǐ as Confucius, and Voltaire kept his portrait like a household saint. Modernity first dethroned him — the New Culture Movement denounced him as the face of feudalism — and then reinstated him. Few mortals have been so many things to so many regimes.

variants.note: Common English name

etymology.derivation: Yù (玉) 'jade'; Huáng (皇) 'emperor, sovereign' — the supreme deity of Chinese folk religion and Taoist cosmology.

pronunciation.approximation: 'YUE-hwong' — say 'ee' with rounded lips and let the pitch drop sharply; then 'hwong' with a soft guttural h, rising like a question.
pronunciation.note: Yùhuáng is Tier 1: the tones are the name's distinctive feature — Tone 4 on 玉 and Tone 2 on 皇 are the tonal equivalents of stress and length, and plain ASCII yuhuang erases the tone system entirely. The registrable form uses tone-marked Pinyin; the hanzi 玉皇 are shown in the Original Script card.

domains.title: Jade Emperor
domains.subtitle: Jade Emperor, Heaven, Sovereignty
domains.lead: Yùhuáng, the Jade Emperor, is the sovereign of the Daoist Heaven: supreme administrator of a celestial bureaucracy of thunder-ministers, star-officers, and registrars of life and death. Canonically ranked just below the Three Pure Ones, in the practice of every household he is the Heaven that receives, files, and answers prayer.

cards.name: The Throne of Heaven
cards.desc: Supreme administrator of the celestial bureaucracy — thunder, rain, plague, and the registers of life and death all report to his court.

cards.name: Jade Sovereign
cards.desc: 玉 yù, 'jade' — the incorruptible stone; 皇 huáng, 'sovereign': Heaven's ruler in the substance of Heaven.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Yùhuáng restores the falling and rising tones — the tone system itself — that plain yuhuang erases.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: 玉皇 attested in Tao Hongjing's Zhen'gao (5th century) and enthroned by Song imperial patronage from 1012.

symbols.name: The jade seal
symbols.meaning: The stamp that authenticates Heaven's decrees; jade itself — unchanging, luminous, and hard — is the substance of his name

symbols.name: The beaded imperial crown (mianguan)
symbols.meaning: The twelve-strand curtain crown of the highest rank, marking him as sovereign of the celestial court

symbols.name: The dragon throne
symbols.meaning: The axis of bureaucratic Heaven: from it issue the commissions of thunder, rain, and the registers of death

symbols.name: The peach of immortality
symbols.meaning: The Queen Mother of the West's peaches, served at the banquet of the gods (Journey to the West, ch. 5)

symbols.name: The memorial and the register
symbols.meaning: Petition and ledger: the machinery by which prayer ascends and fate descends

symbols.name: The Great Luo Heaven (Dàluó tiān)
symbols.meaning: His residence at the summit of the Daoist heavens, above the thirty-two lesser heavens

mythology.lead: The Jade Emperor's mythology is a late, literate construction — scripture, novel, and folk tale jointly building a biography and a government for Heaven. His stories ask the great bureaucratic question: who, exactly, is in charge? The answer, assembled from the fifth century to the Ming novel, is a sovereign with a résumé, a war record, and a court that even comedy cannot overthrow.

myths.title: The Making of a Sovereign
myths.text:
The Daoist canon answers the obvious question — where does Heaven's emperor come from? — with a full sacred biography. The Scripture of the Jade Sovereign's Former Deeds (Gaoshang Yuhuang benxing jijing, in the Ming Daozang) tells of the childless king of the Kingdom of Wondrous Bliss, whose queen, after years of prayer to the Dao, dreams that the supreme Lord hands her an infant wrapped in radiance. The prince, grown, marvels that even his happy kingdom cannot spare him from death; he gives the throne to a worthy minister and withdraws to the mountain to cultivate the Way — through kalpas of austerity, service to prior immortals, and ordeal after ordeal, until he ascends as Yùhuáng, the Jade Sovereign of the clearest heaven.

The scripture thus gives the celestial throne a curriculum vitae: Heaven's ruler is not born but made, refined like an alchemist's elixir across ages no chronicle can hold.

myths.title: The War Against the Demon Host
myths.text:
The same scripture and the popular tradition that grew from it give the future emperor his proving war. While the radiant prince still rules in his father's kingdom, a demon king — lord of black clouds, master of hosts — brings plague and darkness upon the world, and the gods of the older heavens cannot end him. The prince arms himself, and in the great battle that follows his radiance alone routs the demon armies; the defeated host swears fealty, and the victor — refusing even the throne of the conquered — returns to his mountain and his cultivation. Later novels, above all the Ming Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen yanyi), pour the same pattern over heaven itself, where the mandate passes from defeated tyrants to a righteous successor.

The myth's grammar is that of every dynastic founding: the old order falls not because the gods fail, but because the throne must change hands before its holder can be seen at all.

lore.culturalLegacy: His birthday, the ninth day of the first lunar month, is the feast of Tiāngōng — 天公誕 — kept with especial splendor by Hokkien- and Teochew-speaking communities in Taiwan, Fujian, and the diaspora of Southeast Asia, where families set a table of offerings facing the open sky at midnight. Daoist temples everywhere raise his image at the summit of the pantheon wall, beneath only the Three Pure Ones; the Yuan-dynasty murals of Yongle Palace in Shanxi preserve the grandest painted vision of his court. Through Journey to the West and its endless adaptations he is known worldwide as heaven's mild, beleaguered manager. In the full title 玉皇大帝 he remains the household name for the highest authority there is.
lore.archaeology: The god's material record begins with texts: the title Yùhuáng is attested in Tao Hongjing's Zhen'gao (5th century), and the imperial turn came under the Song — in 1012 Emperor Zhenzong announced a revelation from the 'Jade Emperor' and heaped honorific titles upon him, beginning the god's absorption of state Heaven worship. Daoist temple art gives him his body: the Yuan-dynasty murals of Yongle Palace (Ruicheng, Shanxi, 13th–14th century) paint his celestial court procession with the graded regalia of an earthly audience hall, and Ming and Qing temple walls repeat the program across China. His birthday altars, heaven-facing offering tables, and the ubiquitous 'tablet of Heaven' in village shrines are the folk archaeology of a cult that left few excavated monuments because it lived above ground, in the open sky.
lore.syncretism: The Jade Emperor is a late synthesis wearing an ancient title. The name Yùhuáng appears as early as Tao Hongjing's Zhen'gao (5th century), but the fully enthroned emperor is a product of the Tang and Song, when Daoism absorbed the older Lord on High (Shangdi) and the impersonal Heaven (Tiān) of state religion into a single personal sovereign. Canonically he remains, modestly, below the Three Pure Ones — the Dao itself in triplicate — while in practice he is Heaven's chief executive; the hierarchy lets theology and government mirror each other exactly. Popular religion went further: in Fujian and Taiwan he is Tiāngōng, 'Heaven's Duke,' whose birthday outranks every local god's, and Vietnamese communities worship the same figure as Ngọc Hoàng. Buddhist hells, thunder agencies, and star ministries all file their reports to his court.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 玉皇 — 玉 'jade' and 皇 'sovereign'. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Yùhuáng (Tone 4 + Tone 2), per Hanyu Pinyin and the Unihan Database; the registrable form uses tone-marked Pinyin, and the hanzi are displayed in the Original Script card.

etymology.derivation: Greek κράτος 'strength, power, might'; personified as one of the children of the Titan Pallas and Styx.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KRATOS' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.
pronunciation.note: Krátos is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the acute accent on the short penult is the one feature the ASCII 'Kratos' loses; there is no long vowel and no circumflex. In living Greek the acute was musical pitch. The name is a common noun personified — Strength — exactly as Níkē is Victory.

domains.title: Strength
domains.subtitle: Strength, Power, Sovereignty
domains.lead: Krátos is Strength enthroned beside Zeus: the personified might that executes the ruler of heaven's will. Son of Styx and Pallas, brother of Níkē, Bía, and Zelos, he dwells forever at the tyrant's right hand — and speaks Greek tragedy's bleakest doctrine: none is free but Zeus.

cards.name: Strength
cards.desc: Executive force: the power that enacts a decree once Zeus has made it — the will of heaven with hands.

cards.name: Sovereignty
cards.desc: The Greek noun behind -cracy itself: dēmokratíā, aristokratíā, autokratíā — the word that built 'democracy.'

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Krátos recovers the acute pitch accent that plain ASCII kratos flattens.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Attested in the original script as Κράτος — Hesiod's Theogony and Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound.

symbols.name: The adamantine bonds
symbols.meaning: The unbreakable chains Hephaestus forged in ignorance and Krátos fastens without pity (Prometheus Bound)

symbols.name: The Scythian crag
symbols.meaning: The remote cliff at the world's edge where Prometheus is nailed — the geography of force's work

symbols.name: Styx, mother
symbols.meaning: The underworld river whose oath binds the gods themselves — Krátos is born of the most terrible pledge

symbols.name: The house of Zeus
symbols.meaning: His only dwelling: the permanent right, granted after the Titanomachy, to sit forever beside the ruler of Olympus

mythology.lead: Krátos has no independent mythology — no quests, no loves, no temples. His entire dossier is a genealogy, an oath, one terrible scene, and the trace of a word in epic: the binding of Prometheus, in which he is the speaking voice of power.

myths.title: The Children of Styx
myths.text: Hesiod gives Krátos his family in the Theogony (375–383): the river Styx, daughter of Ocean, bore to Pallas four children — Zelos (Rivalry), trim-ankled Níkē (Victory), Krátos (Might), and Bía (Force). They are not decorative attendants. When the Titanomachy broke out, Styx was the first of the gods to bring her children over to Zeus's side, and for that loyalty Zeus granted them a rare honor: they live with him forever, 'for he ordained that they should dwell with him always and have honor beyond the other gods' (Theogony 383–403). Hyginus (Fabulae, preface) repeats the list and calls them primos in omnibus — first among all. The myth explains something precise about Greek ideas of rule: victory, rivalry, might, and force are not Zeus's rivals but his household, bound to him by gratitude and oath.

myths.title: The Will of Zeus
myths.text: Aeschylus stages Krátos in person. At the opening of Prometheus Bound, Might and Force — Krátos and Bía — drag the defiant Titan to a crag at the world's edge, and Krátos addresses the workman Hephaestus with the play's entire thesis: Zeus is new to power and ruthless; old loyalties count for nothing; 'there is no one free except Zeus' (Prometheus Bound 50–52). Hephaestus pities Prometheus and hesitates over the hammer; Krátos has no pity to hesitate with — he only checks that the work is done. Then he leaves the stage, his task complete, and never returns: force has nothing more to say once the chain is set. The drama built the West's first portrait of power as a functionary — efficient, unpersuadable, bored by the suffering it administers — and gave the abstraction a mask the audience could boo.

lore.culturalLegacy: Krátos's cult was nonexistent, but his word built a civilization's self-description. Classical Athens put his name in its constitution — dēmokratíā, the kratos of the dēmos — the same word, with the master changed, that Aeschylus' Krátos had claimed exclusively for Zeus. Every modern -cracy, from democracy to bureaucracy, descends from a god no city ever worshipped. Prometheus Bound, meanwhile, has been read in every age as an anatomy of state violence — by the Romantic rebels, by the generation of Marx, by modern stages that costume Krátos in a uniform. The personification without a temple turned out to have the largest parish of all: everyone who has felt the chain tighten knows exactly who is speaking.
lore.archaeology: No temple, image, or votive of Krátos is attested; his entire material record is textual. The binding of Prometheus was a favorite of Attic vase painters from the sixth century BCE — Hephaestus strapping the Titan to the crag, the Oceanids wringing their hands — but the painters show the smith, not Might; the pairing of Krátos and Bía belongs to Aeschylus' stage, and papyri of Prometheus Bound from Roman Egypt are the god's only 'sites.' Even his mother left barely a footprint: Styx was honored at a single Arcadian spring and a hill in Elis (Pausanias 8.17–18) — a fitting inheritance for the family of oaths: real, but rarely visited.
lore.syncretism: Rome had no Krátos: the personification was too specifically Aeschylean to transplant, and no Latin cult of Vis or Potestas mirrors him. His afterlife is instead linguistic and theatrical. Through the suffix -kratia the word seeded the political vocabulary of the West — dēmokratíā, aristokratíā, autokratíā, bureaucratia: 'democracy,' 'aristocracy,' 'autocracy,' 'bureaucracy' are all his name doing new work. And in 2005 Sony's God of War borrowed the name for a Spartan anti-hero — a character who shares nothing with Hesiod's functionary beyond the word, which is itself the point. Strength recognizes no genealogy: wherever power is enthroned and chains are fastened without pity, the audience still supplies the name.

entries.meaning: He who goes forth shining; the Nahuatl sun god

etymology.derivation: Classical Nahuatl Tōnatiuh, the sun; the fifth sun of the Aztec cosmos, born from the sacrifice of Nanahuatzin.

steps: Nahuatl was recorded by Spanish and native scribes in Latin alphabets from the sixteenth century onward.
Tōnatiuh is the sun deity; the name is attested in the Florentine Codex and colonial devotional texts.
The macron marks a long vowel in scholarly Classical Nahuatl orthography.
The Unicode restoration Tōnatiuh preserves the long vowel; there is no indigenous logographic spelling for the personal name.
provenanceSources: Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl

pronunciation.approximation: 'toh-NAH-tiw' — stretch the first o for two beats; end with a quick 'tiw,' the lips rounding shut at the close.
pronunciation.note: Tōnatiuh is Tier 1: the macron of ō preserves the long vowel that Classical Nahuatl actually pronounced, a phonemic length the ASCII form tonatiuh erases entirely.

domains.title: Sun
domains.subtitle: Sun, Heat, Fifth Age
domains.lead: Tōnatiuh is the Nahuatl sun god of the present age — Nahui Ollin, '4-Movement,' the Fifth Sun. His name, from tōna, 'to be hot, to shine,' names the burning disk that rises only because the gods fed it their own hearts. He is the engine of the Aztec cosmos: war, tribute, and sacrifice all answer his appetite.

cards.name: Sun
cards.desc: The Fifth Sun of the present age, Nahui Ollin — '4-Movement' — who crosses the sky only while fed with hearts.

cards.name: The Shining One
cards.desc: From tōna 'to shine, to be hot' + -tiuh 'one who goes': the name itself means 'he who goes forth shining.'

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The macron of Tōnatiuh restores the long ō Classical Nahuatl actually pronounced; plain ASCII flattens the vowel to a single beat.

cards.name: Attestation
cards.desc: Painted in the Aztec codices with a frontal solar face; in Roman letters in Sahagún's Florentine Codex and the Anales de Cuauhtitlan.

symbols.name: Sun disk with face and tongue
symbols.meaning: The frontal solar face of the codices, often shown with a protruding tongue — the sacrificial blade set in the god's own mouth

symbols.name: Ollin (movement) glyph
symbols.meaning: The trembling, striped sign of earthquake and motion that names the present age — the day-sign of the Fifth Sun

symbols.name: Obsidian knife (itztli)
symbols.meaning: The blade with which Quetzalcoatl opened the gods' breasts to feed the unmoving sun

symbols.name: Eagle (cuāuhtli)
symbols.meaning: The warrior-bird whose spirits — the eagle and jaguar dead — take up the sun's burden from noon onward

symbols.name: Sacrificial blood
symbols.meaning: The nourishment without which the sun stands still; the cosmic debt paid at every temple

mythology.lead: Tōnatiuh's mythology is the mythology of the Fifth Sun — the age we inhabit. The Nahuatl sources preserve the legend of how our sky was lit, and together they make daylight a running debt: the sun was born of a god's courage at Teotihuacan, and it moves only while it is fed.

myths.title: Nahui Ollin — The Sun of Movement
myths.text: Before our sky there were four suns, each destroyed: 4-Jaguar, when jaguars devoured the giants; 4-Wind, when hurricanes swept the people from the earth; 4-Rain of Fire, when the sky rained flames; 4-Water, when the flood came and the people became fish (Anales de Cuauhtitlan; Codex Vaticanus A). After the flood the gods gathered in darkness at Teotihuacan, the 'Place Where the Gods Were Made,' and asked who would light the world. The proud Tecuciztecatl and the humble, pox-scabbed god Nanahuatzin both offered to leap into the great fire. Tecuciztecatl faltered at the flames and leapt only at the shaming of the others; Nanahuatzin, who had no pride to lose, plunged straight in — and rose as the new sun, the moon following ashamed behind him (Florentine Codex, Book VII). Our age is therefore Nahui Ollin, '4-Movement,' and its sign is the earthquake: the sun of the present world moves, and everything that moves can end. The old gods did not make our sky to last — they made it to be paid for.

myths.title: The Sun That Demands Hearts
myths.text: When the new sun rose it would not move. 'How shall I live?' it said. 'I cannot move — feed me, nourish me' (Anales de Cuauhtitlan). The gods understood at once: no sun moves on its own strength. Quetzalcoatl took the obsidian blade, and the gods went willingly to be opened — their hearts fed the fire, and only then did the sun begin its road across the sky. The chronicles and codices name this sun Tōnatiuh, 'he who goes forth shining,' the same deity the fate-books enthrone at 13-Olin in the tonalamatl (Codex Borbonicus; Codex Vaticanus A). The tellings differ on the fire-leaper's name — Nanahuatzin in Sahagún's version, Tōnatiuh in the calendar books — but they agree completely on the economy: daylight is a loan, and the debt is paid in what is most alive. Aztec war, tribute, and temple sacrifice are not cruelty for its own sake in this theology; they are the interest on the world's first meal.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Piedra del Sol — the Aztec Sun Stone excavated beside Mexico City's cathedral in 1790 — hangs in the National Museum of Anthropology as the single most reproduced image of ancient Mexico, its solar face on coins, textbooks, and murals. The muralists of the revolutionary decades, Diego Rivera foremost, drew the Aztec cosmos as the deep past of the modern nation, and the sun's face entered the vocabulary of twentieth-century art. The name Tōnatiuh has returned as a given name in Mexico and in Nahuatl-language revitalization; it names schools, cultural groups, and festivals — a deity's rebirth as civic memory, and proof that a language's oldest word for the sun still knows how to shine in new mouths.
lore.archaeology: The Great Temple (Templo Mayor) of Tenochtitlan, excavated from 1978 onward, was the engine-house of the sun cult: its building phases and offering caches — including the great Tlaltecuhtli earth-monolith and sacrificed warriors — anchor the theology in material practice. The Piedra del Sol, found in 1790 and now the centerpiece of the Museo Nacional de Antropología, bears the frontal face usually identified as Tōnatiuh (though the earth-monster and the night-lord have their defenders). The Codex Borbonicus (Bibliothèque de l'Assemblée nationale, Paris) shows his enthronement in the trecena 13-Olin. Teotihuacan — the pyramids named in the legend as the sun's birthplace — preserves an older, different solar cult a thousand years before the Aztecs, and its Pyramid of the Sun shows how deep the nameless reverence for this site ran.
lore.syncretism: In the colonial centuries Tōnatiuh was mapped onto Christ — the rising sun read as the risen Son, an equation early missionaries exploited from both sides and Nahua communities adapted, so that reverence for the dawn survived inside Christian liturgy (Durán, Book of the Gods; Ricard, The Spiritual Conquest of Mexico). The old calendar lived on under saints' days while the tonalpohualli was driven into the villages. In the twentieth century the figure returned as a national one: the so-called Aztec Sun Stone, excavated in 1790, became the emblem of Mexico, its central frontal face usually identified as Tōnatiuh — though some scholars read the earth-monster or the night-lord there instead. Unlike the Greek Helios, who dissolved into allegory, Tōnatiuh never stopped being worshipped; he changed altars, and then changed back.

entries.meaning: Creator of the earth; primordial ancestor of the Yoruba

etymology.derivation: Yoruba Ọdùduwà, the divine ancestor who descended with a chain at Ile-Ife and founded the Yoruba city-states.

steps: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality.
The underdot marks the open vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ and the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/; these are the obligatory phonemic marks.
Tone marks (grave low, acute high, mid unmarked) are fully written in dictionaries but routinely omitted in everyday Yoruba writing.
The owned Unicode form preserves the underdots and the tone marks the domain could carry; the fully tone-marked dictionary form is documented here.

pronunciation.approximation: 'oh-doo-DOO-wah' — four even syllables; the grave-marked syllables ù and à are low in pitch, sung below the others, not stressed harder.
pronunciation.note: Odùduwà is Tier 1: the restored form carries the Yoruba tone marks — low ù and à — that the ASCII oduduwa cannot write. The marks are the name: a Yoruba speaker reads pitch, not spelling.

domains.title: Progenitor
domains.subtitle: Progenitor, Ile-Ife, First King
domains.lead: Odùduwà is the founder: the heaven-sent ancestor who made the earth firm, founded Ilé-Ifẹ̀, and fathered the dynasties of the Yoruba world. Every Yoruba king claims descent from him, and the Oòni of Ifẹ̀, his living heir, is the acknowledged spiritual head of the tradition.

cards.name: Progenitor
cards.desc: The primordial ancestor of Yoruba kingship — Ifẹ̀ tradition names his sons and grandsons as the founders of the Yoruba towns and their dynasties.

cards.name: Maker of the Firm Earth
cards.desc: He took the materials of creation — a handful of earth, a five-toed cockerel, a chain — and made the dry land on which the world stands (Ifá corpus; oral tradition).

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Odùduwà recovers the low tones that plain ASCII oduduwa flattens — in Yoruba, pitch is meaning.

cards.name: Ifá and Oral Attestation
cards.desc: Attested in the Ifá corpus and Yoruba oral tradition; Yoruba's Latin orthography is a nineteenth-century standardization, so the true attestation is tonal and performative, not alphabetic.

symbols.name: The chain of descent
symbols.meaning: The chain by which Odùduwà climbed down from Ọ̀run, the sky, to the primordial waters — the umbilical cord between heaven and the first city

symbols.name: The five-toed cockerel
symbols.meaning: The sacred fowl whose scratching spread the scattered handful of earth into the world's dry land

symbols.name: The handful of earth
symbols.meaning: The seed-soil of creation given by Olódùmarè — from a fistful of dust, a continent

symbols.name: Red earth of Ifẹ̀
symbols.meaning: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, 'the house of expansion' — the red soil where creation began and where his shrine still stands

symbols.name: The Ade Aare crown
symbols.meaning: The ancient crown of Ifẹ̀, worn by the Oòni only at the Olojo festival and believed by tradition to have been Odùduwà's own

mythology.lead: Odùduwà's story is the Yoruba Genesis: the descent from heaven, the making of dry land, the founding of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, and the fathering of dynasties. It lives in the Ifá corpus and in oral tradition rather than any fixed book, and the tellings disagree with one another — the tradition itself treats the variants as paths to the same city.

myths.title: Seventeen from Ọ̀run
myths.text:
In the beginning the world was water: Olódùmarè, the supreme God, ruled from Ọ̀run, the sky, while Ayé, the earth below, was soft marsh without a place to stand. The orishas petitioned to build a dry world, and Olódùmarè chose Ọbàtálá — Oríṣàńlá, the most senior among them — to lead the mission down, with Odùduwà in the company: in some tellings his younger brother, in others simply the keeper of the god's bag of materials. The delegation received what creation required — a handful of earth, a five-toed cockerel, and a chain long enough to climb from heaven to the waves. The number of the delegates shifts between tellings, sixteen or seventeen, as oral tradition allows. The story is recorded in the tellings collected by Bascom, Johnson, and Idowu from the Ifá corpus and Ifẹ̀ priests.

The myth's quiet claim is that creation in Yoruba thought is delegated: God entrusts the founding of the world to a team, and seniority alone does not finish the job. The one who climbs down will matter more than the one who was chosen to lead — and the tradition already knows it.

myths.title: The Sleep of Ọbàtálá
myths.text:
Before the descent, Ọbàtálá grew thirsty and drank palm wine — and the wine dulled him. He staggered, fell, and slept beside the work he had been sent to do. Odùduwà took the bag from his sleeping brother, climbed down the chain to the primordial waters, scattered the handful of earth onto the waves, and set the five-toed cockerel to scratching; the fowl spread the dust outward into wide dry land, beginning at the place that became Ifẹ̀. When Ọbàtálá awoke and came down to find the creation finished by another hand, the rivalry between the two worship-lines was born. Tradition adds the ritual moral: Ọbàtálá therefore forbade his priests the palm wine that undid him.

The myth explains two lasting facts at once — the founding of Ifẹ̀ and a living taboo in Ọbàtálá's cult — and its judgement is characteristic of Yoruba narrative: creation passes not to the most senior but to the most steadfast, and the instrument of failure is never an enemy, only a pleasure taken at the wrong hour.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ilé-Ifẹ̀ remains the spiritual capital of the Yoruba world: the Oòni is its ritual head, chiefs from every Yoruba town pay ceremonial allegiance, and the Olojo festival draws the diaspora home. The city is also one of Africa's great art-historical sites: the naturalistic terracotta and bronze heads excavated at Ifẹ̀, dating roughly to the twelfth through fifteenth centuries, made the city famous as a medieval centre of masterly casting and modelling, and sit today in Lagos, London, and Paris. The Ifẹ̀ corpus shaped how the world studies Yoruba religion — Bascom's and Idowu's works, and the Ifá traditions themselves, made Ilé-Ifẹ̀ the reference point of the field. And in everyday life the name still does its founding work: to be Yoruba is to know the road back to Ifẹ̀, and Odùduwà is the reason the road exists. Restoring the tones of Odùduwà returns the name to the pitch in which that claim is spoken.
lore.archaeology: The material record of the myth is the city itself. Excavations at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ — beginning with Frobenius's notorious 1910 visit and continuing through the work of Willett, Eyo, and Fabunmi — uncovered the celebrated Ifẹ̀ heads: naturalistic terracotta portrait heads and copper-alloy castings of the twelfth to fifteenth centuries CE, among them the bronze heads found in 1938 in the Wunmonije compound, interpreted in tradition as the shrine images of past Oònis. The iron-crusted Opa Ọ̀rànmíyàn, a monolith over five metres tall, still stands at Ifẹ̀ as the monumental staff of Odùduwà's youngest son, and the sacred sites of the city — Odùduwà's shrine, the Olojo ground, the groves — keep the founding geography walkable. Ifẹ̀'s red earth, the stuff of the creation story, is underfoot everywhere the myth names.
lore.syncretism: In the African diaspora the founder travelled with his people. In Brazilian Candomblé, Oxalá — the counterpart of Ọbàtálá — appears in two aspects, the young warrior Oxaguiã and the ancient creator Oxalufã, and several houses read the younger aspect as the lineal continuation of Odùduwà himself; in Cuban Santería he is remembered under the name Odudua, though Ọbàtálá dominates the liturgy. Within Nigeria the identification flows the other way: Odùduwà has been increasingly worshipped as an orisha in his own right, and in places identified with the sea-god Olókun, an association the lineages themselves debate. In the modern world the name has outgrown religion: Odùduwà functions as a pan-Yoruba symbol of common origin — on university gates, in cultural congresses, and in the political language of Yoruba identity — so that the founder has become, in effect, the patron of the idea of being Yoruba at all.

entries.meaning: Highest Emperor; the supreme god of early Chinese religion

etymology.derivation: Shàng (上) 'above, highest'; Dì (帝) 'emperor, thearch' — the high god of Shang and Zhou religion, later identified with Tian.

pronunciation.approximation: SHAHNG-dee, both syllables falling in pitch — ‘SHAHNG!’ ‘DEE!’, as if a command were travelling downward from on high.
pronunciation.note: Shàngdì is Tier 1 by the mechanical rule: the tone marks are preserved diacritics that ASCII flattens, and the tones are phonemic in Mandarin. The restoration also carries the older sacral sense — on the oracle bones, 上帝 is less a pronunciation than a title: the god who is above.

domains.title: Supreme Deity
domains.subtitle: Supreme Deity, Heaven, Sovereign
domains.lead: Shàngdì (上帝), the “Highest Thearch,” is the supreme god of earliest recorded Chinese religion — the divine sovereign to whom the Shang kings reported through oracle-bone divination and border sacrifice, ancestor of the later concept of Tiān (Heaven), and the distant original of the imperial Temple of Heaven.

cards.name: The Border Sacrifice
cards.desc: The jiào 郊 at the southern suburban altar: the Son of Heaven’s open-air offering to Shàngdì, performed for three millennia.

cards.name: Heaven’s Mandate
cards.desc: 天命 Tiānmìng: dynasties reign by Shàngdì’s charge and fall when the charge is exhausted — the oldest Chinese theory of legitimacy.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The tones in Shàngdì carry meaning; plain ‘shangdi’ flattens the name into something no dynasty would recognise.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Written 上帝 on oracle bones from Yinxu (Anyang), ca. 1250–1046 BCE — China’s oldest readable archive.

symbols.name: The graph 帝
symbols.meaning: The ‘thearch’ sign — the high god’s title on the oracle bones, later inherited by every human emperor.

symbols.name: The oracle bone
symbols.meaning: Turtle plastron and ox scapula, cracked and inscribed: the medium through which the Shang kings reported to Shàngdì.

symbols.name: The southern border altar (郊)
symbols.meaning: Open-air sacrifice on bare ground south of the capital — no roof allowed to stand between offering and sky.

symbols.name: The jade disk (璧)
symbols.meaning: The round jade symbol of Heaven, paired in royal offerings with the square cōng tube of earth.

symbols.name: The Hall of Light (明堂)
symbols.meaning: The cosmological hall where the king faced the directions of Shàngdì’s realm and enacted the seasons (Liji, ‘Míngtáng wèi’).

mythology.lead: Shàngdì has no birth-story and no wandering heroics: the earliest Chinese supreme god rules from above as a sovereign, granting harvest, victory, and the mandate to kings who sacrifice at his altar. What survives is not a cycle of myths but three thousand years of court theology — divination, sacrifice, and the argument over what it means that Heaven is watching.

myths.title: The King’s Reports
myths.text: At Yinxu, the last Shang capital (modern Anyang), the kings spoke with Shàngdì through bone and shell. Diviners cracked turtle plastrons and ox scapulae over heat and read the fractures; the questions — Will the harvest be good? Should the king hunt at X? Will Lady Hǎo’s childbearing be lucky? — were carved beside the cracks, and sometimes the outcomes were recorded after the fact. The inscriptions show a god who governs wind, rain, drought, and disease, accepts sacrifice, and stands above the royal ancestors yet communes with them (Yinxu oracle-bone corpus, ca. 1250–1046 BCE). What survives is not scripture but correspondence: the oldest continuously readable archive on earth is a king’s file of reports to his god. The mythic grammar is already fully formed — heaven sends misfortune when neglected and favour when fed — and it would structure Chinese political theology for three thousand years.

myths.title: The Duke of Zhou’s Proclamation
myths.text: When the Zhōu overthrew the Shang (traditional date 1046 BCE), they faced a theological crisis: how could Heaven’s own dynasty fall? The answer, forged in the Duke of Zhōu’s proclamations, became China’s central political doctrine. The Shang kings had reigned by a charge from on high — the oracle bones already call the god 上帝, and the Zhōu hymns sing ‘Vast is Shàngdì, the ruler of the people below’ (Shijing, Dàyǎ, ‘Dàng’) — but Heaven withdraws its mandate from unvirtuous rulers and bestows it elsewhere: ‘Heaven sees as my people see, Heaven hears as my people hear’ (Shūjīng, ‘Tàishì’). In the transmission the name itself migrates: Shàngdì’s personal sovereignty becomes Tiān, Heaven, the Zhōu’s more abstract guarantor (Shūjīng, ‘Dà Gào’). One conquest thus rewrote the supreme god into a principle — and made every later rebellion a theological argument armed with a scriptural proof-text.

lore.culturalLegacy: Shàngdì’s descendant building stands in Beijing: the Temple of Heaven (Tiāntán), raised under the Yongle emperor in 1420, where the Son of Heaven prayed at the winter solstice in the direct line of the ancient jiào — the longest continuous sacral architecture on earth. His name still means God: the Chinese Union Version Bible of 1919 chose 上帝 for the God of Abraham, a decision that divides Chinese churches to this day (many prefer 神), while Catholicism, after Ricci’s defeat, standardised 天主, ‘Lord of Heaven.’ In scholarship, David Keightley’s work on the oracle bones made the Shang god a test case for how religion and statecraft fused at the very beginning of Chinese civilisation. Few divine names have been fought over so often — by dynasties, Jesuits, Protestants, and philologists — and survived the fighting so intact.
lore.archaeology: The material witness is the Yinxu archive itself: the oracle-bone pits of Anyang, excavated since 1928 after their recognition in 1899 as ‘dragon bones’ in Beijing pharmacies, hold well over a hundred thousand inscribed bones and shells — the working papers of the Shang court’s dialogue with Shàngdì. Around them stand the royal tombs of the Shang necropolis, including the intact tomb of Lady Hǎo (excavated 1976) with its bronzes and sacrificial burials, and the foundry quarters that produced the ritual vessels the inscriptions say were offered at the altars. Three thousand years downstream, the circular Altar of Heaven and Hall of Prayer in Beijing repeat the open-air geometry of the jiào: bare ground, round jade, sky above — nothing in between.
lore.syncretism: The Han dynasty absorbed Shàngdì into a larger heaven: Tiān became the all-encompassing term while the five directional Thearchs (Wǔdì) shared honours once his alone, a syncretism recorded in the ritual debates of the Shǐjì and the Báihǔtōng. The most consequential identification, however, came from Europe. Matteo Ricci, in the Tiānzhǔ Shíyì (1603), argued that the Chinese had always known the true God — Shàngdì and Tiān were China’s names for the Christian Deus — and chose 上帝 as the word for God in his catechism. The Figurists went further, reading the classics as a primitive revelation; Rome disagreed, and the papal rulings of 1707 and 1715 (Ex illa die) condemned the equation. Protestant missionaries reopened the question in the nineteenth century, and modern scholarship still debates whether the Shang Shàngdì was a high god above nature, the supreme ancestor of the royal line, or both at once. Every party has wanted him.
lore.originalScriptNote: Shàngdì is written 上帝 — 上 ‘above, highest’ set over 帝 ‘thearch,’ the supreme god’s title as it stands on the oracle bones. The paleography of 帝 is debated — readings range from a tied bundle of sacrificial wood to the calyx of a flower — but from the Shang bones onward its sense is fixed: the title above all titles, later lent, with a humanising prefix, to every emperor as 皇帝 huángdì.

entries.domain: Lord of the World, Puri, Devotion

etymology.derivation: Sanskrit Jagannātha, from jagat 'world, universe' + nātha 'lord, protector'; the form of Krishna worshipped at Puri.

steps: Sanskrit Jagannātha is written in Devanagari as जगन्नाथ
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: JUH-gun-NAH-thuh — hold the long aa on 'nah', keep the rhythm trochaic, and let the final th be a soft, breathy 'tuh'.
pronunciation.note: Jagannātha is Tier 1 because the Sanskrit form preserves what ASCII flattens: the long ā of -nātha and the geminate n are load-bearing in the IAST restoration, and the name's division jagat + nātha ('Lord of the World') is visible only when the vowel length is written. The earlier placeholder note's claim about 'stress' was wrong — Sanskrit does not mark stress; length and the doubled nasal do the work.

domains.title: Lord of the World
domains.subtitle: Lord of the World, Puri, Devotion
domains.lead: Jagannātha is Viṣṇu as the Lord of the World, worshipped at Puri in Odisha in a form older than any scripture about him: a great-eyed wooden god with no arms, who rides out once a year on a towered chariot pulled by human hands. His mythology is the story of how the world came to Puri — a tribal deity, a king's vow, a carpenter who vanished, and a journey that never stopped.

cards.name: Puruṣottama-kṣetra
cards.desc: Puri, the sacred field where the Lord owns the land itself — in 1238 CE King Anangabhima III dedicated his entire kingdom to him.

cards.name: The Unfinished Hands
cards.desc: The icons have no arms and no legs: the carpenter of the gods vanished before finishing them, and the tradition kept them unfinished on purpose.

cards.name: The Three Siblings
cards.desc: Jagannātha with Balabhadra and Subhadrā on one platform — Kṛṣṇa, his brother, and his sister, worshipped as one household.

cards.name: The Ratha Yātrā
cards.desc: Once a year the Lord leaves the temple and rides a city-high wooden chariot pulled by thousands of hands down the Grand Road to his aunt's house.

symbols.name: The armless form
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty that receives rather than grasps — the Lord needs no hands, because his people's hands are his

symbols.name: The dāru-brahman, the log of Brahman
symbols.meaning: The Lord came to Puri not as an idol but as fragrant timber floating from the sea

symbols.name: The chariot rope
symbols.meaning: To pull it is to be pulled — grace transmitted through the shoulder, not the eye

symbols.name: The Nīlācala, Blue Mountain
symbols.meaning: The hill of Puri the Lord chose as his seat, where the Sabara chief first kept him in secret

symbols.name: Mahāprasāda
symbols.meaning: The sacred food from the world's largest kitchen, eaten by all together without distinction of caste

symbols.name: The round eyes
symbols.meaning: The wide unblinking gaze of the unfinished icons — the Lord watching the world without eyelids

mythology.lead: Jagannātha's mythology is a foundation epic told in temple chronicles and Purāṇic chapters rather than in any single scripture. It tells how the Lord of the World came to the Odia coast: hidden among tribal worshippers, sought by a king, carved by a carpenter who vanished, and carried in person through his own city once every year.

myths.title: The Blue Lord of the Sabaras
myths.text: King Indradyumna of Malwa heard whispers of a wonder: on the remote Blue Mountain of the eastern coast, the tribal chief Viśvavāsu worshipped in secret a form of Viṣṇu called Nīlamādhava, the Blue Lord. The king sent his priest Vidyāpati to find him. Vidyāpati lived among the Sabaras, won the chief's trust, and married his daughter Lalitā; when he was led at last to the hidden shrine, he scattered mustard seed along the path so the king could follow. But a storm swept down and carried the Blue Lord away before Indradyumna arrived. The king fasted on the shore, performed the horse sacrifice at Puruṣottama-kṣetra, and waited. In a dream the god spoke: build a temple, and I will come to you as a log from the sea. The Puruṣottama-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa tells the tale, and the temple chronicle Mādala Pāñjī keeps it. The myth absorbs without erasing: the Sabara chief's line holds to this day the hereditary right to touch the god before anyone else.

myths.title: The Carpenter Who Never Finished
myths.text: One dawn a great log of fragrant reddish wood drifted in from the sea — dāru-brahman, Brahman come as timber, bearing the marks of conch, discus, mace, and lotus. An old carpenter arrived unasked and promised the king three images in twenty-one days, on one condition: no one might open the workshop door. Day by day the king waited; on the fourteenth day — the nineteenth in some tellings — the door was opened, and the carpenter was gone. On the platform stood three figures with huge round eyes and no arms: Jagannātha, his brother Balabhadra, his sister Subhadrā. Indradyumna was stricken, but the sage Nārada consoled him: the Lord had chosen the form his people would love, and the unfinished state was no accident but an invitation. The Mādala Pāñjī preserves the story; the Skanda Purāṇa tells a shorter form. A god who cannot hold anything must be held by his people — which is exactly what happens to him every single year.

lore.culturalLegacy: Jagannātha anchors one of Hinduism's four great pilgrimages — the Char Dham — and Puri's kitchen is the largest in the world, feeding upward of a hundred thousand people a day with mahāprasāda eaten without caste distinction, a daily sacrament of equality run on firewood and hereditary cooks. Every twelve to nineteen years the wooden gods are ceremonially buried and replaced with new neem logs in the rite of Nabakalebara, 'new embodiment' — perhaps the only major cult in which the deity's body is periodically allowed to die. For Odisha, Jagannātha is more than a god: royal inscriptions from 1238 declare him the owner of the kingdom, and modern Odia identity still speaks of the land as his household. And through ISKCON's global Ratha Yātrās and the word juggernaut, the Lord of the World has become, accidentally and thoroughly, a citizen of every city on earth.
lore.archaeology: The present great temple was begun by the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva (r. 1078–1150 CE) and completed under his successors, above all Anangabhima III (r. 1211–1238 CE), whose inscriptions of 1238 declare the kingdom itself the property of Puruṣottama-Jagannātha — a rare case of a state legally deeding itself to its god. The Nīlācala hill beneath the temple held older, humbler shrines remembered in the Purāṇic chapters, and the Skanda Purāṇa's Puruṣottama-kṣetra mahātmya claims sanctity far older than any surviving masonry. The images themselves are perishable by design: neem wood, repainted and repaired on a fixed cycle and wholly replaced at the Nabakalebara rite, so the god's body is a documented sequence of bodies. The chariot-yard, the Grand Road, and the Gundicha temple complete a ritual city-plan without parallel — a town whose main street exists so that its god can leave home once a year.
lore.syncretism: Jagannātha is syncretism made architecture. The tribal layer survives in the Sabaras' hereditary service; the Buddhist hypothesis — stupa, tooth relic, converted shrine — hung over the temple through two centuries of scholarship before the Eschmann–Kulke–Tripathi study (1978) reframed the god as a deliberate layering rather than a conversion. Jain memory claims the early mathas of Puri; the Brahmanical settlement made him Puruṣottama, and the devotional revolution of the Gītagovinda made him Kṛṣṇa. Colonial travellers turned his chariot into an English common noun — juggernaut — and the crown of his modern reception belongs to ISKCON: since 1967–68, Prabhupāda's disciples have staged the Ratha Yātrā in San Francisco, London, and every major city on earth, so that the armless god of one Odia town now rides annually through most of the world's capitals. In Puri itself the Gajapati king still sweeps the chariot floor with a golden broom — a living kingship rite older than every republic around it.

etymology.derivation: Old Norse Jǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *erþō 'earth'; personified as a jötunn and mother of Thor by Odin.

steps: The name Jǫrð is recorded in the Poetic and Prose Eddas, preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts.
Younger Futhark runic inscriptions do not preserve the name directly; the runic spelling is a scholarly reconstruction.
The normalized Old Norse form Jǫrð uses the letter ǫ (o with ogonek) for the rounded back vowel and ð (eth) for the voiced dental fricative.
The Unicode restoration jǫrð.com preserves the normalized Norse spelling; the runic form is displayed as the original script.
provenanceSources: Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic

pronunciation.approximation: YORTH — the first sound is English 'y', the vowel the open 'o' of 'thought', and the name ends on the voiced 'th' of 'this'.
pronunciation.note: Jǫrð is Tier 1: the ǫ and the ð are distinctive letters that ASCII flattens entirely — 'jord' loses the nasalised vowel and the voiced fricative of the Old Norse name.

domains.title: Earth
domains.subtitle: Earth, Mother of Thor
domains.lead: Jǫrð is the Norse earth — not a character with adventures but the ground itself personified: daughter of Night, wife of Óðinn, and mother of Þórr, the mightiest of the gods. The skalds need no stories about her; they call the very land by her name, and every thunder-clap is her son walking.

cards.name: The Earth
cards.desc: Her domain is the ground itself — fields, mountains, graves; she is the oldest of the ásynjur because everything stands on her.

cards.name: Earth Mother of Þórr
cards.desc: By Óðinn she bears Þórr, strongest of the gods — the storm literally born of the earth (Gylfaginning ch. 9; Skáldskaparmál).

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Jǫrð recovers the ǫ and ð that plain ASCII jord flattens; the restoration is the name as the skalds wrote it.

cards.name: In the Eddas
cards.desc: Listed among the ásynjur and invoked in kennings — 'son of Jǫrð' is Þórr's standard style from Bragi to the late skalds.

symbols.name: The land itself
symbols.meaning: She needs no emblem: in skaldic kennings the ground is her body, and 'the meal of Jǫrð' is a kenning for the dust of the earth

symbols.name: Þórr
symbols.meaning: Her son by Óðinn: the thunder-god's strength is earth-strength, and 'Jǫrð's son' is among his commonest titles

symbols.name: Fjǫrgyn and Hlóðyn
symbols.meaning: Her twin names in the poetry — Völuspá calls the thunderer 'Hlóðyn's glorious son' (v. 56) — three masks for a single mother

symbols.name: The dark lineage
symbols.meaning: As daughter of Anarr and Nótt (Night) she belongs to the old giant layer of the cosmos, older than Óðinn's race

mythology.lead: Jǫrð has no saga of her own — the Norse sources never give her a deed. Her 'myths' are her genealogy, her marriage, her three names, and the silence where her temple should be; read together they are the Norse answer to the question of what the ground is.

myths.title: Daughter of Night
myths.text: The Prose Edda (Gylfaginning ch. 9–10) gives Jǫrð the strangest pedigree in the pantheon: she is the daughter of Anarr and Nótt — of Anarr and Night. Her mother Nótt is the giantess who drives the black chariot across the night sky, ancestress of every dawn; her father Anarr is little more than a name in the margin. From Night comes the earth, and from Night also comes Dagr, Day, born of the bright Dellingr — so the earth's brother is daylight itself, and the two are ever turning over the same horizon. The genealogy is a compact cosmology stated as a family tree: darkness precedes and engenders both the ground we stand on and the light that crosses it. When the skalds called Þórr kin of Nótt they were keeping the whole system inside one kenning — the thunder's pedigree runs back past Óðinn to the Night that came before the gods.

myths.title: Wife of Óðinn, Mother of Þórr
myths.text: Snorri lists Jǫrð among Óðinn's wives — Gylfaginning ch. 9 names her in the tally of nine — and the whole mythology leans on the match. Their son is Þórr, strongest of the gods, and the skalds' standard style for him is the double patronymic: son of Óðinn and of Jǫrð. The union is the Norse sky-father/earth-mother formula compressed into a single household — the storm is literally what happens when heaven touches ground. Nowhere do the sources narrate the courtship, and none is needed: this is not a love story but a standing fact, like gravity. Þórr's hammer-fall is the marriage still being consummated; every thunderstorm is the myth told again in weather, and the skalds, who never tired of the kenning, understood that a formula repeated a thousand times is a cult.

lore.culturalLegacy: Jǫrð never died because she never lived anywhere but underfoot. Her name is the ordinary word for earth in Icelandic, Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish jord; English 'earth' descends from her Old English cognate eorþe. 'Mother Earth' — the phrase behind Earth Day, Gaia theory, and a whole modern environmental iconography — is, linguistically, Jǫrð's daughter.
